title: How BJP Used State Power to Win Kolhapur’s Gokul Dairy
description: The BJP was helped by a Maharashtra government ordinance and the votes of four government-appointed directors  to win Gokul dairy’s chairmanship in Kolhapur, overriding the panel elected through a democratic process.
author: Amey  Tirodkar
content:
Gokul Zilla Sahakari Dudh Utpadak Sangh (Gokul district cooperative milk-producing federation) in Kolhapur district, known popularly as Gokul, is Maharashtra’s largest dairy cooperative. Around 5.5 lakh farmers of the district are directly linked to this cooperative, established in 1963. Known for the high quality of its milk, Gokul’s provisional turnover for 2025-26 was Rs.4,185 crore.
The election to the post of the cooperative chairman on November 10 pushed Gokul into the news for all the wrong reasons. The election, won by a BJP-led panel (Chhatrapati Shahu Shetkari Aghadi) backed by Maharashtra’s ruling Mahayuti, is widely perceived to have been manipulated, with many alleging subversion of democratic mandate.
On October 19, in well-publicised elections to the board of directors, the BJP-backed panel won 12 of the 25 seats. The panel led by Congress MLC Satej Patil (Rajarshi Shahu Shetkari Samvichari Aghadi) won 13 seats. The mandate clearly was in favour of the Congress-led panel.
But then this panel found itself in a fix when it came to electing the board chairman. A Gokul by-law requires a quorum of at least 14 board members for the election to be valid. The panel led by Satej Patil had 13. On the day of the election on October 28, all 12 of the Mahayuti-backed board members absented themselves.
In Mumbai, State Medical Education Minister Hasan Mushrif, whose son Navid Mushrif led the previous board, told the media: “People have voted us [the Mahayuti panel] to oppose their [Satej] panel. Not to elect their chairman. So, our members decided to remain absent.” Father and son belong to the Nationalist Congress Party (Ajit Pawar), which is part of Maharashtra’s ruling coalition.
The group led by Satej Patil moved court, and on November 2, the Bombay High Court directed that the election be held on November 10, with notices to all 25 elected board members to remain present.
But on November 6, an ordinance issued by the State government made provision for five government-appointed directors in cooperatives with an annual turnover over Rs.500 crore; four of them would have voting rights. This ordinance amended a clause in the Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act, 1960, which denied voting rights to nominated and government-designated directors in elections for chairmen or other office-bearers.
The 5 members were duly appointed, and the chairman election of November 10 was held after the High Court refused to impose a stay on the ordinance. The balance of power was now in favour of the Mahayuti, whose candidate, Rajesh Patil, won 16 votes—12 from the elected board, 4 from the government appointees—in the election held on November 10. The Congress-backed panel’s candidate, Shashikant Patil Chuyekar, got 13.
Thus, through executive overreach, the BJP seized control of an institution that wields significant political influence over a vast network of farmers who are attached to it and dependent on it.
What happened before the election
The backstory of how Satej Patil’s group came to win as many as 13 seats on the board reflects the dynamics of district-level politics.
The five-year term of the previous board ended in May. In the last five years, Gokul grew spectacularly, establishing 1,400 new cooperative milk societies, which brought up the total number of such societies to 5,418.
In the last election to the board held in 2021, Hasan Mushrif and Satej Patil were on the same side of the political divide. Hasan Mushrif was then a Minister in Uddhav Thackeray’s government. His party, the as-yet-unbroken NCP, had an alliance with the Congress; this alliance won the board, ending the rule of the Mahadevrao Mahadik family, which by then was with the BJP.
By 2026, the Mushrifs and Satej Patil were political adversaries. Yet, Hasan Mushrif was at first reluctant to have his party cooperate with the BJP’s Rajya Sabha member Munna Mahadik, whose family’s control over Gokul his side had broken in 2021, over the 2026 Gokul election. Frontline learnt from reliable sources that Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis himself stepped in to smooth out the differences and make the Mahayuti alliance work for the election. Apart from Hasan Mushrif and Mahadik, another key person for this alliance was Chandrakant Patil, State Higher and Technical Education Minister, who is originally from Kolhapur.
After the board elections were announced, State Dairy Development Minister Radhakrishna Vikhe Patil cancelled the voting rights of the 1,400 new milk societies that were added to the cooperative in the last 5 years. This was seen as a move designed to help the Mahayuti-backed panel. But these societies got back their voting rights by first moving the Bombay High Court and then the Supreme Court.
A panel contesting the board elections needs letters of support from member milk societies. When the Gokul elections were announced, 4,500 member societies, out of a total of 5,418, were supportive of the Mahayuti. But the attempt to cancel the voting rights of 1,400 societies created an undercurrent of opposition.
A senior journalist from Kolhapur, Vijay Chormare, said: “This cancellation of membership was nothing but an SIR process in Gokul. The way the ECI [Election Commission of India] is cancelling the voting rights of citizens rampantly—the same strategy was applied in Gokul. Just as anger against the ECI is palpable all over the country, Gokul members were angry with the Mahayuti even before the campaign got started.”
Satej Patil seized his chance. He personally visited the 5,418 member societies in 3 months and promised them that no member of his family would contest the Gokul elections; all candidates on his panel would be ordinary farmers. This was an important pledge because the Mahayuti alliance candidates were mostly relatives of leaders. The strategy worked, and the victory of Satej Patil’s panel got prominent coverage on Marathi news channels and in newspapers.
Why this desperation?
Countering criticism about the manner in which the BJP seized control of Gokul, Fadnavis keeps saying that the November 6 ordinance was necessary to end “the constitutional crisis in Gokul”. The Congress leader Rahul Gandhi has observed that the BJP snatches power in any way it can when it senses that it is losing.
The question to ask is why the BJP-led regime needed to go out on a limb to win Gokul. Cooperative institutions, it is true, have played an important role in Maharashtra’s politics for five decades. Yet, Maharashtra’s political economy has moved beyond the role played by these institutions. The share of agriculture in the State’s economy has fallen from 40 per cent in 1960 to 15 per cent at present. Urban infrastructure, real estate, and mega projects now dominate the political economy. Gokul, in comparison, is small fry.
Neeraj Hatekar, a professor of economics, explained why Gokul nevertheless has political significance for the BJP: “The BJP wanted to win Gokul because it gives it direct control of and connect with 5.5 lakh farmers of an influential district.”
But Gokul is also directly under the Dairy Development Department and Cooperative Department. This makes it easy for the government to influence decision-making in the cooperative. Then why the desperation to control the board? A senior journalist, Deepak Lokhande, said: “The BJP believes in a vindictive kind of politics. Defeating Satej Patil in Gokul was more important for it than handling Gokul through Mantralaya. To earn that pleasure, it took such extreme step.”
The political scientist Suhas Palshikar believes that the BJP is not bothered about the criticism that it subverts democracy: “Wherever there is a whiff of power, the party would go and grab it by hook or by crook. In the process, the criticism about democratic functioning is not even considered.”
In the larger scheme of things, it was perhaps important for the BJP to thwart the rise of Satej Patil, who is emerging as the Congress’ de facto leader in Maharashtra. He has popular appeal and works hard to win elections. He is also a Maratha, which is a highly political community. Vasant Bhosale, editor of Lokmat (Kolhapur edition), said: “Satej Patil could challenge the BJP like Revanth Reddy of Telangana or D.K. Shivakumar of Karnataka. Winning Gokul would have given him a boost. So, he had to be defeated. Misusing government power and creating an issue out of the quorum rule was part of the game to ensure that.”
Satej Patil made a serious allegation while campaigning for the Gokul election. He said that the BJP wanted to finish the Gokul brand to help Amul grow. “The Central government has created Sardar Patel Multistate Milk Federation in which Gokul will be merged. That’s why a hidden power (“adrishya shakti”) is trying to win Gokul,” he said.
Some experts and commentators in Maharashtra believe that the BJP wants to weaken Marathi institutions. “Gokul is Maharashtra’s institution, a powerful brand. The same thing was tried with Nandini of Karnataka. But the Karnataka voters defeated the BJP and saved their Nandini. In Kolhapur also, people have defeated the BJP. The State government is helping the Gujarati lobby to finish Gokul,” said Deepak Pawar of Marathi Abhyas Kendra.
At any rate, the BJP regime’s manoeuvres have made the Gokul election national news. As the veteran journalist S.M. Deshmukh said: “Earlier, even journalists in Mantralaya used to be unaware of the outcome of these elections because these were locally fought polls. It was rare for the Chief Minister to get involved. But this time a small election became big because big people made their hands dirty in a small election. That’s the problem with Maharashtra politics now. Big leaders think with small hearts.”

title: Why is Wall Street bleeding? $1.5 trillion-plus market value wiped out as AI bubble fears, inflation and Trump’s tariffs rattle investors
description: Wall Street is bleeding as Trump's tariff threats collide with stubborn inflation, rising interest-rate expectations and growing doubts over whether the AI boom can deliver the astronomical profits investors have priced in. | OpIndia News
author: Jinit Jain
content:
The US stock market is witnessing a generational drawdown. On Wednesday, November 25, it witnessed one of its sharpest sell-offs in recent months, with technology stocks bearing the brunt of an investor exodus. More than $1.5 trillion in market value was at risk of being wiped out from the Nasdaq-100 as a combination of renewed trade tensions, stubborn inflation, growing doubts over the artificial intelligence boom and uncertainty over Federal Reserve policy spooked investors.
The Nasdaq Composite plunged 4.15%, shedding nearly 986 points to trade at 22,747.61 during Wednesday’s session. The Nasdaq-100 fell 4.3%, while the S&P 500 declined 2.86% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1.99%. The technology-led sell-off was particularly brutal, with Nvidia losing around 8.6%, Alphabet falling 5%, Amazon declining 4.9% and Microsoft shedding 3.2%.
Intriguingly, equities were not the only asset class to face the heat. Gold and Silver also came under heavy selling pressure. Spot Gold fell more than 2%, while Silver declined 3.8%, as a stronger US dollar and expectations of further interest rate hikes weighed on precious metals.
The market turmoil is being driven by several developments converging at the same time. While Trump’s fresh tariff proposals have provided the latest trigger, the underlying problems run considerably deeper.
1. Trump’s tariff war is back, and investors are getting nervous
The immediate trigger for the latest sell-off is Washington’s decision to propose fresh tariffs on 14 major trading partners, including India, China, Japan, South Korea and the European Union.
The Trump administration has proposed tariffs of up to 25% on imports from India and additional duties of up to 20% on several other economies. China faces a proposed additional 20% levy as Washington accuses Beijing of flooding international markets with cheap manufactured goods.
The measures follow an eight-month investigation under Section 301 of the Trade Act into what the US describes as structural excess industrial capacity among its trading partners.
The problem for investors is that tariffs introduce another layer of uncertainty into an already complicated economic environment.
American companies depend heavily on international supply chains. Fresh import duties could increase the cost of raw materials, components and finished products, putting pressure on corporate profit margins. Businesses could either absorb these costs or pass them on to consumers, potentially creating another round of inflationary pressure.
There is also the possibility of retaliatory measures from affected trading partners. Companies operating across multiple international markets could find themselves dealing with higher costs, disrupted supply chains and unpredictable trade policies.
The tariffs have only been proposed and are not yet implemented. However, financial markets rarely wait for policies to take effect before pricing in their potential consequences.
2. Inflation refuses to cool, putting the Federal Reserve in a difficult position
Another major reason behind the market’s weakness is persistent inflation in the United States.
Data released on Wednesday showed that the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) Price Index, the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge, increased 3.8% year-on-year in October, up from 3.6% in September.
Core PCE inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, climbed to 3.3% from 3.1% in September. The monthly increase was 0.3%.
This is significant because the Federal Reserve has a 2% inflation target. Inflation running considerably above that level makes it difficult for the central bank to justify cutting interest rates.
In fact, expectations have shifted towards further monetary tightening, with investors increasingly pricing in at least a 25-basis-point rate hike before the end of 2026.
The problem for Wall Street is that higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive and reduce the present value of future corporate earnings. This particularly hurts technology companies whose valuations depend heavily on profits expected several years down the line.
There is another complication. The US economy grew at an annualised rate of 4.3% in the third quarter, considerably higher than the 3.5% economists had expected.
While strong economic growth is ordinarily positive for businesses, it complicates the Federal Reserve’s inflation-fighting efforts when price pressures remain elevated. The central bank has less reason to ease monetary policy when economic activity remains robust and inflation is not approaching its target.
Investors who were hoping for cheaper borrowing costs are consequently reassessing their expectations. The prospect of higher rates for longer is particularly bad news for expensive technology stocks.
3. The AI boom is facing its biggest reality check yet
Perhaps the most significant underlying reason behind Wall Street’s troubles is the growing realisation that the artificial intelligence boom may not deliver the returns investors have been expecting.
For much of the past two years, AI has been the biggest driving force behind the US stock market rally. Nvidia, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and other technology giants have attracted enormous investor interest on the promise that artificial intelligence will transform businesses and generate extraordinary profits.
However, the market is increasingly questioning whether the enormous investments being made in AI infrastructure will generate sufficient returns.
Technology companies are spending hundreds of billions of dollars building data centres, purchasing advanced processors, expanding computing capacity and securing energy supplies. This expenditure has fuelled unprecedented demand for semiconductor manufacturers and companies supplying AI infrastructure.
But building infrastructure is not the same as generating profits from it.
Investors want to know when these investments will translate into sustainable revenue and earnings. They are also questioning whether the current pace of capital expenditure is financially justified, particularly when companies are increasingly relying on borrowing to fund their expansion.
The sell-off is not limited to chip manufacturers. Companies operating data centres and providing specialised AI computing capacity are also facing pressure.
CoreWeave and Nebius, two companies exposed to the AI infrastructure boom, suffered steep share-price declines. CoreWeave’s bonds also came under significant pressure, with yields on its 2031 debt approaching 18%.
This is an important warning sign. When investors begin questioning not only the valuations of AI companies but also their ability to finance expansion, the repercussions can spread across the entire technology ecosystem.
The semiconductor index has already suffered a substantial correction, falling more than 43% from its June record high. Nvidia, the biggest symbol of the AI boom, has also been at the centre of the latest market turmoil.
This does not necessarily mean artificial intelligence is a passing fad or that demand for AI technology has disappeared. It does, however, suggest that investors are no longer willing to assign unlimited valuations to companies merely because they are associated with AI.
The market wants profitability, not just promises.
4. Excessive valuations and the unwinding of the AI trade
Another problem is that Wall Street had become heavily dependent on a relatively small group of technology companies.
A handful of mega-cap stocks, particularly those associated with artificial intelligence, account for a substantial share of the market’s value and influence major indices such as the Nasdaq-100 and S&P 500.
When these companies rally, the indices rise disproportionately. But the reverse is equally true. When investors begin selling these stocks, the damage spreads across the broader market.
The volatility surrounding Nvidia illustrates this problem.
The company witnessed a spectacular rally on Monday after Jensen Huang returned as its CEO, providing temporary relief to investors. However, the euphoria did not last. Nvidia shares subsequently reversed sharply, falling around 6% on Tuesday and another 8.6% on Wednesday.
The episode illustrates how sentiment-driven the AI trade has become. Investors are willing to aggressively buy shares on positive developments, but they are equally quick to exit when doubts resurface.
There are also concerns about the valuations attached to companies that have benefited enormously from the AI narrative without yet demonstrating that their infrastructure investments will generate commensurate returns.
When expectations become excessively high, even strong earnings or improved revenue forecasts may not be enough to satisfy investors.
The result is a market increasingly vulnerable to profit-booking and sudden corrections.
5. Regulatory uncertainty is adding another layer of pressure
The political environment is also changing the outlook for technology companies.
The Democratic Party’s gains in the November midterm elections have raised concerns among investors about potentially tougher scrutiny of the AI industry.
Regulatory restrictions, additional compliance requirements and hurdles to building large data centres could slow down infrastructure expansion.
This matters because the current AI investment cycle depends on companies being able to construct data centres rapidly, secure electricity and deploy increasingly powerful computing infrastructure.
Any regulatory intervention or delay could affect the projected returns on investments running into hundreds of billions of dollars.
Investors are consequently assessing whether the scale and speed of AI infrastructure expansion can be sustained under a potentially more challenging regulatory environment.
6. Even Gold and Silver are falling as investors seek liquidity
The simultaneous decline in Gold and Silver is another interesting feature of the current market turmoil.
Gold is traditionally considered a safe-haven asset, but it is not immune to selling pressure when investors anticipate higher interest rates and a stronger dollar.
The US inflation numbers have reinforced expectations of further Federal Reserve tightening. Higher interest rates make non-yielding assets such as Gold less attractive compared with interest-bearing investments.
There is also another possible explanation. During sharp market corrections, investors facing losses in equities may sell profitable or liquid positions in other asset classes to meet margin calls and raise cash.
Silver has faced additional pressure because of its industrial demand exposure.
The decline in precious metals alongside equities therefore reflects more than just a conventional flight away from risk. It also highlights how aggressively investors are reassessing monetary policy expectations and liquidity requirements.
Is this the beginning of a bigger market correction?
The latest sell-off is not an isolated event caused exclusively by Trump’s tariff announcement. Wall Street has been struggling for several weeks as investors reassess technology valuations, inflation expectations and the sustainability of the AI investment cycle.
The Nasdaq-100 briefly touched the threshold of 20% below its October 6 record closing high on Wednesday. A closing level at that threshold would confirm a bear market in the index.
The combination of sticky inflation, potentially higher interest rates, renewed trade tensions and doubts over AI profitability has created an uncomfortable environment for investors.
What makes the situation particularly interesting is that none of these developments, individually, necessarily signals the end of the US economic or technology growth story.
The US economy is still expanding, companies continue to invest heavily in artificial intelligence, and demand for advanced computing infrastructure remains substantial.
However, financial markets operate on expectations. When investors begin questioning whether those expectations have become unrealistic, valuations can correct sharply even when the underlying businesses continue to grow.
That is precisely what Wall Street appears to be experiencing right now.
The AI boom is here to stay. The chips used to power the AI boom are selling at a record pace. All metrics suggest the AI is yet to reach its peak. But the recent correction in the markets, particularly the slump in Anthropic shares, suggest we are well past the time when AI companies got a free pass in commanding unrealistic valuations. We are now, perhaps, entering from the realm of imagination to reality.

title: Prevented court-ordered lighting of Karthigai Deepam at Deepathoon, challenged Madras HC order to remove Periyar statue from temple land: How TVK has outperformed DMK in being anti-Hindu in just six months
description: The TVK government has not only filed review petition against Supreme Court order allowing one-time lighting of Karthigai Deepam at Deepathoon, it has also moved a petition before the Supreme Court, challenging the October 2026 Madras High Court order directing the removal of a statue of anti-Hindu ‘activist’ E. V. Ramasamy Naicker, better known as Periyar. | OpIndia News
category: Editor's picks, Featured, Opinions, Political History of India, Politics
author: Shraddha Pandey
content:
Tamil Nadu is arguably the only state in India where mainstream political parties compete with each other to prove that they are more anti-Hindu than their opponents. For years, the DMK government and leaders openly suppressed Hindu, and even declared intentions to eradicate Sanatan Dharma. Now the over six-month-old TVK government led by CM C Joseph Vijay appears to be aiming to outperform DMK in taking anti-Hindu measures. The TVK demonstrated its anti-Hindu stance through its defiance of the Supreme Court order to light the Karthigai Deepam at the Deepathoon atop Thiruparankundram Hill on 24th November.
TVK government opposed Karthigai Deepam at Deepathoon, filed review petition, arrested Hindus and defied court order: How TVK crushed Hindus to appease Muslims
On 20th November, the Supreme Court allowed the lighting of ‘Karthigai Deepam’ atop the Thiruparankundram hill in Madurai, during the Karthigai Deepam festival on November 24, 2026.
A Bench comprising Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M. Pancholi passed the order with the condition that only authorised persons from the Devasthanam (temple administration) and government officials will be able to conduct the lamp lighting ceremony.
The court granted the interim relief considering the present circumstances. It noted that if the lighting of the lamp was not allowed on the festival, no subsequent relief would be able to make up for that.
This was strictly a one-time measure. Yet since Muslims are against the lighting of Karthigai Deepam merely because the Deepathoon is situated near a Dargah on the same hill, the Muslim-appeasing TVK government blatantly defied the court order.
First, the TVK government, through the HR&CE Commissioner, filed a review petition against the Supreme Court order.
It contended that granting one-time permission amounts to granting final relief at the interlocutory stage itself.
The petition asks whether the Supreme Court should have issued a mandatory interim direction without the petitioners establishing a strong prima facie case and demonstrating that the balance of convenience favoured them.
The petition invoked provisions of the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959.
It highlighted that under Section 28(1), trustees are responsible for administering the affairs of religious institutions. Section 63(e) empowers the Joint Commissioner to inquire into and decide questions concerning established usage in a religious institution.
The TVK government’s review petition says that the question of where the Hindu temple’s traditional lamp should be lit must be addressed through the appropriate statutory and institutional process instead of determining it through an interim judicial direction.
It also argued that there is no established customary or legal right to light the lamp at the stone pillar atop the hill.
Know Your Rights
The review petition also claims that the Hindu petitioners have not presented documentary evidence establishing that the location was historically used for the ceremony.
The TVK government expressed its apprehension that granting even one-time permission for lighting the traditional lamp, Karthigai Deepam, would set a precedent for future claims.
The review petition is worried about the Deepathoon’s proximity to a nearby Islamic shrine named Sikandar Badhusha Dargah.
The CM C Joseph Vijay-led government is concerned that lighting a traditional Hindu lamp at this spot close to a Dargah could pose a risk of disturbing communal harmony.
The Vijay government’s opposition to the Supreme Court order didn’t remain confined to a review petition.
The TVK government mobilised the state machinery to defy the Supreme Court order and ensured that the Karthigai Deepam could not be lit at the Deepathoon.
Heavy police deployment, promulgation of Section 144 in Madurai and other obstructive acts by the TVK government showed that it is just as anti-Hindu as the DMK, in fact, even more desperate for appeasing Muslims.
In the process, hundreds of Hindus, including several BJP leaders, were arrested or detained.
As the TVK government stopped the lighting of the Deepam at Deepathoon on the Thiruparankundram Hill, Hindu Munnani State president Kadeshwara Subramaniam said that the “anti-Hindu” TVK regime will collapse.
On 25th November, the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) government apologised in the Supreme Court after it lit the Karthigai Deepam lamp at the traditional Uchipillayar Deepa Mandapam rather than the Deepathoon stone pillar atop Thiruparankundram hill, in violation of its order.
The state claimed that the order was not executed because of the Board of Trustees.
However, the legal representatives of the Hindu petitioners exposed the deceptive tactics.
“This is like anticipatory breach, anticipatory mentioning. Most unfortunate, My Lords. State tells the High Court some prohibitory orders were. They use the Board of Trustees, and I say this, to say the custom does not permit it, and the sthanikars have said it cannot be done,” they said, adding that the government and the devasthanam joined hands to defend the contravention of the verdict.
Clearly, from legal routes, mobilisation of administrative machinery to deceptive rhetoric, the CM Vijay-led TVK government played every tactic in the book to ensure that the Hindus could not light the Karthigai Deepam at Deepathoon, Muslims remain content, and TVK could dodge contempt charges while also coming across as an upholder of ‘secularism’.
TVK’s anti-Hindu actions are not confined to the Thiruparankundram controversy.
Vijay government filed plea challenging Madras High Court order to remove Periyar statue from Hindu temple land
On one hand, the TVK government filed a review petition against the Supreme Court order in the Karthigai Deepam case.
On the other hand, it moved a petition before the Supreme Court, challenging the October 2026 Madras High Court order directing the removal of a statue of anti-Hindu ‘activist’ E. V. Ramasamy Naicker, better known as Periyar, installed on land belonging to an ancient Shiva temple in Tamil Nadu’s Thanjavur district.
The Vijay government filed a Special Leave Petition (SLP) through the District Collector of Thanjavur on 22nd November 2026.
The High Court order concerns the statue installed on land belonging to the Brahma Sirakandeeswarar Temple at Kandiyur, an ancient Hindu shrine revered by devotees of Lord Shiva.
A bench comprising Justices Velmurugan and Ramakrishnan passed the order while hearing a petition filed by Rama Ravikumar, a resident of Ezhumalai in Madurai district. He had approached the court challenging the installation of the statue on temple-owned property.
The case raises questions about how a statue of a notorious Hinduphobe came to be installed on land belonging to a Hindu temple, particularly when the petitioner claims that the installation never received the necessary approval from the Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments (HR&CE) Department.
The petitioner had filed an inquiry under the Right to Information Act (RTI).
The May 2025 RTI response stated that the HR&CE Department had not granted any permission or approval for installing the statue of EV Ramasamy on the temple property.
The Hindu petitioner’s objection was not limited to the alleged absence of official permission.
He also questioned the presence of an inscription beneath the statue that openly rejects the existence of God and uses derogatory language against those who believe in and worship God.
The inscription reads:
“There is no God, there is no God, there is no God at all. He who created God is a fool. He who propagates God is a scoundrel. He who worships God is a barbarian.”
This is not an isolated case. Similar inscriptions were installed near prominent Hindu temples during the tenure of Dravidian governments.
Despite knowing that these inscriptions are blatantly Hinduphobic and that Periyar was an outright Hindu hater, the TVK government has challenged the Madras High Court order which directed removal of the statue.
This is when TVK and C Joseph Vijay publicly declared earlier that he and his party have accepted Periyar’s broader principles, but they do not accept his atheism or rejection of God.
And yet, the TVK government has an issue with the removal of Periyar’s statue.
Reason? Tamil Nadu’s political landscape.
In Tamil Nadu, the supposed liberal and progressive political parties compete with each to prove that they are more secular, tolerant, inclusive, rational and progressive than others.
However, these are all high-sounding words for opposing, crushing and humiliating Hindus, their beliefs, sentiments and rights.
DMK prevented the lighting of Karthigai Deepam when it was in power; now TVK has done the same.
DMK leader and former Deputy CM Udhayanidhi Stalin gave calls for eradication of Sanatan Dharma, so did TVK MLA VMS Mustafa.
In the Indian Islamo-leftist understanding of secularism and rationality, Hinduism alone is the dogmatic, divisive and dehumanising religion.
Islam, Christianity and other religions are not subjected to such ‘rational’ scrutiny perhaps because of the electoral usefulness of their adherents as a votebank.
From Periyar and Annadurai to DMK and TVK, rationality, social justice, freedom from superstition and smashing patriarchy have always been about scrutinising and mocking Hindus, Hindu Gods, rituals, vilifying Brahmins and appeasing Muslims and Christians.
Periyar’s anti-Hindu activism and how Nehru described him as a lunatic
Born in 1879, Periyar was a vehement anti-Hindu and anti-Brahmin activist.
While contemporary EVR apologists argue that he never advocated racial hatred against Brahmins. Periyar was quite explicit in his expression of his hatred against Hindus.
The magazine Periyar edited published articles praising the ascendancy of Adolf Hitler and warned Brahmins in Tamil Nadu that they should learn from the plight of Jews in Nazi Germany and opt for course correction.
He reportedly used to tell his followers that if they ever encountered a Brahmin and a snake on the road, they should kill the Brahmin first.
Periyar, in his lifetime, spread numerous canards about the Ramayana. All his lies were directed towards slandering the God who is considered Maryada Purushottam by Hindus. His lies ranged from accusing Shri Rama of being casteist to claiming that he killed and mutilated women.
Periyar not only claimed that no ‘North Indian Brahmin’ died in the war against Ravana but further propagated that Lord Rama had married women other than Sita for his sexual pleasure. He had also claimed that Lankan King Ravana was, in fact, a Dravidian King from South India.
Periyar had also burnt pictures of Lord Rama, who is one of the most revered Hindu gods. This is not all; Periyar is notorious for organising a procession in Salem in Tamil Nadu with big cutouts of “Ram”, “Sita” and “Hanuman” garlanded with slippers.
Periyar also broke statues of Lord Ganesha. From rhetoric to action, Periyar exploited every opportunity at hand to express his visceral hatred against Hindus and Brahmins.
Interestingly, India’s first Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru had on many occasions called out Periyar’s Hindu hate. Nehru had gone to the extent of suggesting that Periyar should be sent to a lunatic asylum.
In a letter [pdf] to Madras Chief Minister Kumaraswami Kamaraj on November 5, 1957, PM Nehru stated, “I am much distressed by the anti-Brahmin campaign continuously carried on by E.V. Ramaswami Naicker… I find that Ramaswami Naicker is going on saying the same thing again and calling upon people at the right time to start stabbing and killing. What he says can only be said by a criminal or a lunatic.”
PM Nehru was of the view that anti-Brahmin ‘activists’ such as Periyar should be placed in a mental asylum, meant for the treatment of ‘perverted minds’.
In a November 1957 letter to Tamil Nadu CM Kamaraj, Nehru urged the CM to stop Periyar’s hate campaign against Hindus.
A book on Madras State’s fourth CM, C. N. Annadurai, written by PC Ganesan, also makes reference to PM Nehru dubbing Periyar as an ‘old and senile’ man who deserved to be in a lunatic asylum.
“The Prime Minister Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru considered it a sacrilegious act and in an outburst of anger remarked that “old and senile men like Periyar deserved a place more in a lunatic asylum than in public life,” it quoted PM Nehru as saying.
TVK’s Muslim and Christian appeasement policies
Coming back to the current TVK government in Tamil Nadu, it has been accused of squandering state funds on freebies and Muslim appeasement-driven schemes even as the state’s financial health is deteriorating.
Recently, the TVK government announced that the state government will cover the full undergraduate tuition fees for Muslim female students admitted under the government quota in government, government-aided, and self-financing colleges. For this, the government allocated ₹20 crore.
Minister A M Shahjahan also announced the expansion of the Tamil Nadu Waqf Board scholarship for Muslim girls, from Classes 1-8 to Classes 9-10 at ₹2,000 per year. The scheme is expected to benefit 41,384 Muslim schoolgirls for Rs 8.28 crore.
An announcement was also made about a ‘minorities’ women’s college in Chennai through the Waqf Board, with an initial grant of ₹2.45 crore.
Moreover, the Vijay government has also announced a ₹100 crore interest-free revolving fund for loans to develop income-generating assets like marriage halls, commercial complexes, etc. on Muslim and Christian properties.
The state government will also construct a new headquarters for the Tamil Nadu Waqf Board at an estimated cost of ₹40 crore. The administrative grant for the state Waqf Board will also be raised to ₹5 crore.
In November 2026, the Joseph Vijay-led government in Tamil Nadu decided to regularise encroachments by issuing pattas to thousands of mosques, churches and dargahs.
According to A M Shah Jahan, Minister for Minorities Welfare, the government was working to regularise religious institutions that lack ownership documentation. He informed that minority groups petitioned the government for pattas for unlawful houses of worship that had been on government property for 25-50 years.
Conclusion
Tamil Nadu Hindus are on their own. DMK or TVK, the names change, but their disdain and bias against Hindus remain constant. This disdain finds an outlet in their conduct in matters like the Karthigai Deepam issue and the Periyar statue case.
For them, no length is too far when it comes to appeasing Muslims at the cost of suppressing Hindu rights. It’s not even a cost; they enjoy it.
The BJP, though, is standing firmly and unapologetically with Hindus in the Thiruparankundram issue, and otherwise, they have just one MLA in the state assembly.
While it remains to be seen whether the courts hold the TVK accountable or tell Hindus to accommodate, until a political-ideological turnaround unfolds in Tamil Nadu in view of the civilisational stakes, this mockery of Hindu rights under the pretext of secularism will continue.

title: Who is Yash Maheshwari? Comedian booked over vulgar Chhath Puja jokes; old videos mocking PM Modi and Ram Mandir resurface
description: Patna Police have registered an FIR against comedian Yash Maheshwari over sexually suggestive remarks about Chhath Puja. | OpIndia News
author: OpIndia Staff
content:
Patna Police has booked stand-up comedian Yash Maheshwari following a massive backlash over his sexually suggestive remarks about Chhath Puja traditions and women in Bihar. An FIR has been registered against him at the Patna Cyber Police Station under multiple sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) and the Information Technology Act.
In a post on X on Wednesday, 25th November, Patna Police said the case was registered on 24th November under Case No. 1550/26. The FIR invokes Sections 75(1), 79, 351 and 352 of the BNS, along with Sections 66(C) and 66(D) of the IT Act.
दिनांक 24.11.2026 को सोशल मीडिया प्लेटफॉर्म YouTube पर चैनल @Almostyash (Yash Maheshwari) के माध्यम से बिहार की महिलाओं के प्रति अभद्र एवं आपत्तिजनक टिप्पणी किए जाने के मामले में #पटना_साइबर_थाना में कांड संख्या 1550/26, दिनांक 24.11.2026, धारा 75(1), 79, 351, 352 एवं 66(C), 66(D) IT Act के अंतर्गत #प्राथमिकी दर्ज की गई है। उक्त वीडियो/कंटेंट में बिहार की महिलाओं के प्रति की गई आपत्तिजनक टिप्पणियों से सामाजिक सौहार्द प्रभावित होने एवं विभिन्न समुदायों के बीच वैमनस्य की स्थिति उत्पन्न होने की आशंका के मद्देनजर मामले को गंभीरता से लेते हुए प्राथमिकी दर्ज की गई है। पटना साइबर थाना द्वारा मामले की जांच एवं अग्रतर विधिक कार्रवाई की जा रही है। #पटना_पुलिस सोशल मीडिया पर आपत्तिजनक, अभद्र एवं भड़काऊ सामग्री प्रसारित करने वालों के विरुद्ध सख्त कार्रवाई के लिए प्रतिबद्ध है। @dm_patna @bihar_police @IG_CentralRange @cityspwest @CentralSP_patna @CyberPol_Patna @BiharHomeDept @IPRDBihar @DDNewsHindi @AIRNewsHindi #PatnaPolice #CyberPolice #CyberCrime #BiharPolice #CyberPS #viralvideo #viral
— Patna Police (@PatnaPolice24x7) November 25, 2026
The Patna Cyber Police Station is investigating the matter and taking further legal action. The police also warned that strict action would be taken against those circulating objectionable, derogatory and inflammatory content on social media.
This police action comes after one of Maheshwari’s comedy clips went viral, showing him ridiculing married Bihari Hindu women for applying a long streak of sindoor from their nose to their forehead during Chhath Puja, making obscene references to their husbands’ private parts and using foul language to demean the sacred ritual.
In the name of comedy, Yash Maheshwari made vulgar, sexually suggestive remarks about Chhath Puja and the sindoor tradition followed by Hindu women. Abuses, cheap shots at sacred figures, and outright obscenity, is this what Indian comedians are selling as comedy? What is clout-chasing, and why are comedians crossing every line just to grab attention? @Anurragmishra explains.
— OpIndia.com (@OpIndia_com) November 25, 2026
Comedian deletes Instagram account amid backlash
As public anger refused to die down and legal heat intensified, the controversial comedian deleted his Instagram account as well as the offending stand-up video from YouTube. The sudden disappearance of his Instagram profile came right after angry internet users began digging through his old uploads.
Once the Chhath Puja video blew up, his older Instagram reels and posts started facing severe backlash over previously uploaded derogatory and offensive content, prompting him to wipe his presence from the platform to escape further scrutiny.
Who is Yash Maheshwari?
Yash Maheshwari is a self-proclaimed stand-up comedian from Jaipur who has built a career around what he calls “unfiltered comedy.” He operates a YouTube channel under the handle @almostyash, which has roughly 29,000 subscribers, and it was on this very platform that the latest controversy was triggered.
However, a closer look at his past performances shows that mocking Bihari women and sacred Hindu traditions is not a one-off mistake for him.
In another video, Maheshwari made deeply offensive remarks again targeting Bihari women, claiming that they are “experts in getting beaten by men.” In that exact same routine, he went on to stereotype men from Haryana as habitual offenders and suggested that Bihari women and Haryanvi men should be matched against each other to eliminate crime.
Marry Bihari women to men from Haryana so they can beat them – Yash Maheshwari बिहारी औरतों को पिटना पसंद है और हरियाणवी मर्द को पीटना। दोनों की शादी कर दो , हरियाणवी मर्द बिहारी महिलाओं को पीटेंगे – @samrat4bjp आपकी भी बेटी है । @bihar_police तुम लोगों की भी । I am sharing the video link in the comments, please mass report his channel and video.
— With Love Bihar (@WithLoveBihar) November 24, 2026
Beyond regional and cultural mockery, old clips resurfacing on X from his now-deleted Instagram account reveal a clear pattern of politically motivated content.
In one viral clip, Maheshwari can be heard mocking Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the Ayodhya Ram Temple, falsely alleging, “Modiji got a theft committed at the Ram Mandir.”
In the same video, he tried to provoke BJP workers over the baseless claim, saying in Hindi, “My BJP friends, you remember that a theft happened at the Ram Mandir and Modiji himself got it done. What should be done about it? Will you do something about it, or do nothing, or just leave it like that? Leave it.”
इसकी पुरानी वीडियो सुनिए, आपको खुद समझ आ जाएगा कि यह किस पार्टी का समर्थक है! https://t.co/jRuiDKLCL6
— Social Tamasha (@SocialTamasha) November 25, 2026
He also brought up Congress leader Rahul Gandhi’s unfounded “vote chori” (vote theft) accusation against the Election Commission, adding, “Election theft also happened; should we leave that too?”
EXPOSED! Now it’s becoming clear which party’s ideology Yash Maheshwari is influenced by. and where this vulgarity is coming from. https://t.co/KChIsSjq0G
— JanHit Voice (@HJP2029_2036) November 25, 2026
In yet another clip mocking Prime Minister Modi, he sarcastically called him chai wala and remarked, “My whole day goes by saying just one thing: a tea seller, a tea seller, a tea seller. It feels so good to hear; it is total fun. Even though I do not even drink tea, it still feels like just saying, a tea seller, a tea seller. I just keep saying this.”
Furthermore, in another social media post, he was seen attending the CJP protest and trying to frame it as “Gen Z protests” in India, attempting to link it to the violent unrest seen in neighbouring Nepal and Bangladesh.
Political propaganda disguised as comedy
Looking at his overall digital footprint, it becomes clear that Yash Maheshwari’s old videos and social media activity lean heavily toward biased political commentary and mocking Hindu culture rather than actual stand-up comedy.
Instead of delivering genuine humour, which Yash Maheshwari clearly struggles to do, his content repeatedly relies on anti-Modi and anti-BJP posts, cheap shots at religious beliefs, and narratives that seem aimed at inciting unrest in the country.
By masking political propaganda and offensive stereotypes as “edgy” jokes, his past work shows a consistent pattern of chasing online clout through outrage rather than actual comedic talent.
How the latest Chhath Puja controversy unfolded
The latest controversy erupted after Maheshwari uploaded a stand-up performance titled Morally Questionable Standup Comedy on his YouTube channel on 21st November. A clip from the performance subsequently went viral on social media, drawing furious reactions for its vulgar take on Chhath Puja and Hindu women.
In the viral clip, Maheshwari can be heard mocking the tradition followed by married Hindu women in Bihar of applying a long streak of sindoor extending from the nose towards the forehead during Chhath Puja.
This practice holds religious and cultural significance for women observing the festival, who associate it with their husbands’ long lives and family well-being.
Maheshwari turned this revered custom into a sexually explicit joke by comparing the length of the sindoor streak to the size of a man’s genitalia, suggesting that women wearing longer streaks had husbands with larger private parts.
Using profane language, he mocked the religious belief behind the ritual and even dragged Lord Hanuman into the vulgar joke, stating,
“Meri lambi umar main khud dekh lunga, par tu jo Bajrang Bali ban ke baithi hai na tujhe mujhse kaun bachayega.” Through this comment, Maheshwari also invoked Lord Hanuman, one of the most revered Hindu deities, in a sexually suggestive context, further intensifying the outrage.
The clip was shared on X by user Raj Shekhar Verma (@shekhar_br02), following which several social media users demanded action against the comedian. BJP leader and activist Ritu Jaiswal also condemned the remarks and demanded legal action.
बिहारी औरतों के माँग में सिंदूर डालने के तरीकों पर भद्दा टिप्पणी कर रहा है । छठ पूजा और शादी के दौरान महिलाओं के लंबे माँग भरने की कल्चर पर जोक कर रहा है । बिहारी महिलाओं के अपमान का बदला क्या बिहार पुलिस लेगी ? @bihar_police आपके होते हुए एक स्टेट की पूरी महिलाओं को टारगेट करना भद्दे कमेंट्स पास करना क्या ये अपराध नहीं है? बिहारी महिलाओं के अपमान पर क्या इसे बिहार के थाने में नहीं सड़ाया जा सकता है?
— RAJSHEKHAR VERMA (@shekhar_br02) November 24, 2026
In a post on X, Jaiswal said, “An FIR should be filed against this man in every district of Bihar for making obscene jokes about our great festival of Chhath and those who observe the Chhath fast.” She urged the police to take strict action so that nobody would dare to make such remarks about the festival in the future.
हमारे महापर्व छठ और छठव्रतियों पर अश्लील कॉमेडी करने वाले इस शख्स के खिलाफ बिहार के प्रत्येक जिले में FIR दर्ज होनी चाहिए। ऐसी सख्त कानूनी कार्रवाई हो कि इसे अपनी गलती का एहसास हो और अगली छठ में हमारे महापर्व की महानता का साक्षात दर्शन कर सके। छठ की आस्था और अस्मिता से खिलवाड़ बर्दाश्त नहीं!
— Ritu Jaiswal (@activistritu) November 24, 2026
Yash Maheshwari apologises after facing backlash
Following the controversy and widespread criticism, Maheshwari issued an apology through a video shared on his YouTube channel on Tuesday night, 24th November. Introducing himself as a stand-up comedian, he acknowledged that his comments about Bihar’s cultural traditions were inappropriate.
He said, “Recently, I uploaded a video in which I was talking about certain cultural aspects of Bihar. I think I should not have done that. I completely stand by that, and I apologise. I should not have made those comments in that manner.”
The comedian further claimed that he never intended to hurt anyone’s religious sentiments or offend people celebrating the festival. However, he accepted responsibility for his remarks and admitted that he was wrong.
“It was never my intention to hurt anyone’s religious sentiments, any festival or anyone’s feelings in any way. But I am not sure how it was portrayed, and perhaps it was entirely my mistake that it came across that way. I genuinely accept my mistake,” he said.

title: From Ambulances To Tow-Away Cranes: NHAI Mandates Emergency Infrastructure Before Opening New Highway Stretches
description: The National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) has issued guidelines mandating the availability of Incident Management Services on national highways
author: Swarajya Staff
content:
Infrastructure
Swarajya Staff
Nov 26, 2026 | Updated 09:13 AM GMT+5:30
Save & read from anywhere!
Bookmark stories for easy access on any device or the Swarajya app.
The National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) has issued guidelines mandating the availability of Incident Management Services on national highways before any stretch opens to traffic.
The directive, announced on Wednesday (25 November), requires emergency ambulances, route patrolling vehicles and tow-away cranes to be operational before motorists use newly constructed highway sections.
The guidelines prescribe specific arrangements for different categories of national highway stretches.
Emergency teams will be integrated with NHAI's 1033 National Highway Helpline and coordinate with local police, fire services and hospitals.
On operational stretches, ambulances will be positioned at toll plazas or other suitable locations based on accident data and the requirements of each section.
For national highways entrusted to NHAI by the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, ambulances will be deployed through a centralised agency in accordance with delegated powers of NHAI field offices.
Route patrolling vehicles and tow-away cranes will be arranged through separate tenders or included as part of highway maintenance contracts.
On stretches not entrusted to NHAI but tolled by the authority, deployment will follow procedures laid down by the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways.
Under this arrangement, ambulances will be deployed through NHAI's centralised agency in coordination with the concerned regional office, while patrol vehicles and cranes will be arranged by the respective authority.
The policy aims to strengthen road safety and ensure timely assistance to highway users during accidents, vehicle breakdowns and other emergencies.
By conditioning highway commissioning on physical emergency readiness, NHAI shifts rapid trauma response from an operational afterthought into a mandatory precondition for road clearance.

title: From Tunnel Boring Machines To Excavators: India Clears Rs 11,000 Crore Scheme To Strengthen Domestic Equipment Manufacturing
description: The Union Cabinet approved an Rs 11,000 crore scheme yesterday (25 November) to boost domestic manufacturing of construction and infrastructure equipm
author: Swarajya Staff
content:
Infrastructure
Swarajya Staff
Nov 26, 2026 | Updated 09:06 AM GMT+5:30
Save & read from anywhere!
Bookmark stories for easy access on any device or the Swarajya app.
The Union Cabinet approved an Rs 11,000 crore scheme yesterday (25 November) to boost domestic manufacturing of construction and infrastructure equipment, marking a significant push to reduce India's dependence on Chinese imports.
The Scheme for Enhancement of Construction and Infrastructure Equipment Manufacturing Ecosystem will run for eight years from FY 2026-27 under the Ministry of Heavy Industries.
The government aims to attract Rs 21,000 crore in investments and enable import substitution worth Rs 22,500 crore, whilst increasing exports to around four times their current level.
India's construction equipment industry is the world's third-largest, with a market size of Rs 97,000 crore in FY 2024-25, yet about 45 per cent depends on imports, Information and Broadcasting Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw told media after the Cabinet meeting.
The scheme targets seven categories of equipment currently fully or largely imported, including tunnel boring machines, ship-to-shore cranes, hydraulic excavators, off-highway trucks, loaders, piling rigs and drilling machines.
The initiative includes a two-year gestation period (FY2026-27 to FY2027-28) to set up manufacturing facilities, followed by a five-year incentive disbursement period (FY2028-29 to FY2032-33).
The scheme comprises two main components: sales-linked incentives for original equipment manufacturers and component makers, alongside a grant of up to Rs 375 crore in viability gap funding for setting up a dedicated construction equipment testing facility.
The move comes as China imposed export controls on tunnel boring machines, raising concerns about supply disruptions for critical infrastructure projects.
Industry observers note the timing of the Cabinet's decision, as India depends on China for 45-75 per cent of its import requirements for heavy industrial machinery, including cranes, bulldozers and tunnel-boring machines.
The scheme seeks to strengthen India's manufacturing base under the Atmanirbhar Bharat initiative, with incentives supporting manufacturers including JCB, Caterpillar and Hitachi, as well as component makers.

title: Assam: Union Cabinet Clears Rs 2,014 Crore Greenfield Airport Project At Doloo In Silchar's Barak Valley
description: The Union Cabinet approved the development of a new greenfield airport at Doloo in Silchar, Assam, at an estimated cost of ₹2
author: Arjun Brij
content:
News Brief
Arjun Brij
Nov 25, 2026 | Updated 07:56 PM GMT+5:30
Save & read from anywhere!
Bookmark stories for easy access on any device or the Swarajya app.
The Union Cabinet approved the development of a new greenfield airport at Doloo in Silchar, Assam, at an estimated cost of Rs 2,014 crore today.
The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, cleared the proposal for the Airports Authority of India to construct the facility.
The project will overcome the severe operational and spatial constraints of the existing defence landlocked civil enclave at Silchar Airport and accommodate sustained passenger growth.
Information and Broadcasting Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw stated that the airport will have the capacity to handle 800 passengers during peak hours and an annual passenger handling capacity of 1.01 million.
The proposed terminal building will span 12,351 square metres with modern passenger amenities, sustainable green building principles, and modular expansion capability. The project will be funded entirely from the Airports Authority of India's own internal resources.
The infrastructure includes a 2,705-metre-long, 45-metre-wide Code-4C compliant runway suitable for A-320 aircraft operations, along with construction of a new apron capable of parking six A-320 aircraft and a dedicated isolation bay.
The current Silchar airport operates only as a civil enclave inside a defence-controlled airfield, which restricts its space and operations at a time when passenger numbers are rising steadily.
Doloo, situated in the Cachar District of Assam, serves as the strategic heart of the Barak Valley.

title: We investigated why you keep paying for Gurugram’s endless garbage contract
description: A dormant company, Rs 428 crore of Chinese capital and years of public money later, Gurugram's garbage mountain is taller than ever, and a new Rs 600 crore tender is already out.
author: Anmol Pritam
content:
A dormant company, Rs 428 crore of Chinese capital and years of public money later, Gurugram's garbage mountain is taller than ever, and a new Rs 600 crore tender is already out.
Gurugram’s garbage problem was supposed to be solved years ago. Instead, it has become a never-ending cycle of failed contracts and public money going down the drain.
Ecogreen was hired in 2017 to collect and process waste in Gurugram and Faridabad. A Chinese company invested Rs 428 crore in the firm, and the government paid Ecogreen another Rs 157 crore. The promised waste-to-energy plant never came and the Bandhwari landfill grew into a much taller garbage mountain, polluting groundwater in nearby villages.
Ecogreen was a dormant company owned by the Agarwal family of Ghaziabad until a Chinese firm bought a 99.98% stake in 2017. Within six months, it had won contracts in Lucknow, Gwalior and Gurugram-Faridabad. Company filings show about 80% of the initial Rs 60 crore invested in the Gurugram project went to related parties. Against Rs 428 crore of Chinese investment, only about Rs 60 crore worth of plant and machinery exists on the ground. In 2024, the Chinese firm sold its entire stake for Rs 1 crore and left India.
When Ecogreen’s contract was cancelled in 2024, the government’s answer was to hire nine more companies for Rs 532 crore to clear the mess. Six missed their deadlines and were fined around Rs 20 crore. Yet the state had already paid these firms Rs 311.5 crore. Gurugram then floated another waste-management tender worth over Rs 600 crore.
The garbage keeps piling up, but so does the bill. And the cycle starts all over again.

title: EXCLUSIVE: चीनी कंपनी को ठेके, जनता को कचरे का पहाड़! गुरुग्राम के बंधवाड़ी लैंडफिल का पूरा सच
description: How did a Chinese company get contracts to process Gurugram’s garbage? NL Documentaries investigates the Bandhwari landfill, mounting waste and the public money spent on it.
author: अनमोल प्रितम
content:
गुरुग्राम के बंधवाड़ी में कचरे का पहाड़ लगातार बढ़ रहा है और इसके साथ बढ़ता जा रहा है सरकारी खजाने पर बोझ. आखिर इस पूरे खेल में किसे फायदा हुआ और इसकी कीमत कौन चुका रहा है? देखिए हमारी यह ग्राउंड रिपोर्ट.
गुरुग्राम की कचरे की समस्या का समाधान सालों पहले हो जाना चाहिए था. लेकिन ऐसा होने के बजाय यह नाकाम कॉन्ट्रैक्ट और सरकारी पैसों की बर्बादी का एक अंतहीन सिलसिला बन गया.
2017 में एक प्राइवेट कंपनी इकोग्रीन को गुरुग्राम और फरीदाबाद में कचरा इकट्ठा करने और उसे वैज्ञानिक तरीके से प्रोसेस करने का ठेका दिया गया था. इस कंपनी में एक चीनी कंपनी ने 428 करोड़ रुपये का निवेश किया.
वहीं, सरकार ने इकोग्रीन को 157 करोड़ रुपये का भुगतान भी किया. लेकिन जिस वेस्ट-टू-एनर्जी प्लांट का वादा किया गया था, वह कभी बना ही नहीं. दूसरी तरफ, बंधवारी लैंडफिल पर कचरे का पहाड़ बढ़ता गया और आसपास के गांवों का भूजल प्रदूषित होता रहा.
गौरतलब है कि इकोग्रीन 2017 तक गाजियाबाद के अग्रवाल परिवार की एक निष्क्रिय कंपनी थी. उसी साल एक चीनी कंपनी ने इसमें 99.98 फीसदी हिस्सेदारी खरीद ली. इसके महज छह महीनों के भीतर कंपनी को लखनऊ, ग्वालियर और गुरुग्राम-फरीदाबाद में कचरा प्रबंधन के ठेके मिल गए.
कंपनी की वित्तीय फाइलिंग से पता चलता है कि गुरुग्राम प्रोजेक्ट में शुरुआती 60 करोड़ रुपये के निवेश का करीब 80 फीसदी हिस्सा संबंधित कंपनियों और पक्षों को ट्रांसफर कर दिया गया.
वहीं, चीनी कंपनी के 428 करोड़ रुपये के निवेश के मुकाबले जमीन पर महज 60 करोड़ रुपये की प्लांट और मशीनरी ही मौजूद है. आखिरकार 2024 में चीनी कंपनी ने इकोग्रीन में अपनी पूरी हिस्सेदारी महज एक करोड़ रुपये में बेच दी और भारतीय बाजार से बाहर निकल गई.
2024 में इकोग्रीन का कॉन्ट्रैक्ट रद्द होने के बाद सरकार ने इस गड़बड़ी को ठीक करने के लिए नौ और कंपनियों को 532 करोड़ रुपये के ठेके दिए. इनमें से छह कंपनियां तय समयसीमा में अपना काम पूरा नहीं कर पाईं और उन पर करीब 20 करोड़ रुपये का जुर्माना लगाया गया. इसके बावजूद सरकार इन कंपनियों को 311.5 करोड़ रुपये का भुगतान कर चुकी थी. इसके बाद गुरुग्राम में कचरा प्रबंधन के लिए 600 करोड़ रुपये से ज्यादा का एक और टेंडर जारी किया गया.
करोड़ों रुपये खर्च होने के बावजूद समस्या जस की तस है और एक बार फिर वही सिलसिला शुरू हो चुका है.
देखिए हमारी यह खास पड़ताल.
भ्रामक सूचनाओं के दौर में आपको ऐसी खबरों की जरूरत है, जिन पर आप भरोसा कर सकें. न्यूज़लॉन्ड्री आपके लिए ऐसी ही खबरें लेकर आता है. हमारी पत्रकारिता को मजबूत करने के लिए सब्सक्राइब करें.

title: ‘A day off means job loss’: One year on, Surat’s loom workers say labour codes yet to reach them
description: Many migrants who run Surat’s power looms still work 14-hour days on piece rates, with no contracts and no safe way to complain.
author: Satish Bhartiya
content:
Many migrants who run Surat’s power looms still work 14-hour days on piece rates, with no contracts and no safe way to complain.
Amit Raut* has been caught in a Catch-22 for nearly two decades. The only work that pays enough to keep his family going is the work that is wearing him down.
Raut, about 50, first came to Surat 19 years ago from Ganjam district in Odisha, some 1,600 kilometres away, to work in the city’s power loom factories. Within four years, the pressure and the insecurity amid the clatter of dozens of machines became unbearable. He quit and went home.
In Ganjam, he spent nearly 10 years trying to make ends meet as a labourer. Daily wages there could not run a household, and the work was never certain. Three years ago, he came back to Surat, and to the looms.
Today he operates power looms in the Katargam area for 14 to 15 hours a day, paid by the metre of fabric he weaves. “I don’t receive any benefits like a labour card, PF (provident fund), or ESI,” he says.
Raut’s situation may seem to be an aberration, but it is how a significant portion of Surat’s weaving economy works. The city’s textile trade turns over an estimated Rs 1.5 lakh crore a year, and its looms are run by several lakh migrant workers from Odisha, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Madhya Pradesh. Few of them have any official record of their employment.
On November 21, 2025, the Union government brought four labour codes into force, replacing 29 older laws and promising appointment letters, provident fund, health insurance and leave. As the codes complete their first anniversary, our reporting across Surat’s loom clusters found that little of that promise has reached the factory floor.
It is because of various reasons. The codes’ own headcount thresholds leave many small weaving units outside their strictest provisions. Workers say the rules, such as double pay for overtime, are barely enforced, and that they are too afraid of losing their jobs to ask.
Inside the sheds
Inside a factory in Katargam, more than 50 power looms roared at once, minded by just three workers, roughly 17 machines each. Two of them, drenched in sweat, had plugged in earphones to cut out the din. The third was peeling off a soaked vest.
Many factories we visited looked like ruins (except that ruins are quiet): broken windows, walls unpainted for years, and tin sheds, put up in the name of repairs, that make the interiors even hotter. Workers laboured in shorts and undershirts. The passages between machines were so narrow that one misstep could cause a serious accident. Drinking water was scarce, and emergency exits were hard to find.
What was easy to find were CCTV cameras. They were mounted in most factories, including those with no restrooms or water coolers.
Raut’s own factory, also in Katargam, runs about 66 looms.
“I operate power loom machines for about 14–15 hours every day just to earn Rs 500-800,” Raut says. That works out to between Rs 33 and Rs 57 an hour.
Though he is paid by output, not time, which shifts the cost of every flaw onto him. “My income fluctuates because sometimes the fabric gets damaged in the machine, resulting in lower pay,” he says. “The factories pay between two to five rupees per meter. I get paid three rupees per metre of fabric produced. Under these conditions, my monthly income comes out to between 15,000 and 25,000 rupees.”
Rent takes Rs 6,000 a month and food for the family another Rs 10,000. He also buys his own drinking water. “I spend anywhere between 60-100 rupees on water,” he says. Even the factory’s toilets and rest areas are off limits to him, he claims.
In a good month, Raut saves about Rs 5,000. That is nowhere near enough to educate his children or cover a medical emergency, and he claims getting a day off is difficult. So why stay? “There are six members in my family. My wife, myself, three daughters, and one son,” he says.
An industry that doesn’t count its workers?
Since its first textile ancillary unit opened in 1925, Surat has grown into a network of more than 70,000 traders. The city alone is estimated to have around 7 to 8 lakh weaving units, which employ between 7 lakh and 12 lakh migrant workers.
Naishadh Desai, chairman of the labour organisation Shramjivi Sevalaya, says around 30 lakh workers are employed in Surat’s textile industry, with 95 percent coming from states like Odisha, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, and Madhya Pradesh.
The government’s last baseline survey of the powerloom sector, conducted in 2013, counted roughly 24 lakh power looms across India supporting about 44 lakh jobs. For all of Gujarat, it recorded 5,24,102 looms and 6,63,068 jobs, fewer looms than Surat is now estimated to run on its own. The Ministry of Textiles told Parliament in 2024 that it was framing a new survey. Until one is published, the 2013 count remains the only official baseline.
A worker who does not exist on paper cannot claim provident fund, insurance or gratuity, and in some of the factories we visited, there was no official record of the people at the looms.
Little change
The labour codes were meant to fix some of these issues. Between them, the Code on Wages, the Industrial Relations Code, the Code on Social Security and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions (OSH) Code promised appointment letters, ESIC insurance, free health check-ups, and gratuity, based on certain eligibility conditions.
Workers say they have seen little of it. Asim Sheikh*, 25, a migrant from Birbhum district in West Bengal, says his work conditions and pay have not changed in the year since the codes took effect. “We remain unorganised labour contracted on a temporary basis, which means we can’t demand rights under labour laws,” he says.
A study based on group discussions, by a labour organisation that requested anonymity, earlier claimed that most workers are unaware of overtime. No factory registers workers for ESIC or EPF or pays gratuity, and grievance committees and basic safety measures are virtually absent, it claimed.
Part of the explanation lies in some of the codes. The OSH Code covers establishments with 10 or more workers, and treats a unit as a “factory” only if 20 or more people work there with power. Under the old Factories Act, that threshold was 10. Provident fund is compulsory only for establishments with 20 or more employees, and ESIC is mandatory from 10, voluntary below that. Weaving units with four to 10 workers, a common size in Surat, can slip under most of these lines.
Though the Code on Wages has no such restrictions. It applies to every employee in every establishment, organised or unorganised, and guarantees minimum wage and overtime at no less than twice the normal rate. Even Gujarat’s 2025 amendment to its factory law, which allowed shifts to stretch to 12 hours, kept a 48-hour weekly ceiling and required overtime pay beyond nine hours a day.
Raut works 14 to 15 hours a day and earns the same three rupees a metre in his 14th hour as in his first.
A climate of fear
Shramjivi Sevalaya’s four-storey, 35,000-square-foot building seems deserted. Founded in 1940 to fight for workers’ rights, the organisation registered about 100,000 workers between 1960 and around 2000. Today, barely two to five workers visit in a day.
Its chairman Naishadh Desai says more than 80 union leaders work on labour rights in Surat. “However, even today, more than 90 percent of textile workers here, including those in power looms, are not provided their rights under labour laws,” he said.
The offices of five labour rights organisations we visited were just as empty, with at most one to four workers present.
Sheikh claims, “If a worker attempts to form a union or demand labour law protections, they are fired and blacklisted from finding work elsewhere.”
The same allegation surfaced this autumn, when Surat’s embroidery workers went on strike for shorter shifts and a weekly day off. As per reports, labour leader Malkhan Singh Verma alleged that 300 to 400 workers were dismissed, and that photographs of some were circulated on social media to warn other units off hiring them. Verma, who heads Majdoor Sena Surat, says the pattern is old. “In my experience working on labour rights from 2010 to the present, whenever an organisation, worker, or social activist raises the issue of workers’ rights, they are assaulted, jailed, threatened, and framed in false cases,” he says.
This reporter tried to speak to about 100 power loom workers. Some felt nothing would change; others believed speaking out would cost them their jobs. Not one agreed to be recorded on camera, and many would not even name their factory or its owner.
In Surat’s Parvat Patiya area, a group of people earlier surrounded a reporter who was filming workers. One of them snatched the phone, deleted several videos and issued a warning: “Get out of Surat, and don’t let us catch you filming anywhere again.”
The quiet exit
Bhimadhar Samudra, 59, has run Santoshi Restaurant in Katargam for 26 years. A power loom operator himself some 40 years ago, he has watched his customers dwindle.
“Until 2017–18, around 600 power loom workers used to come to my restaurant for meals in the morning and evening,” he says. “Now only about 100 workers eat here. They no longer have the money to feed themselves properly.”
He has also noticed more workers quitting the looms to look for something else. Rukmini Ben* is about to be one of them. The 45-year-old came to Surat from Jalgaon in Maharashtra 20 years ago and spent nearly 15 of them on power looms, with no job security, provident fund, bonus or safety provisions.
“Our hands make the cloth that goes out to the entire world,” she says, “but no rules or laws are followed in the factory to ensure our hands remain safe.”
Having “wasted” 15 years, she now wants out. “When a worker does not get their rights even after working for years, continuing the job makes no sense,” she says.
For now, she cooks in the evenings after her shift at the loom, and is looking for less physical work such as cooking, gardening or domestic help. “The power loom work makes me weak and fragile,” she says.
‘Sector hasn’t recovered from Covid’
Ramesh Bhai Prajapati, who owns a small weaving unit in Surat, admits that labour laws are disregarded in the city’s factories.
“We are unable to provide facilities like PF or labour cards to workers,” he says. “This is private, informal work, so workers are paid on a daily wage basis. Providing any additional benefits beyond this is beyond our capacity.”
Ramesh employs eight workers and pays them by output. His monthly wage bill is about Rs 1.5 lakh, or Rs 18,000 to 20,000 a worker. Maintenance, cleaning, electricity and materials cost another Rs 30,000 to 50,000. “My monthly net profit ranges from Rs. 1.5-2 lakh,” he says. “Before Covid, it was almost twice as much. The textile sector hasn’t recovered from the lockdown period.”
With eight employees, his unit falls below the thresholds for compulsory provident fund and ESIC, though the Code on Wages’ minimum-wage and overtime rules still bind him.
Ramesh says “we sometimes have to lay off workers” because the textile industry is “currently experiencing a slowdown”. This year has given some owners reasons for strain. In March, amid a gas shortage linked to the West Asia conflict, labour shortages and weak demand, Surat’s power loom units suspended night shifts. By April, industry bodies said nearly 2.5 lakh migrant workers had left the city. In August, a 25–30 percent jump in polyester yarn prices pushed about 1.5 lakh looms to drop a shift or close two days a week.
Larger owners, Ramesh says, have more capital and are in a much better position. “They are better equipped to look after their workers.”
Ashok Jirawala, president of the All Gujarat Textile Federation in Surat, says factory owners help out workers if they face any work-related or other difficulties, and that they are paid their wages on time. He argues that one of the reasons powerloom workers in Surat do not receive certain work-related benefits is that they do not stay with one factory for a long period.
We could not reach the factory owners whose units employed the workers quoted in this report. The workers were afraid that raising concerns about their rights could cost them their jobs, and spoke to us outside factory premises.
A movement tries again
“To enforce workers’ legal rights, the government and factory owners themselves must step forward with a clear policy,” says Mohan Bhai Dabbuwala, secretary of the Surat Textile Labour Union. “But the intent is clearly missing.”
Sandeep Patel, a Surat activist, is among the leaders of a textile labour movement that began a few months ago. “To demand ground-level enforcement of these laws, we held a sit-in protest on August 10 this year,” he says. “On August 24, we submitted a memorandum to the Collector. But there was no response. So we were forced to protest with nearly 2,000 workers on September 12.”
His demands are basic. “We are driving this movement so that statutory provisions under labour laws — such as 8-hour workdays, fair wages, Sunday off, ESI, and worker safety — are actually enforced on the ground.”
Patel says the Surat administration asked his team for a list of companies that were flouting the labour laws. The team’s worker-led survey covered more than 200 companies across textiles and other sectors. “None of them complied with the labour laws,” he claims.
His campaign ran alongside a wider agitation by Surat’s embroidery workers, who struck in mid-August and also protested at the collector’s office on September 12. In late September, the Deputy Labour Commissioner told the embroidery owners’ association, TEJAS, to comply with the four codes. On October 15, police detained around 70 workers and labour leaders before a planned satyagraha, citing a lack of permission.
The owners made a counter-offer: Rs 14,300 a month for an eight-hour shift with a weekly holiday, against the Rs 25,000 to 30,000 workers now earn for 12-hour days. Unions rejected it, along with a Rs 35,000 offer to stay on 12-hour shifts.
“If workers are denied their rights, this struggle will inevitably evolve into a much larger movement,” Patel says.
This reporter reached out to Surat’s labour assistant commissioner on the phone, email and WhatsApp to seek the department’s response to the allegations mentioned in the copy. This report will be updated if a response is received.
For Amit Raut, nothing about the codes’ first anniversary changes his life. “Taking a day off means losing your job.”
*Names of workers changed to protect identity
