title: In Photos | ‘Jantar Mantar is Everywhere’ Protests in 14 Global Cities
description: Indian diaspora groups and allies protested across Europe, North America and Australia under ‘Jantar Mantar is Everywhere’, opposing SIR, police detentions and alleged repression of anti-SIR protesters in India.
author: Anay Samarth
content:
As protests against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) continue in India, solidarity demonstrations were held in at least 14 cities across 10 countries over the weekend under the common banner of “Jantar Mantar is Everywhere.”
The demonstrations took place in Ireland, Germany, Spain, the Netherlands, Australia, Sweden, England, Canada, Czechia, and the United States, echoing demands in India for the withdrawal of the SIR and Kumar’s resignation.
The international demonstrations, organised by at least 15 various diaspora organisations, civil society groups, and students' outfits, followed days of protests across Indian cities, marked by allegations of police brutality, the detention of protesters and journalists, allegations of sexual assault by Delhi Police personnel, and the incarceration of Cockroach Janta Party leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka.

title: Uttarakhand Forest Fires: How Women Are Leading Community Forest Protection
description: Women in Uttarakhand are leading community forest restoration and fire prevention as migration reshapes Himalayan villages. Discover how initiatives in Manar and other villages are protecting forests and livelihoods.
author: Sriroopa Dutta
content:
Every morning, 75-year-old Bhagirathi Devi walks into the forest beside her village in Uttarakhand's Champawat district. She patrols the area, returns home around noon and heads back for another round at 2 pm, often staying until sunset.
Her task is to ensure that nobody cuts trees, damages vegetation or allows cattle to graze where they should not.
For more than two decades, Bhagirathi has helped protect and restore this forest in Manar village. Known locally as Van Amma, she began the effort in 2000, when the woodland had become almost barren following years of excessive grazing and tree felling.
Today, the community-managed forest is also a site of fire prevention.
In a report published by Down To Earth on 31 May 2025, journalist Bhagirath documented how the village's women organised themselves to restore the forest, regulate access, and remove dry leaves and pine needles before the fire season.
According to residents, there has been no forest fire in the restored forest since the initiative began. The Champawat Forest Department has also recognised the effort as a model for fire prevention.
Manar's experience points to something important about forest protection in Uttarakhand: preventing fires is not always about reaching a burning hillside with firefighting equipment. It can begin much earlier, with people who understand the forest, depend on it and have the authority to regulate how it is used.
Across the state's mountain villages, women are increasingly taking on this responsibility.
As men migrate in search of employment, women remain to manage agriculture, livestock and household needs. Their daily work brings them into close contact with forests, making them among the first to notice smoke and respond to small fires.
The Ghost Village question: who is left to protect the forest?
Uttarakhand's migration story is often told through the image of the ghost village: a settlement where houses remain locked, agricultural fields lie fallow, and only a handful of residents remain.
The scale of depopulation is reflected in government figures cited in the 2021 report Locked Houses, Fallow Lands: Climate Change and Migration in Uttarakhand, India, prepared by The Energy and Resources Institute (TERI) and the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research.
According to the 2011 Census, 1,048 of Uttarakhand's 16,793 revenue villages were uninhabited. A subsequent survey by the state's Rural Development and Migration Commission in 2018 identified another 734 villages that had become uninhabited after 2011.
The report notes that depopulation has affected all 13 districts, although the problem is more pronounced in the hill districts.
However, not every village affected by migration is entirely deserted. In many settlements, men have moved to towns and cities for work while women, children and older residents remain. Women continue cultivating fields, looking after cattle, collecting forest produce and caring for family members.
This changes who is available to respond when a forest fire breaks out.
In Manar, Bhagirathi Devi's initiative began with a problem familiar to many women in mountain villages. Before the forest was restored, women had to walk seven to eight kilometres to a neighbouring forest, Siddhmandir, to collect fodder and firewood. Bhagirathi told Down To Earth that this journey took five to six hours every day.
The loss of nearby forest cover had also affected the flow of local springs. Restoring the woodland was therefore not simply a conservation exercise. It was an attempt to make village life more sustainable.
For women who remain, the responsibility is consequently twofold: maintaining households in villages with fewer working-age residents and protecting the natural resources that make those settlements habitable.
Why women are often the first to notice a fire
The reasons women become first responders are closely connected to the division of labour in rural households.
Collecting firewood and fodder, taking cattle to graze, gathering leaves and working on agricultural land are routine responsibilities for many women in Uttarakhand. These activities keep them in and around forests for several hours a day.
When a fire begins, they may notice the first signs of smoke before it becomes visible from the village or reaches the attention of forest officials.
A 2023 paper by researchers Ripu Daman Singh, Surabhi Gumber, R C Sundriyal, Jeet Ram and Surendra P Singh, published in Tropical Ecology, provides important context for understanding this relationship.
Titled Chir pine forest and pre-monsoon drought determine spatial and temporal patterns of forest fires in Uttarakhand Himalaya, the research analysed satellite-derived fire data from 2002 to 2020 across 24 forest divisions in the state.
The researchers recorded 80,440 fire detections over the 19 years. Their analysis found that warmer pre-monsoon temperatures, a greater proportion of chir pine forest and lower winter and pre-monsoon rainfall together explained 56% of the variation in fire incidence.
They also noted that human activities associated with farming and the collection of fuel and fodder influence the likelihood of fires.
The paper specifically recommends examining changes in population distribution and communities' dependence on forests as part of effective fire management.
This is where women's everyday relationship with forests becomes relevant.
They are not simply residents living near a fire-prone landscape. Their livelihoods are directly connected to the condition of that landscape.
A fire can mean losing fodder for cattle, travelling farther to collect fuelwood, spending additional hours searching for forest produce and, in some cases, losing agricultural resources.
The relationship between gender and firefighting is not simply a question of who is more willing to respond. It is also a question of who is expected to undertake the work when the forest that sustains the household is threatened.
In a report published by Mongabay on 8 September 2026, journalist Swati Thapa documented this pattern in Uttarakhand villages.
Researcher Kavya Pandey of the Centre for Wildlife Studies, Bengaluru, told Thapa that traditional gender roles and women's responsibility for household work and caregiving help explain why they are often the first to respond to fires.
This offers a field-level account of a wider connection between women's labour and forest protection.
How a community can stop a fire before it spreads
Manar offers a particularly useful example of what happens when women move beyond responding to individual fires and take responsibility for managing an entire forest.
When Bhagirathi Devi began the initiative in 2000, she brought other women together to form a van panchayat, a community forest-management council. She was unanimously elected its first sarpanch.
The initial work involved clearing and fencing parts of the degraded forest. The women also worked with BAIF Development Research Foundation, a Pune-based organisation involved in silvopasture initiatives in the region.
Silvopasture combines trees, grasses and livestock management. The idea was to restore vegetation while ensuring that the community could continue to access fodder and other forest resources.
With BAIF's support and training, residents fenced the woodland using stones and thorny plants. They cleared invasive species such as lantana and planted native trees and fodder species, including banj oak (Quercus leucotrichophora), angu (Fraxinus micrantha) and utish (Alnus nepalensis).
For two years, grazing was prohibited to allow the vegetation to recover. It took another five to six years for the trees to establish themselves.
According to Manju Manral, the first president of Manar's Silvopasture Management Committee, 11.6 hectares of forest were eventually revived.
The work was not entirely voluntary.
Down To Earth reported that women involved in the restoration received Rs 120 per day from BAIF. They voluntarily contributed 10% of their wages towards maintaining the forest. Each household also contributed Rs 20 a month towards Bhagirathi's salary for guarding the woodland.
A separate 2022 field study by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, BAIF and the Centre for Ecology Development and Research also found that the forest under Manar's van panchayat was healthier than the forest outside its management area.
What the 2026 fire season reveals
In an assessment published on 2 June 2026 on the Indian Institute of Remote Sensing's (IIRS) Sudoor Manthan science portal, researchers Athira V Mukundan, Madhusmita Murmu, Chandra Mohan Bhatt and Arijit Roy analysed forest-fire activity across the state between January and May 2026.
Using NASA's MODIS active-fire data, they recorded:
- January: 200 active-fire detections.
- February: 113 detections.
- March: 178 detections.
- April: 207 detections.
- May: 433 detections.
The May figure represented a 109% increase over April. It also accounted for approximately 38% of all detections recorded between January and May.
Pauri Garhwal recorded the highest cumulative number of detections during the five-month period, at 207, followed by Chamoli with 190 and Tehri Garhwal with 130.
The researchers also used Sentinel-2 satellite imagery to map burned areas in Pauri Garhwal. Comparing images from April with those captured between 25 and 28 May, they identified approximately 838.66 sq km of burned area. Most of this was classified as low-severity burning, while 0.94 sq km fell into the highest severity category.
These figures are satellite-based detections and mapped burn areas, not a count of independently verified individual fires. Nevertheless, they show how quickly fire activity intensified towards the end of the pre-monsoon season.
The 2023 research by Singh and his colleagues helps explain this seasonal pattern.
Most fires in Uttarakhand occur between March and May, when temperatures rise, vegetation dries and fresh pine litter accumulates on the forest floor.
The human cost of these fires can be severe. On 13 June 2024, four forest department personnel died while fighting a blaze in Binsar Wildlife Sanctuary in Almora district. According to a report by The Times of India on 14 June 2024, four others were seriously injured after the firefighting team was engulfed by flames.
For women who fight smaller fires in community forests, the risks are no less real, particularly when they have no protective clothing, footwear or firefighting equipment.
Besides, women's participation does not automatically translate into decision-making power.
A 2026 research chapter by K Nagahama, published in Springer Proceedings in Earth and Environmental Sciences, examines women's participation in a Uttarakhand van panchayat through household surveys, interviews, forest surveys and long-term observations conducted between 2011 and 2023.
The research examines an important distinction: being present in community forest management does not necessarily mean having equal authority over decisions or control over resources.
The problem is also visible in the reporting from Uttarakhand.
In her September 2026 Mongabay investigation, Swati Thapa spoke to Laxmi Kharayat, a field trainer with The Hunger Project, who described cases where women formally listed as van panchayat heads were unaware of their positions, while male family members exercised authority on their behalf.
There is also a gap between the work women undertake and the employment opportunities available to them.
Seasonal fire watchers recruited by the forest department are predominantly men. Women who assist in firefighting often do so without regular wages or access to appropriate protective equipment.
The Forest Fire Prevention and Management Scheme and India's National Action Plan on Forest Fires recognise the importance of early detection, community participation and coordinated firefighting. The challenge is to ensure that these provisions translate into practical support for women at the village level.
This means providing women with training in fire prevention and safe firefighting, protective clothing, gloves, sturdy footwear, communication equipment and access to emergency assistance.
It also means creating paid opportunities for women as seasonal fire watchers and ensuring that they have actual decision-making authority within van panchayats.
Just as importantly, their work should not be treated as an unpaid extension of household responsibilities simply because they are the people who remain in the village.
Forest protection begins with the people who depend on it
Bhagirathi Devi's work did not begin with a firefighting operation. It began with a forest that had become too degraded to support the people living beside it.
By bringing women together, restoring native vegetation, regulating grazing and establishing a system for removing dry litter, the village created a model of long-term community protection.
For women in Uttarakhand's mountain villages, protecting a forest also means protecting the resources that keep their households functioning.
When the forest burns, the consequences reach their cattle, farms, water sources and daily routines. Their leadership has shown that communities can play a significant role in preventing fires, provided they have the authority and resources to do so.
The next step is to ensure that this responsibility does not remain invisible or unpaid.
The women who recognise the first signs of smoke, organise their neighbours and maintain village forests should be treated as essential partners in forest protection, not as an informal firefighting force expected to manage with whatever tools they have at hand.

title: Watching a Press Wallah Discard Charcoal Inspired This Schoolgirl to Design a Solar Ironing Cart
description: For generations, India's neighbourhood press wallahs have relied on burning charcoal to earn a living. Watching one of them dispose of burnt charcoal prompted Tamil Nadu schoolgirl Vinisha Umashankar to explore an alternative.
author: Vaishali Gautam
content:
From school uniforms to office shirts, many of us rely on our neighbourhood press wallahs for freshly ironed clothes. The history of the tool they use goes back over 2,000 years, long before electricity entered our homes.
As early as the first century BC, people in China used metal pans filled with hot charcoal to remove creases from fabric. These heated pans were moved over stretched cloth to smooth out wrinkles.
In medieval Europe, blacksmiths made heavy, flat metal irons known as sadirons. These were heated over a fire or on a stove. Since they cooled down during use, people often kept several irons ready to use in rotation.
Charcoal irons offered another way to keep the metal base hot. Their hollow bodies held burning charcoal. In 1852, a patent was granted for a design featuring a chimney and ventilation openings.
In India, generations of dhobis, istriwallas and neighbourhood press wallahs have earned their livelihoods through washing and ironing clothes. Their work requires an understanding of different fabrics, heat and pressure.
The history of India's laundry trade is also linked to caste and hereditary occupations. For many families belonging to traditional washer communities, the skills involved in washing and ironing clothes have been passed down through generations.
In 1882, American inventor Henry W Seely patented an electric flat iron. His design used electricity to generate heat, eliminating the need to heat the iron over a fire or burn charcoal inside it.
Despite advances in ironing technology, charcoal irons remain a familiar sight on Indian streets. However, burning charcoal exposes vendors to smoke and contributes to air pollution. Producing charcoal can also contribute to deforestation.
At the age of 12, Vinisha Umashankar from Tiruvannamalai, Tamil Nadu, noticed an ironing vendor discarding burnt charcoal on her way home from school. She began researching its environmental impact and looking for a cleaner alternative.
Vinisha designed a mobile ironing cart that uses solar panels and batteries to power a steam iron. The cart could also accommodate mobile phone charging facilities, giving vendors another potential source of income.
The National Innovation Foundation developed a prototype in 2019. Two years later, Vinisha became the youngest finalist for the inaugural Earthshot Prize and, at 15, addressed world leaders at COP26 in Glasgow.
For centuries, people have found different ways to heat irons and remove creases from clothes. Vinisha's invention explores how an everyday service that supports generations of Indian families could become less dependent on charcoal.

title: Meet the Young Innovator Using Data to Understand India’s Vanishing Groundwater
description: A Surat schoolboy built JALAAKAR, an AI groundwater prediction tool that uses rainfall, soil and borewell data to estimate underground water availability.
author: Nishtha Kawrani
content:
A borewell can run dry without much warning. For a farmer depending on it to irrigate crops or a family relying on it for everyday water needs, the question that follows is simple: how much water is actually left underground?
Finding an answer is not easy. Unlike rivers, lakes, or reservoirs, groundwater reserves cannot be seen. Their availability depends on several factors, from rainfall and soil conditions to the rate at which water is extracted. Without reliable estimates, planning how much to draw or where to focus conservation efforts becomes difficult.
A school student from Surat, Gujarat, is exploring how technology could make this information easier to access.
Dheyay Shah has developed JALAAKAR, a machine-learning-based tool that estimates groundwater availability across different talukas using historical records and environmental data. His innovation recently won the national title at vivo Ignite 2026, a nationwide challenge that received more than 6,100 project submissions from school students across India.
Making groundwater easier to understand
India depends heavily on groundwater for drinking water, agriculture and other everyday needs. However, excessive extraction, changing rainfall patterns and growing demand have put pressure on these underground reserves.
One of the difficulties in managing this resource is knowing how much water is available in a particular area. Groundwater levels can vary depending on local geography, the amount of rainfall received, and how much water is being extracted.
This is where Dheyay's project comes in. Instead of relying on isolated measurements, JALAAKAR brings together different sources of information to generate estimates that help people better understand groundwater conditions.
How JALAAKAR uses machine learning
At its core, JALAAKAR uses machine learning to identify patterns in historical groundwater and environmental data.
The tool considers information such as past borewell records, rainfall patterns, and soil characteristics. Each of these offers a different piece of information about underground water reserves.
For instance, rainfall influences how much water can seep into the ground and replenish aquifers. Soil characteristics determine how readily this water can percolate, while borewell records provide insights into changes in groundwater levels over time.
JALAAKAR analyses these datasets to identify relationships and recurring patterns. It then uses what it learns from the historical information to estimate groundwater availability at the taluka level.
In simpler terms, the tool attempts to use what has happened in the past to understand what groundwater conditions might look like in a particular area.
Such estimates could eventually help local communities, farmers, and those involved in water management make more informed decisions about extraction and conservation.
However, predictive estimates are not a substitute for actual groundwater measurements. The tool's accuracy, independent field validation, and suitability for different geographical conditions would need to be established before it can be used for wider water-management decisions.
A young innovator looking beneath the surface
Dheyay's project was recognised at vivo Ignite 2026, where he emerged as the national winner. The competition brought together school students working on ideas that apply science and technology to real-world challenges.
With more than 6,100 projects received, the challenge evaluated innovations on parameters such as creativity, scientific application, feasibility, cost-effectiveness, and potential social impact.
What makes JALAAKAR interesting is the problem it chooses to address. Groundwater management is often discussed in terms of large-scale infrastructure and policy, but it also begins with something much simpler: understanding how much water is available before using it.
Dheyay's work explores how data can help answer that question. While the tool would need further testing and refinement before wider application, it offers a promising starting point for making groundwater information more accessible.
For a young student, looking beneath the surface has meant looking at a problem that affects millions of people. And if developed further, JALAAKAR could contribute to a future where communities have better information to guide how they use and protect one of their most important natural resources.

title: How Tamil and Telugu Cinema Reduces Women Into Symbols
description: From The Paradise to Pushpa 2, women bear the violence of male ambition.
author: Prathyush Parasuraman
content:
A pregnant tribal woman is protesting in the Telugu film The Paradise, starring “natural star” Nani. Immediately, you know that she is going to be punished for her pregnancy. Like Chekhov’s flaming gun, a pregnant woman in Tamil and Telugu cinema is an invitation to imagine the worst—you know violence against her will ensue, just not how. In The Paradise, the woman’s protest is for her tribe to be recognised as a legitimate part of the state. The overlord, under whose clenched fist they live, does not want this.
As punishment, the woman is electrocuted, with her belly clamped to the engine of a revving car. The shock makes her twins slip out of the uterus—the boy survives, the girl dies. The boy will grow up wearing braids, a symbol of his lost, female twin; he will call himself Jadal, meaning braids. As a man, he will lead his tribe to victory.
But not before another pregnant tribeswoman is tortured. This time, the woman will tie up her feet and push until her child rips out of her body and she dies bleeding. This orphan will become the totemic symbol of the future around which the tribe will mobilise itself and finally emerge victorious. The mother’s final words to her child: “Think of this umbilical cord as your white ration card.”
Women are essential to The Paradise for the ways in which they are dispensable. Their presence is necessary. Their personhood, not so much. They provoke the plot and retreat. Or they hover over the narrative like a ghostly presence, exerting force on the events, like a wafting perfume, but without any pressure. Womanhood is stuck in ideas, unable to descend and occupy the body. There is a deep incuriosity built into the female characters; a deliberate effort is made to keep them from becoming compelling persons. It is not an unintentional lacuna, it is an enforced, strategic absence. You can watch the film dance around these characters, never embracing them, only poking at them, and then going back by two steps.
While women might be the object of male gaze, pregnant women quickly become symbols of male hope. Birthing a future generation, they are the object of something far more troubling than objectification—deification. Because, to objectify, you must at least consider the body. With deification, even that body—its marrow, a thing capable of exuding desire—becomes immaterial. Any violence committed on their bodies takes the shape of allegory. All of this is done in the garb of devotion.
To assault them is to threaten a future. To murder them is to wipe off this future. They become vessels, hollowed of presence, emblematic of a future often they will not get to inhabit.
At the cost of the feminine
Giving birth itself is a grisly affair, an original form of body horror. To look away from this, and turn the grisliness into something outside of the body—the electrocuted belly, the tied feet—is precisely the kind of perspective you adopt when you see the body not as something that inherently endures, but as something that must be given more to endure. What does it say about our cinema that it cannot show childbirth, but can make the audience watch a pregnant woman being tortured into childbirth?
This is not merely The Paradise’s cross to bear. In Jailer 2, too, it is a pregnant woman being flogged that revs its hero into action. In Ranabaali, a pregnant woman’s stomach must be ripped open to protect the child—another future buffering.
The woman’s body is a plaything for commercial Tamil and Telugu cinema—that much is incontestable. Women are arrayed, ready to be ravaged, hoping to be eventually saved, entirely instrumental. Mothers are essential to the plot in ways women are not. The violence exerted on these bodies is tactical, careful. There is a relish with which the scenes play out. Shorn of clothes, they are stripped down to sexual shimmer in songs; they pinprick the hero’s conscience by being raped and assaulted; they secrete fragile visions of the world that men will then murder and trample over.
What does it take to see a woman as a woman, and not the idea of a woman—the feminine not as means to an end, but as an end in itself?
For the longest time I thought that cinema’s obsession with rape, assault, and violence against women comes from society, where sexual and domestic violence is endemic—is an epidemic, in fact. It took a few films for me to recognise that rape is not what they care for, male power is. The proliferation of violence on the female body in cinema is entirely a product of directors—men, mostly—refusing to look the women they write in the eye. For how do you meet the gaze of a wispy idea? Of a burdensome ideal?
Given this apathy, it is impossible to see the hero with schoolgirl braids in The Paradise, or the hero donning a sari before ripping apart goons in Pushpa 2: The Rule, as masculinity that is comfortable with the feminine. Rather it is a masculinity that is expanding, not in tandem with but at the cost of the feminine, swallowing what it previously did not inhabit. The Paradise’s heroine, for example, is introduced in a rush, and her role is circumscribed into that of making B-grade films exposing her body, to earn money to pay off a debt. She makes her mother shoot these films.
The camera leers even as it claims that she is doing it under compulsion. This, perhaps, is the best that the film is capable of—to perform criticism as a shrug while revelling in the thing being critiqued. It is, after all, nice to know when being stabbed that the plunged knife felt bad about it.
Prathyush Parasuraman is a writer and critic who writes across publications, both print and online.

title: Vinod Kapri's Pyre and Beckett's Godot: Waiting as Love and Loneliness
description: In Vinod Kapri’s Pyre (2024), an octogenarian couple in a ghost village wait for a son who never arrives, realising that even loving companionship cannot shield them from a world that has long moved on.
author: Zainab S. Qazi
content:
If faith were to have another face, it might resemble the hopeful act of waiting. For what is waiting if not to believe, and keep believing, that the light is here and waiting for us to catch it? That the chase will end any day now, and the self will find solace, even when the world outside is veiled in darkness? What is waiting if not love disguised as faith, a quiet conviction that something, someone out there is worth holding on to?
Perhaps it is no coincidence that Vinod Kapri’s Pyre (2024) begins with the octogenarian couple Padam (Padam Singh Kapri) and Tulsi (Hira Devi) invoking the gods while navigating a hilly and lifeless terrain in Kumaon, Uttarakhand. A few minutes in, Padam suggests that Tulsi jump off the cliff, and the scene cuts to black as the title card appears. For the next hour and a half, the audience is trapped in the circular, often futile, spectatorship of waiting, until the film is gradually enveloped by a bleak landscape where death and life linger in uneasy proximity. What emerges is an existential portrait of loneliness in which even their loving companionship cannot protect Padam and Tulsi from a world that has long moved on, forgetting the last two people who still believe and hold on.
In many ways, Pyre can be read alongside the renowned Irish playwright Samuel Beckett’s seminal tragicomedy, Waiting for Godot. The octogenarian couple share the weariness of Estragon and Vladimir, who tirelessly wait for their waiting to end. The Kumaoni village mirrors the play’s existentialist landscape where, to quote Beckett, “nobody comes, nobody goes, it’s awful!”
In both, sanity is lost to the very act of waiting, and the self is recognised only through the other. Pyre’s elusive Godot—the one who never arrives—is Padam and Tulsi’s son Hariya. The hope of his arrival persists even when his physical absence becomes an inescapable reality. Hariya, like Godot, inhabits a world beyond their reach: close enough to be imagined, too far to be reached. In one poignant scene, Tulsi tells Padam: “Hamara beta laapata ho gaya hai” (We’ve lost our son). Padam replies: “Hamara beta laapata nahi hua hai, Tulsi. Hum khud laapata ho gaye hain” (We haven’t lost our son, Tulsi. It is we who are lost).
What emerges is the peculiar inadequacy of companionship in the face of overwhelming loneliness. This tension lies at the heart of the theatre of the absurd, to which Beckett’s play belongs: companionship sits beside abject loneliness, and two individuals are caught in a temporal loop, spinning within the circularity of time, which seems to have stopped for them even as it moves on for the rest of the world. Their banter as a loving couple, their slow moments of tenderness, and even Padam’s occasional humour, do not quite dispel the desolation surrounding them. There is something deeply absurd and unsettling in the way their affection endures in a life overshadowed by despair and mortality.
Unlike the solitary tree in Beckett’s play, which stands silent witness to the dying spirits of Vladimir and Estragon, nature remains indifferent to the couple’s gradual unravelling in Pyre. Landslides, heavy rains, and cloudbursts become a testament to their dying house, exposing its vulnerabilities and making their already precarious conditions even more difficult to endure. Nature offers neither refuge nor consolation; like the rest of the world, it moves on regardless of the lives trapped within it.
The cost of out-migration
The existential, almost ghostly spirit of the Kumaoni village looms large over many villages in the hills of Uttarakhand today. Rural-urban migration is on the rise, driven by push factors like high unemployment, poor pay, and poverty, compelling young people to leave their hometowns for cities. Kapri’s film brings this issue to light: ageing parents are left behind, waiting endlessly for their children to return. While Hariya’s presumed migration becomes a microcosm of the larger out-migration from the region, the film takes an unexpected turn towards the end, when it is revealed that Hariya is long dead and Padam has been writing letters in his son’s name to keep Tulsi’s hope alive. This is where the film grows even more existential, leaving the audience with a set of unsettling realisations that extend beyond the couple’s predicament: the lies we tell ourselves, the fictions we construct, and the stories we keep returning to in order to make sense of an uncertain, bewildering existence.
Death hovers over the film from the very beginning. Padam urges Tulsi to make their own pyres, for he fears no one would come to pay their last respects. For him, their love alone cannot save either of them, and each anticipates the other’s death with dread. In what I would call the year’s most haunting climax, a lone Tulsi mourns the dead Padam, since she must now live not only in a deserted village but also the absence of her only confidant, her best friend, her shield. And then the most telling image of the home comes to life when goats and heavy rains encircle Padam’s pyre. There is life all around him, yet this is the most lifeless scene of them all, set against a broken home that once sheltered two lives and now bears witness to the loneliness of the one left behind.
We return, then, to the central questions. What would remain of Vladimir if Estragon were gone, too? Perhaps it would resemble Tulsi’s world: a profound silence, with the only one who occasionally interrupted it also now gone. How do we make sense of the futile task of waiting if we have no one to wait with? The most tragic form of waiting is that one day you may be left with neither the person you wait for nor the person you waited with.
Zainab S. Qazi is an independent writer and researcher based in New Delhi. She writes at the intersection of film, media, culture, gender, and politics.
