title: Delhi Police register FIR over comedian's remarks on Bihari women, Chhath Puja
description: The Complaint Seeks Scrutiny Of Video Recordings, Social Media Posts And Other Digital Evidence From An October 24 Comedy Event In Saket
author: PTI
content:
The Delhi Police has registered an FIR over alleged objectionable remarks against women from Bihar and the religious and cultural traditions associated with Chhath Puja at a stand-up comedy event held in south Delhi.
The FIR was registered at Saket police station following a complaint against a comedy programme held at a Saket-based comedy club on October 24. The complaint named stand-up performer Yash Maheshwari.
The complainant alleged that objectionable remarks were made during the programme and sought examination of video recordings, social media posts and other digital evidence related to the event.
The FIR, however, does not mention the comedian's name. It has been registered under Sections 79 (word, gesture or act intended to insult the modesty of a woman), 196 (promoting enmity between different groups on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, language, etc. and doing acts prejudicial to maintenance of harmony), 296 (obscene acts and songs) and 352 (intentional insult with intent to provoke breach of peace) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS).

title: Delhi HC notice to Centre on Saurav Das travel axe, CJP slams those leaking his passport
description: Additional Solicitor General Chetan Sharma Told The Court That The Mumbai Police Had Issued A Look Out Circular Against Das On November 23 And That Discrepancies Pointed Out In His Passport May Also Have A Bearing On His Indian Citizenship
author: Our Web Desk
content:
Delhi High Court on Thursday sought the Centre’s reply on the Cockroach Janta Party’s Saurav Das's plea challenging the government's move to stop him from travelling to attend an event in the UK.
Additional Solicitor General Chetan Sharma told Justice Amit Mahajan,that the Mumbai police had issued a look out circular against Das on November 23 and that discrepancies pointed out in his passport may also have a bearing on his Indian citizenship.
Das was to travel to the UK on November 24 morning and was stopped at Delhi’s Indira Gandhi International Airport.
Das’s lawyer said they were not informed about any look out circular against him.
The court instructed that notices be issued to the regional passport officer and the Union Ministry of External Affairs for the next date of hearing, December 9.
The court developments came a day after the CJP alleged that Das’s passport details had been deliberately leaked.
“Certain BJP-aligned social media handles have now leaked my passport,” Das wrote on X (formerly Twitter) on Wednesday evening.
“This is a matter of serious concern. Will the Ministry of External Affairs clarify whether such leaks of citizens’ passports are a routine affair? Has doxxing been legalised in #NewIndia?
“First, a BJP-aligned lowlife leaked my Delhi residential address,” he wrote. “Then sent propagandist YouTubers who barged into my house while I was out of town. This was followed by fabricated stories about my family life and even a morphed picture of me. Now, my passport is being circulated to peddle yet another stupid, ridiculous narrative.
“It is precisely because of this pattern of targeted harassment that I specifically asked the SEM Court to ensure that my rent agreement is not leaked. I shall be filing a criminal complaint with the relevant authorities against EVERY social media handle involved in circulating my passport.
“And to those who mistake the prevailing climate of impunity for permanent immunity: I am documenting every instance and every handle involved. Governments come and go. When the time comes, they will face the full wrath of law. Fleeing the country will be the only option left for them,” he added.
The CJP’s Abhijeet Dipke also levelled the same allegation.
“Saurav’s passport has been leaked from within the system and is now being circulated by several BJP supporters,” the CJP founder wrote.
“What kind of world are we living in where nobody can access the Prime Minister’s degree, but a citizen’s passport can be leaked and circulated so openly?”
CJP legal head Ratna Singh told PTI Videos: “Saurabh was supposed to travel to the UK. When he reached the airport, he was stopped by immigration. Although he had a valid visa and a valid passport, he was stopped and told that there was a show-cause notice against him, because of which he would not be allowed to travel. The show-cause notice was also emailed to him that same evening, by the immigration department…Our submission before the court was that how can someone's movement be restricted on the basis of a show-cause notice when no valid grounds or specific reasons have been communicated to him for stopping him? His passport is also completely valid, so why was this done?”

title: Supreme Court orders separate warning labels for high salt, sugar and fat on food packs
description: The Order Will Be A Major Setback To Food And Drink Players Such As PepsiCo, Mondelez, Coca-Cola And Nestle That Have Long Opposed Such Labels
author: Reuters
content:
India's top court on Thursday tightened a government labelling proposal for food packaging and criticised what it said were the "double standards" of global companies that resist food warning labels in India but voluntarily apply them in some other markets.
In a challenge brought by health activists disappointed at the government's plan for ingredient warning labels, the Supreme Court ruled the labelling regime should require separate labels to indicate high amounts of salt, sugar and fat, and not just a single one as proposed earlier.
It also said global multinationals should adopt uniform standards across jurisdictions, noting concerns had been raised that product composition often differed from territory to territory.
"If true, such double standards are deeply troubling," the court said, without naming any companies. "A consumer in India is entitled to no less protection, and no less information, than a consumer in the United States or the United Kingdom."
The debate on food safety has intensified in India since India's government opted for a weaker labelling regime after lobbying by Coca-Cola and groups backing Nestle and PepsiCo, which argued warning labels were ineffective. Many companies have implemented such measures voluntarily in European markets, Reuters found.
A can of Fanta sold in London has 63 calories, but the same-sized product in India contains three times as much sugar and 185 calories, Reuters had reported. Health activists in India have repeatedly raised concerns about the amount of sugar in such drinks.
Thursday's order will be a major setback to food and drink players such as PepsiCo, Mondelez, Coca-Cola, Unilever and Nestle that have long opposed such labels. Most foreign companies count India as one of their biggest consumer markets, and executives privately say such measures could impact sales of both local and international food products.
There was no immediate response to the court ruling from the food companies.
Three labels, not one
India is in the midst of an unprecedented food safety crackdown, carrying out nationwide raids against restaurants, amid concern over poor hygiene and standards. The new front-of-pack red warning labels will bring India's labelling regime more in line with markets such as Chile and Mexico that operate strict labelling regimes.
The Supreme Court said the government needed to tighten its proposal, mandating separate hexagon-shaped warning labels for high salt, sugar and fat on the front of packs, not only one as proposed earlier by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India.
The authority shall ensure that a separate hexagon for each "nutrient of concern, each containing the word high fat, high sugar, high salt... rather than a single combined hexagon," Supreme Court judge J.B. Pardiwala said.
Health activists welcomed Thursday's ruling.
"This is certainly a landmark development in the nutritional history of the country," said Rajiv ‌Shankar Dvivedi, the lead counsel for non-profit "3S And Our Health", which brought the challenge.
Pardiwala asked the lawyers why they were not smiling after hearing the decision. When one replied that he represented the food industry, the judge teased by saying once the lawyer finished all 150 pages of the ruling, "perhaps nothing will remain on your face."
"This is larger public interest, national interest," the judge added, calling for strict implementation of the court's orders.
The industry will have one year to adjust to the changes once the labelling law is finalised.

title: Dar-e-Nijaat: Pakistani TV drama screenings cancelled in India after backlash
description: The show, Dar-e-Nijaat, has become a sensation in India but is now embroiled in a political row.
author: Zoya Mateen
content:
Two screenings of Pakistani TV show cancelled in India after backlash
- Published
Until Wednesday, the weekend plans of some television enthusiasts in the Indian city of Bengaluru involved dressing up, having an elaborate dinner and finding out what happens next in the lives of a wildly popular fictional Pakistani couple.
Then geopolitics intervened.
Two private screenings of Dar-e-Nijaat (Door to Salvation), a Pakistani television drama that has become something of a sensation on Indian social media, were called off after an online backlash and police scrutiny.
The serial, which airs on Pakistan's ARY Digital, is available to Indian viewers through some YouTube channels, though the broadcaster's official channel is blocked in India.
The controversy comes amid a renewed appetite for Pakistani entertainment in India, even though cultural engagement remains a sensitive issue following a brief but intense military confrontation between the two nuclear-armed neighbours in May last year.
A similar gathering in Delhi, featuring quizzes and even a virtual interaction with the show's director, had already divided opinion online last week.
In Bengaluru, one screening, scheduled for Saturday at a restaurant, offered a Persian and Arabic dinner alongside two episodes of the serial for a small ticket charge. The other - scheduled at a private theatre and meant only for family members - asked guests to dress in their "best Pakistani ensemble".
As promotional posters circulated online, several social media users questioned the appropriateness of such gatherings and called for police intervention. Both events have since been called off.
The backlash has coincided with calls to block the release of another Pakistani drama in India.
The All Indian Cine Workers Association (AICWA) has written to Prime Minister Narendra Modi demanding that Netflix's upcoming Pakistani series, Jo Bachay Hain Sang Samait Lo (Gather whatever is left), be barred from release in India.
Featuring Fawad Khan, Mahira Khan, Sanam Saeed and other stars with many Indian fans, the series is Pakistan's first Netflix original. Its global premiere is scheduled for 4 December.
In its letter to Modi on Tuesday, the AICWA argued that releasing the series in India would disregard the sentiments of families affected by terrorism. India has long accused Pakistan of supporting cross-border terrorism, an allegation Islamabad denies.
The association has also sought permanent legislation prohibiting Pakistani entertainment content in India. Netflix is yet to clarify whether the series will be available to Indian subscribers.
The developments have revived an old debate in India over whether cultural ties with Pakistan should be kept separate from political differences.
India and Pakistan share a rich cultural heritage, but relations between them have often been fraught since they were carved out of British India as independent nations in 1947.
And cultural exchanges have often been among the first casualties of political tensions. Pakistani ghazal singers with devoted audiences in India have periodically found themselves unable to perform there. Indian films, immensely popular in Pakistan, have disappeared from its cinemas. Artistic collaborations have flourished during periods of relative calm, only to unravel when tensions flare again.
The early 2010s were a particularly fertile period. Pakistani singers Atif Aslam and Rahat Fateh Ali Khan were among the most recognisable voices in Hindi cinema. The launch of the television channel Zindagi in 2014 brought Pakistani serials into Indian living rooms, introducing viewers to stories whose language and emotional worlds were familiar, but whose treatment of everyday life often felt refreshingly different.
By 2016, Fawad Khan was appearing in some of Bollywood's most prominent productions. But attacks on Indian security forces in Uri that year and in Pulwama in 2019, both of which India blamed on Pakistan-based militant groups, narrowed the space for cultural collaboration. Pakistan - which has constantly denied any involvement - also imposed restrictions on Indian entertainment.
Even as formal exchanges dwindled, Pakistani dramas found new audiences in India on YouTube, while music continued to travel across the border through streaming platforms.
But the events of last year disrupted even this relatively informal relationship.
On 22 April 2025, militants killed 26 people, most of them tourists, in Pahalgam in Indian-administered Kashmir. India blamed Pakistan-linked militants; Islamabad denied involvement. In May, India launched military strikes on what it described as terrorist infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-administered Kashmir. Four days of fighting followed before a ceasefire was announced.
Amid widespread anger in India, the government asked streaming platforms to discontinue Pakistani-origin content, while social media accounts of several Pakistani celebrities were blocked.
Fawad Khan's much-anticipated return to Hindi cinema with Abir Gulaal was thwarted when the film was denied permission for release in India. Criticism of India's military action by Pakistani artistes fuelled further anger.
For much of the past year, Indian audiences have encountered Pakistan on screen largely through the prism of national security. In December, millions flocked to watch Dhurandhar, Aditya Dhar's espionage thriller, whose success inspired a fascination with the gangsters, spies and political intrigues of Karachi.
But in recent months, a more familiar kind of fascination with Pakistan has begun to resurface.
Pakistani songs like Alfaaz have become hugely popular on Indian social media, while Dar-e-Nijaat, a story about marriage, heartbreak and domestic life, has found an enthusiastic audience.
Written by the celebrated Urdu novelist Umera Ahmed, the serial revolves around the marriage of Zaryab (Durefishan Saleem), a young woman recovering from a romantic betrayal, and Abu Bakar (Sheheryar Munawar), a deeply religious man.
Though the drama explores questions of faith and redemption, it is Abu Bakar's tenderness towards his wife that has earned him perhaps the highest accolade in the contemporary vocabulary of courtship: a "green flag".
It was this enthusiasm for the drama that prompted the organiser of one of the screenings in Bengaluru to plan an event at a private theatre in her apartment complex.
What she had envisaged as a small family gathering, she said, had been interpreted quite differently once the invitation found its way onto X.
"My family was saying why should we cancel?" she said. But ultimately, she decided to call it off.

title: Kerala: Police investigate fairness cream's alleged link to kidney ailment in 17-year-old Indian girl
description: Doctors who treated the 17-year-old girl say that the cream allegedly contained toxic levels of mercury.
author: Ashraf Padanna , Cherylann Mollan
content:
Police investigate fairness cream's alleged link to Indian teen's kidney ailment
- Published
Police in India's southern Kerala state have registered a case against a fairness cream brand after a 17-year-old girl who used the cream allegedly developed a serious kidney ailment.
The girl's doctor told the media, external that she had developed a disease that impairs the kidney's ability to filter blood due to toxic levels of mercury allegedly found in the cream.
The girl - her name has been withheld to protect her identity - reportedly bought the cream to treat pimples and pigmentation after seeing an ad on social media.
India has an obsession with skin-lightening creams and this has led to a proliferation of brands selling fairness creams, though not all of them are regulated.
Experts say some of these creams may contain toxic metals like mercury and lead, but because they are sold via WhatsApp and other social media platforms, the brands often escape scrutiny of the authorities.
They also say that many of these brands use social media to market products to youngsters, even if they are uncertified and untested.
Laboratory tests revealed that the cream the girl used contained 12,500 parts per million of mercury, far exceeding the permissible limit of less than one part per million for skin-lightening products, Aster MIMS Mother Hospital in Malappuram district, where the teenager was treated, said in a statement.
Dr Satheesh, a nephrologist at the hospital, said that the girl had developed membranous nephropathy - a life-threatening kidney disorder where immune deposits thicken the filtering walls of the kidneys, causing large amounts of protein to leak into the urine.
She added that mercury absorbed through the skin could damage the kidneys' filtration units, leading to blood toxicity. If left untreated, such toxicity could cause kidney failure and severe neurological damage.
The girl said she started buying the fairness cream about a year ago through a social media app and had bought three bottles over the past year.
"The company claimed that continuous use [of the cream] every night would help remove pimples and pigmentation. It also promised visible results with consistent application," the teenager told Onmanorama newspaper.
But after using the cream for a couple of months, she began experiencing fatigue, headaches, dizziness, insomnia and her legs and face began to swell. The teenager told the newspaper that she even struggled to stand upright.
"The teenager was initially brought to the hospital by her parents with severe body swelling and acute physical distress," the hospital said.
"While primary treatment was initiated, the unusual progression of her symptoms prompted doctors to suspect an underlying toxin. Subsequent blood and clinical tests revealed dangerously elevated levels of mercury in her system," their statement added.
Doctors suspected that the mercury could have entered the girl's bloodstream through her skin. They sent a sample of the fairness cream to a laboratory for testing.
The test results confirmed that the cream contained mercury "drastically higher than" the permissible safety limits mandated by the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) for cosmetics in India, the hospital said.
The doctors then treated the girl by administering medicines to eliminate toxins, while managing her kidney-related complications.
She was discharged from hospital after about a month and has been recovering at home.
On Monday, she told the BBC that she was still experiencing some health issues and was finding it difficult to study.
"Since starting treatment, she has shown gradual improvement. However, she is not back to normal yet and it may still take time for her to fully recover," Dr Satheesh said.
Meanwhile, the Kerala police have launched an investigation into the matter and the Kerala State Commission for Protection of Child Rights has also registered a case against the fairness cream manufacturer.
The incident once again puts the spotlight on India's obsession with fair skin, and how people, especially women, are willing to buy creams that may not be regulated as long as they promise to make them fair.
This is because the cultural bias against dark skin runs deep in Indian society and those who aren't fair-skinned often face discrimination.
In recent years, social activists and even Bollywood actors have spoken out about this unhealthy preference for fair skin, challenging the widely-held notion that fairer is better.

title: Pew survey: What India's changing Hindu and Muslim populations tell us
description: India will remain predominantly Hindu, though its Muslim population is projected to grow faster, according to a new survey.
author: Soutik Biswas
content:
India's religious make-up - what a new Pew study says about Hindus and Muslims
- Published
India will remain overwhelmingly Hindu for decades to come, but its religious composition is projected to shift gradually.
A new study by the Pew Research Center, projecting the world's religious populations to 2070, estimates that Hindus will make up 76% of India's population by then, down from 79% in 2020, while the Muslim share will rise from 15% to 20%.
The shift is rooted largely in differences in age and fertility: Indian Muslims are younger than Hindus and, on average, have more children.
The Pew projections place India at the centre of a wider demographic shift across South Asia.
Pakistan is expected to overtake Indonesia as the country with the world's largest Muslim-majority population, with India moving into second place. Bangladesh, too, is projected to see substantial growth in its Muslim population.
The study projects the religious composition of the world over the next 50-year period, drawing on data from 201 countries and territories, covering virtually the entire global population.
It tracks seven religious groups between 2020 and 2070, assuming recent demographic trends continue. Using census and survey data, it establishes each group's size and age profile in 2020, and factors in differences in fertility and religious switching.
The findings place India at the heart of a changing global religious landscape. The country is expected to have the world's second-largest Muslim population by 2070, after Pakistan, with about 334 million Muslims. Pakistan itself will overtake Indonesia as the country with the largest Muslim population, with an estimated 461 million.
Yet the projections offer little support for the more dramatic narratives sometimes attached to India's changing religious composition.
If current demographic trends continue, the Hindu population in the country is expected to grow by 176 million between 2020 and 2070, the report says. It will continue to account for more than three-quarters of the country's population.
Despite a sharp fall in India's overall fertility, Muslim women still have more children, on average, than Hindu women. Pew attributes the shift primarily to demographic momentum.
Indian Muslims had a median age of 24 in 2020, compared with 29 for Hindus.
Between 2025 and 2030, Pew estimates Muslim women in India will have an average of 2.3 children, against 1.8 among Hindu women.
"We expect religious change in India to be driven almost entirely by long-standing demographic differences between Hindus and Muslims: Muslims are younger and have higher fertility rates," Stephanie Kramer of the Pew Research Center told the BBC.
"The fertility gap has narrowed considerably – from more than one child per woman in 1992 to about half a child in recent years and is likely to keep shrinking," she said.
"But Hindu fertility is already below the replacement level, while Muslim fertility is projected to remain above it for another two decades." (A replacement level is one at which new births are sufficient to maintain a stable population.)
The projections are hardly surprising, says KS James, an Indian demographer at Princeton University.
"The fertility gap between Muslims and Hindus is well established and it means Muslim population growth is likely to remain faster for the next few decades. But fertility is declining across all religious communities and the gap is expected to narrow further," he told the BBC.
"Ultimately, they will converge," he says, adding that the projections do not point to anything dramatically different in India's demographic trajectory.
Demographers push back against claims, often amplified by Hindu right-wing groups, that Muslims will eventually outnumber Hindus. There is no evidence of any significant religious conversion driving population change in India, they say, and the projections do not support such "alarmist scenarios".
The wider South Asian picture is equally revealing, according to the report.
Pakistan's Muslim population is projected to more than double to 461 million by 2070, overtaking Indonesia as the world's largest. India will rank second, with 334 million Muslims, while Bangladesh's Muslim population will rise to 218 million. India and Nepal, meanwhile, will remain the world's only Hindu-majority countries.
There appears to be a global story behind these regional shifts.
By 2035, Muslims are projected to overtake Christians as the world's largest religious group, according to the report. By 2070, their numbers are expected to reach 3.64 billion, up from 2.02 billion in 2020.
Christianity, meanwhile, will have just under three billion followers. Muslims will account for 36% of humanity, compared with 26% today.
But the most dramatic transformation may be taking place thousands of miles west of South Asia, in Africa.
Christianity's centre of gravity is moving steadily away from Europe and the Americas towards sub-Saharan Africa.
The report says that if recent trends continue, more than half of the world's Christians are expected to live there by 2070, compared with 31% in 2020. Pew forecasts that the Democratic Republic of Congo will overtake the United States as the country with the largest Christian population.
The steepest decline is expected to occur in Europe. If current trends continue, by 2070 Europe will be home to 11% of the world's Christian population, down from 22% in 2020, the report says.
The US is projected to lose its Christian majority by 2065, although Christians will remain the country's largest religious group in 2070.
One reason for this changing religious landscape is the growing number of people identifying with no religion.
In UK and France, the "religiously unaffiliated" are projected to become the majority by 2070. South Korea is expected to follow suit.
Yet their share of the world's population is forecast to fall from 24% to 17%, largely because of a decline in China's population.
China accounts for about two-thirds of the world's religiously unaffiliated population. Its expected population decline will more than offset growth in secular populations elsewhere, the report says.
By 2070, there are other unexpected shifts.
The US is projected to become the world's fifth-largest Hindu population, with immigration driving much of its growth.
And Australia's unaffiliated population will overtake Christians as the country's largest group.
Buddhism, meanwhile, faces a demographic squeeze. Its population is expected to fall by more than half in China, Japan and South Korea, reflecting the ageing and shrinking populations of East Asia. Laos and Mongolia are projected to lose their Buddhist majorities.
There are, of course, caveats. These are demographic projections, not predictions of everything that might happen. Pew assumes that recently observed patterns of fertility, migration and religious switching - or conversions - will continue.
"There are many events that could affect religious group populations (including wars, natural disasters, epidemics and changes in economic or social circumstances) that are not analysed here," the report admits.
India's baseline also required projecting the 2020 religious composition from the 2011 census, because the subsequent census had been delayed
Still, the broad direction is unmistakable.
South Asia will remain indispensable to the world's religious story, not just because of India's enormous Hindu population but because of the growing weight of its Muslim populations. Africa will increasingly shape Christianity's future, while Europe and parts of East Asia become more secular.
Clearly, by 2070, the world's religious landscape may look markedly different, shaped less by conversion than by the uneven arithmetic of births, deaths and migration.

title: Govt responds to ThePrint report on Chinese satellites’ unusual manoeuvres days before Pahalgam
description: According to a report by a space surveillance firm, exclusively accessed by ThePrint, a Chinese satellite Yaogan-35 01A altered its orbit to make more passes over Pahalgam on 16 April 2025.
author: Keshav Padmanabhan
content:
New Delhi: The Ministry of External Affairs Wednesday said it has taken note of media reports on the Chinese satellites making unusual manoeuvres days before last year’s Pahalgam terror attack last year, and promised that “appropriate measures” will be taken when necessary.
First reported by ThePrint, last year, China’s Earth-observation satellites carried out around 37 unusual manoeuvres focused on Pahalgam in Jammu and Kashmir. Days later, terrorists attacked the area, killing 26 people.
In response to ThePrint’s coverage on the Chinese satellites, Randhir Jaiswal, the official spokesperson for the Ministry of External Affairs, said, “We have seen some media reports on the issue. We continue to closely follow developments which have a bearing on our security and will take measures as appropriate”.
According to a report by Digiantra, a space surveillance firm, exclusively accessed by ThePrint, a Chinese satellite Yaogan-35 01A altered its orbit to make more passes over Pahalgam on 16 April. Other satellites carried out similar manoeuvres on the day of the attack.
The report does not allege collusion between China and Pakistan days before the attack, but points to a possible pattern of cooperation between the two countries. In response to the Pahalgam terror attack, India launched Operation Sindoor on 7 May.
The military strikes targeted terror complexes across Pakistan. Islamabad escalated the situation through attacks on Indian civilian and military infrastructure, leading to an 87-hour conflict.
Tensions between the two countries remain high. As a result of the Pahalgam terror attack, India also announced that the Indus Waters Treaty will be held in abeyance in response to continued cross-border terror attacks.
Last year, ThePrint also exclusively reported that requests for satellite images of the Pahalgam region had increased from a US-based satellite company, weeks before the terror attack.
Islamabad has also increased its cooperation in the space sector with Beijing, as it looks to strengthen its own space programme.
Ties between India and China have slowly stabilised in the last two years. Both countries clashed in Eastern Ladakh at Galwan during the summer months of 2020, which led to a decline in political ties.
In October 2024, India and China announced an agreement to disengage at the friction points across the Line of Actual Control. Since then, the two countries have instituted a number of confidence-building measures, including resumption of direct air services and the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi travelled to China in August 2025 to attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit, while Chinese President Xi Jinping travelled to India in September 2026 to attend the BRICS Summit.
(Edited by Anupama Yadav)

title: Meta top execs held closed-door talks with Congress amid protests on content curbs—Reuters report
description: Congress raised concerns about rise in curbs on its leaders’ accounts, and about allegations that Meta favours BJP, Reuters report says, citing sources. Meta has denied favouritism.
author: Reuters
content:
New Delhi: Meta‘s top executives in India held closed-door talks with the country’s opposition Congress party as the two sides try to defuse protests against the US firm’s content moderation practices, four people familiar with the matter said.
Meta‘s Aman Jain and Natasha Jog, two key executives in India, represented the company at the meeting at Congress headquarters on Tuesday, one person said.
They raised concerns about protests targeting Meta‘s offices and the depiction of CEO Mark Zuckerberg in posters. Congress raised concerns about a rise in restrictions on its leaders’ accounts and posts, and about allegations that Meta favours Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), three other people said. Meta has denied any favouritism.
The meeting marked Meta‘s first direct engagement with the party since protests by its youth wing began on Friday.
The Youth Congress has demanded that Meta restore accounts taken down on government orders and explain how its algorithms restrict posts, and its members have clashed with police near Meta‘s offices in Hyderabad, Mumbai and Gurugram.
Congress did not immediately respond to a request for comment, while Meta said it moderates content in India in accordance with the law. Meta executives Jain and Jog did not respond.
Meta made no commitments to the party during the meeting and explained that it was bound by local laws, said one of the people, who had direct knowledge of the discussions. The executives also emphasised that Meta was neutral towards all political parties, the person said.
The dispute adds to political pushback for Meta in its biggest market by users, where it restricted more than 5.4 million posts or accounts under local laws in the first half of 2026, up from about 70,000 in all of 2025, company disclosures show.
Meta attributes the rise to India’s amended IT rules that require faster and more proactive takedowns, but it has triggered a debate over free speech as the government steps up demands to remove online content.
The protests took a fresh turn in recent days as posters and banners depicting Zuckerberg in a white shirt, khaki shorts and black cap, the traditional uniform of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), appeared in cities like Delhi, Kolkata, Patna, Mumbai and Bengaluru. The RSS is a Hindu nationalist volunteer organisation that is the ideological parent of the BJP.
“This is Congress Model: Vandalise offices of private companies,” BJP national spokesperson Pradeep Bhandari wrote on X on Saturday.
(Reporting by Munsif Vengattil, Aditya Kalra and Saurabh Sharma; Editing by Tomasz Janowski and Kevin Buckland)
Disclaimer: This report is auto generated from the Reuters news service. ThePrint holds no responsibility for its content.

title: Exclusive: चीन ने पाकिस्तान के लिए लॉन्च किए 5 सैटेलाइट, भारत के हर इंच की होगी 24×7 निगरानी
description: भारत पर चीन की सैटेलाइट निगरानी को लेकर दिप्रिंट की यह तीसरी एक्सक्लूसिव रिपोर्ट है.
author: सौम्या पिल्लई
content:
नई दिल्ली: चीन और पाकिस्तान मिलकर सैटेलाइट का एक ऐसा नेटवर्क बना रहे हैं, जो भारतीय क्षेत्र पर लगातार नजर रख सकता है. अंतरिक्ष निगरानी से जुड़ी एक रिपोर्ट में कहा गया है कि 2025 में भारत-पाकिस्तान के बीच हुए संघर्ष के दौरान दोनों देशों के बीच अंतरिक्ष में यह सहयोग और मजबूत हुआ.
बेंगलुरु की अंतरिक्ष निगरानी स्टार्टअप दिगंतारा की एक रिपोर्ट के मुताबिक, जिसे दिप्रिंट ने खास तौर पर देखा है, ऑपरेशन सिंदूर के दौरान भारतीय सैन्य ठिकानों और अन्य रणनीतिक जगहों पर नजर रखने के लिए चीन की अंतरिक्ष क्षमताओं, जिसमें सैटेलाइट डेटा भी शामिल है, का इस्तेमाल किया गया हो सकता है.
रिपोर्ट में सबसे अहम खुलासों में से एक चीन के हाई-रेजोल्यूशन ऑप्टिकल रिमोट-सेंसिंग सैटेलाइट याओगान-41 की भूमिका से जुड़ा है. भारत और पाकिस्तान के बीच 88 घंटे तक चले सैन्य टकराव के दौरान इस सैटेलाइट की भूमिका रही.
रिपोर्ट में कहा गया है, “चीनी सैटेलाइट याओगान-41 पूरे भारतीय उपमहाद्वीप पर लगातार नजर रख सकता है. दोहरे इस्तेमाल वाला यह सैटेलाइट ऑपरेशन सिंदूर के दौरान भारतीय एयरबेस पर नजर रख रहा था.”
रिपोर्ट में ऑपरेशन सिंदूर के दौरान भारत के खिलाफ याओगान-41 के खास इस्तेमाल की बात कही गई है. साथ ही यह भी बताया गया है कि चीन और पाकिस्तान अंतरिक्ष निगरानी का एक ऐसा नेटवर्क बना रहे हैं, जिसमें भारत का एक इंच भी हिस्सा निगरानी से बाहर न रहे.
जनवरी 2025 और जून 2026 के बीच पाकिस्तान ने छह सैटेलाइट ऑर्बिट में स्थापित किए. इनमें से पांच—पाकिस्तान रिमोट सेंसिंग सैटेलाइट-अर्थ ऑब्जर्वेशन 1 (PRSC-EO1), पाकिस्तान रिमोट सेंसिंग सैटेलाइट-2 (PRSS-2), HS-1, PRSC-EO2 और PRSC-EO3—को चीनी रॉकेटों के ज़रिए, चीन की सुविधाओं से लॉन्च किया गया था.
इन सभी सैटेलाइट्स को अलग-अलग भारतीय क्षेत्रों पर नज़र रखने के लिए तैनात किया गया है. साथ ही ये चीन के सैटेलाइट नेटवर्क को भी मजबूत करते हैं.
पाकिस्तान और चीन के सैटेलाइट की संयुक्त पृथ्वी-निगरानी क्षमता से भारतीय सैन्य ढांचे, सैनिकों की आवाजाही, सीमा पर बने ठिकानों, एयरबेस, नौसेना के ठिकानों और रणनीतिक संपत्तियों पर ज्यादा लगातार नजर रखी जा सकती है.
रिपोर्ट में कहा गया है, “चीन ने पाकिस्तान के लिए पांच सैटेलाइट लॉन्च किए, जिससे ISTAR, भारतीय संपत्तियों की निगरानी और अंतरिक्ष निगरानी की क्षमताएं बढ़ीं.”
ISTAR एक सैन्य प्रणाली है, जो सैटेलाइट, ड्रोन, विमान, रडार, जमीन पर लगे सेंसर और खुफिया नेटवर्क से मिली जानकारी को एक साथ जोड़ती है. इससे सेना को अपने विरोधी की गतिविधियों और क्षमताओं की विस्तृत जानकारी मिलती है.
विशेषज्ञों का सुझाव है कि चीन जब अंतरिक्ष में अपनी महत्वाकांक्षाएं बढ़ा रहा है, तो भारत को भी अंतरिक्ष में अपनी मौजूदगी बढ़ाने के लिए अपनी क्षमताओं पर काम करना होगा.
पाकिस्तान के सैटेलाइट
दिगंतारा की रिपोर्ट से पता चलता है कि चीन की मदद से पाकिस्तान के सैटेलाइट लॉन्च करने का सिलसिला 2025 से काफी पहले शुरू हो गया था. 2018 से ही PRSC-EO1, PakSat MM1, ICUBE-Q, PRSS-1 और Pak TES 1A जैसे सैटेलाइट भारतीय क्षेत्र पर नजर रख रहे थे. इन्हें ऐसी कक्षाओं में रखा गया था, जो चीन के पहले से मौजूद सैटेलाइट नेटवर्क को मजबूत करती हैं.
सैटेलाइट का यह बेहद सावधानी से तैयार किया गया नेटवर्क इस तरह काम करता है कि जब एक सैटेलाइट किसी खास क्षेत्र की पहुंच से बाहर जाता है, तो दूसरा उसकी जगह ले लेता है. इससे उस क्षेत्र पर लगातार नजर बनी रहती है. एक तरह से ये पाकिस्तानी सैटेलाइट चीन के पहले से बड़े सैटेलाइट नेटवर्क में मौजूद छोटे-छोटे अंतर को भर रहे हैं.
इन सैटेलाइट की कक्षाएं भी इस तरह चुनी जाती हैं कि जिन क्षेत्रों पर नजर रखनी है, उनकी निगरानी अलग-अलग कोणों, दूरी और स्पष्टता से की जा सके.
उदाहरण के लिए, PRSS-1 पाकिस्तान का पृथ्वी-निगरानी सैटेलाइट है. इसे जुलाई 2018 में PakTES-1A के साथ लॉन्च किया गया था. इसमें इलेक्ट्रो-ऑप्टिकल इमेजिंग उपकरण है, जो दो तरह की मुख्य तस्वीरें लेता है- पैनक्रोमैटिक और मल्टीस्पेक्ट्रल.
पैनक्रोमैटिक तस्वीरों में सही परिस्थितियों में करीब एक मीटर आकार की वस्तुओं या चीजों की पहचान की जा सकती है. मल्टीस्पेक्ट्रल तस्वीरें इलेक्ट्रोमैग्नेटिक स्पेक्ट्रम के अलग-अलग हिस्सों से जानकारी जुटाती हैं. इससे पेड़-पौधों, जमीन के इस्तेमाल के पैटर्न, जलाशयों और सतह की दूसरी विशेषताओं की पहचान करने में मदद मिलती है.
पाकिस्तान की अंतरिक्ष एजेंसी, स्पेस एंड अपर एटमॉस्फियर रिसर्च कमीशन (SUPARCO) के मुताबिक, PRSS-1 दुनिया में किसी भी जगह की दोबारा तस्वीर लेने की क्षमता रखता है. इसके लिए चार दिन का समय लगता है.
उदाहरण के तौर पर, अगर PRSS-1 सोमवार को दिल्ली की तस्वीर लेता है, तो करीब चार दिन बाद वह दिल्ली की एक और तस्वीर ले सकता है. वह दुनिया के दूसरे हिस्सों में मौजूद जगहों के लिए भी ऐसा कर सकता है. इससे वैज्ञानिकों और अधिकारियों को जमीन पर होने वाले बदलावों पर नजर रखने में मदद मिलती है.
PRSS-1 के सैटेलाइट से ली गई तस्वीरों को प्राप्त करने, प्रोसेस करने और सुरक्षित रखने के लिए इस्लामाबाद और कराची में ग्राउंड स्टेशन हैं.
2024 में लॉन्च किया गया PAKSAT-MM1 एक संचार सैटेलाइट है, जिसे चीन की मदद से विकसित किया गया है. इसे पाकिस्तान और आसपास के क्षेत्रों में दूरसंचार सेवाएं देने के लिए बनाया गया है.
इसमें चार फ्रीक्वेंसी बैंड में काम करने वाले उपकरण हैं. C-बैंड का इस्तेमाल टीवी प्रसारण और संचार के लिए, Ku-बैंड का इस्तेमाल प्रसारण, VSAT (बहुत छोटे एपर्चर टर्मिनल) कनेक्टिविटी और मोबाइल बैकहॉल के लिए, Ka-बैंड का इस्तेमाल हाई-स्पीड ब्रॉडबैंड और ज्यादा क्षमता वाले इंटरनेट के लिए और L-बैंड का इस्तेमाल सैटेलाइट आधारित ऑगमेंटेशन सेवाओं (SBAS) के लिए किया जाता है. ये सेवाएं पोजिशनिंग और नेविगेशन की सटीकता बेहतर कर सकती हैं.
दूसरी ओर, PRSC-EO1 पाकिस्तान के नए रिमोट-सेंसिंग सैटेलाइट कार्यक्रम का हिस्सा है. इसमें ऑप्टिकल सेंसर का इस्तेमाल करके पृथ्वी की सतह की तस्वीरें ली जाती हैं.
इन सभी सैटेलाइट्स को चीन से तकनीकी और लॉन्च संबंधी मदद मिली है.
2022 में पाकिस्तान की SUPARCO और चाइना ग्रेट वॉल इंडस्ट्री कॉरपोरेशन (CGWIC) ने कई सैटेलाइट लॉन्च करने के लिए एक समझौते पर हस्ताक्षर किए थे. CGWIC, चाइना एयरोस्पेस साइंस एंड टेक्नोलॉजी कॉरपोरेशन (CASC) की एक सहायक कंपनी है.
इस समझौते के तहत पाकिस्तान को लंबे समय तक चीन के रॉकेटों और उनसे जुड़ी तकनीकी सेवाओं का इस्तेमाल करके कई सैटेलाइट लॉन्च करने की व्यवस्था मिली.
जमीन पर मौजूद निगरानी व्यवस्था भी मददगार
दिगंतारा की अंतरिक्ष निगरानी रिपोर्ट में एशिया-पैसिफिक ग्राउंड-बेस्ड स्पेस ऑब्जेक्ट ऑब्जर्वेशन सिस्टम प्रोजेक्ट (APOSOS) में पाकिस्तान की बढ़ती भागीदारी को भी चिंता का विषय बताया गया है.
APOSOS एक बहुराष्ट्रीय अंतरिक्ष निगरानी नेटवर्क है, जिसे एशिया-पैसिफिक स्पेस कोऑपरेशन ऑर्गनाइजेशन (APSCO) के तहत शुरू किया गया था. इसके संचालन और डेटा प्रबंधन में चीन की अहम भूमिका है. यह परियोजना अंतरिक्ष में मौजूद वस्तुओं, जिनमें सैटेलाइट भी शामिल हैं, को देखने और उनकी गतिविधियों पर नजर रखने के लिए जमीन पर लगे ऑप्टिकल टेलीस्कोप का इस्तेमाल करती है.
दिलचस्प बात यह है कि APOSOS के पहले तीन निगरानी केंद्रों या स्टेशनों में से एक पाकिस्तान में बनाया गया था. हर केंद्र में 15 सेंटीमीटर एपर्चर वाला ऑप्टिकल टेलीस्कोप है. अलग-अलग केंद्रों से मिलने वाला निगरानी डेटा चीन की राजधानी बीजिंग में चाइनीज एकेडमी ऑफ साइंसेज की नेशनल एस्ट्रोनॉमिकल ऑब्जर्वेटरीज के केंद्रीय केंद्र में भेजा जाता है. बाकी दो स्टेशन पेरू और ईरान में हैं.
पाकिस्तान न सिर्फ APOSOS का सदस्य है, बल्कि उसके एक केंद्र की मेजबानी भी करता है. इससे उसे भौगोलिक फायदा मिला है और वह दुनिया के अलग-अलग हिस्सों से होने वाली निगरानी तक पहुंच बना सकता है. इस जानकारी का इस्तेमाल कक्षा में घूम रहे सैटेलाइटों पर नजर रखने के लिए किया जा सकता है, जिनमें भारत की अंतरिक्ष संपत्तियां भी शामिल हैं.
(इस रिपोर्ट को अंग्रेज़ी में पढ़ने के लिए यहां क्लिक करें)
यह भी पढ़ें: भारत विरोध से आगे बढ़ रहा नेपाल का राष्ट्रवाद, नौकरी-विकास नया एजेंडा

title: Modi Govt Tells HC Saurav Das's Passport 'Discrepancies' Can Affect His Citizenship - The Wire
description: Questions have been raised on the timing of the circular, which appear to have been issued more than seven years after the Cockroach Janata Party spokesperson's passport was issued to him.
author: The Wire Staff
content: New Delhi: The Narendra Modi government told the Delhi high court that a ‘look out circular’ was issued against youth activist Saurav Das on the night of November 22-23 – seemingly, hours before he was to depart for London – and that the alleged discrepancies in his passport could affect his citizenship.The spokesperson and co-convenor the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) was stopped at the Delhi airport as he was setting out for the United Kingdom, where he was due to deliver a lecture at the Oxford University.Additional Solicitor General Chetan Sharma told Justice Amit Mahajan that that on the intervening night of November 22-23, the Maharashtra Police has issued a look out circular against Das, LiveLaw reported.Das has to challenge the same before an appropriate forum, ASG Sharma said.When Senior Advocate Akhil Sibal, who represented Das, said that no information on this had been given to Das and asked for a copy of the circular, Sharma said it could not be furnished.Sibal said that pendency of a show cause notice does not mean that Das will be stopped from flying abroad which is a fundamental right.Questions have been raised on the timing of the circular, which appear to have been issued more than seven years after Das’s passport was issued to him.The Hindu had reported a day ago how the Regional Passport Office (RPO) in Chennai served a show-cause notice to Das, asking him to clarify the place of birth listed in his passport application. The notice said the office had received inputs that his application of August 8, 2019 contains “particulars (place of birth) furnished in it are incorrect” and that the passport issued on August 21, 2019 was “obtained by material suppression of facts.”ASG Sharma claimed in court today that an inquiry was initiated by the SSP of Pondicherry on August 20 on the veracity of Das’s place of birth, address and parentage as he had left column of his father’s name blank. Das’s parentage has been the topic of intense speculation in social media circles opposed to the CJP’s politics. However, as The Hindu‘s Vijaita Singh has pointed out, the RPO notice seeks a clarification on “place of birth” not the “father’s name”.Sharma also claimed that the issues with Das’s passport can have a bearing on his citizenship.“There are multiple discrepancies so an inquiry is done. Pursuant to the inquiry, on November 23, a show cause notice and advisory were issued at 7:32 PM and 7:56 PM… Assuming he travels abroad and he does not attend the meeting [regarding his passport] or he attends and a discrepancy is found which goes to the very root of the matter. It can also have a bearing on his citizenship,” Sharma said, according to Bar and Bench.In an extraordinary move, the Madras high court on October 30 issued notice on a plea seeking inquiry into his antecedents.Das and the CJP has noted on social media that copies of Das’s passport have been released by “BJP-aligned social media handles.”

title: Between April and June This Year, YouTube Took Down 34.4 Lakh Videos in India, Highest in the World - The Wire
description: YouTube was also the most targeted Google service in India in a separate dataset tracking removal requests from Indian courts and govt agencies, accounting for 3,399 of the 4,006 requests between Jan and June.
author: The Wire Staff
content: New Delhi: YouTube removed 34.4 lakh videos uploaded from India between April and June 2026, the highest takedowns from any country, increasing by 28% from the previous quarter. This accounted for nearly 31% of the 1.1 crore videos YouTube took down worldwide under its Community Guidelines, according to YouTube’s Community Guidelines Transparency Report.The US was next in the list at 12.4 lakh, followed by Indonesia at 9.2 lakh. Of the reasons for taking videos down, child safety accounted for 68.2% of removals globally, while 98.6% of the videos were taken down following flagging by automated systems.According to the Guidelines, YouTube identifies the country of upload using the uploader’s IP address and publishes the reasons for removal only at the global level.Several independent media houses and journalists, including The Wire, have faced these YouTube video takedowns in recent years.YouTube was also the most targeted Google service in India in a separate dataset tracking removal requests from Indian courts and govt agencies, accounting for 3,399 of the 4,006 requests between January and June 2026.These requests rose 61% from the preceding six months and covered 65,091 items, coming third on the list after Russia and South Korea. At least 2,870 requests – nearly 72% – were made by police, while courts accounted for 695 requests. Defamation was the most frequently cited reason, appearing in 2,130 requests. Further, Google removed 19,883 items for violating local laws. Meanwhile, it took no action on 19,402 items and said it lacked sufficient information to act on another 17,473.The latest figures come amid reports of heightened surveillance of social media posts and accounts. The Wire has previously reported on the Union home ministry’s Sahyog portal which has, since October 2024, allowed takedown orders to be issued by central ministries, state governments and police, constituting an expansive censorship mechanism.The use of the Sahyog portal has raised many questions especially as it seeks to bypass the limited blocking powers contained in Section 69A of the IT Act, which in 2015 the Supreme Court upheld in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India. While Google, Meta and ShareChat are among the companies that have complied with the government to use the portal, X refused to comply.According to PIB Fact Check, the Sahyog portal has flagged 2.98 lakh URLs for takedown between March and July 2026, and state governments accounted for over 82% of them. In November, an RTI reply reportedly showed that Gujarat Police had issued 5,358 takedown notices covering 1,90,633 URLs through the portal.

title: Is This a Recent Clip of RSS Members Attacking a Mosque in Ghaziabad? No!
description: Fact-Check: An old video is going viral on social media, falsely claiming to show RSS members armed with swords attacking Jamia Masjid in Ghaziabad.
author: Anika K
content:
A video is going viral on social media, claiming to show Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) members armed with swords attacking Jamia Masjid in Ghaziabad, Uttar Pradesh.
- One of the posts sharing the video is captioned, "RSS members in Ghaziabad armed with swords surrounded Jamia Masjid, Muslims trapped inside and several injured. Police response remains unclear, Ghaziabad police seems compromised?"
How did we find out?: We ran a reverse image search on the video using Google Lens, which led us to a post by journalist Rana Ayyub from 2022 with the same visuals.
- The post, uploaded on 12 April 2022, is captioned, "In BJP (Bharatiya Janata Party) ruled Madhya Pradesh, a massive crowd of Hindu radicals with swords, axe in front of a mosque, playing Islamophobic songs with police being spectators. Can the world ignore the silence of Narendra Modi. (sic)"
- We found another post carrying the same visuals, stating that it shows a Hindutva mob with swords in front of Shahi Jama Masjid in Sarangpur, Madhya Pradesh.
- Independent news platform Muslim Mirror published a report on 12 April 2022 about CPI(M) questioning the PM's silence over the communal incidents that happened during Ram Navami.
- The report shared a visual that matches the viral video with a caption that suggests it shows 'Hindu extremists threatening Muslims at a mosque in Sarangpur, Madhya Pradesh.'
- Based on the information, we were able to geolocate the area on Google Maps and confirm that it matches the visuals from the viral video.
- The Official account of the Ghaziabad Police Commissionerate commented under the viral claim that the information is misleading and false.
- They stated that no such incident has occurred within their jurisdiction.
Conclusion: The video is not recent. It dates back to 2022 and shows an incident where a Hindutva mob with swords surrounded a mosque in Sarangpur, Madhya Pradesh.
(Not convinced of a post or information you came across online and want it verified? Send us the details on WhatsApp at 9540511818 , or e-mail it to us at webqoof@thequint.com and we'll fact-check it for you. You can also read all our fact-checked stories here.)

title: Moratorium or Step-Up EMI: Which Costs a New Business Less?
description: Compare moratorium and step-up EMI options for business loans. Understand interest costs, repayment schedules and which structure may suit your cash flow.
author: Partner
content:
The first year of a business almost never matches the plan. Revenue shows up later than promised. Setup costs run over. And the owner is still hunting for customers when the first instalment falls due.
Lenders have seen this movie before, and many offer repayment designs meant to soften the opening months. Two are common. The first is a moratorium, a stretch at the start when you pay no principal. The other is a step-up EMI. Instalments start small and get bigger each year. Both help, under the right conditions. Neither is free. Which one costs a new business less? You have to look past the relief in month one and ask what the loan costs by the final instalment.
How does a moratorium work?
It's a window at the start of the loan, often three to twelve months, in which you don't repay principal. What happens to interest depends on the sanction terms. Some lenders collect interest monthly during the pause. Others don't collect it at all. They add it to the loan balance instead, which is called capitalisation.
That difference matters. Interest runs at the contracted business loan interest rate for the whole moratorium, paid or not. When it's added, you begin repaying with a balance bigger than what you borrowed, and every later month's interest is worked out on that bigger number. Add the fact that repayment now has to fit into a shorter stretch, and the instalment ends up higher than it would be on a standard schedule.
What the interest total hides is breathing room. A new business can use its cash in the months when cash is scarcest, for stock, hiring or marketing, without an instalment competing for the same money.
How does a step-up EMI work?
Same tenure, different shape. A step-up EMI (some lenders call it graduated repayment) raises the instalment in stages, usually once a year. Early payments are lower than a standard EMI would be. Later ones are higher. The bet is that the business will be earning more in years two and three, and that the payment can grow with it.
Smaller early instalments mean less principal gets repaid at first, so the balance stays high for longer, and interest is charged on that bigger balance. That's why a step-up loan costs more in total than a standard one. The extra is usually smaller than people fear. It's still real.
Then there's a risk a moratorium doesn't carry. The payments are scheduled to climb whether or not revenue does. Have a weak third year, and you still face an instalment well above the first.
Which one costs less overall?
Usually the gap isn't huge, but numbers help. Take a ₹30 lakh loan over five years at an assumed 14% a year, interest on the reducing balance, no fees. The moratorium lasts six months. The step-up plan raises the instalment by 10% a year.
Illustrative, but there's a pattern. Every relief option costs more than the standard schedule. Rank the three relief options and the moratorium with interest paid as it falls due wins on cost. The step-up plan is second. Capitalised interest makes the other moratorium the priciest. A business loan calculator will redo all this for your actual figures. Try different pause lengths and step percentages and see what changes.
But the lowest total isn't the only target. A new business that can't meet ₹69,805 in month three has no use for the cheapest schedule on paper.
Fitting the structure to the business
Take two owners. Meera is opening a café. She'll spend four months on interiors and equipment before the first customer walks in. A six-month moratorium makes sense for her, because for most of that time there's no income at all. Karan runs a small packaging unit that already sells every month, just not enough yet. He expects orders to grow as two new clients ramp up. A step-up schedule fits him: low payments now, higher ones as the orders arrive.
Swap them and trouble starts. Meera on a step-up plan would be paying instalments while the café is still a construction site. Karan on a moratorium would be sitting on a bigger balance he never needed to defer.
Both plans fail in the same way, though. If revenue doesn't show up as forecast, the heavier payments waiting in years two and three land on a business that can't carry them. Lenders usually ask for projections to justify the structure. Use them as a test of your own plan, not only as paperwork for the bank.
Before you sign
Here's a mistake that happens more than it should. An owner signs for a six-month moratorium, assumes the first six months are "free", and finds out later that interest was piling onto the balance the whole time. The first full instalment arrives, and it's a shock.
The fix is boring, but it works. Read the sanction letter and the Key Fact Statement before you sign anything. Lenders must provide that statement for retail and MSME term loans sanctioned on or after 1 October 2024. Find out what happens to moratorium interest. Find out how many instalments come after the pause.
And find the annual percentage rate once charges are in. Fixed or floating matters too, because a floating rate can change what you pay mid-loan. Pre-payment terms are worth a look as well. Since 1 January 2026, RBI directions have limited pre-payment charges on many floating-rate loans to micro and small enterprises. Conditions vary by type of lender, so check yours.
Final thoughts
Try a small test at your desk. Put the schedule in a spreadsheet, shave 20% off the revenue you expect, and watch the later instalments. Panic? Then ask the lender for something gentler.
So, moratorium or step-up? Neither beats a plain schedule on cost. The better question is which one your business can actually use. A moratorium shelters the first months. A step-up plan eases the first few years but leans on growth after. Compare total interest, test the later instalments against a gloomy forecast, and choose the one your cash flow can carry.

title: 5 New Frog Species Discovered in Arunachal Pradesh
description: Five new frog species have been discovered in Arunachal Pradesh after five years of research. Meet the tiny horned frogs, including India's first snail-eater.
author: Nishtha Kawrani
content:
Imagine walking through a forest in the Eastern Himalayas after sunset. The ground is damp, fallen leaves gather beneath towering trees, and the sounds of insects fill the night air. Somewhere among the undergrowth, a tiny frog sits almost unnoticed, blending into its surroundings.
In forests like these, some of nature's most fascinating discoveries are easy to miss. And a recent scientific study has brought five such hidden inhabitants into the spotlight.
Researchers from the University of Delhi and Harvard University have identified five previously unknown species of horned frogs in Arunachal Pradesh, following five years of fieldwork in the Eastern Himalayas. The discovery has also revealed something unusual about one of them: it feeds on land snails, making it the first known snail-eating frog recorded in India.
The research offers a fascinating glimpse into the biodiversity that India's forests continue to hold.
Meet the five newly discovered frogs
All five species belong to the genus Jingophrys, commonly known as diminutive horned frogs. These tiny to medium-sized amphibians are distinguished by horn-like projections of skin around their eyes, which give them their distinctive appearance.
The five newly identified species are:
- Tanii horned frog (Jingophrys taniitatii): Named after the Tanii tribe of Arunachal Pradesh, the name also incorporates 'tatii', the Apatani word for frogs and toads.
- Snail-eating horned frog (Jingophrys tanogogo): Named after the Apatani word for snails, this species has an especially unusual diet.
- Siang horned frog (Jingophrys siangensis): Named after the Siang region of Arunachal Pradesh, where it was discovered.
- Hrdy's horned frog (Jingophrys hrdy): Named in recognition of a long-time supporter of herpetological research and conservation biology at Harvard University.
- Wu-Larson's horned frog (Jingophrys wularsoni): Also named to recognise supporters of research and conservation at Harvard.
The names of three species acknowledge the region's local communities, language and geography, while the other two honour individuals who have supported scientific research.
A frog that eats snails, shells and all!
Among the five discoveries, Jingophrys tanogogo stands out for its unusual feeding behaviour.
While examining the species, researchers used advanced three-dimensional micro-CT imaging to study its internal anatomy. They found entire land snail shells inside the frog's gut.
This makes it the first known snail-eating frog recorded in India and the first documented instance of snail-eating behaviour in the family Megophryidae.
It is a remarkable finding because it expands what scientists know about the feeding habits of this group of amphibians.
Five years of research in challenging terrain
Identifying these frogs was no easy task. The research team included Sonali Garg, S D Biju, Tage Tajo, Radhakrishna Upadhyaya K, and James Hanken, who carried out extensive explorations across the Eastern Himalayas.
The researchers encountered temperatures as low as minus 4 degrees Celsius while navigating the mountainous terrain. Since these frogs are nocturnal, much of the fieldwork involved searching for them at night, often without a place to stay.
Local tribal communities also played an important role, sharing their knowledge of the region and supporting the researchers during their field explorations.
Beyond identifying new species, the team used DNA analysis to understand their evolutionary history. Their findings suggest that the diversification of these frogs coincided with the rise of the Himalayan mountain ranges and the intensification of the Asian monsoon millions of years ago.
Why these discoveries matter
The findings draw attention to the Eastern Himalayas as an important centre of biodiversity and evolution. The number of Jingophrys species recorded in India has increased seven-fold through this research, while the known diversity of the genus worldwide has more than doubled.
Yet, there is still much to learn. Some of these frogs are extremely secretive and appear in remote forests only during short breeding seasons. Further research will be needed to understand their ecology, behaviour and conservation needs.
For now, these five discoveries offer a reminder of how much life remains undocumented in India's forests. Sometimes, finding an entirely new species does not require looking beyond a distant wilderness. It simply requires looking a little closer at the world beneath our feet.

title: Deccan Mahseer Conservation: 10 Lakh Fish Released in Ujani
description: Maharashtra's Ujani Reservoir is receiving 10 lakh Deccan Mahseer fingerlings as part of a BNHS-led restoration initiative. Discover how 45 lakh native fish, aquatic plant restoration and invasive species removal aim to revive freshwater biodiversity.
author: Sriroopa Dutta
content:
A fish that had nearly disappeared from Maharashtra’s Ujani Reservoir decades ago is getting another chance to swim in its waters.
The Deccan Mahseer, once found in abundance in the Bhima River basin, had become increasingly rare by the 1990s as pollution, invasive fish species and destructive fishing practices took a toll on the reservoir’s native aquatic life.
Now, in October 2026, the Bombay Natural History Society (BNHS), with support from the Cipla Foundation and Tata Power, released 45 lakh (4.5 million) native fish fingerlings, including 10 lakh Deccan Mahseer (Tor khudree), popularly known as the ‘Tiger of the River’, alongside more than 21,000 aquatic plants into Maharashtra’s Ujani wetland near Bhigwan.
According to BNHS, the restoration programme responds to decades of ecological degradation in Ujani, where invasive fish, deteriorating water quality and destructive fishing practices have contributed to the decline of native species.
Why did the fish disappear?
Ujani Reservoir, formed by the Ujani Dam on the Bhima River, is an important freshwater ecosystem spanning parts of Pune, Solapur and Ahilyanagar districts.
Over the years, however, its aquatic biodiversity has come under pressure from invasive fish, pollution and fishing methods that capture even young fish before they can reproduce.
According to the BNHS, around 35 native fish species have become locally extinct in the reservoir, while another 40 are at risk of disappearing.
Invasive species such as suckermouth catfish, tilapia and African catfish have spread through its waters.
The BNHS-led restoration programme has also identified the impact of invasive aquatic vegetation, which can obstruct waterways, affect oxygen levels and compete with native plants.
The scale of the intervention reflects the extent of the problem. BNHS and local fisheries societies have removed more than 178 tonnes of invasive fish from the reservoir over the past year.
Additionally, nearly 6,500 tonnes of invasive vegetation, including water hyacinth, Ipomoea and Prosopis, have been cleared from approximately 2,000 hectares of the catchment area.
The October stocking programme included 10 lakh Indian major carps, comprising rohu, catla and mrigal, alongside more than 22 lakh fingerlings of other native species, including kavdas, nukta and bobari.
What makes the Deccan Mahseer important?
The Deccan Mahseer, also known as the blue-fin mahseer, is a freshwater fish belonging to the carp family. Its historic distribution includes the Krishna River system and its tributaries across parts of Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Telangana.
A 2019 scientific review, titled Mahseer (Tor spp.) Fishes of the World: Status, Challenges and Opportunities for Conservation, published in the journal Reviews in Fish Biology and Fisheries, examined the distribution, conservation status and threats facing mahseer species.
This is the Deccan Mahseer, revered as Lord Vithoba's beloved "Devmaasa". Found in Indrayani river, it is now endangered due to pollution & deadly water hyacinth growth on Anand Doha. A case of authorities' indifference😢 ##goodbadugly #saverivers Image: iNaturalist (1/2) https://t.co/5aTWC0UhK4
— Pune River Revival (@PuneRivers) May 22, 2024
The researchers identified the northern and central Western Ghats, particularly the Krishna River system, as the historical range of the Deccan Mahseer. Its tributaries include the Indrayani, Mula-Mutha, Koyna, Tungabhadra and Panchaganga.
The review also highlighted how artificial propagation and large-scale fish stocking since the 1970s expanded the species' distribution beyond its original range. Some introduced populations have even shown invasive characteristics, affecting native fish populations in other river systems.
Another study, published in Fisheries Research in 2011, examined the sustainability of Deccan Mahseer fisheries in the Western Ghats using catch data collected with the participation of local fishers.
Researchers Rajeev Raghavan, Anvar Ali, Neelesh Dahanukar and Alison Rosser studied six fishing sites and found that catches frequently included immature fish. Their assessment also indicated that exploitation rates exceeded sustainable levels at most of the sites studied.
A 10-year plan to bring the fish back
The Ujani restoration programme included a dedicated partnership between BNHS and Tata Power for the conservation of the Deccan Mahseer.
Under the arrangement, Tata Power has committed to supplying 10 lakh mahseer fingerlings over 10 years. The fish are being bred with support from its facility at Valvan in Lonavala.
According to BNHS's October 2026 conservation newsletter, Dr Unmesh Katwate, head of the BNHS Wetland Eco-Restoration Project, visited the facility on 9 October to assess the available fingerling stock and preparations for their release.
The newsletter also records a separate initial release of 8,000 fingerlings near Palasnath Temple in Ujani Reservoir on 22 October. The site was selected after considering its depth, water quality and habitat conditions.
The organisation is also working with local fisheries societies and government departments to encourage more sustainable fishing practices.
For Ujani, the return of the Deccan Mahseer is therefore part of a larger restoration exercise.
Whether the mahseer can establish a self-sustaining population in the reservoir will become clearer through continued monitoring in the coming years.

title: This 26-YO Pays Weavers Up to 35% More To Keep a 300-YO Tamil Nadu Craft Alive
description: Bhavani’s Jamakkalam weaving has a 300-year history, but its artisan numbers have fallen sharply. Discover how a young entrepreneur is opening new markets for this traditional Tamil Nadu craft.
author: Avantika Krishna
content:
Look closely at a Jamakkalam, and you might spot a smile. Hidden in its traditional stripes is a pattern called Pallu Mutham, meaning pearl-like teeth. A 26-year-old entrepreneur recognised its potential.
That entrepreneur is Varsha Sivakumar, who grew up in Bhavani, Tamil Nadu, surrounded by Jamakkalam looms. Today, through House of Jamakkalam, she works with 30 to 35 weavers to bring this traditional textile to new buyers.
Full story
But what exactly is Jamakkalam? This thick, striped cotton weave originated nearly 300 years ago in Bhavani and neighbouring Kumarapalayam. First woven by the Jangamar community, it became a familiar part of Tamil households.
Wedding trousseaus, temple courtyards and everyday homes once made up its market. The craft even received a Geographical Indication tag in 2005–06. Yet, recognition could not prevent its biggest problem: dwindling demand.
History of Jamakkalam
In two decades, Bhavani's active weaver population reportedly fell from 20,000 to around 3,000. Cooperative orders declined, finished pieces piled up unsold, and younger generations began choosing other occupations over weaving.
Varsha saw this differently after a classroom presentation in 2017. At the National Institute of Fashion Technology, a guest lecturer presented Jamakkalam as a craft worth studying. Varsha wondered why she had overlooked it.
She returned to the weaving clusters, documented techniques and listened to artisans. Her biggest discovery? The craft did not need an entirely new design language. Its existing patterns simply needed to reach contemporary buyers.
Read Varsha's story
Take the Smiling Pouch. Its distinctive appearance comes from Pallu Mutham, a traditional arrangement of stripes that already resembles a woven smile. Varsha did not invent the pattern. She recognised what generations had created.
There is another important change. House of Jamakkalam absorbs the higher cost of finer yarn, pays upfront and offers 30–35% premiums on complex orders, without penalising artisans for flawed pieces.
Instagram has also connected the weavers to overseas customers, particularly Sri Lankan Tamils commissioning Jamakkalams for weddings. Varsha's ambition is regular monthly orders for every loom. The 300-year-old weave is finding new homes, one order at a time.

title: Sonia Gandhi’s Memoir and the Politics of Right-Wing Abuse
description: Sonia Gandhi’s memoir challenges decades of right-wing abuse, from the RSS’s attacks on the Nehru-Gandhi family to the BJP’s politics of hate.
author: Aditya Sinha
content:
Page 139 of Sonia Gandhi’s staid memoir Belonging: A Journey of Love contains a startling sentence about her first baby, a boy who lived only a few hours: “In one of the right-wing opposition papers, an item appeared: ‘Indira Gandhi failed in her attempt to become the grandmother of a bastard child.’” This single sentence sums up the right-wing in all its avatars, of which the BJP is one: a movement whose lifeblood is nastiness, and that takes pride in its insensitivity.
Sonia’s second born was Rahul Gandhi, Leader of Opposition, who recently told an interviewer: “I saw my mother being brutalised, humiliated, abused and the type of absolute filth, even the most so-called honourable people, which has not been said, and she will not say (sic)... But the pettiness, the nastiness, the abuse of a woman. As a son, I found that to be completely disgusting.”
He was privately enraged, and who could blame him? His mother, sitting at that interview alongside Priyanka, tried to shrug it off. “You think, theek hai,” she phlegmatically said.
Rahul should dislike Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who has called Sonia several things over the years, especially when he was Chief Minister of Gujarat. He called her a “Jersey Cow” (and Rahul a “hybrid calf”) during the 2004 parliamentary election; he said shopkeepers in Gujarat would not hire her as a clerk (or Rahul as a driver); he called her a white-skinned lady (which is actually a good thing in many parts of racist India); he’s called her “pastaben”, “shetangana”, and “Surpanakha”; and after he became Prime Minister, at an election rally in 2018, he called her “Congress kividhwa”.
Modi’s negative tactics are not new for the right wing. After all, one of their leading lights, Nathuram Godse, murdered the Father of the Nation, M.K. (Mahatma) Gandhi. Godse was an intimate of RSS ideologue V.D. Savarkar, who begged the British for mercy and refused to participate in the 1942 Quit India movement. The newspaper Agrani, associated with Godse, referred to Gandhiji as “this Bania who is a traitor to his community”.
The RSS mocked the Mahatma throughout the 1940s: it too called him a traitor. “Mahatma Gandhi wanted to keep the Muslims in India so that the Congress may profit by their votes at the time of election,” the RSS’s most virulent ideologue, M.S. Gowalkar, said. “We have the means whereby such men can be silenced...”
And when Partition-time violence broke out between Hindus and Muslims, the RSS publication Organiser said about Gandhiji: “Nero fiddled when Rome burnt.” It also accused him, bizarrely, of “Islamic preaching and appeasement”.
Three days before Gandhiji was assassinated, Mahant Digvijaynath of the Hindu Mahasabha called him “anti-Hindu” and called for his expulsion to Pakistan, a solution that even today the BJP and its trolls advocate for dissidents and opponents.
It is not surprising, then, that when Indira Gandhi became Prime Minister in 1966, the socialist Ram Manohar Lohia called her Goongi Gudiya and the right wing followed suit, attacking her in the bitterest terms. The irony, of course, is that the right wing lionised her after she broke Pakistan into two with the 1971 war, calling her “a leader with guts”.
Nastiness and abuse are clearly part of the BJP’s genetic structure, but they would have remained a fringe political movement had it not been for the voting public. This same Indian public rejected “Maunmohan Singh”, as Modi called him, though in hindsight it is obvious that he ran the country so well that 20 years ago, Westerners expected India to rival China. Modi has proved the adage that authoritarians don’t know how to manage the economy.
From this, one can only infer that Indians, traditionally a self-loathing and cowardly lot, love nastiness. Nobody in India was alive during Mughal rule, yet all Hindus seem to think they were responsible for all of India’s ills. No one seems to acknowledge that India had one of the world’s leading GDPs before the British arrived. Yet malice and the politics of “othering” make many a Hindu feel empowered.
A politics of venom
It is telling that right-wing movements around the world rely on venom, the prime example being US President Donald Trump. He refers to “the Biden crime family” when his own family’s corruption is well-documented: son-in-law Jared Kushner is attempting to make billions from Gaza and from an end to the Russia-Ukraine war. Trump has seen his own net worth rise as President, from $2.3 billion in 2024 to $7.3 billion currently. His holding in Nvidia stock reportedly gained $15 million after he forced Nvidia’s board to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, despite serious national security concerns; this may be the straw that breaks the camel’s back and gets him impeached.
The cruelty of nationalist-populists is running out of steam globally, thanks to the cost of living, corruption, and war. Even Modi appears listless these days, doubling down on his strongman behaviour: refusing to release Umar Khalid from imprisonment, preventing Cockroach Janta Party leaders from going abroad, and still trying to push through, by hook or by crook, the Delimitation Bill that will skew Parliament. He is apparently trying to get the parliamentary numbers by roping in the opportunistic Sharad Pawar, a man who threw a tantrum over Sonia Gandhi’s foreign origins and was thrown out of the Congress party. (She’s been an Indian citizen since 1983.)
This columnist is still reading Sonia’s memoir, a tough task given its lack of literary quality. Perhaps as a person she is vanilla; her account is of a callow girl when she meets Rajiv Gandhi, marries him, and learns to live with Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. However, over the years Sonia has become something of an autodidact and a voracious reader. The memoir details many anecdotes that illustrate how her mother-in-law trusted her deeply and implicitly. This is enough to show how shallow Modi’s, and the RSS’s, abuse has been, how one-dimensional right-wing politics is, and it ought to put an end in any reader’s mind to any question of her “belonging”.
Aditya Sinha is a writer living on the outskirts of Delhi.
