title: Who qualifies as a journalist? Supreme Court raises question of media protection at protests
description: Court Asks Journalists' Unions To Submit Evidence Of Alleged Detention, Assault And Use Of Excessive Force During October Protests In Delhi
author: PTI
content:
The Supreme Court on Thursday said it would examine who qualifies as a journalist and whether accredited media persons are entitled to greater protection than self-proclaimed reporters while covering protests, bringing the distinction between professional journalists and social media content creators into focus.
A bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana observed that journalistic freedom must be balanced with the administration of public order and law.
The top court referred pleas concerning the alleged detention of seven journalists, assault and obstruction of media personnel covering protests in Delhi on October 10 and 11, 2026, to a high-powered committee headed by former Supreme Court judge R Subhash Reddy.
The bench asked the petitioners to submit relevant material before the five-member committee to establish whether the journalists were present at the protest sites and whether they were subjected to excessive force.
"You will go back to the committee which we have constituted to factually demonstrate whether your petitioners were, in fact, present there. If present, whether they were subjected to excessive force.
"Whether they were subjected to force and, if subjected, whether such force was excessive in relation to the proportion necessary for maintenance of public order," Justice Bagchi observed.
Justice Bagchi also said self-proclaimed journalists may not enjoy the same protection as accredited journalists.
The Kerala Union of Working Journalists and the Delhi Union of Journalists, in their pleas, alleged that journalists were forcibly removed from reporting sites, prevented from recording events and subjected to physical force.
According to the petitions, accredited journalists covering the protests were restrained, dragged away, manhandled and detained despite displaying their press credentials.
Senior advocate PV Dinesh, appearing for the petitioners, said seven journalists associated with established media organisations, and not reel-makers, had been taken into custody.
"The question is, when established journalists, who are recognised journalists, are covering events, can they be taken into custody?" the lawyer submitted.
The Delhi Police had earlier told the Supreme Court that social media "reel-makers" and influencers could not claim the same protections as journalists covering protests.
In an affidavit, the city police submitted that journalists "constitute a distinct category" from social media content creators who use cameras and microphones to make reels for commercial gain. It argued that the latter cannot automatically claim the protections afforded to the press while covering protests.

title: NCP (SP) chief Sharad Pawar admitted to Mumbai hospital, Supriya Sule shares update
description: The 85-year-old NCP (SP) Chief Was Recently Hospitalised In Pune For A Chest And Respiratory Infection
author: PTI
content:
NCP (SP) chief Sharad Pawar was admitted to Mumbai's Breach Candy Hospital on Thursday after he appeared to suffer from dehydration, his daughter and party working president Supriya Sule said.
Confirming his hospitalisation in a post on X, Sule said the 85-year-old veteran leader needed to slow down and reduce his travel.
“Admitting Baba (father) to Breach Candy hospital. Looks like dehydration. He needs to slow down and travel less. Baba just doesn’t listen. He loves his work too much. Thank you for your concern and good wishes,” she said.
Sule was attending a meeting called by NCP (SP) state president Shashikant Shinde at the party office in Nariman Point when she left midway to be with her father, party sources said.
This is not the first time the veteran leader has required hospital care in recent weeks. Pawar was recently admitted to Pune's Ruby Hall Clinic on November 2 after complaining of chest pain and cough. He was subsequently treated for a chest and respiratory infection.

title: Congress sues Meta and Centre over takedowns of Rahul Gandhi's posts ahead of state elections
description: The Party Argues That Meta's System Is Blocking Posts That Are Not 'exactly Identical' Copies Of Content Previously Ordered Removed, Including Birthday Greetings, Tributes And A Wedding Invitation Featuring Rahul
author: Reuters
content:
Congress has sued Meta and the federal government, saying that an automated content-removal system is blocking political posts and images of opposition leader Rahul Gandhi ahead of state elections.
The filing takes a week-long Congress campaign against Meta from the streets to the courtroom, and highlights Prime Minister Narendra Modi's automated takedown mandate, under which the Facebook and Instagram parent has restricted more than 5.4 million posts in the first half of 2026, up from about 70,000 in all of 2025.
In a court filing dated November 25 in the Delhi High Court, seen by Reuters, Congress' youth wing social media head Manu Jain said the rules have become "an instrument for the suppression of lawful political expression".
The case leaves Meta's operations in India, the company's biggest market, caught between a government whose rules strip platforms of legal protection if they fail to comply, and an opposition demanding it push back.
Congress argues that Meta's system is blocking posts that are not "exactly identical" copies of content previously ordered removed, including birthday greetings, tributes and a wedding invitation featuring Gandhi. Meta says it moderates content in India in accordance with the law.
Meta declined to comment. India's IT and home ministries, which are named as co-respondents in the lawsuit, did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.
Modi's government has maintained that such laws are essential to prevent the proliferation of illegal and harmful content online in a market of over 1.1 billion internet users.
Congress is urging the court to strike down the mandate for automated takedowns and also order Meta to restore the posts, as well as disclose blocking criteria.
Hearings are expected to begin in the coming days.
"Automated tools" mandate
India amended its IT rules in February to require large platforms to use technical measures "including automated tools" to find and block any post "exactly identical" to content already removed under a court order or a written government notice. Before that, platforms were asked only to "endeavour" to use such tools.
To comply, Meta has been restricting "100% identical copies of content, at scale and in country" under India's amended IT rules, its transparency report shows. The company says it is still testing and refining the system given the "unprecedented nature of this effort".
Meta says it is required to automatically restrict content at scale in only a "limited" number of countries, which it says explains the higher volumes.
Congress says the automated system is catching far more than exact duplicates. It is blocking birthday greetings, tributes and even a wedding invitation because they carry the photograph or name of opposition leader Gandhi, while "no order, notice, reason or even a 'legal request' has been disclosed," the petition said.
In one case cited in the petition, a November 8 birthday greeting from a youth wing leader to a colleague, showing the colleague standing beside Gandhi, was blocked the same day.
"We restricted access to this content through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements," the notice to the user read.
India is also one of seven markets, including Brazil and Hong Kong, where Meta does not tell users which government authority sought a restriction, citing "legal obligations and regulatory considerations", its transparency report shows. Elsewhere, it does so in most cases.
Wider offensive by Congress
The automated takedown system "distorts the level playing field" needed for a free and fair election, especially as party workers rely on Meta's platforms to reach voters ahead of state polls due early next year, the petition says.
Facebook and Instagram have 400 million and 515 million users respectively in India, according to research firm DataReportal.
Congress has put up large hoardings in several cities depicting Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg in the traditional uniform of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, the ideological parent of Modi's party.
Congress' youth wing has protested near Meta offices and clashed with police in several cities in recent days. The BJP has accused the protesters of vandalising the offices of private companies.
At a closed-door meeting this week reported by Reuters, Congress told Meta to push back against first-instance takedown orders, as Elon Musk's X has done, a source told Reuters. X is currently engaged in a legal battle against the government over its content-removal system.
Meta told Congress at the meeting that it is neutral towards all political parties and bound by local laws.

title: Anant Singh daughter wedding: The big fat nuptials of politician's daughter making headlines in India
description: Half a million people are estimated to have attended the wedding of Shivangi Singh, daughter of Anant Singh.
author: Geeta Pandey
content:
The big fat wedding of politician's daughter making headlines in India
- Published
The big fat wedding of a politician's daughter in the northern Indian state of Bihar has been making headlines for its over-the-top celebrations in the country's poorest state.
The wedding of Shivangi Singh, daughter of Anant Singh - a legislator in the state assembly - culminated on Wednesday after days of high-voltage celebrations that included plans for a horse race.
Hundreds of thousands of people, including the speaker of the state assembly and several prominent local and national politicians, attended Wednesday's ceremony at the family's ancestral home in Nadawa village, about 65km (40.4 miles) from the state capital, Patna.
At a press conference earlier this month, Singh - a five-time legislator from the Mokama constituency - had said "everyone has been invited... Not only from Bihar, but from across India and Pakistan too".
And reports from the ground yesterday said it seemed "everyone did turn up".
Media reports estimated that half a million people attended the wedding, turning the village into a large fairground and stalling traffic for several hours on the road leading to and from Patna.
Six helipads were set up in the village to receive important guests, and more than 150 dishes, including eight million pieces of sweets, were prepared by hundreds of cooks in temporary kitchens.
The biggest attraction at Wednesday's wedding was meant to be the horse race, for which 52 horses had been brought in. But it was postponed at the last minute because of the huge crowds that turned up to watch the event, with many spilling on to the racing ground.
A viral video from a pre-wedding practice session for the race showed tens of thousands of spectators gathered to watch, with several hundreds perched high above the ground over an electricity tower to get a better view.
Last week, the legislator shared a video on his X account of a white SUV costing between 1m-2m rupees (£8,300-£16,500; $10,800-$21,600), announcing that it would be the prize for the winner. A motorcycle and a scooter were promised as the second and third prizes.
The finale is now planned for Thursday.
The bride, Shivangi, a Delhi university graduate, arrived in a Land Cruiser while the groom Rishikesh Kumar, an MBA from Georgia State University in Atlanta, came in a convoy of 151 cars.
Anant Singh also made a grand entry, rising through the sunroof of an SUV as a sea of supporters pressed in around it, news channel NDTV reported. He "was arriving for his daughter's wedding, and he did it in a style that would upstage any groom".
Media reports said the groom received a car worth 23m rupees, as well as gold and silver, from the bride's family, although Singh has not revealed how much the wedding cost.
The scale of the wedding is not comparable to the 2024 festivities India saw during the marriage of Anant Ambani, the youngest son of Asia's richest man Mukesh Ambani.
But the extravagant wedding in Bihar, a state where one in every three citizen is counted as multidimensionally poor, has been dubbed "a royal wedding" and become a huge talking point.
One political rival - Neeraj Kumar, a Bihar legislative council member - has also called on the investigative agencies to look into where the money for the wedding came from.
The interest in the wedding, though, has less to do with the couple than with the father of the bride, a controversial politician.
Popularly known as "Chhote Sarkar" (Hindi for younger lord or mini government), Singh is often described as a "bahubali" - a word that translates as strongman and is used to describe powerful local leaders in many parts of India.
In videos on his social media accounts, Singh is often seen twirling and turning up the ends of his moustache - a gesture of pride and masculinity.
Local people say he travels in a convoy of 20-25 cars and a local journalist said that, on one occasion, Singh chased away tax officials who visited him by turning up with live snakes wrapped around his neck.
Singh first won Mokama in 2005 and has retained it in subsequent elections in 2010, 2015, 2020 and 2025.
According to the affidavit he submitted to the Election Commission before last year's polls, he described himself as a social worker who has businesses and agricultural land.
He declared that his combined wealth with his wife added up to 1bn rupees and that there were more than two dozen criminal cases pending against him. In some of these cases, he's accused of serious crimes such as murder, attempt to murder, extortion and rioting.
According to reports, he's done several stints in prison, external, but the only time he was not a legislator in the past two decades was in 2022 when he was convicted and sentenced for 10 years in jail. It was in a case from 2019 when arms and ammunition, including an AK-47 assault rifle, were seized from his home.
The state assembly disqualified him, but he remained on bail and appealed against the court order. He contested and won last year's election and returned to the assembly.
He's also been named as the main suspect in a murder case during last year's election and the Supreme Court has ordered him to surrender by 1st December. Singh, who spent three months in jail in connection with the case, has said in interviews that he would abide by the court order.

title: Lahori Zeera, Campa Jeera: Cumin-laced fizzy sodas are giving the cola giants a tough fight in India
description: Cumin-laced sodas are capturing a bigger market share in India as demand for homegrown flavours goes up.
author: Nikhil Inamdar
content:
Cumin-laced fizzy sodas are giving cola giants a tough fight in India
- Published
It began as an impromptu kitchen experiment.
Saurabh Munjal, Nikhil Doda and Saurabh Bhutna - three cousins in India's north-western Punjab state - were messing about at home post dinner one evening, when Doda casually brewed up a tangy cumin-flavoured fizzy soda using regular pantry ingredients.
They enjoyed its earthy, piquant taste so much that they decided to explore options to sell it commercially.
Cumin-laced sodas had always been sold at street-side stalls in India, but it was a broken market of local companies. Not many had built a carbonated beverage brand around the flavour.
The trio persuaded their families to invest some capital and launched Lahori Zeera in 2017. Zeera is the Hindi name for cumin.
Almost a decade on, the drink has become a bit of a sensation in India, challenging the entrenched monopoly of global cola giants, especially in the all-important mass-market ten-rupee ($0.11; £0.078) beverage category - it will close this year with revenues of $115-120m.
Its popularity reflects a growing consumer preference for distinctly Indian flavours and drinks perceived to be more healthy, say analysts.
Lahori Zeera is one of several cumin-flavoured soda brands that have mushroomed across the country over the past decade.
There's Jeeru from Mumbai-based Xotik Frujus, Campa Jeera from billionaire Mukesh Ambani-owned Campa Cola and at least half-a-dozen other variants from regional players including Fizz Jeera Masala from House of Bindu.
Bindu launched their cumin soda nearly 25 years ago, but sales were flat until some years ago, according to Megha Shankar, a director with the company.
"Now it is the fastest growing category among carbonated beverages," Shankar told the BBC. "Its contribution to our revenues has doubled from 20% to 40% in the last five years."
Soaring demand for the product has pushed House of Bindu to widen its footprint across the country, after being largely based in southern India for over two decades.
Parle Agro, external, one of India's oldest consumer brands, also rolled out its own cumin soda brand Dhishoom nationally last year after exclusively selling it in rural markets since 2012.
Online orders for these fizzy drinks, meanwhile, were up 900% this summer according to a report from one of India's online delivery companies.
The cumin frenzy is reshaping India's non-alcoholic beverages market, which was valued at $32 billion in 2024 and projected to double by 2033.
According to a report from Kotak Mutual Fund earlier this year, Lahori Zeera, Campa and other smaller challengers - now dubbed as India's "ethnic beverages market" - collectively doubled their share of India's carbonated soft-drinks market to around 15% by September last year, while the combined market share of Coca-Cola and PepsiCo fell from roughly 93% to 85%.
"This is a "Jio moment" for beverages. Just as telecom incumbents bled market share when data prices crashed, beverage incumbents are bleeding volume," the Kotak report said, drawing an analogy to the disruption caused by the entry of Reliance-owned Jio Telecom in India's telecoms market in 2016.
"In global markets, established duopolies rarely lose more than 1-2% share annually; an 8% swing in less than a year is a structural disruption."
Saurabh Munjal, CEO of Archian Foods which manufactures Lahori Zeera, told the BBC that the company has "always been in a situation where we are sold out each year. We've doubled our capacity to 1.2 million bottles per day last year and are still unable to meet demand".
For decades, the colas have had a dominant presence in India, appealing to the aspirational part of the population as lifestyle products that were cool to consume.
With millions of dollars in marketing budgets splashed out on billboards, Bollywood stars and cricket championships, they sold a very western idea of hydration to India, says Munjal.
But home-grown brands are now mounting a serious challenge with a combination of smart distribution, attractive pricing and a turn towards nostalgic Indian flavours such as cumin, raw mango, kokum fruit and tamarind.
Munjal says that for long, there has been a tendency among consumer brands in India to either westernise Indian products or "Indianise" western products. But with Lahori Zeera, which uses the tagline "apna desi thanda", meaning India's own cold drink, his desire is to change that.
Shankar says her brand has also recently launched a zero-sugar version of their cumin soda to capture the growing market for healthier non-cola drinks.
This success notwithstanding, sustaining this winning trajectory will not be easy for these ethnic beverage brands, say analysts. The very factors that propelled their rise could also limit growth.
"The million-dollar question is how big can the cumin-flavoured drink market become. And I suspect it won't become as big as the colas," Rajiv Agarwal, a professor at Mumbai-based SP Jain Institute of Management, who advises family businesses on strategies to succeed against multi-national corporations, told the BBC.
The 10-rupee price point, which accounts for the bulk of sales volumes in India's cumin-flavoured carbonated drinks market, is another double-edged sword.
While it has driven up sales, the soaring cost of plastic, packaging, sugar and other raw material amid the global energy shock could start to hit margins, which are already very thin.
Raising prices, meanwhile, could affect volumes, forcing brands to further reduce bottle sizes, something the cola companies had resorted to a few years ago.
Then there is always the threat of bigger, deep-pocketed players coming in to disrupt the category.
"Competition is extremely aggressive," says Agarwal. And the established global players are better organised in terms of systems, processes, distribution channels and bottling arrangements.
Coca Cola, which had acquired the cumin-flavoured Rimzim brand in the 1990s, is strengthening its play in this category and reportedly doubled production last year.
But the challenges haven't deterred the ambitions of the homegrown players.
"Indian flavours need to find a global spotlight," says Munjal, who is looking to tap the global market in the coming years.
"For generations, we've grown up drinking colas of the world, but I hope the next generations will drink the zeeras of India."

title: Landeed, Fractal Analytics: The AI start-ups fixing India's broken roads and messy land records
description: From legal-tech to healthcare, dozens of Indian AI start-ups are solving uniquely Indian challenges.
author: Nikhil Inamdar
content:
The AI start-ups fixing India's broken roads and messy land records
- Published
In 2020, Sanjay Mandava flew down from Chicago to Chennai in southern India to resolve a personal land dispute.
Over the next few months, he was running around between government offices to access a dozen records that would conclusively prove that the property belonged to his family.
Just a sale deed dating back to when his parents bought the land was not enough. Authorities asked him to produce a string of other documents.
Frustrated by the experience, he built Landeed - an AI-led digital platform that enables users to aggregate fragmented, multi-source land-records, verify titles and conduct legal checks at the click of a few buttons, across 24 states in India.
He's solving a problem that is uniquely Indian.
"In the US or UK, when you purchase a property, the government verifies ownership. In India by contrast, we follow presumptive titling - the buyer is responsible for establishing ownership. A sale deed merely records the transaction - multiple other documents may be needed to prove title," Mandava told the BBC.
These include building certificates, property tax receipts and land survey maps among others.
The system is rife for misuse - property disputes account for a bulk of civil litigation cases in the country where some 80% of household wealth is held in real estate.
Landeed has mapped large swathes of India using geo-spatial technology and data from state land revenue departments, registration offices, survey records and municipal databases.
Using this, it has linked registered properties to their official land identification and survey numbers and ownership records.
An additional AI-layer can read these titles, extract information and spot inconsistencies within minutes - a process that takes lawyers and brokers several days.
With the largest repository of title data in the country, consisting of 1.8 billion documents, the app is now used by millions of individual and enterprise customers while doing real estate transactions.
The app is among a burgeoning list of Indian start-ups trying to address some of India's most complex challenges in sectors ranging from legal-tech to healthcare, infrastructure, education and agriculture using AI.
Unlike the US and China which have a global dominance in building frontier language models like ChatGPT, India's AI revolution is happening downstream in data centre infrastructure and consumer applications rather than in research.
Start-ups are solving issues for everything from pothole detection to tribal language translation to assisting overworked public-health professionals with medical tasks - often working with highly fragmented, multilingual datasets in extremely cost sensitive industries.
Bengaluru-based YouTube teacher Gaurav Sen's AI app detects potholes using a dash-cam, satellite-based navigation and an AI vision model to analyse images.
It then identifies civic officials responsible for fixing them and sends them this data. He got viral attention recently given how widespread the menace of potholes is across India's urban sprawls.
On last count, there are at least half a dozen other similar offerings that map and report road damage to authorities across the country.
"A municipal corporation can take the app and use it on public buses and taxis, to access real-time, updated data on road conditions," Sen told the BBC.
In Mumbai on India's western coast, Fractal Analytics - among the few Indian listed AI companies - has deployed its AI tool "Vaidya" in hospitals run by the local civic authority.
The app allows citizens to receive AI-generated, simplified summaries of their lab reports in multiple languages, identify nearby healthcare facilities based on their needs and gives doctors AI-guided pre-consultation support such as medical history and medication details of patients.
It also provides hospital administrators with a public health dashboard based on aggregated, anonymous insights from lab reports accessed through its tie-up with municipal hospitals, giving them crucial visibility into emerging infections or other disease trends.
This boom has led to a surge in funding for AI start-ups - up 265% year-on-year according to Inc42, external, a start-up information platform. They raised over $1bn in the first nine months of this year amid a relatively muted fundraising environment for the broader ecosystem.
Yet, these companies face an uphill task in commercialising their ideas and taking them beyond pilot.
"The cost of building in India is sometimes much higher than what Indian customers are willing to pay," Fractal's co-founder Srikanth Velamakanni told the BBC at his sprawling office overlooking Mumbai's film city.
"The computing power needed to run an AI model is the same whether it is built in India or the US - but American customers have a far bigger paying capacity than those here."
Indian AI founders are also being forced to build around scarcity, with availability of high quality chips at the right scale and price, a major impediment for many.
"I believe I am building one of the most impactful things for this country," says Mandava.
"But I am starved for GPUs [chips that perform millions of calculations and help train AI models]. I have a hellish time trying to acquire them," he says.
The country has promised its start-ups 38,000 GPUs through its government-led AI mission, external, but demand for this compute power is far greater than supply.
Cumbersome regulation and bureaucracy are other major challenges.
Without these fundamental issues being addressed, there's a risk that Indian AI companies will build shallow solutions that a next generation of founders will immediately make redundant, say experts.
"Someone like a Google will probably laugh if I tell them of my pilot. To make it sustainable and hard to replicate, it will have to be much more sophisticated," says Sen, displaying a self-awareness of where his product currently stands.
From a lack of experienced talent to the struggle to turn successful pilots into recurring government contracts to heavy dependence on expensive foreign technology, Indian founders are powering through many odds.
"We can still do it. We don't want protection, but propel us, give us the weapons to compete against the best," Mandava says, when asked what he wants from policymakers.
"To quote Jay-Z - I can't help the poor if I'm one of them," he adds.
Follow BBC News India on Instagram, external, YouTube,, external X, external and Facebook, external.

title: Rahul’s Israel reset lasts a week. Congress goes back to calling Gaza war ‘genocide’
description: Days after Rahul Gandhi backed strong India-Israel ties while condemning both sides, Congress' Pawan Khera returned to the party's earlier line, calling Israel's actions in Gaza 'genocide'.
author: Apoorva Mandhani
content:
New Delhi: Days after Congress leader Rahul Gandhi’s remarks in Chicago on India-Israel relations seemed to signal a slight shift in his party’s stand, the Congress on Wednesday appeared to revert to the original position as it spoke of “genocide in Gaza”.
Speaking at the Chicago University last week, Rahul had asserted that India should maintain strong ties with Israel, including defence cooperation, while condemning both the 7 October Hamas attacks and Israel’s actions in Gaza. This approach was a marked shift in the party’s approach.
Only in June this year, Congress leader Sonia Gandhi had castigated the Modi government for its “stony silence” and “inaction” on Israel’s “Gaza genocide”. Rahul, skipping any mention of ‘genocide’, had drawn criticism from the Left and also a section of the Left-liberal intelligentsia.
However, in what seems like another shift in the party’s stance, Congress spokesperson Pawan Khera Wednesday once again called Israel’s military actions in Palestine “genocide”, and urged India to “stand firmly for the Palestinian people’s right to their land, self-government and dignity”.
Khera was responding to the Indian government giving USD 2.5 million to the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA), as a part of its annual contribution of USD 5 million for the year 2026-27.
He asserted that there was “no need whatsoever to congratulate the BJP government” on this grant, saying, “Given Israel’s genocide in Gaza, no amount of aid can ever be enough to rebuild what has been lost”. He then asserted that India “must reiterate a clear and unequivocal position in support of negotiations for a sovereign, independent, viable and secure State of Palestine, coexisting in peace with Israel.”
“No amount of money or financial assistance can compensate for the denial of dignity, freedom and fundamental rights,” he wrote in a post on X.
There is no need whatsoever to congratulate the BJP Government for committing $2.5 million to Palestinian refugees. Given Israel’s genocide in Gaza, no amount of aid can ever be enough to rebuild what has been lost.
One can only hope that this Government, and governments across… https://t.co/5SJavniahj
— Pawan Khera 🇮🇳 ಪವನ್ ಖೇರಾ (@Pawankhera) November 25, 2026
‘All for relationship with Israel’
Khera’s remarks come days after Rahul Gandhi’s comments in Chicago attracted widespread criticism.
“We have a good relationship with Israel. We buy weapons from Israel, but with all due respect, we are bigger than Israel. We are a country of 1.5 billion people, and our foreign policy should be based on what’s good for us and not what’s good for someone else. I condemn what happened in October. It was absolutely horrible, should never have happened. Killing of innocent people is absolutely wrong, but I also condemn what Israel has done in Gaza. And one cannot get away from both the wrongs,” Rahul said.
“As far as the relationship with Israel goes, there are strategic reasons why we have a relationship with them, and why we buy weapons from them. Frankly, we have to buy the best weapons and they happen to produce very good weapons. I’m fully for having a good relationship with Israel, but India has to play on the global stage and show its weight on the global stage. And that shouldn’t be hampered by anybody, whether that is Israel, US, Russia or China,” Rahul added.
Reacting to Rahul’s remarks, former Kerala chief minister Pinarayi Vijayan wrote on social media platform X that Rahul’s remarks “expose the Congress party’s glaring hypocrisy on Palestine”.
“At a time when Gaza is witnessing one of the most devastating genocides of our time, with thousands of innocent children among its victims, he openly advocates stronger ties with Israel and arms purchases from a state responsible for their slaughter. His attempt to strike a diplomatic balancing act in the face of this catastrophe is indefensible,” he wrote.
Vijayan also alleged that Rahul’s position undermines the legacy left behind by Jawaharlal Nehru, whose foreign policy, he said, “stood firmly against imperialism and in solidarity with the Palestinian struggle”.
CPI(ML) general secretary Dipankar Bhattacharya had also lashed out on Facebook, calling Israel a “genocidal regime”, and asserting that there can be no independent foreign policy of India which advocates strong strategic ties with Israel.
Sharing an article on Rahul’s statement, Bhattacharya wrote, “India’s existing strategic relationship with Israel, the growing Adani-led corporate trade including arms supply, and sinister use of Israel’s surveillance technology and security model has already done enough damage to India’s international image, foreign policy credibility and above all the health of our own internal democracy and governance. We must end it sooner rather than later and must not rationalise it in the name of India’s defence or national security needs.”
(Edited by Viny Mishra)

title: BJP mobilises Sri Rama Sene as Karnataka weighs repeal of anti-conversion, cow slaughter laws
description: The Karnataka Protection of Right to Freedom of Religion Act, 2022, and Karnataka Prevention of Slaughter and Preservation of Cattle Act, 2020 was passed by the erstwhile BJP govt.
author: Sharan Poovanna
content:
Bengaluru: The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), the principal opposition party in Karnataka, met with Sri Ram Sene controversial head Pramod Muthalik to shore up support to oppose the likelihood of D.K. Shivakumar-led government from repealing the anti-cattle slaughter and anti-conversion laws.
Although it is not official yet, the state government has indicated the possibility of repealing the Karnataka Protection of Right to Freedom of Religion Act, 2022, and Karnataka Prevention of Slaughter and Preservation of Cattle Act, 2020 at the winter session of the state legislature in Belagavi.
“I met with Sri Pramod Muthalik, founder of Sri Ram Sene, in Bengaluru today, and we discussed several issues. We held extensive discussions on several matters concerning the protection of the interests of the Hindu community in the state, including the designs of this anti-Hindu Congress government, which is seeking to repeal the law banning cow slaughter,” BJP state chief B.Y. Vijayendra said in a post on X.
Several pro-Hindu groups, including Muthalik-led Sri Ram Sene, Vishwa Hindu Parishad (VHP) and others have also threatened protests if the government attempts to repeal the legislation.
The Congress party, which enjoys the backing of minority groups like Christians and Muslims, is under pressure to repeal the two controversial BJP-era laws.
In October, Christian and Muslim spiritual and community leaders demanded the Congress government fulfil its 2023 poll promises of repealing contentious legislations that targeted specific minority and oppressed communities.
Rev. Peter Machado, the Archbishop of Bengaluru, and Mohammed Yahya Damudi, the convener of the Karnataka Rajya Muslim Okkoota (KRMO), told reporters the ruling party should repeal both the laws as well as the immediate implementation of the proposed Karnataka Hate Speech and Hate Crimes (Prevention) Bill, 2025.
Shivakumar has been under pressure to make good on the 2023 poll promises that helped the Congress storm to power with a clear majority. However, the Congress government–both under Siddaramaiah and Shivakumar–have not been able to withdraw the two contentious legislations despite the administration enjoying three years in power.
The hate speech Bill was sent from Karnataka’s Lok Bhavan to President Droupadi Murmu for her consideration on the grounds that the Bill was flawed. All three bills were passed by the previous BJP government between 2019 and 2022.
The Congress had earlier claimed that it lacked a clear majority in the Upper House of the state legislature which impeded the smooth passage or withdrawal of bills. In October, the BJP-led National Democratic Alliance (NDA) managed to retain three and wrest control of another MLC seat in the elections.
The Congress now has 37 members in the Karnataka Legislative Council as against 24 of the BJP and seven of the Janata Dal (Secular). There are five vacant seats and one Independent in the 75-member house. By this count, the NDA has 31 seats in total.
Despite the party-wise tally, minority groups have intensified their demands seeking a repeal of the contentious laws as delays have been adding to the brewing discontentment among the core support base of the Congress.
This includes anger from the Muslim community over the denial of MLA tickets in the Davangere by-elections and follow-up action against two prominent community leaders, including the removal of Nasser Ahmed as the chief minister’s political secretary.
(Edited by Tony Rai)

title: Instagram ‘Auto-Blocking’ Rahul Gandhi Posts: Youth Congress Moves Delhi HC, Meta Meets Leaders - The Wire
description: The plea alleges that posts by the IYC and its members on Instagram and Facebook are being made unavailable in India without notice, reasons or a hearing. It suspects Meta's automated system treats Rahul Gandhi's name and picture as keywords.
author: The Wire Staff
content: New Delhi: The Indian Youth Congress (IYC) has moved the Delhi high court on Thursday (November 26) claiming that Instagram is automatically restricting posts that carry the name or photograph of Leader of Opposition (LoP) in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi. The petition challenges the constitutional validity of Rule 4(4) of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021.The plea filed by IYC national secretary and head of its social media department Manu Jain says that posts by the IYC and its members, workers and office-bearers on Instagram and Facebook are being made unavailable in India without notice, reasons or a hearing. It suspects Meta’s automated system treats Rahul Gandhi’s name and picture as keywords.The posts it lists as restricted between September 29 and November 23 include photographs of party workers with him, a wedding invitation sent to him, birthday wishes, tributes to former Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi and a post on his University of Chicago lecture. One such post, on his interaction with students and faculty there, was blocked on November 19 and restored the same day, Live Law reported.“The petitioner apprehends that the automated tool has been made to treat the name and the image of Shri Rahul Gandhi as a keyword, so that any post carrying them is blocked automatically. The notices also warn that the account “could be restricted in India” if such content is shared again, and each block is counted against the account as if it were a breach of the Community Standards of Respondent No. 3. Many accounts of ordinary citizens are now close to permanent suspension,” the plea states, as per the Live Law report.Meta’s notices say the content was restricted “through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements” under the IT Rules. Yet no blocking order, legal request or reasons have been shown to the IYC or the affected users, the petition says.The IYC is contesting Rule 4(4), as amended in February, to the extent it makes significant social media intermediaries use automated tools to proactively restrict information “exactly identical in content” to material already removed under Rule 3(1)(d).It argues this exceeds the IT Act, 2000 and violates Articles 14, 19(1)(a), 19(1)(c) and 21 of the constitution. The safeguards of Section 69A, which the Supreme Court relied on in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, are missing here, it adds. The party clarifies that it does not object to automated removal of content showing rape or child sexual abuse, the report added.The plea mentions two advisories, dated October 8 and 10, from the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, which asked intermediaries to exercise greater diligence. It says these are being enforced alongside the automated blocking.It seeks disclosure of any orders or requests and of the keywords or criteria used, a declaration that Rule 4(4) is unconstitutional to that extent, quashing of both advisories, restoration of the posts, and a direction to Meta not to restrict content or accounts merely because they feature Rahul Gandhi.Meta meets CongressSeparately, Meta representatives have met Congress functionaries, including the head of its social media department, on Tuesday (November 24) amid IYC protests over alleged bias in content moderation and suspended Instagram accounts. Neither side has commented officially. As per a report published in The Hindu, Congress sources said that the Delhi meeting was held at Meta’s request.The IYC has protested outside Meta offices in Hyderabad, Mumbai and Gurugram, alleging that Congress leaders’ political content is curbed while similar posts by Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) leaders stay up.Meta was represented by Aman Jain and Natasha Jog, and Supriya Shrinate attended for the Congress, according to the report. Meta reportedly said most of its takedowns concerned AI-generated content, but Shrinate is said to have countered that similar AI content from the BJP targeting Congress leaders was not being removed.The Congress leader also reportedly pointed out that the protests began after the Instagram handles of IYC chief Uday Bhanu Chhib and All India Congress Committee (AICC) in-charge for the IYC, Manish Sharma, were blocked. IYC sources told TH that the handles have since been restored.

title: Union Govt Argues FRA Need Not Be Pursued in Andaman & Nicobar, But That’s Wrong, Experts Say - The Wire
description: The Union government has argued that the Forest Rights Act need not be implemented in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, but experts say the law applies and that the rights of indigenous communities cannot be bypassed in the name of development.
author: Aathira Perinchery
content: Bengaluru: The Calcutta high court has deferred the final hearing regarding allegations pertaining to forest rights violations linked to the union government’s infrastructure projects proposed on the Great Nicobar Island in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, per a report by the Hindu.The final hearing will now be heard on January 12, 2027, because the Union government sought time to file more information, including an additional affidavit. On November 25, at the hearing in the Calcutta HC, the government argued that the Forest Rights Act, 2006, (FRA) does not need to be implemented in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, the Hindu reported.However, experts told The Wire that both the FRA and the Aboriginal Tribes Regulations, 1956, are applicable in the islands, and that any government claim suggesting otherwise is wrong.Petitions regarding violation of rights under FRAThe Calcutta high court has been hearing a batch of petitions alleging violations of rights under the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006, that will come about due to the Rs 92,000 crore-worth projects on Great Nicobar island. These include an international transshipment container terminal, a greenfield airport, a township, a power plant and linked tourism facilities.Also read: Gram Sabha that Cleared Great Nicobar Island Project Didn’t Meet 50% QuorumThis project will mean felling rainforest trees on 130 square kilometres of forest land. Social scientists have also raised concerns that diverting some of this land from the tribal reserve will affect the Shompen and Nicobarese indigenous communities who live on the island. The Shompen are listed as a Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group (PVTG), and still choose to remain in low contact with outsiders.The rights of both communities are recognised under regulations including the FRA and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands (Protection of Aboriginal Tribes) Regulation.Activists, including a former official of the Union tribal and environment ministries, have filed petitions alleging that the communities’ rights under the FRA have been violated in the process of clearing the project, including in the way the gram sabha consent (which is mandatory under the FRA) was obtained.In August 2025, the Tribal Council of Little and Great Nicobar had highlighted these FRA violations in a letter to Jual Oram, the Union minister for tribal affairs, alleging that the island administration had made a false representation to the Union government in August 2022 by claiming that processes under the FRA had been completed on the Islands when it had not been done.On November 25 at the Calcutta high court, however, the Union government argued that the FRA is not implemented in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, the Hindu reported. This, the government claimed, was because the Protection of Aboriginal Tribes Regulations, 1956, was already operational there.The petitioners rebutted by noting that the Islands administration had already issued a certificate claiming that FRA rights have been settled, and that this is what was being challenged.On Wednesday, the Additional Solicitor General of India Vikramjit Banerjee also submitted that the Union government wanted to once again raise preliminary objections on the maintainability of some of the petitions, and that it wanted to submit one more affidavit pertaining to tribal rights, with some additional documents.‘They are lying’The FRA already recognised and vested forest rights with the communities when the FRA was enacted, commented Bijor C.R., who examines natural resource conflicts and governance issues.“The FRA provides for a procedure to determine, verify, and approve the rights so recognised and vested, examine them by the SDLC [Sub-Divisional Level Committee, which examines forest rights claims passed by gram sabhas], recognise, record and issue titles. So their rights are already recognised and vested. In the case of A&N Islands, in addition, their rights are already recognised and vested through Aboriginal Tribes Regulations, 1956,” he told The Wire.Moreover, the Union ministry of tribal affairs had clarified that in such cases, a proactive recognition of these recognised rights under FRA is also to be done, Bijoy added. This was not done. Per the ministry, in cases where the rights of people have been already documented (such as in Mizoram), Collectors may give a certificate to this effect to substantiate that no further procedure with regard to FRA is required. But this too has not been carried out, he pointed out.“Therefore, it is not only a violation of Aboriginal Tribes Regulations, 1956 but also the FRA,” he told The Wire.Also read: ‘Flagrant Violations’ of Tribal Rights in Great Nicobar Projects: Jairam Ramesh Writes to Minister Jual OramThe ministry also states that in all cases where forest rights holders are being displaced, they have to be adequately compensated through proper livelihood plans in accordance with the provision of Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013. This too has not been done and has been violated,” he told The Wire.“So when they say that the rights have been settled, they are lying,” he said‘Brazen callousness’: Jairam RameshThe Modi government came with a clear strategy to further stall and delay the high court proceedings, even after assuring the Supreme Court that it would cooperate to have the hearings completed as scheduled and having them argued yesterday itself, commented former environment minister and senior Congress leader Jairam Ramesh.“The hearings have now been put off to January 13, 2027, because the Modi Govt suddenly discovered the need to file new affidavits,” he said in a post on social media platform X.“Meanwhile, this ecological disaster of a project continues to get bulldozed through. Bids were invited on Oct 26th to demarcate the entire 166.1 sq km area earmarked for the project that includes about 122 sq km area of biodiversity-rich forest land. The boundary is itself of about 43 km. Tenders were thus invited just a month before the Calcutta High Court hearings demonstrating the utter contempt that the Modi Govt has for democratic processes. Its mind is made up and can be summed up thus: ‘Let the challenges meander their way through the courts but the project will go forward unhindered.’ This is brazen callousness. The havoc that it will cause is foretold.”The court will hear the matter on January 13, 2027, when the petition that specifically deals with tribal rights and the FRA will be heard. Following this, the court has agreed to also hear the Attorney General’s submissions on behalf of the government on January 22.

title: Two Private Screenings of Pakistani Television Drama Series Dar-e-Nijaat Cancelled in Bengaluru - The Wire
description: The event was promoted as the “first-ever screening in Bengaluru” of episodes 34 and 35 of the series. The event was also supposed to be followed by a Persian and Arabic dinner.
author: The Wire Staff
content: New Delhi: Following objections and police scrutiny, two private screening events of Pakistani television drama series Dar-e-Nijaat, which were scheduled to be held in Bengaluru on November 28 and December 5 have been cancelled by the respective organisers, reported The Hindu.Prior to the cancellation, the screenings were advertised through promotional posters on social media. Earlier, the first screening which was being organised by The Bloom Society Sister’s Club, was scheduled for November 28, from 6 p.m. onwards, at a Persian and Arabian cuisine restaurant in Frazer Town.The event was promoted as the “first-ever screening in Bengaluru” of episodes 34 and 35 of the series. The event was also supposed to be followed by a Persian and Arabic dinner.The second screening, was being organised by The Star Club. It was supposed to be held on December 5 at a private theatre in the city.“We are getting in touch with the organisers to know more details about it. If anything is to be done on the ground, it will be done,” Bengaluru chief commissioner of Police R. Hithendra told The Hindu.Both the organisers confirmed to the newspaper that the screenings had been called off. The organiser of the first event said that following backlash, the Persian- and Arabic-themed dinner planned as part of the event had also been cancelled.The move comes at a time when the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting has asked Netflix to ensure that content originating in Pakistan is not streamed in India.Certain cinema groups have asked for the Pakistan-based Netflix web series Jo Bachay Hain Sang Samait Lo to not be released in India.The All India Cine Workers Association has written to Prime Minister Narendra Modi asking him to stop the release.The ministry has asked Netflix to adhere to its advisory dated May 8, 2025, and ensure that streaming content originating in Pakistan is not available in India, PTI reported, based on unnamed sources’ comments.

title: Did Nitin Nabin Say India Invited Pak to SCO Summit Under China’s Pressure? No!
description: Fact-Check: A deepfake is going viral on social media with false claims that it shows BJP leader Nitin Nabin stating that India invited Pakistan to the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation under pressure from China.
author: Anika K
content:
A video is going viral on social media, claiming to show the national president of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), Nitin Nabin, stating that India invited Pakistan to the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) under pressure from China.
The claim: In the video, Nabin can be heard saying that India did not invite Pakistan to the SCO summit of its own accord.
- He says, "India has an agreement with China to reclaim the 200 square kilometres of Indian territory that China has occupied, and prevent any further encroachment.
- He goes on to say, "For this, China has insisted that India must invite Pakistan to the SCO summit, or else it will not move forward with this agreement"
How did we find out?: We conducted a keyword search and couldn't find any credible sources sharing it or reporting on it.
- Following this, we ran a reverse image search on the video, which led us to a report by ANI with the same visuals.
- In the video, Nabin talks about how India's economy used to be described as fragile and how, under Prime Minister Narendra Modi's leadership, India has emerged as the world’s fourth-largest economic power.
- He goes on to talk about the people who go abroad and disrespect India, as they lack trust in the figures provided by international institutions and have no interest in national development.
- He doesn't mention the SCO, China or Pakistan.
Is it AI?: We ran the video through Hiya Deepfake Voice Detector, a tool that detects AI-generated audio, and it flagged the audio as AI.
- We ran the video through DeepFake-O-Meter, an AI detector, and nine of its detectors flagged it as AI.
- The official BJP Facebook account posted to clarify that the viral video of Nitin Nabin is a deepfake and that the statements attributed to him are completely false.
Conclusion: The video is a deepfake and doesn't show real footage of Nitin Nabin stating that India invited Pakistan to the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation under pressure from China.
(Not convinced of a post or information you came across online and want it verified? Send us the details on WhatsApp at 9540511818 , or e-mail it to us at webqoof@thequint.com and we'll fact-check it for you. You can also read all our fact-checked stories here.)

title: CJP To Hold Constitution Day Rally In Nagpur Honouring Ambedkar
description: CJP leaders to organise 'Save Democracy, Save Constitution' rally in Nagpur on Constitution Day, paying tribute to Dr B.R. Ambedkar at Deekshabhoomi and highlighting constitutional values.
author: The Quint
content:
The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) is set to organise a 'Save Democracy, Save Constitution' rally in Nagpur on 26 November 2026, coinciding with Constitution Day. CJP leaders, including founder Abhijeet Dipke and co-convenor Ashutosh Ranka, began the day by paying tribute to Dr B.R. Ambedkar at Deekshabhoomi, a significant Buddhist monument in the city. The rally is scheduled for 4 pm and will also feature actor Prakash Raj.
As reported by Hindustan Times, Dipke described Constitution Day as a "very holy day for everyone in the country" and emphasised the importance of honouring Dr Ambedkar, the principal architect of the Indian Constitution. The leaders' visit to Deekshabhoomi, where Ambedkar and his followers converted to Buddhism in 1956, underscored the symbolic significance of the site for the day's events.
According to The Hindu, Constitution Day marks the anniversary of the adoption of the Constitution by the Constituent Assembly in 1949. The day is observed nationwide with tributes to Ambedkar and other framers of the Constitution, and is often used by political parties and civil society groups to reaffirm their commitment to constitutional values.
As highlighted by Deccan Herald, Prime Minister Narendra Modi referred to the Constitution as "a priceless heritage of Indian democracy" and called on citizens to strengthen the values enshrined in the document. The government has promoted Constitution Day since 2015 to increase public awareness of constitutional principles.
"Today is a very holy day for everyone in the country because, on this day, Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar gave us the Constitution, on which our country is running and moving forward," Dipke stated after his visit to Deekshabhoomi.
In the context of Nagpur, the CJP rally aims to address concerns regarding the functioning of democratic institutions, particularly the Election Commission of India. Coverage revealed that Constitution Day has evolved from being observed as Law Day to a broader commemoration involving public awareness campaigns, educational activities, and political events across the country.
Nationally, Constitution Day is marked by various political parties and organisations through marches, readings of the Preamble, and public rallies. Reporting indicated that in other states, such as Uttar Pradesh, the day is used by parties to consolidate support among Dalits, minorities, and backward communities, reflecting the enduring legacy of Ambedkar and the Constitution in contemporary politics.
Legal experts and commentators have noted the significance of Constitution Day in reaffirming the moral and legal foundations of the Republic. Analysis showed that the day serves as a reminder of the ongoing responsibility to uphold justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity as outlined in the Constitution.
"Constitution is not a mere lawyers' document; it is a vehicle of Life and its spirit is always the spirit of Age," Dr Bhim Rao Ambedkar is quoted as saying, highlighting the living nature of the Constitution.
Other regions have also marked the occasion with special sessions and commemorative events. In Haryana, officials responded by organising a special session in the state assembly to reinforce commitment to constitutional principles and democratic values among elected representatives.
Note: This article is produced using AI-assisted tools and is based on publicly available information. It has been reviewed by The Quint's editorial team before publishing.

title: Venice Biennale 2026: Meet the 5 Indian Artists Whose Creations Helped India Win the Visitors’ Lion
description: ndia wins the Visitors’ Lion at Venice Biennale 2026. Meet the five Indian artists and discover the stories behind their award-winning artworks.
author: Nishtha Kawrani
content:
When the Delhi house where artist Sumakshi Singh spent her childhood summers was demolished, she found an extraordinary way to bring it back. Using delicate white threads, she recreated its doors, windows, stairs and even its gates.
Thousands of kilometres away in Venice, Italy, her childhood home became part of an exhibition that drew around 4.5 lakh visitors.
Alongside her work stood a towering bamboo structure inspired by Indian construction sites, a miniature Ladakhi settlement made from discarded egg trays and paper, and sculptures inspired by India’s natural landscapes.
On 25 November 2026, these creations earned India the Visitors’ Lion for Best National Participation at the Venice Biennale, one of the world’s biggest international art exhibitions. The award was decided by public vote.
Behind the winning exhibition, titled Geographies of Distance: Remembering Home, are five Indian artists who took inspiration from everyday materials, childhood memories and generations-old traditions to explore something we can all relate to: what it means to call a place home.
Here are the five artists and the fascinating stories behind their creations.
1. Sumakshi Singh: A house recreated in thread
Artwork: Permanent Address
Imagine walking into a house that is no longer there.
That is the experience Sumakshi Singh creates with Permanent Address, an intricate, life-size reconstruction of her family home in Delhi. The artist has recreated the house using embroidered thread and water-soluble fabric.
The house was built in 1951 by Singh’s grandparents, who came to India during Partition. It became the venue for family weddings, reunions and childhood sleepovers. It was also where she spent afternoons learning to knit and embroider with her grandmother.
Years later, when the house was demolished, the same craft helped her recreate the place she had always called home.
2. Asim Waqif: Bamboo that tells a story of changing cities
Artwork: Chaal
Using 12 tonnes of bamboo sourced largely from Assam and West Bengal, artist and architect Asim Waqif built a 30-foot-high structure in Venice without using a single nut or bolt.
The bamboo pieces are bent and tied together, forming a structure that resembles the scaffolding that supports buildings across Indian cities.
The choice of material is central to the artwork. Bamboo has long been used in traditional construction, but modern building practices increasingly favour materials such as steel and aluminium.
Waqif’s installation draws attention to this shift and the risk of losing traditional skills, such as bending and tying bamboo to build scaffolding.
3. Ranjani Shettar: A garden suspended in the air
Artwork: Under the Same Sky
In contrast to Waqif’s towering structure, Ranjani Shettar’s installation feels like stepping into a floating garden.
Inspired by flowers and natural growth, Under the Same Sky features sculptural forms suspended from the ceiling. Shettar created the flower-like sculptures using handwoven cotton fabric, steel and lacquer.
Working from her studio near Sagara in Karnataka, Shettar has used these materials for nearly two decades. Her installation allows visitors to experience the garden from within.
4. Skarma Sonam Tashi: Bringing Ladakh’s homes to Venice
Artwork: Echoes of Home
What does a traditional Ladakhi settlement look like when recreated thousands of kilometres away?
Artist Skarma Sonam Tashi offers an answer through Echoes of Home, an installation inspired by the architecture and landscape of Ladakh.
Using papier-mâché, cardboard, egg trays and old paper, he creates a miniature settlement that evokes the region’s traditional homes, built using earth, stone and timber.
Growing up in Ladakh, Tashi was familiar with traditional homes built using locally available earth, stone and timber. Designed for the region’s harsh climate, these houses help keep families warm during winter and cool during summer.
As concrete and steel buildings increasingly replace traditional homes, his artwork draws attention to generations of knowledge that Ladakh risks losing.
5. Alwar Balasubramaniam: When nature becomes the artist
Artworks: Drift and Not Just for Us
Sometimes, the most compelling artwork is made from something as familiar as the ground beneath our feet.
For these works, artist Alwar Balasubramaniam, also known as Bala, uses clay and soil sourced from rural Tamil Nadu to create sculptural panels.
The surfaces are marked by natural cracks and fissures, capturing the effects of time and environmental forces. Rather than smoothing over these imperfections, the artist makes them the focus of the work.
While the artwork was being created, peacocks, monkeys and snakes passed through the work in progress, leaving their marks on it.
It is a reminder of the idea behind his work: the earth is home to every living creature.
Five artists, one idea of home
India returned to the Venice Biennale after seven years with an exhibition built around materials familiar to millions of Indians: bamboo, thread, cotton, paper and earth.
Through their creations, the five artists brought stories of Partition, traditional architecture, family memories, craftsmanship and India’s changing landscapes to an international audience.
With around 4.5 lakh visitors and an award decided by the public, their exhibition showed how stories rooted in everyday Indian life could resonate with people across the world.

title: Before Directing Ramayana, Nitesh Tiwari Was an IIT Bombay Grad Who Quit His Tech Job to Write
description: From a four-month software job to a film reaching 130+ countries, discover the unconventional career journey of IIT Bombay alumnus and Ramayana director Nitesh Tiwari.
author: Avantika Krishna
content:
When Nitesh Tiwari left a software company after four months, he had no film career waiting for him, only an IIT Bombay engineering degree and an interest in writing.
Nearly three decades later, he has directed Ramayana: Part 1. Released on 5 November 2026, it travelled to more than 130 countries and crossed ₹1,000 crore in worldwide gross collections in its opening week, according to a Prime Focus investor presentation. Yet Tiwari’s route to the director’s chair began in a college hostel.
The campus where storytelling began
Tiwari graduated from IIT Bombay in 1996 with a BTech in Metallurgical Engineering. He did not arrive on campus thinking of a career in cinema; its extracurricular culture introduced him to performance and writing.
Hostel competitions brought students into theatre, one-act plays and miming. Encouraged by a senior, Tiwari entered the Freshy Miming Competition and won. He then won the senior competition for four consecutive years and directed hostel plays in his third and fourth years.
He told Hindustan Times in 2022 that the response to his performances sparked his interest in dramatics and writing. Engineering, he said, later helped him think analytically while structuring screenplays.
During his third year, he interned at advertising agency RK Swamy BBDO, where he decided to give writing a chance. His experience reflects the influence of campus theatre in shaping creative careers.
From software to advertising, then cinema
After graduating, Tiwari joined a software company. He kept questioning whether he wanted to do that work for the rest of his life. Four months later, he quit, choosing to try writing before the comfort of a salary made it harder to change direction.
He joined FCB Ulka at one-fourth of his software salary, Hindustan Times reported. Three of the five agencies he applied to rejected him. Ulka hired him after a copy test and a poem, despite initially questioning why an IIT graduate wanted to write.
Advertising became a substantial career. IIT Bombay’s alumni profile says Tiwari spent 18 years in the industry: four at FCB Ulka, three at Lowe Lintas and 11 at Leo Burnett. He rose to become Chief Creative Officer at Leo Burnett in Mumbai. Advertising taught him to write for audiences and collaborate.
His entry into filmmaking was not part of a mapped career plan. Tiwari and fellow advertising professional Vikas Bahl had written Chillar Party but could not find a director willing to take on a film featuring children and a dog. They decided to direct it themselves rather than abandon the script. In a 2019 interview with Scroll, Tiwari described the move as an unplanned step into filmmaking.
Released in 2011, Chillar Party won the National Film Award for Best Children's Film and Best Original Screenplay. Tiwari went on to direct Bhoothnath Returns, Dangal and Chhichhore. He also co-wrote Nil Battey Sannata and Bareilly Ki Barfi. His journey is among the engineering graduates who found their way into filmmaking.
A much larger canvas
Dangal became a defining point in his career. The 2016 film, based on wrestler Mahavir Singh Phogat and his daughters Geeta and Babita, became a major international commercial success, including in China, where it reached audiences well beyond the usual Hindi-film market.
Tiwari received the Filmfare Award for Best Director in 2017, according to IIT Bombay’s alumni profile. Chhichhore, released in 2019, returned him to the campus setting that had shaped his early creative life. His career also reflects the relationship between theatre and cinema in the making of performers and storytellers.
His latest assignment, Ramayana, takes that storytelling journey to a different scale, drawing on an epic familiar to audiences across generations. The two-part adaptation brings together a large cast and a global production and distribution effort. The first instalment was released in Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam.
Prime Focus’s November 2026 investor presentation described it as the widest global release for an Indian film, with screenings in more than 130 countries and major premium formats including IMAX, Dolby Cinema, ScreenX and 4DX.
The company also reported that the film crossed ₹1,000 crore in worldwide gross collections in its opening week. The figures come from the production company’s disclosure. A second instalment is planned.
His journey was not an overnight leap from engineering to cinema. It passed through years of advertising, writing and collaboration. It began with a decision to leave a job after four months and give writing a chance; it has since taken him from hostel performances to a film released across continents.

title: 5 Indian Businesses Creating Social Impact Through Their Business Models
description: Here are five Indian businesses creating social impact through inclusive hiring, affordable healthcare, rural livelihoods and women’s entrepreneurship.
author: Avantika Krishna
content:
What comes to mind when you think of a successful business? Crores in revenue, thousands of employees, a presence across the world, or perhaps a celebrated CEO?
Now consider a few other measures of success. How many women earned their first independent income? How many people with disabilities found a workplace where they could build a career? How many families could afford life-saving medical treatment? How many rural artisans could earn a living without leaving their villages?
Recent conversations around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s management practices have brought a larger question into focus: what truly makes a good business leader?
Closer to home, these five Indian enterprises offer a different perspective on success. From hospitality and healthcare to waste management and handicrafts, they show how building a profitable business can go hand in hand with creating meaningful opportunities and improving people's lives.
Making room for every ability
At Lemon Tree Hotels, learning Indian Sign Language is part of employee training. It helps colleagues communicate with one another and makes everyday working life more accessible for employees with hearing disabilities.
Patu Keswani, the founder of the hotel group, began hiring people with disabilities in 2007. Over the years, the company has adapted its training programmes to accommodate people with different needs.
Deaf employees receive training with the help of sign language interpreters, while colleagues with low vision are provided accessible learning materials. Some neurodivergent employees undergo internships lasting more than six months to help them settle into their roles.
According to its 2025–26 annual report, Lemon Tree employed 305 people with disabilities and another 635 people from socially and economically disadvantaged backgrounds across its owned, leased and managed hotels.
Much like several inclusive cafés across India, the hotel chain demonstrates how adapting workplaces to people's needs can open up meaningful career opportunities.
Taking village crafts to the world
In 1978, Nand Kishore Chaudhary began Jaipur Rugs with two looms and nine artisans. He wanted to connect rural craftspeople directly with larger markets, helping them earn through skills they had developed over generations.
According to the founder's website, the business has grown to work with around 40,000 artisans across 600 villages in five Indian states. Around 80 percent of them are women.
For many of these women, weaving offers an opportunity to earn from their homes without having to migrate to cities or travel far for work.
As The Better India previously reported, the company delivers raw materials to artisans' homes and collects the finished carpets from them.
Through its Manchaha initiative, artisans also get the freedom to create their own rug designs, drawing inspiration from their surroundings, experiences and imagination.
Their craftsmanship has found customers across the world while creating livelihood opportunities closer to home.
Making life-saving surgeries affordable
For a family struggling to afford heart surgery, the cost of treatment can stand between a loved one and potentially life-saving medical care.
It was this challenge that cardiac surgeon Dr Devi Shetty sought to address when he founded Narayana Health in Bengaluru in 2001.
His hospital model focuses on performing a large number of surgeries, making efficient use of medical equipment and reducing procurement and operational expenses.
The savings help bring down the cost of treatment for patients.
A 2017 case study by The Commonwealth Fund documented that Narayana Health had brought the average cost of open-heart surgery below US$2,000 at the time.
By rethinking how hospitals operate, Dr Shetty built a business model that demonstrates how greater efficiency can help more families access specialised medical care.
Helping waste pickers become entrepreneurs
When Lotfar moved to Bengaluru in 2010, he was struggling to make ends meet as a waste picker.
A 2022 report by Tata Trusts documented how his life changed after he began working with Hasiru Dala. By then, he owned four trucks and employed around 20 other waste pickers.
Founded in 2015 by Shekar Prabhakar, Nalini Shekar and Marwan Abubaker, Hasiru Dala Innovations is a waste management enterprise that helps informal waste workers build more secure livelihoods and run their own businesses.
These entrepreneurs provide waste collection and management services to residential communities, offices and events. They earn through service fees as well as the sale of recyclable materials.
By 2022, the enterprise had supported 24 waste-picker entrepreneurs, who had, in turn, created employment opportunities for around 300 other waste pickers.
The model brings the people who have long helped keep our cities clean into the business of managing their waste, giving them opportunities to grow as entrepreneurs.
From making papads to becoming business owners
In 1959, seven women in Mumbai borrowed Rs 80 and began making papads. Their aim was simple: to earn an income of their own.
What began as a small venture became Shri Mahila Griha Udyog Lijjat Papad, one of India's most recognisable household brands.
According to its official website, the enterprise provides self-employment to around 45,000 women across 83 branches in 16 states.
What makes Lijjat particularly interesting is its shared ownership model. Its women members participate in running the enterprise, and the profits and losses of each branch are shared among its members.
For thousands of women, a skill they already possessed became a means of earning an income and having a stake in the business they helped build.
More than six decades later, the enterprise offers an example of what women can achieve when they have access to economic opportunities and collective ownership.
These five enterprises have taken different paths to growth. Yet, each offers a valuable lesson in how businesses can widen access to opportunities, recognise overlooked talent and help people build better lives for themselves.
Perhaps, alongside asking how much a business earns, we could also ask a question that deserves just as much attention: Who grows when the business grows?
