title: 'A Muslim will be Deputy in UP if Chandrashekhar becomes CM': Owaisi at mega Samajik Parivartan Morcha rally
description: Lucknow, Nov 26 (UNI) AIMIM chief Asaduddin Owaisi and Azad Samaj Party president Chandrashekhar Azad, MP from Nagina, jointly held a mega rally of their newly…
content:
'A Muslim will be Deputy in UP if Chandrashekhar becomes CM': Owaisi at mega Samajik Parivartan Morcha rally
Manoj Bhadra
Lucknow, Nov 26 (UNI) AIMIM chief Asaduddin Owaisi and Azad Samaj Party president Chandrashekhar Azad, MP from Nagina, jointly held a mega rally of their newly-launched Samajik Parivartan Morcha in Lucknow on Thursday.
At the rally, Chandrashekhar Azad was announced as the Chief Minister candidate, with Owaisi announcing a Muslim as his Deputy CM. At the rally, claimed to have an attendence of around one lakh supporters, held at the Ramabai ground, AIMIM chief Owaisi said, "Akhilesh Yadav has taken everything from Muslims. He has reduced them to a vote bank. Our large turnout sends a message to the Samajwadi leader that the public will not fall prey to your deception."
He said that now 'Abdul' will not just spread the carpet but will help make Chandrashekhar the Chief Minister. Owaisi challenged the SP and Congress leaders, saying, "Compete with me in a speech; I will knock you out in five minutes." He also said that "if speaking the truth and advocating for the rights of the poor is provocation, then I will do it". Nagina MP Chandrashekhar said that if he comes to power, his party will provide women with Rs 25,000 per month. Justice will be served not by bulldozers, but by the Constitution.
"If Chandrashekhar becomes CM, Abdul will become Deputy CM. He will also appoint a backward class brother as Deputy CM," he announced. Chandrashekhar said, "The media will ask us where the money will come from. I want to tell you that the Chief Minister spends Rs 7,000 crore on advertising. We will give that money to women". Owaisi said, "We have come here to make Chandrashekhar the Chief Minister."
He added that the Constitution didn't begin with any Gods or Goddesses, but rather with "We the People of India." He stressed that "we must learn to use our vote; otherwise, this era of oppression will continue and we will not receive our rights". He said that there is a union of hearts with Chandrashekhar, and this will always remain. He added that "if it means sacrificing our lives to save the Constitution, we will accept that". According to him, if the Constitution is weakened, it will become a matter of life and death for Dalits and Muslims.
Chandrashekhar said, "The Samajik Parivartan Morcha will work to oust the Bharatiya Janata Party." "We have a big heart. We are not small-minded. You have so much power that with your vote you can put anyone you want in power. You can also throw anyone you want to the ground. If these people offer Rs20,000 to come to power, I declare that we will give Rs25,000 to every woman," he declared.
Chandrashekhar said, "The names of parks have been changed. Similarly, in Lucknow, the Ambedkar Green Park was renamed Janeshwar Mishra Park. We have no problem with Janeshwar Mishra. They could have built a new one. Those who try to garner votes by using Baba Saheb's name, hate him so much that you changed the name of the park built in his name. The public will not forgive."
Chandrashekhar said, "When our government is formed, false cases against farmers and laborers will be withdrawn. When I was contesting elections in Nagina, you sent me money. I still have some of it. Seeing those notes brings tears to my eyes. They are stained with your sweat. I will return them to you with interest." The AIMIM chief said that if the Constitution is weakened, the state will be ruled by Thakur and Yadav raj, which would lead to the oppression of Dalits and Muslims. He described "Chief Minister Chandrashekhar" as the leader of the poor and Muslims.
Owaisi claimed that Baba's time in Uttar Pradesh will be over, referring to CM Yogi Adityanath. He said that Baba had claimed over 10 million Hindu votes had been deleted, learning this through AI. He blamed Yogi Adityanath for the "devastation" in Uttar Pradesh. He said that "Chandrashekhar Azad and I will not rest until the vulnerable get justice". Owaisi said that "we would rather die than remain silent."
Launching a scathing attack on the Samajwadi Party and Akhilesh Yadav, Owaisi alleged that while dancing occurred in Saifai, children were suffering in Muzaffarnagar. He alleged that Akhilesh Yadav only wants the Muslim community's votes and that now the Muslim community will no longer roll out the carpet, but will instead want a share in power. Owaisi said he visited Chandrashekhar's home and ate with his mother. He said he was ready to go to any poor person's home and do anything he could.
Owaisi said he asked Akhilesh Yadav if he would field a Muslim from Karhal. According to him, Akhilesh Yadav retorted, "You're losing because you're practicing nepotism." Owaisi retorted, questioning the SP's politics. Owaisi reiterated that the situation is changing and the Muslim community will no longer be merely a vote bank. He said that Muslims will no longer be playing the carpet but will demand their rights and full participation in power.
Chandrashekhar said, "Kashiram Sahib used to say that one's own hut is better than others' palaces. I love my own hut. I have no concern for others' palaces. This government has robbed SC/ST children of the right to reservation in the four medical colleges of Kannauj, Saharanpur, Jalaun, and Ambedkar Nagar." Chandrashekhar said, "For 75 years, all political parties have said they will bring you good days. They will remove your poverty. They will remove your helplessness. They say they will bring you into the mainstream.
"Our SC, ST, OBC and minority communities are still marginalized. You have two options. One, rely on fate and wait. The other, follow Babasaheb's advice and become two fists. Stop begging. Babasaheb had said that 'political power is the master key,' meaning political power is the golden key, through which you can solve all your problems."
UNI MBD RN

title: Govt sees fresh Trump tariffs as 'leverage', not 'done deal'; will concentrate on finalising trade pact
description: Jayanta Roy Chowdhury New Delhi, Nov 26 (UNI) Top officials in India see the fresh threat of tariff
content:
Govt sees fresh Trump tariffs as 'leverage', not 'done deal'; will concentrate on finalising trade pact
Jayanta Roy Chowdhury
New Delhi, Nov 26 (UNI) Top officials in India see the fresh threat of tariff imposts by President Donald Trump's administration on India and 13 other trade partners as a "leverage" or bargaining tool rather than a "done deal". Top Commerce Ministry officials told UNI on Thursday, India is in any case "moving towards signing a bilateral trade deal with the US" and that, "The new tariff threat is best understood as leverage, not a done deal."
Washington on Wednesday proposed fresh duties of roughly 15-25 per cent on a host of countries including India under Section 301, of the US Tariff Act which allows administration to levy higher duties on countries whose trade policies are considered discriminatory, unjustifiable or unreasonable, towards the US.
"The rates are not yet in force, and the US trade representative has explicitly said Indian tariffs would be capped at 17 per cent if a bilateral deal is signed, or could rise to 25 per cent if talks fail," officials dealing with the issue explained to UNI. The fresh US tariffs have targeted India's industrial subsidies, labour policies, financial rules, and non-tariff barriers, besides India Inc.'s reliance on Chinese imports in critical sectors like pharmaceuticals, medical devices, steel, solar technology, and information technology.
Pinak R Chakravarty, former Secretary (Economic Relations) in the Ministry of External Affairs, also added that the tariffs announced last night, "are a replacement legal route after the US Supreme Court struck down Trump's earlier sweeping tariffs under emergency powers," leaving a 10 per cent baseline rate and could be subjected to further legal scrutiny by the US judiciary. "The tariffs are a bargaining chip rather than a fixed policy, which is why they speak of 17 per cent with a deal and 25 per cent without," pointed out Chakravarty.
For Indian exporters, who saw their exports to the US rising by 11 per cent in the April-September 2026-27 half year period to USD 50.80 billion, the main worry seems to be US-based buyers delaying purchases, seeking price reductions, or for rerouting supply chain lines till tariff levels are finalised. "While the immediate tariff implications are significant, this should also be viewed as a short-term phase in a much longer economic relationship," said Rupa Dutta, former Principal Economic Advisor to the Ministries of Commerce and Industry.
The economist added that an agreement could provide greater certainty for Indian exporters and businesses, but its eventual impact will depend on the terms negotiated and how it is implemented. "We should therefore remain cautiously optimistic and wait to see how the agreement progresses, particularly with regard to the final tariff framework and the extent to which its implementation may require congressional approval in the US," Dutta said.
The terms Washington is seeking in ongoing trade negotiations are, however, likely to go beyond tariff cuts. Top officials suggested a "final deal" could not only require India to curb industrial subsidies, prevent Chinese goods from being rerouted through India, align some export controls with the US," but also "open up more agricultural and industrial goods markets," which would help win the current administration brownie points with American voters in the farming and industrial hinterland. However, "this (opening up contentious agricultural markets in grains, dairy products, fruits and vegetables) in turn could be politically problematic for our government," pointed out officials. Till now, India has delayed formal signing of any trade deal until the US tariff structure becomes "crystal clear" and in negotiations made it clear that the US cannot bully India like any other smaller economy, given its importance in any supply chain diversification away from China, especially in areas like critical minerals, AI architecture etc. Officials said they would continue "negotiating rates but not principles."
India will keep insisting that any final deal locks in a low, predictable ceiling and includes exemptions for labour-intensive exports such as textiles, gems, pharmaceuticals and auto components, said officials. At the same time, India will continue to diversify its export market away from the US by concentrating on new growth continents such as Africa. Where India's exports rose by 44 per cent in the first half of the current fiscal, and Latin America, where Indian exports saw a rise by 14 per cent to Brazil and 26 per cent to Mexico in H1 of 2026-27. Besides, Indian officials said they would also work to deepen trade with traditional markets such as the EU, UK, Gulf States, Japan and Southeast Asia "so that the US market carries less marginal weight". Indian economic and trade pundits believe that India's strongest defence against Trump tariffs cannot be retaliation in the manner in which China has responded, as India does not have the trade leverage to bargain with but rather to adopt postures which would make "its position in the US supply chain too important to be treated as a tariff target."
UNI JRC AAB

title: Rebel TMC MPs face crucial test as Delimitation Bill threatens to deepen defection battle
description: New Delhi, Nov 26 (UNI) The 20 rebel Trinamool Congress MPs who have aligned themselves with the National Citizens Party of India (NCPI) could face an explosiv…
content:
Rebel TMC MPs face crucial test as Delimitation Bill threatens to deepen defection battle
Shahid K Abbas
New Delhi, Nov 26 (UNI) The 20 rebel Trinamool Congress MPs who have aligned themselves with the National Citizens Party of India (NCPI) could face an explosive political and constitutional test during the forthcoming winter session of Parliament, with their possible support for a government-sponsored Constitutional Amendment Bill on delimitation potentially putting their Lok Sabha membership at further risk.
If they vote in favour of the BJP-led NDA government's proposal in defiance of a formal whip issued by the Mamata Banerjee-led Trinamool Congress leadership, they could face an additional ground for disqualification under the anti-defection law, unless their claim to protection under the merger provisions of the Tenth Schedule is accepted by Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla. For the dissident MPs, the impending constitutional confrontation could prove to be a decisive moment in their attempt to establish a separate political identity.
Having broken away from the Trinamool Congress following the party's defeat in the West Bengal Assembly elections in May, the 20 parliamentarians have thrown their weight behind the NDA government and are seeking recognition as a separate parliamentary group aligned with the NCPI. However, their political realignment remains under a legal cloud, with disqualification petitions initiated by Trinamool Congress national general secretary Abhishek Banerjee challenging their departure from the party and seeking their removal from the Lok Sabha.
The immediate question is whether the rebels will demonstrate their allegiance to the government by supporting its proposed delimitation legislation at a time when their own parliamentary status remains unresolved. Their 20 votes could provide the NDA with additional strength in a politically sensitive constitutional exercise. But the same votes could also complicate their legal position if the Speaker ultimately rejects their claim that their departure from the Trinamool Congress is protected under the merger exception.
Under Paragraph 2(1)(b) of the Tenth Schedule, a member of a House belonging to a political party is liable to disqualification if he or she votes or abstains from voting contrary to a direction issued by that party without obtaining prior permission, unless the party condones the action within 15 days. Thus, if the Speaker continues to treat the rebels as members of the original Trinamool Congress parliamentary party and rejects their merger defence, voting against a duly issued party whip could provide an additional basis for disqualification.
The implications would be particularly serious because the 20 MPs are already facing allegations that they voluntarily gave up their membership of the Trinamool Congress by aligning themselves with another political formation. Defying the parent party's formal direction in a crucial constitutional vote could strengthen the complainants' case and further complicate the rebels' legal defence. If disqualified, they would lose their Lok Sabha membership and their seats would fall vacant, necessitating by-elections. The central legal issue, however, is whether the rebels can successfully invoke Paragraph 4 of the Tenth Schedule, which provides protection in cases of a merger.
The provision does not confer immunity merely because two-thirds of the members of a legislative party decide to leave their original political party and join another formation. It requires a merger of the original political party with another political party, with the merger being recognised for the purposes of the anti-defection law when at least two-thirds of the members of the legislature party concerned agree to it. The rebels contend that they represent 20 of the 27 effective Trinamool Congress members in the Lok Sabha, comfortably exceeding the constitutionally prescribed two-thirds threshold. Numerically, their argument appears persuasive. But the more fundamental question is whether the original Trinamool Congress itself has merged with the NCPI or whether the MPs have merely defected to another political formation while invoking the numerical strength of their parliamentary group.
The distinction is significant in view of the Supreme Court's interpretation of the merger provision in its May 2023 judgment in the Maharashtra political crisis. The apex court made it clear that the original political party and its legislature party cannot simply be treated as interchangeable entities. While the two-thirds requirement is an essential condition for invoking the merger exception, it does not eliminate the requirement of a merger involving the original political party.
The Speaker will therefore have to examine the substance and validity of the alleged merger rather than rely exclusively on the numerical strength claimed by the dissidents. If their merger defence is accepted, the rebels would have a substantially stronger legal position. Paragraph 4 would protect them from disqualification on the ground of defection, while their legally recognised political affiliation would become relevant in determining which parliamentary whip applies to them. In that eventuality, a direction issued by the original Trinamool Congress leadership would not automatically bind them in the same manner as it would members who continue to be legally affiliated with the parent party.
However, if the Speaker rejects their merger argument, their political alignment with the NCPI and support for the NDA could come under closer scrutiny under the anti-defection provisions. A formal Trinamool Congress whip directing its MPs to oppose the constitutional amendment would make their position particularly vulnerable. The uncertainty has been compounded by the delay in the Speaker's decision on the disqualification petitions, despite the Supreme Court's intervention.
On September 23, the apex court expressed concern over the time taken by the proceedings and described the three-month delay as a red flag. While declining to prescribe a rigid calendar deadline, it stressed that the matter should be decided expeditiously within a reasonable period and indicated that it would continue monitoring the proceedings. The disqualification battle has now entered a significant procedural phase.
On November 24, the 20 rebel MPs submitted their individual replies to Speaker Om Birla on the final day of the deadline granted by the Lok Sabha Secretariat. Each response reportedly runs into 17 to 18 pages and seeks to establish that their decision to align with the NCPI did not violate any constitutional or parliamentary provision. NCPI chief whip and rebel Trinamool Congress leader Kakoli Ghosh Dastidar has maintained that the MPs have followed the prescribed procedures and submitted their defence against the disqualification petitions.
Speaker Om Birla had earlier indicated that the proceedings would be expedited after receiving responses from both sides. The completion of the reply-filing exercise has consequently removed one of the immediate procedural hurdles before the Speaker takes up the substantive issues. The timing assumes added significance because the government could seek to revive its delimitation agenda during the winter session. The controversy has already exposed the difficulties facing the NDA in securing the special majority required for constitutional amendments.
The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026, introduced in April as part of the government's proposed delimitation framework, failed to secure the constitutionally prescribed majority in the Lok Sabha. Any fresh attempt to advance the exercise would once again require the government to mobilise support beyond its existing parliamentary strength. Under Article 368, a Constitutional Amendment Bill must be passed separately by each House by a majority of its total membership and by at least two-thirds of the members present and voting.
Depending on the provisions sought to be amended, ratification by at least half of the State legislatures may also be necessary. For the NDA, therefore, the support of the 20 dissident MPs could be politically useful, although their votes alone would not guarantee the passage of the proposed legislation. For the rebels, the opportunity to demonstrate their political usefulness to the government comes with the considerable risk that their voting conduct could become another issue in the pending disqualification proceedings. Importantly, the recording of their votes in the Lok Sabha would not automatically settle their legal status or protect them from subsequent disqualification.
The Speaker would still have to adjudicate the petitions under the Tenth Schedule. Equally, disqualification cannot be presumed merely because the parent party alleges a violation of its whip. The constitutional process requires consideration of the applicable provisions, including whether prior permission was obtained or the action was subsequently condoned within the stipulated period. Meanwhile, the dispute over the Trinamool Congress's political identity has acquired a parallel dimension.
The Election Commission of India has summoned both the Mamata Banerjee-led All India Trinamool Congress and the Ritabrata Banerjee-led Democratic Trinamool Congress for a hearing in New Delhi on November 27 over their rival claims to the original party name and its twin-flowers-on-grass election symbol. Both factions have submitted affidavits and supporting documents to establish their respective claims. The Mamata Banerjee faction has reportedly submitted extensive documentation, including affidavits bearing the signatures of the party chief, 17 MPs from both Houses of Parliament and 38 MLAs. The rebel faction has also submitted supporting material.
The Election Commission's proceedings, following the Supreme Court's September 28 directions, are expected to examine the rival claims relating to organisational and legislative support before deciding the dispute over the party's original identity. However, the Election Commission's proceedings and the Speaker's disqualification proceedings involve two separate constitutional and legal questions. The Commission's decision under Paragraph 15 of the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968, concerns recognition of rival factions and their entitlement to the party name and election symbol.
The Speaker's decision under the Tenth Schedule concerns the liability of individual MPs to disqualification for defection. Consequently, recognition of a faction by the Election Commission would not, by itself, conclusively establish the validity of its merger defence under the anti-defection law. The rebels are thus seeking legitimacy on two different institutional fronts: recognition of their political formation through the Election Commission and protection of their parliamentary membership through the Speaker. A favourable outcome in one proceeding would not necessarily guarantee success in the other.
For Mamata Banerjee, the stakes extend beyond the immediate loss of 20 MPs. Allowing elected parliamentarians to cross over and support the NDA without facing the consequences of the anti-defection law could undermine her authority over the party organisation and parliamentary wing and potentially encourage further political realignments. The disqualification petitions are therefore also an attempt to defend the organisational and political integrity of a party confronting a major electoral setback and an unprecedented internal rupture.
For the BJP-led government, the dissidents' support could provide an additional political advantage in a contentious constitutional exercise. But projecting their votes as evidence of a legally established merger would be premature, given that the Speaker's decision remains pending and the Election Commission is separately examining the rival claims to the party's identity. Ultimately, the winter session could become a defining moment for the 20 rebel MPs. Their most consequential decision may not simply be whether to support or oppose the government's delimitation proposal, but whether they can cast their votes without exposing their parliamentary membership to further legal jeopardy.
If the Speaker accepts their merger defence, they could emerge with their Lok Sabha positions intact and their political realignment on a stronger legal footing. If he rejects it, defiance of a formal Trinamool Congress whip could add another damaging dimension to their already precarious position. The coming weeks could therefore determine not merely the parliamentary arithmetic surrounding a crucial constitutional amendment but also whether the 20 dissidents can transform a political rebellion into a legally sustainable realignment. For them, the fundamental question is no longer simply which side of the House they choose to support, but whether the anti-defection provisions of the Constitution will allow them to continue occupying their seats.
UNI SKA AAB

title: In Numbers: How Different Religions May Grow Over The Next 50 Years
description: Christians are projected to remain broadly stable at 2.2 per cent, while the share of Buddhists and other religious groups is expected to decline slightly.
author: Subham Singh
content:
The world's religious composition is expected to change significantly over the next five decades, with Muslims projected to grow faster than any other major religious group.
According to projections by Pew Research Center, the global Muslim population is expected to increase by 80 per cent between 2020 and 2070, far outpacing overall world population growth of 29 per cent during the same period. Christians are projected to grow by 30 per cent, while Hindus are expected to grow by 17 per cent. In contrast, Buddhist populations are projected to shrink by 23 per cent, and the number of religiously unaffiliated people is expected to decline by 10 per cent.
The projections suggest that fertility rate will play the biggest role in shaping the future religious landscape.
Higher Fertility Remains A Major Driver
One of the clearest reasons behind the faster growth of Muslim populations is fertility. While fertility rates are projected to decline across nearly all religious groups over the coming decades, Muslims are expected to retain the highest fertility rate among major religions, as per Pew Research Center.
During 2020-25, Muslim women worldwide are estimated to have an average of 3.1 children, compared with 2.5 among Christians, 2.3 among Jews, 1.9 among Hindus, and 1.6 among Buddhists. By 2065-70, fertility is projected to decline across groups, but Muslims are still expected to have the highest average at 2.2 children per woman. Christians are projected to fall to 2.1, Jews to 2.0, and Hindus to 1.7.
The gap is smaller than it is today, but it remains large enough to produce substantially different population trajectories over time.
In addition to higher fertility, Muslims also have one of the youngest population profiles globally. A younger population means a larger share of people are entering child-bearing ages, which contributes to population growth even as fertility rates gradually decline.
Taken together, these demographic factors help explain why Muslims are projected to add people at a much faster pace than any other major religious group through 2070.
India Mirrors The Broader Trend
India, home to the world's largest Hindu population and one of the world's largest Muslim populations, is also projected to see changes in its religious composition over the next five decades.
The share of Hindus in India's population is projected to decline from 79.4 per cent in 2020 to 75.8 per cent in 2070, a drop of 3.6 percentage points.
Over the same period, the share of Muslims is projected to increase from 15.2 per cent to 19.6 per cent, a gain of 4.4 percentage points.
Christians are projected to remain broadly stable at 2.2 per cent, while the share of Buddhists and other religious groups is expected to decline slightly.
The projections do not suggest a shift in India's religious majority. Hindus are expected to remain by far the country's largest religious group in 2070. However, the data indicate that demographic differences, particularly fertility patterns and age structures, could gradually alter the relative shares of religious communities over time.

title: Maharashtra's New Power Model Aims To Turn Excess Solar Into 24x7 Supply
description: The model shifts responsibility for sourcing, scheduling and balancing power to suppliers, while allowing MSEDCL to retain control over deployment of the procured electricity.
author: Press Trust Of India
content:
Maharashtra is pioneering a new model of renewable energy procurement that seeks to convert surplus daytime solar generation into reliable Round-the-Clock (RTC) electricity, addressing a growing challenge for power distribution utilities as renewable capacity expands.
Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Co Ltd (MSEDCL) floated a tender earlier this year to procure 2,500 MW of RTC renewable power for 25 years via tariff-based competitive bidding and an e-reverse auction, according to people with knowledge of the matter.
The tender effectively converted 5,000 MW of non-firm solar capacity into 2,500 MW of firm power by combining renewable energy with other generation sources and storage, they said.
The Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission (MERC) described the arrangement as "unique and bespoke", saying it would enable MSEDCL to "effectively utilise and convert the 5,000 MW of non-firm solar power...into a firm source of power".
Unlike conventional power procurement contracts, the supply-based arrangement does not require bidders to own dedicated generation assets. Suppliers can source electricity from multiple generators and technologies but must meet stringent annual, monthly and peak-hour supply obligations, including a minimum 51 per cent traceable renewable energy component, they said.
The model shifts responsibility for sourcing, scheduling and balancing power to suppliers, while allowing MSEDCL to retain control over deployment of the procured electricity.
Consumer economics are central to the arrangement. MERC noted that MSEDCL's discovered tariff of Rs 5.90 per unit compares favourably with levelised tariffs of Rs 6.31-8.90 per unit for recent long-term thermal power procurement. The tariff is fixed for the 25-year power purchase agreement, with suppliers bearing the risk of fluctuations in input power costs.
Four bidders offered a combined 6,250 MW. Adani Power Limited (APL) won the contract after quoting Rs 6.30 per kWh initially and securing the lowest tariff in the e-reverse auction, followed by Lalitpur Power Generation Company (Rs 6.34/kWh), MB Power (Rs 6.48/kWh), and Sterlite Grid 42 (Rs 9.50/kWh).
APL received the Letter of Award (LOA) and the Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission (MERC) adopted the Rs 5.90/kWh tariff, they said.
The tender also imposes substantial delivery obligations, with penalties for non-performance reaching up to 400 per cent of the applicable tariff in specified cases. MERC described the bidding process as "fair, transparent, and competitive", citing substantial market response.
The model seeks to address a growing imbalance in India's electricity market: solar generation peaks during daylight hours, while demand continues after sunset. Better utilisation of surplus solar power could reduce renewable energy curtailment, improve transmission network utilisation and limit inefficient backing down of thermal power plants.
The approach is beginning to find traction elsewhere. West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Company Ltd (WBSEDCL) has recently concluded a similar 2,500 MW RTC procurement, comprising 1,750 MW and a 750 MW greenshoe option. Its contract provides for a first-year tariff with subsequent escalation linked to the Wholesale Price Index (WPI), the people said.
The two procurements could provide a template for other states seeking to integrate larger volumes of renewable energy without compromising supply reliability or increasing the burden of under-utilised conventional generation assets.
The broader significance is a shift in renewable power procurement from buying intermittent green electricity to securing dependable, round-the-clock power with a substantial renewable component. As India's solar capacity expands, such arrangements could become increasingly important in balancing clean-energy ambitions with the need for reliable and affordable electricity.

title: Akhilesh Yadav On Stage, Azam Khan Says 'Wish He Spent 6 Months In Jail'
description: Azam Khan said he went through severe mental and physical distress during his five-and-a-half years in prison.
author: Vaibhav Tiwari
content:
Old wounds reopened for Azam Khan on Thursday. With a tinge of pain across his face and mild resentment in his voice, the Samajwadi Party's most recognisable Muslim face recalled his over five-year-long imprisonment, stating it would take party chief Akhilesh Yadav at least six months in jail to understand what he went through during his incarceration.
The politician, who often deploys sarcasm to attack opponents - and sometimes even his supporters - made the remark at the Samajwadi Party's UP manifesto launch event, with Akhilesh Yadav sitting on the stage just metres from the dais.
"I just told Akhilesh that I sometimes told Abdullah (his son) and others in jail that I wished Akhilesh would also come to jail for six months....so that he could know the truth about how the days and nights go by and what happens," he said.
Khan said he went through severe mental and physical distress during his five-and-a-half years in prison. He alleged that during a jail transfer, authorities separated him from his son, Abdullah Azam.
READ | Azam Khan's 'Biryani' Jibe At Asaduddin Owaisi Amid Tussle For UP Muslim Votes
He said they were transported in separate vehicles, inducing fear that they might be killed in a fake police encounter.
"They made me stand on one side and my son on the other, taking us in separate vehicles. When I asked why he was being taken separately, there was no answer. I told my son, 'Son, today might be our last meeting. If we don't meet here, we will meet in the hereafter,'" Khan told the gathering.
The former Rampur MP accused the BJP-led government, jail administration, and enforcement agencies, including the Enforcement Directorate (ED), of subjecting him and his family to extreme atrocities.
He later asked the audience to forgive him if he "misspoke" because of the toll five-and-a-half years in a "dark cell" took on his body, heart, and mind.
Over the past 5 years, Khan got bail in several cases. However, before he could step out of jail, he would be arrested in another case, resulting in an almost unbroken chain of imprisonment.
READ | Akhilesh Yadav Makes Mamdani-Like Promise, Cites A Socialist Ideologue As Inspiration
Earlier this month, he was arrested by the Enforcement Directorate in a money-laundering case on the day he was to walk out of jail on bail in a separate case. The Allahabad High Court later granted him interim bail, which the Supreme Court upheld. "The heavens are not going to fall," the top court remarked.
Since his jailing, Khan has made several cryptic remarks that sparked speculation that his relationship with Yadav soured. In 2022, he said he hadn't met the Samajwadi Party chief for three years.
Yadav, however, later met him in jail on several occasions and publicly opposed his imprisonment.
READ | 'Heavens Won't Fall': Supreme Court Refuses To Pause Azam Khan's Interim Bail
His jail remark notwithstanding, Khan and Yadav presented a united front at the launch of the manifesto.
Khan expressed strong confidence in Yadav's political future.
"Speaking about Akhilesh Yadav today, I can say that he will be Chief Minister again and again, and perhaps even much more. He won't be just here; he will go much further," he added.
