title: Parliament Set to Reconvene on November 30 Amid Delimitation Bill Buzz - The Wire
description: While the BJP-led government’s delimitation-linked Lok Sabha expansion plan to implement women’s reservation was defeated in a special session in April, parliamentary arithmetic has changed since then. Opposition parties have accused the government of assaulting the Constitution by announcing the session on Constitution Day.
author: Sravasti Dasgupta
content: New Delhi: Amidst speculation that the Narendra Modi-led Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government will make a fresh bid to reintroduce its contentious delimitation-linked Lok Sabha expansion plan to implement women’s reservation, the Union government has ended days of speculation about when parliament would reconvene. The dates announced on Thursday (November 26) say that the session will resume on November 30 for “essential government business”.The government’s announcement has come 105 days after the monsoon session was adjourned sine die on August 13. When parliament meets again on November 30, it will be after the longest mid-session gap in history. The sittings will not be part of the winter session but a continuation of the monsoon session, which has not yet been prorogued.In a statement on X, Union minister for parliamentary affairs Kiren Rijiju said that the government has requested the Lok Sabha Speaker and the Rajya Sabha Chairman to “reconvene Lok Sabha on Monday, 30th November, 2026 and Rajya Sabha on Wednesday, 2nd December, 2026”, respectively, to transact essential government business.“Subject to exigencies of the business, the sitting of both Houses may conclude on 3rd December, 2026,” he wrote.The government had used the implementation of the women’s reservation bill to bring in a delimitation-linked Lok Sabha expansion plan, calling it the Nari Vandan Adhiniyam, 2023 (the 128th constitutional amendment Bill). It passed unanimously in parliament in September 2023. It provided for 33% reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and state legislatures but tied it to delimitation following the next census.The Modi government failure to push through a constitutional amendment for the first time in the Lok Sabha also led to the defeat of the accompanying delimitation Bill. The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill did not get the required two-thirds majority of the House. Both these Bills, working together, had sought to make large-scale changes that would not just increase the strength of the Lok Sabha to 850 but fundamentally alter parliamentary arithmetic as well as Union-state relations.Also read: In a First, Modi Govt’s Delimitation-Lok Sabha Expansion Plan Fails in ParliamentCrucially, the 131st Amendment Bill also sought to remove the freeze on delimitation imposed in 1976 and instead provided for the 2011 census to be used to determine the allocation of Lok Sabha seats among states and the boundaries of parliamentary constituencies, by referring to the “latest published census”. Opposition parties had contested this as the 2027 census was already underway.The constitutional amendment had received 298 votes in favour and 230 against, with the government falling short by 54 votes to get it passed.Since then, the BJP-led National Democratic Alliance (NDA) has gained in numbers, following defections in the Trinamool Congress, Shiv Sena (Uddhav Balasaheb Thackeray) and Aam Aadmi Party (AAP). The exit of the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) from the INDIA bloc following the Congress ending its alliance with the party after the Tamil Nadu Assembly elections has also led to speculation about whether the party will vote in favour of any new delimitation Bill.All eyes are also on whether the Nationalist Congress Party (Sharad Pawar), a key member of the INDIA bloc, will support the legislation with MP Supriya Sule saying on Wednesday that the party would support “if it is in country’s interest.”While opposition parties had earlier said that the government had not prorogued the monsoon session because it was attempting to bring the delimitation bill back through a special session, experts said that the session from November 30 will only be a continuation of the monsoon session.“Since the monsoon session has not been prorogued, it will be a continuation of that session,” said former Lok Sabha secretary general P.D.T Achary.‘Assault on constitution’, say opposition partiesMeanwhile, the opposition has accused the Modi government of choosing Constitution Day to announce the session, calling the bid to push delimitation by manipulating a majority.“On the evening of Ambedkar Jayanti on April 14, 2026, the Modi Govt had made the Delimitation Bills public that met their well-deserved fate on the night of April 17, 2026. Now on Constitution Day, after 105 days of Operation Lotus, the Modi Govt announces a special session, hoping that it will get its super-tainted two-thirds majority to pass a Constitution amendment bill,” said Congress MP Jairam Ramesh.“Can there be a great insult to and assault on the Constitution? The fight is on,” he wrote.Communist Party of India (Marxist) MP John Brittas accused Modi of specifically choosing Constitution Day for this announcement, calling it a “dark and shameful chapter in Indian democracy.”“What is being done in the name of delimitation – amalgamation, merger, acquisition and buyout designed to manufacture a majority – is nothing short of an assault on the constitution. The greatest tragedy is that this is unfolding on Constitution Day, seventy-seven years after its adoption. A constitution meant to safeguard the people’s mandate is being manipulated to defeat it,” he said.Rashtriya Janata Dal MP Manoj Kumar Jha accused the BJP of “cooking” the numbers with the “finest cookware available.”

title: ‘Midnight Momo’ is Indie Filmmaking at its Finest  - The Wire
description: Made on a shoestring budget of €4,000, Tenzin Yeshi’s directorial debut was somewhat of a sleeper hit at DIFF 2026.
author: Siddhant Vashistha
content: There is something particularly cruel about being trapped in a shift that never seems to end. In Tenzin Yeshi’s Midnight Momo, this familiar anxiety of working life acquires a science-fiction dimension. Set inside a Tibetan momo restaurant in Queens, New York, the film follows Kunga (played by Yeshi), whose already chaotic closing shift becomes considerably more complicated when a series of unexpected visitors arrive. Then midnight strikes, and Kunga finds himself back at the beginning of the same fifteen minutes.Yeshi’s directorial debut was somewhat of a sleeper hit at the Dharamshala International Film Festival (DIFF) 2026. At the outset, it is all but a time-loop comedy but then it becomes a commentary on Tibetans in exile, immigrants, food, the service industry, and the current state of American politics, and it does so without being hard or corny.Cinematography meets funny dialogueThere are few dull moments in Midnight Momo. This is partly owing to the dialogues that use pop culture and referencing themes of sex, being a worker, the immigrant condition, and food itself. The dialogues stitch the film onto larger issues at times yet the film does not take itself or the audience too seriously. This works in its favour as the monologues indulge in cultural commentary through humour, without being patronising. It also falters at times; some exchanges stretch beyond their natural duration, with monologues occasionally interrupting the film’s otherwise lively rhythm. Nonetheless, the attempt is admirable. Not all the performances are equally assured, and the screenplay sometimes seems more interested in articulating its ideas than allowing them to emerge organically through character and action. Yeshi as Kunga, Rinzin Ngodup as the conflicted yet humorous Kalden, and Stephanie Jeane as Vivian have all delivered breakout performances.The chinks in its acting and dialogue armour are, however, ironed out by its fine cinematography. This is DOP Tenzin Gurmey’s first big project. It has moments of greatness, with a fearlessness for experimentation and trying something new. The film is shot raw on an iPhone and then rendered for 4K viewing. Gurmey’s mobile camera navigates the restaurant’s confined interiors with an energy that recalls theatre as much as conventional filmmaking. The extended takes and restless movements give the film a sense of immediacy, as though the audience were caught inside the same frantic shift as its characters. The camera movements, arrangement and choreography of characters, and lighting in such a small and restrictive space such as a restaurant is probably the highlight of ‘Midnight Momo’. MusicThe background score is another strong suit of the film. The soul-funk jazz beats sit seamlessly on top of the film’s pace. The music not only creates rhythm and colour to it but also adds to its element of amusement. The score is another ode to the film’s indie character as it was made by musician Tomoki Iwata while tending to her toddler. She worked with Yeshi, who she is also married to, to add the music in the post-production of the film, between nap breaks. Yeshi asked her to create some jazz beats, like songs, and she created a dozen for the movie. While some of the songs act as the actual backing soundtrack to the scenes, others have been chopped up and used as moments to highlight certain lines.A political filmFor all the fun it has, Midnight Momo is consciously a political film as going against the tide of commercial cinema and making an indie film is a deeply political act. Then the fact that it is a Tibetan story made by Tibetan Americans is a rare feat. In an interview to FilmHounds, Yeshi said, “I had to do it by myself and that’s why I stepped into the role of writer and director, to create more Tibetan American stories.” The film makes an active attempt at telling us a bit about Tibetan history, the condition of immigrants, Tibetan or otherwise, in the US, and the preservation of said culture abroad. The presence of ICE agents, the way immigrants are harassed, and “the exiled momo condition”. Jackson Heights, with its overlapping immigrant communities provides not merely a location but an essential part of the film’s imagination. The restaurant functions as a temporary refuge, workplace and meeting point, where the boundaries between friendship, obligation and survival are constantly negotiated.Midnight Momo’s gumption given budget constraints and limited resources is remarkable. The film manages to make a lot out of very little. It is especially inspiring for independent filmmakers because it demonstrates that filmmaking does not necessarily require expensive equipment, elaborate sets or industry backing. What it needs is a strong vision, resourcefulness and a story worth telling. Midnight Momo embodies the idea that you don’t need permission or a huge budget to make movies; sometimes, all you need is a phone, a location, a community and the courage to create.Siddhant Vashistha is an independent journalist.

title: In UP Poll Run-up, Adityanath, Maurya Jostle Over CM Face, Mask Ambitions Behind Lotus Symbol - The Wire
description: Both leaders swear by the lotus, but their remarks expose the unresolved contest over who gets to wear the crown after the 2027 polls.
author: The Wire Staff
content: New Delhi: The run-up to the electoral contest in the most populous state is bringing the rivalries within the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) out into the open. Chief Minister Adityanath is vying for a third term while Deputy Chief Minister Keshav Prasad Maurya has said the party might choose someone other than the incumbent.The tug-of-war is evident from their public statements, and the lotus symbol has become a shield for both leaders to voice their ambitions while trying not to cross the red line of ‘party discipline’.Maurya spoke first in the latest round of sparring, when he made the chief minister face appear ambiguous by saying the BJP would seek votes on the lotus symbol and not an individual leader’s face. Adityanath asserted his position in turn, saying, “Who is who and who is not, that is known to all.”Maurya escalated matters, saying the chief minister would be chosen after the elections and that it could be Adityanath or someone else.On Wednesday (November 25), at an ABP event in Lucknow, Adityanath was asked which constituency he would contest from and he said that Gorakhpur had been his seat for very long and he would contest from there if the party wanted him to. He was also asked about the chief minister face, which is code for whether he was likely to remain in the top post next year.Also read: BJP Heads for UP Polls in Disarray, With 209-Candidate ‘Conspiracy’ Exposing Internal MistrustTo this, Adityanath responded with the “everyone knows who is who” barb and also said that the BJP’s lotus symbol was bigger than him. He generalised the remark, saying “all” party leaders would contest under the lotus symbol, effectively shutting Maurya down without naming him.Maurya had said two days earlier that Adityanath was the BJP’s “current” chief minister and that a BJP chief minister “would emerge again” after the polls.“As for who exactly that BJP chief minister will be, that is something decided only after the elections,” he told reporters.“The chief minister will be decided after the elections through the established procedure, under which members of the legislative party elect their leader. It could be Yogi Adityanath or someone else,” Maurya said, as per a Hindustan Times report. He also downplayed the subtext of the war of words, saying the party fought elections led by the prime minister.There is more to the Maurya-Adityanath jostling than personal ambition. The deputy CM belongs to the Kushwaha-Maurya community, an OBC group, and is an important BJP face for this constituency. Meanwhile, Yogi has wooed elite-caste voters by identifying himself as Kshatriya-Rajput.The votes of most Hindu communities, however, are essential for the BJP to secure victories. That is why, even the appearance of a power struggle could be as much a part of the BJP’s caste-balancing exercise as its internal leadership contest.The saffron party has not fielded Muslim candidates for two election cycles in Uttar Pradesh, nor have its attempts to woo voters from sections of the community been viewed as serious. This raises its dependency on Hindu social groups, even as polarisation along communal lines has remained among its primary electoral tactics across the country.

title: 'Beaten, Abused, Denied Water': Protesters Allege Brutality by Delhi Police
description: Students, journalists and lawyers detained during protests demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation allege they were assaulted by Delhi Police in custody. Several also describe religious discrimination by officers.
author: Fatima Khan
content:
(We bring you such stories at great risk to our reporters. Support our work by becoming a member.)
When Dharmendra Goswami, 25, was picked up by the Delhi police from the protests against the Election Commission of India on October 5, he thought that the worst they would do is keep him in detention for a few hours. Instead, Goswami, a student, was thrashed by police officials on his face and limbs at the Parliament Street Police Station, he alleged. When he was being transferred to Delhi Cantt. Police Station, he said, the cops remarked that he “must be a Muslim, here as a paid protestor hired for Rupees 500”. “Remove his pants and check if he is Muslim,” one of the cops in the car said, Goswami alleged. Immediately, the student told them his surname and confirmed that he is not a Muslim but a Brahmin.

title: 'Want to Wait Before Sending Cadre': Is Bhim Army Keeping Away From CJP 2.0?
description: To protest or not to protest? "Our vulnerability cannot become a reason to deny us political agency," an anti-caste activist tells The Quint.
author: Rakhi Bose
content:
"Two police constables deleted my videos and broke my mic. They then detained me after abusing my caste," Vivek Jatav, 24, tells The Quint.
Jatav, a resident of Faridabad, Harayana, had anticipated that Delhi would become a fortress on 10 October, the day of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protest at Jantar Mantar. So he left his home early in the morning of 9 October and reached Delhi, having made arrangements to stay at a "safe" location at night before joining the protest the next day.
He never reached Jantar Mantar, in fact no one did. As per his, and scores of other protesters' and mediapersons' accounts, police had put up barricades extending upto nearly five kilometres of the protest site.
He was on his way to the area, trying to enter from the direction of Karol Bagh, when he claims he saw the police violently assaulting and detaining some people.
"I started filming them. But two cops, they appeared to be constables, came to me and detained me. I don't know what station or force they were from. They put me in a police vehicle that was parked nearby. One of them took my phone and deleted the videos I had shot. They broke my mic and damaged my phone."

title: We Identified the Lathi-Wielding Hindutva Goon Who Says 'Girls Sold for Rs 300'
description: The man brandishing lathis, making hateful and gendered remarks against women protestors is Deepak Sisodia. A self-proclaimed 'gau-rakshak' who claims to be part of the Hindu Raksha Dal, The Quint finds out.
author: Aliza Noor
content:
A huge group of Hindutva groups descended in Central Delhi's Connaught place on 9 and 10 October to disrupt the anti-Gyanesh Kumar protests. The Quint reported from the ground how right-wing mobilised and yet there was little to no police action against them even as they assaulted and harassed protestors in their presence.
One of these men, wearing a tilak and donning an orange scarf, walked around and gave bytes to a few media-persons making remarks like: "Inn cockroacho ko theek kardenge" (we will fix these cockroaches) and making hateful remarks against Congress leader Rahul Gandhi and YouTuber and independent content creator Dhruv Rathee.
Another video of his went viral wherein he said, "Jitne bhi keh rahe hainna ek kachori do samosa...300 mein bik ke aayi hain, hum bhi khareedte hain ladkiya." (All these girls who raised the 'ek kachodi do samosa slogans,' these girls have been sold for Rs 300, we also buy girls). The Quint watched many videos and managed to identify him. He is Deepak Sisodia, a self-proclaimed Gau-rakshak from Faridabad who claims to be part of the Hindu Raksha Dal (HRD).

title: A Bengaluru Mum Turns 100+ Kg of Fabric Waste Into Reusable Birthday Party Decorations You Can Rent
description: Bhavna Kanoria’s Bengaluru startup Matter Party turns textile waste into reusable party decorations for children’s birthdays, with kits from Rs 1,750.
author: Nishtha Kawrani
content:
What’s a birthday party without balloons? For Bengaluru-based entrepreneur and mother of two, Sowmya Jagannath, this was a question she found herself thinking about while planning her daughter’s birthday. She wanted to try something different, but would her daughter feel that something was missing?
Her daughter loves animals, so Sowmya chose colourful fabric decorations in green and earthy shades. Fabric bunting hung across the room, bringing the animal-themed party to life. There were no balloons to inflate or plastic streamers to pull down after the guests left. Instead, the decorations could be packed away and used again at another celebration.
The children had fun, and all of Sowmya’s initial worries turned out to be unnecessary. Neither her daughter nor the other children missed the balloons.
The decorations came from Matter Party, a Bengaluru-based startup that rents out reusable party décor made from post-consumer textile waste. Founded by Bhavna Kanoria in March 2025, it offers themed fabric decorations that families can rent, return and pass on for another celebration, instead of buying new items that may be discarded after a single use.
For Bhavna, the idea began at home, when her own daughter asked for a planet-themed birthday party. The two made buntings from an old sari, finding a way to make the occasion special with fabric they already had.
That small experiment stayed with Bhavna. It would eventually become a business built around a simple question: could celebrations be beautiful, convenient and less wasteful at the same time?
How an old sari sparked a business idea
Bhavna has a master’s degree in English literature, studied interior design and previously worked as a designer. She had also explored ways of making gifting more thoughtful through earlier ventures, including a gift registry service called Giftistree and Scift, a social gifting platform that allowed people to donate to a cause instead of giving physical presents.
The idea for Matter Party, however, took time to develop. After making the fabric bunting with her daughter, Bhavna left it on the back burner for a few years. Towards the end of 2024, she returned to it, thinking about how the same principle could work on a larger scale. Matter Party launched in March 2025.
Her first rental was for a Lohri celebration rather than a birthday party. The booking came through a friend of a friend, giving her an early opportunity to see how the idea might work beyond her own home.
The business now sources post-consumer textile waste through Hasiru Dala, a Bengaluru-based waste management organisation with a textile recovery facility. Bhavna buys discarded fabric by weight, with material sorted by colour, and sends it to a tailoring unit to be stitched into decorations.
“I work on the designs and handle much of the finishing myself, including attaching cords by hand. The leftover scraps are returned to the recovery facility,” she says.
The result is a collection of reusable decorations in around 35 themes, from unicorns and dinosaurs to Superman, Harry Potter, rainbows and rustic-chic themes. Families can mix and match colours to suit their party.
Lightweight and fitted with cords at both ends, the pieces can be tied to existing fixtures without complicated installation.
Once a party is over, the kit is collected and prepared for its next outing. Bhavna irons the fabric, spot-cleans it with soap and water, replaces cords where needed and checks the decorations before they are rented out again.
The aim is to keep the materials in use for as long as possible.
For these decorations to make their way into more homes, Bhavna knew she had to make renting them as easy as possible for busy parents.
What makes parents choose reusable decorations?
When Bhavna began offering reusable party décor, she realised that leading with sustainability did not always persuade people to try it.
“People may not choose it just because it is sustainable,” she explains. For many parents, the first questions are more practical: Will the decorations look good? Will they suit the theme? Will they be easy to put up? Will renting them be worth the cost?
That understanding has influenced how she presents Matter Party. She wants families to choose the decorations for their designs, range of choices and convenience, without feeling that they have to compromise on how their child's birthday party looks. The reduced pricing is another part of making the service accessible.
The startup currently offers two rental options: a Mini Kit for Rs 1,750, which includes 8-10 buntings and fringes, suited to home parties and smaller venues, and a Party Kit for Rs 3,500, with 16-20 buntings and fringes for larger spaces such as clubhouses and gardens. Both kits also include door or backdrop nets, wreaths and a ‘Happy Birthday’ banner. A refundable security deposit is charged separately. Customers can book through WhatsApp, choose a kit and arrange for delivery before their event.
The decorations are collected after the celebration, so families do not have to find storage space for items they may use only once a year.
Bhavna has also tried to make the process of putting up and taking down the decorations simple. The kits arrive ready to use, with cords that can be tied to existing fixtures, and customers can pack them back into the provided bag after the party.
Optional party helpers are also available through a service partner for families who need additional support.
Sowmya found that the rental model made financial sense, too. When she compared the cost with what she had spent buying decorations separately, she realised how quickly individual purchases could add up.
“I had done a calculation of the cost of the balloons and the buntings and all the other stuff that I had bought the previous year, and this was actually cheaper than that. We don't realise because we buy it in parts. One balloon package, one streamer package, then this and that. By the time you add it all up, it actually comes up to the same thing, if not more,” she says.
For Bhavna, this is the kind of shift that could help reusable décor reach more families: it needs to meet their everyday needs as well as help them reduce waste.
'The children don't miss the balloons'
Sowmya has used Matter Party for celebrations built around her children’s changing interests. Along with her daughter’s animal-themed party, her son has had a Harry Potter-inspired celebration in red and black, and the family has also tried a cricket theme.
“The themes will be there, but colours are always the easiest thing to put together in terms of adding that vibe to the party. I love that she has so many different colour options,” she says.
The designs have also drawn attention from other parents. At her daughter’s birthday in September, guests could not stop admiring the décor.
Those conversations have given Sowmya a chance to talk about the idea with other families. An earlier conversation with Bhavna about balloons and the impact they can have on animals had encouraged Sowmya to try celebrating without them.
“I was almost scared because I was like, ‘Oh my God, if I don't have balloons at the party, how will I manage? Will my daughter be okay?’” she recalls.
But the children were happy without them.
“Nobody missed the balloon completely. Sometimes you have to take these steps to experience yourself; a balloon is not everything for a party,” she says.
Shwetha, another Bengaluru-based mother of two girls aged 13 and nine, came to Matter Party for a similar mix of thoughtful design and a more sustainable approach.
“I would try and reuse as much as possible, but having said that, options were limited. So I was very pleased that Bhavna came out with a solution which was a little more comprehensive,” she says.
Shweta has since used the kits for her daughters’ birthdays, including garden and rainbow themes. She likes the range of choices and the convenience of having the décor delivered and collected. A small placard explaining that the decorations are sustainable also gives guests a way to understand the idea.
“Keeping sustainability aside, the design is impeccable. She's thought of various options that you would want to host a party. It's definitely something that people should go for even keeping sustainability outside of it,” Shweta says.
For Bhavna, feedback like this reinforces the importance of making reusable décor attractive and practical in its own right.
Over 100 kg of fabric gets a second life
Since its launch, Matter Party has upcycled more than 100 kg of post-consumer textile waste and catered to 64 parties and events.
For now, the startup operates only in Bengaluru. Bhavna is mindful of the emissions involved in transporting the kits over long distances and does not want expansion to undermine the purpose of the business.
She is also exploring collaborations with party venues, cafés, restaurants and other vendors, along with workshops in schools that could help children understand how celebrations can generate less waste.
The business has grown through repeat customers and word of mouth, but Bhavna knows that making sustainable choices commonplace will take more than one rental service. It also means helping families see that they do not have to give up the excitement or personal touches that make a birthday special.
That change can extend beyond the decorations. Sowmya, for instance, has given plants as return gifts at her daughter’s birthday and has chosen plantable pencils and stationery on another occasion.
Shweta says using the kits has made her think about what else she might change when planning an event.
Bhavna has noticed a similar openness among children in her own family. Her niece and nephew, aged three and six, have started telling their friends to avoid waste. For her, it is a reminder that children can adapt to different ways of celebrating, particularly when those choices are part of the experience from the beginning.
Helping families celebrate with less waste
Bhavna hopes to grow Matter Party without losing sight of what made her start it: the possibility of making a familiar part of family life less wasteful, without making it less joyful.
She does not expect parents to change every habit at once. Choosing reusable decorations, skipping balloons or rethinking return gifts can be a starting point.
“The aim is to make these options feel normal rather than like an extra effort reserved for particularly environmentally conscious families,” she adds.
That is also why she wants to expand through local partnerships instead of simply shipping kits across the country. For her, the way the business operates matters as much as the product it offers.
A birthday party may last only a few hours, but the decorations can be part of many more celebrations. For Bhavna, that is the possibility she wants more parents to discover: the colourful bunting that made one child's birthday special could bring just as much joy to another child, without either family having to buy everything new.
All images courtesy of Bhavna Kanoria and Sowmya Jagannath

title: What Happens to Your Old Clothes? Inside a Mumbai Network Turning 17500 Kg Into Income for Traders & Artisans
description: What happens to your old clothes after you give them away? Inside a Mumbai network connecting discarded textiles with the workers who reuse and resell them.
author: Raajwrita Dutta
content:
“Bhandiwala, bhandiwala.”
For years, the familiar call was part of how 35-year-old Anil Datanini earned a living. Like other bhandiwalas, he collected old clothes, traditionally exchanged for utensils, and sold what could be reused.
He had entered the trade at around 15, following work his family knew well. After moving from Gujarat to Mumbai, he continued sorting textiles and finding buyers for them.
But there was one thing he could never count on: how much material he would find. Some days brought plenty of clothes; on others, hours spent looking for them yielded very little.
That began to change in January 2026, when Anil partnered with Textile Waste Innovation Network (TWIN), a Mumbai-based enterprise founded by 29-year-old Vikram Shahi.
Instead of sourcing everything himself, Anil now receives a more regular supply of used clothes, which he sorts, prepares and sells through markets in villages and rural areas.
“Now the material comes to us regularly, so we can work properly,” he says. “We sort it according to the quality and condition and then send the reusable clothes to villages.”
Anil says he currently earns between Rs 25,000 and Rs 30,000 a month, sometimes more. For him, the greater relief is being able to plan household expenses and save with more confidence.
His experience captures an important part of TWIN's approach.
According to its founder, the network has collected around 17,500 kg of used textiles and reached more than 650 households. It is doing so by working with waghari workers and bhandiwalas, whose experience in collecting and reselling clothes has long kept usable fabric in circulation.
From his mother's cupboard to Mumbai's beaches
When Vikram was growing up in Mumbai, he watched his mother exchange old clothes for steel utensils with a bhandiwala. He understood the exchange, but wondered what happened to those clothes afterwards.
Born in Bihar, with family roots in Sitamarhi, Vikram moved to Mumbai with his parents when he was three.
In 2017, while studying information technology at Mumbai University, he began volunteering at clean-up drives. At Versova beach that monsoon, he noticed clothes mixed in with the plastic waste.
He saw more discarded textiles during subsequent clean-ups, including around festivals such as Holi. In 2019, he began organising drives of his own with support from Bhumi NGO.
The question from his childhood returned: where did damaged clothes go when they were no longer useful to their owners?
In 2022, Vikram enrolled for a master's in social work at the College of Social Work, Nirmala Niketan, Mumbai. A term paper on waste management helped him explore what happens to post-consumer textiles, meaning clothes and other fabrics discarded after use.
“Post-consumer textile waste was not getting the kind of attention I felt it deserved,” he tells The Better India.
The gap became clearer in 2024, when he joined ReCircle as a sales executive. He had initially applied to work in plastic waste management, but was offered a role involving textiles instead.
“At that point, I did not know much about textile waste, but once I started working on it, I realised there was a huge gap in the collection system,” he says.
People had familiar ways of passing on clothes that were still wearable: donating them, giving them to relatives or exchanging them for utensils.
Torn T-shirts, worn-out bedsheets and other unusable fabric were more difficult to deal with. Even where recycling or upcycling options existed, there was no obvious route connecting a household's unwanted textiles to the people who could process them.
A 1,200-kg experiment in the Mumbai monsoon
In August 2025, while working full time on education initiatives, including STEM labs in schools, Vikram and a few friends organised a textile collection drive in Vasai.
They gathered around 1,200 kg of material, despite heavy monsoon rain complicating the collection.
“I was still working at the time, so we were doing this mostly on weekends,” he recalls. “The first drive itself gave us confidence that people actually had this problem and were looking for a solution.”
TWIN was formally registered on 30 October 2025. Vikram continued his job until February 2026, when he began focusing on the enterprise full time.
He wanted to make textile collection easier for households while giving existing recovery workers a more dependable source of material.
“We are not trying to replace the existing recovery network. We are trying to build on it and create a more organised collection layer around it,” he explains.
What happens to clothes after TWIN collects them?
TWIN collects used textiles from households, housing societies, schools, colleges, hotels, companies, NGOs and other bulk generators across the Mumbai Metropolitan Region. Household pickups are described by the enterprise as free.
A resident can request a collection through TWIN's website or WhatsApp chatbot, sharing their name, location and details of the textiles.
The team records the request, including the quantity and type of material, in a customer relationship management system (CRM) before verifying it and assigning a collection partner.
The enterprise works with waghari and bhandiwala workers, providing training, checking backgrounds and assigning collection areas by PIN code. This helps coordinate pickups that were previously handled more informally.
The collected clothes are then sorted by condition, fabric and possible next use.
That step determines whether a shirt can be worn again or whether a damaged bedsheet might be more useful as raw material for another product.
“Sorting is one of the most important parts because every textile cannot go to the same place,” Vikram says. “We look at the condition, quality and what the next best use can be.”
Wearable clothes are prioritised for reuse. Workers sell them through their existing networks in villages and second-hand markets, where buyers, including farmers, can find affordable clothing. A smaller share goes to communities through NGO partners.
Fabric unsuitable for wearing can take a different route.
TWIN sends suitable material to upcycling partners, including The Kapda Project and artisan groups, to be made into bags, pouches and bottle holders.
It also helps connect these products with buyers, including through organisations such as Sparkling Wings and Prayas Foundation.
Lower-grade textiles may be downcycled into mats, rags or wiping cloths for industrial use.
Recycling remains at the pilot stage, with TWIN and its partners testing which materials can be processed further. The network therefore offers several recovery routes, rather than claiming that every collected item becomes a new garment or recycled fibre.
For residents, the idea is straightforward: clothes that have outlived their original use need different destinations.
TWIN says it accepts wearable and torn clothes, bedsheets and curtains, but not wet or soiled material. That distinction matters when someone is clearing out a cupboard and wondering what can actually be collected.
‘Now we get clothes regularly, so there is more work’
TWIN currently works with around 15 to 20 informal textile recovery workers, of whom seven to 10 are connected to a more regular supply.
Some receive around 200 to 300 kg of sorted textiles from the warehouse in a week, while others collect material directly from households.
Anil, who has lived in the Sion-Dharavi area, says this has changed how he organises his work.
Earlier, much of his time went into finding textiles before he could begin sorting and selling them. Now he can spend more of it preparing clothes for buyers.
“We had to go and search for clothes ourselves,” he says. “Sometimes we would get material and sometimes we would not. The supply was not regular.”
For 22-year-old Bhavesh Dattani, the difference feels familiar.
He grew up in Dharavi, where his family continued a clothes-trading livelihood after his grandparents moved from Gujarat.
Before joining TWIN in December 2025, he went from neighbourhood to neighbourhood exchanging utensils for clothes.
“The barter system takes a lot of time. We have to go from place to place and ask people for clothes, and we do not know how much we will collect,” he says.
Now, he receives reusable garments from the team.
“Now we get clothes regularly, so there is more work and the income is also more regular,” he adds.
He does not specify his earnings, but says having material available more consistently has improved his working routine.
Another worker, Vikram Shankar Chekhaliya, about 45, comes from a family in Gujarat that has worked with textiles for generations.
Associated with the initiative since its early stages in July 2025, he had previously sourced, sorted and sold clothes independently, including lower-value fabric used for wiping.
“Sometimes we would get good clothes, and sometimes there would be very little material. Now there is a regular supply, so it becomes easier to plan the work,” he says.
These workers already know how to assess clothing and where it can be sold.
What TWIN is trying to add is a more predictable connection between the households discarding textiles and the markets that can use them.
Who earns what when an old shirt is sold again?
Although household pickups are free, the enterprise earns through the sale and recovery of collected material, as well as service-based work with organisations.
Reusable clothes move through existing traders and markets, allowing workers to earn from their sale. TWIN also generates revenue from recovered textiles.
Upcycled products made by partner artisans create another income stream when they are purchased by organisations or corporate clients.
Lower-grade materials can be sold for uses such as industrial wiping, while business-to-business services add to the model.
“The idea is not just to collect waste and then store it,” Vikram says. “There has to be a value chain after collection. We need to make sure the material moves to the right person or the right organisation and that there is a revenue stream to sustain the system.”
Vikram began with his own resources. TWIN has also received support from Mumbai Ekatra, a citizen-focused grant programme, particularly for its upcycling work.
According to Vikram, the enterprise has generated about Rs 3 lakh in business revenue, with another Rs 3 lakh worth of potential business in the pipeline.
It has yet to turn profitable, he says, with much of its income being put back into building the collection and sorting network.
17,500 kg of clothes collected. What comes next?
The WhatsApp chatbot, launched in June 2026 after TWIN initially relied on Instagram and a Google Form, has made it easier to organise incoming requests.
Vikram says it recorded more than 300 registrations in its first month.
The team can also track where clothes are coming from, how much is collected and which partner should handle each pickup.
Technology helps manage the movement of textiles, but the recovery itself still depends on people who know how to sort, repair, reuse or sell them.
For now, the work is focused on Mumbai. Vikram hopes to expand to other cities, adapting the collection network to the workers, markets and waste patterns already present in each place.
There are challenges ahead. Recycling is still being tested, the enterprise is not profitable and only part of its worker network currently receives a regular supply.
But the model has begun to connect two needs that often sit apart: households looking for a responsible way to part with old textiles, and workers looking for material they can earn from.
For Anil, that connection has a practical meaning.
He still sorts clothes, finds buyers and does the work he has known since his teens.
What has changed is the amount of time he needs to spend searching for the next batch, and the confidence that there will be work to return to.
All pictures courtesy Vikram Shahi.

title: Shot During Kasab’s Arrest on 26/11, This Retd Cop Now Helps Families With Last Rites & Legal Issues
description: Mumbai officer Sanjay Govilkar was shot while helping capture Ajmal Kasab alive on 26/11. He survived, and now serves through books, an NGO and legal help for the vulnerable.
author: Vidya Gowri Venkatesh
content:
On the night of 26 November 2008, Mumbai Police officer Sanjay Govilkar was shot while helping capture terrorist Ajmal Kasab at Girgaum Chowpatty.
Across Mumbai, terrorists were attacking several locations. People across India followed the news from their homes, fearful of what might happen next. Police officers responded across the city, and many lost their lives in the process.
Sanjay survived the bullet injury. Years later, he continues to speak about that night, the colleagues he lost, and the work that has filled his life beyond the police force.
From writing books to helping families through an NGO he founded with friends, he has found different ways to serve people.
The Better India spoke to the former officer about the arrest of Kasab and the experiences that shaped his life afterwards.
‘Unfortunately, he never returned’
“I consider myself very lucky, as the bullet Kasab fired at me hit the left-hand side of my abdomen and not the right,” he smiles.
Around the time of the attacks, Sanjay had been excited about the release of his book, Stopwatch. He was going around his colleagues' desks to distribute copies to everyone.
Shortly before the attacks began in Mumbai, he visited his boss Hemant Karkare's cabin to give him a copy.
“Hemant sir was not there for some reason, so I left a copy for him on his desk. Unfortunately, he never returned,” Sanjay recalls.
The night he helped capture Kasab alive
“As the attack unfolded, we were tense, but we had only one goal: to serve our nation. The moment I heard that my boss, Hemant sir, had been attacked and lost his life, I was upset,” he shares.
Later that night, Sanjay and his fellow police officers confronted Kasab at Girgaum Chowpatty. During the encounter, Sanjay was shot.
“My colleague wanted to immediately shoot him down, but I convinced him to arrest him, as he was a key witness,” Sanjay shares.
Capturing Kasab alive became an important part of the investigation and trial that followed.
“After the arrest, I was immediately rushed to the hospital, where I received treatment for five to six days. I was asked to stay away from the news and was given counselling by a group of doctors. Finally, when I was discharged, I saw that all the noise was settling. My doctors and my family took great care of me,” he smiles.
The experience left Sanjay with a sense of pride in his service, though he is careful to share the credit with his colleagues.
When asked how it feels to have achieved something so significant, he says, “I am extremely proud of serving my country, and I would never want to take advantage of this.”
He goes on to credit his entire team for the recognition.
Why a police officer began writing about health
While Sanjay says that being a cop and serving the country was his duty, he was always driven by another passion away from work: writing.
Sanjay has so far written and published five books, all of them on health, mental health and relationships.
One of those was Stopwatch, the book he had just published when the 26/11 attacks took place.
“At one point in my career, I was posted as an immigration officer at the airport and had erratic shifts. This took a toll on my health and prompted me to write the book Stopwatch. It is a must-read for all people who work night shifts,” he shares.
Sanjay maintains clear boundaries between his profession and passion.
“I never let my professional experiences shape my writing. I incorporate the lessons I have learnt, but never let them influence my writing,” he says.
‘My biggest asset is my close friends’
His friendships have also shaped another important part of his life. Together with his close friends, Sanjay runs Jeevarang, an NGO inspired by a deeply personal experience.
“Twenty-five years ago, I lost my grandmother. She was very dear to me. We cremated her in my village, and the next day, when we visited the site to collect her ashes, we saw dogs feeding on the remains. I was heartbroken by what I saw,” he shares.
The memory stayed with him and became one of the reasons he wanted to help families give their loved ones a dignified farewell.
Through Jeevarang, Sanjay and his friends assist families who have lost their loved ones across 21 villages in Maharashtra. They provide support in cash or kind, depending on what the families need.
The NGO began operations in 2007 and also encourages writers by sponsoring the publication of their books.
A fraud case that inspired his next chapter
Sanjay retired from the police in July 2026. But his interest in helping people facing difficult situations has continued into his retirement.
He now runs his own legal and risk advisory firm.
The idea goes back to a case he encountered during his police career, involving a mother and daughter who lost their livelihood to online fraud.
“I came across a peculiar case in my career in 2009. Online fraudsters tricked a mother and daughter. They were told they had won a lottery and were asked to pay a huge sum of money. The women were innocent and, assuming they would receive a large amount, they sold their small pull-cart shop in Mumbai and lost all their money. The department, however, intervened and cracked the case. This incident stayed with me, and I decided that I wanted to help people who feel stuck in legal issues. That’s when I came up with this idea,” he shares.
The mother and daughter's experience stayed with Sanjay, much like what he had witnessed after his grandmother's cremation years earlier. Both experiences influenced the work he eventually chose to pursue outside policing.
When Sanjay speaks about 26/11, he credits his colleagues for what they achieved together. In the years since, he has continued to act on the concerns that have stayed with him, from helping families arrange a dignified farewell to supporting people facing legal difficulties.
Individuals seeking guidance or assistance with legal matters and risk-related concerns can find information about the services offered by Govilkar Legal & Risk Advisory on its official website. The firm aims to help people understand complex legal situations and consider their next steps.

title: Can Congress Turn Anti-AAP Sentiment Into A Comeback in Punjab?
description: Punjab’s 2027 Assembly election could offer the Congress a path to revival as anti-incumbency against AAP grows and the Akali Dal and BJP struggle to regain ground.
author: Zaid Bin Shabir
content:
On November 4, Rahul Gandhi returned to Punjab, a State where the Congress party has historically known how to sway voters and win elections. Launching the campaign for the Punjab Assembly elections in Sangrur, an Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) stronghold, Rahul attacked the AAP’s record in government and argued that Punjab needed a government that worked for the State rather than being “run from Delhi”.
The rally came at a time when the Congress, the ruling party in only one northern State, Himachal Pradesh, is trying to add momentum to its national-level recovery with a win in a State that had once been its stronghold. Also, after improving its Lok Sabha tally from 44 seats in 2014 to 99 in 2024, the party has increasingly sought to project Rahul as a more assertive opposition leader, taking on the Modi government.
But in Punjab, Rahul’s pitch was not simply an extension of that national campaign. His appeal to sentiments around Punjab’s distinct political identity builds on an older Congress-Punjab relationship.
For much of its post-Independence history, the Congress remained one of the principal political forces in Punjab as its journey intertwined with some of the many consequential changes in the border State. The party’s fortunes declined elsewhere following the BJP’s Modi wave, which swept away many of the Congress’ traditional strongholds after 2014. Yet Punjab, which brought the Congress back to power as recently as 2017, managed to buck the trend.
But voters in this outlier State have always shown little preference for continuity, which often results in the incumbent ruling party’s ouster. This happened in 2022 when the AAP mopped up 92 of Punjab’s 117 Assembly seats. The Congress, with just 18 seats, was roundly defeated. The State’s voters had built a new consensus that created a third political front.
“In 2022, the AAP was the only party that came into the fray without any baggage from the past,” said Sikander Singh, head of Misal Baba Sawan Singh Attari Dharna Dal, a Nihang Sikh group. “The driving force, which persuaded us to vote for it, was the AAP’s Delhi governance model, which had seemingly brought some relief to people there.”
However, with the passage of time, the ground beneath the AAP’s feet shifted. In the 2024 Lok Sabha election, it won only 3 seats while the Congress bagged 7 of the State’s 13 parliamentary constituencies. Growing popular disenchantment with the AAP government, which started drawing criticism well before the general election, was perceived to be the cause of this reversal. From governance issues to religious matters, Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann’s government has repeatedly found itself cornered.
Two years after the 2024 election, the AAP is out of power in Delhi and faces strong anti-incumbency in Punjab. Many observers believe that the situation creates a window for the AAP’s political opponents. With the Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) struggling to recover its lost credibility and the BJP yet to establish a strong political base, political observers believe Punjab might become the first State to witness a Congress resurgence.
‘Price of power’
The AAP came to power promising a break from the politics of the Congress, the SAD, and the BJP. But its track record on its poll promises is severely contested. “People had very high expectations of the AAP,” said Jagrup Singh Sekhon, former professor of political science at Guru Nanak Dev University, Amritsar. “They thought the problem of drugs, gangsterism, law and order, unemployment, and mounting fiscal and agrarian crises would be addressed. But the AAP did not live up to those expectations.”
Popular discontent has coalesced around the problem of drug addiction. The government campaign on the issue, “Yudh Nasheyan Virudh”, was launched with much fanfare but has not yielded the desired results. The ruling party is perceived to be responsible for the mess.
“As we would fight to save our crops, so now we fight to save our generations,” said Sikander Singh. “The AAP promised to end the drug menace. Instead, drugs have become more easily available. Drugs and the AAP have devoured Punjab.”
The political damage has also acquired a consequential religious dimension. The acting jathedar of the Akal Takht, the highest temporal authority of Sikhs, has declared Mann “Guru Dokhi” (betrayer of the Guru) and “Khalsa Panth Virodhi” (anti-Khalsa Panth).
The State government’s record has also been complicated by the increasingly visceral question of who controls the Punjab’s government. The AAP government has been accused of allowing the ruling party’s central leadership in Delhi to exercise an outsized influence over the State. The impression is that the State’s affairs are being dictated by people with little understanding of, or empathy for, Punjab and its people.
Jagtar Singh, a senior journalist based in Punjab, said: “Immediately after the AAP formed the government, the perception in Punjab was that it was being run by people from Delhi. It was an open secret. Punjabis don’t like Delhi dictating the State, but the interference level keeps rising.”
The extent of that disconnect became apparent when Bhagwant Mann vacated his Lok Sabha seat after becoming Chief Minister in 2022. Barely three months later, the AAP lost the Sangrur bypoll. “It showed that the party’s connection with the people began to take a hit from the very beginning,” Jagtar Singh said.
The AAP, fighting to hold on to its last fort, has attempted to make Mann its Punjab face. Another move has been to drop eight sitting legislators, including Agriculture Minister Gurmeet Singh Khudian, in the party’s second list of candidates for the Assembly election, announced on November 12. But the damage, many observers believe, may be hard to reverse.
Sekhon observed: “The damage is already done. Once the Punjab elections are over, I don’t see the AAP continuing as a national party. The AAP may become a marginalised party. That’s the price of power in Punjab.”
The revival bid
Punjab has five principal contenders heading into next year’s election. Each is fighting, in its own way, to recover the political ground it has lost.
The SAD, one of Punjab’s oldest parties, is struggling to reclaim the political space it once occupied almost by default. The Badals’ centralisation of the party weakened its electoral base. Further, its alliance with the BJP—whose centralised model sat uneasily with the SAD’s regional identity—eroded its credibility. By the time the Akalis walked out over the controversial farm laws, they had already ceded much of their Sikh identity or Panthic political space to splinter groups and neo-Panthic forces such as the Akali Dal Waris Punjab De.
The SAD was reduced to three Assembly seats in 2022 and one parliamentary seat in 2024. Other groups filled the vacuum with Waris Punjab De chief Amritpal Singh and independent candidate Sarabjeet Singh Khalsa winning two core SAD strongholds, Khadoor Sahib and Faridkot, in 2024. Sarabjeet Singh Khalsa’s father was one of the assassins of former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi.
Sekhon said: “The BJP has nothing to lose. But if there is any restructuring of the seat-sharing arrangement then the [Shriomani] Akali Dal has a double challenge, and it is already marginalised. People still identify problems [of drugs, corruption, sacrilege, and gangster culture] with its leaders.”
He added: “This accumulation of baggage makes the SAD-BJP reunion as much a risk as a political opportunity.”
The radical political space also appears to be narrowing. “The era of Amritpal [style of politics] has passed,” Sekhon said. “There was a particular momentum in 2024, especially in rural, agrarian constituencies, where voters wanted to teach Arvind Kejriwal and Narendra Modi a lesson and Amritpal became a vehicle for that anger.” His Akali Dal (Waris Punjab De) later contested the Tarn Taran Assembly bypoll but lost.
The BJP has failed to build an independent electoral presence in Punjab, either in seats or in vote share, notwithstanding its 24-year alliance with the SAD. In other States, the BJP has created a record of starting out as a weaker ally to a strong regional party and gradually growing into the dominant force. The did not happen in Punjab.
Ashutosh Kumar, professor of political science at Panjab University, Chandigarh, argued in his study “The 2024 Parliamentary Elections and Punjab Politics: Commonalities, Exceptionalism, and Takeaways” (published in the Journal of Sikh & Punjāb Studies in 2024) that the BJP is likely to remain a force in Punjab despite its electoral setbacks. But its growth, he noted, will depend on whether it can move beyond cultural nationalism and religious mobilisation, take clearer positions on issues concerning Punjab and Sikhs, and shed its anti-farmer image. The party also needs stronger State-level leadership, he argued, as its national leaders have little traction in Punjab and leaders brought in from the Congress, including Captain Amarinder Singh, Sunil Jakhar, and Manpreet Badal, have failed to give it the political momentum it needs.
The Congress, unlike the SAD and the BJP, is not trying to build a new political base. Notwithstanding its crushing 2022 defeat, the party retained a State-wide organisation and a large social coalition. Its seven Lok Sabha seats in 2024 offered enough evidence that voters who abandoned the party in 2022 had not necessarily moved beyond it.
Kumar observed that the Congress has retained a cross-community base that can become electorally decisive if the AAP’s support continues to erode. According to him, the Congress managed to retain its old social base at a time when political loyalties were becoming fragmented in Punjab.
Sekhon explained why the Congress has an advantage: “Today, the AAP is no longer the outsider that promised to disrupt Punjab’s established political order. It is the incumbent defending its record. While others are caught in some major crisis or the other, the Congress has returned to being a principal challenger, its most comfortable role in Punjab.”
The Congress, meanwhile, has sought to contain factionalism by bringing in Sachin Pilot as Punjab in-charge and former Indian hockey team captain and three-time MLA Pargat Singh as State Congress president. “The combination has helped control the strife to a great extent,” Sekhon said.
Harjeshwar Pal Singh, a professor of history, also said that the Congress has a solid base in Punjab. “It has a presence in almost every district, every village, and every mohalla. It has leaders known across the State,” he said. “That is a strength which cannot be created overnight and other parties currently lack it.”
The Punjab edge
This will be the first State election in northern India since the Cockroach Janata Party(CJP) protests forced the Modi government to confront a series of political controversies. The agitation against the former Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan and then the protests over voter exclusions through the Special Intensive Revision have added to the political goodwill of Rahul Gandhi, as Leader of the Opposition in Parliament, and of the Congress as the major opposition party.
Uttar Pradesh, like Punjab, will also go to the polls next year. But in Uttar Pradesh, the Congress remains one among several political players. The BJP, the Samajwadi Party, and the Bahujan Samaj Party all have considerable influence in the Uttar Pradesh contest. Punjab is different.
Politics in Uttar Pradesh is influenced by politics at the national level. In contrast, Punjab has remained more immune to national developments. “Punjab has never been swayed by the ‘national constituency phenomenon’, attempted earlier by the Congress and now by the BJP, both polity wideparties,” Professor Ashutosh Kumar wrote in his 2024 study. “The latter’s repeated attempts to contest elections on national issues like national security, Article 370, citizenship, exalted status of India on the global stage, has not cut much ice in the State. On the contrary, even in the Lok Sabha elections, local issues like drugs, mafia hold, the farming sector distress, have remained decisive.”
He added: “At a time when there has been a growing perception about a large-scale ideological shift from middle to right-wing conservatism, visible in the ascendance of cultural nationalism in the plains and hills of north, central, and western India, Punjab again seems immune from it, despite having a sizeable Hindu population.”
That distinctiveness, in addition to Punjab’s social composition, has created a natural advantage for the Congress. Unlike other political parties, the Congress has usually drawn support across Sikh, Hindu, and Dalit constituencies.
“Punjab, along with Kerala, is a State that is most productive for the Congress because it is a catch-all party,” explained Harjeshwar Pal Singh. “It does not cater to one particular social group. It has historically brought different identities into the same political coalition.”
No room for complacence
The Congress may have emerged as the principal challenger to the AAP, but the voters who want the AAP out still have to decide which party they believe can replace it. This is where this election differs from the 2022 election, as Sekhon explained: “The 2022 election was altogether different. People had an option then that was relatively free of the political record of the established parties. This time, almost all the parties are sailing in the same waters. It’s not a vote for the best party but a choice of lesser evil.”
That difference could have implications for the Congress’ prospects.
“The biggest advantage of the Congress is that it does not have to convince Punjab to accept it as a political force,” said Harjeshwar Pal Singh. “The question is whether it can convince different social and religious groups that they have a common political interest in bringing the Congress back.”
The calculation could also become particularly important among Punjab’s floating voters who have repeatedly shifted their loyalties. “Punjab’s floating voter is not necessarily looking for the party with the strongest ideology,” said Sekhon. “She is looking at which party can actually form the government. Once the voter starts believing that one party has the capacity to win, the floating vote begins moving in that direction.”
That is where the Congress’ rise as the principal opposition becomes electorally significant. It makes the party a plausible choice for voters who want to punish the AAP but may not be entirely sure of whom they want to reward, said Sekhon.
Yet, there is no room for complacence. “The Congress cannot assume that every voter who is unhappy with the AAP will automatically come to it,” said Jagtar Singh. “Punjab has shown many times that people can reject one party without necessarily choosing the traditional alternative. The Congress has to make itself the obvious alternative. If the voter thinks there is uncertainty about the Congress, the anti-government vote can still be divided.”
There is also a limit to what Rahul Gandhi can do for the party. His confrontation with the Modi government and his association with the farmers’ cause have given the Congress an additional political resonance in Punjab. But the Assembly election will eventually be decided on questions of local relevance.
“Rahul Gandhi can create a political atmosphere, but the Punjab election will be fought by the State leadership,” said Harjeshwar Pal Singh. “People will ask who is going to run Punjab, what they will do about drugs, employment, farming, and law and order. The Congress has to give them an answer that is bigger than simply defeating the AAP.”
Indeed, an anti-incumbency vote many not be easy to consolidate. “People in Punjab defeat a party, they don’t elect a party,” said Jagtar Singh. “They can decide that a government has to go without having already decided which party should replace it.”
Zaid Bin Shabir is a journalist based in Srinagar.

title: O.P. Sharma: Remembering India's last pictorialist
description: Exploring the life, experiments and enduring legacy of O.P. Sharma.
author: Rahaab Allana
content:
The revelation, if it comes at all, will come in a small fraction of a second with an unconscious gesture, a gleam of the eye, a brief lifting of the mask that all humans wear to conceal their innermost selves from the world. In that fleeting interval of opportunity the photographer must act or lose his prize. —Yousuf Karsh
A woman emerging through the surface of a painting as if stepping out of a dream; a shipwreck that seems to etch a moment from W.H. Auden’s elegiac poetry; a black cat fixates on the viewer, apparition-like, in a graveyard, much like a frame lifted from a Murakami novella; angular shards of light create anthropomorphic forms at the Ellora caves; supernatural beams of light emanate from a portrait, like in a 1980s sci-fi film poster; as Bismillah Khan is lost in a rhapsodic trance, a musical instrument materialises like a mirage around him. Such is the ethereal image-making of O.P. Sharma, widely regarded as India’s last pictorialist. He passed away on November 6, at the age of 89, in Delhi.
Just a few weeks ago, while viewing “Light and Magic: The Birth of Art Photography” at the Tate Modern in London, I stood enraptured, once again, in front of a work by him from the 1960s. It was profoundly moving to see this master artisan, portraitist, and technical wizard in the company of some of the world’s greatest image-makers. The recognition was timely though long overdue—and yet it left me wanting more. More images and a suitable commendation.
My own deep interest in his oeuvre had been initiated through his 1998 solo exhibition catalogue, presented by Art Heritage gallery in Delhi, authored by the prolific critic of his time, K.B. Goel. Later, in 2010, pictorialism as a field became a disciplinary concern, while I was co-curating “The Artful Pose: Early Studio Photography in Mumbai (c. 1855–1940),” which included atmospheric images from the 19th and early 20th centuries, at the city’s Dr. Bhau Daji Lad Museum. And finally, in 2020, after persistent efforts, and some absurd coincidences (there was another younger artist of the same name at Triveni Kala Sangam whom I had mistakenly scheduled to meet), I was extremely privileged to have, finally and formally, encountered “O.P.” at his home in Bharati Artists’ Colony in Delhi’s trans-Yamuna area.
Interestingly, the colony came into being some decades after artists resettled in Delhi post-Partition; among them were B.C. Sanyal, Kanwal and Devayani Krishna, Dhanraj Bhagat, and P.N. Mago, who in 1949 founded the Delhi Silpi Chakra, a mutual-aid society and salon for artists (Satish Gujral and Richard Bartholomew would join it later). Born from a desire to retreat from the city centre, the colony paired homes with attached studios to give artists an ideal environment for creative productivity.
Nervously excited at the prospect of an engagement with the genius, I arrived for our meeting accompanied by my friend, Srinivas Kuruganti, former photo editor of TheCaravan. O.P. ji sat at one end of the living room, lamplight illuminating his profile; on the wall next to him was a garlanded photograph of his late wife/creative partner, Chitrangada, daughter of the very same noted modernist artists, Kanwal and Devyani Krishna. Surrounded by black-and-white prints, photo catalogues and books, he was peering intently at a newspaper article. He looked up at us from under those distinctive bushy eyebrows, smiled a welcome. Srinivas soon started filming. O.P. spoke about photography as the bedrock of his personal and professional life, ending almost every sentence with a mild ironic “samjhe?” (do you understand?) For many months, Srinivas and I contemplated whether he had endearingly named us “Sanjay”.
What attracted me most to O.P.’s thought and ethic was his unwavering conviction that photography as a craft and profession was most intensively developed by the passionate, dedicated, largely self-taught practitioner. As he remarked in a 2020 interview (to Diva Gujral), “Pictorial photography is the mother of all branches of photography”; and its biggest contributors are amateurs “who spend their time, money, energy and their life to discover new things”. And he was absolutely firm on how images should be “made”—not just “taken”—and developed: as analogue prints, with each frame pictorially conceptualised before the shot, and with desired effects created in the darkroom.
****
Over the years, it was clear that O.P. ji needed to be adequately recognised. And so, immersive discussions began in connection with the Alkazi Foundation’s planned tribute (in partnership with Art Heritage gallery) to his work at Shridharani Gallery in Delhi, in an exhibition titled “O.P. Sharma and the Fine Art of Photography: 1950s-1990s” (2024). This moment brought us—Sukanya Baskar (the assigned lead curator) and me (her collaborator)—into close contact with O.P. time and again, and to those nearest to him, his son and daughter-in-law, Aseem Sharma and Mohita Junnarkar, dedicated and loving caregivers.
After each session we were treated to delicious cutlets and samosas from a Nathu’s outlet in the neighbourhood. It was very rewarding to eventually open his show on Teacher’s Day, in the very same gallery which had hosted his first exhibition in 1963. O.P. eventually spent days at the exhibition, interacting with former students and conducting walkthroughs. We observed how he had touched the lives of so many in the city. They all came to pay their respects and absorb his astute observations on image-making.
Fascinating insights
Discussions with O.P. ji yielded fascinating insights. O.P.’s engagement with the medium began in 1954, inspired by the work of Armenian-Canadian photographer Yousuf Karsh (opening quote) at an international exhibition hosted by the UP Amateur Photographic Association in Lucknow. During his university studies there, a physics professor taught him to develop black-and-white film, triggering his lifelong obsession with the darkroom and technical experimentation; he gave up fine arts and committed himself to photography. “My interest grew, and eventually, my naani [maternal grandmother] presented me with a twin-lens reflex German camera but she also told me she could not spend any more money on this. Therefore, I used to walk from my home to the college, to save four annas to buy film and paper,” O.P. recalled in a 2018 interview. He learnt aspects of the craft from senior members of the Lucknow Camera Club.
Arriving in Delhi in 1958, O.P. ji joined Modern School as a teacher; he set up its photography unit and darkroom, and began a four-decade career during which he trained generations of students and furthered his own professional excellence. His future father-in-law, Kanwal Krishna, taught art at the school; its director, the prolific M.N. Kapur, himself an enthusiastic lensman, was an anchor. The Kapur daughters, Geeta (later a renowned art critic) and Anuradha (later a renowned theatre director) posed for O.P., who spent endless hours in his studio and the school darkroom, absorbed in technical experiments. Modern School is just down the road from Mandi House, Delhi’s hub of cultural venues where greats from every discipline—theatre, classical music and dance, literature, visual arts—regularly performed; concerts were also frequently held on the school campus. O.P. photographed many virtuosos on stage and invited them to his studio to sit for portraits—portraiture was a genre in which his skills found sublime expression.
O.P.’s Rasa Bhava Darshan project—an extended collaboration with the veteran Bombay theatre/film actor Sajjan Lal Purohit, completed in phases between 1960 and the mid-1970s— drew on Manmohan Ghosh’s translation of Bharat Muni’s Sanskrit treatise Natya Shastra to visualise the eight primary rasas and 49 bhavas of classical Indian aesthetics as a photographic portrait series. Working with scholar/dramaturge Brij Vallabh Mishra, Sajjan posed while O.P. photographed; the massive suite of images was entirely shot in the actor’s home.
A selection was exhibited between 1979 and 1980. In the exhibition brochure, O.P. described his use of Miranda and Asahi Pentax 35mm cameras, 500-watt photoflood lamps, and natural light to play with tonal values of grey; the images were finalised in a Kodak D-23 developer, and printed on Agfa-Gevaert paper. This stunning series was published as a book in 1998, and was meant to be rendered as a 25-minute film on 16 mm, incorporating paintings by Ram Kumar. It was through Sajjan that O.P. and Chitrangada found work in the Indian film industry; the couple created publicity stills for Do Boond Pani (1971); Siddhartha (1972); Chhupa Rustam (1973); and Shalimar (1978).
From 1980 onwards, O.P. ji and Chitrangada directed the Camera Art Institute at Triveni Kala Sangam, the holistic arts institution at Mandi House, conceptualised in 1950 by Sundari Shridharani and Uday Shankar. O.P. ji soon joined, and directed his pedagogy towards both theory and practice, especially printing and technical processes. Photographer Chandan Gomes, a former student, recalls “looking up in awe at a quiet, scholarly gentleman” with “immaculately combed hair, a gentle smile and a piercing gaze”, who “spoke with a calm certainty that made you listen to him with complete concentration” (“Remembering the Photographic Legacy of O.P. Sharma” by Chandan Gomes, published in Critical Collective on October 24, 2024).
Echoes of Surrealism
The restrained demeanour belied O.P.’s rigour; he was a perfectionist and formidable taskmaster, and those who could not grasp principles of optics to the required high level failed the course. Sifting one day through the papers in his studio with Sukanya Baskar, we found pages liberally marked in red ballpoint, with words and phrases enthusiastically circled and underlined.
Through the 1980s, he explored camera-less techniques of image production: controlling light or using chemicals to imprint photosensitive paper and create photograms, photomontages, sodium sulphite prints and collages. This radical experimentation echoed Western movements of the 1920s such as Surrealism and New Vision, and O.P. became known for his invention of what he called the “C-effect”, which produced distinct swirl patterns and infused the image with movement. He also wrote do-it-yourself instruction manuals in English and Hindi. And to O.P. goes the credit for having August 19—the day the French government officially announced the invention of the daguerreotype by chemist-artist Louis Daguerre in 1839—declared as World Photography Day in 1991. He had personally written to as many as 200 photographic societies, artists, and institutions around the world to gain support for this cause.
Along with technological innovation and teaching, and in alignment with his belief in his medium as a social and cultural good, O.P. devoted much time and energy to founding photography groups in different cities and promoting their work. These included the Amateur Photographic Society of Agra (1959), the Foto Arte Group (1974), and the India International Photographic Council (IIPC), established in 1983 and active to this day. The IIPC organised educational workshops, published a monthly journal, and created spaces for discussion, critique and documentation, thus ensuring custodianship of pictorialist legacies.
This last-mentioned endeavour acquired great significance in the context of the intense ongoing debate between Indian photographers and photojournalists about the primacy of genre: the value, necessity, and relevance of documentary realism versus those of pictorialism. Jury members of the First Indian Biennale of Photography, organised by the Lalit Kala Akademi in 1989, included O.P.’s close associate T. Kasinath, the then Director of the Photo Division of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, who actively pushed for the recognition of pictorial photography. However, submissions to the Second Indian Biennale of Creative Photography in 1993, in which O.P. participated, clearly indicated that despite methodological and thematic expansion, pictorialism as an aesthetic choice was now on the wane.
O.P. had long considered contemporary photography to be awash with misconceptions—about the digital era, about rules of composition, about the intricate analogue grammar now seemingly lost to point-and-shoot generations. “If a photograph is technically poor, it is only half a photograph. Unless you understand each and every part of the photographic process—from pressing the shutter to producing the final print—you can’t produce a good image,” he declared in a 2018 interview. Kodak founder George Eastman’s famous tagline, “You press the button, we do the rest”, was read by O.P. as an admission that many of us do nothing but mechanically press buttons.
The last few years have been special. I was honoured to guest-edit Aperture magazine’s Delhi issue in 2021, titled Looking Out, Looking In. The master’s dazzling, mesmeric portrait of Geeta Kapur, embodying both his technical virtuosity and creative philosophy, was selected by the Aperture editors for the cover. “A photograph on its own is like an uncut diamond,” he remarked as we reviewed captions for his 2024 tribute show. “Only when you understand every part of the photographic process—as Ansel Adams and Edward Weston did—and refine and polish the stone, does it become a Kohinoor!”
Rahaab Allana is Curator/Publisher, Alkazi Foundation for the Arts, New Delhi.
