custody, and what are its constitutional consequences.Without expressing any opinion on merits, the bench disposed of a plea by the KUWJ about the alleged detention and manhandling of seven journalists and relegated them to the court-appointed inquiry committeeOn Thursday, the apex court disposed of a plea by the KUWJ concerning the alleged detention and manhandling of seven journalists, relegating them to the court-appointed inquiry committee without expressing any opinion on merits.Earlier, the Delhi Police in its affidavit stated that social media influencers, content creators and reel makers would not get the same protection as accredited journalists.The Delhi police argued that content creators are not covered by the Supreme Court’s earlier directive exempting media personnel from restrictions imposed by the Delhi Police to regulate the movement of those present at the protest sites.“The Delhi Police has, at no point, sought to obstruct, impede or interfere with the bona fide discharge of journalistic duties, whether during the protests in question or otherwise,” said the affidavit filed by the Delhi police.The Wire had previously reported that over October 10 and 11, the Delhi Police detained journalists from across mainstream and independent media as they attempted to cover protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.Journalists covering the demonstrations were stopped, dragged by the police and shoved into buses and taken to holding locations including Chhatrasal Stadium, regardless of whether they displayed press cards. This, despite the Supreme Court saying on October 11 that journalists cannot be stopped from working.Reporters Without Borders has noted that at least 16 journalists were detained on October 10 alone, with around a dozen more detained the following day.The Wire has maintained a list of named journalists detained across both days, October 10 and 11, 2026, which can be read here.The petitions on the issue before the Supreme Court include those by the Network of Women in Media, India, Free Speech Collective, Delhi Union of Journalists and Kerala Union of Working Journalists.

title: Behind the Bisleri Scare: How Do Carcinogens End Up in Drinking Water?
description: From water treatment to packaging, understand how chemical contaminants can affect packaged drinking water and what safety standards are in place.
author: Raajwrita Dutta
content:
You twist open a sealed bottle of water and drink without a second thought. It's clear, it's sealed, and it's been purified.
Behind that bottle is more checking than most of us realise. Since November 2024, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has treated packaged drinking water as a "high-risk" food. The label doesn't mean the water is dangerous. It means the product gets stricter scrutiny: inspections before a licence is granted, annual inspections, and regular testing of both the water and its packaging.
Those checks exist because some things in water can't be seen, smelt or tasted. A recent case shows why they matter.
FSSAI has sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International Pvt Ltd after a water sample from its Goa plant was declared unsafe. The sample reportedly contained bromate at 12 micrograms per litre, above the limit of 10. A referral laboratory later also found polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, or PAHs.
Bisleri disputes the findings. It says independent testing found bromate within the limit, that its water is safe, and that it will cooperate with the regulator.
Whatever the outcome, the case raises a question most of us have never thought to ask: if water has been purified, how can chemicals linked to cancer end up in it?
Here's what bromate and PAHs are, how they get into water, what levels are considered acceptable, and what the rules say about keeping them out.
What happened at Bisleri's Goa plant?
On 30 September 2025, FSSAI officials collected six samples from Bisleri's Goa facility. According to the company, five met the standards. The sixth showed bromate at 12 micrograms per litre, two above the limit.
Bisleri says it appealed on 22 November 2025, and the sample went to a referral laboratory. That lab found bromate within the limit, but detected PAHs.
Bisleri also had the same sample tested at an FSSAI-approved lab, which it says found bromate within the permitted limit. It sent those results to FSSAI's Western Regional Office on 2 February 2026. After that, the company says, it heard nothing more and assumed the matter was closed.
FSSAI, however, declared the sample unsafe and sanctioned prosecution under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. It has also said it plans to test more samples from Bisleri and other packaged water companies.
A prosecution sanction is not a conviction. And because the labs reported different results, it matters to separate what each test actually found from what is still disputed.
How does bromate get into water?
Surprisingly, bromate often comes from the very step meant to make water safe.
Many bottlers disinfect water with ozone, a powerful gas that kills bacteria and viruses. But some water sources naturally contain bromide. When ozone meets bromide during treatment, the reaction can produce bromate. The World Health Organization (WHO) says this treatment process, called ozonation, is the main reason bromate shows up in drinking water. Normally, it isn't found in water in any significant amount.
How much forms depends on four things:
- how much bromide was in the water to begin with
- how much ozone is used
- the water's pH (how acidic or alkaline it is)
- how long treatment runs
Get the balance wrong and levels can climb. The WHO has recorded bromate anywhere from under 2 to 293 micrograms per litre in ozone-treated water.
Bromate can also form when chlorine-based disinfectants are produced using salt that contains bromide impurities.
So bromate in water doesn't necessarily mean the source was polluted. It can be a by-product of cleaning the water, which is why the treatment process itself needs close watching.
How much is too much?
Bromate worries scientists because it caused cancer in laboratory animals.
The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classifies potassium bromate as Group 2B, or "possibly carcinogenic to humans". Its 1999 review found strong evidence of cancer in animals, but not enough evidence in humans.
That difference matters. A chemical being a possible cancer hazard doesn't mean every exposure carries the same risk. How much is present, and for how long someone is exposed, both count.
The WHO's provisional limit for bromate in drinking water is 10 micrograms per litre (0.01 milligrams per litre). India's standard for packaged drinking water, BIS IS 14543:2024, also lists bromate as a chemical that must be tested.
In the Bisleri case, 12 micrograms is two above the limit. That's a regulatory concern, but it doesn't mean anyone who drank the water will develop cancer or fall ill. Judging the real risk would need three things: how concentrated it was, how much someone drank, and for how long.
Two things are true at once. Detecting a chemical doesn't automatically make water unsafe, because it's the amount that counts. And staying within the limit doesn't mean manufacturers can stop checking.
What are PAHs, and how do they get into water?
PAHs are a large family of chemicals, built from two or more linked rings of carbon atoms. They form mainly when things don't burn completely, such as coal, wood, petrol and other organic material. Vehicle exhaust, factory emissions and other burning release them into the air and the environment.
PAHs don't dissolve easily in water. Instead, they tend to cling to tiny particles. According to the WHO, one known route into drinking water is the coal-tar coating used inside older water pipes to stop them corroding. Pollution from burning can also settle on soil and water, and wash into water sources as runoff.
One PAH, benzo[a]pyrene, is a particular concern because it can cause cancer. The WHO's limit for it is 0.7 micrograms per litre. But PAHs are not all alike. One compound causing cancer doesn't mean they all carry the same risk.
Finding PAHs in a sample also doesn't tell us how they got there. In the Bisleri case, we would need to know which compounds were found, and in what amounts, to judge how serious the finding is or where it came from.
What about the plastic bottle?
Bromate comes mainly from treatment, not the bottle. But scientists have looked at whether chemicals can leach from packaging into water.
A 2022 study in the Bulletin of Environmental Contamination and Toxicology tested PET bottles and low-density polyethylene water packets in India. It found that the amount of plasticisers seeping into water depended on the packaging material, how long the water was stored and how hot it got.
Leaching was higher at high temperatures, especially in recycled PET bottles and plastic packets. That's a good reason to pay attention to packaging and storage. But the study looked at phthalates, not bromate or PAHs, so it doesn't show that bottles caused either contaminant discussed here.
What checks are already in place?
Under FSSAI's 29 November 2024 order, packaged drinking water is a high-risk food category. This means:
- manufacturers must be inspected before they get a licence or registration
- inspections happen once a year
- centrally licensed manufacturers need an annual third-party food safety audit by an FSSAI-recognised agency
From 1 January 2026, a new FSSAI testing scheme also requires manufacturers to:
- test their source water at FSSAI-notified, NABL-accredited labs before using it, and test any new source before it's used
- test for microbes every month, and for several chemicals every quarter
- test every parameter in the standard at least once every six months
- test monthly if a parameter fails, until three batches in a row pass
The packaging is covered too. Bottles, jars and caps must be tested every six months for "overall and colour migration", meaning whether material or colour seeps from the packaging into the water. Manufacturers must keep these records for inspection.
How does a failed sample end up in court?
The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, sets out the steps (Sections 42, 46 and 47):
- A Food Safety Officer collects a sample and sends it to a Food Analyst, who usually has 14 days to report.
- If the manufacturer disputes the result, it can appeal to the Designated Officer, who can send the sample to a referral laboratory.
- If the findings show a violation serious enough to prosecute, the case goes to the relevant authority for sanction.
In the Bisleri case, the company challenged the first result, the sample went to a referral lab, and FSSAI then sanctioned prosecution. Bisleri's independent results and its response are part of a dispute that will now be settled through the regulatory and legal process.
Should consumers be worried?
Chemical contaminants can't always be detected by taste, smell or look. Clear water isn't necessarily free of chemicals.
But the Bisleri findings concern one regulatory sample. They don't prove that all packaged water, or every batch from the company, is unsafe.
Safe drinking water depends on consistent testing and monitoring. Purification is non-negotiable, but the chemicals that can form during treatment, and contamination from storage and pipes, deserve just as much attention.

title: Kerala Orchid Conservation: 27,000 Orchids Rescued, 71% Survive
description: Kerala researchers rescued 27,324 native orchids threatened by road development and relocated them to three sites in Kozhikode. A 2026 study recorded 71.4% survival, highlighting how orchid rescue and relocation can support biodiversity conservation.
author: Sriroopa Dutta
content:
When trees along a road are marked for felling, the loss extends beyond their shade and canopy.
For thousands of orchids growing on their trunks and branches, the removal of a single tree can mean losing their entire habitat.
In Kozhikode, Kerala, researchers faced this challenge as road-widening projects threatened mature trees supporting native orchids. Instead of allowing the plants to be lost along with the trees, they began rescuing and relocating them to other landscapes.
A study published on 15 October 2026 in the scientific journal Plants has now documented the outcomes of this effort.
Researchers assessed 27,324 native orchids belonging to 21 species that were relocated to three sites in Kozhikode. After monitoring them for 12 to 24 months, they found that 19,511, or 71.4%, had survived.
Why roadside trees matter to orchids
Unlike terrestrial orchids that grow in soil, epiphytic orchids grow on the trunks and branches of other plants.
They use trees as support, relying on their bark, moisture, shade and surrounding canopy conditions to survive. When a mature host tree is felled, the orchids growing on it can lose their habitat at once.
The scale of this dependence is evident from an earlier survey in Kerala.
A 2025 study, Distribution and Abundance of Native Orchids on Roadside Trees in a Global Biodiversity Hotspot, recorded nearly 10,000 orchids belonging to 13 species on approximately 600 trees across Wayanad. The trees represented 72 different taxa, and the orchid population included six regional endemics.
The October 2026 study notes that road construction and widening have increasingly threatened these mature host trees and the orchid communities they support.
The researchers involved in the latest study included Mithun Venugopal and Pradeep N Sukumaran of the KSCSTE-Malabar Botanical Garden and Institute for Plant Sciences in Kozhikode, and Viswambharan Sarasan of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, in the UK.
More than 17,000 native orchids representing 22 species had initially been transferred to Sarovaram Biopark as part of the earlier rescue programme.
The subsequent effort also involved relocating orchids to two other sites: the Malabar Botanical Garden and Kappad Beach.
Three sites, different survival outcomes
The researchers examined how the rescued plants adapted to three distinct environments, all located in Kozhikode's coastal region.
Sarovaram Biopark, an urban wetland with mangrove cover, provided a humid and relatively sheltered environment. The Malabar Botanical Garden offered a mix of shaded, marshy and moderately elevated areas.
Kappad Beach, meanwhile, exposed the orchids to stronger winds, direct sunlight and salt spray.
The differences were reflected in their survival. According to the study, Sarovaram recorded the strongest overall establishment, while the exposed coastal location presented greater challenges for the plants to take root and survive.
However, Kappad recorded the highest flowering rate among surviving orchids, at 35.6%.
It also had the highest proportion of flowering plants producing capsules, at 62.3%. At Sarovaram, the corresponding figures were 26.3% and 34.8%, while the Malabar Botanical Garden recorded 27% and 40.1%, respectively.
What the findings mean for conservation
The study also examined 6,126 rescued orchids belonging to 12 regionally endemic species. Of these, 3,368 survived, translating to a survival rate of 55%.
The group included eight species endemic to India and four shared between southern India and Sri Lanka.
This was lower than the overall survival rate of 71.4%, highlighting the additional challenges involved in relocating species with more restricted natural distributions.
The researchers found that some high-altitude and mist-forest-associated orchids also managed to survive and reproduce after being moved to lower elevations, although their establishment depended more on the receiving site.
Orchids of India Calanthe biloba Lindl. #Orchids #India #Conservation #Biodiversity @ForestDeptt @Sdg13Un https://t.co/mZDyHDj2Mc
— Dr. Sanjeet Kumar (Ecologist) (@BiotechSanjeet) October 19, 2026
Beyond survival, the researchers also looked at whether the rescued orchids could reproduce in their new surroundings. They found capsules containing embryos among the relocated plants, indicating that some had progressed beyond simply adapting to their new locations.
However, the team stresses that relocation is not a substitute for protecting natural habitats. It is an additional conservation measure for situations where the removal of orchid-bearing trees cannot be avoided.
Before a tree is marked for felling to make way for a wider road, there may be dozens of plants growing quietly on its trunk and branches. For orchids, the loss of that tree can mean the loss of an entire habitat. Identifying these plants before construction begins can make room for infrastructure without overlooking the smaller ecosystems that depend on the trees being removed.

title: Eurasian Otters in Kashmir: New Study Documents Their Return After Decades
description: Eurasian otters are reappearing in Kashmir after decades. A new 2026 study documents sightings across the Lidder, Rambiara and Sindh rivers and examines the conservation challenges facing the species.
author: Sriroopa Dutta
content:
This story is part of The Better India’s new wildlife series, Species in Focus: 52 species. 52 stories. 52 reasons to protect India’s wildlife. One species at a time, the series explores India’s rare, endangered and lesser-known wildlife, their habitats, behaviour, ecological roles and conservation status.
For years, the sight of an otter swimming through Kashmir's rivers had become rare.
Once found across the Jhelum River basin, the Eurasian otter (Lutra lutra) had nearly disappeared from the valley, its numbers declining amid fur-driven poaching, habitat destruction and water pollution.
Now, after decades of little evidence of its presence, the elusive mammal is being spotted again in Kashmir's waterways.
A study published in the journal Biological Diversity on 23 October 2026, titled Re-Emergence of Eurasian Otter (Lutra lutra) in the Valley of Kashmir, India: A Conservation Triumph and a Challenge, documents recent sightings and field evidence of the species in the valley.
Authored by Irfan Khursheed Shah and Sohail Ahmad Wagay, the study brings together reports that suggest the otter is reappearing after decades of near-local extinction.
The researchers identify historical hunting for fur, habitat destruction, and water pollution as major reasons behind the species' decline.
Srinagar had once served as a commercial centre for the valley's pelt and fur trade. Although wildlife protection measures introduced from the late 1970s onwards helped curb hunting and the trade, the otter population had already fallen sharply.
The return was first noticed in 2025
According to the October 2026 paper, the first widely reported public evidence of the otter's return emerged in June 2025, when a video of an animal in a tributary of the Lidder River went viral.
Viewers initially mistook it for a crocodile.
The researchers say that professional enhancement of the footage helped establish that the animal was a Eurasian otter, a species that had become unfamiliar to many residents.
Following the video, camera traps were installed along the Rambiara and Lidder tributaries in July 2025.
Although these did not capture the animals, researchers photographed spraints (otter droppings), which can help establish an animal's presence in an area.
Another video subsequently surfaced from Ganderbal district, showing an otter feeding on a fish in the Sindh stream, another tributary of the Jhelum. Together, these records provided evidence of the animal's presence across different parts of the valley.
The findings also build on earlier field research. A separate study published in the IUCN/SSC Otter Specialist Group Bulletin in January 2026 documented Eurasian otters in the Hirpora Wildlife Sanctuary, along the Rambiara River catchment in Shopian district.
The Wildlife Trust of India researchers Tanushree Srivastava, Manvi Singh, Muneeb Nazir and Ishwar Narayanan, along with Sohail Ahmad Wagay of the J&K Department of Wildlife Protection, recorded an initial direct sighting during fieldwork in March 2024. They subsequently conducted a systematic survey between April and June 2025, covering a 12-km stretch of the river.
The team recorded 21 signs of otter presence, including one direct sighting, spraints, pugmarks, tracks, fish-feeding remains, and camera-trap photographs.
The study reported an average encounter rate of 0.34 signs per kilometre and a camera-trap capture rate of 4.31 captures per 100 trap nights.
However, neither study establishes the total number of otters now living in Kashmir Valley.
Why the return matters for freshwater ecosystems
The Eurasian otter is classified as Near Threatened on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List.
It is a semi-aquatic mammal that inhabits rivers, streams, and other freshwater environments. As a top predator, it helps regulate prey populations and is considered an indicator of freshwater ecosystem health.
A separate finding from the Hirpora study also points to the importance of involving local communities in conservation. Only 15% of respondents recognised the Eurasian otter, although 92% supported its conservation.
More than half reported declining fish populations in the area, indicating potential ecological pressures that also affect otter habitats.
What could threaten their return?
The October study cautions that the conditions in Kashmir's waterways have changed considerably since the period when otters were commonly reported.
Urban expansion over paddy fields, conversion of agricultural land into apple orchards and construction along riverbanks have reduced and fragmented potential habitats. The decline in traditional irrigation canals has further affected the network of waterways available to the animals.
The researchers also identify river pollution from heavy metals, pesticides, microplastics, and plastic waste as potential threats.
Destructive fishing practices involving chemicals and electric currents, human disturbance and the increasing presence of stray dogs could further affect their survival.
We are into the middle stage of our ’13 Weeks of Otters’ series, and next up we have one that the IOSF are very familiar with, the Eurasian Otter! Photo by Terry Evans! #Conservation #Eurasian #Otter #Wild https://t.co/NBY5RQ0ZNR https://t.co/CklFyxizXv
— International Otter Survival Fund (IOSF) (@IOSF) August 8, 2022
Climate change presents another challenge.
Changes in water levels, floods, landslides and prolonged dry spells can damage or expose the sheltered riverbank spaces, known as holts, where otters rest and raise their young. The researchers also flag the possibility of conflict with expanding trout farms, which are an increasingly important source of livelihood in the valley.
What conservation efforts need to focus on
The October 2026 paper recommends a coordinated conservation plan involving researchers, wildlife authorities and conservation organisations.
This includes protecting and improving river habitats, addressing pollution, preventing hunting and monitoring the species across its newly documented locations.
It also calls for public awareness campaigns to address misconceptions about otters.
The researchers recommend educational initiatives in schools, awareness material in local languages and outreach at tourist destinations to help residents recognise the species and understand its behaviour.
The authors note that otter encounters rarely result in harm to humans globally, and that most interactions are neutral.
Better public understanding, therefore, is an important part of ensuring the animals can persist in waterways shared with people.
For now, the recent records establish the Eurasian otter's presence in Kashmir's river systems, rather than a confirmed recovery of its population.
Sustained monitoring and protection of these freshwater habitats will be necessary to determine whether the species can establish a lasting presence in the valley.

title: India’s Healthcare Crisis: Why Quality and Accountability Fail
description: India’s healthcare system boasts world-class hospitals, yet diagnostic errors, unsafe medicines and commercial interests expose deep inequalities. Who protects patients? Demand accountability.
author: Ameer  Shahul
content:
In his review of Congress leader Sonia Gandhi’s Belonging: A Journey of Love in a Malayalam newspaper, A.K. Antony, former Defence Minister, recounted a personal experience. A prolonged spell of weight loss had led him to consult four premier hospitals, including the prestigious All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi. He was diagnosed with cancer in 2014. Before starting treatment, he informed Sonia about it. She advised him to wait and facilitated an urgent medical consultation in the US. The subsequent assessment attributed his weight loss to protein deficiency rather than cancer. In the review, Antony thanked Sonia for helping him avoid what could have been an expensive, painful, and entirely unnecessary course of cancer treatment.
Sonia herself had chosen to undergo surgery to remove a precancerous growth in her pancreas at the University Medical Centre in Rotterdam, even though, she asserts in the book, she had complete confidence in the doctors who treated her breast cancer at Sir Ganga Ram Hospital in New Delhi in 2010.
Their narratives raise deeply uncomfortable questions about the reliability of medical diagnosis in India. Four hospitals, including one of the country’s foremost tertiary-care institutions, and two superspeciality private hospitals, apparently failed to identify the underlying problem in Antony’s case. Remember this was not an ordinary citizen struggling to navigate an unfamiliar healthcare system. Antony was Defence Minister at the time, with access to the country’s most distinguished medical professionals and institutions.
What, then, is the experience of the millions of ordinary Indians who have neither the resources nor the connections to seek a second opinion abroad?
The above anecdotes are not proof of Indian healthcare being poor overall. But they are an invitation to examine a much larger malice: the quality of healthcare delivered by institutions that millions of Indians trust with their lives.
India has invested considerably in building hospitals, medical colleges, specialist institutions, and diagnostic infrastructure. It is true that we have some extraordinarily accomplished doctors and world-class medical facilities. But Antony’s experience proves that such capacity and infrastructure need not translate into clinical excellence always. A hospital can have the most sophisticated equipment, an impressive building, and internationally trained specialists and still fail patients in the most crucial step: correct diagnosis.
Diagnosis is the foundation of medical treatment. An incorrect diagnosis can send patients down an entirely wrong treatment pathway, exposing them to unnecessary procedures or medication, financial expenditure, and psychological trauma. In some cases, it can delay the treatment of the actual condition until it becomes much more difficult to manage. Therapies administered for a non-existent disease can also have far-reaching implications on the person’s health.
The problem can partly be attributed to the growing commercialisation of diagnostics. Investigations which should be guided by clinical necessity can become part of a revenue-generating chain. Patients are often asked to undergo multiple tests, sometimes at different facilities, without being adequately informed about its necessity or the interpretation of results.
The proliferation of diagnostic centres without proper accreditation and external quality assessment is further cause for extreme concern. We need stronger standardised reporting and accountability for diagnostic errors. A test result is only as useful as the quality of the laboratory, the interpretation of findings, and the clinical judgement that follows.
There is also a fundamental distinction between technological sophistication and medical competence. A hospital possessing an advanced MRI scanner or sophisticated laboratory facilities does not automatically possess the clinical judgment required to use them appropriately.
These scenarios force us to ask a difficult question. Are we measuring the success of healthcare institutions by the buildings they construct, the number of beds they add, and the revenue they generate, or by their diagnostic accuracy, treatment outcomes, and patient safety?
The quality crisis does not end at the diagnostic centre or the hospital pharmacy. It extends to the pharmaceutical industry.
The reputation of Indian pharmaceuticals cannot become a shield against scrutiny of manufacturing quality, regulatory enforcement, and access to medicines.
The pharmaceutical market is characterised by considerable information asymmetry. Patients generally have little ability to assess the quality of a medicine, its manufacturing standards, bioequivalence, or the reliability of its supply chain. They depend on doctors, pharmacists, and regulators to protect them.
Substandard and spurious medicines, manufacturing deficiencies, and failures in quality control raise questions about the effectiveness of regulatory oversight. The problem is not confined to small manufacturers. Quality assurance must cover the entire manufacturing ecosystem, including large companies, contract manufacturers, and suppliers of active pharmaceutical ingredients.
India needs stronger risk-based inspections, transparent publication of inspection findings, independent testing, and swift action against repeat offenders. Drug recalls must be timely, traceable, and publicly accessible.
There is one more concern worth flagging: the growing commercial influence over prescribing practices. Pharmaceutical marketing tactics like doctor engagement and incentives influence the relationship between the prescriber and the manufacturer. The patient, who ultimately pays for the treatment, is often the least informed participant in this transaction. A medicine is not merely a commercial product. Its quality can determine whether a patient recovers, remains ill, or suffers additional harm.
Inadequacy of life-saving medical devices
Medical devices are an under-examined dimension of India’s healthcare quality crisis. From cardiac stents and orthopaedic implants to diagnostic equipment, surgical instruments, and intensive-care devices, modern medicine increasingly depends on sophisticated technologies. These devices can save lives, restore mobility, and improve the quality of treatment. But they also introduce risks when manufacturing standards, clinical validation, procurement practices, and post-market surveillance are inadequate.
The issue is particularly important because a substantial part of the medical device market in our country depends on imports, even while domestic manufacturing is expanding. A device approved for use is not necessarily a device that will perform identically across every clinical setting. Its safety depends on manufacturing consistency, proper installation, calibration, maintenance, and the competence of the medical professional fixing it.
Implantable devices present an additional challenge. Once a cardiac stent, artificial joint, or another implant is placed inside a patient, identifying a defect or adverse outcome can be difficult. Patients may not even know the manufacturer, model, or batch number of the device implanted in their bodies to address possible complications caused by the device later.
India needs a much stronger system of device traceability, mandatory adverse-event reporting, independent performance testing, and transparent disclosure of device-related complications.
The regulation of medical devices cannot stop at granting market approval. It must follow the device throughout its life cycle, from manufacturing and importation to clinical use and post-market surveillance.
Across hospitals, in diagnostics, in pharmaceuticals, and with medical devices, the one problem that recurs is accountability. Issues are fragmented and nobody wants to own up to them. The hospital blames the diagnostic laboratory. The laboratory points to the limitations of the test. The doctor may attribute the outcome to the patient’s underlying condition. The device manufacturer will question the manner in which his product was used. The pharmaceutical company will insist that its medicine met the prescribed specifications. Meanwhile, the patient is left to bear the consequences.
India’s regulatory architecture must therefore move beyond licensing and procedural compliance towards measurable healthcare outcomes. We need publicly accessible information on hospital-acquired infections, diagnostic accuracy, surgical complications, readmissions, medication errors, device failures, and treatment outcomes. Equally important is the need for independent mechanisms through which patients can seek redressal.
We must also strengthen public healthcare. Institutions such as AIIMS, Christian Medical College Vellore, Jawaharlal Institute of Postgraduate Medical Education and Research, National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro Sciences, and the Cancer Institute (Adyar) demonstrate that India has the institutional and professional capabilities to deliver high-quality medicine. Public and trust-run hospitals must be strengthened, not displaced by an increasingly commercialised healthcare ecosystem.
A healthcare system should be capable of identifying disease correctly, treating it safely, and accepting responsibility when it fails. For the patient, the difference between these capabilities is not academic. It can be the difference between recovery and suffering, financial security and ruin, or even life and death.
Ameer Shahul is the author of the best-selling books Heavy Metal, Vaccine Nation, and The Silent Syndicate: How Global Finance is Destroying India’s Healthcare.

title: COP31 and the climate crisis: Why the focus must shift to solutions
description: COP31 exposed divisions over fossil fuel phaseout and climate finance. Why global climate policy must prioritise adaptation, innovation and just transitions.
author: Raghu Murtugudde
content:
The Conference of the Parties 31 or COP31 that just concluded in Antalya, Türkiye, was the longest and was also the first one to be organised by two countries. Türkiye was the host, while Australia played a special role as the President of Negotiations. Negotiations were extended by two days but were accused of doing backroom negotiations without involving all parties or being open about the secret dealings. It is now also branded as the worst COP by some countries and NGOs.
The sticking point was the same as the one in Brazil at COP30. And that was to explicitly mention the phasing out of fossil fuels in the cover text as a major outcome of COP31 negotiations. With the absence of the US, other major oil-producing countries blocked any statements on phasing out of fossil fuels. Fossil fuels are now being called the “F” word, and many countries continue to invest heavily in producing fossil fuels. Major fossil fuel producers tried to push electrification (35 by 35, i.e., 35 per cent renewables by 2035) and carbon capture as effective steps towards eventually reaching fossil fuel phaseout. The knee-jerk reactions to such suggestions only underscore the tunnel vision on emissions without acknowledging the lack of pathways to phasing out fossil fuels right now.
The European Union broke the consensus that is required to approve the cover text at COPs. Roadmaps for phasing out fossil fuels are being put out by several countries now with their own strategies for accomplishing this goal. The tyranny of consensus has once again led to failure at a COP. Climate finance and other issues continue to struggle as well. The overall process is doing better on climate mitigation, albeit progressing much more slowly than desirable. Adaptation struggles as always since it is neither ideal for global leadership nor attractive as an investment option for banks and financiers. Even the development banks conflate economic development projects with adaptation programmes.
What is clear as daylight is that all the headlines are about the impacts of global warming, the threat of crossing the warming thresholds, the lack of political will for climate actions, the unwillingness to phase out fossil fuels, or the insufficiency of climate finance for developing countries. It is impossible to find any significant attention on investing in innovations and training the design engineers, doctors, and social scientists for all the solutions and adaptations needed. Where will the solutions for climate mitigation, carbon capture, phasing out fossil fuels, and adaptations in critical sectors such as agriculture and food, water, energy, transportation, buildings, health, etc., emerge from if nobody is paying attention to them? Will grand statements about phasing out fossil fuels drive innovations for solutions? Or is it better to start producing cover statements on solutions and finances to drive just and equitable innovations and designs to transition to a safe and sustainable world?
Mitigation is all political now
Climate change and global warming narratives always scream implicitly and explicitly about the need for mitigation. The agreed-upon warming target for 2100 in the Paris Agreement of 2 degrees Celsius and then reduced to 1.5 degrees Celsius is now the rallying cry for accelerating mitigation efforts and updating national commitments to reducing emissions. Countries continue to struggle internally and on international stages with the socioeconomics, geopolitics, climate justice, and just transition issues that come with the tunnel vision on the warming targets. The relentless push for mitigation despite all other pocketbook and economic development issues is leading to election outcomes in some countries that indicate how disconnected the climate negotiations may have become from everyday lives of common people and the political realities. One tunnel vision always brings an opposing tunnel vision. Even the most progressive countries are struggling with their commitments to climate actions.
The side effects of these rather unscientific global warming targets are also the cacophony about natural climate variability such as the noise about the “super” El Niño and the alarm about crossing the 1.5 degree Celcius threshold. Super El Niño is another unscientific concept with no clear science to explain what special impacts it may bring at local scales. Especially since global warming patterns are now confounding the El Niño impacts and the models continue to struggle to predict the impacts at hyperlocal scales. No clear guidance is available to help anticipate, prepare for, respond to, and recover from disasters and risks. The same goes for this magical global warming threshold as to the impacts in one’s backyard. How are adaptation projects and programmes to be designed and financed with so much noise then?
Adaptations avoid losses and benefit economies
Adaptation programmes and projects are critical to blunt the impacts of global warming. But they are very contextual, location- and sector-specific. They are also about avoiding losses and inducing economic and ecological co-benefits rather than about making profits. The more successful adaptations are in mitigating the risks, the less willing societies may become in sustaining finances for continuing those projects and programmes.
The local nature of adaptations with only co-benefits for economies makes adaptation an unclear investment option for banks and private financiers. Insurance companies may underwrite risks, but pitching adaptation as purely risk mitigation or risk avoidance programmes may limit their long-term goal of building resilience. Resilience is the foundation for ensuring that the risks from global warming and other natural and human-made disturbances do not disrupt economic development and the steady progress towards sustained climate actions for sustainability and net zero.
As long as climate finances are seen as charitable work and not a collective choice for investing in global economic development, COPs will always struggle to line up new financial commitments. The narratives may have to shift from insisting on unrealistic texts on what can be phased out to being more explicit on how and if anything can be phased out. Whether it is the fossil fuels or the emissions. We should not totally dismiss optimal use of fossil fuels with effective carbon capture if that brings consensus on making real progress.
Can COPs focus on climate solutions rather than just aspirational and unrealistic statements?
Global warming is here, and impacts are seen every day in every corner of the world. No country, rich or poor, and no species in the natural-human earth system is spared now. And yet the drive at COPs has been on addressing the symptoms and not the disease. Human lifestyles are energy-intensive, and energy is carbon-intensive. The narratives have to focus on optimistic visions for the future that provide rich standards of living for all without devouring the environment and without emitting or capturing greenhouse gases.
It is highly unlikely, if not impossible, to find our way out of our energy-intensive lifestyles, but it can be a feasible goal to decarbonise energy. All rich countries have achieved high standards of living with high environmental impacts. The remaining countries are striving to achieve higher standards of living, and they have no option right now but to increase their environmental footprints to get there. Instead of the tunnel visions on emissions reductions which have struggled, the paradigm can be at least to transform the narrative to climate solutions in all sectors with just transitions.
The pathways to climate solutions and investments to drive the science, technology and carbon-free living may be a way to get us away from the survival-level street fights at COPs and the relentless lobbying for status quo. Without a clear path and an obvious destination, humans are incapable of changing paths, neither at individual levels nor at group, national or global levels.
The destination of staying under a certain warming threshold may seem sufficient as a cover text, but it does not come with any clear vision of who gets what by achieving this target. The tyranny of consensus may need to end to make progress with a majority rule.
Raghu Murtugudde is Emeritus Professor, University of Maryland; Visiting Professor, Kotak School of Sustainability, IIT Kanpur.

title: Ujani Dam Data Centre Faces Protests from Farmers and Fisherfolk
description: Farmers and fisherfolk oppose Maharashtra’s proposed AI data centre near Ujani Dam over threats to land, water, livelihoods and power supply.
author: Gautam  Nirmal Doshi
content:
“Whoever is against the construction of the AI data centre, please raise your hands,” came an announcement around 11:30 am on November 13 during a Gram Sabha held in Ranzani village in Maharashtra’s Solapur district, by the banks of the Bhima river. Every villager present, young and old, including onlooking children, raised their hands in unison. “The AI data centre and all remaining projects should be cancelled,” said many.
Villagers from Ranzani, the neighbouring Hingangaon village on the other side of Bhima, and the Bhimanagar area that surrounds the Ujani Dam, which holds the 337 square kilometre Ujani Reservoir, are all opposing the proposed construction of not only a 1.4 gigawatt (GW) hyperscale data centre but also a 2 GW floating solar power project and a 1.8 GW Battery Energy Storage System (BESS). The plans for all these were finalised without consulting farmers, fishermen, and other residents.
The projects are a scaled-down version of initial plans that included a green hydrogen plant and a small modular reactor (SMR) nuclear project. After public backlash and citing feasibility concerns, District Collector S. Karthikeyan announced the cancellation of two of the five projects on November 4. The projects are public-private partnerships (PPP) between the State government’s Water Resources Department, JW Global, and The SEED Consortium Partners, with an initial projected investment of Rs.1.65 lakh crore. The 1.4 GW hyperscale data centre represents almost 70 per cent of this investment.
The projects are envisioned under the banner of making the area a “Sustainable Eco-Enterprise District” or SEED, using 568.15 hectares of land on either side of the Bhima river. It envisages the creation of 40,000 temporary jobs and 2,800 permanent jobs. With almost all local farmers and fishermen unequivocally against the project, fearing its harmful effects on the environment, the question that arises is: who is the development for?
With the mask of decarbonisation initiatives amid rising power and water-centric burdens of data centres adding to the other concerns around data centres, it begs the question why such projects are being implemented in agricultural and fishing areas where livelihoods of entire villages are at stake.
In Maharashtra, this is the second uproar against a data centre, the first being at Thane, where residents are opposing the upcoming 400-plus MW data centre in Balkum.
Speaking at a press conference on November 4, Karthikeyan announced that “not a single guntha of land of farmers will be acquired for the project”. He added: “There will be no compulsory land acquisition. Whatever land is with Maharashtra’s irrigation department, only that will be used. It will be given to the MIDC, which will then tie up with the private company.”
On the concern that some of the land proposed for the projects was farming land, Karthikeyan said: “We’re not going to evict or destroy farms and start the project. We will work out a fair compensation with the farmers.” He said that over 112 hectares (of the 586 hectares required for the project) are currently used by around 70 farmers.
Speaking to Frontline, farmers spoke of how their parents or grandparents had given up land some 50 years ago for the construction of the Ujani Dam. “My family gave up several acres for the Ujani Dam. A lot of that land is unutilised, so as per the law, shouldn’t we get it back?” said Vishwas Shahurao Deokar, a farmer from Hingangaon.
Deokar was referring to Section 101 of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in the Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 (or the LAPR Act, 2013), which states that “when any land acquired under this Act remains unutilised for a period of five years from the date of taking possession, the same shall be returned to the original owner or owners or their legal heirs, as the case may be, or to the land bank of the appropriate government by reversion in the manner as may be prescribed by the appropriate government”.
The land was acquired for building a dam, which is considered a public purpose. But the data centre, with the BESS and floating solar panels serving the data centre, are private ventures.
Colin Gonsalves, a senior advocate at the Supreme Court, said: “The data centre is not a public purpose. When the government acquires land for a public purpose, it must be utilised accordingly. The land vests with the government, so if they don’t use it for a dam and say they want to use it for another public purpose, like a public hospital, that would be permissible. But this data centre is not a public purpose.”
However, if the matter is escalated to the courts, there is a chance that it can be argued that the data centres are being used for a public purpose, Gonsalves added. This is because, in the Union Budget 2022-23, the government included data centres in the “Harmonised List of Infrastructure”, which treats them like national highways, airports, and power grids that have public purposes.
Also Read | A data centre mired in controversy
Even though there is no direct utilitarian benefit for farmers or fishermen, the data centres set up by private companies could be deemed to hold a public purpose, if questioned.
The farmers from Hingangaon said that they just want their land back. They wanted to know why the project could not come up on barren land and why it had to be near the Ujani Dam area. “We grow sugar cane, bananas, pomegranates, wheat, and more here. This is fertile land,” said Deokar. According to Karthikeyan, the area near the Ujani Dam was chosen because of its grid connectivity and proximity to a highway.
First phase and evictions
In August, several families in the Bhimanagar Government Colony, not far from the Ujani Dam, were served eviction notices on the grounds that they were occupying government land. The first phase of the project begins in Bhimanagar.
The families of Arifa Sikandar Pathan and Gauri Sunil Dosane (who are neighbours), with two and seven members respectively, have nowhere else to go. “They gave us notice to leave our homes in just five days. We were not told where to go, but were just told there is some area set aside within this village itself. We went to their [government’s] office and got an extension of six months,” Pathan said.
While many vacated their homes hurriedly, several such families are staying on, unsure what to do. “Soon after the notice, they shut off our water supply and electricity for 10-15 days. There’s a school here that was rebuilt less than a year ago. Where will these children go now?” said Dusane.
Vimal Gaikwad comes from Ranzani to farm on the land near the colony. “My family gave several acres for the construction of the project for barely any compensation because they were happy that the dam would benefit the entire community. And it did. But now why are they clearing trees and houses so swiftly? I have been here for over 50 years; I have all the documents about the acquisition,” she said.
A JCB earth mover stands parked near Pathan and Dusane’s homes, the modern symbol of upheaval. Adjacent lies almost an acre of cleared and deserted land. The land clearing was stopped after the public backlash. “There were many peacocks here; so many of them died when they came to cut the trees and clear the land,” said Vimal, who has been actively protesting the proposed projects.
When we reached the Agricultural Produce Market Committee (APMC) in Indapur, along the Ujani Reservoir and near Pune’s district border with Solapur, people were leaving the bustling designated mandi where fishermen sell their freshwater catch. The reservoir has a diverse range of fish. Fisherfolk were wrapping up accounts and shutting shop. When asked, everyone Frontline spoke to was against the proposed floating solar power project.
The 2GW floating solar power plant will cover around 30 sq km, which accounts for 9 per cent of the Ujani Reservoir’s water.
Worried fisherfolk
Naseer Dawood Sheikh, a fisherman from Indapur, said: “This project will affect our livelihoods. Three generations of my family were fisherfolk. What else will we do? There are tens of thousands of us across both districts; we depend on fishing in the reservoir. And it’s not just fishermen; our entire villages depend on fish for sustenance. The government has so much land. Why don’t they take the solar plant elsewhere?”
A common concern was that, with 30 sq km cordoned off for the solar project, fishermen would be forced to fish in other areas, thus reducing everyone’s overall catch. (During his November 4 press conference, Karthikeyan claimed that fishing routes and breeding would not be affected, and that the solar project would be introduced in a phased manner.)
The fisherfolk who fish in the Ujani Reservoir have been protesting since August this year, also seeking the cancellation of a proposed private contract for fishing rights, which was cancelled in September. But the floating solar power project worries them.
Nandkumar Nagare, president of Maharashtra Rajya Machhimar Sangharsh Kruti Samiti, said: “Over 30,000 people are directly dependent on fishing; they have no other alternative. The solar power project and the data centre will increase the temperature in the surrounding land and water; besides, there will be the constant jarring noise of the data centre. People in the surrounding 4-5 villages will be forced to leave for good.”
Nagare was referring to the “data heat island effect”, a term coined by researchers. According to a paper led by Cambridge researchers, the land surface temperatures around AI data centres rise by an average of 2 degrees Celsius, with a peak limit up to 9 degrees Celsius as a result of heat dissipation. The heat can be felt up to 10 km away.
Fishermen like Kiran Mohandar Dare fear being displaced again, something his family dealt with during the construction of the Ujani Dam. “Earlier generations of my family were farmers. We had to give up our land and relocate. We switched to fishing. Now this. This project can be done elsewhere, not here.”
Water quality concerns
Next to Bhimanagar, a road running along a canal leads to its source. “All the greenery along this road will be destroyed,” said Kishore Sonawane, from Indapur, pointing to the numerous trees on either side of the road. It’s a hot November afternoon, and only one fisherman on a small boat is attempting a catch near the shore, with most others finishing before sunrise. The noise of water pumps dominates the soundscape and a faint but foul smell from the water is noticeable. This is another concern the fisherfolk share.
“The water is turning greener and it’s also dirty; we cannot use it for drinking or cooking. You can smell it,” said Pandurang Palare, a fisherman. The fishermen complained that this could be affecting the quality of fish as well. Farmers share the same concern. “We are noticing declines in our yield due to the water quality,” said Gyaneshwar Gaikwad, a farmer from Ranzani.
According to a paper published in 2023 in the Bulletin of Environment, Pharmacology, and Life Sciences, tests on water samples from 10 different locations in the Ujani Reservoir “showed horrendous physical condition issues and may lead to various diseases”.
This is primarily due to rapid urbanisation and the resultant discharge of untreated or partially treated domestic and industrial contaminants into the Mula and Mutha rivers, and the Mula-Mutha (the confluence of both rivers in Pune), which flow eastward for about 60 km before merging into the Bhima river, which flows into the Ujani Reservoir.
The paper concluded that the Ujani Reservoir’s water quality was “marred with high grade pollution. Hence, the Ujani water is not suitable for the household utilisation and also for agriculture without purification”.
“The authorities know the problems here. But no one cared to come here and help us improve the water quality all these years, and now everything is being handed over in a hurried manner to make the data centre,” farmers from Hingangaon told Frontline on November 13.
Water usage amid crisis
In his November 4 press conference, Karthikeyan also said that the total water to be utilised by the proposed facility and the adjacent campus, including the proposed residential areas, would not exceed 0.5 thousand million cubic feet (TMC), about roughly 14,150 million litres per year, which is less than 1 per cent of the reservoir’s capacity of 117 TMC.
“The floating solar power project will prevent the natural evaporation of 1.5-1.7 TMC of the reservoir’s water. Thereby, no additional water will be utilised and, in fact, there’s a net positive of 1-1.2 TMC for the reservoir,” he added.
He said that this was possible because of a newer direct-to-chip closed-loop dry cooling mechanism to be used, which reduces water consumption in a data centre compared to traditional methods of cooling through evaporation towers.
An annual usage of 14,150 million litres translates to 38-39 million litres a day, which is enough for 6.9 lakh people in rural areas or 2.8 lakh people in urban areas, as per the Central government’s benchmarks of 55 litres per capita per day (lpcd) for rural and 135 lpcd for urban populations.
Data centres need distilled or purified water for cooling purposes. However, farmers said that since the water is already polluted, the total water used will be higher than the stated 0.5 TMC. The data centre, they said, will need excess water to filter out the required 0.5 TMC for cooling and other purposes.
The Ujani Reservoir supplies water to the districts of Pune, Solapur, and Ahiliyanagar. The proposed data centre’s use of water has come under the spotlight also because this year, drought was declared in 305 of Maharashtra’s 358 talukas, including all 11 talukas in Solapur. Local news reports indicate that over 229 tankers were sent across 198 villages as of November 17, as roughly 4 lakh people faced severe water scarcity.
In late October, the Karnataka government sought the release of 7 TMC of water from the Ujani Dam for villages along the Bhima in Vijayapura district. However, that has not yet been granted. Given such concerns, farmers are vehemently opposed to a water-guzzling data centre. “We feel our villages will become like a desert. People will leave to look for different jobs,” said Sandip Maruti Mane, a farmer in Ranzani. “We have said time and time again that the entire village is against these projects; we have no option but to protest.”
Fears of energy deficit
The proposed 1,800 MW BESS stores power during surplus supply and helps meet excess demand during a supply deficit. BESS is one of the energy storage solutions being implemented across the country. Another is Pumped Storage Projects (PSPs). The Maharashtra government has ordered fast-tracked environmental clearances for 55 PSPs in the State, concentrated in and around the ecologically diverse Sahyadri range. In the last month, PSPs have come under the spotlight in Maharashtra with the proposed felling of over 32,000 trees for the construction of the Saidongar-I project in Karjat taluka. That project met with protests from villagers and opposition parties. Saidongar-I has been temporarily halted and uncertainty looms over its future as the project aims to clear 233 hectares of forest cover.
The Central Electricity Authority (CEA) projects 73.93 GW of storage capacity in the country by 2031-32. Of this, the PSPs will have a storage capacity of 26.69 GW, with BESS projects accounting for the remaining 47.24 GW.
The push for such storage solutions comes against the backdrop of rising electricity demands and increasing capacities through renewable sources, and to ensure grid stability.
For Maharashtra, specifically, it also comes against the backdrop of rising power cuts during the hotter months owing to demand surge and a lack of supply. In June this year, the Maharashtra State Load Despatch Centre reported load shedding for several hours at a stretch in places. The electricity shortfall was around 28 million units (MU), with the lack of generation accounting for 23 MU.
Farmers in Hingangaon, Ranzani, and Indapur in Pune district said that they get only six hours of electricity on their farms. “During summer, because of load shedding, there are days when we don’t get electricity at all and have to make do,” said Deokar. Some farmers said they get six hours of power every alternate day.
By the early 2030s, the State government plans to sanction 6 GW of power specifically to data centres in Maharashtra, approximately 15 per cent of the State’s entire power demand, assuming maximum demand reaches 40 GW (with current power demand being 30-32 GW and assuming a growth in demand at a CAGR of 4 per cent).
Also Read | Data centre push gets a drought reality check
Currently, connectivity amounting to 2 GW has been given to data centres, of which 200 MW is operational. A large number of data centres are being added in the State in a very short period of time, with the 1.4 GW data centre at Ujani the largest yet, and they are coming on an already burdened power grid.
“This is why we are introducing green data centres,” said Karthikeyan. “Around 50 per cent of the energy demand will be met by solar.”
But data centres work 24 hours; they require a constant power source and have to draw power from the grid itself using the existing high-voltage transmission network rather than connect directly to a solar/wind plant or microgrid. The solar panels also feed into the grid, but solar generation fluctuates.
The proposed projects guarantee 2,800 jobs and 40,000 temporary jobs, the latter primarily construction work. While Karthikeyan has listed various types of jobs ranging from IT and cybersecurity engineers to boat operators and solar panel cleaners, the farmers are doubtful about how villagers will benefit. Krishna Tate, a farmer and activist from Indapur, said: “The well-paid jobs are for AI, data, and IT engineers who will not be from these villages. People from outside will fill these vacancies.”
On November 14, Dhairyasheel Rajsinh Mohite-Patil of the Nationalist Congress Party-Sharad Pawar (NCP-SP), an MP from Madha constituency, under which the proposed projects fall, told mediapersons: “In my constituency and Indapur taluka, we have questions about the projects that remain unanswered. If we are not given an adequate response by the [District] Collector by November 26, we will hold a candlelight march on November 27 to the executive engineer’s office.”
Regardless of the government’s response, villagers are not ready to stop raising their voices against the planned projects, which were started without consulting them. “If the projects are not cancelled, we are ready to protest every day and also willing to put our lives on the line,” a group of 7-8 farmers told Frontline after the Gram Sabha in Ranzani.

title: West Bengal Gets Rs 1 Lakh Crore Road Infrastructure Package With Rs 14,000 Crore For Kolkata Ring Road

author: Arjun Brij
content:

Arjun Brij
Nov 26, 2026 | Updated 04:34 PM GMT+5:30

Union Road Transport and Highways Minister Nitin Gadkari has announced road infrastructure projects worth Rs 1 lakh crore for West Bengal.
Speaking at an NHAI event in Kolaghat, Purba Medinipur today, Gadkari said the Centre would ensure adequate funding for infrastructure projects in the state.
He said road projects worth Rs 35,000 crore, covering around 450 km, were currently under construction, while projects valued at nearly Rs 40,000 crore had already been completed.
He also assured Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari that financial resources would be made available for road development, adding, “Do not worry about money. You will get tired of asking (for projects), but I will not get tired of providing funds.”
Among the major projects announced are the four-lane Siliguri-Guwahati corridor, estimated to cost Rs 26,000 crore, the Siliguri-Darjeeling corridor worth Rs 6,000 crore and the Kolkata ring road project, which is estimated at Rs 14,000 crore.
He attributed India's infrastructure expansion to the government's focus on connectivity since 2014 and said West Bengal could contribute significantly towards the country's ambition of becoming the world's third-largest economy.
Referring to road and flyover development in Maharashtra, Gadkari highlighted innovative financing and market-based resource mobilisation as ways to fund large infrastructure projects.

title: Flight-Style Meals Now Available On Vande Bharat Sleeper Trains Following Passenger Complaints

author: Arjun Brij

The Indian Railway Catering and Tourism Corporation (IRCTC) introduced a compact flight-style food menu on three Vande Bharat Sleeper routes—Mumbai-Bengaluru, Howrah-Kamakhya, and New Delhi-Varanasi.
The shorter menu was introduced on 1 November as part of a pilot project aimed at improving food quality and hygiene on long-distance trains.
The number of items in a meal has been cut from roughly eight to 10 to just four.
For breakfast, passengers on the Mumbai–Bengaluru service can choose idli-vada with chutney and sambar, poha, or upma, whilst lunch and dinner will include chapati, rice, dal, and a main course, with a choice of chicken or a vegetarian option.

The meals are now made by well-known cloud kitchens like TajSATS and Mayfair Group, with the Mayfair Group serving the Kamakhya line, TajSATS in Howrah, and Sarovar Portico Group for the remaining two Vande Bharat sleeper trains.
The change aims to address passengers' ongoing complaints about the quality and cleanliness of meals on long-distance trains.
Passenger complaints have dropped by around 10 per cent, suggesting travellers are happier with the change.
If this pilot delivers satisfactory results, the same menu style could be extended to other long-distance railway services, including premium trains.

title: Tata Trusts Seeks High Court Injunction Against Chandrasekaran Reappointment, Claiming Invalid Board Vote
description: The Sir Dorabji Tata Trust and the R. D. Tata Trust filed suits today in the Bombay High Court against Tata Sons and six of i
author: Swarajya News Staff
content:
News Brief
Swarajya News Staff
Nov 26, 2026 | Updated 04:20 PM GMT+5:30
Save & read from anywhere!
Bookmark stories for easy access on any device or the Swarajya app.
The Sir Dorabji Tata Trust and the RD Tata Trust have filed suits in the Bombay High Court against Tata Sons and six of its directors, challenging the reappointment of N Chandrasekaran as executive chairman for a third five-year term.
The legal action marks a significant escalation in a governance dispute that has simmered since September, when the Tata Sons board approved Chandrasekaran's reappointment for another five years beginning in February 2027.
The dispute centres on Article 121 of Tata Sons' Articles of Association, which the trusts contend requires the affirmative vote of a majority of directors nominated by Tata Trusts for specified board decisions.
At the 17 September board meeting, the two trust-nominated directors split their votes, with Noel Tata opposing Chandrasekaran's reappointment whilst Venu Srinivasan supported it.
The resolution ultimately passed with four directors voting in favour after independent director Harish Manwani, who chaired the meeting, exercised his casting vote.
Tata Trusts, which holds around 66 per cent of Tata Sons, argues that the chairman's casting vote cannot substitute for the mandatory affirmative voting requirement under Article 121.
The trusts are seeking a declaration that the September resolution is invalid, illegal and void, along with damages of Rs 600 crore through the Sir Dorabji Tata Trust and Rs 180 crore through the RD Tata Trust, besides 18 per cent annual interest.
The legal challenge comes ahead of a crucial Tata Sons board meeting scheduled for 30 November, where key decisions including the proposed listing of Tata Sons are expected to be discussed.
The trusts have sought urgent interim relief to prevent the chairman from using a casting vote at the upcoming meeting if nominee directors are split in their opinions. A single bench of the Bombay High Court is likely to take up the suits for hearing tomorrow.
