title: Uncomfortable Truths About India’s Fight Against Global Warming - The Wire
description: Economically, India has been pursuing a compensatory rather than a disciplinary form of neoliberalism but nevertheless being fundamentally neoliberal in character, has dramatically increased inequalities of income and wealth.
author: Achin Vanaik
content: Most commentators in the mainstream and legacy media as well as on social media news and opinion outlets have written favourably about the Indian government’s performance at the recently concluded Conference of Parties (COP31) concerning climate change even though for the first time no final consensus text emerged. There were two main reasons for this. There was no agreement on what should be the annual target figure in the Climate Adaptation Fund to be collectively provided for vulnerable developing countries. Moreover, what has been collected falls miserably short of the levels that had been earlier agreed upon at the previous COPs. India, among others, was right to call attention to and criticise this failing. The second reason is that a number of countries including major emitters of Green House Gases or GHG refused to accept that the term “phase out” of fossil fuel production be included in the text to be finalised. Rare was the article or post in India that mentioned let alone highlighted or sharply criticised the fact that India was one of the countries that also opposed its inclusion. This was in contrast to many other countries both advanced and in the Global South that demanded its inclusion.Third-largest emitterIllustration: Pariplab Chakraborty.India is the third largest emitter of GHG annually after China and the US. But one way of minimising this when it comes to assessing and assigning country-level responsibilities to greatly reduce such emissions is to stress that in per capita emission terms India ranks 92nd. Let us look more closely at this excuse. The most conservative estimate of India’s upper and middle classes that would have in per capita terms levels of emission closer to the average per capita level in many of the advanced countries is 220-230 million.Were this size deemed a country it would rank as the 7th most populated country. A less conservative estimate of the size of this Indian social layer is around 350 million or close to the total population of the US while some put the more accurate figure as above 400 million. What this emphasis on per capita emissions does is to allow the better off sections of society and the Indian government to hide their emissions culpabilities behind the bottom 50% of the population which generates far fewer levels of emissions.Furthermore – and this should be obvious when it comes to assessing country-wise culpability – global warming in the environment is affected by total country emissions not by its per capita levels. The logic that follows is simple, India (and China) should provide much more financial support to the global “Loss and Damage” fund for poorer countries than they do and to generally take much more responsibility to address this global problem than they are willing to admit to doingEcological and economic inequality: a connected parallelIndia justifies its policy of fossil fuel production now and in the future on the grounds that as a developing country it needs faster and higher growth in the short and medium term precisely to help the poorer sections of society. Economically, India has been pursuing a compensatory rather than a disciplinary form of neoliberalism but nevertheless being fundamentally neoliberal in character, has dramatically increased inequalities of income and wealth. In essence, this is a ‘trickle down’ approach to the generation and distribution of income. But so what? Doesn’t a rising tide lift up all boats, big or small! Yes, high growth does have a broad or generalised effect in cumulatively improving the financial condition of the poor over time. And this has happened in India over the decades though by how much is sharply disputed as is the definition of what kind of overall package of goods should constitute the poverty line to actually assess the degree of improvement of the poor.But here is a key question – is the social inequality in the contribution to ecological degradation, briefly referred to earlier, reinforced by greater social inequality in income and wealth? Is this what is happening in India? The average annual growth rate in GDP during the period 1950-80 was what the economist Raj Krishna then called the “Hindu rate of growth” of 3.5% to 4%. In the period 1980 to 2015 the average annual growth rate was 6.07%. However, Lucas Chancel and Thomas Piketty have shown that the average annual growth in real income of the bottom 50% of the Indian population during the span of 1951-1980 was higher than its average increase in the period 1981-2015. They also compared the period of rule by the British Raj and the first decades of independent India. So in 1982 the top 1% share of National Income dropped from 21% in 1940 to 6% while the pre-tax Gini coefficient fell from 46 in 1951 to 40 in 1982.In the decade since 2015 in India should we be surprised that financial inequalities between top and bottom layers should have accelerated just as the rate of ecological degradations – of GHG emissions, denudation of forest cover, sinking water tables, faster melting of Himalayan glaciers and snows, etc. has also accelerated?Prioritising the urgent need for mitigationActivists at COP31 were emphatic that the growing pre-occupation with adaptation measures like carbon capture, let alone with other forms of geo-engineering such as solar radiation management, stratospheric aerosol injection, iron filings in the oceans was a deliberate and serious diversion of attention and commitment to the necessity of still prioritising the pursuit of mitigation through dramatic reduction of fossil fuel production and use. Regarding the rising interest in solar radiation management, on February 14, 2024 when the Israeli genocide in Gaza was going on, an Israeli start-up called “Stardust Solutions” because of concerns of possible negative effects, carried out in Gaza and not in Israel itself, a dispersal of a cloud of tiny reflective particles some 60,000 feet in altitude as a test of its efficacy with no doubt lessons to be learnt for future development of such technologies and sale elsewhere in the world.Regarding mitigation, let us not talk about countries having to rapidly shut down their existing sources of fossil fuel production whether of oil, gas or coal. The least disruptive policy demand is simply this – don’t make any new investments in fossil fuel exploration and production.How many countries are at least prepared to do this? Well, Denmark, Spain, Ireland, France have banned any new investments in fossil fuel exploration and production and also set future dates for a full ‘phase out’ i.e., ending all fossil fuel production and not just ‘net zero emissions. Among important countries that oppose such a commitment and are continuing to make newer investments is, rather surprisingly, Norway. The country is much appreciated for its strong welfare policies and practices, but is exploring for excavations new sites in the North and Barents Seas.Then come the usual nefarious suspects that are fully prepared to make such investments. They are, as to be expected, the US, Russia, Canada, Australia, Japan and China despite it being a leader in developing renewable forms of energy production. Finally, there is also another country much lauded by what can be called our non-official “advisers to the Prince for its ‘sensible’ pursuit, ecologically speaking, of the ‘national interest’ – the Modi government of India!Achin Vanaik is a retired professor of international relations.This piece was first published on The India Cable – a premium newsletter from The Wire – and has been updated and republished here. To subscribe to The India Cable, click here.

title: ‘Sunrise on the Reaping’: A Sweeping Prequel Chronicles the Cost of Youthful Idealism - The Wire
description: The Hunger Games films have been critiqued for following a repetitive structure, regurgitating the same points, again and again. I think there’s a reason for it, because fascism is a cyclical event, across the world.
author: Tatsam Mukherjee
content: While watching the sixth film in the Hunger Games franchise, it occurred to me how the books (and as a result, the films) always took place from the point-of-view of a young protagonist. The original trilogy (2012-2015) was spearheaded by Katniss Everdeen (a star-making turn by Jennifer Lawrence across four films; part 3 was split in two parts). The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes (2023), a prequel telling the origin story of young President Snow (played by Donald Sutherland in the earlier films, and Tom Blythe as his younger version), as a musical tragedy, was an audacious move. And now, in Sunrise on the Reaping – the protagonist is a young Haymitch Abernathy (played by Woody Harrelson in the earlier films, and Joseph Zada in the new one). The Hunger Games films came out in the midst of a deluge of YA (young adult) dystopian novels, and I remember losing interest in them towards the end. It’s only when I rewatched the second, third and fourth film (primarily because of an over-enthusiastic wife who was waiting for this film with bated breath) did I realise how prescient some of those images from 2014-2015 were for 2026. Katniss Everdeen using a camera crew to unmask the Capitol levelling districts with their formidable weapons reminded me of the journalists braving bombardments in Gaza. The image of a young girl becoming the face of the resistance is something we might have seen closer home, with someone like Neha Bora (among others), who have anchored the protests in the Indian capital in the last few months. Even in the latest film, Haymitch willing to be a ‘kamikaze tribute’ to break the Capitol’s machine of sadistic entertainment – broadcasting dozens of tributes killing each other – brought to mind the dozens of young undertrials in India, willing to cremate their futures for a cause that might not bear fruits in their lifetime.The Hunger Games films have been critiqued for following a repetitive structure, regurgitating the same points, again and again. I think there’s a reason for it, because fascism is a cyclical event, across the world. The same arcs regenerate themselves in different parts of the world, again and again. Hope is snuffed out by tyrannical regimes, the ruling class believes it will rule forever. And there are many failed uprisings along the way, before overthrowing the tyrants.A scene from the trailer of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping (2026). Photo: YouTube/Lionsgate MoviesSet 40 years after the events of The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, around the second quarter quell (effectively, the 50th Hunger Games), the film opens with Haymitch (Zada) strutting around District 12 on his 18th birthday. It’s the day of reaping too, where two ‘tributes’ will be picked at random, to compete in the Hunger Games organised by the Capitol. For the uninitiated, the games are a form of punishment for the districts waging war on the Capitol, half a century ago. However, in a quarter quell – the 25-year anniversary – the tributes double. As everyone [including those reading this review] might have already guessed by now, Haymitch is chosen as a tribute.The beats are similar as the earlier films, the tears of the family as the tributes leave for the Capitol. The grimness being replaced by strategy for allies in the gaming arena, the show one has to put up for ‘sponsors’ (who can courier supplies to tributes in the arena), and the cunning machinations of the game-makers ensuring all tributes are brought to their peril, one way or another.One thing I truly enjoyed about Sunrise on the Reaping was the short bursts of performances by the film’s supporting cast. Glenn Close in the two scenes as the rude Capitol escort, Drusilla Sickle, is a riot. So is Elle Fanning, as a young Effie Trinket (played by Elizabeth Banks in the earlier films). Jesse Plemons, one of the most exciting actors working today, is a cipher throughout the film – as Plutarch Heavensbee – much like the late Philip Seymour Hoffman (who played the older version of the character, in what was his last screen performance). There’s never a moment when Plemons, like Hoffman, betrays Plutarch’s loyalties. As President Snow, Ralph Fiennes is the only odd casting. I suspect casting Voldemort was a business decision, rather than a creative one. Fiennes brings a deadpan monotone to a character who sounded almost musical in Sutherland’s iteration, and earnest/poisoned in Blythe’s version. It’s a missed opportunity, because the antagonist has remained the fulcrum of the franchise. Ralph Fiennes in a scene from the trailer of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping (2026). Photo: YouTube/Lionsgate MoviesAs a young Haymitch, Joseph Zada ably shoulders a significant portion of the film. It’s the work of a ravenous young actor willing to look silly for his breakout role. I particularly enjoyed him imitating Harrelson’s Southern drawl. The imagined violence and the gore on the screen seemed particularly mismatched, and I kept wondering if the culprit was the Indian censor board, or a studio chasing a younger certification.The fan-service in Sunrise on the Reaping is sincere and effective, however, what touched me the most about the film was the systemic humiliation a young man must endure, after everything is taken away from him. Director Francis Lawrence, having made dystopian thrillers like I Am Legend (2007) and The Long Walk (2025) more recently, making his fifth film in the franchise, is no stranger to isolation and the psychological damnation that comes with it. I liked how he brought an unabashed sweeping quality to the source material. Haymitch’s tragedy is that he survives, despite his best efforts. And survival is hardly the same thing as freedom. Watching him go about his life, I couldn’t (once again) help but think of the many young undertrials in India today, whose best years are being devoured by a regime that doesn’t need to pronounce their guilt to punish them. Some, like Haymitch, might live to see times change. Perhaps, some might not. Resistance, as the games remind us, belongs to no single generation.*The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is playing in theatres

title: Ramlila Maidan Rally: The Tide is Turning - The Wire
description: The rally is a sign that the BJP's dominance is no longer beyond contestation. The question is whether the INDIA bloc can build on this momentum and turn it into a viable political alternative.
author: Zoya Hasan
content: The political ascendancy of the right is facing growing resistance across the world, both on the streets and at the ballot box. The right-wing cycle may be running its course, as developments elsewhere, particularly in the United States, appear to suggest. The midterm elections offer an important indication of the electoral vulnerabilities of right-wing dominance. Whether this signals a similar turning point in India is a more complex question, given the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)’s organisational reach and the social and political consolidation underpinning its dominance. Yet, the growing mass mobilisation suggests that India’s political terrain, too, is becoming increasingly contested.INDIA – with Congress at its centre – pulls off biggest political meeting in decadesAgainst this backdrop, the November 1 Chalo Dilli rally at Ramlila Maidan marks a significant escalation in the challenge to the BJP-led National Development Alliance (NDA) government. Over the past few months, disparate streams of protest have increasingly converged around electoral malpractice, manipulation of voter rolls and the erosion of democratic institutions. The Congress-led Indian National Developmental Inclusive Alliance (INDIA) bloc brought these protests together in one of the largest political mobilisations Delhi has witnessed in decades. Thousands of people marched along Minto Road to Ramlila Maidan, united by the demand to restore public confidence in India’s electoral process.More significant than the size of the crowd, however, is what it reveals about the changing political mood. The conduct of elections and the institutional safeguards underpinning them have become matters of wider public concern, extending well beyond party politics. The rally sent a strong message of disapproval to the ruling party and the Election Commission of India (ECI), whose actions have raised serious questions about its role in safeguarding electoral democracy. It also underscored the Congress’s centrality to the campaign and Rahul Gandhi’s emergence as its principal political voice. His leadership has given the INDIA bloc greater political visibility and a more clearly defined focus. The two major events over the past three weeks – the October 12 march from Barakhamba Road to the Supreme Court and the rally at Ramlila Maidan – demonstrated the party’s renewed organisational capacity and its ability to bring its cadres onto the streets.Around focal point of SIR, various grievances coalesceThe special intensive revision (SIR) of electoral rolls has become the principal bone of contention because of the staggering scale of exclusions. More than 13 crore names were omitted from the draft electoral rolls across the states and Union territories covered by the revision. The difficulties voters have faced in establishing their eligibility, producing documents and securing their place on the rolls have raised serious questions. These are particularly significant given reports that only around 1,600 alleged ‘infiltrators’ (ghuspaithiyas) have been identified as far as six states with an electorate of 9.86 crore voters are concerned, even though detecting such elements was presented as a principal justification for the exercise. The contrast has fuelled perceptions of electoral wrongdoing and intensified anger among voters and party cadres. A right ordinarily taken for granted has become a source of uncertainty and contestation for millions of voters. More significantly, the burden of proof has shifted from the state to the electorate. Questions about the fairness of elections are no longer confined to allegations by political parties but have entered public discourse.Although the SIR and electoral fairness provided the unifying political focus, the mobilisation also brought wider grievances into the political arena. The gathering gave voice to issues ranging from agrarian distress, unemployment and access to education to women’s safety, inflation and livelihood insecurity. The defence of voting rights and electoral accountability thus provided a common political platform for articulating multiple social and economic discontents. For many of those present, the struggle over the vote was inseparable from broader demands for social justice and the protection of minority rights.Opposition unity, widening social supportThe main takeaway was the unity it brought to the opposition ranks, something that may have surprised the BJP. The active participation of INDIA bloc parties alongside the principal opposition party reflected an unusual cohesion among forces that have often struggled to act collectively. Clearly, unity is possible when there is a compelling common issue and a political force capable of providing direction and coordination.The breadth of support for the rally reflected the diversity of India, while its inclusive character spoke to citizens as equals, transcending identity politics and the Hindu-Muslim binary. Photo: PTI/Salman Ali.The significance of the mobilisation also lay in its social diversity. It was not a sectarian protest, nor was it confined to any particular identity or category of people. Its breadth of support reflected the diversity of India, while its inclusive character spoke to citizens as equals, transcending identity politics and the Hindu-Muslim binary.A further significance lay in the participation of political parties alongside movements and organisations that have traditionally operated outside party politics. Recent weeks have witnessed an unprecedented coming together of the youth movement around the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), Left student organisations and civil society groups, and the Congress and INDIA bloc, which have provided a wider political platform and national focus. This convergence has given the campaign a wider social base and political reach than any of these forces could have achieved independently, while recognising that its durability remains an open question.To move forward, a shared agenda is a must – and it won’t be easyThe future of this conjunction remains uncertain, particularly in the case of the CJP, which supported the protest but was not physically present at the Ramlila Maidan rally. Whether it will work alongside political parties or pursue an independent course remains to be seen. Sustaining the convergence of diverse social and political forces will require a shared agenda and the organisational capacity to carry the mobilisation forward. Ultimately, mobilisation must translate into electoral gains and a shift in the balance of political power.The challenge of sustaining this mobilisation is compounded by the shrinking space for pursuing these concerns through parliamentary channels. Repeated adjournments, the government’s refusal to engage with allegations of vote theft and the rejection of notices seeking the chief election commissioner’s removal have left little room for substantive parliamentary debate on the SIR and the ECI. Yet the government insists that parliament is the appropriate forum for raising these issues, even as it resorts to repression against public protests, as it did on October 10 when it prevented the CJP from protesting against the SIR. By accusing protesters of fomenting anarchy while insisting that these matters be raised in parliament, the government effectively denies the legitimacy of street protest as a means of political dissent.Backlash against the rightThese growing protests in India need to be seen in the wider international context. Across several countries, the political dominance of the right is facing growing electoral and popular resistance. Protests have erupted across countries including France, Belgium and Spain, as well as Albania and Italy, around demands for affordable housing, employment opportunities for young people, relief from the rising cost of living and greater investment in education. Alongside these protests, developments at the ballot box also point to challenges to right-wing politics. Brazil’s Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defeated the far-right challenger Flávio Bolsonaro in the presidential runoff, while a student-led movement in Serbia brought down the incumbent government. These developments differ in their political contexts and trajectories, but together they suggest that the right’s political ascendancy is neither inevitable nor irreversible.Illustration: Pariplab Chakraborty.The Ramlila Maidan rally is significant in this context. It marks an important political moment because discontent with the BJP is beginning to find a wider and more organised political expression. The BJP remains a formidable force, but its dominance is no longer beyond contestation. The question is whether the INDIA bloc can build on this momentum and turn it into a viable political alternative. The tide may be turning; the rally, and importantly the cohesion it demonstrated, has made that possibility more tangible. It could also slow the BJP’s efforts to reshape India’s electoral architecture through the SIR, delimitation and One Nation, One Election, with the larger objective of entrenching a permanent ethnic majority.Zoya Hasan is professor emerita, Centre for Political Studies, Jawaharlal Nehru University.This piece was first published on The India Cable – a premium newsletter from The Wire – and has been updated and republished here. title: Delhi Teens Make Rs 140 Classroom Air Purifier
description: Discover how Project Vayu is helping Delhi schools tackle indoor air pollution, with classroom tests reporting a 60% drop in harmful PM2.5 levels in an hour.
author: Nishtha Kawrani
content:
A classroom fan spins above a group of children bent over their notebooks. As the teacher moves between desks and lessons continue, the fan keeps the air circulating. But in a city like Delhi, where pollution often makes its way indoors, circulating air does not necessarily mean breathing clean air.
For thousands of children studying in schools that cannot afford expensive air purifiers, this is an everyday reality. They spend several hours a day inside classrooms, often with little protection from fine particulate matter suspended in the air.
Two Delhi teenagers, Krish Aggarwal and Samarth Meattle, decided to look at this problem differently. Instead of asking schools to invest in expensive purification systems, they wondered if the fans already fitted in classrooms could be made to do more.
Their idea took shape as Project Vayu, an initiative that has developed an affordable filter that fits over ordinary table and wall fans, helping turn them into air purifiers. At approximately Rs 140 per filter, the innovation offers schools a way to tackle indoor air pollution without having to invest in entirely new equipment.
"Growing up in Delhi, we've personally experienced the effects of air pollution," the duo say. "What bothered us was that while some schools could afford expensive air purifiers, thousands of students in under-resourced schools had no protection."
What if a classroom fan could also clean the air?
Rather than building a new appliance from scratch, Krish and Samarth decided to work with the infrastructure schools already had.
The biggest technical challenge was developing a filter that could trap fine particulate matter, particularly PM2.5, without restricting the airflow of an ordinary fan.
"We experimented with different designs before arriving at our balloon-shaped filter, made from electret media with electrostatically charged fibres," they explain.
The filter uses electrostatically charged fibres that attract and capture tiny airborne particles. It fits over an existing table or wall fan with the help of an elastic lining. Once the fan is switched on, the airflow inflates the filter into a balloon-like shape, increasing its surface area for filtration.
There is no need for additional motors, electrical modifications or specialised installation. The filter can be fitted in under a minute, without tools.
To develop and test the technology, the teenagers approached Hollingsworth & Vose, a filtration media manufacturer. They initially emailed the company's India team with their idea and were surprised by its willingness to support them.
The company provided filtration media free of cost and collaborated with the team on research and development.
"The technology to clean air already exists. Schools just can't afford it. By using fans that classrooms already have, we eliminated the need for expensive motors and additional infrastructure," they say.
This support has helped keep the manufacturing cost at approximately Rs 140 per filter.
What difference can a Rs 140 filter make?
For the young innovators, developing an affordable product was only half the task. They also needed to establish whether it could make a measurable difference to indoor air quality.
According to the founders, independent and external testing, along with joint research and development with Hollingsworth & Vose, has produced encouraging results.
In a closed room measuring approximately 200 square feet, PM2.5 concentrations reportedly dropped from 158 to 11 micrograms per cubic metre within an hour of using the filter, a reduction of over 90%.
The results, however, depend on the room's size and conditions. In a larger classroom, the team recorded a 60% reduction in PM2.5 levels over an hour, with further reductions over several hours of use.
There is also a visible reminder of the particles being trapped.
"One of the most striking things is seeing the filters turn from white to grey or even black after a few weeks of use. It's a visible reminder of just how much particulate pollution is present in classrooms," they say.
From 295 classrooms to thousands of students
Getting schools to trust an unfamiliar technology developed by high school students was not easy.
Initially, many institutions were understandably hesitant. Demonstrations and explanations of the testing behind the filters, however, helped the team build confidence.
Project Vayu began with a pilot covering 295 classrooms and approximately 8,000 students. The initiative has since expanded to more than 10 schools and has reached around 20,000 students. The team has also installed filters in several under-resourced medical clinics.
Their work has not been without challenges. Identifying schools, securing permissions and navigating institutional processes have often slowed installations.
"Balancing Project Vayu with academics has definitely been challenging. A lot of our time goes into approaching schools, coordinating installations, and following up on approvals," they say.
The effort has also brought recognition. Krish was named to the 2026 Diana Award Roll of Honour for his work with Project Vayu. For him, the recognition belongs to everyone who helped build the initiative, including Samarth and their collaborators.
"Project Vayu has taught me that innovation doesn't always require inventing something entirely new. Sometimes it's about making existing technology more accessible," Samarth adds.
What's next for Project Vayu?
The duo now hopes to expand Project Vayu to more schools across Delhi and eventually other parts of India. They are keen to work with government bodies, school principals, teachers and organisations that can help take the filters to children who need them.
Their ambition is rooted in a simple belief: access to cleaner air should not depend on how much a school can spend.
For Krish and Samarth, the idea was never just about making a fan work differently. It was about looking at something already available in classrooms and asking how it could serve children better.
And sometimes, making a difference does not require an entirely new machine. It begins with finding a new purpose for something that is already there.
All images courtesy of Krish Aggarwal

title: Dharwad Women Farmers Preserve 250+ Indigenous Seeds, Win Rs 10 Lakh Award
description: Meet the Bibi Fatima Women's Self-Help Group in Dharwad, Karnataka, which has conserved 250+ indigenous seed varieties, supported 5,000 farmers across 30 villages and won the Rs 10 lakh Plant Genome Saviour Community Award in 2026.
author: Sriroopa Dutta
content:
A handful of seeds can carry generations of farming knowledge.
In Karnataka's Dharwad district, a group of women has been collecting, preserving, and sharing these seeds, helping farmers continue cultivating indigenous crops suited to the region's rainfed conditions.
On November 12, 2026, the Bibi Fatima Women's Self-Help Group (SHG) from Teertha village in Kundgol taluk received the Plant Genome Saviour Community Award, along with a cash prize of Rs 10 lakh, a citation, and a memento.
The recognition acknowledges the collective's efforts to conserve more than 250 indigenous seed varieties and revive traditional millet-based mixed cropping systems across 30 villages in Dharwad's rainfed farming areas.
The initiative began in 2018, when farmer Bibijaan Maulasaab Halemani brought together 14 other women to establish the collective.
According to Bibijaan, her interest in seed conservation came from her father, who also preserved seeds.
Speaking to The New Indian Express in a report published on November 5, 2026, she said, “My father used to conserve seeds, and I too developed an interest and took to seed conservation.”
She established the SHG and its seed bank in 2018, with the aim of making good-quality indigenous seeds accessible to farmers and encouraging traditional crop cultivation.
A seed bank with more than 250 varieties
The group's community seed bank preserves a wide range of indigenous crops, including:
- - Jawari (sorghum)
- - 70 varieties of finger millet
- - 25 varieties of little millet
- - Two varieties of browntop millet
- - 10 varieties of foxtail millet
- - 25 varieties of horse gram
- - 10 varieties of chickpea
- - 25 varieties of paddy
- - Three varieties of green gram
- - Around a dozen oilseed varieties
- - Several varieties of vegetables
These varieties form part of the region's traditional agricultural diversity. The indigenous millet varieties, in particular, are adapted to local agro-climatic conditions and can withstand variations in weather.
The collective has also worked to revive millet-based mixed cropping, in which farmers cultivate multiple crops together rather than depending on a single crop.
According to the United Nations Development Programme's Equator Initiative, the group now supports more than 5,000 farmers across 30 villages. Its work includes promoting multi-cropping, maintaining community seed banks, and encouraging sustainable agricultural practices.
Beyond seed conservation, the collective has expanded into agricultural processing and livelihood activities.
It operates a solar-powered millet processing unit, which helps women produce value-added millet products. The initiative also works on livestock rearing, horticulture, and improving household food and nutritional security.
Recognition for community-led seed conservation
The national award is not the group's first recognition for its work.
In August 2025, the United Nations Development Programme announced Bibifathima Swa Sahaya Sangha as one of the 10 winners of the Equator Prize 2025. The award recognised community-led initiatives working on nature-based solutions under the theme 'Nature for Climate Action', with a focus on women's and young people's leadership.
According to the UNDP's August 20, 2025 announcement, the collective received recognition for its work combining traditional agricultural knowledge, seed conservation, renewable energy and climate-resilient farming. Each winning initiative was awarded $10,000.
For the women of Dharwad, their work continues to centre on collecting indigenous seeds, keeping traditional crop varieties in cultivation and helping farming communities access planting material suited to their local conditions.

title: IIT Roorkee Creates New Spring to Double Drinking Water Supply in an Uttarakhand Village
description: Researchers from IIT Roorkee created a new spring in an Uttarakhand village, doubling daily drinking water availability. Discover how they did it.
author: Sriroopa Dutta
content:
In the mountain villages of Uttarakhand's Tehri Garhwal district, the amount of drinking water available to families can change dramatically with the seasons.
Many households depend on natural springs fed by rainfall and water stored underground. As summer approaches and these springs begin to lose their flow, families are left managing increasingly limited supplies.
For residents of Unchaun village in the Kirtinagar block, seasonal water shortages have been a concern.
And their experience is shared by several other villages in the region.
A 2023–24 annual report by Himmotthan Society documents a similar challenge in Sabli village, also in Tehri Garhwal.
A survey conducted in June 2022 found that all 52 households depended on a local spring for drinking water during summer because piped supplies were either unreliable or unavailable.
The spring's flow dropped from 30 litres per minute during the monsoon to just five litres per minute in May and June. Over four summer months, the village faced an estimated water deficit of 14 lakh litres.
These figures offer a glimpse into how difficult the dry months can be for communities that depend on mountain springs.
Now, researchers at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Roorkee have developed a new spring in Unchaun, using scientific research to locate and bring underground water to the surface.
According to a Ministry of Education announcement on 2 November 2026, the intervention has increased daily drinking-water availability from approximately 500 litres to 1,000 litres or more during the lean season.
The interesting part is how the researchers identified where this water could be found.
Where does a Himalayan spring get its water?
The intervention is part of IIT Roorkee's project, Rejuvenation of Drying Springs in Takoli Gad Catchment of Tehri District, Uttarakhand.
Led by Professor Abhayanand Singh Maurya from the Department of Earth Sciences, the project draws on two studies examining how Himalayan springs are replenished and how water moves through underground rock formations.
The research was conducted in the Takoli Gad watershed, a 143-square-kilometre area in the Lesser Himalayas, within the Alaknanda River basin.
The first study, published in the Hydrological Sciences Journal in October 2026, examined where spring water comes from and how it travels underground.
Researchers studied rainfall patterns and used measurements of different forms of hydrogen and oxygen, including radioactive tritium, to trace the movement and replenishment of groundwater.
Their findings revealed just how important the monsoon is for sustaining Himalayan springs.
Approximately 82% of spring-water recharge in the studied watershed comes from monsoon rainfall. Winter precipitation contributes around 10%, while pre-monsoon rainfall accounts for the remaining 8%.
In simpler terms, much of the water that eventually emerges from these springs enters the ground during the rainy season.
Some of it remains stored underground, helping sustain water sources even months after the monsoon has ended.
The researchers also examined how long water stays underground before emerging through springs.
A second study, published in Applied Geochemistry in 2026, looked at how the rocks beneath the hills influence the chemical composition of spring water.
It found that interactions between water and carbonate rocks play an important role, alongside seasonal rainfall, soil carbon dioxide and human activities.
Together, these studies helped researchers understand how springs are replenished, what influences their water quality and where groundwater might be available.
IIT Roorkee Research Doubles Water Availability in a Himalayan Village During Lean Season Turning scientific research into tangible impact, IIT Roorkee has developed a new spring in Unchaun village, Tehri Garhwal, Uttarakhand, increasing lean-season drinking-water availability from approximately 500 litres to 1,000 litres or more per day. Led by Prof. Abhayanand Singh Maurya, Department of Earth Sciences, the initiative combines scientific understanding of spring-recharge dynamics, groundwater processes and geophysical investigations with targeted recharge interventions to address seasonal water scarcity. Supported by Namami Gange, National Mission for Clean Ganga, Ministry of Jal Shakti, Government of India, the project demonstrates the potential of research-driven solutions to strengthen rural water security. Building on two research studies published in Hydrological Sciences Journal and Applied Geochemistry, the initiative highlights how scientific insights can translate into effective, locally relevant interventions for Himalayan communities. With Prof. K. K. Pant, Director, IIT Roorkee, emphasising research with societal impact, this effort reinforces the Institute's commitment to advancing sustainable solutions for critical environmental and water challenges. #IITRoorkee #WaterSecurity #HimalayanWater #NamamiGange #SpringRejuvenation #GroundwaterRecharge #ResearchForImpact #SustainableDevelopment @iitroorkee @Director_IITR @cleanganganmcg @DoWRRDGR_MoJS
— IIT Roorkee (@iitroorkee) November 2, 2026
How the team brought underground water to the surface
The researchers began by studying the rock formations beneath the hillside to identify areas capable of holding and carrying groundwater.
Once they located promising water-bearing layers, they estimated their depth and extent.
The team then designed trenches along the uphill slope.
These trenches help slow rainwater flowing downhill, allowing more of it to seep into the soil and replenish underground water reserves.
At a suitable water-bearing layer, the researchers created a controlled opening that allowed groundwater to emerge at the surface.
This resulted in a new spring near the road leading to Chandrabadni Temple.
The reported result is an increase of at least 500 litres of drinking water available daily during the lean season, a potentially important improvement for households that depend on local sources.
Could this help other Himalayan villages?
Across the Himalayas, springs are an important source of drinking water, particularly in remote villages where other supplies can be unreliable.
The Unchaun project offers one way of addressing seasonal shortages: studying how water moves beneath a particular hillside before deciding where to intervene.
As Professor Maurya explained in the Ministry of Education release, “Understanding the source, movement and seasonal behaviour of spring water is essential to addressing water scarcity.”
The project has shown promising early results, but its long-term success will depend on whether the new spring continues to provide water through changing seasons.
Researchers will need to monitor its flow and water quality over time.
For now, the intervention offers a potentially useful approach for other Himalayan villages facing similar shortages, while showing how research into something as familiar as rainwater can help address everyday water needs.

title: Basava Mantapa controversy tests BJP and Congress ties with Lingayats
description: The Basavanna book controversy puts the Congress and BJP under pressure as both parties seek to retain the support of Karnataka’s Lingayat community.
author: Sujay B.M.
content:
The Karnataka Cabinet decided on Thursday, November 19, to forfeit Basava Mantapa, a Kannada book by the US-based writer Ravi Hanj, after Lingayat groups said it insulted Basavanna, the 12th-century social reformer and anti-caste crusader. Hanj was detained at Kochi airport in Keralam on Saturday, November 21, as he was about to leave the country.
The dominant Lingayat community, which considers Basavanna its ultimate leader, reacted strongly to the book, released on November 15, and to an interview Hanj gave to the YouTube channel of the Kannada daily Vishwavani. Basavanna is one of the foremost social reformers of Karnataka. In January 2024, the Congress-led State government declared him the State’s cultural icon. Police have registered FIRs against Hanj and the journalist and publisher Vishweshwar Bhat.
Days after the Cabinet decision, a notification forfeiting the book was passed. Forfeiture means that every copy of a book is declared to belong to the government, which can then seize it. Under Section 98 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023, a State government can issue such a declaration by notification, stating its grounds, if a book appears to contain matter punishable under specified provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023. These include promoting enmity between groups and deliberate acts intended to outrage religious feelings.
Once a book is declared forfeited, any police officer can seize copies wherever they are found in India, and a Magistrate can authorise a search of premises where copies are suspected to be held. The declaration can be challenged only before the High Court.
Posting on X, Home Minister Priyank Kharge accused Hanj of “distorting the history of Guru Basavanna and deeply hurting the sentiments of Kannadigas”. “He initially attempted to create the impression that he had left India for the United States. However, verification by the Home Department established that he was in a neighbouring State. He has been traced and a formal notice has been issued directing him to appear before the investigating authorities,” he added.
The book, which Frontline has accessed, accuses Basavanna of ambition and claims that “… Once Bijjala [Kalachuri king] started realising that Basavanna had placed his people in positions of power or once Basavanna opposed Bijjala, the stage of political polarisation to murder Bijjala and assume power started…”
It also claims that Basavanna died by suicide, which the Lingayat community contests. The book condemns the movement that seeks separate religion status for Lingayatism and personally attacks its leaders. In 2018, the Congress government led by Siddaramaiah recommended to the Union government that Lingayatism be granted separate religion status. The Narendra Modi-led Union government rejected the recommendation. The BJP and conservative sections had accused the Congress of “dividing” Hindu society. It also argues that untouchability was not prevalent in ancient Indian society and emerged only as a reaction to the arrival of Islamic rulers.
The book compiles articles Hanj wrote for Vishwavani, which Bhat heads. Hanj, a Kannadiga, has settled in the US and taken American citizenship. In the interview, Hanj cited a famous vachana (a Kannada devotional verse) of Basavanna, Kalabeda kolabeda husiya nudiyalu beda (Do not steal, do not murder, do not lie), as an example of Basavanna’s contradictions, accusing him of indulging in the very acts he condemned in the verse. Hanj has since apologised for his comments.
Political reactions
Criticising it at a press conference, Large and Medium Industries Minister M.B. Patil of the Congress, who is a Lingayat, said: “A man named Ravi Hanj has referred to a great vachana by Basavanna [Kala Beda Kola Beda] and has [directed it to] Basavanna himself. He is a criminal… This is not limited to one Ravi Hanj. There are many such people. It started with Kondi Manchanna in the 12th century. There have been several Kondi Manchannas over 800 years. They cannot tolerate Basavanna, the Basava Dharma and those vachanas.”
Speaking to Frontline, Congress MLA B.R. Patil, a veteran Lohiaite, or follower of the socialist leader Ram Manohar Lohia, said: “Such books are attempts by people who don’t believe in the casteless, egalitarian principles and equal society espoused by Basavanna. Whenever an opponent cannot be defeated with ideas, people resort to such personal slander and vilification. Such slanders are not confined to Basavanna but are happening with Gandhi, Ambedkar and Karl Marx as well.”
The situation is trickier for the BJP. Bhat is widely considered close to the RSS and its affiliates, and the controversy caught the party off guard. On the defensive, BJP leaders have condemned the book too. Prominent Lingayat leaders in the BJP, such as former Chief Minister B.S. Yediyurappa and his son, State president B.Y. Vijayendra, have expressed displeasure with the book.
Speaking to Frontline, the BJP MLA Arvind Bellad, who is Deputy Leader of the Opposition in the Karnataka Legislative Assembly and also a Lingayat, criticised Hanj’s comments on Basavanna. “Ravi Hanj is mad. Does anyone speak that way about Basavanna? Earlier, I have also read his articles on Vishwavani. Just because he has some literary skills, can he say whatever he wants? He is against the egalitarian principles of Basavanna that fought against untouchability. Our community [Veerashaiva Lingayats] stands on the concepts of the vachanas. Naturally the community is hurt by this controversy.”
Bellad agreed with the Congress-led State government’s decision to forfeit the book. “Such people who vitiate peace in the society must be arrested and placed before bars.” Much of civil society has condemned the book, though some scholars say banning a book is undemocratic. Others feel the line between freedom of expression and hate speech, which disturbs public tranquillity, is thin.
Fissures in the Mahasabha
The controversy has also set off a clash within the All India Veerashaiva Lingayat Mahasabha, the apex body of the Veerashaiva Lingayat community. Community leaders have criticised the Mahasabha’s State president, Shankar Bidari, a former DGP of Karnataka, and Manu Baligar, a former president of the Kannada Sahitya Parishat, for attending the book launch.
In a letter to Eshwar Khandre, the Mahasabha’s All India president and Rural Development and Panchayat Raj Minister, M.T. Subhash Chandra, a vice patron of the Mahasabha, urged that Bidari be suspended as State president. “Participating in the book launch of Basava Mantapa, Bidari has not only praised the anti-Basava author of the book Ravi Hanj but also congratulated him on behalf of the Mahasabha. This is a treason against the Mahasabha… Before more damage happens from such a person, I urge you to suspend Shankar Bidari,” the letter added.
Apart from the forfeiture, the letter sought legal action against Vishwavani and Bhat.
Many parts of Hanj’s book are in tune with the Hindutva ideology of the Sangh Parivar, but the BJP cannot afford to antagonise the Lingayats, its most significant support base.
Since the decline of the Janata Dal (United) in Karnataka, the BJP has drawn substantial support from the Lingayat community. The BJP has never won a simple majority on its own (113 of the 224 seats in the Karnataka Legislative Assembly). It won 110 seats in 2008 and 104 in 2018, and later assumed power through “Operation Lotus”, which drew opposition MLAs to its fold.
On both occasions, the Lingayat community was perceived as the BJP’s main support base. Yediyurappa is widely seen as the tallest Lingayat leader of the present day. Forcing him to make way for Basavaraj Bommai as Chief Minister in 2021 is widely perceived as one of the reasons for the BJP’s defeat in the 2023 Assembly election.
Though the BJP got the largest share of Lingayat votes even in 2023, a marginal shift of Lingayats towards the Congress, coupled with other developments, helped the Congress win 135 seats, with 42.88 per cent of the votes against the BJP’s 36 per cent.
The Lingayat community, dominant in north and central Karnataka with pockets of presence in the south, was believed to make up over 15 per cent of the State’s population. However, the socio-economic and educational survey report submitted in 2024 by the Backward Classes Commission under K. Jayaprakash Hegde estimated the community at 11.09 per cent. The community rejected the figure as “undercounting” of its numbers. The Siddaramaiah-led government set the report aside in June 2025.
Even at the lower estimate, the community’s social and political capital keeps it central to the State’s politics. Since Yediyurappa’s political retirement, there has been a leadership vacuum in the Lingayat community across parties. Vijayendra, though the BJP’s State president, is yet to become a universally accepted leader within the party.
The Congress is watching the situation closely and trying to win over the community. The State government’s quick action in forfeiting the book and detaining Hanj could help it make inroads. A senior Veerashaiva Lingayat Mahasabha leader told Frontline that Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar, though a Vokkaliga (a land-owning community dominant in south Karnataka), was trying to win over the community. “Since Shivakumar became the chief minister, he has taken decisions in favour of Lingayats. The decision to forfeit the book is a major one. He has also appointed five Lingayats as vice chancellors of various universities. He is trying to win over the support of the community. Lingayats do not insist on only supporting leaders from their caste. Even in the past, former Chief Minister Ramakrishna Hegde [Brahmin] was widely trusted and supported by Lingayats.”
The regional Janata Dal (Secular), an alliance partner of the BJP, has little stake in the contest for Lingayat votes, since it is seen as a party that rests mainly on Vokkaliga support and is confined to south Karnataka.
How the two national parties handle the controversy, and the Lingayat community, will bear on their electoral prospects in the 2028 Assembly election.

title: The importance of Asaduddin Owaisi
description: The AIMIM leader’s willingness to fight elections in Uttar Pradesh is billed as vote-splitting, but his real role is to give Muslims a voice that mainstream anti-Hindutva formations have taken for granted.
author: Ajaz Ashraf
content:
All India Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen leader Asaduddin Owaisi, in his speech opposing the motion of thanks on the President’s address on June 10, 2014, listed four events that had defiled India’s post-Independence history. These were the assassination of Mahatma Gandhi in 1948, the genocide of Sikhs in 1984, the destruction of the Babri Masjid in 1992, and the anti-Muslim pogrom in Gujarat in 2002.
BJP members in the Lok Sabha erupted, stung by Owaisi’s audacity to taunt them a fortnight after they had come to power. Not one to be cowed, Owaisi said he stood before them as a son of Ehsan Jafri, as a brother of Ishrat Jahan, and as an uncle of Mohsin Sadiq Sheikh. Jafri, a former MP, was hacked to death in 2002 in Gujarat, where Jahan too was killed in a fake encounter, while Sheikh was a Muslim techie lynched in Pune days earlier.
For a man who delivered such an extraordinarily bold speech, and whose ardour in highlighting the trials and tribulations of Muslims hasn’t diminished since, it must hurt or anger that he is accused of being the BJP’s Trojan horse. This charge against Owaisi has resurfaced following his forging of an alliance with Chandrashekhar Azad’s Aazad Samaj Party-Kanshi Ram (ASPKR) in Uttar Pradesh, where the Assembly election is due in February-March.
Those who accuse Owaisi of playing the BJP’s game do so out of their worries over Hindutva’s illiberalism and its propensity to demonise and target Muslims. Only a united anti-Hindutva front can defeat the BJP, given its wide social base in Uttar Pradesh, they argue. Since Owaisi can’t, even in alliance with Azad, dethrone the BJP, he shouldn’t, as a votary of Muslim interests, contest and split the community’s votes to whatever degree.
Owaisi should have, they argue, left the dominant anti-Hindutva alliance of the Samajwadi Party and the Congress to wage an unimpeded battle against the BJP. Not only has he sought to enhance his appeal by aligning with Azad’s ASPKR, a Dalit party, but he has also been directing his fury against the SP-Congress alliance and the BJP in equal measure. The votes Owaisi would garner would be those of the SP-Congress alliance, since Muslims mostly exercise their franchise to defeat the BJP.
The predominant concern of Muslims to vote out the BJP has led anti-Hindutva formations to take their support for granted, Owaisi argues. In power, they didn’t pull the community out of the economic morass in which it languishes. And now, out of power, they haven’t mounted resistance to the lynching and killing of Muslims in fake encounters, or to the destruction of mosques and mausoleums, nor have they improved their representation in legislatures.
The hypocrisy of anti-Hindutva blocs
The conduct of anti-Hindutva formations is hypocritical, Owaisi argues, for they wouldn’t be even within smelling distance of power without the support of Muslims. He advocates that Muslims should leverage their votes to strike a better bargain for the community. Since the BJP isn’t an option for them, they should vote en masse for the AIMIM.
Such strategic voting has a twofold advantage: the possibility of losing Muslim support will persuade anti-Hindutva formations to work harder for the community. Or, they will enter into an alliance with the AIMIM, in the same manner as regional and national political parties do with outfits representing a caste. Either way, it is a win-win situation for Muslims.
This political strategy has been a subject of discussion among educated, middle-class Muslims for well over a decade. It has acquired salience today because of Owaisi’s popularity in the Modi years. Owaisi has fearlessly opposed the attacks on Muslims and espoused their interests, couching his arguments in constitutionalism and drawing upon the arguments of the founders of the Indian Republic, especially B.R. Ambedkar. He represents the fantasy of Muslims to speak in the public sphere as he does.
Owaisi wasn’t always positioned against anti-Hindutva formations. After being elected to the Lok Sabha in 2004 from Hyderabad, he supported the United Progressive Alliance at the Centre and the Congress government of undivided Andhra Pradesh. He broke away from them in 2012, after the State government allowed, in violation of a High Court order, for the Bhagyalaxmi temple, abutting the iconic Charminar monument, to be covered with tarpaulin. The makeshift temple didn’t exist until the late 1950s, as the Archaeological Survey of India’s photos show.
Since then, he has played solo in the Indian political theatre, hoping to grow his AIMIM on the support of Muslims. His limited success has been inadequate for bargaining on the community’s behalf. The AIMIM won two seats in the 2014 Maharashtra Assembly election, came second in three, and had a vote share of 0.93 per cent. Five years later, the AIMIM again bagged two seats, came second in four, and secured a vote share of 1.34 per cent.
In 2024, the party was down to one seat and a vote share of 0.85 per cent, partly because it contested only 17 seats, in comparison to 24 in 2014, and 44 in 2019. But it came second in five seats. The AIMIM has developed a stable support base in certain constituencies—Malegaon Central and Aurangabad Central, for instance—where it pulls thousands upon thousands of votes every election.
The AIMIM famously won five of the 20 seats it contested in the 2020 Bihar Assembly election, on a vote share of 1.24 per cent. Four AIMIM MLAs defected. Yet, in 2025, the AIMIM retained all five seats, came second in another two of the 28 seats it fought in, while its vote share crawled up to 1.85 per cent. The party came third in 13 seats. In three of them, though, its presence led to losses for the Grand Alliance.
The ‘vote-splitter’ charge
Although the AIMIM’s growth has been incremental, leaders of anti-Hindutva formations dub Owaisi a “vote-splitter”. This is because they know his popularity is greater than his party’s electoral performance suggests, and could become an important factor in a scenario of social plates shifting. Besides, with elections increasingly becoming a neck-and-neck competition, they wish to minimise as far as possible the number of Muslims drifting to Owaisi from them.
It is to accelerate this process of drift that Owaisi has tied up with Azad, who positions himself as an alternative to Mayawati’s Bahujan Samaj Party, which is witnessing a downward spiral. Owaisi and Azad symbolise the coming together of Dalits and Muslims, a dream of subaltern thinkers and activists. The two social groups together constitute roughly 40 per cent of Uttar Pradesh’s population.
Many, including Muslims, question why Owaisi doesn’t conquer his home State of Telangana before venturing into the Hindi heartland, pointing out that the AIMIM contested 20 of 119 Assembly seats in 2014, eight in 2018, and nine in 2023. Contrast these figures with the number of candidates the AIMIM fields in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh.
One reason could be that 52 per cent of Telangana’s Muslims reside in Hyderabad and neighbouring Rangareddy districts, reducing the chances of the predominantly Muslim-based AIMIM winning elsewhere. Yet it does seem the AIMIM appears content with regularly winning seven Assembly seats in Hyderabad, in contrast to its feverish efforts to expand in the Hindi heartland.
Owaisi’s detractors also wonder why he hasn’t attempted to build a Dalit-Muslim combine in Telangana, where the two social groups together account for 30 per cent of the State’s population. Owaisi would, though, point out that the AIMIM elected Hyderabad’s first Dalit mayor—K. Prakash Rao—way back in 1986, and at least two more in later years.
In addition, academics Rochana Bajpai and Adnan Farooqui, in their study of Owaisi, point out, “In the 2015 Aurangabad Municipal elections, the party fielded thirteen Dalit candidates, of whom five won in reserved seats with substantial margins.” Since then, fielding Dalit and other Hindu candidates has been a consistent pattern in the AIMIM’s electoral strategy.
Yet both Owaisi and Azad face a formidable challenge in becoming significant players in Uttar Pradesh. In the 2022 Uttar Pradesh Assembly election, the AIMIM didn’t win even one of the 95 seats it contested and managed a vote share of 0.49 per cent. It polled over 10,000 votes in only six constituencies. The ASPKR crossed the 10,000-vote mark in just one of the 100 seats it fought in, with a measly vote share of 0.13 per cent.
Owaisi hasn’t been able to translate his popularity into votes because poor Muslims, unlike those in the middle class, are not networked into the system that could protect them from the onslaught of Hindutvawadis. They would rather vote out, say, Chief Minister Adityanath, their unrelenting tormentor, than calculate whether his successor would be beneficial to them; he wouldn’t, at least, subject them to everyday communal abuse.
Owaisi’s real importance to Indian politics is that he is the vent through which Muslims release their anger and discontent against the BJP—and also against anti-Hindutva formations. His speeches are cathartic for Muslims. Owaisi is acutely aware of his role, for Bajpai and Farooqui quote him telling them, “A Muslim who feels let down by mainstream parties is coming to me, but God forbid, tomorrow he may go to fundamentalists, what is the alternative for him?” Those stridently critical of Owaisi exercising his democratic right to contest in Uttar Pradesh need to rethink and take into account the meaning Owaisi personifies.
Ajaz Ashraf is a senior journalist from Delhi and the author of Bhima Koregaon: Challenging Caste.

title: What is the Real Reason Behind the Gold Price Crash?
description: Gold and silver prices have plunged amid global market turmoil. Modi claims credit, but household debt, gold loans and market forces tell another story.
author: Mitali Mukherjee
content:
In a script straight out of Bollywood, with power, corruption, spies, romantic affairs and a blockbuster stock listing all in the mix, the AI trade is seeing a massive sell-off globally. The irony is that the most human and fallible emotions have brought this frontier technology to its knees: greed and hubris. The weight of the debt these AI companies are saddled with seems to be causing panic in the stock markets and the world at large. US tech stocks have logged their worst session since the COVID-19 outbreak in the same week that AI colossus Anthropic had a spectacular listing, rising 17 per cent and raising an eye-watering $81.3 billion in its initial public offering.
In the very near term, the sell-off has triggered a rally in Indian stocks and the rupee. Foreign investors have bought $12 billion of shares so far in November, the largest-ever monthly inflow and some relief from the pasting the Indian currency and markets received for most of this year. India is the world’s “AI-free trade”, but something else is playing out in global markets that could have a far bigger impact on India and its people.
Triggered in part by forced selling to cover the deep losses AI and technology-related stocks have seen in the US, and also by the fear of steepish interest rate hikes coming from various central banks, gold has fallen with a ferocity that has been startling to watch.
Global gold prices fell nearly 10 per cent over just the past week, and while markets across Asia have also seen sharp cuts in gold prices, two markets are seeing physical gold demand surge—India and China.
The crash in gold prices is playing out in very different ways across India. For those who invested in precious metals through mutual funds or exchange-traded funds, the fact that silver has crashed over 60 per cent from its January peak, and gold over 30 per cent, means that there are gaping holes in the value of their investments. Those who trade on exchanges like the Multi Commodity Exchange are probably smarting from margin calls and major losses.
For India’s wedding-season buyers, though, this unforeseen fall in gold and silver has meant buying jewellery is clearly cheaper, and it is no surprise jewellery showrooms are buzzing with activity. As an aside, it would be very revealing to know how many of these purchases are being made in cash versus digital payments.
Modi’s claim
Against this backdrop of what is clearly a global reset in gold and silver prices come Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s claims that credit this correction in gold prices to himself and to his appeal earlier this year to Indians, asking them to avoid non-essential gold purchases for a year.
A few points to note here. First, what time periods are we assessing when talking about a Modi-led correction in precious metals? In November, international gold prices fell by more than 30 per cent from their January record of $5,594.82 per ounce (about $180 per gram). In contrast, the Prime Minister points to a fall in domestic prices by comparing prices one day before his announcement. The reversal in international gold prices started in January of 2026, much before any appeal from the Modi government exhorting people to stop buying gold.
Second, in May of this year, the Centre more than doubled import duties on gold and silver from 6 per cent to 15 per cent, a move, in part, to dissuade people from importing gold by making it more expensive and also to curtail the slip and slide of the rupee by decreasing the foreign currency needed to buy that gold.
And finally, as the World Gold Council data report explains, the numbers for gold and its purchase in India are a “volume and value” story. India’s gold market had a modest second quarter, with demand rising sharply in the third quarter of the year, specifically on the back of jewellery demand. Despite the gap between the volume of gold bought and that in 2025, the value of demand has risen through the first nine months of 2026: demand fell 12 per cent to 444 tonnes, while value increased 38 per cent to Rs.6,688 billion ($71 billion).
So, while the Prime Minister may be marking this relief in gold prices as a personal victory, the data and trends tell a different story. Both the spectacular rise and equally dazzling fall of gold have less to do with any clarion call from the Prime Minister and more to do with a global rally and consequent sell-off. For a while Indians bought smaller quantities of gold because it was simply too expensive and out of reach, especially imported gold. The broad picture for 2026 confirms that both consumers and investors have continued to allocate substantial sums to gold: high prices limited how much could be bought but certainly not the sums involved in these purchases; in its simplest terms, this year you get less for more.
Stress at gold lenders
Against this tale of who bought and when, the biggest red flag is early reports trickling out from gold-financing non-banking financial companies like Muthoot Finance, IIFL Finance, Bajaj Finance, and Manappuram Finance. All of them have reported an increase in stage 2 assets, which are loans showing early stress or delinquency. The ferocity of the fall in gold and silver prices means there is a real danger of defaults, which may bring distress for both the loan companies and, importantly, their lenders.
The relationship that Indian households have with gold and silver is not as simplistic as the Prime Minister would like to believe. It has always been an emotional investment, treated as not just the safest asset to own, but also a matter of pride and the ultimate refuge.
So, while the short term may provide a window of buying for some, in the longer term, deep and prolonged damage to prices will not be good news for Indian households that are already stretched with loans and struggling with rising household costs.
During early gold rushes like the 1849 California Gold Rush, thousands of hopefuls with no mining background flooded the rivers and hills. What they found in plenty was wet pyrite, a mineral that glinted and gleamed just like the precious metal but soon came to be called “fool’s gold”. And perhaps, just as Indians know the value of gold, they can also tell the difference between real accomplishments and bogus claims.
Mitali Mukherjee is Director of the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism, University of Oxford.
