title: Parliament's Four-Day Sitting From November 30, No Question Hour Or Zero Hour
description: Parliament's four-day special sitting will begin on November 30 in the Lok Sabha and December 2 in the Rajya Sabha, with no Question Hour, Zero Hour or Private Members' Business.
author: Madhuri Adnal
content:
Parliament's Four-Day Sitting From November 30, No Question Hour Or Zero Hour
The Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha secretariats on Thursday issued separate bulletins announcing the schedule for the upcoming four-day parliamentary sittings. Both notices confirmed that there will be no Question Hour, Zero Hour or Private Members' Business during the session.
Earlier on Thursday, Union Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju said the government had requested Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla and Rajya Sabha Chairman CP Radhakrishnan to reconvene the two Houses.
AI-generated summary, reviewed by editors
The special sittings come amid speculation that the government may bring back the Delimitation Bill and the Constitution Amendment Bill seeking to implement 33 per cent reservation for women from 2029. The Union Cabinet is also scheduled to meet at 1 pm on Friday.
According to the Lok Sabha bulletin, the Lower House will reconvene at 11 am on Monday, November 30, after being adjourned sine die on August 13. The government had not prorogued the Monsoon Session.
As a result, the session technically remains open. Under Rule 15 of the Lok Sabha's Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business, the Speaker can call a sitting of the House without requiring the President to summon a fresh session. A corresponding provision applies to the Rajya Sabha.
The Lok Sabha Speaker has directed that the second part of the eighth session of the 18th Lok Sabha resume on November 30 under Rule 15.
The provisional calendar has set aside November 30 and December 1, 2 and 3 for parliamentary business. The sittings are scheduled to end on December 3, depending on the government's business requirements.
The Rajya Sabha will reconvene at 11 am on Wednesday, December 2, according to a separate bulletin issued by the Upper House secretariat. The notice said the 271st session, which was adjourned sine die on August 13, had been reconvened by the Chairman to transact essential government business. It is scheduled to conclude on December 3, subject to business requirements.
Both Houses have confirmed that the sittings will not include Question Hour, Zero Hour or Private Members' Business.

title: How The Numbers Stack Up For NDA Since April To Push Women's Reservation, Delimitation Bills
description: The Centre is hoping to secure support for the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill in the upcoming Parliament session, with the DMK, NCP (SP) and rebel TMC MPs indicating they may back it.
author: Madhuri Adnal
content:
How The Numbers Stack Up For NDA Since April To Push Women's Reservation, Delimitation Bills
The Centre may have a better chance of passing the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill when Parliament meets later this month, with several Opposition parties and breakaway groups indicating that they could support the legislation this time.
The bill, which was defeated in April, seeks to increase the maximum strength of the Lok Sabha from 543 to 850 seats and provide 33 per cent reservation for women in Parliament and state assemblies ahead of the 2029 general elections. The government had failed to secure the two-thirds majority required for its passage after the Opposition voted against it.
AI-generated summary, reviewed by editors
Since then, a series of political realignments has changed the numbers in the Lower House. 20 Trinamool Congress MPs have broken away and joined the Nationalist Citizens Party of India (NCPI), while 6 Shiv Sena (Uddhav Balasaheb Thackeray) MPs have moved to the Eknath Shinde-led Shiv Sena. The Shiromani Akali Dal, which has one Lok Sabha MP, has also joined hands with the BJP.
These developments have raised hopes within the NDA that it could get closer to the required majority. However, support from parties outside the ruling alliance will still be important.
The DMK is among the parties that could influence the outcome. With 22 MPs in the Lok Sabha and eight in the Rajya Sabha, the party has indicated that it is willing to reconsider its position if the Centre gives written assurances that states will receive a proportionate increase in their Lok Sabha seats.
A senior DMK leader said the party would examine the revised provisions before taking a decision. "If the wording of the bill has changed, we will certainly be open to supporting it. We will meet tomorrow or soon after and decide our course of action," the leader said.
The DMK's position is particularly important given its earlier opposition to the legislation. The party, once a close Congress ally, has also seen its relationship with the national party deteriorate after the Congress backed the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam to form the Tamil Nadu government following the Assembly elections this summer.
The Sharad Pawar-led Nationalist Congress Party (Sharadchandra Pawar), which is part of the INDIA bloc, has also left the door open to supporting the bill. The party has eight MPs in the Lok Sabha and one in the Rajya Sabha. It had voted against the legislation in April.
NCP (SP) working president Supriya Sule has made it clear that her party's support will depend on the changes proposed by the government. She has listed three conditions: implementation of women's reservation, a 50 per cent increase in Lok Sabha seats across all states, and adequate representation for Opposition parties in the delimitation commission.
Sule has also argued that the growing population in parliamentary constituencies makes delimitation necessary. She said MPs are finding it increasingly difficult to represent constituencies with rising populations.
"The population in parliamentary constituencies is increasing and it is becoming difficult for MPs like me to manage it," said the Baramati MP.
The party will examine the bill before deciding whether to support it. "If they align with the three issues we have raised, we can support the bill," Sule said.
Speaking to reporters in Mumbai, she said the NCP (SP) would not rule out backing the legislation if it served the country's interests. She cited instances when parties across the political divide had supported government decisions on national issues, including the response following the Pahalgam terror attack and the passage of the GST and women's reservation bills.
"The same could happen with the delimitation bill if its provisions are in the country's interest. Who knows?" she said.
The 20 rebel Trinamool Congress MPs are also expected to support the government. Their proposed merger with the NCPI, however, is yet to receive the Lok Sabha Speaker's approval. Until then, they continue to be recognised as Trinamool Congress MPs in official records, a senior Lok Sabha official said.
"We are with the NDA. We support the delimitation bill," a senior member of the rebel group said, requesting anonymity.
What numbers does the government need?
Passing a Constitution amendment requires a two-thirds majority of members present and voting in each House, in addition to the support of a majority of the House's total membership. The amendment must also be ratified by at least half of the state legislatures.
The Lok Sabha currently has 540 members, with three vacancies. The government needs 360 votes to pass the bill, while 180 votes against it would be enough to prevent its passage.
In April, the bill received 298 votes in favour and 230 against.
The Opposition has since lost around 26 votes following the split in the Trinamool Congress and the exit of six Shiv Sena (UBT) MPs. If the DMK and NCP (SP) also extend their support, the government could move considerably closer to the numbers it needs.
The coming Parliament session will therefore be crucial in determining whether the Centre can secure the backing that eluded it during the April vote.

title: Centre Expands UAPA Action Against Zakir Naik's IRF, Gives States More Powers
description: Centre authorises states and UTs to exercise UAPA powers over funds and premises linked to Zakir Naik's Islamic Research Foundation.
author: PTI
content:
Centre Expands UAPA Action Against Zakir Naik's IRF, Gives States More Powers
The Centre has authorised states and Union territories to exercise powers related to funds and premises under the stringent Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, in relation to fugitive preacher Zakir Naik's Islamic Research Foundation (IRF), which was declared an unlawful association earlier this month.
In a gazette notification issued on Thursday, the Ministry of Home Affairs invoked powers under Section 42 of the anti-terror law to issue the directive to state governments and Union territory administrators. The ministry had extended the ban on the IRF as an unlawful association through a notification dated November 13 under sections 3(1) and 3(3) of the Act.
AI-generated summary, reviewed by editors
"The Central government declared the Islamic Research Foundation an unlawful association vide notification number S.O. 6182(E) dated November 13, 2026, published in the Gazette of India; in exercise of the powers conferred by Section 42 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, the Central government hereby directs that all powers exercisable by it under sections 7 and 8 of the said Act shall also be exercised by the state governments and the Union territory administrations in relation to the above said unlawful association," the notification said.
Section 7 of the UAPA pertains to the powers of the government to prohibit the use or transfer of funds, securities and other financial assets suspected of being used or intended for the purposes of an unlawful association. It also allows authorised officers to investigate such financial dealings, whereas Section 8 empowers the government to notify premises, including houses and buildings, suspected of being used for the activities of an unlawful association.
Following the notification, the authorities can regulate access to a premises and restrict the use of movable properties found there.
On November 13, the Centre extended the ban on fugitive preacher Zakir Naik's IRF for another five years under the stringent UAPA. The ban was to expire on November 14. Naik, a resident of Maharashtra, was on a trip abroad when the government banned his organisation in 2016. Since then, he has been living in Malaysia. In 2017, his passport was also revoked at the request of the National Investigation Agency (NIA), which registered a case against him.
India has been pursuing legal and diplomatic measures against Naik since November 17, 2016, when the Central government declared his organisation an unlawful association citing allegations of promoting enmity and hatred between religious communities.
In May 2017, India approached INTERPOL for a Red Corner Notice (RCN) against Naik, providing subsequent clarifications in August and October. However, during its 102nd session in late December 2017, the Interpol Commission deemed the request premature because a charge-sheet had not been filed at the time of the initial application.
Based on a fresh court warrant issued on November 24, 2017, the Indian agencies submitted a renewed RCN request to INTERPOL on January 3, 2018, a response to which remains awaited. India had also formally transmitted a provisional arrest and extradition request to Malaysia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs on January 19, 2018, after it was confirmed that Naik had been granted permanent residency status.

title: Quit before being removed, PM told: Kharge targets Modi over Shah and Adityanath
description: At A Lucknow Meeting, Congress Chief Says Modi, Amit Shah And Yogi Adityanath Are Eyeing The Prime Minister’s Post And Claims The BJP Fears Defeat In Uttar Pradesh
author: Piyush Srivastava
content:
Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge has suggested that Narendra Modi quit before his own people dethrone him, appearing to claim that Amit Shah and Yogi Adityanath harboured prime ministerial ambitions.
“We don’t know what is going on between Modi and Shah, but a third person has also emerged recently in Uttar Pradesh. He is eyeing the PM’s chair. Shah is also eyeing the PM’s chair. Modi, however, is not willing to leave the chair. I suggest he leave it himself,” Kharge told a public meeting at the state party headquarters in Lucknow on Thursday.
The reference to the “third person” appeared to be to Adityanath.
The Congress president was in Lucknow to attend a party event marking the adoption of the Constitution on November 26, 1949. Kharge led a Samvidhan Raksha March (Protect Constitution March). The local administration allowed him to address the meeting but didn’t permit the procession.
Kharge claimed Modi and Shah had realised that the BJP would lose the Uttar Pradesh elections. “That is why he (Modi) is speaking less aggressively than before, he is perturbed,” the Congress leader added.
“The truth is that Modi doesn’t know how the country is running. Recently he addressed a meeting and accused companies of profiteering. Modi himself told the seminar that companies had not increased wages and hirings. I am not saying this, he himself complained to them that they didn’t make investments although he had divested public sector undertakings, waived taxes and given them everything they wanted,” Kharge said.
“Unfortunately, he realised this only when elections are round the corner. Every item is being imported from China, but Modi is silent.”

title: Samajwadi Party pledges jobs, Rs 5 meal and leash on mafia ahead of  2027 UP polls
description: Akhilesh Yadav Promises 25 Lakh Government Jobs, Pensions For Elderly Women And A Farm Loan Waiver, While Pledging Rs 5 Meals And Action Against Land Grabbers
author: Our Special Correspondent
content:
Samajwadi Party president Akhilesh Yadav on Thursday promised 25 lakh government jobs and employment opportunities for 2 to 3 crore youths over five years, an annual pension of Rs 40,000 for elderly women and a farm-loan waiver if his party comes to power in Uttar Pradesh after the 2027 Assembly polls.
Free laptops will be distributed to students completing Class XII, Akhilesh announced, building on a popular scheme of his government during the SP’s 2012-2017 tenure.
Unveiling the party’s manifesto along with senior SP leaders here, Akhilesh said: “Our resolve is to give government jobs to 25 lakh youngsters and employment in other sectors to 2 to 3 crore young people in five years.”
Promising financial assistance to vulnerable sections of society, he said elderly women would receive Rs 40,000 annually as pension and the amount would be directly transferred to their bank accounts. Labourers, women workers and artisans would also be given an annual pension of Rs 40,000, the former Uttar Pradesh chief minister said. “Samajwadi canteens will be opened for PDA (backwards, Dalits and minorities) women and the poor, where meals will be available for Rs 5,” he said.
Akhilesh also promised an immediate farm loan waiver and said a corpus of Rs 15,000 crore would be created to ensure that sugarcane growers receive their payments within 24 hours.
The SP chief promised better law and order in the state. Since the law-and-order situation under SP rule had faced repeated questions and the BJP reminds people about the “patronage to outlaws”, Akhilesh said on Thursday: “Goondas, the mafia, land grabbers and criminals will be sent to jail if we come to power. A special task force will keep an eye on land grabbers.”
Where’s Congress?
The SP president refused to reply to a question on why ally Congress was not present when he unveiled the SP’s manifesto.
He ridiculed the reporter for asking the question and said: “I know you. We will talk about it later.”
Akhilesh said he would release two more manifestos before the elections, including one for women.
Annoyed Azam
SP general secretary Azam Khan, the SP’s most prominent Muslim face, suggested in his speech that his party leaders didn’t try to understand his problem when he was in jail.
“I used to tell my son (Abdullah Azam) and others that Akhilesh should also be here for six months to understand the ordeal I passed through,” Azam said.
Muslim, OBC promise
AIMIM chief Asaduddin Owaisi said Uttar Pradesh would get a Muslim and an OBC deputy chief minister, besides Dalit leader Chandrashekhar Azad as chief minister, if their Samajik Parivartan Morcha formed the government.

title: Congress sues Meta, govt for ‘censoring’ Rahul Gandhi-related posts ahead of state polls
description: Party Challenges IT Rules In Delhi HC, Alleging Automated Tools Blocked Political And Personal Posts Featuring Rahul Gandhi Without Notice Or A Hearing
author: Amiya Kumar Kushwaha, Reuters
content:
The Congress has sued Meta and the Centre, saying that an automated content-removal system is blocking political posts and images of Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi ahead of state elections.
The filing takes a weeklong Congress campaign against Meta from the streets to the courtroom and highlights Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s automated takedown mandate, under which the Facebook and Instagram parent has restricted more than 5.4 million posts in the first half of 2026, up from about 70,000 in all of 2025.
In a filing dated November 25 in Delhi High Court, Congress’s youth wing social media head Manu Jain said the rules had become “an instrument for the suppression of lawful political expression”.
The case leaves Meta’s operations in India, the company’s biggest market, caught between a government whose rules strip platforms of legal protection if they fail to comply, and an Opposition demanding it push back.
The petition specifically flagged multiple contents that Meta made “unavailable in India” between September 29 and November 23.
“The one feature common to all of them is the photograph or the name of Rahul Gandhi, Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha,” the petition filed by Indian Youth Congress national secretary Jain said.
Jain filed the petition in Delhi High Court through advocate Rishav Ranjan, seeking to strike down Rule 4(4) of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021.
Rule 4(4) of the IT Rules, effective since February, requires social media intermediaries to deploy automated tools to proactively identify and render inaccessible information that such tools treat as identical to information previously disabled under Rule 3(1)(d), without notifying the publisher, providing reasons, or offering any opportunity to be heard.
Under Rule 3(1)(d), social media platforms must remove unlawful information upon receiving actual knowledge through a court order or notification from the appropriate government.
According to the petition, these posts included ordinary political and personal content, such as a wedding invitation given to Rahul, a birthday wish from a party worker to another, a tribute to a former Prime Minister on his birth anniversary, photographs of party workers with Rahul, a post about a 3,000km march undertaken by an IYC district office-bearer, and an IYC post about a lecture given by Rahul at the University of Chicago.

title: Sheikh Hasina: Why her planned return from India has Bangladesh on edge
description: The ousted prime minister's December homecoming plan deepens Dhaka-Delhi tensions and risks fresh unrest.
author: Soutik Biswas
content:
Sheikh Hasina's planned return puts Bangladesh on edge - and India in a bind
- Published
Sheikh Hasina has repeatedly vowed to return to Bangladesh.
Now the ousted prime minister has put a date on her homecoming - 16 December - and even outlined how she intends to make the journey.
The government in Dhaka, which had previously dismissed the prospect, is taking her latest declaration more seriously.
Hasina, 79, who fled to Delhi in August 2024 after a student-led uprising ended her 15-year rule, plans to go back on Victory Day, the anniversary of Bangladesh's triumph over Pakistan in the 1971 liberation war, her spokesperson said.
She was sentenced to death after being convicted of crimes against humanity for her role in the crackdown, in a trial held in her absence that raised questions about due process. Her Awami League party is banned in Bangladesh. The UN says as many as 1,400 people were killed by security forces during the uprising.
The government says she would be arrested immediately if she returned and has promised to carry out the death sentence.
Hasina now wants the Bangladesh government to arrange a flight from Delhi. If that fails, she could travel commercially or cross the land border.
"She is even prepared to walk into Bangladesh," Abu Obaidha Arin, a key aide to Hasina, told the BBC.
India and Bangladesh share a 4,096km (2,545 mile) border across five Indian states - West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. Her supporters, Arin said, had identified nine possible crossing points. "This is a carefully thought-out, precise plan. This is serious."
Dhaka has responded with defiance, insisting Hasina must be extradited.
"Reality and desire are different things," Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs, told reporters in Dhaka. "[The reality is] she's not a regular commercial passenger. She can only be brought back in handcuffs."
India's foreign ministry said on Wednesday that Hasina's extradition request was being examined through the "established process", adding that a voluntary return would be a separate matter.
Many in Dhaka believe Hasina's declaration is more than a promise of homecoming.
They believe it is an attempt to test the government's authority, force her way back into the political conversation and exploit divisions among the parties that united to oust her. It also threatens to turn India's unresolved problem of sheltering a former ally into a more immediate diplomatic crisis.
The date is significant. Hasina is invoking Victory Day to reclaim her place in Bangladesh's founding narrative. Aides say she has spent months trying to keep her party alive in exile.
Arin says Hasina has been in regular contact with party leaders and workers through interactive audio conversations on Telegram, keeping alive a network that might otherwise have been difficult to sustain from exile.
Over the past 18 months, he says, she has held more than 300 such meetings, reaching supporters across all 64 districts and the country's 300 constituencies. They are organised through the Awami League's 78 units and "can last four or five hours".
The meetings allow Hasina to listen directly to party workers, hear their grievances and understand what is happening on the ground, Arin says. He insists the response has been substantial and claims the party "could mobilise five million people to welcome her along the route from the border to Dhaka, forming a human chain".
"We have the organisational capacity to make that happen," he says.
That may be an ambitious claim. The Awami League remains a mass party with millions of supporters, but it is banned and largely shut out of mainstream politics. Much of its leadership is abroad, in jail or underground. Police have arrested supporters and filed thousands of cases against party workers.
Yet its supporters have continued to take to the streets, staging flash protests that have grown more frequent and confrontational in recent months.
Several districts have reported bomb attacks, arson and vandalism, though responsibility for some incidents remains disputed.
Gopalganj, Hasina's ancestral district, has proved particularly difficult for the authorities to control.
Awami League supporters have attacked police stations, external, torched vehicles and targeted homes and offices belonging to ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) leaders, reports say. Highways have been blocked, external with felled trees and burning tyres, bringing traffic to a standstill. In some areas, police have withdrawn, external amid fears of further attacks.
Supporters have staged 40 demonstrations and more than 140 riots up to 23 November, according to data from conflict monitoring group Acled (Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project). At least 11 people, including two civilians, have been killed in political violence this month, six directly linked to the unrest, the group says.
The party's ability to cause disruption, however, is not necessarily evidence of a broad resurgence.
Many in Dhaka remain sceptical that Hasina will actually return, viewing the announcement as a means of galvanising a demoralised party.
Yet the Awami League has achieved something politically: it is back in the conversation. Immediately after Hasina's fall, even mentioning the party was taboo. Now its future is being debated across the political spectrum.
Shafiqul Alam, editor of the English-language daily Daily Waadaa and former press secretary to the Muhammad Yunus-led interim government, believes the party is "exploiting cracks in the unity forged during the uprising".
He told the BBC that "disagreements" over the July Charter, external, proposed constitutional changes and the referendum have "widened divisions" between the elected BNP government and rivals Jamaat-e-Islami and the youth-led National Citizen Party (NCP).
"The Awami League sees an opening," Alam told the BBC. "The party believes this is an opportune moment to take to the streets, exploiting a weakened police force and divisions among the forces of the July uprising."
Analysts say if Hasina returns it could just as easily deepen hostility as revive her party's fortunes. The government has framed the sporadic recent violence as terrorism, while supporters insist their demonstrations are peaceful and accuse the authorities of repression.
The larger question is whether Bangladesh can sustain the exclusion of a political constituency as substantial as the Awami League without creating another source of instability.
For India, the dilemma is increasingly difficult to manage.
Delhi has sheltered Hasina, but her public remarks have angered Dhaka, which wants her extradited. India has sought to repair ties through diplomatic outreach and talks on trade, border security and other bilateral issues, but relations remain strained.
The chill is striking: nearly 10 months into his tenure, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has yet to visit India.
A trip was reportedly in the offing in August, but Hasina's press conference in Delhi proved a setback to efforts to reset relations.
Avinash Paliwal, who teaches politics and international studies at SOAS University of London, argues that Hasina's latest announcement has "shifted the burden of choice to Dhaka rather than Delhi".
Delhi, he says, "feels it has tried its best" to work with Rahman's government over the past 10 months - "from appointing a political heavyweight as high commissioner, external with cabinet rank to offering fresh talks on security and trade".
"The failure of this outreach has left India disillusioned with Dhaka. India seems to have decided that bilateral relations will likely remain tense whatever it does, so there is little reason to stop Hasina from stirring the political pot."
Delhi has the leverage to restrain Hasina from making political statements on Indian soil, Paliwal argues, but may not want to exercise it.
Nor, in his view, is it in India's interest to see the Awami League permanently excluded from Bangladeshi politics.
"The political party still enjoys pockets of support across Bangladesh and is weaved into the social and political fabric of the country," he says. "So, yes, it is in India's interest, and also in Bangladesh's long-term interests, to rehabilitate the Awami League and take the path of political reconciliation."
That view is increasingly contested in Dhaka.
"There is a perception in Bangladesh that India wants to rehabilitate the Awami League. There are issues India has not resolved, including the extradition of Hasina. India has also not renewed the transit facilities that could benefit Bangladeshi garment exporters, while the Ganges water treaty, external is nearing expiry without much progress. But has India done enough to win back trust?" says Alam.
"For now, only tourist and medical visas have resumed. Everything else remains in limbo."
A Dhaka-based foreign-policy expert, who asked not to be named, says the two countries remain locked in "mutual frustration".
Hasina, he says, remains central to the impasse. "She remains the elephant in the room, but we also have to find a way to move beyond Hasina."
Paliwal argues that the least damaging outcome for India would be Hasina returning to face a fresh trial, with the Awami League rehabilitated under a different operational leadership.
"It will reintroduce a degree of balance in Bangladeshi politics, and will afford India space to protect its long-term interests and equities better," he says.
For now, 16 December is not yet a confirmed journey. But Hasina has already succeeded in making her return a question that neither Dhaka nor Delhi can ignore.
"December could be chaotic. Everyone in Dhaka is on edge," says the foreign-policy expert, warning of protests and confrontation as Hasina's proposed return date approaches - and the possibility that it could be postponed yet again.
"Hasina is unlikely to return, as she would face a death sentence. But her comments have clearly galvanized her supporters," says Pearl Pandya, Acled's South Asia analyst.
But the impasse is also complicating India's ties with Bangladesh. As Paliwal puts it, the "next window of serious negotiations will now open only after Hasina returns to Dhaka, or Dhaka relents under pressure and returns to the table".

title: Why Trump's new tariffs are less of a threat
description: Other countries have rerouted trade in response to his first tariff salvo, now they are looking beyond Trump's tenure.
author: Faisal Islam
content:
Faisal Islam: Why Trump's new tariffs are less of a threat
- Published
There was none of last April's fanfare, the Rose Garden reveal, the gameshow blue board or "Liberation Day" rhetoric surrounding Trump's tariff announcement this week.
Instead there is something rather tentative about this latest exercise with talk of further negotiations.
"We expect to have a broad, even a plurilateral negotiation to talk about excess capacity and how to resolve it," US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC.
Around the world the view is that this week's announcement is an attempt to shore up the domestic legal underpinning of these tariffs, more than a fundamental change in the Trump trade agenda.
The tariffs are also not due to come in until January or possibly February, after a period of consultation. There has already been eight months of process and hearings, and the rates announced are upper ceilings, often up for negotiation. It's quite the contrast to the overnight shock meted out to the world last April.
Still, the US is making the argument that large swathes of the rest of the world, including allies, are harming the US goods trade position by supporting their own industries. This is the basis for the tariffs, in large part replacing the previous tariffs justified on "forced labour" provisions.
The UK, which was unaffected by the new tariff announcements, remains caught by the forced labour provisions, albeit at a rate of 10% extra on global tariffs. There was no move in response to the UK's digital services tax.
It means for many important countries there are now two legal bases upon which the Trump tariffs rest, after the Supreme Court struck down the original emergency basis earlier this year. A group of 25 states has taken the Trump administration to court to strike down the forced labour tariffs.
The tariffs will have to be finalised under a Democrat Congress, which has influence, but not power. The Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries said this week that the new House would in its first 100 days "move aggressively to… repeal the Trump tariffs".
The Chinese rate of 20% is the truce rate from last year's Trump-Xi deal. The truce is due to expire in mid-January. Beijing's response was muted, no retaliation, criticism of industrial overcapacity as a "false issue", and a call to implement the Xi-Trump deal. The leverage over China has weakened, with the US share of its exports dropping to around 10% this year, down from 15%, just two years ago, and 19% in 2018.
- US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China 
  - Published1 day ago
- New UK-EU treaty has 10-year termination clause 
  - Published14 hours ago
However, the most interesting spot to focus on is closer to home for Trump. Over half of Canada tariffs are authorised under "Section 338" of the 1930s Smoot-Hawley act. There is already a Senate Bill to repeal them, and it is possible that there would be enough rebel Republicans in the House and Senate to threaten to over-ride any Presidential veto. The incoming Senate Finance Committee chair Ron Wyden last week said Democrats were focussed on "figuring out a way to beat Trump and his veto".
Before that an interim deal is being sought, and Democrat senators such as Chris Coons are appearing on Canadian TV, telling CBC, external: "Frankly, if you can get an interim deal, I'd take it, and then put it to us in the new majority to legislate an even better deal."
The rest of world is watching the machinations in Washington and also looking beyond Donald Trump's tenure.
It pays to look at how the initial Trump trade-quake has reshaped the pattern of world trade already.
The rest of the world has rerouted its trade flows around Donald Trump's tariff wall, proving far more resilient than expected. In cash terms, China's exports so far in 2026 are down about 8% on 2024, but that is more than 25 times made up for by its increased exports to everywhere else.
Canada has seen flat exports to the USA since tariffs, fewer cars and lumber, but pricier flows of energy. Its exports, especially commodities, to the rest of the world have rocketed.
This means that next month's G20 summit at the president's Miami resort is an important moment. In general US allies have not rocked the boat, accepting the lower level of tariffs as part of the new reality. Could the middle powers choose to upset their host in Florida next month?
The bigger question however, is how much the Democrats decide to keep of the America First trade agenda. It will not be all, but nor will it be nothing. Economists now expect some of these tariffs to stay in place for years.

title: Rishabh Pant: India star joins New Zealand club match under false name
description: India wicketkeeper Rishabh Pant unexpectedly joins a club game in Christchurch before the second Test against New Zealand and scores 54 off 21 balls.
author: Ffion Wynne
content:
Pant joins New Zealand club match under false name
- Published
India wicketkeeper Rishabh Pant made a surprise appearance for a club team in Christchurch under the false name 'Stan Stan'.
Pant, 29, played for the Open House Swingers against The Chosen Ones and smashed 54 from 21 balls in a 16-run win.
His appearance came a day before India's second Test against New Zealand, which begins at the Hagley Oval at 22:00 GMT on Thursday.
Open House player Mohammad Safi told the New Zealand Herald that he had seen Pant on an electric bike in the city and approached him, saying that his team were a player short.
Safi also said that Pant was not immediately recognised by many on either side, and he turned up in a purple tracksuit and had to borrow kit.
New Zealand captain Tom Latham said Pant's appearance was "brilliant" and showed his "real character", while India bowling coach and former South Africa quick Morne Morkel said he "nearly fell off my chair" when he saw the footage that circulated on social media.
The first Test in Wellington ended in a high-scoring draw, where Pant scored 128 in India's only innings of 720-9.
Pant is regarded as one of the world's most entertaining cricketers, and has scored 3,853 runs in his 53 Tests at an average just shy of 45.
Of those to have scored more than 2,000 Test runs for India, only Virender Sehwag and Kapil Dev have a better strike-rate than Pant's 74.43.

title: EXCLUSIVE: Insurers, brokers seek changes to IRDAI’s proposed overhaul of distribution framework
description: Insurance regulator tells ThePrint there is broad support for reform objectives. But stakeholders raise concerns over commission caps, tighter expense limits, viability of smaller players.
author: Udit Bubna
content:
New Delhi: Insurers, brokers and other stakeholders have sought changes to the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India’s (IRDAI) proposed overhaul of insurance distribution, raising concerns over commission caps, tighter expense limits, the viability of smaller players and the impact on certain insurance products.
The insurance regulator told ThePrint that there is broad support for the objectives of the reforms, including greater transparency, better market conduct, curbing mis-selling and ensuring better value for policyholders. Stakeholders, however, want phased implementation, expense limits that account for insurer size and business models and greater consideration of the viability of small-ticket policies.
IRDAI said it is examining the submissions, and has constituted an expert committee to advise on refining the proposals and ensuring their smooth implementation.
The IRDAI’s consultation paper, ‘Recalibrating Economics of Insurance Distribution’, released on 23 September, seeks to restrict distribution costs, reintroduce product-specific commission limits, tighten expense-management norms and make insurance sellers more accountable for mis-selling.
One recurring concern raised by insurers is the proposed reduction in Expenses of Management (EoM) limits, which determine the overall expenses an insurer can incur, including commissions, administrative costs and other operating expenses.
IRDAI has proposed bringing EoM of life insurance companies down to 15 percent of gross direct premium income (GDPI) within two years, and 12.5 percent within five years. For general insurers, it proposes reducing the limit from 30 to 25 percent within two years and 20 percent within five years, while shifting the benchmark from gross written premium to domestic GDPI.
Standalone health insurers are also proposed to move from a 35 percent limit to 25 percent within two years, and 20 percent within five years.
Responding to ThePrint’s queries, IRDAI said that insurers want to implement the revised expense limits over a longer period, while some have suggested scale-based limits linked to the insurer’s size. The concerns reflect apprehensions that smaller insurers, which may have relatively limited scale and higher operating costs, could find it more difficult to survive the tighter expense norms.
Stakeholders have also flagged the proposed restriction on bundling credit life cover with loan products, arguing that such insurance provides protection to borrowers and that the economics of high-volume, low-premium business must be taken into account.
The issue is particularly relevant to bancassurance, where banks distribute insurance products, including those linked to loans. IRDAI’s proposals seek to ensure that borrowers are not compelled to purchase insurance as a condition for obtaining a loan, and retain the freedom to choose their insurer.
Intermediaries, particularly brokers, have also raised concerns to IRDAI over the proposed commission caps.
The consultation paper proposes different commission ceilings depending on the product, distribution channel and effort involved in selling a policy. For instance, commissions on first-time individual health insurance sales are proposed to be capped at 15 percent for distribution entities and 20 percent for agents. On renewals, the proposed limits are five percent and 10 percent, respectively.
For third-party motor insurance on new vehicles, the proposed commission is nil for distribution entities and 2.5 percent for agents and associates. On individual pure-term life insurance, the proposed first-year commission is 25 percent for intermediaries and 30 percent for agents, with renewal commissions of 7.5 percent and 10 percent, respectively.
IRDAI said different segments of brokers provided feedback based on their business models, with concerns primarily relating to the commission caps and architecture, including the proposed consolidation of intermediary categories.
The proposed structure seeks to bring distributors under three broad categories—Insurance Distribution Entities, Insurance Distribution Persons and Market Infrastructure Institutions—replacing a fragmented framework.
The Insurance Brokers Association of India (IBAI), which represents licensed insurance brokers, had earlier opposed aspects of the proposed commission caps and lower expense limits, while supporting measures aimed at preventing mis-selling and compulsory bundling.
Also Read: Insurance sold, not chosen: Why IRDAI wants to put the customer back at the centre
What lies ahead
IRDAI has constituted an expert committee of independent economists and insurance professionals, chaired by Dr Indu Bhushan, IAS (Retired), former Chief Executive Officer of the Ayushman Bharat Mission, to advise on refining the proposals after the feedback.
The committee, constituted on 23 November, has been asked to submit its report by 31 December 2026. It will examine the proposals and recommend appropriate changes, including transition pathways for smaller insurers and distributors.
“Suggestions backed by sound economic and business reasoning that also serve policyholders’ interests will be given due consideration,” IRDAI said in its response to ThePrint. The regulator will undertake any additional analysis or detailing required before framing the draft regulations.
The feedback received from stakeholders and the expert committee’s recommendations will be considered before the draft regulations are published for public comments under the IRDAI (Procedure for making Regulations and Subsidiary Instructions) Regulations, 2026.
The regulator will consider the comments received at that stage before notifying the final regulations.
IRDAI said the basic objectives of the reforms will remain unchanged – rationalising distribution costs, ensuring policyholders get better value and encouraging insurers to compete on the price and quality of their products rather than on distributor payouts.
The reforms are currently expected to take effect from 1 April 2027, though the exact date and transition arrangements will be specified in the final regulations.
(Edited by Nardeep Singh Dahiya)

title: A loyal Modi cheerleader takes on Modi’s ‘Chota Bhai’. Ramdev’s changing relationship with BJP
description: The yoga guru rose to prominence during the 2011-12 anti-corruption campaign that set the tone for BJP’s march to power. So, what's behind his changing rhetoric?
author: Apoorva Mandhani
content:
New Delhi: Yoga guru Ramdev seems to have got the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in a bind. Once a prominent voice against the erstwhile United Progressive Alliance (UPA) government over black money and corruption, Ramdev has trained his guns at Dhirendra Krishna Shastri, who has a growing following among the BJP brass, including Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
The Patanjali founder rose to prominence during the 2011-12 anti-corruption campaign that set the tone for the BJP’s march to power. He backed the BJP’s 2014 Lok Sabha campaign and Modi’s prime ministerial bid. Cut back to 2026, the yoga guru has joined Gen Z causes, alleging corruption in government recruitments and poor facilities in schools.
That aside, Ramdev has lashed out at Shastri, who is touring poll-bound states, including Punjab and Uttar Pradesh, to spread the message on ‘Hindu unity’. The Bageshwar Dham chief’s kathas (religious narrative) are being organised and attended by several sitting MLAs belonging to the BJP as well as other parties.
At an event Sunday in Jamshedpur, Ramdev called Shastri a “fool” and a “hypocrite” for his statements calling Lord Krishna ‘tedha’ (crooked). What further seems to have irked him is Shastri’s call for Hindus to hold both ‘mala’ (rosary) and ‘bhala’ (spear) in their hands.
“Taking the name of Sanatan, some frauds, some hypocrites, selfish and greedy people even tell Sanatanis to take a ‘mala’ in one hand and a ‘bhala’ in the other,” Ramdev lashed out without taking Shastri’s name.
“You will save Hindus and the country by taking a spear? Then what will this police do, what will this paramilitary do, what will the military do, what will the constitution of the country and democracy do? Those who instigate Hindus like this cannot be in the interest of Hindus.”
To the discerning observer, Ramdev’s outburst isn’t just a war of words between two ‘babas’. One of Modi’s earliest cheerleaders from the saffron brigade is now picking up cudgels against a darling of the Hindutva regime. Shastri’s glowing clout was evident when PM Modi called him a ‘chhota bhai’ (younger brother) during the visit to Bageshwar Dham in Chhatarpur, Madhya Pradesh in February, 2025.
This isn’t the first time that Ramdev has spoken against the current establishment. During an Independence Day address in Haridwar, Ramdev alleged corruption and the influence of money in the government job selection process. “Fix these scams, otherwise Ramdev may have to protest again.”
Political observers like Professor M.M.Semwal view his latest remarks as an extension of this ability to “gauge public sentiment”.
“Back in 2011-12, when the India Against Corruption (IAC) movement happened against the UPA government, Ramdev sensed the tide then and was extremely active in it,” Semwal from the political science department at HNB Garhwal University told ThePrint.
“His recent support for the agitation against paper leaks is consistent with his earlier responses to emerging public sentiments and his ability to engage with issues that carry wider socio-political significance.”
Uttarakhand Pradesh Congress Committee president Ganesh Godiyal believes that Ramdev’s statements are a reaction to the people’s sentiments towards the BJP government.
“He’s particularly keenly aware of public aggression. And now his statements are changing in response to public aggression. So, I believe his words are a reaction to the public’s actions. His faith is eroding. He’s beginning to feel that the BJP governments at the center and state have betrayed and betrayed the people,” the PCC chief told ThePrint.
In contrast, Uttarakhand Assembly Speaker Ritu Khanduri Bhushan asserted that there is “nothing political” about Ramdev’s recent statements.
“The two of them were sharing the stage just a few hours before he (Ramdev) went on a rant, but I feel that there could be some statement that Baba Bageshwar must have made that hurt him, maybe that is why he said whatever he did…It can happen between two people,” Bhushan, a BJP leader, told ThePrint.
To a query on Ramdev’s statements on the students’ protests, Bhushan said, “That is a decision he must have taken. He is also heading a huge organisation in Uttarakhand.” She was referring to Ramdev’s empire that is headquartered in Haridwar from where he and his associate Acharya Balkrishna head several ventures under the banner of Patanjali.
Also Read: Ramdev is trying to manufacture relevance with his pitch to Gen Z
‘Political currents’
Ramdev’s role in the IAC upsurge gave him prominence on the national stage, leading to his proximity with the BJP bigwigs. In 2015, the Manohar Lal Khattar government appointed Ramdev as Haryana’s brand ambassador for yoga and Ayurveda. It also announced Cabinet minister-equivalent status for him but he declined the offer.
That was in the past. In his Independence Day address, Ramdev criticised India’s education and government recruitment systems. At Patanjali Yogpeeth, he warned the authorities about the protests intensifying if concerns regarding irregularities in education and government recruitment were not addressed.
He also called for breaking the “walls of hatred” in the country. “Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra, Dalit, Adivasi, Vanvasi, Hindu, Muslim, Sikh, Christian, Jain, Buddhist have stood before one another with such enmity and opposition as if they are thirsty for each other’s blood.”
As for his observation of Shastri, Ramdev spoke against the Bageshwar Dham head’s call that the Hindus should unite and save the nation.
“In the name of making fanatic Hindus Sanatani, to promote the tense culture, to spread poison in the society, to create division in the society and to create divisions — first create divisions then loot—and by using conspiracies create religious frenzy, communal frenzy, political frenzy, economic frenzy, social frenzy among the people and then tell them, Hindus you are in danger, we will save you,” Ramdev said in Jamshedpur.
“Whom will you save, what is your standing? Since the creation, Sanatan has been there, is there and will remain there.”
Ramdev’s ability, according to the political observers experts, to gauge public sentiment puts him in a position to travel in the direction of the political currents of the country.
Semwal asserted that Ramdev was instrumental in promoting Ayurveda and yoga across the country. At the same time, he has been vocal in the political landscape and has not shied away from expressing his views on matters of public importance.
“Ramdev supported the Gen Z agitation against paper leaks. It seems that he demonstrates the ability to gauge public sentiment and the direction of the political currents in the country. His recent stance may be understood in the context of his longstanding engagement with issues of public concern,” Semwal explained.
‘Ideological differences’
Within the BJP in Uttarakhand, where Ramdev is based primarily, there still seems to be an admiration of his contribution towards promoting yoga in a way that only few spiritual leaders have managed to do. However, there is a curiosity over his latest statements.
Vasudha Pant, founder trustee of the Green Hills Trust in Almora, who is associated with the BJP, said that she visited Ramdev’s yoga retreats in the past, and has never found any of his speeches objectionable.
“It isn’t that he (Ramdev) does not know Dhirendra Shastri personally. Now they were sharing the same stage a day before his remarks, and the next day he called him a hypocrite and a fraud. I don’t understand how that happened,” she told ThePrint.
On Ramdev’s remarks on the students’ protests, she opined that while everybody has the right to protest, it should be left to the people without politicising the issue.
“This is the era of social media…When youngsters are putting forth their points, what is the need for outsiders to jump in. Then it becomes a competition about who is in cahoots with them…I don’t think everybody has the right to jump into such things, whether they are our politicians, or parties, or our sadhu-sant (seers),” she told ThePrint.
BJP Uttarakhand state president Mahendra Bhatt said that Ramdev is a man of independent thought and has never gone against nationalism. “He is not a member of the BJP, but he has always supported the BJP’s actions. We always take his words as a suggestion. He can answer why he said what he said, but he knows that if anyone can give the student movement the right direction, it is the BJP and Modi,” Bhatt told ThePrint.
His deputy Rajendra Singh Bisht acknowledged that Ramdev raising concerns of students “demonstrates his social sensitivity”. However, he said that it would not be appropriate to interpret this as a change in his support for the BJP.
There may be “ideological differences within the seer community,” he said. “I believe that Ramdev’s thoughts should be viewed in the context of his extensive social and national contributions, and not just from a political perspective.”
On Tuesday, Ramdev came out before the media in Haridwar where he signalled ending the row. “He (Shastri) is like my son. He is also like my younger brother and disciple. Therefore, I reprimanded him with all my authority for things that I found inappropriate and hurt me. He also accepted my reprimand with love. This is also his greatness,” the 60-year-old yoga guru-cum-entrepreneur told reporters.
(Edited by Tony Rai)

title: Modi addressed pay packet of India’s factory workers. Why growth in wages has been stagnant
description: Discourse over stagnation in wage growth has predominantly focused on developments of the past 2-3 years. But analysing data over four decades reveals a more significant narrative.
author: Bidisha Bhattacharya
content:
New Delhi: Prime Minister Narendra Modi, addressing the FICCI annual general meeting (AGM) last Thursday, put a pointed question to business leaders: “Did you increase the salaries of your employees [despite the reduction in basic corporate tax]?”
In doing so, he directly addressed the stagnation in wage growth in the private sector. And the data corroborates his concerns.
In the fiscal year 2024-25, the average factory worker’s earnings were approximately Rs 2.28 lakh, reflecting a 5.3 percent increase over the previous year, the latest Annual Survey of Industries shows.
However, with consumer prices rising by 4.6 percent year-on-year, the real wage increase was a mere 0.7 percent. In FY 2023-24, real wage growth was 0.1 percent, and in FY 2022-23, real wages declined.
Excluding the recovery from the pandemic-induced downturn, real wage growth has remained below 1 percent in five of the past six years.
The political discourse over stagnation in wage growth has predominantly focused on the developments of the past two to three years. But the same survey has been monitoring India’s manufacturing sector since 1981-82. Analysing this data over four decades reveals that the stagnation in wage growth is not merely a consequence of the pandemic or a temporary anomaly; rather, it represents the latest phase in a prolonged, gradual transformation in how benefits are distributed within Indian manufacturing.
This disparity can be illustrated with a simple comparison: the garment worker and the oil refinery worker.
Also Read: Real wages grew just 0.01% over the last 5 years and contracted in Haryana & UP, Ind-Ra report finds
Four decades of a shrinking slice
In the Indian economy, a worker employed in an oil refinery contributes approximately Rs 43.6 lakh in value annually. In contrast, a garment worker in factories located in Tiruppur or Noida contributes around Rs 5 lakh. Despite the refinery worker generating nearly nine times the economic value, their remuneration is only about two and a half times greater than that of the garment worker, with earnings of Rs 4.25 lakh compared to Rs 1.76 lakh of the refinery worker.
Every manufacturing facility generates value, defined as the difference between its sales revenue and its expenditures on raw materials, fuel, and machinery depreciation. Economists refer to this as net value added, and the allocation of this value between labour and capital has long been a central inquiry in the field.
In the early 1980s, wages for factory workers in India constituted approximately 30 percent of this value. Following the 1991 economic reforms, this proportion slipped into a prolonged decline, reaching a nadir of 10.6 percent in FY 2007-08. Subsequently, it recovered steadily over the next decade, reaching 18.9 percent in FY 2019-20, before declining again post-pandemic. In 2024-25, it stood at 16.5 percent. Over the same four decades, the share of net value added going to profits rose from about 23 percent to around 50 percent, according to calculations based on the Annual Survey of Industries.
The transformation observed is partly attributable to modernisation. Indian factories have become significantly more capital-intensive than in 1981, with machinery now commanding a larger share of returns. This trend also illustrates the evolution of factory work.
In the fiscal year 2019-20, 38 percent of factory workers in India were employed through contractors rather than directly by firms. By FY 2024-25, this proportion increased to 42 percent.
Contract workers generally receive lower wages, get fewer benefits, and possess limited bargaining power. This dynamic explains how factories were able to increase their workforce by approximately 30 lakh workers between FY 2021-22 and FY 2024-25 without substantially increasing individual wages.
Why productivity doesn’t reach the pay packet
Returning to the context of the refinery and garment factory, standard economic theory posits that a worker’s compensation is approximately equivalent to their contribution to output. As a result, industries with higher worker productivity should ideally offer higher wages.
However, Indian factories only partially adhere to this principle. The value added per worker across industries ranges from approximately Rs 5 lakh to over Rs 40 lakh, yet annual wages remain within a narrower range of approximately Rs 1.8 lakh to Rs 4.3 lakh. Notably, the industries employing the largest workforce, such as food processing, textiles, and apparel, offer wages below the national average.
What accounts for the lack of responsiveness of wages to productivity?
Arthur Lewis, who was later awarded the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, provided a definitive explanation in 1954. In his influential paper on “economic development with unlimited supplies of labour,” Lewis explained that in nations where a significant portion of the population remains engaged in low-productivity agricultural work, wages in modern industry are determined not by the output of a factory worker but by the potential earnings from agricultural work, supplemented by a modest premium to incentivise the transition. As long as this labour reserve persists, factories can continue hiring at approximately the same wage level, with the benefits of increased productivity accruing primarily to capital.
Wages begin to rise significantly only when this labour reserve is depleted, a phenomenon economists now refer to as the Lewis turning point.
India, with nearly half of its workforce still employed in agriculture, exemplifies Lewis’s model. This explains why wages in the refinery and garment sectors are comparable despite substantial differences in productivity: both sectors recruit from the same extensive pool of individuals whose alternative employment is small-scale farming or casual labour.
Lifting the floor and the ladder
The Lewis model provides a pathway for economic advancement. The primary strategy involves accelerating the transition of workers from low-productivity agriculture to manufacturing and service sectors, which can accommodate them on a large scale. This shift tightens the labour market for those remaining in agriculture, thereby exerting upward pressure on wages. Labour-intensive sectors such as apparel, footwear, and food processing, where India holds a comparative advantage, are expected to generate the majority of these employment opportunities.
The second strategy focuses on enhancing productivity within industries that currently employ the largest workforce. If workers in the garment and food-processing sectors could achieve productivity levels closer to the national average, there would be greater potential for wage increases.
This requires investment in advanced machinery, expansion of factory capacity, and stronger export market linkages, all of which can be facilitated by India’s recent trade agreements.
The third strategy is to establish a minimum wage. The four labour codes, effective since 21 November, 2025, provide for a national floor wage to reduce the disparity between contract workers and directly employed workers. If set judiciously, this can raise the lower end of the pay scale without causing job losses. Additionally, the codes’ provisions on contract labour aim to reduce the disparity between contract workers and directly employed workers. A year on, implementation is still catching up. By October this year, only six states and Union Territories had notified rules under all four codes, and the national floor wage itself is yet to be notified.
Furthermore, the Ministry of Statistics’ inaugural household income survey, currently underway, will provide comprehensive data on income trends across various employment types, addressing a longstanding gap in policymaking.
India’s economic narrative has traditionally focused on output, investment, and exports. Historical data spanning four decades indicates that increased productivity does not inherently lead to higher wages. The critical factor is a labour market characterised by worker scarcity, which enhances their value. Achieving this condition is the pivotal challenge India now confronts.
(Edited by Amrtansh Arora)
