title: Sonia Gandhi's Memoirs Draw Right-Wing Outrage, but Her Critics Gloss Over Savarkar's Real Legacy - The Wire
description: Savarkar's record is pockmarked with contradictions. So much so, even his contemporary admirers choose to ignore some aspects of his legacy.
author: Ram Puniyani
content: Congress leader Sonia Gandhi’s autobiography is currently generating considerable discussion. Different aspects of the book are coming to light, while commentaries on it continue to appear across social media.One incident related to the book took place in Mumbai. Several leaders from the Eknath Shinde-led Shiv Sena faction held a press conference in the city, during which they tore out a few pages of the book. According to them, Gandhi’s autobiography portrays Vinayak Damodar Savarkar as someone who helped the British.They strongly objected to this portrayal, arguing that he was among the bravest of revolutionaries, having been sentenced to two life terms and deported to the Cellular Jail, popularly known as Kala Pani.Savarkar’s grandnephew, Satyaki Ashok Savarkar, has filed a case against Gandhi over the remarks in the autobiography.On page 201, the book describes the anguish experienced by Gandhi’s mother-in-law, Indira Gandhi, following the Allahabad High Court verdict and the nationwide protests against her government. There was pressure on her to resign. Indira said, “If I resign, the party will be split and scatter and RSS will have its way…How can we allow it? We fought them all these years. They’re going to destroy the country.”Further, Gandhi writes, “I know these people. I know their history. I know what their aim is…”Indira’s antipathy to the RSS was deep and real. Gandhi writes, “While Congress freedom fighters were fighting assaults and imprisonment at the hands of British rulers, senior ideologues of RSS like Vinayak Damodar Savarkar were writing mercy petitions to their colonial masters and their members were colluding with British authorities as informers.”(Here, the book makes a slip, Savarkar, though the progenitor of Hindutva ideology, was not part of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh.)Also read: During the Quit India Movement, the Hindu Mahasabha Played the British GameBut Gandhi is on the dot about the mercy petitions Savarkar wrote and about the RSS helping the British in its war efforts. Interestingly, those tearing pages from Gandhi’s book don’t appear to know that even the RSS’s second Sarsanghchalak or topmost leader, M.S. Golwalkar, made several derogatory remarks about Savarkar in his book, Bunch of Thoughts.As the Indian Express recently reported, Congress leaders have been asking why the Shinde Sena had “not objected to Golwalkar’s book, too, saying it calls Savarkar’s Hindutva “negative” and refers to him as a ‘traitor’.”Savarkar is held in high regard by many, particularly in Maharashtra. But his life had a complex trajectory. He was an anti-British revolutionary in the initial phase of his life. While studying law in England, he was involved in political activities and was sentenced to two life terms for waging war against the state and abetting the murder of Nashik District Magistrate A.M.T. Jackson.But he could not bear the harsh conditions of jail life, and so began to write mercy petitions to the British. The result was his release and internment in Ratnagiri. Here he initiated anti-caste activities and inter-caste dining. He also established the Patit Pavan temple in 1931, with the aim of allowing Hindus across caste boundaries, including Dalits (then referred to as the Depressed Classes), to worship together.These aspects of his life have contributed to his stature in Maharashtra. He was also a poet and writer, and several of his works remain popular. He is credited with writing about the 1857 uprising, which he described as the First War of Indian Independence.His writings inspired many later freedom fighters. In recognition of his contributions, a commemorative postage stamp was issued in his honour, and his portrait was also installed in parliament on February 26, 2003. It was unveiled by then President Dr A.P.J. Abdul Kalam.Savarkar’s mercy petitions, now part of many of his biographies, show his total surrender to the British. In these petitions, he promised the British to help them implement Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms, their other policies and to serve them loyally. During his jail term itself, he wrote Essentials of Hindutva, the book that laid the foundation of the two-nation theory, arguing that there are two nations in India, Hindu and Muslim.He was totally opposed to the concept of composite Indian nationalism as conceived by the national movement led by Mahatma Gandhi.Savarkar was president of the Hindu Mahasabha from 1937 onwards, and during his tenure the Mahasabha collaborated with the Muslim League. It joined ministries led by the League in Bengal, Sindh and the North-West Frontier Province. The resolution for the partition of the country was moved while the Hindu Mahasabha was part of this coalition.Also read: Full Transcript: ‘Savarkar and Hindu Mahasabha Stayed Firmly Outside the Freedom Movement’Nathuram Godse, the man who assassinated Mahatma Gandhi on January 30, 1948, was a staunch follower of Savarkar, and the two are known to have met regularly. Savarkar was getting a hefty pension (allowance) of Rs 60 from the British government. He also supported Godse in running his newspaper, Agrani. One of the cartoons the paper published was of Ravan Dahan, the ritual burning of effigies of Ravana during Dussehra celebrations.In that cartoon, Syama Prasad Mookerjee, guided by Savarkar, is shown slaying Ravan. The ten heads of Ravan had Gandhi close to the centre, surrounded by Nehru, Patel, Bose and Maulana Azad, amongst others.Savarkar was one of the accused in Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination case, but was acquitted. Later, the Commission of Inquiry into the Conspiracy to Murder Mahatma Gandhi, led by former Supreme Court judge Justice Jeevan Lal Kapur between 1966 and 1969, concluded that the facts, taken together, were “destructive of any theory other than the conspiracy to murder by Savarkar and his group”.So the point about Savarkar is not whether he was imprisoned in the Andaman Islands or whether he was sentenced to two life terms totally 50 years. The point is that Savarkar went from opposing British rule to working for the British government.Interestingly, RSS leaders hold him in high regard for laying the theoretical foundations of Hindu nationalism, rooted in ideas of Aryan ancestry, the geographical conception of the Hindu nation extending from the Sindhu [River Indus] to the ocean, and Brahminical culture.The defence minister and senior BJP leader Rajnath Singh once said that Savarkar wrote those petitions on the advice of Mahatma Gandhi. But Savarkar began writing his petitions in 1911, when Gandhi was in South Africa. Some go to the extent of claiming that he, every night, flew on the wings of a bulbul to visit his motherland from across the Andaman sea – such was his devotion to the nation.Ram Puniyani is president of the Centre for Study of Society and Secularism.

title: India, Globally: A Country of Protest - The Wire
description: A monthly highlight of how the world is watching our democracy.
author: The Wire Staff
content: The Narendra Modi government frequently posits India as a ‘Vishwaguru’ or world leader. How the world sees India is often lost in this branding exercise.Outside India, global voices are monitoring and critiquing human rights violations in India and the rise of Hindutva. We present here monthly highlights of what a range of actors – from UN experts and civil society groups to international media and parliamentarians of many countries – are saying about the state of India’s democracy.Read the monthly roundup for October 1-31, 2026.International media reports CBC News, Canada, October 8Susan Ormiston reports on Google building its largest AI data centre, outside the US, in South India, “clearing 600 acres of land” to do so. Environmental and human rights advocates warn that the data centre will consume huge amounts of water in an already dry region, and electricity too. Unlike young tech professionals, the villagers interviewed did not think that the promise of jobs would be realized. A farmer told Ormiston, “Our land is gone and our land is our livelihood”. New York Times, US, October 11Mujib Mashal analyses the dent in Narendra Modi’s “strongman” persona exposed by the clampdown on a wave of youth protests that broke out in October. As “violent scenes” from Delhi became viral, Mashal writes that this is “exposing the rough edges of Modi’s rule and the limits of his formula for maintaining power”. Modi’s strategy of “boxing in opponents” is not working since the youth movement “increasingly draws on a cross-section of society”. “Digital savvy” combined with “Hindu nationalist ideology” is not working with Gen Z. Mashal adds, “the once-battered opposition is feeling invigorated, trying to widen the crack opened by the young people”. France 24, France, October 13AFP highlights innovative protest strategies used by Indian youth in the recent protests. These range from batman masks, flash mobs, a digital dashboard which mapped and matched the movement of detainees with volunteer drivers and sometimes doctors, and protestors who held on to each other to “wriggle out” of police buses. These are some of the ways in which protestors are turning “ingenuity into a form of resistance”.Al Jazeera, Qatar, October 16Mahmodul Hassan reports on allegations by the tribal community in Koraput district of Odisha of forged signatures and thumbprints as government acquires the community’s ancestral land for an Adani bauxite mining project. Al Jazeera’s investigation reveals forgery of signatures and thumbprints even of dead and fictitious people. Arpitha Kodiveri, Assistant Professor of Political Science at Vassar College, finds this part of a trend of the “illegal administrative practice of implementing the consent provision without adhering to procedure and law” in Odisha and elsewhere.The Economist, UK, October 18The Economist reflects on the “deadly seriousness” with which Indians take the right to vote. Particularly that the recent interference with the sanctity of elections constitutes “a step too far”. As long as Indians believe that “they have the power to punish their rulers come election day, they will put up with a lot” – electoral fraud like booth capture is seen “as part of the game”. However, the question of whether the game itself is fixed is now bringing citizens to the brink. Associated Press, US, October 23Erika Kinetz and Piyush Rai report on “hundreds” of targeted shootings by the police in Uttar Pradesh of Muslims accused of cow smuggling. Nearly 93% of identifiable victims were Muslim. Known as “Operation Lame”, critics describe this as amounting to “extrajudicial punishment, religious persecution and intimidation.” While police defend the shootings as self-defence, human rights advocates warn they undermine the rule of law and reinforce majoritarian politics.Reuters, UK, October 26 Aditya Kalra reports on how media houses owned by Ambani and Adani are among the 21 Indian news publishers who are challenging the government’s privacy law in court. As India’s Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA), they are arguing that the law will seriously damage investigative journalism and compromise the identity of the sources. This is “the most high-profile challenge” to the privacy law so far. For the challenge to include businesses headed by billionaire industrialists allegedly close to and favoured by the Prime Minister is significant.BBC, UK, October 26Nikita Yadav reports on the growing censorship faced by cartoonists in India, particularly in the wake of the Gen Z protests which deployed humour in highly visible ways. Digital platforms are blocking access for independent cartoonists. Cartoonists in newsrooms are responding to pressure with self-censorship. It is hopeful that cartoonists are supporting one another and finding ways to adapt.Here is a montage of newspapers across the world with front-page stories on the October protests in India and the Modi government’s response.Prominent papers in the US, UK and Japan led with the story on their front pages, while others have carried headlines befitting of the nature of the protests and the Modi government’s crackdown on its own young citizens. https://t.co/XUSXOCEqj7— The Wire (@thewire_in) October 12, 2026Indian diaspora and international civil society groupsOn October 11, InSAF India held the second memorial event for Professor G.N. Saibaba. Nandita Narayan and Karen Gabriel recalled Saibaba’s integrity as a teacher and commitment to Adivasi struggles. Vipanchika Bhagyanagar asked friends to carry on his legacy of fearless critique accompanied by action. Saibaba’s daughter, Manjeera, while noting the very limited time she had with her father after his release, shared how much he still wanted to do, most of all, start a university for Adivasi youth. All agreed that Saibaba would have welcomed the youth-led protests taking place in India today.On October 27, protests organised by Survival International and joined by South Asia Solidarity and other groups outside London’s Science Museum urged the Museum to end its continued association with the Adani Group. Protestors warned that the proposed Great Nicobar mega-project threatens the Indigenous Shompen people and fragile rainforest ecosystems. Genocide scholars have called the project a “death sentence for the Shompen”. Survival International’s Executive Director Caroline Pearce said how the museum is complicit in “reputation-washing” Adani and demanded it “choose the Shompen not sponsorship”, citing risks of displacement, ecological destruction and the loss of Indigenous livelihoods. The Indian diaspora across the globe holds protests in solidarity, calling for electoral accountability in India:Parliamentarians and public officias advocateUS Congresswoman Pramila Jayapal tweeted her deep concern about “the actions of the Indian government to purge 130 million people from the voting rolls, on October 14. Experts sayUnited Nations experts issued two statements regarding the state response to the protests taking place in India. On October 10, the UN’s Human Rights spokesperson Thameen Al-Kheetan called for the release of demonstrators, lawyers, journalists and others, invoked the right to peaceful assembly and urged the authorities “to engage in meaningful dialogue to address the broadly held concerns expressed”. On October 20, twelve Special Rapporteurs, members of two working groups and one independent expert, noted that “this crackdown reflects a broader, troubling pattern” in which Indian authorities have been “repeatedly alerted” against the use of undue restrictions on peaceful assembly, excessive force and arbitrary detentions, and highlighting “the gender-specific impact”. They called for an independent investigation into the conduct of law enforcement and affiliated forces. Human Rights Watch (HRW) issued a statement on October 13 expressing its concerns on the forceful state response to the protests in India. Elaine Pearson, the HRW Asia director, noted that “Peaceful protest and freedom of expression are fundamental rights protected under the international human rights law that India’s leaders claim to uphold”. HRW asked the Indian government to publicly direct security forces to respond to protests in accordance with the UN Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms by Law Enforcement Officials. HRW released another statement on October 28, calling India’s voter-roll revision “arbitrary and deeply flawed”. It highlighted the disproportionate impact on women, Muslims and marginalized communities. HRW urges authorities to “immediately scrap the voter roll revision process that has denied India’s most marginalized people their right to vote and other government services”. Umar Khalid was one of five laureates from around the world who received the Human Rights Defenders at Risk award from the human rights organisation Front Line Defenders (FLD). Khalid was recognised for his leading role “in the peaceful and democratic civil movement against the unconstitutional and anti-Muslim amendments to India’s citizenship laws”. The awardees receive support to bolster their protection and visibility. Gilles Verniers, a political scientist at the Centre for International Studies at Sciences Po, Paris, highlights several striking similarities between recent student protests in India and France. In both countries, protestors are targeting not a particular law or reform, but the entire system; using satire as a weapon (like the deliberately misspelt signs aimed at the failure of schools carried by French students); in both, the “street and screen feed off each other”; “politicians follow, not lead” with Opposition parties rushing in to express solidarity after the movements were initiated, and the unprecedented police brutality “adds fuel” to the protests.The Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders, a partnership of the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT), draw attention to the incarcerated film maker Vishal Singh’s deteriorating health. Calling for adequate and specialised medical care, the Observatory invoked the need to respect the humanity and dignity of prisoners as per Article 10 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), to which India is a state party.India scores 24.1 on the 2026 Global Hunger Index, placing it in the “serious hunger” category, substantially above the global average (18.1). India stands 100th out of 122 countries. Despite improvement, 9.8% experience undernourishment. Nearly three out of every ten children under five remain stunted. Child wasting, which records children who have low weight for their height, has worsened to 19%. The International Crisis Group (ICG) released a report – A Trigger in Jammu and Kashmir: Militant Violence under Indian Central Rule – assessing developments seven years after New Delhi revoked Jammu and Kashmir’s semi-autonomous status. ICG finds that “bitterness festers” among the people of Kashmir despite “improvements in security”. This is occurring alongside the failure to “uproot militant groups which have gone underground”. ICG advocates that the Centre “reconsider its heavy-handed approach to governance in Jammu and Kashmir” and also restore statehood “with the aim of strengthening local rule and depriving insurgents of their main rallying cry”. Read the previous roundup here.

title: The Public Impeachment and Moral Verdict Against the Election Commission of India - The Wire
description: Minor fixes cannot paper over what has happened. Mandates have been distorted. Parties have been decimated. Crores have been disenfranchised. And the institution meant to prevent it all stood by, and also facilitated it.
author: Gurdeep Sappal
content: The public impeachment of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar was not an event designed for television airwaves. Nor was it meant to feed social media reels and memes. It gave voice to a collective anguish. An institution entrusted with the most sacred task of our republic has stopped discharging its constitutional duties. Worse, it is using its humongous powers to undermine democracy itself.The charge sheet is long. Consider it count by count.The charge sheetOver the last two years, voluminous evidence has been placed before the Election Commission (EC) about unauthorised access to its servers and software. In Maharashtra, evidence was submitted that electoral rolls were being altered through a private app. There has been no investigation to date. Rahul Gandhi demonstrated at a press conference how the commission’s OTP-based system was being misused to tamper with voter lists in Aland, Karnataka. Again, the commission did not bother to investigate.There are hundreds of documented cases of misuse of Form 7 by unauthorised persons to delete the names of bona fide voters. Filing a false objection is a criminal offence punishable with up to a year in prison. Yet not a single inquiry has been initiated by the EC which is the sole authority to do so. When the Karnataka CID began an investigation into mass deletions in Aland, it sent the commission 18 reminders over 18 months seeking basic data. The commission didn’t cooperate. It never wanted to uncover the crime.Media reports have recorded several instances of software loopholes and irregularities in the commission’s systems. None received a meaningful response. A reasonable citizen can draw only one conclusion. The software was allowed to remain porous and insecure, while powers that the constitution vests in district and local officers were steadily centralised in Nirvachan Sadan.An SIR that surrendered its own purposeWhen Rahul Gandhi exposed the commission’s failure to protect the sanctity of the rolls, Gyanesh Kumar did not order an inquiry. He ordered a Special Intensive Revision (SIR). What had been done clandestinely was now given a legitimate design.The SIR set out, ostensibly, to verify citizenship. When challenged in the Supreme Court, the commission conceded that it does not have the power to conclusively determine citizenship. The facade was surrendered. The charade continued.Also read: The ECI Software Deleted 5.38 Lakh Bengal Voters With Auto-Generated Rejections Without Citing a ReasonA hundred crore citizens were sent scrambling for documents, mapping names in voter lists that were decades old. About 15% were struck off. And now, with the summary revision announced in October, the commission has quietly returned to the old system of enrolment. No answers. No explanation. No remorse.Nor does it engage with political parties in a manner befitting a constitutional body. When the Leader of the Opposition (LoP) in the Lok Sabha placed evidence before the nation, the commission did not set out to verify it. It questioned his standing to raise it, and dared him to file an affidavit or apologise. When a high court directed that polling records be shared with a candidate, the rules were amended to restrict access. Then the commission ordered that CCTV and webcast footage of polling be destroyed 45 days after results, unless challenged in an election petition. Evidence that might have settled the dispute is being erased by design.An institution that will not investigate itself cannot complain when the people do.Beyond the reach of lawAll this happens behind a wall of legal protection. The 2023 law gave complete immunity to election commissioners from civil and criminal proceedings for official acts. CEC can’t be impeached, as it has full protection of Modi’s government. For all practical purposes, the CEC answers to no one.Also read: ‘Treason Against Constitution’: Opposition Holds Symbolic Public Impeachment of CEC Gyanesh KumarSo what is an opposition to do? Sit quietly and accept the demolition of democracy as a fait accompli? The Congress conceptualised democracy in India, made it functional and nurtured it through a century of struggle. It cannot stand by while that inheritance is hollowed out. It has led the opposition and the people onto the streets. It has marched to the President. It has petitioned the Supreme Court. And now it has held a public impeachment.The inquiry the Raj could not controlThis is not a new idea. It is woven into our freedom struggle. In April 1919, General Dyer’s troops fired into a peaceful crowd at Jallianwala Bagh. The colonial government appointed the Hunter Committee to inquire into the “disturbances”. The Congress refused to accept an inquiry run by the very power that had pulled the trigger. It set up its own Punjab Inquiry Committee. Mahatma Gandhi, Motilal Nehru, C.R. Das, Abbas Tyabji and M.R. Jayakar went from town to town, recording the statements of ordinary Punjabis.Their report had no legal power. It could not punish a single officer. Yet more than a century later, it is largely through those testimonies that we remember Jallianwala Bagh massacre. The official inquiry gave the Raj its version. The people’s inquiry gave India its memory.Two years earlier, Gandhi had done the same in Champaran. Ordered to leave the district, he refused. He and his colleagues wrote down the complaints of thousands of indigo cultivators, one statement at a time. The evidence was so overwhelming that the government had to appoint its own committee, with Gandhi as a member. The tinkathia system was abolished soon after. A people’s hearing had forced an official one.In the 1990s, the Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan held jan sunwais in the villages of Rajasthan. Muster rolls were read aloud before the very labourers who were supposed to have been paid. Officials had no answer. Those hearings grew into the right to information movement, and finally into the RTI Act of 2005. Beyond India, the Russell Tribunal on Vietnam had no court behind it, yet it shaped how the world judged that war. In each case, the hearing drew its strength not from the law but from the evidence and the public it spoke to.It worksThe pressure is already telling. The evidence placed before the public by Rahul Gandhi, and the protests that followed, have exposed what was meant to stay hidden. Cracks have appeared within the system itself. The two election commissioners recorded objections to the CEC’s decisions on the SIR. The Maharashtra chief electoral officer (CEC) has sought discretion for field staff on ECINET. Officials in Goa have contradicted the commission’s own claims.Also read: The BJP Forgets That a Protest Is Also About JoyFor eight years, the Congress asked for machine readable voter lists, which were available until 2018, so that the rolls could be properly scrutinised. The commission refused, citing privacy. After the protests, it has meekly agreed to provide searchable rolls. Two electoral registration officers (EROs) in Pilibhit have been suspended and named in an FIR, and a statewide re-examination of the rolls in Uttar Pradesh has been ordered. The edifice of non accountability is beginning to crumble.It is worth recalling that the opposition was never irrational. In March 2025, the commission itself proposed linking voter IDs with Aadhaar. The Congress supported it. The commission then dropped the idea without explanation and moved to a dubious SIR instead.But these corrections are too little and too late. Minor fixes cannot paper over what has happened. Mandates have been distorted. Parties have been decimated. Crores have been disenfranchised. And the institution meant to prevent it all stood by, and also facilitated it.Recalling the prophecy by Dr Ambedkar in the Constituent Assembly, the system so laboriously built by the founders is being dismantled by the EC headed by Gyanesh Kumar.This cannot be allowed to lapse. The public impeachment has recorded the public sentiment. The public verdict will follow.Gurdeep Singh Sappal is a Permanent Invitee to the Congress Working Committee and former editor/CEO of Rajya Sabha Television.For our full coverage on the SIR and the issues it has brought to citizens, click here.

title: Jeeva Subramaniam Left Home at 13, Worked in Hotel Housekeeping and Now Plays a Key Role in the Tamil Film Dorothy
description: Trans actors have rarely found substantial roles in Tamil cinema. After years on the industry's margins, Jeeva Subramaniam moved from hotel housekeeping and temple shows to makeup rooms and Dorothy, now celebrated by transgender audiences across Tamil Nadu and Telugu-speaking states.
author: Avantika Krishna
content:
At 13, Jeeva Subramanian arrived in Chennai with Rs 300 her mother had given her. Her brother had accompanied her to the city, but left her at Koyambedu bus stand. Unfamiliar with the place and with nowhere else to go, she waited for him to return.
“I did not know anyone in Chennai. I thought my brother would come back to take me, so I kept waiting in the same place. I would go to the public toilet, wash myself and my clothes, and return to where I had been sitting. I kept thinking he would look for me there,” she recalls.
Two days passed before Jeeva realised that he was not coming back. By then, she had spent nearly three days at the bus stand. A woman who worked there cleaning the premises eventually approached her and offered to find her a job.
That conversation led to Jeeva’s first job in Chennai, at a shop inside the bus stand. She earned Rs 40 a day, with food and accommodation provided by the employer, though her wages were held back for seven days at a time.
“I was only 13. That was my first job in Chennai. They gave us food and a place to stay, so I continued working,” she says.
The job lasted about two months. When it ended, the bus stand became her refuge again. She slept within sight of a police booth because she felt safer there, and took up whatever work she could find, including carrying vegetables at the Koyambedu market in the early hours of the morning.
At the time, Jeeva knew she was a girl, but did not know what it meant to be transgender or that there was a community of people like her. “I lived with the feeling that I was a girl. I did not know there was a transgender community. I was a child. I did not understand what was happening around me,” she says.
From surviving to finding her place
Jeeva eventually found work clearing used banana leaves after wedding functions at a marriage hall. But workers were asked to leave once a wedding was over, and she was again left searching for somewhere safe to stay. A visitor at one of the functions gave her a contact for a housekeeping company. Through it, she found work at a sweets outlet in Vadapalani, earning Rs 2,200 a month, along with food and accommodation.
Around this period, Jeeva began to understand her identity and gradually encountered other transgender people. Dance offered another possibility.
She joined a dance school and began performing at programmes, sometimes wearing wigs for devotional and glamour songs. When the programmes stopped, she was once again left looking for work. A friend helped her find occasional performances, but that too came to an end when he moved to Dubai.
Her next opening came through cinema, where she began working as a touch-up assistant. She had already developed an interest in acting, but expressing that ambition was not easy. People questioned whether she was good-looking enough to act, and once they learnt she was transgender, some became reluctant to employ her.
“I used to tell people that I wanted to act, but they would ask me, ‘What are you going to do by acting? Are you beautiful enough?’ They would dismiss the idea. After they found out that I was trans, people became hesitant to take me for work. Some of the other assistants would keep teasing me,” she says.
There were, however, people who stood up for her. Actor Bala Singh, with whom she worked for several years, was particularly protective. Jeeva remembers him telling others, “She is my daughter. Why are you talking about her like that?” She also worked with actors including Anushka Shetty, Taapsee Pannu, Shriya, and Ramya Nambesan.
Actor Shriya encouraged her to learn makeup, a skill that could support her financially. Jeeva went on to work as a bridal makeup artist, doing makeup for around 400 brides. But discrimination followed her into this profession too, and a bad experience eventually forced her to give it up.
Even as she found ways to earn, the search for a stable home remained unresolved. The rooms she could afford were often in poor condition, with rainwater entering the house and collecting up to her knees. The 2015 Chennai floods damaged her home and left her with very little. A friend, Sheela, took her in and gave her food and shelter.
These experiences had already taught Jeeva how precarious everyday life could be. But it was on a film set that she encountered a moment of acceptance that would change how she saw her place in the industry.
The embrace that changed her relationship with cinema
By the time she was called to work on Dharma Durai, Jeeva was considering leaving Chennai. She had worked for years, tried different jobs and felt that none of it was taking her anywhere. She accepted the opportunity partly because she admired actor Radhika.
The shoot, however, was difficult. People in the crowd used slurs against her, and she found it hard to continue performing. She broke down and cried. Actor Vijay Sethupathi noticed what was happening, intervened, and asked the crowd to stop. He told them, “She is my younger sister,” before hugging Jeeva and kissing her forehead.
For someone who had experienced rejection and abuse, the gesture carried a meaning that went far beyond the film set.
“An embrace may be a normal thing for other people, but it did not come to me so easily. I cannot even put into words what I felt that day. When he hugged me, I closed my eyes for a moment, and it felt as though the whole universe was spinning around me. Nobody had hugged me like that before. He kissed me on the forehead, and I held on to him and cried,” she says.
Director Seenu Ramasamy then encouraged her to continue with the scene, telling her that the very people insulting her should one day whistle and applaud when they saw her on screen.
“He could have said that they should get someone else to do the scene. Instead, he told me to act with confidence. That gave me the courage to go back and perform. That is the magic of Dharma Durai for me,” she says.
The film was released in 2016, and Jeeva began to be recognised by people who had seen her on screen. Her father, too, called her “my daughter”, a moment she remembers with particular happiness. But the recognition did not translate into a steady livelihood. People who had earlier hired her as an assistant began to see her only as an actor and stopped calling her for makeup work.
“I had to start running around for work all over again. Earlier, at least I was working as an assistant. After the film, people would say, ‘You have become an actor. How can we call you for assistant work?’ Nobody called me. I struggled ten times more than I had before. There were days when I could not find food. I would go to the Vadapalani temple and eat the food they distributed. I even went to Hyderabad and stayed in a small lodge, calling actors and asking them to take me on as a makeup assistant so I could pay my rent,” she says.
Being visible on screen, she realised, did not necessarily mean being accepted off it. Jeeva continued looking for work, taking up roles in films and short films. One of her short films went on to win 58 awards, while her work brought her opportunities in projects including Airaa, Darbar and Suzhal. But she did not want recognition to be mistaken for charity. She wanted opportunities to demonstrate her ability, and that determination would be tested again when she auditioned for Dorothy.
Proving what she could do in Dorothy
When the team behind Dorothy approached Jeeva, they initially felt she looked too young for the character. They were looking for someone older and heavier. Jeeva, who weighed around 64 kg, decided to gain weight and shape the character’s appearance herself. She gained 13 kg, choosing a cotton saree, double nose studs, a bun and grey hair to complete the look. She took photographs of herself and sent them to the team.
“I told them, ‘Give me one opportunity. Only if you give me a chance can I prove myself.’ I wanted them to see that I could do the character. I put together the look, took the photographs myself and sent them. I was determined to get this opportunity,” she says.
Jeeva also performed the physically demanding sequences herself, without a body double. During one sequence, she was hurt, and actor Karthi helped her up and checked on her. When the crew applauded her performance, he came over and hugged her.
“He came running and hugged me tightly. He even helped me because I had been hurt. I felt that same kind of embrace I had received years ago during Dharma Durai,” she says.
The film became another turning point. At a rough-cut screening, Jeeva was moved by what she saw and hugged director Karthik Subbaraj. He told her they would take the film to Canada. At the Toronto International Film Festival in 2026, she experienced a warm welcome from people who had watched her work. Actor Rajinikanth also praised her performance.
Yet, even as her work travelled beyond India and more people began recognising her, the difficulties she faced away from the camera did not disappear. In fact, being more recognisable sometimes made finding a house even harder.
The struggle to find a home continues
Jeeva has been searching for a house for around six months. A property that would ordinarily be rented for Rs 10,000 has been quoted to her at Rs 30,000. She once paid an advance of Rs 40,000 for a house, only for the landlord to return the money after neighbours objected to a transgender woman moving into their street.
The questions she faces from brokers and landlords are often invasive. They ask how many people will visit her, whether she intends to bring clients home, and how many people she will bring in each day. In one instance, a broker suggested that she would have to pay far beyond the advertised rent. Jeeva has also been told that a house could be rented to her only if a male acquaintance signed the agreement, because the landlord did not trust her on her own.
“I have been looking for a house for six months. If a house normally costs Rs 10,000, they tell me it will cost Rs 30,000. I paid Rs 40,000 as an advance for one house, and then the people in that street said that a transgender person should not be allowed to live there. They told the owner to return my advance. This is what keeps happening,” she says.
She recalls being asked questions that implied she was offering sexual services. When she explained that she went to work and could pay only what she earned, she was told not to pretend to be poor. A transgender woman who approached the same broker was quoted Rs 35,000 and managed to secure a house, Jeeva says, making her feel that access to housing can depend on how much a landlord believes a person can pay.
The uncertainty has affected her daily life. Her belongings have been packed and unpacked repeatedly as brokers promise that a house will be confirmed the next day. She has kept much of her household packed for months and says she has cried after conversations with people who were supposed to help her find a place.
Jeeva has also approached the government for assistance. She says she was once told that a house could be allotted to her, but the property was around 50 km away, making it impractical for her work. When she sought an allocation closer to the city, she was told that housing categories had specific allocations for several communities but no separate percentage for transgender applicants. She is now trying to secure an appointment with the minister to submit a formal request.
“I do not want anyone to give me a house for free. If I have to pay Rs 4 lakh or Rs 5 lakh, I am willing to do that. Just allot me a small house. I have faced so many things in life, but I have cried more over this house problem than over many of the other things that happened to me. Every time I go to look at a house, the questions people ask me are so humiliating. I do not even know how to answer them,” she says.
She has a simple request: “I want a small house of around 400 square feet, a house that is mine. I do not want to keep proving to people that I am a good person, that I am respectable, or explaining where I am going and what work I do. I just want to sleep peacefully in my own house.”
The contrast is difficult to ignore. Jeeva has appeared on screens watched by audiences across countries, received appreciation from some of Tamil cinema’s most prominent names and represented a community that rarely gets such visibility. Yet she is still made to answer questions about whether she can be trusted with a rental home.
A celebration, and a wish for ordinary life
The difference between being seen and being allowed to live freely is something Jeeva has experienced in smaller, everyday ways too. She recalls that, in earlier years, Diwali was not a festival she celebrated with others. She would buy enough rice and lentils to last a few days, shut the doors and keep to herself. After Dorothy, she decided to mark the festival differently. She bought a cake and cut it for Diwali.
“It may seem like a small thing, but it gave me so much happiness,” she says.
For Jeeva, the cake was not simply a festive purchase. It was a moment in which she allowed herself to celebrate, rather than spend the day withdrawing from the world. It was also a reminder that the life she wants is not defined only by film roles, awards or public recognition. It includes the ordinary freedoms that many people take for granted: a secure place to return to, the ability to celebrate without fear and the dignity of not having to explain herself to strangers.
She continues to look for work and a home, while hoping that the attention around Dorothy will lead to more opportunities. She would like to win a National Award one day. But when she speaks about what she wants beyond cinema, her wish is strikingly modest.
After years of being pushed out of homes, workplaces and public spaces, Jeeva is asking for a place where she can close the door at the end of the day and rest without having to prove that she belongs there. The applause may follow her from one theatre to another, but what she is still waiting for is a home of her own.

title: After a US Tech Career, Kalaiselvi Turned Her Father’s Farm Surplus Into ‘Aruvi Eco Organics’ in Tamil Nadu
description: Kalaiselvi founded Aruvi Eco Organics in Tamil Nadu to turn surplus farm produce into natural food products, reduce waste and create local livelihoods.
author: Raajwrita Dutta
content:
By the time the amla ripened at her father's farm in Iduvai, Tamil Nadu, there was more fruit than the family could consume or sell fresh. Around 25 trees were bearing heavily, and the harvest would not wait for buyers.
For Kalaiselvi, a former software professional who had spent nearly a decade working in the United States, the surplus presented a question: Could the fruit be preserved and sold long after its season had passed?
That question led to Aruvi Eco Organics, which now makes more than 25 products, from amla jaggery candy and dried fruit to herbal teas and leaf powders. Kalaiselvi estimates that processing helps the farm use nearly 60 percent of its suitable surplus produce, depending on the season. The venture also supports a six-member core team.
“My father laid the foundation for our venture through his commitment to organic farming. My contribution has been to build on that legacy by trying out how we can process the produce, reduce avoidable losses, and make natural food products available to more people,” she tells The Better India.
A return to her father’s farm
Kalaiselvi grew up in an agricultural family in Iduvai. In 1999, her father, Subramaniam, began developing their ancestral land into what the family called Aruvi Farm, growing amla, sapota, mango and guava without chemical pesticides.
She remembers planting seeds during childhood summer holidays at her aunt's house. Her parents encouraged their daughters to study while keeping a connection to the land, but her own ambitions took her towards computers.
After studying computer science and engineering at Kongu Engineering College, she worked in Chennai before moving to the US in 2006 to join her husband. Her IT career included stints at AT&T, Frontier Communications, Verizon and Highmark in Pittsburgh, where she worked as an application developer.
In March 2015, the couple returned to India with their two young children. Her father-in-law was facing serious health issues, and they wanted to be closer to their parents and raise their children here.
They settled in Chennai, where Kalaiselvi spent time helping the children adjust, then worked in recruitment and scientific publishing. She also started Kana Bags, an initiative making cloth bags as alternatives to plastic ones.
When the pandemic disrupted that venture in 2020, with the children's classes moving online, the family began spending more time on the farm in Iduvai. Kalaiselvi saw firsthand the labour behind her father's harvest, and the problem that accompanied it.
“I got a closer understanding of the effort behind cultivation and the challenges that come with storing and managing the harvest,” she recalls.
The amla crop was particularly abundant. Even with buyers, fresh fruit had a limited window in which it could be sold.
“Instead of looking at the surplus just as produce that could not be sold in time, I started seeing it as an opportunity to create value-added products,” she says.
From a dryer in the living room to a food business
Her father showed her a newspaper article on value addition, and she joined an online session offered by Tamil Nadu Agricultural University.
She began experimenting with drying amla and sapota, initially using a coir-tray dryer that cost about Rs 28,000. She installed it in her Chennai living room; her father sent fruit from the farm by overnight parcel twice a week.
The early batches taught her that turning fruit into a product was more complicated than finding a recipe.
She sought training at the ICAR-Krishi Vigyan Kendra in Tirupur, Tamil Nadu Agricultural University in Coimbatore and the National Institute of Food Technology Entrepreneurship and Management.
Over roughly two years, she learnt about handling produce, moisture, food safety, packaging and shelf life. Guidance from a food technologist at the Krishi Vigyan Kendra also helped her understand which ideas could be made consistently and sold commercially.
“A recipe may work once, but achieving the same taste, texture, and quality consistently across batches is a completely different challenge,” she says. “I had to experiment repeatedly, understand how ingredients behave during processing, and learn how factors such as drying, moisture, and storage affect the final product.”
Training introduced her to around 25 possible products. Rather than produce everything, she and her father chose ideas that suited what grew on the farm and their preference for avoiding artificial colours, flavours and synthetic preservatives.
In 2021, the family also tested selling sapota and mango directly to consumers. Their first order was for sapota, but the pilot reinforced how difficult it could be to find buyers before fruit spoiled.
By April 2022, the family had moved permanently to Iduvai. Working alongside Subramaniam, Kalaiselvi made the experiments more systematic, and Aruvi began commercial sales towards the end of that year.
A June 2023 video about her journey on the agricultural YouTube channel Tamizhan Agri helped introduce the products to a wider audience.
What goes into making 25+ natural food products
Aruvi's catalogue has grown to more than 25 products, including over a dozen made with amla. Alongside jaggery-sweetened amla candy are dried mango and sapota, moringa and curry leaf powders, herbal infusions and products made from jamun seeds.
“I never set out to build a large product line. Each new addition came from identifying an opportunity to make better use of what we grew and finding ways to meet customer needs,” Kalaiselvi says.
The choices extend to packaging. Aruvi uses cotton bags for its herbal dip teas instead of nylon mesh.
Produce is harvested, sorted and cleaned, with damaged portions removed. Depending on the product, the team cuts or deseeds fruit before drying or further processing.
The team checks each batch for appearance, texture, aroma and moisture, then packages and stores it carefully. Samples are sent to a NABL-accredited laboratory at Tamil Nadu Agricultural University in Coimbatore for nutritional and quality assessment.
Working without synthetic preservatives makes consistent processing and storage especially important. The family farm supplies most ingredients, with additional produce sourced from farmers and producers around Tirupur when needed.
For Kalaiselvi, this is where her previous career has proved useful. The discipline of software development, she says, helped her approach new recipes through testing, documentation and problem-solving, even as she learnt the practicalities of working with seasonal crops.
The people behind every packet
As orders grew, Aruvi's work created roles beyond the family. Six people now make up its core team across farming, processing, packaging and operations. For some, the change has meant a dependable income; for others, a chance to use or develop new skills.
Mahalakshmi, 41, joined in February 2024 after spotting a banner advertising work at the farm gate.
A single mother raising two children, she had previously worked in tailoring and papad-making units. She began by collecting leaves and fruit, then learnt food processing from Kalaiselvi.
Today she helps maintain the workspace, stitches cotton tea bags and operates the amla-deseeding machine.
“I did not have much knowledge of food processing or how farm produce could be turned into different products,” she says. “At Aruvi Eco, I got the opportunity to learn new skills under the guidance of Kalaiselvi ma’am.”
Earning Rs 5,000 a week has made a difference at home. Her daughter is in college and her teenage son is studying for a diploma. Where she once sometimes turned to relatives for help with education expenses, she says she can now meet more of those costs herself.
“Today, I feel proud that I can earn and take care of many of my family’s needs myself,” she says. “Apart from being my only source of income, this job is an opportunity to build a better future for my children.”
Ramar and his wife Uma joined in March 2026. They had moved to Tirupur in search of work and were employed at a stitching unit when they saw an advertisement for jobs at Aruvi.
Ramar has a degree in agriculture and now handles planting, watering, pruning and tree care under Subramaniam's guidance. Uma works with fruit and flowers in processing.
He earns Rs 6,000 a week and she earns Rs 4,000. Together, they support three children and their elderly parents.
“I was happy to get an opportunity to return to agriculture, while my wife could contribute to food processing,” Ramar says.
Sasikumar's connection with the farm goes back further. He joined as a helper in January 2008 and gradually learnt planting, tractor operation, maintenance, plumbing and electrical repairs.
Today he manages much of the daily farm work and coordinates packing and dispatch. His wife, Sumithra, stitches cotton tea bags from home using a machine supplied by Kalaiselvi.
When a customer complained that a tea bag floated instead of staying immersed, Sasikumar suggested adding two stitches. The adjustment worked and became part of the process.
“I never imagined that a job I started as a helper would allow me to learn so many skills and take on such responsibilities,” he says. “I feel that my experience matters and that I can contribute ideas that make a real difference to the business.”
A longer life for the fruit, and a new beginning after 40
Kalaiselvi estimates that nearly 60 percent of suitable surplus produce that might previously have gone unused is now processed.
It is an approximate, seasonal figure, rather than a fixed share of everything the farm grows. Processing also means the family has more ways to earn from fruit instead of relying only on fresh-produce prices during a short harvest window.
By December 2024, Aruvi had reached more than 4,000 customers and recorded around 450 orders in one month.
Sales have come through its website, Amazon and WhatsApp, while exhibitions, farmers' markets and food events have helped people across India discover the products. Some ingredients are sourced from neighbouring producers, giving the business opportunities to connect with other growers too.
Growth comes with its own demands. Availability changes with each season, small batches take planning, and products without synthetic preservatives need careful hygiene and moisture control.
Kalaiselvi has had to learn about equipment, investment, pricing and winning customer trust.
“Perhaps the biggest challenge was changing our own mindset. From thinking like farmers who wanted to avoid wastage to thinking like entrepreneurs who had to create a product, a brand, and a market around that surplus,” she says.
She hopes to improve processing capacity and quality checks, work with more local farmers, reach retailers and business customers, and create more jobs.
But she keeps returning to the person who made the journey possible: her father, who began tending the ancestral land long before she imagined working on it herself.
“Today, the farm means much more to me than a piece of ancestral land. It is a part of my family’s history, a teacher, a workplace, and the foundation of Aruvi Eco,” she says.
She was over 40 when she began learning food processing. Starting again meant being a beginner after years in an established career, a possibility she hopes other women will consider too.
“I started this journey in a completely new field after 40, and there were many things I had to learn from scratch,” she says. “That experience has given me a strong belief that women, and anyone who feels it is ‘too late’ to begin something new, should not let age stop them.”
What began as a question about unsold amla has become a way to carry forward her father's work, give the harvest more time to find a buyer and build livelihoods around the farm she once visited on holidays.
All pictures courtesy Kalaiselvi.

title: Before UNESCO Comes Calling, Explore 9 Indian Natural Heritage Contenders Responsibly
description: Seven Indian natural heritage sites are now on UNESCO’s Tentative List. Discover what makes them significant and how to explore them responsibly.
author: Avantika Krishna
content:
India's most extraordinary landscapes do not always announce themselves with grand monuments or marked tourist trails. Some are hidden beneath tropical forests, others rise out of the sea, and a few preserve evidence of geological events that unfolded millions of years ago.
Now, several of these remarkable places are attracting international attention. India's UNESCO Tentative List has expanded in 2026, with two particularly fascinating natural heritage additions in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands: the Karst-Mud-Volcano Complex of Baratang and the Andaman Subduction Volcanoes, comprising Barren and Narcondam islands.
These additions build on seven natural heritage properties submitted in August 2025, taking the story beyond a handful of destinations to a remarkable cross-section of India's geological history.
But what makes these places special, where can travellers experience them, and what should visitors know before setting out? More importantly, how can we explore them without damaging the very landscapes that make them extraordinary?
A landscape shaped by two kinds of volcanoes
The first of the two new natural properties is the Karst-Mud-Volcano Complex of Baratang, on Great Andaman Island, about 100 km north of Sri Vijaya Puram (Port Blair).
Picture a forested island where the ground opens into limestone caves, narrow fissures, and underground chambers. Over millions of years, marine organisms, including shells and corals, accumulated and compacted to form the limestone. Rainwater gradually dissolved parts of this rock, creating the intricate cave systems found here.
But the island has another geological surprise. Its mud volcanoes, locally called Jalki, release slurries of mud, water, and gases rather than molten rock. Unlike conventional volcanoes, these formations do not erupt magma. They are driven by pressure and movement within underground sediment layers.
After remaining dormant for around 20 years, Baratang's mud volcanoes became active again in 2025. The Geological Survey of India identified the mud volcano as a Geo-Heritage Site that year. The caves also support specialised subterranean ecosystems, making their conservation important beyond their geological appeal.
The second property, Andaman Subduction Volcanoes, brings together Barren Island and Narcondam Island. Both emerged from the tectonic processes associated with the Indian Plate moving beneath the Burma microplate.
Barren Island, approximately 138 km northeast of Sri Vijaya Puram, is South Asia's only active volcano. Its first recorded eruption dates to 1787. More recently, it recorded mild eruptions in September 2025, followed by an ash plume rising approximately 1.2 km in January 2026.
Narcondam, meanwhile, presents a different picture. Its densely forested volcanic landscape rises 710 metres above sea level and supports species found nowhere else, including the Narcondam hornbill. Unlike Barren Island, which is known for its surrounding marine environment, Narcondam is not open to tourism. Access is restricted, and visitors should not attempt independent trips or landings.
These islands are important precisely because their ecosystems remain relatively undisturbed. A UNESCO listing should not be mistaken for an invitation to explore every part of them.
Seven more landscapes that tell India's geological story
The two Andaman additions join seven natural properties submitted to UNESCO in August 2025. Together, they reveal just how varied India's geological heritage is.
In Maharashtra, the Deccan Traps at Panchgani and Mahabaleshwar preserve evidence of enormous volcanic eruptions around 66 million years ago. Their successive lava flows created the distinctive stepped rock formations of the region. Visitors should stick to established viewpoints and avoid disturbing exposed geological formations.
Off Karnataka's Malpe coast, the St Mary's Island Cluster is famous for its unusual columnar basalt formations. These polygonal rock structures developed as molten lava cooled and contracted approximately 85 million years ago. The islands are accessible by ferry, subject to seasonal conditions. Resist the temptation to collect rock fragments or climb fragile formations.
Meghalaya's Meghalayan Age Caves include Mawmluh, Mawsmai, Arwah and Krem Puri. Mawmluh Cave is particularly significant because a mineral deposit found there helped establish the Meghalayan Age, the youngest stage of the Holocene geological epoch. Cave formations take thousands of years to develop, so visitors should never touch, scratch or break them. Explore with authorised guides.
Nagaland's Naga Hill Ophiolite in Kiphire district offers a glimpse into the Earth's ancient oceanic crust and upper mantle. Ophiolites are fragments of ocean floor pushed onto land through tectonic activity. The landscape also has ecological significance, making local guidance and respect for wildlife essential.
In Andhra Pradesh, Erra Matti Dibbalu, or the Red Sand Hills, near Visakhapatnam, displays striking red and brown sedimentary formations. Wind and water erosion have shaped these hills over time, preserving evidence of changing environmental and climatic conditions. Visitors should avoid walking over unstable formations or leaving waste behind.
Further south, the Natural Heritage of Tirumala Hills includes the Eparchaean Unconformity and the Silathoranam natural rock arch. The latter is particularly fascinating: its formation represents an exceptionally old geological history, with the rocks in the region recording more than a billion years of Earth's past. The surrounding hills also carry religious significance, so visitors must respect temple and forest regulations.
Finally, Kerala's Varkala Cliffs expose layers of the Warkalli Formation, dating to the Mio-Pliocene period. Their striking sedimentary bands overlook the Arabian Sea, while natural springs add to their geological importance. However, the cliffs face pressure from increasing tourism and construction. Visitors should keep away from unstable edges and follow safety instructions.
The responsibility that comes with discovery
A place becoming popular can bring income to nearby communities, but it can also put pressure on fragile ecosystems. The challenge is to ensure that tourism does not destroy what makes these destinations worth visiting.
Before travelling, check local entry permissions, seasonal restrictions, and forest department guidelines. Some locations, particularly caves and protected islands, have restricted access. Never assume that a place being on UNESCO's Tentative List means it is open to unrestricted tourism.
Choose local guides and community-run stays wherever possible. Carry reusable water bottles, avoid single-use plastics, and take all waste back with you. Do not collect rocks, fossils, shells or other natural material. At coastal destinations, avoid disturbing marine habitats, and at forest sites, keep noise levels low and maintain a safe distance from wildlife.
There are already examples of tourism supporting conservation across India. In Nagaland's Khonoma village, community-led tourism allows visitors to experience local culture while supporting conservation efforts. Similarly, community-led travel companies are creating opportunities for travellers to contribute directly to local livelihoods.
Travellers can also take inspiration from five Indian journeys that support wildlife and nature conservation and learn from sustainable travel practices that minimise waste and respect local ecosystems.
India's geological heritage is not simply a collection of spectacular views. These landscapes preserve evidence of volcanic eruptions, shifting tectonic plates, ancient oceans and evolving ecosystems. Their importance extends far beyond their potential as tourist destinations.
Being included on UNESCO's Tentative List is an important step towards international recognition, but it is not the finish line. The real achievement will be ensuring that these places remain intact for generations to come.
After all, the best way to experience a natural wonder is to leave it just as wonderful for the next person.

title: Arpita Singh: The Playful Imagination Behind the Paintings
description: Artist Arpita Singh combined a childlike imagination with political awareness, technical mastery, and an enduring curiosity that kept her art evolving across generations.
author: Udit Bhambri
content:
When I was 8 years old, I came across a painting titled “Amina Kidwai with Her Dead Husband”. It was part of an exhibition about couples. I remember walking past it and then stopping in front of it. At first, it was the pink that drew me in, along with the teacups, pink flowers, and clouds. It seemed like a rather joyous painting. But the longer I stood there, the more uncomfortable I became. There were two figures at a distance from each other. A woman, with what appeared to be a black shawl on her lap, sat apart from a man who seemed to be looking towards her. She, however, was looking away. The title horrified me. Why was this man not lying down if he was dead? This was, after all, an 8-year-old’s understanding of death. Why was the word “dead” even there? Gradually, the pink didn’t seem quite as pink, the blue wasn’t quite as blue, and even the teacups lost their cheerfulness. I walked away, but the painting stayed with me.
Perhaps that is what art does. It unsettles you just enough to remain with you, sometimes for reasons you cannot quite articulate.
Arpita Singh was a name I kept encountering after that. I would look for her work in exhibition catalogues, galleries, and invitations. I loved the name and, whenever I came across it, I would seek out the paintings. Yet I didn’t own a single work until 2021, when I finally met her properly. What followed was something of a collecting rampage. But much more importantly, Arpita became an extraordinarily dear friend, almost immediate family. Very quickly, the giant of an artist became secondary to the person: gentle, kind, playful, funny, silly, and endlessly curious.
Almost 30 years after first seeing the painting, I finally asked her about “Amina Kidwai with Her Dead Husband”. She told me that she used to visit her neighbour Amina Kidwai every day at 5 o’clock for tea. On the morning her husband, Mr Kidwai, passed away, Amina, almost instinctively, handed Arpita a black shawl and asked her to pass it to him because he must be feeling cold. Arpita was stunned. She understood that someone we love does not simply disappear when they die. They continue to inhabit our lives, our gestures, and our imagination. He did not need to be lying down, with closed eyes, or absent from the picture. He was very much present because he was present for her. And while she could not look at him, he was looking at her. That, I realised, was a love story.
People often describe Arpita’s paintings as dreamlike. I think some of them are nightmares dressed up as dreams. She once explained that her figures were not floating. They were simply there. We live in a world governed by gravity, but her world had no such laws. Her figures were anchored to her canvases, entirely present within their own universe.
Her work is also frequently described as childlike. But there is a difference between making childlike work and approaching the world with the imagination of a child. At 90, Arpita had managed to preserve that imagination. Picasso famously spoke of learning to paint like a child, and I think Arpita retained precisely that freedom: the looseness, the playfulness, the willingness to let a painting surprise her. This was despite being extraordinarily well-read, politically alert, and deeply engaged with the world. Reading was almost a ritual for her. She followed the news, devoured books, and was endlessly interested in what was happening around her.
Colour was central to this freedom. She spoke of Naples yellow, Holbein’s brilliant pink, titanium white, ultramarine, and terra verte with an intimacy that made these colours seem like old acquaintances. Yet, for all her extraordinary command of colour, she was equally remarkable as a draughtsman. Her drawings were so fine, so intricate, that people would often ask whether they were prints. They almost resembled etchings. She had also spent nearly 10 years studying nothing but lines and dots. But her exploration never stopped at the surface. She cut paper, created layers, experimented with dimensions, and worked with needles, pin marks, and scratches. She was extraordinarily physical with paper. Sometimes she would rub glass against its surface because of the way it caught the light, reminding her of miniature paintings. She would also rub down the surface of a canvas, allowing the impasto to peel and its underlying layers to emerge. For her, a painting was never simply a finished image. It was an accumulation of discoveries.
An extraordinarily funny private shorthand
There was also an entire private language in her work and in her life. Animals, alphabets, and seemingly ordinary objects became codes. A koala, an elephant, a porcupine, or a baby seal could carry a particular meaning. X, L, H and K each had their own associations. Over time, I began to recognise that even her emojis had a vocabulary of their own. A dushman could be a friend; a friend could be a backstabber; a snake could mean something entirely different from what one ordinarily associates with a snake. Someone might become a tablecloth simply because of the way they dressed. These were not necessarily judgments but observations, intuitions, and feelings translated into an extraordinarily funny private shorthand. She took her feelings very seriously, but herself never too seriously.
She was equally particular about the generosity of artistic exchange. She often wondered why artists no longer critiqued one another as they once did. Her generation had grown up seeking criticism, not taking offence at it. It was a culture of generosity rather than competition. She missed that distinction between criticism and critique: the latter coming from a genuine desire to understand, engage and help another artist. Yet she was sensitive to the times we live in. She would sometimes hold back an observation, wondering whether the person receiving it was as ready to receive as she was to give. She was careful not to hurt anyone, even while yearning for the intellectual honesty she had once experienced.
Her curiosity, however, never diminished. She was fascinated by younger artists, unfamiliar names, and international practices. After I visited an Anthony Gormley exhibition, she made an entire work around the idea of “Anthony Gormley’s Men and Arpita’s Women”. He was making sculptures of men; she was painting women. The observation found its way into a work that, on the surface, might suggest something entirely different, almost a meditation on migration. She would ask me to send her pictures of artists she hadn’t encountered. She had no embarrassment about admitting she didn’t know a particular international name. She simply wanted to see, understand, and discover.
Perhaps the swans will come back another year
Once, she showed me a sketch full of swans and told me it would become her next painting. When I eventually saw the finished canvas, there wasn’t a single swan. It was an abstract, textured work. I asked her where the swans had gone. She smiled and said, “The swans did not come this year.”
I once asked her when she knew a painting was successful. Her answer was characteristically unexpected: a work was successful only if it told her what to do in the next one. It might offer a colour, a texture, a composition, a technique, or simply an idea. Even at the very end, just before signing, a painting could reveal something that would lead to another. Its success lay not in its completion, but in what it made possible.
I keep returning to that thought, and to the swans. Perhaps, at the end of this canvas, Arpita found a hint of what she wanted to do next. I hope she did. Because Arpita will continue to live on: in the minds of those who loved her, in the lives she touched, and in the extraordinary world she has left behind for us to enter. She will continue to look at us through her paintings, reminding us to remain curious, to be playful, to be a little silly, and never to take ourselves too seriously. And, at the same time, to remain stoic, strong, and firm in what we believe.
Perhaps the swans will come back another year. Until then, there is still so much to discover in the world she has left us.
Udit Bhambri is a Mumbai-based art collector who was a close friend to the artist and an ardent fan of her work.
