title: Dogra scion raises Sheshnag concern over roadwork near lake and fragile Kashmir ecology
description: Vikramaditya Singh Urges Jammu And Kashmir Authorities To Monitor BRO Work Near Sheshnag Lake, Citing Concerns Over Tree Felling And The Region’s Fragile Ecosystem
author: Muzaffar Raina
content:
Vikramaditya Singh, the scion of the erstwhile Dogra royal family, on Thursday voiced concern over the Sheshnag “road maintenance work”, saying the region’s ecosystem was under stress and cannot afford irreversible damage.
The concern came as PDP president Mehbooba Mufti stepped up pressure on the Omar Abdullah-led government in Jammu and Kashmir over the work, demanding cancellation of an MoU with the Border Roads Organisation (BRO) in January. Several social media handles, however, flagged an official order showing that the road-maintenance work had been assigned to the BRO by the Manoj Sinha-led administration in 2022.
Vikramaditya, son of Dr Karan Singh, said it was “our collective duty to preserve the natural beauty and unique ecology of Jammu and Kashmir for future generations”. The century-long Dogra rule is widely believed to have provided greater institutional and state patronage, with some accounts dating the formal beginning of the Amarnath Yatra during its rule in 1872.
“The (recent) felling and burning of protected Chinar and Chestnut trees in Kashmir, along with BRO road construction in close proximity to the sacred Sheshnag Lake, are deeply concerning developments,” Vikramaditya said on X. “The experiences of Uttarakhand and Nepal serve as stark reminders of the consequences of unchecked/over-development and environmental neglect. The fragile ecosystem of Jammu & Kashmir, already under considerable stress, cannot afford such irreversible damage. I urge the J&K Government and the concerned authorities to take serious cognisance of these activities and ensure strict monitoring before it is too late.”

title: Ex-MP jail release overturned: Supreme Court orders Anand Mohan to return to prison
description: The Court Directs Former Bihar MP To Surrender Within A Month After Uma Krishnaiah Challenged His Premature Release Under State’s Remission Policy
author: Our Bureau
content:
The Supreme Court on Thursday quashed the Bihar government’s remission policy that had granted relief to former Bihar MP Anand Mohan, whose premature release in 2023 from a life sentence in connection with the 1994 lynching of district magistrate R. Krishnaiah had triggered a nationwide outrage.
A bench of Justice Dipankar Datta and Justice Sheel Nagu, while quashing the remission granted to Mohan, directed the former lawmaker to surrender within a month to the jail authorities.
Despite facing life imprisonment for leading a mob that lynched Krishnaiah in 1994, Mohan walked out of jail on April 24, 2023, under the Bihar government’s remission policy, which has been challenged by the slain IAS officer’s wife.
The apex court passed the order after hearing senior advocate Sidharth Luthra appearing for Uma Krishnaiah, wife of the murdered district magistrate, who questioned the Bihar government’s decision on the ground that it was contrary to several Supreme Court judgments that convicts are not entitled to any automatic release upon completion of 14 years of imprisonment.
According to the petition filed by Uma in the apex court, the life imprisonment sentence given to a convict as a substitute for the death sentence must be viewed differently and segregated from the ordinary life imprisonment given as the sentence of first choice.
Life imprisonment, when awarded as a substitute for a death penalty, has to be carried out strictly as directed by the court and is beyond remission, the petition said.

title: United protests against SIR held in Delhi and state capitals on Constitution Day
description: Left Parties, Farmers’ Unions And Civil Society Groups Demand Scrapping Of The SIR, While INDIA Bloc Plans Rallies In Bhopal, Ahmedabad And Kolkata
author: Our Special Correspondent
content:
The Congress, the Left and civil society groups on Thursday held protests in Delhi and all state capitals to mark Constitution Day, focusing on the SIR.
Resuming the poll-roll-related movement, which had been put on the back burner just before Diwali, all major Left parties and groups representing farmers, women and students protested on Mandir Marg.
AISA president Neha Bora said: “On one hand, Constitution Day is being celebrated (by the government) in Central Delhi.... On the other hand, the soul of universal adult franchise under the Constitution is being torn by this government.”
The Sanyukta Kisan Morcha, the biggest umbrella group of farmers’ unions, demanded “implementation of the assurance of December 9, 2021, on enacting an MSP law, loan waiver, no privatisation of electricity and not signing the India-US Trade Deal, scrapping the SIR... and removing and prosecuting (chief election commissioner) Gyanesh Kumar and re-notify Jantar Mantar as the site of peaceful protest in the capital city, New Delhi.”
A Trinamool MP told The Telegraph: “The INDIA bloc will hold its next rally against the SIR and Gyanesh Kumar on December 12 in Bhopal, tentatively on December 19 in Ahmedabad and in Calcutta after January 15.”

title: Marital rape: Millions of wives in South Asia unprotected - study
description: More than 100 countries have outlawed marital rape, but a large part of South Asia has not.
author: Geeta Pandey
content:
Millions of wives in South Asia unprotected from marital rape - study
- Published
Failure to fully criminalise marital rape leaves millions of women and girls unprotected in eight South Asian countries, where intimate partner violence is 35% higher than the global average, says a new study.
More than 100 countries have outlawed marital rape, but a large part of South Asia - India, Afghanistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh - remain among the three dozen countries which haven't.
The only South Asian country where rape within marriage attracts the same penalty as any other rape is The Maldives.
Nepal and Bhutan have criminalised marital rape, but apply lesser penalties, says the study by Samaj, a coalition of women's rights groups in the region.
South Asia's marital rape laws largely stem from British colonial rule, says Ranjeeta Silwal of Equality Now, a global women's rights group part of Samaj.
The law, dating to 1860 in India and Bangladesh and 1885 in Sri Lanka, lists exceptions to rape - including sex by a man with his adult wife.
Campaigners say the law is outdated and forced sex is rape, regardless of the perpetrator. Experts warn marital sexual violence harms women's physical, psychological, emotional and sexual well-being.
More than 100 countries have criminalised marital rape, including the UK, which changed its law in 1991. But the exemption remains in India, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh.
Pakistan removed the marital rape exception in 2006, but no higher court has confirmed that rape laws apply within marriage. A recent high court ruling, meanwhile, granted husbands broad immunity for non-consensual sex.
Since returning to power in 2021, the Taliban have steadily dismantled women's protections in Afghanistan.
A new penal code introduced in January made matters worse, Silwal says. Under it, a husband can be prosecuted for violence against his wife only if he causes a broken bone, open wound or severe bruising. Even then, he faces just 15 days in prison if convicted.
Unsurprisingly, the code makes no mention of marital rape. But its narrow definition of punishable violence effectively denies women protection against it.
"The idea comes from the belief that consent for sex is implied in marriage, that marriage is a threshold where consent ends," Silwal told the BBC.
"But it shows a lack of awareness, it shows we are still treating women as property, that we are still very patriarchal."
The report comes amid renewed debate over marital rape across the region.
In India, 10 petitions challenging the law are pending before the Supreme Court, which is due to begin final hearings on 9 December.
Courts have delivered contradictory rulings over the years, with some judges acknowledging the law's archaic nature and urging parliament to criminalise marital rape.
There was outrage last year when a court let go a man whose wife had died after he brutally raped her.
But the Indian government, religious organisations and men's rights activists have opposed petitions in the top court, saying criminalisation of marital rape would be "excessively harsh".
Rights groups in Bangladesh have also challenged the marital rape exception, arguing it violates constitutional rights to life, liberty and protection from torture and cruel treatment, the report says.
"Those who oppose criminalising marital rape say it would undermine the family unit and break them apart. And family is very important in our countries," Silwal says.
"They say it will affect our religious and cultural values and worry that there would be false accusations against men."
Also a change in law, she says, may not necessarily mean justice for survivors.
Silwal points to Bhutan where marital rape is a criminal offence but it's treated as a petty misdemeanour and is punishable by one month to one year.
In Nepal, the punishment for rape is between six and 20 years, but it's only up to five years for a husband who rapes his wife.

title: Indians turn to start-ups to care for ageing parents as young become more mobile
description: Changing family structures in India are driving demand for start-ups offering services for eldercare.
author: Rachita Prasad
content:
Indians turn to start-ups to care for ageing parents as young become more mobile
- Published
Arindam Bhattacharyya, an advertising executive based in Jakarta, had an unexpected wake-up call in 2024.
His parents, based in India's Kolkata city, were visiting him when his father had a health crisis. Bhattacharyya managed to get him medical care but when it was time for them to go back, he faced a question familiar to many Indians - how do you care for your parents when you can't be there in person?
Between 2020 and 2050, the number of people aged 60 and above globally is projected to double to 2.1 billion, according to the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA). India is expected to mirror this - by 2050, one in every five Indians will be above the age of 60, close to 21% of the total population.
Until a few decades ago, there was little discussion in India on caring for elderly people as the expectation was that families would step in, the UNFPA notes, external.
This, however, has been complicated by factors including the shrinking of joint families. As younger people move away from their families, and with limited social infrastructure to support the elderly, a gap is only widening, experts say.
Some frame this as an opportunity.
Government think-tank NITI Aayog says the senior care industry in India is valued at around $7bn (£5.56bn) - it is expected to grow rapidly and offer huge opportunities for healthcare companies.
Many start-ups are already moving in. These companies are looking to address several areas including senior living, home care and technology-enabled services. While their goal is to help older adults live and age more independently, their customers are often the children of the people they help.
Bhattacharyya says he now relies on two start-ups to monitor his parents' health, coordinate care and arrange emergency medical support.
"These services are a big help but I still monitor everything closely [from Jakarta]," he said.
An area seeing an uptick is organised senior living, mainly due to higher incomes and changing family structures. But some experts believe that demand is far ahead of supply.
Companies like Manasum Senior Living, Primus Senior Living, Ananta Living and Vedaanta Senior Living are building projects especially for senior housing and care, even as there is growing interest from traditional real estate developers.
Real estate management firm Colliers International Group estimates current senior living demand at around 2-2.2 million units in India while only around 25,000 units are available.
Anantharam Varayur, a former tech executive, co-founded Manasum Senior Living after he saw many older people in India living restricted lives compared with their peers in the US.
In 2015, when he first set up a promotional stall at an event by a large Indian community in the US, hoping to draw interest from younger Indians due to their familiarity with the concept, hardly anyone came to ask questions - he thinks this was due to the "stigma" associated with leaving older family members in an "old age home", as they are traditionally called in India.
But things have changed - his company already has 900 operational units, mostly in Bengaluru and Goa, and plans to scale up to 10,000 units by 2030, including a luxury project.
They get enquiries from senior citizens whose children live abroad, couples with adult children with special needs, older single people, and even younger people planning for the future.
But there are also many older people who prefer staying in their family homes or apartments and need support.
Earlier, attendants and nurses were seen as an addition to family caregivers. Today, they are often taking on primary caregiving roles.
What was once a fragmented, hyperlocal market run by small agencies is now seeing the rise of firms that offer end-to-end home-care services and use technology to scale up. Examples include Emoha Elder Care Services, Care24 and KITES Senior Care, among others.
But given the sensitive and intimate nature of the caregiving industry, finding the right personnel and retaining them is a big challenge.
"Failure to adequately train the workforce will lead to an acute shortage of skilled people amid rising demand," warns a report by ratings firm CareEdge.
The challenge goes beyond skills. Caregivers also need thorough vetting and specialised training to support a demographic that is vulnerable to fraud, financial scams and other forms of exploitation.
NITI Aayog has recognised this issue and highlighted the need for a national caregiving policy to build a professional and inclusive caregiving ecosystem in India.
Entrepreneurs are also looking at ways to address the social and emotional needs of clients.
In 2022, former Tata Group chairman Ratan Tata's investment in start-up Goodfellows generated a lot of public interest. The company's tagline explains what it does - "Everything Grandkids Do!"
Founder Shantanu Naidu says that they are not aiming to replace family, but to fill a void by offering spirited, empathetic youth companions for elderly clients for some quality time together or even to just help them with technology.
While Naidu's start-up is tapping human emotional intelligence, some entrepreneurs are using artificial intelligence to solve real-life challenges.
In Bengaluru, companies like Kubo Care and NoBlink.ai combine AI-powered monitoring services with wall-mounted radar devices at homes to monitor people's movements to alert emergency services if they faint or fall.
Prajith Nair, co-founder of NoBlink.ai, says that they aim to "build at scale so that it is available at economical and affordable cost".
He says that the company is currently selling these systems to senior living projects at 13,500 rupees ($141.74; £106.42) per device and a monthly monitoring fee of onwards of 50 rupees per room, one tenth the price of what some similar products abroad.
But despite many start-ups aiming to keep prices competitive, affordability is a big concern.
Varayur says buying a one bedroom-hall-kitchen unit in a senior living project can cost 6m rupees, with additional payment for maintenance and food. The cost can vary according to the facilities chosen.
Demand is high, but this is out of reach for most elderly Indians.
NITI Aayog says 78% of India's elderly population is without a pension, which could restrict their ability to access these services. Households with at least one elderly person have a lower monthly per capita income of around 3,568 rupees as compared with 4,098 rupees for a unit without an elderly member.
That's why start-ups can't be the only solution, experts say.
Japan has addressed issues faced by its ageing population by introducing a mix of long-term care insurance, public nursing facilities, social exchange programmes and community-based support systems. India's neighbour China has spent years grappling with an ageing population, rolling out measures to encourage younger people to marry and boost births as its workforce shrinks.
Earlier this year, Kerala became the first Indian state to pass a landmark law for senior citizens centred on rights to affordable care, legal aid, digital inclusion and safe public spaces.
Industry experts say India still has time before it reaches a demographic crossroad. But caring for millions more elderly citizens will require robust support systems. A strong ecosystem of businesses serving senior citizens could play a role in bridging that gap.

title: Floods: Building boom in Nepal and India's Uttarakhand puts 300,000 people in path of potential Himalayan disasters, study suggests
description: The construction of tourism facilities, housing, and infrastructure has surged in parts of Nepal and India's Uttarakhand.
author: Navin Singh Khadka
content:
Building boom puts 300,000 people in the path of potential Himalayan disasters
- Published
At least 300,000 people in parts of the Himalayan region could now be living in the path of potential disasters, a new study suggests.
Researchers found that the amount of built-up land in high-risk zones in northern Nepal, parts of south-eastern Tibet and a corner of India's Uttarakhand had grown by about 45% between 2016 and 2023.
In areas particularly threatened by flooding from glacial lakes, development increased even faster, rising by almost 78% over the same period, according to the peer-reviewed study published in Scientific Reports.
The team of scientists behind it said the true number of people under threat could be much higher, as they only analysed a specific territory and not neighbouring areas which face similar risks.
The study was carried out before August's devastating mass floods which left more than 1,400 dead and thousands missing in Nepal. More recently there have been several smaller incidents, including flooding along the Budhi Gandaki river on 11 October that damaged 200 houses, swept away five bridges and left five people missing.
Nine researchers from the UK, Nepal and India looked at areas up to 50km (30 miles) downstream from Himalayan rivers, as well as around 1,360 glacial lakes.
They found significant development in these areas - including an expansion of tourism facilities, infrastructure development and real estate.
It's clear in Pokhara, a major tourism hub at the foot of the Himalayas that's grown significantly in the past 30 years to cater for a massive increase in visitors.
Mayor Dhana Raj Acharya says it's a huge challenge to deal with the risk posed by the Seti Gandaki River, which stems from the Annapurna mountain range and flows right through the city. Many old buildings are just 5m (16ft) from river banks, he says, despite new rules requiring them to be further away.
"Where we move them, and how we do that, is the real challenge."
To the north is the world-renowned Annapurna trekking region that has also seen a major increase in settlements along river banks - some hit by recent floods and landslides.
Phurpa Chhiring Lama, who runs a homestay there, feels helpless. Normally all of his 20 rooms are occupied at this time of year - the peak trekking season - but now only five are. "We have been doing this business for more than 40 years, but we've never seen this kind of disaster."
Krishna Gauchan, whose hotel is close to the glacier-fed Modi river, is worried too. "This river can flood if the glacier collapses or if the glacial lake bursts out and we are living in constant fear."
Tourism investors promote some of these spots as destinations without factoring in the risks, suggests Khagendra Poudel, a geographer at a local campus of Tribhuvan University. It's similar to what's happening in parts of north India's Himalayan valleys which host major pilgrimages.
The president of the Hotel Association Pokhara admits tourism businesses have expanded "without any proper planning" in the region and been promoted "haphazardly".
"By the time disasters hit, it is too late," says Laxman Subedi. "As a professional body we are trying to create awareness among tourism entrepreneurs and investors."
But it's not just tourism. The regions surrounding the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers have seen a significant rise in the construction of hydropower plants.
"As river valleys become increasingly populated, development decisions being made today will shape disaster risk for decades to come," warns the study's lead author, University of Leeds glaciologist C Scott Watson.
And even more buildings may be under threat than those identified by the researchers.
The study categorised buildings at risk as all those that were within 50 vertical metres (164ft) of a river or glacial lake's surface.
But during the catastrophic flooding on 26 August, locals in Rasuwa district say the river level had risen by 70m (230ft) at some points - so even buildings that were relatively far from the river banks were hit and buried by debris-sludge.
The risks in all of these areas are largely driven by warming in the Himalayan region, which scientists say is happening at twice the global rate. This has sped up the melting of glaciers, icefields, snowpacks, and ground that's normally frozen all year.
This can, in turn, destabilize mountain slopes which are also frequently shaken by earthquakes, unleashing devastating disasters downstream.
The rapid melting is also filling up and expanding glacial lakes until they burst, causing deadly floods. Nepal alone has documented around 30 of these events since 1940.
Another issue is that rising temperatures cause rain to reach high altitudes where it used to only snow, leading to slope failures, rock and ice falls, and other disasters.
Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah raised the dangers of climate change at his recent UN General Assembly speech, where he said his country was paying a "colossal price" for a crisis it did not create.
"Every major disaster threatens to erase years of development. And it forces a poor country to borrow money to repair damage it did not cause."
Alton Byers, a mountain geographer at the University of Colorado who was not involved in the study, says it should serve as a "springboard" to bring about more effective early-warning systems and other precautionary measures.
But achieving that will be a challenge. Campaigners say building regulations aren't implemented on the ground and through the years, development has been haphazard in too many places.
Roads, hydropower projects, hotels and market towns have expanded on the low, flat land along rivers, which is accessible and buildable, says Prof Surya Raj Acharya, an urban planning expert and registrar at the University of Nepal.
Those responsible have often ignored safeguards including keeping off the river bank, he adds.
"A fragile ecosystem like the Himalaya demands stricter planning and building regulations than elsewhere, yet these rules have been weak and poorly enforced."
Authorities in Nepal say they are working to address these issues. Settlements within 15m (49ft) of the riverbank along the recently devastated Rasuwa-Bhotekoshi corridor will soon be banned, according to the national disaster agency. Similar rules are being introduced in other river corridors soon.
"It is a challenging job because people in many places have sentimental attachments with their land and property but we cannot ignore the increasing risks," says chief executive Dharam Raj Uprety.
A similar story has unfolded across Nepal's western border in India's Uttarakhand state, where maximum tourism limits and environmental regulations have been bypassed in the name of economic growth, claims activist Anoop Nautiyal.
On paper there are zoning rules prohibiting the construction of houses and infrastructure too close to river banks, "but on the ground we see no implementation of such rules.
"You can see rampant construction all over."
The Uttarakhand government on 12 October approved new floodplain zoning rules to regulate land use and development. "Its objective is to protect life, property and important infrastructure from possible flood damage while maintaining the natural flow of flood waters," the state's cabinet decision read.
But Basanta Raj Adhikari, director of the Centre for Disaster Studies at Tribuvan University, thinks it will not be possible to mitigate such threats completely.
Insurance grades, he suggests, could be another way to encourage people to build in less risky areas. If authorities were to map places as high, moderate and low risk, he believes insurance coverage would "follow accordingly" ensuring people who build homes in safer areas get better protection.
But for now, the pace of construction across the region shows no signs of slowing.
  - Published12 October

title: Is a transwoman a ‘woman’ & can she invoke sexual offence laws? The high courts are divided
description: The divided interpretation of the same law leads to the question: Is constitutional recognition of gender identity sufficient to ensure access to criminal justice?
author: Ruchi Bhattar
content:
New Delhi: Every time a transgender woman seeks legal redress for sexual crimes under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), the question of whether she is a ‘woman’ comes before the possibility of remedy.
Precedents aren’t hard to find, but they are mixed: seven high courts have ruled on this interpretation, five including trans women under BNS protections, and two not doing so.
The Supreme Court is also expected to take up this question when it hears the challenge to the Transgender Amendment Act of 2026. The amendment, coming into force in May this year, did away with self-perceived gender identity, making medical board scrutiny or authority identity certificates mandatory for such identification.
This, petitioners say, violates Articles 14, 15, 19 and 21 of the Constitution, and is inconsistent with NALSA vs Union of India (2014), a Supreme Court judgement that legally recognised transgender persons as a ‘third gender’ and affirmed their right to self-identify their gender.
This divided interpretation of the same law leads to the key question: whether constitutional recognition of gender identity is sufficient to ensure access to criminal justice, or specific legislative changes are needed to ensure that transgender survivors are not left navigating an uneven framework of protections.
On paper, the law revolves around Section 63 (rape) and Section 69 (sexual intercourse by deceitful means, such as a false promise of marriage) of the BNS which apply specifically to a woman. ‘Woman’ is defined as a ‘female human being’ in the BNS—which includes transgender persons in its general definition of pronouns, but does not make sexual offence victims gender-neutral.
Replacing the Indian Penal Code (IPC) with the BNS eliminated Section 377, which previously covered non-consensual sexual acts against adults regardless of gender. The only remaining dedicated protection is Section 18(d) of the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2019, which covers physical, sexual, verbal, emotional and economic abuse, carrying imprisonment from six months up to two years plus a fine.
In contrast, rape under Section 64(1) of the BNS carries a minimum sentence of 10 years’ rigorous imprisonment, extendable to life.
Also Read: Can transwomen access women’s shelters, washrooms? Plea brings gender vs sex debate to SC
Inclusionary verdicts
This month, the Bombay High Court held that allegations of sexual assault and outraging the modesty of a woman can be sustained even when the victim is a transgender person who identifies herself as a woman.
It rejected the discharge application of Vishal Ingle, an Agniveer in the Army, who was accused of sexually assaulting a transgender woman on the promise of marriage. The court held that even if the victim did not possess a certificate of transgender identity at the time of the alleged incident, it would not prevent invoking the penal provisions of the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2019.
The court also relied on the Supreme Court’s 2014 judgment in National Legal Services Authority vs Union of India, which held that “it is entirely for the transgender to self-identify her gender and that this self-determination cannot be questioned by others”. It further noted that Section 4(2) of the Act, which expressly recognised a transgender person’s right to self-perceived gender identity, was in force when the alleged incident took place last year.
In 2019, the Uttarakhand High Court in 2019 ruled in favor of the transwoman, holding that gender identity must be determined by a psychological test and self-identification—as established in NALSA vs Union of India (2014)—rather than biological sex or DNA.
A transgender woman who had undergone sex-reassignment surgery and obtained official recognition to be addressed as “she” filed a complaint, alleging she was repeatedly raped and blackmailed. The investigating officer subjected her to a DNA test, concluded she was biologically male, and registered the FIR under Section 377 IPC (unnatural offences) instead of Section 376 IPC (rape of a woman). The court had directed authorities to treat the petitioner as female for all legal purposes and affirmed that a transgender woman identifying as female is included within the definition of ‘woman’ in sexual assault prosecutions.
In 2018, a transgender woman who faced sexual harassment challenged the constitutionality of Section 354A of the IPC (sexual harassment of a woman, now Section 75 BNS) before the Delhi High Court. She argued that the provision violated Articles 14, 15, and 21 of the Constitution insofar as police authorities interpreted the word ‘woman’ strictly to exclude transgender victims from registering complaints.
The Delhi Police assured the court that, in line with the NALSA judgment, complaints by transgender persons identifying as women would be registered under Section 354A. Recording this undertaking, the high court affirmed that transgender women are entitled to invoke women-centric sexual harassment provisions without needing a statutory amendment.
In a 2019 verdict, the Madras High Court passed a ruling after a cisgender man and a transgender woman (who identified as female and was intersex/transgender) solemnised their marriage at a temple in Tuticorin, local registration authorities refused to register the marriage. Officials contended that a transgender woman did not qualify as a ‘bride’ under Section 5 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955.
The high court overturned the refusal, ruling that the term ‘bride’ is not static, and must be interpreted in light of constitutional guarantees of equality and dignity. The court held that a transgender person who identifies as a woman has the sole right to self-determine her gender—regardless of medical procedures—and must be legally recognised as a woman across statutory frameworks.
This Madras High Court ruling forms the foundational precedent cited by the Andhra Pradesh and Bombay High Courts in extending criminal protections to trans women.
In 2025, the Andhra Pradesh High Court ruled on the same issue. A transgender woman married a man according to Hindu rites and customs in January 2019. After her husband abandoned her and ceased communication, she lodged a complaint alleging mental cruelty and dowry harassment under Section 498A IPC (now Section 85 BNS) and the Dowry Prohibition Act. The husband and his family petitioned the high court to quash the case, arguing that a transgender woman is not a ‘woman’ and cannot bear children.
The high court rejected the biological argument as “completely incorrect and legally unsustainable”, holding that denying a trans woman legal protection based on reproductive capacity violates Articles 14, 15, and 21. The court affirmed that a transgender woman is legally recognised as a woman and is fully entitled to invoke criminal provisions meant to protect women from marital abuse.
Exclusionary approach
In a 2024 case from the Himachal Pradesh High Court, a transgender woman whose Aadhaar card listed her gender as female alleged that the accused man entered into a sexual relationship with her on a promise of marriage.
According to her complaint, the accused and his father pressured her to undergo sex-reassignment surgery before the wedding, only for him to break off the engagement and arrange a marriage with another woman after her surgery was completed. The police booked the man under Section 69 of the BNS (sexual intercourse by deceitful means) and Section 18(d) of the Transgender Persons Act 2019.
In granting bail to the accused, the court held that Section 69 of the BNS applies strictly when the victim is a ‘woman’, defined under Section 2(35) BNS as a “female human being”. Because Section 2(10) BNS separately recognises “male, female, or transgender” by importing the definition from the 2019 Act, the court concluded that Parliament had placed transgender persons in a distinct legal category. Consequently, Section 69 BNS could not be invoked, leaving the complainant restricted to remedies under Section 18(d) of the 2019 Act only.
In October this year, the Allahabad High Court ruled also on the issue. In this case, a Bareilly-based transgender woman underwent sex-reassignment surgery in April 2023 and subsequently entered into a relationship with the accused, who allegedly had sexual relations with her on a false promise of marriage before backing out.
Following an FIR under Section 69 BNS, a medical panel report noted that while her genitalia had been surgically altered, she lacked a uterus. The accused sought bail, arguing she did not meet the statutory definition of ‘woman’.
In an October bail order, the high court ruled that ‘woman’ in Section 69 BNS refers exclusively to a biological female human being. Pointing out that Parliament chose not to adopt the Parliamentary Standing Committee’s recommendation to include transgender women in BNS sexual offence provisions, the court held that even after sex-reassignment surgery, a transgender woman remains legally classified as a “transgender person” rather than a “female human being”.
The Allahabad High Court distinguished past rulings from other high courts relied upon by Amicus Curiae Mayuri Mehrotra. Key judgements, such as the Uttarakhand High Court’s ruling of 2019 and the Andhra Pradesh High Court’s ruling of 2025ؙwhich had extended protection to transwomen under earlier penal laws—were held inapplicable.
Also Read: Delhi to make education job ads gender-neutral after SC intervention on transgender applicants
‘The system is not meant for us’
For transgender women, the question of access to criminal law protections is not merely about how courts interpret the word ‘woman’. It also concerns whether they can approach the police, have their complaints registered and be taken seriously when reporting violence or discrimination.
Jane Kaushik, a transgender rights activist who had approached the Supreme Court in Jane Kaushik vs Union of India over discrimination in employment on the basis of gender identity, described the exclusionary interpretation adopted by the Himachal Pradesh and Allahabad High Courts as “deeply discriminatory” and “transphobic”.
Arguing that transgender women are women, even while their identities and experiences may differ, she drew a comparison with differences among cisgender women: that distinctions in physical characteristics or reproductive ability should not determine whether someone is recognised as a woman.
“I am a different kind of woman. I am a transgender woman, I am proud of my identity, but still I am a woman,” Kaushik said recalling her attempt to seek legal recourse for employment discrimination. This, she said, also exposed the absence of an effective grievance-redressal mechanism.
Kaushik said she was unable to get an FIR registered. Instead, her complaint was recorded at a women’s help desk, which she said is a bird’s-eye view of what women must have to go through before they reach court.
“I went there with all of the proof and evidence. And they just registered my complaint at a normal women’s help desk. That was just a normal complaint, that was not an FIR,” she said.
She said the experience left her without an effective avenue to seek justice, particularly in smaller towns where institutions could be influential and the police lacked sensitisation to transgender concerns.
The barriers, she said, are even more pronounced when transgender women report sexual violence. Many do not approach police stations because they fear that their complaints will not be acted upon, and that the system is not built for them.
Kaushik added that police officers may themselves lack the understanding needed to handle complaints involving transgender survivors. Kaushik said misconceptions about sexual violence, including the assumption that rape can only occur against someone with a vagina, further complicate the reporting and investigation of offences against transgender women.
For her, the differing high court interpretations are also part of a wider pattern in which transgender persons struggle to secure recognition, employment, education and basic rights.
‘A forced thirding’
Mihir Rajamane, a doctoral researcher at the University of Oxford, has examined the divergent rulings and highlighted that the exclusionary judgments represent a minority position and that both cases he had examined involved Section 69 of the BNS, a provision that has itself been contested in criminal law.
“There is a ruling out there which says that trans women may not be women, when it comes to certain laws. And that can affect how, especially in the jurisdiction whose high courts have issued rulings, police officers register cases,” he said.
Rajamane pointed to the history of the transgender struggle on getting the police to register complaints, recalling mobilisation in Bengaluru in 2002 to ensure that the police registered a case. He said that the distinction between transgender women and persons who identify as a third gender is crucial to understanding the legal dispute. According to him, some courts have conflated transgender identity with third-gender identity, thereby denying transgender women the ability to identify and be recognised as women.
On the definition of ‘woman’ as a ‘female human being’ under the BNS, Rajamane said the phrase did not necessarily exclude transgender women. “The fact that it uses the phrase adult human female doesn’t mean that it necessarily excludes transgender women,” he said, adding that the exclusionary interpretation may stem from a reading of ‘female’ as a biological category.
He also pointed to what he termed a “forced thirding” of transgender persons, where courts assume that a transgender person necessarily belongs to a third-gender category rather than recognising their self-identification as a woman or a man. “There are many misconceptions about, you know, that transgender people have certain, like, intersex persons, for example. So those kinds of misconceptions, I think, are what’s behind these kinds of rulings,” he said.
On whether the BNS deliberately excluded transgender women from sexual offence protections, Rajamane argued that the statute should be read alongside the Supreme Court’s NALSA judgment. “I don’t think the BNS textually excludes transgender women,” he said, arguing that the NALSA judgment recognises both the right to self-determine one’s gender and the existence of gender identities outside the binary. “Whenever BNS uses [the word] ‘woman’, it naturally includes transgender women”, he said.
Judicial training, legal aid and reform
Rajamane said the way forward lies not only in challenging exclusionary rulings but is also in institutional reform: challenging the transgender amendment through legal and political avenues, implementing judicial training on LGBTQI+ rights, and ensuring that District Legal Services Authorities are equipped to assist transgender persons.
He said a module on LGBTQI+ persons prepared by the Supreme Court around 2020-2021, to his knowledge, had not been implemented through national or state judicial academies. “Actually implement those into judicial training,” he said, stressing the need for judges to be sensitised to transgender rights and the legal principles of self-identification.
He also said District Legal Services Authorities should be familiar with the rights of transgender persons under criminal law and other legislation so they can assist in filing complaints, securing legal representation and accessing remedies.
Kaushik considers the 2026 transgender law amendment to be part of a broader attempt to erase transgender identities and weaken the community’s ability to demand rights and welfare from the government. She argued that the absence of political representation further makes the community vulnerable to exclusion.
As the Supreme Court considers challenges relating to transgender rights, Kaushik said the issue is not simply whether a particular provision of the BNS applies, but whether transgender survivors can access a justice system that they often believe is inaccessible to them in the first place.
On whether cases arising from the divergent high court rulings would be heard alongside the challenge to the Transgender Amendment Act, Rajamane said he expected the issues to be considered separately, although there could be overlap. Since the NALSA judgment itself is being questioned in the amendment challenge, overlap is likely, he said.
(Edited by Nardeep Singh Dahiya)
