title: Elderly prisoners’ inclusion to fixed review window, new Delhi jail rules modify emergency parole system
description: The amendments make three principal interventions in the existing parole framework.
author: Alfreza Ahmed
content:
New Delhi: Prisoners over 70, as well as those who are infirm or terminally ill, have been brought within the ambit of Delhi’s emergency parole regime as the government moves to widen the circumstances in which temporary release from prison can be considered.The change is part of the Delhi Prisons (Amendment) Rules 2026, notified on 25 November.
The amendments make three principal interventions in the existing parole framework: they widen the scope of emergency parole under Rule 1212A, recast the process for obtaining police and probation reports under Rule 1213, and substitute Rule 1219 governing cases where a convict is unable to furnish surety (a financial guarantee furnished to secure compliance with the conditions of release).
The most substantive change is to Rule 1212A. The provision now expressly permits emergency parole to be considered in situations involving an epidemic or natural disaster, or old age (only for prisoners above 70), infirmity or terminal illness, as well as other circumstances warranting an immediate easing of the prison population.
This does not mean that emergency parole, or even the eight-week period contemplated by the rule, has been introduced for the first time.
Rule 1212A already allows the government to grant up to eight weeks of emergency parole in one spell, in addition to regular parole, in the event of an epidemic, natural disaster or other circumstances requiring an immediate easing of the prison population. The rule also left it to the government to decide whether the period spent outside prison would count towards the prisoner’s sentence. Those features have been retained.
The amended rule also states that the number of emergency-parole spells may be increased where the situation warrants. The release, however, is not automatic. Rule 1212A uses discretionary language, providing that the government “may” grant parole, subject to prescribed conditions.
Also Read: Delhi HC says furlough not an absolute right. A look at the rules of conditional release from jail
Parole verification gets a two-week window
The amendment also changes the mechanics of an ordinary parole application.
The substituted Rule 1213(iv) requires the prison superintendent to forward the application to the police station where the First Information Report was registered, as well as the police station concerned with the prisoner’s last known address and the place where the prisoner proposes to stay during parole. The investigating agency must also be approached, while a copy is to be sent to the district deputy commissioner or senior superintendent of police.
The amendment seeks to tighten the verification process by fixing timelines for reports from agencies involved in considering a parole application. Unlike the earlier rule, which did not prescribe a fixed period for the police to furnish its report, the substituted Rule 1213(iv) requires the report to be submitted within two weeks of receipt of the request. The prison superintendent will also have to seek the probation officer’s report within two weeks of the parole application.
While parole decisions depend on inputs beyond a prisoner’s eligibility, including police and probation reports, the amended rule now requires these reports to be furnished within a defined two-week period.
The amendment also does away with certain procedural requirements relating to police reports under sub-rules (vi), (vii) and (viii) of Rule 1213 while bringing the verification process within a common two-week timeline.
What happens when a convict cannot furnish surety?
The government has also substituted Rule 1219, which deals with a different problem: a prisoner has secured parole but is unable to satisfy the surety condition attached to the release.
Under the new provision, where a convict cannot furnish the required surety, if any, within four weeks of being served with the parole order, the prison superintendent may, upon an application by the convict, recommend relaxation of the parole condition to the competent authority.
There is, however, an important qualification: the amended provision applies where the convict is being released on parole for the first time. A recommendation by the superintendent also does not by itself waive the condition. The power to relax it remains with the competent authority.
Taken together, the changes broaden the scope of emergency parole while tightening timelines for verification and addressing cases where the inability to furnish surety delays a convict’s release.
(Edited by Nardeep Singh Dahiya)

title: 87.5% girls, women, LGBTQ+ people feel unsafe in Delhi local parks, says new report
description: The annual gathering at Vasant Udyan in Vasant Vihar, ‘Hain Haq Hamara Hissedari’, was attended by hundreds. They refused to let darkness drive them out of the neighbourhood park.
author: Manisha Mondal
content:
New Delhi: More than 87 per cent of women, girls, and LGBTQ+ persons in Delhi feel unsafe in their neighbourhood parks after dark, while more than 14 per cent do not visit these parks at all, a new report has found.
Titled ‘Everyday Journeys: Women’s and Girls’ Access to Footpaths and Public Parks in Delhi’, the study was launched on the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women and Girls. The Centre for Equity and Inclusion (CEQUIN), which published the report, works to prevent gender-based violence across Delhi-NCR, Haryana, Rajasthan, and Bihar.
According to the report, 87.5 per cent of women, girls, and queer persons feel unsafe while walking to the nearest bus stop or metro station after dark.
“A woman should not have to explain why she is outside, whether she is there for work, leisure, pleasure or nothing at all. She has a right to be there. The more women occupy these spaces, the safer and more accessible they become,” said Laura Prabhu, co-founder of CEQUIN. “By keeping women away, we are not solving the problem. We are curtailing their rights, limiting their participation in public life and, ultimately, holding back half the population that contributes to the economy.”
Reclaim the park
On Wednesday evening, the annual gathering, Hain Haq Hamara Hissedari, was attended by hundreds at Vasant Udyan in Delhi’s Vasant Vihar, refusing to let darkness drive them out of a neighbourhood park.
The gathering came in the wake of the alleged rape of a 17-year-old girl at Ashta Kunj Park in September. The incident brought the safety of women in Delhi’s public parks under scrutiny. These green spaces, often the only breathing room in the choking capital, have since seen access restrictions, with several parks that have multiple gates shutting some of their entrances in the evening.
CEQUIN, along with 60 other civil society organisations, came together to reclaim the park and discuss women’s safety through poetry, dance performances, and conversation. The study by CEQUIN is also a part of this effort.
The organisation conducted the survey online in Hindi and English, circulating it through WhatsApp, CEQUIN’s community networks, schools, colleges, and partner organisations.
Of the 1,588 respondents, 38.1 per cent were girls aged 8-17, 46.9 per cent were women aged 18-35, and 13 per cent, aged 36-59. Nearly 70 per cent of them lived in JJ clusters, resettlement colonies, unauthorised or regularised colonies, and urban villages, while 16.6 per cent lived in planned colonies, DDA flats, or housing societies.
Also read: What is Punjabiyat? Not a settled inheritance but ‘a living element’
Dark and broken footpaths
More than 79 per cent of the respondents said that men’s behaviour makes it unsafe to walk in the park. About 80 per cent of them could not name a single authority responsible for footpaths and parks.
Nearly 90 per cent of the transgender women, trans men, and non-binary and genderqueer people surveyed said that they do not feel safe in parks after dark.
The respondents complained about the poor condition of roads and footpaths. Most of them take detours or negotiate to avoid harassment during journeys in poorly lit stretches.
The organisation has submitted its recommendations to the Supreme Court of India following the violence across the capital.
Prabhu stressed that most people do not complain about these issues. When they do, they do not necessarily get the response they’re looking for.
“We need to think about how to circumvent these barriers. Is there a way for women to file complaints anonymously, particularly about public infrastructure? How do we ensure that authorities are held accountable and that citizens know whether action has been taken on their complaints?” she asked.
The survey also pointed out “mobility” as a primary issue.
It revealed that even if almost half of the respondents stay within a 20-minute walking distance of a bus stop, metro station, or public walk, 87.5 per cent feel unsafe to walk after dark. Around 54 per cent of respondents also said that they do not feel safe in a park during daylight.
Prabhu pointed out that Delhi needs a solution and not a “protectionist approach” that restricts women from moving freely in parks.
“We need some kind of convergence model, perhaps anchored at the district administration level, where these multiple authorities can come together. We can also look at models such as multi-stakeholder committees where citizens are formally engaged,” she added.
She also stressed the need for active feedback, perhaps from RWAs and local NGOs.
“Citizens should have a platform through which they can raise concerns and engage with the authorities,” Prabhu said.
(Edited by Prasanna Bachchhav)

title: Bengal Police Are Demanding Documents From Voters Awaiting SIR Tribunal Orders. The CEO Office Doesn't Know Why - The Wire
description: The Wire has seen an order from West Bengal Police Headquarters that set the exercise in motion. But no order allowing the police to verify the documents of voters waiting at the tribunals has been made public.
author: Aparna Bhattacharya
content: Kolkata: Police in several districts of West Bengal have begun going from house to house asking voters whose cases are pending before the appellate tribunals constituted as part of the special intensive revision (SIR) for their documents, several say. Whenever asked, police have not been able to show residents copies of any official orders. Today, the visits reached the Supreme Court, where petitioners told the bench that the state was acting on its own, without the Election Commission’s knowledge. The bench suggested they raise the matter before the Calcutta high court.The Wire has seen an order from West Bengal Police Headquarters that set the exercise in motion.The officers who are tasked with compiling the electoral rolls on the ground say they have been left out of the process entirely. Several booth-level officers (BLOs), assistant electoral registration officers (AEROs) and electoral registration officers (EROs) say they have not been told about the exercise, and block development officers (BDOs) whom The Wire spoke to, say they are unaware of it. The office of the Chief Electoral Officer (CEO), West Bengal, has said it issued no such directive. “There is no directive from the office of the CEO,” Arindam Niyogi, Additional Chief Electoral Officer, West Bengal, told The Wire. The Wire has learnt of police visits in districts of Malda, Jalpaiguri, Dakshin Dinajpur, Purba Bardhaman, Bankura, South 24 Parganas, Hooghly, Howrah, Paschim Medinipur, North 24 Parganas and Murshidabad. In most places, they began on November 24 and 25.The police order The order, No. 1754/DGP(L&O)/26, is dated November 23, 2026, and signed by the director general and inspector general of police (Law and Order). It is addressed to every police commissioner in the state except Kolkata’s, and to the superintendents of police of every district and police district.Its subject reads: “SIR Adjudication and Tribunal Appeals Report – Appeals Against Exclusion and Inclusion Across All 294 Assembly Constituencies of West Bengal”.“All CsP and SsP are hereby requested to visit the website https://appeal.civicresearch.in/ and examine the data pertaining to their respective jurisdictions in connection with SIR adjudication and tribunal appeals against exclusion and inclusion across all 294 Assembly Constituencies of West Bengal,” it says.“The data available on the website shall be downloaded, carefully analysed as per instructions given today in Video Conference (VC) and a comprehensive report in respect of the respective jurisdiction shall be submitted to this office positively by 30/11/2026.”It ends, “The matter may be treated as MOST URGENT.”What the police are asking forA checklist released by a Bengal police station.A checklist issued by the Kotwali police station in Paschim Medinipur, seen by The Wire, asks for each voter’s name, voter ID (EPIC) number, assembly constituency and booth number, and a contact number. It then asks whether the voter has each of six documents, and tells the officer to collect a self-attested copy of any the voter has.A note at the foot of the checklist tells officers in charge of police stations to deploy their staff for the work. “A Soft copy of all the collected reports must be sent to the DIB office by 6 PM everyday over email,” it says, referring to the District Intelligence Branch. “All the verifications must be completed by 28th November, 2026.”The checklist carries no letterhead and no reference to the Election Commission, the tribunals, or any court order.‘Can be considered an Indian citizen’A second document, seen by The Wire, goes further. Headed “Simplified Check List for Deleted Voters”, it is written in Bengali, and its first line sets out its purpose. “A deleted voter can be considered an Indian citizen if they can give any one of the proofs below,” it says. It lists six kinds of proof. A ‘simplified’ checklist released by a police station in Bengal. The first is a land deed executed before 1987 in the name of the voter’s biological father, mother, grandfather, grandmother or great-grandfather. The second is a pension payment order or an Indian passport in the name of one of those ancestors. The third is a Class X or equivalent certificate from before 1987, whether the person appeared in the examination or passed it, in the voter’s own name or an ancestor’s. The fourth is a caste certificate, birth certificate or other document issued by a government authority before 1987, again in the voter’s or an ancestor’s name. The last two concern the electoral rolls, either an ancestor’s name on the roll after the 2026 SIR, or on the rolls of 1971.Two of its dates are considered cut-offs under the citizenship law. Under the Citizenship Act of 1955, a person born in India before 1 July 1987 is a citizen by birth, whatever the nationality of their parents. In Assam, 24 March 1971 was the cut-off for the National Register of Citizens. The SIR itself relied on West Bengal’s roll of 2002.The list matches what voters in Murshidabad district’s Suti assembly constituency told The Wire police had asked them for at the outpost, including old land deeds and documents from before 1987, such as a pension payment order or a passport.The electoral roll records who may vote. Under the electoral law, it is the electoral registration officer who decides whether a person is eligible to be on it, and, for those struck off during the SIR, the appellate tribunals. The law gives the police no such role, and no power to declare anyone a citizen or not. Election officials left out, then includedA BLO in Paschim Medinipur told The Wire that people in his area had begun calling him on the morning of November 26. Police had come with a format, he said, asking voters whose names were before the tribunals or under adjudication to write down their constituency, part and serial number, and the documents they had submitted. “Neither the ARO nor the AERO has told us anything about this. The police have not informed the BLOs either,” he said. “People in the area are frightened.”But by November 27, the exercise had reached the block offices, and the officers who run the electoral roll on the ground. That morning, messages forwarded to booth-level officers (BLOs) in at least two assembly constituencies in South 24 Parganas told them to bring voters “under adjudication” to the block office at 11 am, along with photocopies of six documents including their tribunal application, school certificate, birth certificate, Aadhaar card, voter ID card, and land documents. The BLOs themselves were told to bring the final voters’ list and the 2002 roll. “All BLOs are requested to inform those in adjudication to come to the BDO office today with those documents,” a follow-up message said.A voter, asking to remain anonymous, has shared the recording of a BLO’s phone call with him with The Wire. In it, the BLO asks the voter to gather documents from everyone in the area whose name is under adjudication. “The BDO has asked us to bring in the documents at 11. They sent the message yesterday at 12:20 [am],” the BLO is heard saying in the call. He asks the resident to collect photocopies of whatever documents each person has – a birth certificate or an Aadhaar card – pin them together, write each person’s name at the top, have them sign it, and drop them off to him before he goes to school. Most BLOs are government school teachers.The voter is heard asking the BLO whether the documents are the same ones which police were asking for. “Who knows, they didn’t say anything like that,” the BLO is heard saying.The Wire has reached out to this BLO as well. They said that the BDO had called him at midnight to tell him about furnishing these documents. A day ago, BDOs had said they knew nothing of the police visits. A first-time voter from Satgachia in South 24 Parganas, said he had heard about this drive from the BLO. “No notice has come from the police station. The BLO messaged me,” he told The Wire. Summoned in groups, in SutiIn Suti, in Murshidabad, voters have been called to a police outpost in groups of five or six, on consecutive days, according to the BLO for booth 241 in the Suti Assembly constituency, who requested anonymity as they spoke to The Wire. Of the 246 voters in his booth whose names were struck off during the SIR, 241 have appealed to the tribunals, he said.On November 25, people from the police station came to the area with civic volunteers, read out the names of voters with appeals pending, and told them to report to the police outpost, he said, citing voters who had gone there. At the outpost, the voters told him, police asked to see old land deeds, whether their names were on the 2002 roll, and whether they had any document from before 1987, such as a land deed, a pension payment order, a passport or an OBC certificate. They were also asked for current birth certificates, and whether their names were on the 2026 roll.“The BDO office hasn’t informed us of anything, nor do we, as BLOs, have anything from the Election Commission,” said the BLO, a schoolteacher. When the voters called him to ask why the police were summoning them, he told them he did not know. “Election work is supposed to be done by the Election Commission, and your verification is supposed to happen at the tribunal, not at the police station,” he said he told them. Suti comes under the jurisdiction of the Jangipur police district.Also read: Election Commission Says Around 6,000 Voters in Bengal Are Still ‘Under Adjudication’. In Just 22 Seats, the Real Number is Almost 30,000Elsewhere in North 24 Parganas, documents are being gathered by civic volunteers attached to police stations, not by police officers, according to Communist Party of India (Marxist) leader Kallol Majumdar. In parts of Sonarpur, in South 24 Parganas, on the night of November 25, police in plain clothes went to the homes of people whose names were not on the rolls after the SIR and told them to come to the police station “at 11 pm the following night,” according to a resident The Wire spoke to. In the same area, the resident said, a team which said it came on behalf of the government told some people who had received money under the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana housing scheme to return it. A BLO of Bankura district told The Wire that on November 25, the police ‘form’ was sent to Muslim voters whose cases were pending before the tribunals in villages across the district. The Wire has not been able to verify whether the forms indeed went to voters of one community, or to everyone with a case before the tribunals.In Howrah, police from Golabari police station set up a camp in a school, called voters whose names had been deleted to the camp, and began collecting their documents, said Umar Awais of the Association for Protection of Civil Rights (APCR), West Bengal. APCR has written to the Director General of Police and the Chief Secretary asking under what authority the police are acting.People arrive with their documents at a Howrah school. Photo: By arrangement.What the police order saysThe written order issued by the West Bengal Police Headquarters asks police chiefs to analyse data and send a report. It says nothing about visiting voters, calling them to police stations, collecting their documents, or deciding whether anyone is a citizen. Whatever officers were told to do with the data was set out “in Video Conference”, not on paper. That may explain why officers at voters’ doors could not show an order that covered what they were doingThe order comes from the state police’s Law and Order wing, not from the Election Commission or the office of the Chief Electoral Officer.The data the police were told to useThe website named in the order, appeal.civicresearch.in, is published by the Civic Research Group, which compiles public data on the SIR’s adjudication and appeals in West Bengal, constituency by constituency. The Group, comprising of independent researchers have been seeking legal opinion but refused to make a statement.The Wire has worked with the Civic Research Group in its reporting on the SIR, including its analysis of appeals against the inclusion of voters cleared by judicial officers. The group published the data to open the revision’s outcomes to public scrutiny. In the Supreme CourtToday, in the Supreme Court’s hearing on Bengal’s SIR, Senior Advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan and advocate Prashant Bhushan told the court of these visits, LiveLaw reported.““Apparently the police has been discharged with the duty to people whose appeals are pending… individuals being asked to furnish documents… they have been told it has to be done by 29th,” Sankaranarayanan said.The deadlines given have varied from place to place. Sankaranarayanan said voters had been told to finish by November 29. The Kotwali checklist set November 28 as the deadline for completing the verification, and the Headquarters’ order asked for reports by November 30.Bhushan said that if appeals are still pending when municipal corporation elections are held, those whose appeals are pending should be allowed to vote. The bench, headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, suggested that the issue be raised before the Calcutta high court. An MLA’s noticeA notice issued in the name of Sumitro Chatterjee, the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) MLA for Naihati, asks everyone whose name is pending before a tribunal to contact their police station. Those who have received a call from an officer at their police station, it says, “must” go there on November 26 or 27, and bring their birth certificate, other original documents and photocopies of every document. BJP MLA Sumitro Chatterjee’s notification on his Facebook page.Amit Paik, a representative of Chattopadhyay, claimed the Election Commission has sent the order. “The ECI has sent it to the BDO and SDO levels, to the administration. The administration, from the SDO and BDO levels, is sending it to every police station. So the police administration is verifying these people’s documents.”This version differs from what the Bengal CEO told The Wire and is also at odds with what BLOs and block development officers have said – that they were never told of the exercise.The lists, he said, were of voters whose names are before the tribunals, and had also gone to municipal officials. “The police administration is contacting everyone based on the names the Election Commission has sent them,” he said. The Commission had said earlier that voters with cases before the tribunals would not have to fill in Form 6 again, he added. “They will be verified, and after that, a decision will be made on whether their names will be added or deleted.”Paik did not have the written order. Instead, he said there had been a meeting with the administration at which the MLA was present. What the law saysUnder the law that governs the electoral roll, deciding whether a person is entitled to be on it is an electoral function, not a policing one. Sections 13B and 13C of the Representation of the People Act, 1950, give the job of preparing and revising the roll to electoral registration officers and their assistants, and Sections 22 and 23 give them the power to delete and add names.The CEO’s office set out who does what in the SIR in a press note of October 28, 2025, issued under the Commission’s instructions of the day before. House-to-house enumeration, and the identification of absent, shifted, dead and duplicate voters, fall to BLOs. Issuing notices, examining documents, holding hearings and deciding whether a name stays or goes fall to EROs and AEROs. The police are given security at hearing centres and the maintenance of law and order, and no role in checking voters’ documents.The Supreme Court, in its order of January 19, 2026, directed the Director General of Police and district superintendents to ensure “that there are no law and order problems at the location and that the entire activity proceeds smoothly”. The Commission passed that direction on to the state’s chief secretary, the director general of police and the Kolkata police commissioner on January 21. In its order of February 9, the court again tied the police to law and order, and gave the consideration of documents and objections to EROs. When it handed the remaining adjudication to judicial officers on February 20, it asked district superintendents of police to provide assistance and logistical support.None of these orders gives the police any independent authority to examine voters’ documents or decide who stays on the roll. The law does allow EROs to engage additional staff for revising the roll, under Section 13B(2), and the police can investigate suspected crimes. But no order allowing the police to verify the documents of voters waiting at the tribunals has been made public.Why it mattersJawhar Sircar, a former Chief Electoral Officer of West Bengal and former Rajya Sabha member, said the police had always been kept at arm’s length from the revision of electoral rolls. “As soon as the Supreme Court directed Bengal’s appellate tribunals to first verify the names ‘wrongly struck off’ the voter list and include them, the government sent the police into the field. I have never seen this before. What will the police explain to voters going from house to house now? Have the police become BLOs? Instead of dealing with theft, robbery, extortion and hooliganism, will the police now do this work on behalf of the ruling party?” he said.“The police have no jurisdiction here. Who will be a voter and who will not be a voter is not for the police to decide,” Mohammed Salim, state secretary of the CPI(M), told The Wire. “The police SPs must explain on whose orders civic volunteers or police from the stations are going door to door.”More than 38 lakh appeals are pending before the tribunals, all of which are in Kolkata. They include about 22 lakh by voters struck off during the SIR, and about 16 lakh filed by officers of the CEO’s office against voters judicial officers had cleared. The voters now being visited by police are, for the most part, people who have already submitted documents, been heard, and are waiting for a judge’s decision on whether they stay on the roll.The documents the police are asking for go beyond those the Election Commission listed for the SIR. And the reports go not to an election officer but to the District Intelligence Branch.The Wire has sent questions by email and WhatsApp to the Director General of Police, West Bengal, Siddhinath Gupta, asking who ordered the exercise, under what law, why the reports are being sent to the District Intelligence Branch, whether civic volunteers have been authorised to collect documents, why voters have been summoned to police stations late at night, whether police are using a checklist that describes who “can be considered an Indian citizen”, and on what authority, how the voters to be visited were chosen, and what will be done with the information collected. This report will be updated if he responds.

title: Why the Thiruparankundram Lamp-Lighting Issue Needs to Be Addressed Sooner Than Later - The Wire
description: A British-era survey pillar has become a communal boilng point in Tamil Nadu. The judiciary must defuse it immediately.
author: MG Devasahayam
content: “Thiruparankundram will be the next Ayodhya,” declared H. Raja, a senior Tamil Nadu Hindu Munnani/BJP leader and a Hindutva fanatic, in February last year. True to this declaration, communal elements in Tamil Nadu, which includes some legal brains, are whipping up a frenzy over the non-lighting of the ‘deepam’ (lamp) on the ‘deepathoon’ (lamp pillar) at the Thiruparankundram Hillock during the Karthigai Deepam festival on November, 24, 2026. This hillock is believed to be the first abode of Lord Murugan.There is a cacophony of noises seeking the dismissal of the Joseph Vijay-led Tamil Nadu government for breakdown of constitutional governance, the arrest of Madurai’s District Collector, for contempt of court and allegations of grave hurt to Hindu ‘sentiments.’ The very next day Tamil Nadu governor Rajendra Arlekar invoked powers under Article 167(b) of the Constitution of India and sought a detailed factual report from the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) government, explaining why it failed to implement the Supreme Court’s order. The cacophony is so loud and bizarre that some Hindu Munnani, an Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh front, elements are demanding an affidavit from the chief secretary on the role played by Chief Minister Vijay in the matter as he is a Christian. There is also the absurd demand that the Supreme Court should invoke its extraordinary powers under Article 142 of the Constitution for lighting the lamp at the deepathoon in the next seven days! Supreme Court’s orderOn November 20, 2026, the Supreme Court, while staying the ‘perfunctory order’ of the Madras high court, based on ‘false’ findings, permitted the petitioners to light the Karthigai Deepam at the disputed deepathoon on November 24 as a one-time arrangement for the 2026 festival. There were several conditions to the permission, including a direction that “only a team authorised by the temple administration could light the lamp.” This “permission for one-time arrangement” was not carried out due to administrative and religious reasons.The young district collector of Madurai, Nishant Krishna, who was assigned by the top court as the nodal officer in charge of carrying out its order, apologised to the court and stated that the district administration could not implement the directive due to opposition from the Arulmigu Subramaniya Swamy Temple Trust. He stated that the temple administration did not allow lighting the Karthigai Deepam at the deepathoon, citing a violation of established practices and rituals.Also read: Why Supreme Court’s Thirupparankundram Order is ContradictoryTamil Nadu government also told the Supreme Court that it could not implement the order because the temple administration did not authorise the team to light the ceremonial lamp, as per the requirement in the court order. The lamp was instead lit at its traditional location near the Uchipillaiyar temple.Explaining this, the temple trust made a statement saying that the board members decided against lighting the lamp at deepathoon to protect age-old traditions, customary practices, Agama regulations and established worship practices. It said: “The festivals, poojas, religious rituals, and the Karthigai Deepam festival conducted at the temple have been observed for generations based on religious traditions, customary practices and Agama rules. In particular, as per the age-old practice followed at the temple, the Karthigai Maha Deepam is traditionally lit at the Deepa Mandapam located near the Uchipillayar temple atop the hill, directly above the sanctum sanctorum of the presiding deity.” The commissioner of Tamil Nadu’s Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department had moved the Supreme Court seeking a review of its inexplicable order while staying the Madras high court’s findings on the nature of the pillar and the land on which it stands. The apex court did not dispose of the review petition, thereby allowing such a sensitive matter to hang!In this matter the Supreme Court has not issued a Writ of Mandamus under Article 32 of the Constitution that would be binding on the government and temple authorities. The order was more of an advisory nature giving “permission as one-time arrangement” to be facilitated by the district collector. According to the conditions, only a team authorised by the temple’s administration could light the lamp. The trust decided to light it in accordance with “religious traditions, customary practices and Agama rules,” and not the whim of a few Hindu Munnani petitioners and a perfunctory court order. A review petition against this order is still pending. Why then all this frenzy and cat-calls?A pillar near a dargahTherein lies a sordid tale. The pillar at the centre of the controversy is said to be a deepathoon, a ceremonial structure meant for lighting lamps. The stone pillar is located atop the Thiruparankundram hillock, which houses both the Arulmigu Subramania Swamy and the Sikkandar Badhusha dargah. The deepathoon there is located approximately 50 metres from the dargah, while the Subramaniya Swamy temple is at the base of the hillock.The present dispute centres on the lighting of a lamp at the deepathoon near the Dargah during the Karthigai Deepam festival. Petitioners belonging to Hindu Munnani, who sought the deepathoon lighting, argued that the pillar lies on temple land and should be used for the ritual. Meanwhile, the dargah management and other parties contest claims over the hilltop, access and the pillar’s status.Historically the lamp is lit at the Uchipillayar temple. In multiple legal battles, successive governments backed by the temple priests have supported this arrangement. In 1994-95 Hindu Munnani precipitated matters demanding the lamp to be lit at the pillar, calling it a deepathoon, close to the dargah. The objective was clear: trigger a communal feud to pursue the Hindutva agenda in the state. However, this did not succeed since courts continued to reject this demand. Also read: A Lamp Was Lit, But Tensions Remain Over the Thiruparankundram Karthigai DeepamIt was under these circumstances that in November 2025, one Ravikumar moved the Madras high court, seeking a direction to the temple to light the lamp at the pillar, or permission to light it himself on December 3, 2025. A December 2025 order by Justice G.R. Swaminathan held that the pillar was a deepathoon and directed the temple to light the lamp there in addition to the customary site near the Uchippillaiyar temple. When the temple did not carry out the order on December 3, the judge initiated contempt proceedings and allowed Ravikumar and 10 others to light the lamp with Central Industrial Security Force protection. Their access was blocked by the police, on grounds of a prohibitory order issued by the district collector. A division bench upheld the December 3 order. Yet the lamp was not lit at the pillar that year. The state then approached the Supreme Court in appeal. A British-era survey markerThe Tamil Nadu government and the temple’s trust say that the pillar is not a traditional lamp-lighting structure, but an old survey marker. Now, a new report by the state government appears to offer evidence supporting that claim. It identifies the disputed pillar as part of a massive 200-year-old British-era project, to map the Indian subcontinent, launched in 1802. The report, in fact, documents hundreds of similar survey stations across Tamil Nadu. Titled “Documentation of the Great Trigonometrical Survey Stations in Tamil Nadu,” it was jointly compiled by the state’s Departments of Survey and Settlement and Archaeology to locate, document and preserve the remains of this old surveying network called the Great Trigonometrical Survey (GTS). The massive survey eventually covered 2,400 kilometres, reaching the Himalayas in 1841. Surveyors often chose hilltops because they offered clear views of distant locations. So, they built permanent stone pillars there to mark their survey stations. According to the government report, the pillar on Thiruparankundram hillock is one such structure.The high court steps in againIt is now clear that the deepathoon is a mere survey marker and has nothing to do with any religious practice or traditions. The substantive case is pending adjudication in the Supreme Court. Yet, a division bench of the Madras high court, comprising Justices G.R. Swaminathan and M.D. Sumathi, summoned Madurai’s district collector and commissioner of police on November 24 and told them that the writ petitioners apprehend that for political reasons, and to appease a section of the public, the apex court’s order would not be implemented. They cited the promulgation of a prohibitory order dated November 23, 2026, under Section 163 of the BNSS by the district collector. They recalled the defiance of the court’s order last year and noted that the “present trend is disturbingly reminiscent of the said past.” The judges further ordered: “Article 144 of the Constitution of India mandates that all authorities, civil and judicial, in the territory of India shall act in aid of the Supreme Court. The District Collector is a civil authority and Article 144 will squarely apply to him. Since officials brazenly defied judicial orders last year in connection with the Karthigai Deepam event, we deem it necessary to remind the District Collector that he is a public servant who is answerable only to the Honourable Supreme Court of India in this case. He shall ignore any contra advice given by any other authority. We are sure that no law officer worth his salt will counsel him to act in contravention of the order dated 20.11.2026. No doubt, a review petition has been filed before the Honourable Supreme Court in respect of the order dated 20.11.2026, but no order has been passed in the said review petition.”Questions that need answersAll these judicial proceedings have created a communal crisis in Tamil Nadu and raise several pertinent questions that need prompt answers:On what basis did the Madras high court hold that the pillar was a deepathoon and directed the temple to light the lamp there? Did it make a full inquiry and consult archeological experts before pronouncing the judgment? Why did it initiate contempt proceedings and allow Ravikumar and 10 others to light the lamp with Central Industrial Security Force protection?On what basis did the division bench uphold Justice Swaminathan’s order?On what grounds did the apex court issue a ‘perfunctory order’ allowing the lighting of lamp, after staying the high court’s perfunctory findings?Why has Justice Swaminathan shown extraordinary interest in this Hindu Munnani petition as if it were his personal matter; to the extent of summoning the collector and intimidating him with harsh directives? When there is no Writ of Mandamus how does Article 144 of the Constitution come into play?In sum and substance, l’affaire Thiruparankundram is a judiciary-induced crisis which needs to be resolved immediately by the judiciary itself, lest Tamil Nadu plunges into a Hindutva-style communal feud! M.G. Devasahayam, formerly of an IAS, is coordinator of the Citizens’ Commission on Elections.

title: A Homeless Barn Owl Has Become the New Face of Dissent in Kashmir - The Wire
description: Environment experts in Kashmir said that the younger generation in the Valley was experiencing the first-hand consequences of the climate change as opposed to just reading about them in the books, which is why the visuals of a homeless barn owl struck an emotional chord.
author: Shakir Mir
content: Over the past one week, people scrolling their mobile screens in Kashmir are greeted by strange visuals: a lonely barn owl hovering in the empty skies. The bird cranes its neck from side to side, as if trying to look for something that it cannot find. Gliding through the cold autumnal nights, the owl rests on a perch of the charred remains of what was, until last week, a lifesize Chinar (Oriental Sycamore) tree at Srinagar’s Shalimar neighbourhood, right next to the famed Mughal-era Shalimar Gardens. However, the tree caught fire mysteriously last week. In a matter of minutes, the embers glowing inside of its hollowed interior gave way to thick plumes of smoke before the fire engulfed the entire tree. The Chinar Chowk at the Shalimar area of Srinagar, where a centuries old Chinar tree was cut down after it caught fire. Photo: Shakir Mir.“The fire began at 9:30 am after some people tried to burn a fire from the leaf litter so that they could warm themselves,” Parvaiz Ahmad, a local resident and eye-witness to the tree’s burning, told The Wire. “The police and fire service tried to douse the flames but failed. Eventually, its charred branches drooped dangerously low enough to pose a public threat while also disrupting the electricity supply as the power wires ran underneath it,” he said. “They had to cut it down.”Rising concerns over ‘development’ spreeBut in a place like Kashmir, where ecological risks posed by various developmental projects have stirred a lot of political anxiety recently, the axing of what many describe as a Mughal-era Chinar tree has tapped right into these concerns, galvanising a torrent of popular backlash. Since then, there have been mounting questions over the accountability that surrounds a slew of new developmental projects – highways, ring roads or the widening of traditional pilgrimage routes – which involve flattening the delicate alpine tracks or the felling of hundreds of thousands of trees.These concerns also readily acquire political salience, as they come in the backdrop of the seven years of reading down of Article 370, which enshrined various land laws that restricted the scope of land-related changes in J&K, including conversion, re-use, or appropriation of land for uses other than agricultural. Notified by the Jammu & Kashmir administration in October 2020, the new laws (and amendments) removed the old legal fetters, along with the bureaucratic red tape that could have otherwise made the commissioning of such projects difficult to begin with.At the same time, however, the new forest protection laws with stringent safeguards against ecological degradation – such as The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 – were also implemented in J&K. But as activists tell The Wire, their enforcement has been lax due to lack of awareness in the general public. In recent times, the forest fires on the hills of Hari Parbat in Srinagar; axing of Chinar trees for a road widening project in Ganderbal; cutting down of over 500 conifer trees across the Anantnag and Marwah forest divisions for the Singhpora–Vailoo tunnel project; pruning of a century old Sweet Chestnut tree at the premises of Kashmir University; and the presence of JCB excavator at high-risk Sheeshnag glacial lake in South Kashmir; have deepened worries over fate of regional ecology as the government steps up the work on infrastructural projects.A popular political memeThe popular anguish against what is being seen as widespread ecological “vandalism” is now finding expression through a new face: a homeless barn owl.Instagram feeds in Kashmir are full of videos featuring the owl as it flutters from one branch to another, looking for the lost Chinar tree where it is likely to have nested. A lot of Kashmiri social media users also set the screengrabs from homeless barn owl clips as their display pictures to show solidarity. The hollow of the burnt Chinar tree in Srinagar where the Barn Owl is likely to have nested. Photo: Shakir Mir“The barn owls find homes in Kashmir’s Chinars. It’s a relationship that transcends time,” Museum of Kashmir, a popular Instagram account that posts on culture, history and politics, told The Wire. “For me, the owl returning to its nest is a personification or metaphor for how Kashmiris perch on the edge while their homes and homeland face ecological collapse and political disenfranchisement”Others have posted AI-generated clips of the owl in which the bird appears grief-stricken, shedding tears, and a Bollywood song blares in the backdrop: “Leave me to my own devices. I am alive. That’s enough.” Residents of Shalimar told The Wire that the barn owl appears regularly at dusk. “We see it almost everyday after the Isha (fifth and last prayer of the day) namaz,” said 21-year-old Mir Zaid. “It is as if the bird knows that people would be coming out of their mosques. It stays here for hours. People turn up to see it and record videos.”Chinar as metonym for KashmirThe fabled Chinar tree has for centuries symbolised the sense of belonging in Kashmir. Although Chinar also grows in some other Himalayan regions of India, it is hard to find the tree in such large numbers outside Kashmir. Its abundance in Kashmir is often credited to the region’s ancient trade and cultural connections to wider Central Asia. In its effort to promote the conservation of Chinars, the J&K government recently completed the geo-tagging of around 30,000 trees across the region. The trees feature badges that display QR codes containing information of that particular Chinar tree. In the case of the fallen Chinar at Shalimar, the database reveals that its height was 55.6 feet, while its GBH (Girth at Breast Height), which is the circumference of a tree trunk measured at a standard breast height, was 47 feet.Chinar’s leaves, which come with long, flame-like serrations, have long held a semiotic power for the local community, which is why it features prominently in Kashmir’s cultural iconography. The autobiography of Sheikh Abdullah, a prominent Kashmiri political figure of the 20th century, is also called Aatish-e-Chinar (The Blazing Chinar). “Owls of all types in Kashmir largely use Chinar trees for nesting,” Aaqib Hussain, a wildlife biologist with the J&K chapter of Wildlife SOS told The Wire. “The tall Chinars not only provide them shelter but also give them a panoramic view of the streets below, which is important for them as they hunt little birds and rodents.”Hussain said that the owl’s behaviour shows it lost its nest after the Chinar tree at Shalimar was cut down. “Owls take a lot of things into account before choosing a place for nesting. It might not be very easy for this owl to find a different spot and owls are generally very territorial,” he said. Aaliya Mir, the Project Head and Education Officer at Wildlife SOS, said that the visuals of the owl clearly show the bird was in distress. “The bird has lost his habitat and he is returning again and again to locate it. It is very likely that he had a nest inside the tree with chicks in it,” she told The Wire.Mir said that owls nest deep inside the hollows of Chinar trees and that such nests are generally beyond the reach of human beings. “Winters are generally tough times for owls because the food is scarce. The loss of habitat represents a dire situation for them. Eventually, hunger takes a toll and they often resort to cannibalism, feeding on their own spawn.”Environment experts in Kashmir said that the younger generation in the Valley was experiencing the first-hand consequences of the climate change as opposed to just reading about them in the books, which is why the visuals of a homeless barn owl struck an emotional chord.“In the last six to seven years, we have seen the physical manifestations of global warming, which includes threats of fires, floods and water scarcity. This generation understands how time to salvage the earth is narrowing,” said Raja Muzaffar Bhat, a prominent climate campaigner in Kashmir. “It haunts them. The future politics of Kashmir will be fought over climate.”

title: WebQoof Recap: Of Misinformation Around Bisleri, China, AI Videos & More
description: WebQoof Recap| From misinformation about Bisleri water after a notice was issued by the FSSAI to a deepfake of BJP national president Nitin Nabin, here are five of the most viral pieces of misinformation we debunked this week.
author: Team Webqoof
content:
From misinformation about Bisleri water after a notice was issued by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) to a deepfake of Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) national president Nitin Nabin stating that India invited Pakistan to the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) under pressure from China, here are five of the most viral pieces of misinformation we debunked this week.
1. Did Nitin Nabin Say India Invited Pak to SCO Summit Under China’s Pressure? No!
A video is going viral on social media, claiming to show BJP's Nitin Nabin, stating that India invited Pakistan to the SCO under pressure from China.
- In the video, Nabin can be heard saying that India did not invite Pakistan to the SCO summit of its own accord.
However, the claim is false, as the video is a deepfake.
Read our fact-check here.
2. Viral Video of Chinese Helmets With Integrated Airbags Is AI-Generated
A video showing an airbag opening up around a falling biker's helmet has gone viral on social media, where users have claimed that it shows innovation from China, which has introduced bike helmets featuring integrated airbags.
But...?: The video is an AI-generated one and doesn't show real visuals of such a helmet.
Read the full report here.
3. Is Bisleri Water ‘Unfit for Drinking’? Not Really, Here's What You Need to Know
Posts alleging that the water brand Bisleri has been declared 'unfit for drinking' due to the carcinogenic chemicals in it are being widely circulated on social media.
- Social media users are sharing this claim following a notice issued by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) regarding Bisleri's packaged drinking water.
According to a post released by Bisleri, the sanction of prosecution against Bisleri is in regards to a batch produced in September 2025 at Bisleri's Verna manufacturing facility in Goa.
Furthermore, according to news agency ANI, the FSSAI clarified that only one sample from one batch, Batch No. GO 270, was found to be non-compliant and that an order prohibiting its sale has been issued.
So, one failed test doesn't mean all of Bisleri's water is unfit for consumption.
Read the full report here.
4. Video of Houses on Fire in Bangladesh Shared With Misleading Communal Angle
A video showing a massive blaze in the Kalia area in Bangladesh's Narail district has gone viral on social media.
The claim: Some of those sharing this video have claimed that it shows a targeted attack against Hindus in Bangladesh, with CNN News 18's Editorial Affairs Director Rahul Shivshankar exclaiming that "BANGLADESH CANNOT BECOME A HUNTING GROUND FOR HINDUS! (sic)."
But...?: The claim is misleading, as the arson was politically motivated and has no communal angle to it.
Read our fact-check here.
5. Promo Clip From a Film Shared With False Claim About Woman Faking Harassment
A video is going viral on social media, claiming to show a woman taking a selfie-style video where she is filming herself leaning on a man and forcing herself on him for views.
- Deepika Bhardwaj, journalist and men's rights activist, shared the video with a caption that compared the woman in the viral video to the Shimjitha Musthafa case, where a woman faked being molested on a bus.
- However, the claim is false.
- The original clip is from a promotional video for an upcoming Marathi film titled Janak.
Read the full report here.
(Not convinced of a post or information you came across online and want it verified? Send us the details on WhatsApp at 9540511818 , or e-mail it to us at webqoof@thequint.com and we'll fact-check it for you. You can also read all our fact-checked stories here.)

title: 6 Indian Childhood Games to Get Your Kids Moving, Laughing & Off Screens This Winter Break
description: Discover 6 traditional Indian games for children, from Stapu and Lagori to Kho-Kho, that encourage active play, teamwork and fun away from screens.
author: Nishtha Kawrani
content:
“Just five more minutes!” If you've ever tried getting a child to put down a phone or tablet, chances are you've heard this familiar refrain.
But long before cartoons were available at the tap of a screen and games came with colourful animations, childhood entertainment looked a little different. It meant chalk-drawn squares on the floor, marbles tucked into pockets, endless rounds of hide-and-seek and friends gathering in the neighbourhood until someone called them home.
The best part? Most of these games needed little more than a few friends, some open space and a generous dose of imagination.
Bringing these old-school games back can be a fun way to encourage children to take a break from screens, get moving and spend quality time with others. Here are six Indian childhood favourites worth introducing to the next generation.
1. Hopscotch (Stapu)
All you need is a piece of chalk and a little space to get started. Draw a series of numbered boxes on the ground, toss a small stone into one of them and ask children to hop through the squares on one foot, skipping the box containing the stone.
Known as stapu in many parts of India, hopscotch is a simple game that can keep children entertained for hours. It encourages balance, coordination and concentration, while giving them a chance to cheer each other on.
2. Seven Stones (Lagori)
A game that brings together teamwork, speed and a little strategy, lagori is a favourite that deserves a comeback.
Stack seven flat stones on top of one another and divide the players into two teams. One team tries to knock down the stack with a ball, while the other attempts to rebuild it before getting hit by the ball. The opposing team tries to stop them by tagging players with the ball.
The game gets everyone running, dodging, planning and laughing. It is also a wonderful way to introduce children to teamwork and friendly competition.
3. Carrom
Rainy afternoon? Too hot to play outside? Bring out the carrom board!
This classic indoor game needs a board, striker and carrom coins. Players take turns flicking the striker to pocket their coins, aiming to clear the board before their opponents.
Carrom is a lovely way to bring the family together. It helps children practise hand-eye coordination, patience and strategic thinking. Parents can even make it a family tournament, complete with playful challenges and a little friendly rivalry.
4. Tip-Cat (Gilli-Danda)
Think of it as a traditional Indian game that puts hand-eye coordination to the test. Gilli-danda uses two wooden sticks: a small tapered one (the gilli) and a longer one (the danda).
Players use the longer stick to flick the smaller one into the air and then hit it as far as possible. The game can be played in an open ground with simple rules agreed upon by everyone.
It is a wonderful way for children to enjoy outdoor play, practise coordination and discover a game that entertained generations before smartphones existed.
5. King, Minister, Thief, Soldier (Raja, Mantri, Chor, Sipahi)
This is a fun indoor game that needs just four players and a few small slips of paper.
Write the names Raja, Mantri, Chor and Sipahi on four slips and distribute them among the players. The person who gets Raja reveals their identity, while the others have to figure out who the Chor is. The Mantri gets a chance to guess, and the Sipahi can help with the investigation, depending on the rules the group decides.
With guessing, suspense and plenty of laughter, this game can turn an ordinary afternoon into a mini detective adventure.
6. Tag and Chase (Kho-Kho)
A playground favourite, kho-kho is a fast-paced team game that keeps children on their toes.
Two teams take turns chasing and dodging. Players from the chasing team sit in a row, facing alternate directions, while one active chaser tries to tag opponents. By calling 'kho' and transferring the chase to a teammate, players must think quickly and move strategically.
Besides being a great way to get children running, kho-kho encourages teamwork, agility and quick decision-making.
Making room for play
The idea isn't to ban screens altogether or make children feel guilty about enjoying their favourite digital games. Instead, it is about making space for other kinds of fun, too.
Parents can start small by setting aside 20–30 minutes for a family game, inviting neighbourhood children over for an afternoon of outdoor play or teaching their little ones a game they enjoyed growing up.
After all, childhood doesn't always need a screen, a scorecard or a fancy toy. Sometimes, all it takes is a chalk-drawn square, a few friends and the freedom to play.

title: Filmmaker Aditi Anand Shares What It Takes to Raise a Child as a Same-Sex Couple in India
description: Filmmaker Aditi Anand and her partner Susan Dias share their journey of building a family through adoption, navigating parenthood as a same-sex couple, and raising their son with the support of loved ones.
author: Nishtha Kawrani
content:
What does it mean to build a family beyond traditional labels? Filmmaker Aditi Anand and her partner Susan Dias share their journey of love, adoption, and queer parenting in India.
Aditi, 42, founded the production houses Little Red Car Films and Neelam Studios. Her film credits include Tere Bin Laden, No One Killed Jessica, Paan Singh Tomar and Chillar Party.
Susan, 37, has been with Aditi for over a decade. Together, they co-founded Native Brews and petitioned the Supreme Court for marriage equality and legal recognition of same-sex parents.
Aditi grew up surrounded by both sets of grandparents and their siblings. She fondly calls this close-knit extended family a 'herd of elephants', bound by care and shared memories.
All four grandparents lived through Independence and Partition. Their stories taught Aditi that a nation is something people participate in and build, not something distant.
Like many queer people in India, Aditi once struggled to imagine marriage or children. Coming out, she says, can mean telling parents that the future they pictured may not happen.
Aditi and Susan met in 2012. “There's life before Susan, and there's life after,” Aditi says. Their relationship helped her imagine adulthood, hope, and a future of her own.
Susan says they have navigated careers, cities, happy times, and difficult ones through nearly 14 years together. Shared values, beyond love, helped them decide to start a family.
Aditi had always wanted to adopt, while Susan was clear she wanted a family. They supported each other's wishes, making the decision through trust and mutual understanding.
The couple waited until they felt financially and emotionally ready. They also considered what needed to change in their lives and how society might respond to their family.
Susan says the couple has received love and acceptance from people around them. Their son is growing up with grandparents, great-grandparents, close friends, and godparents.
Susan believes family includes both natal and chosen relationships that form life's essential support structures. Their son once said he would run away from home to stay with a close family friend.
Aditi jokes that life as a couple felt like a gritty noir. After their son arrived, they found themselves in a Sooraj Barjatya film, moving from independence to interdependence.
Aditi says parenthood taught her she need not be a “brick wall” and can express fear and process difficult emotions. Their son has brought curiosity into her life, while Susan says parenting has made her calmer and more aware of his future.
Aditi hopes queer families in India will become more visible. For her, family has no fixed rules. It is built with people who raise, choose, teach, and grow alongside one another.

title: Sustainable Architecture in Yercaud: A Home Built Around Nature
description: In Yercaud's Shervaroy Hills, architect Malli Saravanan designed Whispers of the Wild around an existing tree, a sloping landscape and the memory of a disappearing stream. The 2,400-square-foot home offers a different way to think about building in ecologically sensitive terrain.
author: Sriroopa Dutta
content:
Imagine walking into a house and finding a stream flowing beneath your feet.
Not outside the entrance or in a garden designed to resemble a natural waterbody, but directly beneath a transparent glass floor.
Look up, and there is a tree framed by glass walls and a glass roof. Walk a little further, and the architecture opens towards a valley, allowing the surrounding landscape to become part of the experience.
This is Whispers of the Wild, a residential project by MAWI Design, led by Chennai-based architect Malli Saravanan, in Yercaud, Tamil Nadu.
But the most interesting thing about this house is not what its architects added to the landscape. It is what they chose not to take away.
Spread across a 10,000-square-foot plot in the eco-sensitive Shervaroy Hills, the 2,400-square-foot residence was designed for a family of six. Completed in 2024, it occupies two levels and sits within Wild Orchid, a 100-acre residential community that follows an eco-sensitive development approach.
“We wanted the terrain to flow naturally over here and then bring the entire thing out,” Saravanan tells The Better India.
“I wanted much of it to remain tucked into the landscape, with its built form designed to sit beneath the surrounding tree canopy.”
The tree that became the centre of the design
When the MAWI Design team first visited the property, they found a sloping site with a valley opening up on one side.
A mature tree occupied a prominent position on the land, its canopy extending across the site.
Instead of treating it as an obstacle around which the building had to be designed, the architects decided to make it the focal point.
The team first conducted a total-station survey and mapped the trees across the property. This helped them understand where the existing vegetation stood and how the proposed structure could be positioned without cutting them down.
“We made sure that we didn't want to cut any of the trees, and we tried to work around them without cutting the tree,” Saravanan explains.
The design was subsequently broken into three architectural fragments, allowing the tree to remain at the centre of the composition.
“As visitors enter the house, their first visual connection is with this tree. The private and communal spaces open towards an L-shaped deck that wraps around it, creating a shared outdoor space overlooking the valley.”
“The tree is not retained as a decorative feature. We tried to retain this tree as the hero of the site and started building a story around this tree,” he says.
The same idea extends to the interiors.
The living, dining and kitchen areas follow an open-plan arrangement, while the communal deck creates a transition between the house and the outdoors.
The master bedroom, meanwhile, projects outwards in a cantilevered form. Its glass frame opens towards a panoramic view of the valley.
Saravanan points out that the corners have been kept free of columns to preserve the expansive views.
“We don't have any TV walls and stuff, so the bedrooms are designed to open towards nature, too,” he says, describing the decision to make the surrounding landscape the primary visual experience.
A stream that disappeared, and an attempt to bring back its memory
One of the most distinctive features of Whispers of the Wild is its entrance foyer.
Here, the team separated two building blocks to create a transition space that feels open rather than enclosed.
They also introduced a cascading water feature beneath a glass floor.
There is a story behind this intervention.
“We tried to pull out the rocks that were there at the site. And then we set up a water feature so that when one comes into this foyer space, the flooring is completely glass, so the water will be flowing underneath,” Saravanan says.
The experience is deliberately immersive. The glass floor reveals the water below, while glass on the opposite side reflects the trees. A glass roof completes the visual connection with the surroundings.
What happens during heavy rainfall?
The team incorporated rainwater harvesting and constructed a storage tank to collect water from the roof and other catchment areas for use within the house.
“Since it is a slope side, we have made sure that when there is heavy rain, the water gets collected and then it is harvested inside the ground, and the overflow gets down to the valley,” Saravanan says.
There is, however, an important distinction in the project's assessment of water systems. Saravanan confirms that the team conducted a soil test and a general site survey, but did not undertake a separate hydrological assessment.
What happens when the house borrows from the landscape?
The walls of the house incorporate locally available random rubble stones, many sourced from within the property or nearby areas.
Saravanan explains that construction activity in and around Yercaud often brings up large boulders when soil is excavated. Some of these were already available on the property, while smaller stones were sourced from nearby community areas.
“We use this material as a kind of expression of the context. We use the same material in the exterior and also in the interior, so that we create a very timeless kind of palette inside the house,” he says.
The rubble stone is used as an exterior-facing element over brick construction, rather than as the primary structural wall. According to Saravanan, the thickness and overall mass of the wall contribute to thermal comfort within the house.
The flooring uses leathered Kota stone.
Saravanan wanted the sensation of walking indoors to resemble the experience of walking outdoors. The stone's natural texture and coolness were important considerations.
“For us, the first thing is experiential. The second is the sustainable aspect of it, and third is the aesthetics,” he explains.
Oxide finishes and other natural materials complete the palette.
The intention was not to create a polished, artificial version of nature, but to let the materials sit comfortably within the surrounding landscape.
The team also retained the site's existing vegetation, including fruit-bearing plants and a fig tree. Saravanan says they avoided introducing non-native plants.
The one notable addition was bamboo, planted along the property boundary.
It serves two purposes. The community has a pathway running along the edge of the property, and the bamboo provides visual privacy for the residents. It also contributes to the sensory experience of the house.
“We love the rustling sounds. So whenever there is wind, you listen to the rustling sounds, and it adds to the overall experience of the space,” he says.
Does wildlife find a place here, too?
A house in a hillside landscape cannot be understood only through its architecture.
The Shervaroy Hills have their own distinctive vegetation, including shrubs and fruit-bearing plants. Saravanan says the team tried to retain the existing flora and make the new landscape blend with the region.
He has also noticed changes in the presence of birds and other smaller wildlife around the property.
“Butterflies, birds, and peacocks started coming after this,” he says, adding that peacocks are frequently seen around the house.
A home that changes how its residents experience nature
Interestingly, Whispers of the Wild was not originally conceived as a permanent retirement home.
The client, 67-year-old Chandrapratapan from Salem, purchased the property.
“One of our favourite things about living here is never knowing what we might see in the morning. Peacocks often wander by in the garden, squirrels move between the trees, and occasionally we spot a mongoose passing through. We've started recognising different birds by their calls. The old tree is probably the busiest spot on the property, with birds and insects constantly moving through it,” he shares with The Better India.
“This has made us much more aware of all the life we share this place with. We love that we've been able to preserve much of what was already here — the trees, the slope and the natural landscape,” Chandrapratap adds.
Saravanan also believes this reflects a shift in how people think about their homes.
“We are in a very rushed world, with all these tensions and pressure, running here and there. At the end of it, people want to spend time for themselves,” he says.
He has noticed more people looking beyond metropolitan neighbourhoods for homes that offer a connection with nature and a sense of calm.
For him, this is not simply about having a second home or spending money on elaborate interiors. It is about the relationship between people, their surroundings and the communities they live in.
Can building with nature also make financial sense?
There is another question worth asking. Is this approach financially viable, or is it an architectural luxury accessible only to people who can afford expensive homes in the hills?
Saravanan puts the construction cost of Whispers of the Wild at approximately Rs 1.3-1.4 crore.
He considers this reasonable for a project of its scale and location, particularly because transporting materials to a hill station and arranging labour can increase construction costs.
“We had all those good elements around the site. We wanted the site not to be manicured. We wanted things to be imperfect and just flow seamlessly,” he says.
“We don't know where that new landscape starts or where the new construction starts. It should feel like it's very well lived in, especially the exterior parts.”
The project does not establish that this approach is cheaper in every situation. Its costs depend on the terrain, construction requirements, materials and site conditions.
But it offers an example of how existing natural features can become part of the architectural experience rather than being removed and recreated.
Before building on a hillside, what should architects reconsider?
For Saravanan, the first step is to understand the site before drawing up the building.
“First, we need to understand the existing terrain, the flora, the fauna, and the existing site conditions. Making less impact on nature is the first fundamental thing they need to consider,” he says.
He believes the value of a mature tree, for instance, cannot be measured simply in terms of the money required to plant another one.
“Today, we can buy anything, but a well-grown tree like this, with whatever money they want, they can't buy it.”
He also emphasises the importance of keeping the building footprint small.
At Whispers of the Wild, the architects used cantilevered sections and elevated portions to reduce the amount of building mass touching the ground. The intention was to allow the landscape to continue around the structure.
“If the footprint is very small, it is always better. It is the idea that a building does not always need to begin with a cleared, levelled piece of land,” he adds.
