title: General Strikes Return as Europe Confronts Austerity
description: Europe’s youth and workers are taking to the streets against austerity, militarisation and declining public services, reviving the general strike as a force for international solidarity.
author: Susan  Ram
content:
These past few weeks have seen mass protests ignite across broad swathes of Europe. From France in the West to Serbia in the East, an extraordinary eruption of activism has transformed the continent into a crucible of protest, a testing ground not for NATO’s latest weapons but for people’s ability to assert their collective power and fight back.
The scale of this continent-wide autumn of discontent is astonishing. Street protests, in many cases youth-led, have unleashed and given form to cross-national outpourings of accumulated frustration and anger. In every sense, these are the wages of austerity. They are the fruit of decades of stagnant wages, underfunded public services, unaddressed needs, destroyed hopes and the wanton waste of human capabilities. Whether the focus of mobilisation is a housing crisis that is pricing people beyond any hope of a decent home (Spain and Portugal), or a crumbling public infrastructure that spells dilapidated classrooms and acute teacher shortages (France), or the threatened return of conscription in goose step with national and European Union militarisation plans (Germany), hundreds of thousands of people across Europe have simply had enough.
That many have taken inspiration from the uprising of French schoolchildren, beginning in mid-September, is evident in the number of education-related protests across the continent. Demonstrations specifically targeted at lamentable school conditions, cuts to higher education and other facets of the war on children and young people have been held in Belgium, Austria, Denmark, Ireland, Greece, Italy, and beyond. Germany’s nationwide mass protests against conscription have also included calls for better higher education funding and relief from rising living costs.
Even where mobilisations have been triggered by specifically local issues (in Albania, for instance, the Trump family’s “development” designs on Sazan Island, whose pristine environment harbours a world-famous flamingo sanctuary), the focus of mass protests has speedily broadened; after all, what does it tell you about a government that’s willing to let key representatives of the global billionaire class seize and despoil an irreplaceable national asset?
One aspect of the developing situation has been the reactivation of the general strike on the continent where it first took shape close to two centuries ago. Over the span of two months, this longstanding weapon of the organised working class has been unsheathed across Europe, especially in Italy, Spain, and France, the three powerful economies at the centre of this ongoing popular revolt.
In Italy, where discontent with the far-right Meloni government is at historic levels, two trade union-sponsored general strikes have been held within the space of four weeks: on October 30 and November 20. On November 11, Spain staged its first general strike since the great Iberian strike of 2012. The previous week, on November 5, tens of thousands of French workers downed tools in a one-day mass strike called by the country’s five main trade union confederations. By the end of the month, the phenomenon was spreading elsewhere: to Greece, for example, where a one-day general stoppage is in progress as I write on November 25.
Historical perspectives
As its name suggests, the general strike is one that mobilises a significant proportion of workers across a broad swathe of different sectors. Its origins can be traced back to the industrial revolution in Britain, and the concomitant emergence of a new, as yet unorganised, urban proletariat. In the 1840s, working-class anger at the 1832 Reform Act, by whose terms the vast majority of working people were denied the right to vote, crystallised around the Chartist movement and its 1838 list (or charter) of political demands.
In the context of this nascent working-class movement, miners in the Black Country, to the north and west of Birmingham, struck work in May 1842 against proposed wage cuts. The stoppage quickly spread to the Staffordshire potteries and onwards into the mills of Lancashire and Yorkshire. By August, half a million workers had downed tools. Strikers “marched from town to town, from factory to factory, pulling the plugs on furnaces and calling on their fellow workers to join the strike” (Paul Foot, The Vote, 2005: p. 111). The world was witnessing its first general strike.
Soon, cross-sectoral strikes were erupting elsewhere in Europe, and beyond. Addressing the new phenomenon in the first volume of Das Kapital, Marx, who had spoken at a Chartist public meeting in 1848, saw it as contributing to workers’ sense of themselves as, together, constituting “the agent of production”, and to their awareness that if they stopped, then so did production.
But it was the German-Polish Marxist Rosa Luxemburg who, early in the twentieth century, provided the general strike with its most systematic theoretical exploration. Drawing lessons from the 1905 Russian Revolution, which she’d just witnessed at first hand, Luxemburg was struck by the galvanising impact of a series of general strikes in Russia, beginning with the great St. Petersburg textile workers’ strikes of 1896 and 1897. In her tract The Mass Strike (1906), she noted the tendency of strikes involving large-scale industry to develop into directly political struggles; the economic became political and the political economic. Out of this intermingling, there had emerged in Russia a new form of organisation, the soviet or workers’ council, and a plethora of new possibilities.
Twenty years later, in a Europe devastated by war, this potential was put to the test during Britain’s 1926 General Strike, a comprehensive, nine-day, multi-sector stoppage that to this day retains the ability to send shivers down establishment and bourgeois spines. Sparked by private coalmine owners’ bid to impose a wage cut on 1.2 million locked-out pit workers, the strike began as an official one, called (with some reluctance) by the General Council of the Trade Unions Congress (TUC). It was distinguished by the enthusiasm and militancy of its one and a half million participants, which a half-hearted union leadership constantly sought to rein in, and by the no-holds-barred application of state force to crush it: battalions of troops marched through the port city of Liverpool as if for battle, and emergency powers were invoked to give the police multiple new grounds for arrest.
But even this historic rendition of the general strike would be dwarfed by events four decades later when, in May 1968, an estimated ten million French workers, roughly two-thirds of the total workforce, walked off the job, bringing the country’s factories, transportation and public services to a comprehensive halt. Even the considerable repressive powers of the state, at the time being liberally applied to France’s upstart student rebels, were hard put to it to cope with a situation whose gravity and swiftly escalating revolutionary potential at one point drove President Charles de Gaulle to (briefly) flee the country for Germany.
Back to 2026
Europe’s current general strikes are taking place in a context far removed from the Trente Glorieuse, the French term for the three post-war decades of economic growth and relative prosperity. With trade union membership in long-term decline, the continent’s depleted ranks of organised labour are seeking new ways to combat the entrenched, life-sapping realities of austerity, authoritarianism and militarisation. There’s a growing emphasis on experimentation, coalition-building and cross-border actions that help foster international perspectives and solidarity.
This new impetus was evident on October 30, when dockworkers from across Europe participated in an international day of action against war, genocide and militarisation. In this global mobilisation of port workers and grass-roots civil society organisations, embracing 22 countries and more than a hundred ports, a key role was played by Italy’s USB (Unione Sindicale di Basa/Unions from the base), a grass-roots, rank-and-file driven trade union confederation with a magnificent record of building solidarity with Palestine.
The significance of this action should not be underestimated. While adapting to new circumstances, the general strike continues to flex its muscles. As mass protests continue across Europe, with zero expectation of any serious response from governments bent on squeezing more from their citizens to feed insatiable military ends, we may, possibly, be at the start of something new: an internationally co-ordinated movement against austerity and war.
Susan Ram has spent much of her life viewing the world from different geographical locations. Born in London, she studied politics and international relations before setting off for South Asia: first to Nepal, and then to India, where fieldwork in Tamil Nadu developed into 20 years of residence.

title: Thirupparankundram: The Unequal Burden of Religious Proof
description: The Thirupparankundram cases expose differences in how courts assess religious custom, essential practices, and constitutional rights.
author: R. Vanchinathan
content:
Thirupparankundram is a rocky hill on the southern edge of Madurai. At its foot stands the Arulmigu Subramaniya Swamy temple, one of the six abodes of Murugan. On its summit stands the dargah of Sikkandar Badhusha. For about a hundred years, the two have shared the hill under a court decree of 1923.
Every year, on Karthigai Deepam, the temple lights a large lamp on the hill. It lights it at the Deepa Mandapam, near the small Uchi Pillaiyar shrine, halfway up the hill. In November 2025, a group of petitioners asked the Madras High Court to allow the lamp to be lit at another spot as well, a stone pillar higher up, near the top of the hill, a short distance from the dargah.
A year later, the matter reached the Supreme Court. On November 20, 2026, a Bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M. Pancholi allowed the temple to light the lamp on that pillar once, on November 24, as what the order called “a limited, one-time arrangement”.
The order, passed in Hindu Dharma Parishad v. Union of India, along with the State’s appeals, put on hold the findings recorded in paragraphs 1 to 141 of the High Court’s judgment, in so far as they concern the challenge before it. The Bench was careful to add, in paragraph 15, that the permission “does not proceed upon any finding that the stone pillar is, or has historically been, a place of customary religious observance”. It also said that it was not deciding whether lighting the lamp there is an “essential religious practice”.
The case will be heard again in the second week of January 2027. On November 21, Tamil Nadu’s Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments (HR&CE) Commissioner asked the court to review the order, arguing that it gave the petitioners what they had asked for without any finding that they had a right to it. On November 24, the lamp was lit only at the customary Deepa Mandapam near the Uchi Pillaiyar shrine, and not at the pillar, even though the Supreme Court had permitted it there and the High Court had, that afternoon, directed the authorities to comply.
On November 25, counsel for the District Collector informed the same Bench that the lamp had not been lit at the pillar. According to reports of the hearing, the State said that the temple administration had not authorised the team to perform the ceremony there. Counsel for the petitioners referred to a statement issued in the name of the temple’s board of trustees, which cited custom for lighting the lamp only near the Uchi Pillaiyar shrine. He also told the court that the temple’s sthanikars had since denied approving the statement. The Bench declined to initiate contempt proceedings on its own. “No suo motu; file the necessary petition, we will issue appropriate orders if required,” Justice Aravind Kumar said. Among the contempt petitions filed since then is one by advocate V. Ramasubbu against the Madurai District Collector and three other officials. A fresh plea seeking directions to light the lamp at the pillar has also been filed. On November 26, the Bench said these would be heard the following day.
The Supreme Court was right to be careful not to decide whether the pillar was a customary site for lighting the lamp. But having read the judgments concerning both the temple and the dargah, I find it difficult to understand why the courts demanded such different standards of proof from the two communities. When someone goes to court claiming a religious practice, who has to prove it, and how much proof is enough?
What is an “essential religious practice”?
Article 25 of the Constitution guarantees every person the freedom to profess, practise, and propagate religion. That freedom has limits. The State can still regulate religion in the interest of public order, morality and health, and for social reform.
Over the years, the courts developed what is now known as the “essential religious practices” test to decide which practices are entitled to constitutional protection.
In the Shirur Mutt case of 1954 (Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Mutt, AIR 1954 SC 282), the Supreme Court said that what is essential to a religion must be found in that religion’s own teachings. In 1961, in the Supreme Court narrowed this in Durgah Committee, Ajmer v. Syed Hussain Ali (AIR 1961 SC 1402). The judgment said only practices that are “essential and integral” to a faith would be protected.
Also Read | Thirupparankundram: Tamil Nadu skips lighting lamp on pillar despite SC order, HC direction
Under this test, a person seeking constitutional protection for a religious practice is generally expected to establish that the practice is essential to her religion. Courts have often refused such protection where they have found the practice to be merely optional.
Scholars have long warned about what this does to the courts. In a 2017 article in the BYU Law Review, the legal scholars Faizan Mustafa and Jagteshwar Singh Sohi described the Supreme Court as “acting as clergy”: to apply the test, judges must decide for themselves what a faith requires.
The political scientist Ronojoy Sen, in a 2007 study for the East-West Center, showed how the court’s rulings have ended up defining and reshaping religious practice itself. My concern here is whether the courts have exercised that authority in the same manner when dealing with different religions.
The test itself has few defenders left. Before the nine-judge Bench now re-examining its validity, the Union government urged the court to move away from it, and other parties called it “unstable” and “unworkable”. That Bench reserved its judgment in May 2026.
1958: What Muslim butchers had to prove
In the 1950s, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, and Madhya Pradesh passed laws banning cow slaughter. Nearly 2,500 Muslim butchers of the Qureshi community challenged these laws in the Supreme Court, in 12 petitions. The case is known as Mohd. Hanif Quareshi v. State of Bihar (AIR 1958 SC 731).
Among other things, the butchers argued that sacrificing a cow on Bakrid was part of their religion, and so protected by Article 25. A five-judge Bench led by Chief Justice S.R. Das did not accept this.
To find out what Islam requires, the court did not turn to Muslim scholars. It turned to an English translation of the Hedaya, a book of Hanafi law, made by Charles Hamilton in the colonial era. The Hedaya says that “the sacrifice established for one person is a goat and that for seven a cow or a camel”.
From this, the court reasoned that a Muslim could sacrifice a goat or a camel instead. The cow was one option among several, so its sacrifice was optional. And an optional practice was not protected.
The court also counted lack of evidence as going against the butchers’ plea. It noted that “no affidavit has been filed by any person specially competent to expound the relevant tenets of Islam”. It observed that many Muslims did not sacrifice cows at all, and that Mughal emperors such as Babar and, “it is said”, Akbar, Jehangir, and Ahmad Shah had banned cow slaughter.
The lawyer and author Abhinav Chandrachud points out in Republic of Religion (Penguin, 2020) that the court reached its conclusion about Islam through a colonial translation.
A sharper criticism came much earlier, from the legal scholar Upendra Baxi. Writing in the Journal of the Indian Law Institute in 1967, he observed that the court’s “rigorous methods” for finding out what Islam required “were not extended to the determination of the Hindu’s reverence for the cows”. The court simply accepted that reverence as a fact and counted it in favour of the ban.
In 2005, a seven-judge Bench extended the same reasoning to bulls and bullocks (State of Gujarat v. Mirzapur Moti Kureshi Kassab Jamat, (2005) 8 SCC 534).
Whether the court interpreted the Hedaya correctly is a separate debate. What deserves attention is the standard of proof demanded of the butchers. It was not enough for them to show that they had been practising cow sacrifice on Bakrid. They had to establish that Islam required them to do so. Their claim under Article 25 failed because they could not establish this to the court’s satisfaction.
2025: A lamp on a disputed pillar
On November 3, 2025, the temple’s Executive Officer turned down a request to light the lamp on the stone pillar. He is an official of the State’s HR&CE Department, which administers the temple. He said that by custom the lamp was lit at the Deepa Mandapam. The temple’s sthanikars, its hereditary priests, certified that this was the practice laid down in the Agamas, the scriptures that govern temple worship.
The petitioners then went to the Madurai Bench of the Madras High Court with writ petitions. A writ petition is a direct request to a High Court to enforce a legal or constitutional right, and it is usually decided on documents, without a full trial.
The lead petitioner, Rama Ravikumar, is described in several news reports as the founder of the Hindu Tamizhar Katchi, a Hindu activist outfit. The State, its HR&CE Department, and the dargah opposed the plea.
What the hill’s history says
There was little in the historical record to establish a custom of lighting the lamp at this particular pillar. In a suit filed in 1920 (O.S. No. 4 of 1920), the Subordinate Court at Madura ruled in 1923 that the temple owned almost the entire hill, while recognising the Muslim defendants’ ownership of the Nellithope area, the flight of steps leading to the mosque, and the top of the rock on which the mosque and its flagstaff stand. Although the Madras High Court reversed this ruling in 1926, the Privy Council restored the original judgment in 1931. Summarising those findings in his order of December 1, 2025, Justice Swaminathan himself recorded that Hindus had tried “to put up lights at the summit of the hillock on which the mosque stands” in 1862 and again in 1912. Both times, a magistrate stopped them because “it was not customary to put a light there”.
Whether those attempts were made at this very pillar is itself disputed. The single judge understood them to have taken place elsewhere, while the dargah, in its 1975 written statement, linked them to the stone pillar.
In 1996, in writ petition No. 18884 of 1994, the High Court directed that the temple light the lamp “ordinarily” at the traditional mandapam near the Uchi Pillaiyar shrine. The temple could allow another spot only with prior approval under the HR&CE Act, and only at least 15 metres from the dargah.
In 2014, two more writ petitions, one of them asking for a lamp to be lit at “the top of the hill”, were dismissed. The appeals against the dismissals failed in 2017.
December 2025: “not custom, but right”
On December 1, 2025, Justice G.R. Swaminathan allowed the petitions seeking permission to light the lamp at the top of the hill (W.P.(MD) No. 32317 of 2025 and connected cases). The State and the dargah had argued that the petitioners should first go before the HR&CE authorities and prove a custom of lighting the lamp at the pillar. The judge brushed that aside.
“The question is not one of custom. The question is one of right,” he wrote. Even if lighting the lamp at the pillar was not a custom, he held, it was necessary to assert the temple’s ownership of that part of the hill. He compared it to the High Court closing its own gates one day a year, so that the public cannot claim a right of way through them.
A worshipper’s right, he said, covers “not only ‘what is’ but also ‘what ought to be’”. The petitions were allowed about four weeks after the Executive Officer’s reply.
The lamp was not lit at the pillar that December. A prohibitory order was issued under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, the provision used to bar gatherings when trouble is feared. Justice Swaminathan quashed it on December 4, and contempt proceedings followed. A Division Bench later stayed those proceedings on March 17, 2026.
January 2026: The burden is turned around
On January 6, 2026, a Division Bench of Justices G. Jayachandran and K.K. Ramakrishnan upheld the single judge’s order (W.A.(MD) No. 3188 of 2025 and batch). This Bench did look at the Agamas, but it turned the question of proof around.
It read for itself the Saiva texts Thirumanthiram and Meikanda Sastramand said that “from our limited research” it could find no text requiring the lamp to be lit only directly above the deity. It treated the priests’ statements as hearsay.
Then it held that the State (including the HR&CE department) and the dargah had “failed to produce formidable evidence” that the Saiva Agamas forbid lighting the lamp at a place not directly above the deity in the sanctum. The court, not the temple’s own priests, decided what the scripture says.
What is particularly striking in this judgment is that the burden was placed on those opposing the petition. Instead of requiring the petitioners to establish their claim through scripture or custom, the court required the respondents to establish that the practice was prohibited.
The Bench also dismissed fears of communal trouble as an “imaginary ghost”. These findings are now on hold by order of the Supreme Court, but they are the reasoning on which the lighting of the lamp was first ordered.
Same hill, a different rule
Earlier, in 2025, the High Court dealt with another religious practice on the very same hill.
The dargah says it has long held a Kandoori, a feast at which animals are sacrificed and the meat is shared. On December 25, 2024, the police stopped a group carrying a goat up the hill for the ritual, and on December 31 the Revenue Divisional Officer told the dargah to go to a civil court. Writ petitions seeking a ban on animal sacrifice on the hill followed (W.P.(MD) No. 2277 of 2025 and connected cases).
On June 24, 2025, a two-judge Bench gave a split verdict. Justice J. Nisha Banu would have dismissed the petitions. She found that animal sacrifice at the dargah had been “prevalent as a religious practice from time immemorial”, noted that the District Collector’s own report confirmed this, and held that under Article 25 the practice could not be stopped without a law.
Justice S. Srimathy disagreed. She directed the dargah to go to a civil court and prove that animal sacrifice, and prayers on Ramzan and Bakrid, were practised there before the 1920 suit. A civil suit is a full trial, with evidence and witnesses, and it can take years.
Justice Srimathy’s direction echoed the temple administration’s own position. The temple had told the court it would not permit any new ritual on the hill “not conducted prior to the date of Privy Council judgment” in the ownership dispute. No such cut-off was applied to the lamp on the pillar. Had it been, the claim would have struggled: nothing in the record showed a lamp was lit at the pillar before 1920, and the only recorded attempts to light the summit before then, in 1862 and 1912, were stopped as not customary.
The case then went to a third judge, Justice R. Vijayakumar. On October 10, 2025, he held that animal sacrifice was not an essential religious practice, since it was “not followed in all the Mosques/Dargahs”, and that it could not be allowed until a civil court ruled on the custom. In February 2026, the Supreme Court declined to interfere with that ruling.
Separately, on January 2, 2026, Justice Srimathy passed an interim order limiting the dargah’s Urus festival to 50 participants and barring animal sacrifice and non-vegetarian food anywhere from the foot of the hill to the top.
Within roughly six months, on one hill, the dargah was sent to a civil court to prove a century-old custom before it could hold its feast. The pillar petitioners, in a writ petition decided within a month, were told custom was not the question, and the other side was then asked to disprove a scriptural bar.
The point was made before the Supreme Court too, LiveLaw reported. Senior Advocate Huzefa Ahmadi, appearing for the dargah, argued that a new custom must be established through a suit, not a writ petition. Senior Advocate Narender Hooda, appearing for a priest who supports the State, pointed out that the dargah had been refused permission for animal sacrifice, while the claim about the pillar was allowed in a writ petition.
Can these judgments be distinguished?
One possible distinction between the two cases concerns the ownership of the hill. On this view, Thirupparankundram is not an “essential practices” case at all. It is about property: who owns which part of the hill, who may climb it, and where the temple may assert the ownership it has held since the 1923 decree. Quareshi case was a challenge to a law that banned a practice; here no law banned anything, so the cases cannot be compared.
It is true that the Quareshi case concerned the validity of a law and that neither Bench of the High Court formally applied the essential religious practices test. But I do not think these differences are sufficient to distinguish the cases.
This dispute, too, began with the State saying no. An HR&CE official refused to light the lamp at the pillar, and the petitioners challenged that refusal, just as the butchers challenged a ban. Justice Swaminathan did mention the temple’s ownership, but he decided the case as “one of right”, the worshippers’ right.
The Division Bench treated it as a petition “seeking enforcement of a religious practice in protection of fundamental right”, grounded in Article 25(1). And if this really were a dispute over ownership, it would belong in a civil court. That is exactly where the dargah was sent over the Kandoori.
There is also an argument to be made under the HR&CE Act itself. Section 28(1) requires a temple to be run according to its usage, meaning its established ways. Section 63(e) lets the Joint Commissioner decide what “the established usage” of a temple is.
On this view, where the lamp is lit is simply a question of the temple’s usage under a statute, and the essential practices test has nothing to do with it.
Applied to this case, however, the argument works against the petitioners. The established usage at Thirupparankundram is the Deepa Mandapam. The 1996 order says the lamp is lit there “ordinarily”. The Executive Officer and the priests said the same, and the respondents told the court the pillar had not been used for more than a century.
Under the Act, anyone who wants to change that would have to prove a different usage before the Joint Commissioner. That is exactly what the State and the dargah asked for, and exactly what the High Court refused. “The question is not one of custom,” the single judge replied, and the Division Bench held that the Section 63(e) route was “neither an alternate remedy nor an efficacious remedy”.
In fact, if the dispute is examined purely as a question of established usage under the HR&CE Act, the reasoning adopted by the High Court becomes even more difficult to justify. And on the same hill, a dispute over custom, with no law under challenge, was enough for the third judge to apply the essential practices test against the dargah.
Another question is whether the Division Bench was justified in placing the burden on the State. It could be argued that the court only held the State to its own claim: the State said the Agamas forbid lighting the lamp elsewhere, showed no text, and lost the point.
I would have found this reasoning more persuasive had the State been seeking to alter the existing practice at the temple. The lamp has been lit at the Deepa Mandapam by long usage, which the 1996 order recognised as the ordinary place. Normally, whoever asks a court to change a long-standing practice has to justify the change. Here the existing practice was made to justify itself from scripture, while the new demand did not have to show any past practice at all.
Some will point to Sabarimala, where the temple board, not the lawyers’ association that challenged the custom, had to show that keeping women out was an essential practice. The court refused to give the exclusion that status “in the absence of any scriptural or textual evidence”.
But the board bore that burden because it was the one claiming constitutional protection for a practice that kept others out. At Thirupparankundram, it was the petitioners who invoked Article 25; the State relied only on the temple’s established usage, which excludes no one. In my reading of Sabarimala, the burden falls on the party seeking constitutional protection for religious practice. At Thiruparankundram, that party was the petitioners.
The Supreme Court’s interim order, of course, has not decided the question of essential religious practices. But it does not rule the question out. Paragraph 15 says it does not “determine whether” the lighting “constitutes an essential religious practice”, which leaves the question open. Paragraph 8 places the dispute among the questions on Articles 25 and 26 now before a nine-judge bench.
The court has also put the High Court’s findings on hold, and paragraph 13 says the permission is “not in recognition or enforcement of any asserted customary, religious or proprietary right”. That is a sensible position for an interim, one-time order. But it also meant the lamp was to be lit before anyone had decided whether the petitioners had a right to it.
Questions have also been raised about why the HR&CE Department is opposing the judgment. Some may see this as politics, with the department appealing a judgment that protects its own temple’s ownership, as if a Waqf Board were to appeal a win for a dargah. But the judgment did not go in the department’s favour. It overturned the Executive Officer’s decision and ordered the lamp lit at a spot the department had opposed.
The temple’s ownership of the hill, settled in 1923, is not in question before the Supreme Court. And under the Act, HR&CE is the body required to uphold the temple’s established usage. Defending that usage in appeal is its legal duty, not a conflict of interest.
Coming back to the Quareshi case, it is true that much of the judgment dealt with cattle preservation and livestock economics under Article 48, the directive principle on protecting cattle. But the religious claim was still decided by the court’s own reading of a legal text, and Abhinav Chandrachud argues that the economic reasoning gave a secular face to a decision about faith.
What consistency would require
Broadly, the court has two approaches open to it, and whichever it eventually adopts, I would argue that it must be applied consistently across religions.
The first is to hold every claimant to the same burden. A claim that rests on custom, as both the Kandoori and the lamp did, would go to a civil court or to the HR&CE Joint Commissioner, who under Section 63(e) of the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959, decides “the established usage” of a temple, and the claimant would prove the custom. A claim for protection under Article 25 would require the claimant to show the practice is essential to the faith, as the butchers and the dargah were made to.
These are different inquiries, but the burden in each should fall the same way, whoever is asking. The dargah faced both; the lamp petitioners faced neither.
The second is to give a community’s sincere belief real weight. In the Ayodhya title suit (M. Siddiq v. Mahant Suresh Das, (2020) 1 SCC 1), the court accepted that Hindu worshippers genuinely believe Ram was born at the disputed site, without ruling on whether that belief is historically true. That was not an Article 25 ruling, but it shows the courts can take a community’s faith at its word. If that respect is to be given, the Bakrid sacrifice and the Kandoori feast are entitled to it as much as the lamp.
I cannot see any constitutional justification for demanding proof of essentiality from one religious community while dispensing with that requirement for another.
Where this goes next
The Supreme Court’s own order points to where this can be settled. Paragraph 8 notes that these questions overlap with the Sabarimala reference before a nine-judge Constitution Bench, which heard arguments on the essential practices test from April 2026 and reserved its judgment on May 14.
One of the questions before that bench is how far courts can go in deciding what is essential to a religion. Judges of the court have voiced the same unease before. In the 2018 Sabarimala judgment, Justice D.Y. Chandrachud wrote that the essential practices inquiry had “led the court to don a theological mantle”, and Justice Indu Malhotra, dissenting, warned against courts judging religious practices by their own idea of what is rational. Thirupparankundram gives it a concrete case: will courts test every faith by the same measure?
Also Read | Thiruparankundram controversy: Unholy fight over holy ritual
There is another detail worth noting about the composition of these Benches. Justice Aravind Kumar sat on the Bench that, in February 2026, declined to interfere with the Kandoori restrictions, and on the Bench that allowed the lamp on November 20. He is also a member of the nine-judge Sabarimala Bench.
This is no reflection on the judge. The February order declined to disturb a High Court ruling, and the November order is a one-time arrangement that expressly decides nothing. But it does mean that a judge who has heard both sides of this hill sits on the Bench now answering the questions of law on essential practices referred from the Sabarimala review. The review petitions themselves will be decided only after it rules.
When the Supreme Court takes up the matter again in January, I hope it addresses the difference in the standards of proof demanded in these cases. A person approaching an Indian court under Article 25 should not have to worry that the burden of proving a religious practice will depend on the religion they belong to.
R. Vanchinathan is a Chennai-based lawyer and the author of two Tamil books on law, including one on India’s new criminal codes. He worked as a Research Officer with the High-Level Committee on Union-State Relations, chaired by Justice Kurian Joseph and constituted by the Government of Tamil Nadu. The author is not Advocate S. Vanchinathan, who is counsel in the Thirupparankundram litigation. Views are personal.

title: Tamil Nadu's dissolution of Kurian Committee raises questions on federalism
description: The TVK government's decision to dissolve the Kurian Committee leaves its work on Centre-State relations unfinished and raises questions about its commitment to federalism.
author: R. Vanchinathan
content:
Praveen Chakravarty’s “A committee ain’t the cause”, published on November 18 in The New Indian Express, defends the Tamil Nadu government’s decision to dissolve the High-Level Committee on Union-State Relations chaired by Justice Kurian Joseph. His case is that a committee is a tool, federalism is the cause, and the cause will outlive the tool. It helps to know who is making this defence. Chakravarty is a Congress MP who entered the Rajya Sabha in June with backing from the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK). In other words, he is defending the government that gave him a seat in Parliament. My own stake is plain: I was a Research Officer on the Kurian Committee until the evening it was dissolved.
The Kurian Committee was asked to examine the Constitution provision by provision, along with the laws and policies that govern Union-State relations, and to recommend measures to secure “utmost autonomy” for the States without prejudice to the unity of the country. Part I was submitted on schedule on February 16, with 10 chapters and roughly 100 recommendations. Part II was about 60 per cent complete, and it covered emergency provisions, Central agencies, and the legislative, administrative, and fiscal relations between the Union and the States. Chakravarty has argued that since Part I is in the public domain, little is lost, but that is not true. In fact, the depth of Part I showed what the committee could have done had it been allowed to continue.
Chakravarty is right that a body created by executive order can be dissolved by one, but it was not the legality of the dissolution that was in question, but its prudence. Equally, the precedents he cites, the DMK replacing the members of the Child Rights Commission in 2022, and Kerala closing the Loka Kerala Sabha, do not fit the argument. In the former case, the standing commission can keep working with new members; and the latter is about an expatriate forum, not a research committee.
Also, the manner of shutting down the commission was not honest. After the TVK took office in May, Minister Vanni Arasu spoke in the Assembly on May 13 against closing the committee. The committee was asked to continue but with one condition: the Secretary and Research Officer, a former Registrar of the University of Madras and a respected economist who had served on the State Planning Commission, was asked to leave because the government doubted his political leanings. Despite his leaving, the committee was dissolved just six months later. The committee’s staff were removed one by one: the office assistants and accountant in August, and the translator in October. When the dissolution order came on the evening of November 6, ahead of a long weekend, it did not seem to be issued by a government that was sure of its reasons.
Chakravarty’s sharpest charge is that the political associations of the members raised doubts about their neutrality. The member whose family ties he alludes to, Prof. M. Naganathan, resigned on May 4, six months before the dissolution. The remaining member, K. Ashok Vardhan Shetty, is a retired IAS officer who has served governments of every stripe. Working closely with any Chief Minister is what senior civil servants do. The committee chair was a former Supreme Court judge; was his neutrality also suspect?
A fairer test of the committee might be to see how its work was received. Justice J. Chelameswar called Part I timely and scholarly. Advocates Gautam Bhatia, Faizan Mustafa, and Sanjay Hegde commended it. Two serving BJP Union Ministers wrote in praise of it. As did sitting judges of four High Courts, a former Election Commissioner, and a former Union Finance Secretary. Chakravarty’s own colleagues in the Congress offered warm praise: Siddaramaiah said Karnataka shared the concerns expressed in Part I, while Mani Shankar Aiyar urged that its work be followed up, regardless of the outcome of the Tamil Nadu election. That the DMK cited the report in its campaign is not enough to counter this.
The government’s main defence, which Chakravarty unquestioningly accepts, is that the State Law Commission duplicates the committee’s work. That, however, is not the case. The Law Commission, which has been reconstituted every three years since 1994 on inherited terms, carries Centre-State relations as one line in a general brief on law reform.
The dissolution order also calls the committee non-statutory, but so is the Law Commission.
The dissolution order and Chakravarty’s article seem to indicate that it is only a question of files being transferred. The rigour, however, might not be that easy to replicate. The committee strove to ensure that no recommendation in Part I contradicted another; equally, the committee was careful that nothing in Part II would collide with Part I. Keeping 100-odd proposals across 25 chapters consistent with each other is a Herculean task, and only a team that carries the whole design in its head can do it.
Moreover, handing the work of a former Supreme Court judge to another body headed by a former High Court judge appears to this writer to be a needless slight to Justice Kurian Joseph.
There are two situations in which a committee’s work is rightly handed over to someone else. One is when the committee has not worked and has missed its deadlines. The other is when its output is poor and has been badly received. Neither applies here. Indeed, it was the exact opposite. The report was delivered on time, and it was praised across party lines. One wonders if perhaps that was the problem. The committee would ordinarily have delivered Part II by May 2027. Now, handing over the work to a body with no team, no timetable, and no deadline is a reliable way to ensure the report never lands.
Minister with no jurisdiction
There is also the question that Chakravarty avoids: Who wanted this? The committee came under the Public (Law and Order-F) Department, which reports to the Chief Minister. Yet, when the decision to dissolve it drew criticism, it was Law Minister C.T.R. Nirmal Kumar who responded, even though his department had nothing to do with the committee. The government’s own order names the Secretary, Public Department, as our single point of contact; the Law Department appears only in the copy list. Nirmal Kumar’s name surfaced first in September, in media reports of pressure on Justice Kurian Joseph to resign.
In his six months in office, the Chief Minister did not meet Justice Joseph even once; neither has he commented on the issue since. Nirmal Kumar came to the TVK through the AIADMK, after years in the BJP. Meanwhile, a prominent political voice that welcomed the dissolution was the BJP Tamil Nadu’s chief spokesperson, Narayanan Thirupathy. It is pertinent to ask why a Minister with no jurisdiction was so invested in ending a committee on federal distribution of powers, and why is the Chief Minister silent?
A question for the Congress
Even more puzzling is Chakravarty’s defence. His party fights the BJP on the subject of federalism; his party leader resolutely reminds Parliament that India is a Union of States. Yet here is a Congress MP lending his pen to a decision driven by a former BJP man and cheered on by the BJP. Does the party high command have anything to say about its member’s stance? One may fairly ask whether federalism for the Congress is a matter of principle or convenience.
Chakravarty says federalism belongs to no party. I agree. That is exactly why the committee should have been allowed to finish its task. Its recommendations would serve every State, including one headed by a TVK government. Today, nobody asks which party appointed the Rajamannar Committee. They read its report.
A committee is not the cause. But a cause with nobody doing the work is only a slogan.
R. Vanchinathan was a Research Officer with the High-Level Committee on Union-State Relations (Justice Kurian Joseph Committee), Government of Tamil Nadu.

title: Who gets to tax Google? India’s fight for a fair share of the global digital economy
description: Digital platforms can earn from Indian users without a physical presence. They resemble a 'shop with no door'. Customers and revenue are present, but the old rules struggle to identify a taxable entrance. Tax treaties can further restrict rights that domestic law might otherwise provide. | OpIndia News
author: Divyansh Tiwari
content:
A trade permit helped turn a dispute in Bengal into war in 1763. More than two centuries later, India’s digital tax debate raises a similar question, who decides the rules when income is earned in one country and booked in another?
A privilege granted by Mughal emperor Farrukhsiyar in 1717 was stretched beyond its purpose by the East India Company, disadvantaging local merchants. The EIC misused the dastaks, or duty-free trade passes and gained an unfair advantage over local tradesmen. Mir Qasim, the Nawab of Bengal, abolished inland duties for everyone. In March 2025, India scrapped its six per cent equalisation levy on online advertising payments to non-residents. The question endured: should the country whose market generates income have a right to tax it?
A distinction has to be made between source-based taxation, where income is generated, and residence-based taxation, where a company is headquartered or managed. Rules generally require a foreign business to have a permanent establishment, an office, branch, factory or dependent agent, before its profits can be taxed locally. Digital platforms can earn from Indian users without a physical presence. They resemble a ‘shop with no door’. Customers and revenue are present, but the old rules struggle to identify a taxable entrance. Tax treaties can further restrict rights that domestic law might otherwise provide.
The historical section traces international tax rules through British influence over Indian tariffs, including the 1896 debate over cotton duties and excise taxes, the Ottoman Public Debt Administration’s collection of revenues after default, and the League of Nations’ 1920s work that favoured residence-based taxation. The comparison with colonial capitulations concerns fiscal autonomy, it does not equate them with modern tax treaties.
India’s own record also warrants scrutiny. Under the 1982 India-Mauritius treaty, certain gains on Indian shares could be taxed only in Mauritius, where they often went untaxed; the Supreme Court upheld the relevant CBDT circular in the 2003 Azadi Bachao Andolan case. After the Court ruled in 2012 that Vodafone’s offshore transaction was not taxable under the law as it stood, Parliament amended the law retrospectively. Vodafone and Cairn pursued arbitration. India repealed the tax in 2021 and issued refunds. Later treaty changes and the 2026 Tiger Global ruling sought to close parts of the Mauritius route and clarify treaty eligibility.
The world of the digital economy is the real test now for taxation rules. Indian users’ searches, clicks and online behaviour help platforms target advertising and create value. It separates data sovereignty into protection, control and value, arguing that taxation should focus on where value is created, not where a server stores information. India’s significant economic presence test recognises digital activity without a physical office, although treaties can limit it. The equalisation levy risked double taxation, trade friction and higher advertising costs for Indian businesses. OECD initiatives, Pillar One and Pillar Two, offered alternatives, but disputes over profit allocation and the 2026 US carve out raised questions about equal treatment.
The UN tax convention was first advanced by African countries over similar concerns in 2022. India supported a process intended to move negotiations from the OECD’s 38-member forum to a member-state-led UN forum. The United States withdrew in February 2025. Drafts released in July 2026 covered a framework convention and protocols on cross-border services and tax disputes. As the next round of talks for the convention approaches, India’s priorities at Nairobi should be stronger source country taxing rights for specified digital and cross-border services, predictable dispute resolution, and an equal place in global rule-making.
The article tests these proposals against six objections. A deal without the United States, effects on Indian companies abroad, data protectionism, investor uncertainty, gross versus net taxation, and the UN’s slow pace. These concerns require safeguards, sensible thresholds, double-tax relief and transparent procedures, not a return to a narrower rule-making club. The aim is to make stronger taxing rights compatible with certainty for businesses and fair treatment abroad.
In Kalidasa’s Raghuvamsha, King Dilipa’s tax system is described as the sun drawing moisture and returning it as rain. Taxation should work in the same spirit: value drawn from a country’s people and markets should help sustain public goods. India is not asking for special treatment. It is asking for rules that work both ways.
Read the full article here on Chapter 1 Magazine.

title: Fifth S-400 System To Guard Pakistan Border After Russian Delivery In Early 2027: Report
description: India will station its next S-400 air defence system along the border with Pakistan once Russia delivers it by February 2027, Hindustan Times reported
author: Arun Dhital
content:
News Brief
Arun Dhital
Nov 27, 2026 | Updated 02:05 PM GMT+5:30
Save & read from anywhere!
Bookmark stories for easy access on any device or the Swarajya app.
India will station its next S-400 air defence system along the border with Pakistan once Russia delivers it by February 2027, Hindustan Times reported.
The fifth unit, expected to arrive in January or February 2027, will complete the $5.43-billion agreement India and Russia signed in 2018 for five S-400 systems. Citing senior military sources, the newspaper said a team of Indian officials will travel to Russia in December to inspect the system before it is dispatched.
The long-range S-400 can track and shoot down hostile aircraft, missiles and drones, and is reported to have a range of up to 400 km.
India has so far received four of these systems. Three are positioned along the western front facing Pakistan, while the fourth is based in the eastern sector.
The S-400 played a significant part in Operation Sindoor in May 2025, when India struck terror infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir in response to the Pahalgam terror attack.
The S-400 Triumf (Sudarshan Chakra in India) is a mobile, long-range surface-to-air missile (SAM) system developed by Russia's Almaz-Antey. Entered into Russian service in 2007, it is designed to detect and destroy aircraft, drones, cruise missiles, and ballistic missiles within a 400 km radius.

title: India's Carrier-Building Capability May Die The Same Slow Death As Its Submarine Lines
description: In July 2022, Cochin Shipyard Limited (CSL) handed Indian Naval Ship (INS) Vikrant over to the Navy and was left with an empty berth where India's fir
author: Prakhar Gupta
content:
Defence
Prakhar Gupta
Nov 27, 2026 | Updated 01:35 PM GMT+5:30
Save & read from anywhere!
Bookmark stories for easy access on any device or the Swarajya app.
In July 2022, Cochin Shipyard Limited (CSL) handed Indian Naval Ship (INS) Vikrant over to the Navy and was left with an empty berth where India's first home-built aircraft carrier had taken shape. In a statement marking the handover, the shipyard noted that the skills built on the carrier would serve the country well "if sustained".
More than four years later, the government has yet to act on that warning. The second Indigenous Aircraft Carrier, or IAC-2, has been argued over, shrunk, and repackaged, but it has not been ordered. It has yet to receive even the Acceptance of Necessity, the first formal approval in India's defence procurement process.
The cost of this delay goes well beyond the number of carriers the Navy operates. India has twice built the hard-won ability to make conventional submarines and twice let it wither for want of a follow-on order. The carrier line now faces the same fate, and the decision that would prevent it cannot wait much longer.
How The Second Carrier Shrank
For most of the last decade, successive Navy chiefs described IAC-2 as a 65,000-tonne ship, sometimes called INS Vishal, that would carry 55 to 60 aircraft. It would also give the Navy the three carriers it had long sought, so that two could be at sea while the third was in maintenance. In December 2019, Admiral Karambir Singh, then the Navy chief, said the service needed a carrier of that size.
Two months later, the plan ran into India's first Chief of Defence Staff (CDS). General Bipin Rawat argued that with two carriers already in hand and the submarine fleet dwindling, "our priority should be for submarines". In a May 2020 interview he went further, warning that carriers, as surface ships, could be "knocked off by missiles" and that the Indian military was not an expeditionary force. He also pointed to a carrier's hidden costs in crew, aircraft, and escorts, and suggested that the Navy might have to choose between IAC-2 and nuclear-powered attack submarines.
The argument outlived Rawat, who died in a helicopter crash in December 2021. Those who favoured submarines went on saying that carriers were expensive targets poorly suited to grey-zone threats, and that the same money would buy more in nuclear submarines and underwater drones.
The Navy gave ground one step at a time. In December 2022, three months after Vikrant was commissioned, Admiral R Hari Kumar, then the Navy chief, said IAC-2 might be a copy of Vikrant rather than the larger ship long promised. In late 2023, the Defence Procurement Board gave in-principle approval to a roughly 45,000-tonne repeat costing about Rs 40,000 crore, leaving the final call to the Defence Acquisition Council (DAC), which the Defence Minister chairs.
In October 2024, the government cleared the construction of two indigenous nuclear-powered attack submarines. By February 2025, the Navy had set aside its three-carrier plan for the time being, and IAC-2 was recast as a replacement for the ageing, Russian-origin INS Vikramaditya rather than an addition to the fleet.
Why The Navy Would Not Choose
Through all of this, the Navy refused to accept that it had to pick between carriers and submarines, and its first technical argument was about air cover. A submarine can deny an enemy the use of the sea, but it cannot shield a fleet from air attack or keep watch over a wide stretch of ocean. Naval officers argued in 2020 that aircraft flying from Indian airfields could not fill that gap, because their usefulness falls away the farther the fleet sails from the coast. "Air operations are integral to naval operations. Airpower at sea is required here and now," Admiral Karambir Singh, then the Navy chief, said that December.
Vice Admiral Pradeep Chauhan, a retired naval officer, explained what that phrase means in practice. Aerial refuelling can carry shore-based fighters out to a distant fleet, he wrote in 2021, but it cannot put them overhead the moment a threat appears. Only fighters already on a carrier's deck can do that.
The second argument was about survivability, the critics' strongest charge, and here the Navy's case rests on the size of the ocean and the speed of the ship. Admiral Nirmal Verma, Navy chief from 2009 to 2012, pointed out that a carrier can move 600 nautical miles a day, which forces an enemy to search about a million square nautical miles of ocean before it can aim a missile. Chauhan calculated in 2014 that a warship's radar covers only about 0.2 per cent of the Arabian Sea, so watching all of it at once would take some 471 ships. An attacker has to find, identify, track, and strike a carrier, and each step exposes the patrol aircraft and tankers the attacker depends on to the carrier's own fighters. In March 2025, Admiral Dinesh K Tripathi, Navy chief from 2024 until May this year, called the image of the carrier as a sitting duck "a misnomer", since a carrier sails at the centre of a battle group, ringed by destroyers, frigates, submarines, and its own air cover.
Among retired officers, Admiral Arun Prakash, a former Navy chief, rejected Rawat's preference for shore-based aircraft in November 2020 and argued that if China ever sent three carriers into the Indian Ocean, "aircraft carriers are the only answer to such a situation." Commodore Srikant Kesnur, a former head of the Navy's Maritime Warfare Centre, wrote in August 2022 that setting carriers against submarines was a comparison of "apples versus oranges". A submarine's great strength is stealth, he argued, while a carrier can pressure or deter an adversary before a war as well as during one.
The Navy's strongest argument came in May 2025, when, during Operation Sindoor, it sent the Vikrant carrier battle group into the northern Arabian Sea. According to the Navy, the deployment kept Pakistan's naval and air units in a defensive posture, mostly inside harbours or close to their own coast. Tripathi drew the lesson in May this year, a day before he retired. "Aircraft carriers remain central to maritime power projection, sea control, deterrence and strategic influence," he said.
The Navy has now settled on what it wants. In January this year, Admiral Tripathi confirmed that a repeat order of Vikrant was under active consideration, modified with lessons from the first ship's design, construction, and early service, and with capabilities the Navy expects to need in future. The design exists, and the yard that built the first ship is ready to build the second. CSL has even built a 310-metre dry dock, inaugurated in January 2024 at a cost of about Rs 1,800 crore, that can handle carriers of up to 70,000 tonnes.
What the project lacks is a decision, which the Navy had hoped to secure in 2026 but which has not come with the year nearly over. In February, a brokerage tracking CSL noted that the shipyard's order book had stayed largely flat since 2021-22 and blamed the deferral of IAC-2. A market analysis published in April did not expect the carrier to be ordered before 2029.
That timeline should worry the Navy, because 2027 is only weeks away and Vikramaditya is ageing. The carrier was commissioned in 2013, but it was rebuilt on a Soviet hull launched in 1982. Naval sources said late last year that it would likely be retired around 2037, unless an assessment due around 2035 found it worth a mid-life upgrade (MLU) that could keep it at sea for another 15 years. The same sources cautioned that such an upgrade might come with huge price tag. If the Navy decides against it, Vikramaditya has about a decade of service left in the Navy.
A new carrier will need at least that long, since naval officers have said a carrier takes 10 to 12 years from the date of sanction to enter service, and Vikrant took 13 years from the laying of its keel in 2009 to its commissioning. CSL believes a repeat order would move faster, but even on the Navy's own estimate, a carrier sanctioned in 2027 would join the fleet between 2037 and 2039. One sanctioned in 2029 would arrive between 2039 and 2041. In either case, the Navy faces years with a single carrier, which means no carrier at all whenever that ship is in refit. India has lived through this before, when Vikramaditya was in a long refit from early 2021 and Vikrant was not yet ready, and the Navy went more than a year without an operational carrier.
The Submarine Lesson India Keeps Ignoring
The deeper cost of the delay is harder to see, because building Vikrant created an industrial base that India did not have before. When supplies of warship-grade steel from Russia stopped, the Navy, the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), and the Steel Authority of India Limited (SAIL) developed an Indian equivalent, called DMR 249A. Some 550 Indian vendors, nearly 100 of them small and medium enterprises, supplied the project, and about 76 per cent of the ship was indigenous. In January this year, Madhu S Nair, who led the shipyard as its chairman through Vikrant's delivery, retired after 37 years at the yard. Kesnur had warned of exactly this in 2022, when he urged the government to start the next carrier quickly, before retiring engineers took their expertise with them as they had from submarine building in the 1990s.
India has seen this happen twice before with conventional submarines. In 1981, it signed a contract with Howaldtswerke-Deutsche Werft (HDW) of West Germany for four Type 1500 submarines. The first two were built in Germany, and the other two were assembled at Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders Limited (MDL) in Mumbai and commissioned in 1992 and 1994. They were meant to start an Indian submarine-building industry, but allegations of kickbacks led to HDW's blacklisting, costs soared as the Deutsche Mark strengthened, and the option to build more was abandoned. After INS Shankul was commissioned in 1994, MDL had no submarine to build for more than a decade.
The skills built under the German programme drained away in those years. When MDL began building the French-designed Scorpene under a 2005 contract, much of that expertise had to be rebuilt. The first boat, INS Kalvari, was due in 2012 but was commissioned only in December 2017, the Navy's first new conventional submarine in 17 years. Vice Admiral Arun Kumar Singh, a former Commander-in-Chief of the Eastern Naval Command, has explained why such skills are perishable. A submarine welder who is out of practice for more than three months "has to be recertified", he said, because a submarine's survival depends on the welds of its pressure hull.
The lesson should have stuck, because the Navy's 1999 plan for two parallel production lines and 24 submarines by 2030 was built around keeping construction continuous. In November 2016, Defence Minister Manohar Parrikar warned that the skilled workforce built on the Scorpenes had to be retained. "To retain it, we need to have more construction of submarines," he said.
Parrikar's warning went unheeded even as MDL grew more capable, and by 2022 its chairman was saying the yard had needed no French help after the second Scorpene. Yet since the last of them, INS Vaghsheer, was commissioned in January 2025, the line has had no new submarine to build. Project 75 India, the follow-on that was meant to run alongside the Scorpenes, has drifted since its first approval in 2010. When its contract is finally signed, India will be going back to Germany for a submarine design. Its partner will be ThyssenKrupp Marine Systems (TKMS), which took over HDW in 2005, so the programme returns India to the same Kiel yard it walked away from after the kickback scandal. In October this year, the Defence Secretary said the deal for its six boats was in its final stages, but the first boat will arrive only about seven years after the contract is signed. A proposal for three more Scorpenes, first put to MDL in August 2023, remains "under consideration".
South Korea started only a few years later, with the same German firm, and took the opposite path. In the late 1980s, it signed with HDW for Type 209 submarines, bought the first boat from Germany, and built the rest in its own yards. It then moved on to nine larger Type 214 boats with air-independent propulsion, and after building some 18 submarines without a break, it had the skills to design its own. The first of these 3,000-tonne boats, the Dosan Ahn Changho of the KSS-III class, was commissioned in 2021, and the South Korean Navy now operates 21 submarines across three classes.
Korea has also become an exporter, beginning in 2011, when Indonesia ordered three submarines from a Korean yard. That order made South Korea only the fifth country, after Britain, France, Russia, and Germany, to export one, and Jakarta signed for three more in 2019. This year, the Dosan Ahn Changho sailed some 14,000 kilometres to Canada to compete for a 12-boat order. Canada chose TKMS in July, in what Prime Minister Mark Carney called "a difficult, close decision between two highly qualified suppliers". South Korea now competes for orders against the German firm that taught it, while India, which began with the same firm, is going back to it for a design.
The Decision Cannot Wait
The carrier line now stands where the submarine line stood in the mid-1990s and again in 2025. The ship has been delivered and the yard has proven itself, and the people who know how to build a carrier are still there, though they will not remain there for long.
The Navy, former officers, and the carrier's performance in Operation Sindoor have already made the case for IAC-2. The Navy has accepted a smaller ship and a replacement role to make that case easier to approve. What remains is for the Defence Acquisition Council and the Cabinet to clear the project and for the Ministry of Defence to sign a contract with CSL. A repeat order now would keep the yard's carrier skills, its supplier base, and the Navy's design team intact, and it would leave room to build a larger third carrier later.
If the decision slips to the end of the decade, CSL may have to relearn how to build a carrier, much as MDL had to relearn how to build a submarine, and the Navy will pay for that lesson a second time.
Prakhar Gupta (@prakharkgupta) is a senior editor at Swarajya.

title: India To Manufacture Bullet Train Wheels Domestically At Ramkrishna Titagarh's Chennai Facility
description: High-precision wheels for India's bullet trains will be manufactured at Ramkrishna Titagarh Rail Wheels' facility in Chennai, Railway Minister Ashwini
author: Swarajya Staff
content:
Infrastructure
Swarajya Staff
Nov 27, 2026 | Updated 01:17 PM GMT+5:30
Save & read from anywhere!
Bookmark stories for easy access on any device or the Swarajya app.
High-precision wheels for India's bullet trains will be manufactured at Ramkrishna Titagarh Rail Wheels' facility in Chennai, Railway Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw announced on Thursday (26 November).
The manufacturing of the bullet train wheels at the facility, located at Gummidipoondi near Chennai, will mark a significant step towards domestic manufacturing of critical high-speed rail components.
The minister described this as part of a push to build every piece of these trains domestically.
Vaishnaw visited the RKTR Forged wheel factory at Gummidipoondi during his Tamil Nadu tour yesterday.
The move aims at reducing Indian Railways' import dependence by inviting industry to set up facilities to produce wheels for semi-high speed trains like Vande Bharat and high-speed bullet trains.
The manufacturing plant at Gummudipoondi is set to become Asia's second largest forged wheel manufacturing plant with a capacity to produce 228,000 forged wheels every year.
RKTR signed the contract for manufacturing and supply of forged wheels under the Atma Nirbhar Bharat scheme, with total supply of around 15.40 lakh wheels over twenty years.
Trial production has started at the Chennai plant, with 300 trial forged wheels currently under Indian Railways inspection, and partial production planned from November or December 2026.
The facility is a joint venture between Ramkrishna Forgings and Titagarh Rail Systems, representing a major milestone in India's railway self-reliance initiative.
India announced eight bullet train projects, with one corridor under construction and new lines like Bengaluru-Chennai and Hyderabad-Chennai announced in the latest budget.
The Ramkrishna Titagarh Rail Wheels factory in Gummidipoondi is ready to produce high-strength wheels for export to Europe.

title: Case of aggravated contempt: ASI to SC on Deepam row
description: The Archaeological Survey of India has accused the Tamil Nadu government of 'aggravated contempt' for obstructing its officials from lighting the Karthigai Deepam at the disputed Deepathoon pillar, defying a Supreme Court order. The Supreme Court has asserted that its orders cannot be diluted, while the Tamil Nadu government has apologised, blaming temple authorities.
author: Text Feed
content:
The Supreme Court is addressing allegations of "aggravated contempt" against the Tamil Nadu government by the ASI for failing to comply with an order to light the Karthigai Deepam at the disputed Deepathoon pillar, highlighting the judiciary's firm stance on its directives.
Key Points
- The ASI accused the Tamil Nadu government of "aggravated contempt" for preventing its officials from accessing the Deepathoon pillar for Karthigai Deepam.
- The Supreme Court stated its orders cannot be diluted and warned against creating constitutional chaos.
- The Tamil Nadu government apologised to the Supreme Court on Wednesday, blaming temple authorities for the non-compliance.
- The Karthigai Deepam was lit only at its customary Uchipillayar mandapam on November 24, not at the disputed Deepathoon pillar as ordered by the SC.
- The Supreme Court is confining its hearing to the non-compliance of its November 20 order.
The ASI told the Supreme Court on Friday that the Tamil Nadu government committed "aggravated contempt" by not allowing its officials to go near the Karthigai Deepam at the disputed Deepathoon pillar, with the top court making it clear that its orders could not be diluted.
A bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M Pancholi said it would set right anybody trying to create constitutional chaos.
ASI Alleges 'Aggravated Contempt'
Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for the Archaeological Survey of India, told the bench that the ASI was informed by the temple trustees that no instruction regarding their entry was received from higher officials.
"The ASI team was halted at a certain point by the local police at 3 pm and was not permitted to go near the lamp," Mehta said.
"My respectful submission is... this is a case of aggravated contempt and administrative arrogance. The government has been opposing from the beginning," the SG said.
Mehta submitted that the lamp should be lit at Deepathoon before the contemnors were heard.
"My request on behalf of the ASI is that, in view of the admitted position that the order is not complied with. Before the contemnors are heard, they should purge themselves of contempt by ensuring the lamp is lit.
"The way in which police had functioned leaves nothing to be said. There are videos available which show the entire premises was packed by police. My request is please ensure that ... (some) other agency monitors this," he said.
Arguments From Both Sides
Senior advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan, appearing for the Madurai Collector, contradicted Mehta's submission and said that ASI officials were consulted and multiple meetings were held with them.
He said the top court should first decide whether any prima facie contempt was committed.
Senior advocate Sidharth Luthra, appearing for the Madurai Police Commissioner, told the court that over 5,000 personnel were deployed to ensure no breach of law and order took place and prohibitory orders were passed.
"We will see whether you are shedding real or crocodile tears," the bench told the Madurai Police Commissioner.
Court Focuses On Non-Compliance
As the hearing commenced, the top court clarified that it would not go into the main matter and would confine itself to the non-compliance of its November 20 order permitting the lighting of the Karthigai Deepam lamp at Deepathoon as a one-time measure on November 24.
The court was hearing contempt petitions and other applications on the controversy surrounding the non-lighting of the ceremonial lamp at the disputed Deepathoon pillar.
Senior advocate S Guru Krishna Kumar, appearing for contempt petitioner Karthikeyan, submitted that the Tamil Nadu government had decided at the outset that it would not permit the lighting of the lamp and the preliminary report submitted by them was like a confession.
"The Collector was also to consult the ASI in this regard. The onus has been completely let down. The preliminary report is like a confession. They did everything except for the lamp being lit. The only reason is the board of trustees not giving permission. The board has never contested the matter. They are bound by the order of the court," he said.
The hearing is underway.
Tamil Nadu Government Apologises
On Wednesday, the Tamil Nadu government apologised to the top court over the non-lighting of the ceremonial lamp at Deepathoon and blamed the Arulmigu Subramaniaswamy temple authorities for it.
Despite the apex court's permission, the Karthigai Deepam was lit only at its customary Uchipillayar mandapam at Thirupparankundram on November 24 and not at Deepathoon.

title: 29 Women Rescued In Delhi Spa Raids
description: Delhi Police has successfully busted four alleged prostitution rackets operating from spa and massage centres in central Delhi, leading to the rescue of 29 women and the apprehension of 15 individuals, including spa owners, managers, and customers. The raids were conducted on Thursday after verifying intelligence through decoy customers.
author: Text Feed
content:
Delhi Police has successfully dismantled four alleged prostitution rackets operating under the guise of spa and massage centres in central Delhi, rescuing 29 women and apprehending 15 individuals.
Key Points
- Delhi Police busted four alleged prostitution rackets operating from spa and massage centres in central Delhi.
- Twenty-nine women were rescued during the operations on Friday.
- Fifteen individuals, including spa owners, managers, and customers, were apprehended.
- Raids were conducted on Thursday in Paharganj, Nabi Karim, and Karol Bagh after deploying decoy customers.

Delhi Police has busted four alleged prostitution rackets operating under the guise of spa and massage centres in central Delhi, rescuing 29 women, an official said on Friday.
Police Action Against Illegal Operations
Police also said that they have apprehended 15 people, including spa owners, managers and customers.
