title: Indian driver wins $1.3m in life-changing lottery prize
description: A truck driver's fortunes have changed overnight after he won a Diwali lottery in the northern Indian state of Punjab.
content:
Indian driver wins $1.3m in life-changing lottery prize
Baljinder Singh, a truck driver from the northern Indian state of Punjab, has won a 120m rupee [£978,000; $1.3m] lottery with a ticket that cost him just 500 rupees. But Singh says the big win won't change his life. He plans to carry on working as a truck driver. Meanwhile, celebrations are under way at his home, with family members distributing sweets to mark the win.

title: Catherine visits Mumbai maternity hospital on the last day of royal trip
description: The Prince and Princess of Wales ended their three-day trip to India on Wednesday, the couple's first international tour since 2022.
content:
Catherine visits Mumbai maternity hospital on the last day of royal trip
The Prince and Princess of Wales ended their three-day trip to India on Wednesday, the couple's first international tour since 2022.
Catherine visited a maternity hospital in Mumbai and was seen comforting a grieving mother who lost a baby after giving birth to premature twin girls.
William met actors Kareena Kapoor, Saif Ali Khan and filmmaker Karan Johar during a visit to a film production company.
The couple also met Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi, with a Kensington Palace spokesperson saying they discussed the "strength and importance of the UK–India bilateral relationship".

title: Fugitive gangsters’ list doesn’t end with Goldy Brar. Half dozen more wreak havoc from foreign soil
description: In the wake of an intensified crackdown in North America, ThePrint takes a look at some of the top fugitive gangsters who have been operating their criminal syndicates from abroad.
author: Mayank Kumar
content:
New Delhi: Gangster and designated terrorist Satinderjit Singh alias Goldy Brar returned to the top of Canada’s most-wanted list with a reward of up to 2,50,000 Canadian dollars for information about his whereabouts.
Similarly, the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) reiterated its most-wanted status and a bounty of up to $1 million for information on him. Days earlier, American authorities had detained a top member of his syndicate in a big breakthrough.
In the wake of an intensified crackdown in North America, ThePrint takes a look at some of the top fugitive gangsters apart from Brar, who have been operating their criminal syndicates from abroad.
Rohit Godara
Born as Rawat Das Swami in Rajasthan’s Bikaner district, Godara is identified as one of the key figures in the syndicate run by jailed gangster Lawrence Bishnoi and Brar. He is involved in more than two dozen cases of firing and murder related to extortion.
Criminal activities forced him to flee to Dubai on a fake passport in 2022. Godara works from Europe, as per police records. His rise to notoriety came after Sukhdev Singh Gogamedi, the president of a Karni Sena breakaway faction, was shot dead at his Jaipur residence in October 2023.
The footage of the chilling murder carried out by three shooters was captured on a CCTV camera installed at the residence. Hours later, a social media post appeared purportedly in Godara’s name, taking responsibility for the murder.
According to the records of police in Rajasthan and other northern states, Godara has at least 32 cases ranging from extortion to murder. The National Investigation Agency (NIA) also has a couple of cases against him, including the one on the Gogamedi killing.
The FBI alleged him to be heading the organised crime syndicate of Bishnoi and Brar in European countries. “Defendant GODARA directed the European operations of the Bishnoi OCG (Organised Crime Group). In their respective areas of control, as well as in other areas around the world, defendants SINGH and GODARA directed targeted killings, shootings, kidnappings, maimings, assaults, extortions, and drug trafficking,” the FBI documented in the indictment.
Harry Boxer
Like Godara, Boxer is a native of Rajasthan and original name is Harichand Jat. He comes from a farming background. Boxer had emerged as one of the top henchmen of the Bishnoi gang operating from the US.
His run came to an end earlier this month when the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detained him based on inputs from Indian agencies, including the Rajasthan Anti-Gangster Task Force (AGTF).
According to police records, Boxer graduated from a college in Bansur, prepared for recruitment examinations for the police, the Army, and the Staff Selection Commission (SSC), and later pursued boxing before allegedly transitioning to organised crime.
He fled abroad in 2023 using a fraudulently obtained passport, initially went to Dubai, then moved to the US via the Dominican Republic, and finally entered the US via the ‘Donkey Route’ across the Mexican border, settling in California.
Boxer rose to notoriety in August 2025 when an audio clip emerged in which he purportedly took responsibility for the shooting at comedian and television host Kapil Sharma’s cafe in Canada. This was followed by threats to producers, directors, and actors, urging them not to work with Bollywood actor Salman Khan, with whom the Bishnoi gang reportedly holds a grudge over the killing of blackbucks in 1998.
The gangster faces more than 30 cases, ranging from murder, attempt to murder and extortion, across Rajasthan, Delhi, Haryana and Maharashtra.
Goldy Dhillon
A native of Rajpura in Punjab’s Patiala district, Dhillon is also a top associate of the Lawrence Bishnoi-Goldy Brar crime syndicate. Based in Canada, Dhillon is accused of coordinating shooters and providing them logistical support for extortion-related firing as well as fatal shootings in North America.
His name cropped up in a probe related to more than two dozen cases of targeted killings as well as extortion in Canada, such as the firing on Kapil Sharma’s cafe as well as in his home state of Punjab.
While these gangsters are the main faces running the operations of the Bishnoi gang, its rivalry with the gang run by Armenia-based Lucky Patial is responsible for the majority of the bloodshed on the streets and in the organised crime syndicate.
Lucky Patial
A native of Chandigarh, Patial has emerged as the leader of the Bambiha gang, earlier run and led by slain gangster Davinder Bambiha, who was killed in a police encounter in 2016. He gained infamy in 2012 when he was booked for the murder of kabaddi player Saudagar Singh in Mohali. He was booked in another chilling murder of Akali Dal worker Gurjant Singh in 2014 in Mohali.
Patial was sentenced to life in 2015 but jumped parole. Around 2019, he fled the country and has moved between several countries, with the police tracing his last known location to Armenia.
The rivalry with Bishnoi is attributed as the reason for almost all gang rivalry killings in the northern states. His men took responsibility for the killing of Goldy Brar’s cousin Gurlal Brar in 2020 and then Youth Akali Dal leader Vicky Middukhera in 2021. This was followed by Bishnoi and Brar hatching a conspiracy to kill Punjabi singer Siddhu Moosewala in 2022.
According to police records, Patial runs his crime syndicate from Armenia, with the help of other foreign-based associates and more than 300 shooters in northern Indian states of Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan and Delhi.
Balwinder Singh Doni alias Doni Bal
Hailing from Beas in Punjab’s Amritsar district, Doni Bal has emerged as one of the top members of the Bambiha syndicate and has been responsible for several targeted killings in the Majha region.
In 2025, Bal and his operatives were implicated in the killing of kabaddi player and promoter Rana Balachauria in Mohali. His name came up last month in the killing of assistant sub-inspector Iqbal Singh, who was shot dead outside his residence at Tarn Taran’s Naushera Pannuan village.
Based in the UK, Bal has been working in tandem with Brazil-based Prabhdeep Singh alias Prabh Dasuwal and Gurvinder Singh alias Gurvinder Afridi, who was deported earlier this month.
Gangsters-turned-terrorists
While the abovementioned gangsters are calling the shots from abroad, carrying out killings and extortions through their operatives, several such fugitive gangsters have also been associated with the banned outfits such as the Babbar Khalsa International (BKI) and the Khalistan Tiger Force (KTF).
Arshdeep Singh Gill alias Arsh Dalla
Born at Dala village in Punjab’s Moga district, Gill has been in Canada since 2018. According to the Indian security agencies, Dalla met the now-slain chief of KTF and designated terrorist, Hardeep Singh Nijjar, at the Guru Nanak Sikh Gurdwara. After Nijjar’s killing in June 2023, Dalla rose to the de facto chief of KTF.
Dalla had around 70 cases against him, ranging from extortion, smuggling of weapons and narcotics and terror-related cases across several districts of Punjab, police dossiers show.
Designated as an individual terrorist, India had sought his provisional arrest in July 2023, which was declined by Canada.
Lakhbir Singh alias Landa
Landa has been one of the top associates of Pakistan-based chief of the Babbar Khalsa International, Harwinder Singh alias Rinda.
The native of Punjab’s Harike town fled India in 2017 and operates from Canada. Over time, as his command and control over the business of drugs and illegal arms increased, his rise to notoriety was marked by RPG attacks on a police station in Tarn Taran as well as the audacious attempt to carry out an explosion at the Punjab Police’s intelligence headquarters in Mohali in 2022.
The Punjab police trace the emergence of Landa’s criminal operations in the Majha region and a feud with rival gangs to a killing in May 2021 carried out by gangster Daya Singh alias Preet Sekhon.
Shiromani Akali Dal worker Amandeep Singh alias Aman Fauji and his associate Prabhjit Singh were shot dead by two car-borne men in May 2021. The Punjab Police had found that Landa had given Sekhon Rs 6 lakh for the killing. The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) had declared him an individual terrorist under the provisions of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, or the UAPA.
(Edited by Tony Rai)

title: How US ex-Dy Secy of State Strobe Talbott described post-Pokhran II reset in India-US ties in 2004
description: In 2004 Walk the Talk interview, US ex-Dy Secy of State Talbott recalled talks with Jaswant Singh, equation between Indira Gandhi & Henry Kissinger, PV Narasimha Rao & Bill Clinton.
author: Shekhar Gupta | Walk The Talk
content:
Strobe Talbott, former US Deputy Secretary of State and president of the Brookings Institution, was among the key figures involved in reshaping India-US relations at a particularly fraught moment in their shared history.
A reporter with Time magazine before entering government, Talbott accompanied then US Secretary of State Henry Kissinger on his 1974 visit to India, when relations between the two countries were strained by Cold War tensions and India’s nuclear ambitions.
In a 2004 episode of Walk the Talk, ThePrint Editor-in-Chief Shekhar Gupta spoke to Talbott about the thread of India-US relations, the 1998 nuclear tests, his talks with Jaswant Singh and the Clinton administration’s approach to India and Pakistan, Musharraf’s role in the peace process, and the threat posed by the proliferation of nuclear weapons.
Here is a complete transcript of the interview, edited for clarity:
Shekhar Gupta: Hello and welcome to Walk the Talk. I’m Shekhar Gupta, and my guest today, well, I can give you a long introduction: President of the Brookings Institution, former Deputy Secretary of State, one of the most respected writers, columnists and analysts on world affairs. Strobe Talbott, welcome to Walk the Talk.
Strobe Talbott: Thank you very much. And what a nice setting for us to be chatting here.
Shekhar Gupta: Knowing you as somebody who’s not just written about foreign affairs and given a new direction to so many ideas in the last quarter century, but as somebody who was a co-architect of a completely new Indo-US relationship.
Strobe Talbott: It’s wonderful to be back here.
Shekhar Gupta: And you’ve been an old traveller to India.
Strobe Talbott: It has been 30 years since I first came to India. It was in 1974. I was in your line of work as a reporter. I was accompanying Henry Kissinger when he came here to see Indira Gandhi in 1974.
Shekhar Gupta: A lot has changed since. Indira Gandhi and Henry Kissinger, those were very frosty days. I mean, as frosty as the weather today. Does it remind you of Washington?
Strobe Talbott: Yeah, but I remember the visit that he made quite well. There was actually quite a bit of mutual respect between them. I think the relations between Indira Gandhi and Henry Kissinger were better than the relations between India and the United States.
Shekhar Gupta: Or between Indira Gandhi and Nixon, for that matter.
Strobe Talbott: That’s for sure. Yes, absolutely.
Shekhar Gupta: But describe to me how exactly it was then, because in 30 years everything has changed completely. The year 1974 was Pokhran, the eve of the Emergency. It was a very different Mrs Gandhi in a very different India.
Strobe Talbott: Well, I think the big difference, of course, is that 1974 was still very much in the depths of the Cold War. And even though it was not literally the case, and shouldn’t have been the case, India and the United States ended up on opposite sides in the Cold War. That was the overall geopolitical context of what was not a good relationship for a very long time between our countries.
Shekhar Gupta: Well, Jaswant Singh said on this show some time back to me. I think the line that he quoted to me from Madeleine Albright, he said Madeleine said to me, “50 years in our relationship, the mice ate away.”
Strobe Talbott: Yeah exactly. I mean, there’s a phrase that’s come out of Washington in the last couple of years: “If you’re not with us, you’re against us.” But there was a little bit of that same attitude towards India going back to John Foster Dulles, when Prime Minister Nehru went to Bandung, was one of the co-founders of the Non-Aligned Movement.
In Washington, and particularly on the part of Secretary of State Dulles, the Non-Aligned Movement was seen as only slightly better than the other side in the Cold War. And India, in particular, was seen to be, to use a famous word, tilting more towards the Soviet Union than towards the United States.
Shekhar Gupta: Those were interesting years because I’ve read some of the stuff that Dulles has written, you know, stuff that’s been declassified by the State Department. I can see that he was truly fascinated by Nehru’s personality. In one place, for example, he writes a long note to Eisenhower on how Nehru had a tendency of getting excited in the middle of a conversation and climbing on the back of the sofa and sitting there. And he writes the whole three paragraphs in wonderment, saying, “How do you deal with this man?” Then there’s stuff from Eisenhower that says it’s quite well known that what works with Nehru is personal appeal, and not as much policy and ideology and stuff like that.
Strobe Talbott: Yes, but you know, Shekhar, President Eisenhower himself actually had a rather warm feeling towards India and Nehru. You may recall, indeed, that Eisenhower invited Nehru to his farm in Gettysburg. And while he didn’t make a great deal out of it publicly, Eisenhower wanted to have a somewhat better relationship.
Shekhar Gupta: That comes across because I think there are also descriptions of their discussions about China, on which Nehru had a very different take. But that’s a fact. Somehow India and the US have had a very different worldview over the past decades, except now, in the past five years or 10 years.
Strobe Talbott: Yeah. No, I think one of the reasons that President Clinton, whom I worked for for eight years, was so eager to have a better relationship with India was that he sensed the end of the Cold War created an opportunity that none of his predecessors had. He would have liked to have initiated a quantum improvement in the US-India relationship during his first term. For a variety of reasons, he just didn’t get around to it.
Shekhar Gupta: But if you were advising the President on his South Asia policy during the Cold War, would you have advised him to handle it differently?
Strobe Talbott: Well, in a way I did, since I was writing. I wasn’t in the capacity of a presidential adviser. I was a journalist, and as you know very well, we journalists give advice to anybody.
Shekhar Gupta: We’ve all heard about your book. I think it’s called Engaging India: Democracy, Diplomacy, and the Bomb. It’s a very pregnant title. Give me a teaser and tell me how this fits into this sort of Indian ideological upbringing.
Strobe Talbott: Well, of course, as you and your viewers know very well, the issue of the extent to which India’s defence was going to have a nuclear weapons component has been debated and deliberated in this country for a very long time. It was in the background, I would even say in the foreground, of Pokhran-I, which is to say the so-called Buddha smile test of 1974, the peaceful test. And indeed, that was one of the principal topics of conversation between Indira Gandhi and Henry Kissinger on that trip in 1974 that brought me to India for the first time. On the subject of nuclear weapons, and whether they are necessary and indeed imperative for a major country to both protect its own security interests and play a global leadership role, the United States and India have had a disagreement really for over 30 years. And that disagreement was muted and managed when India had what it claimed was only a peaceful nuclear capacity. But when India, in May of 1998, decided that it was going to have an unambiguous…
Shekhar Gupta: …had to give up the hypocrisy.
Strobe Talbott: Well, as I would put it, have an unambiguous. It’s undeclared. It was going to go from having an undeclared nuclear capability to having a declared nuclear capability. Then that disagreement became front and centre, and it really brought the relationship to perhaps the lowest point it had ever been, which is saying a great deal.
Shekhar Gupta: You mean worse than it was during the Bangladesh war?
Strobe Talbott: Oh, I think so.
Shekhar Gupta: The Seventh Fleet, Enterprise?
Strobe Talbott: Well, we didn’t have naval vessels off your shore. But in terms of the intensity, the importance, the stakes of the disagreement between us, I think it was a new low in a relationship that had never had very many highs. Now, it was against that backdrop that President Clinton decided we had to intensify our engagement.
Shekhar Gupta: And there was real anger in Washington.
Strobe Talbott: Fury, including on the part of the President of the United States, for all kinds of reasons. First of all, President Clinton felt frustrated and disappointed. He had wanted to use the second term of his presidency in order to have a much closer relationship with India. He felt that that was now going to be difficult, if not impossible.
Second, he attached a very, very high priority to non-proliferation, persuading countries throughout the world that having nuclear weapons was unwise and unnecessary in terms of advancing their own interests. And he was very concerned about what the consequences would be in the India-Pakistan relationship. Of course, one of the first things that all of us in Washington worried about when India tested was: Was Pakistan going to test? And the answer was yes, of course Pakistan would test, although we made an effort to persuade them not to.
Shekhar Gupta: So describe to me the first moments when the news came in.
Strobe Talbott: Well, it was a bad day, a bad way to begin a week. It was on a Monday morning in May of 1998. It’s the opening scene in my book. I came to the office expecting a more or less normal week, at least by State Department standards. And then, and this made the irony, of course, all the more painful, we learned what had happened quite a few hours before from CNN. In other words, we didn’t even get the news from our vaunted intelligence services.
Shekhar Gupta: It means CNN is getting better than the CIA.
Strobe Talbott: Yes. And when I heard the news from CNN, the first thing I did was to pick up the phone and call my counterpart at the CIA to get some more information. He didn’t know what had happened. So he was not only getting the information from CNN, he was getting it from the State Department, which had gotten it from CNN, which was about the worst of all possible worlds from his standpoint. But then we moved into very high gear to try to figure out.
Shekhar Gupta: In fact, one of your colleagues at Brookings and a well-known analyst in India, Steve Cohen, then said the problem with intelligence people is they don’t read anything that’s not marked classified. So if they’d only read the BJP’s election manifesto, they would have known what was coming.
Strobe Talbott: Yeah, but Shekhar, actually, let’s look at it a little more seriously than that. Yes, of course, if we had been listening very carefully to the hints that we had gotten, our level of expectation, if not suspicion, would have been much higher. Indeed, as you know, there were villagers around Pokhran who knew what was coming because of all of the preparations. There was even a story that had gotten into a Sikh community newspaper in Canada predicting the test. But here’s one of the reasons why we didn’t know. Our attention was focused elsewhere. This was a period when we had more or less a crisis going on Iraq. Huge problems in the Balkans. And it was simply a question of information overload and attention deficit.
Shekhar Gupta: But would you say that we Indians have been pretty good at keeping these secrets?
Strobe Talbott: Yeah, and for good reason from your standpoint. Because a couple of times previously, which I also recount in the book, India had been very close to testing, or at least keeping open the option of testing at Pokhran, and the United States had found out and used diplomatic channels, particularly Ambassador Wisner, when he was here, to persuade your government not to do it.
Shekhar Gupta: That was a well-known case during Narasimha Rao’s prime ministership.
Strobe Talbott: Yes. And, by the way, it was during precisely that episode, Shekhar, that I first became aware of the name Jaswant Singh, because he was a spokesman, of course, for the BJP. He had some rather forceful and eloquent things to say on the subject of what appeared to be American pressure to stop India from testing. And I remember being struck at the time by the eloquence and firmness of his comments.
Shekhar Gupta: We will come to Jaswant Singh. And how you changed the course of history. I think in 14 meetings, in seven countries, three continents over two years. But before that, tell me exactly what happened. There’s a lot of speculation here as to what happened during Narasimha Rao’s time, when we were about to test but did not test.
Strobe Talbott: Back during Prime Minister Rao’s premiership. Well, I think what happened is more or less what’s been in the press at the time. We, the United States government, took the information that we had, brought it to the Prime Minister through his personal secretary at the time, and said, “Here’s what we think you’re going to do. We think it would be a huge mistake.” President Clinton got into the exchange directly. There was no formal promise that the government wouldn’t test.
Shekhar Gupta: But you mean Clinton called Rao?
Strobe Talbott: Yes, yes. There was no formal promise. But there was clearly the message. The American message was received, and the test didn’t happen.
Shekhar Gupta: But did Clinton call Rao and hold out a threat?
Strobe Talbott: It wasn’t a threat. It was more a strong argument that this would just be contrary to everybody’s interests.
Shekhar Gupta: And what was your sense? Do you think Narasimha Rao actually wanted to test, or do you think it was some elaborate, clever game that he was playing? He was a clever leader.
Strobe Talbott: Yes, I actually discussed the issue of India’s possible test directly with Prime Minister Rao when he came to Washington to see President Clinton. President Clinton used his own private meeting with him in the Oval Office to make the case not to do it. And then President Clinton sent me in to see him in his hotel room afterwards to deliver the message even more clearly. I had the impression that he was genuinely torn. On the one hand, he was under considerable pressure from various forces within his own government. On the other hand, he understood the logic of the long-standing Congress party position of what might be called nuclear ambiguity.
Shekhar Gupta: That’s been one charge that the BJP has always laid at the door of the Congress party, that the Congress party buckled under American pressure and we did not. And if it was left to the Congress party, they would have compromised India’s nuclear interests.
Strobe Talbott: Well, my own view is that that’s a way of describing the situation with a point of view, that is, that it was absolutely right to test. You won’t be astonished, Shekhar, that I don’t happen to share that point of view. But this is a disagreement that’s now passed into history. Once India made a decision that it was going to test, and once it tested, we, the United States and the world, were confronted with a new reality. Then the question became not concentrating all of our rhetorical and political efforts on recrimination, but trying to figure out what to do next. Where now? How do you make the best of a situation which is far from ideal?
Shekhar Gupta: And that brought Jaswant Singh into the picture.
Strobe Talbott: Yes.
Shekhar Gupta: So tell me a little bit about how it started and how it went on. Fourteen meetings, as I said, seven countries, three continents, two years.
Strobe Talbott: Well, it started, I think, because of an important and positive decision at the level of the two leaderships, that is to say, Prime Minister Vajpayee and President Clinton. Both of these men, who did not have a close personal relationship at that point, and each had some reason for annoyance with the other. President Clinton was, as I say, not just annoyed but furious over India’s decision to do this because of what he saw as all the dangerous and negative consequences. Prime Minister Vajpayee had a reason to be annoyed at the United States because the United States immediately triggered every sanction.
Shekhar Gupta: Let me ask you the front-benchers’ question now. In this engagement, who got more for his country? You for the US or Jaswant for India?
Strobe Talbott: Well, I’ll answer that in two parts. The great American Secretary of State Dean Acheson once famously said that he never read a memorandum of conversation in which the author comes off second best. My book is an exception to that because, insofar as it’s an extended memorandum of conversation between myself and Jaswant Singh on the nuclear issue, on the non-proliferation issue, Jaswant comes off better than I do, in that he accomplished more of what I think was the Indian strategy in that dialogue than the United States did. Which is to say, he and the Indian side held firm against any significant concessions to or acquiescence in the strong requests of the United States.
But the more important point is that there was an overarching goal in the dialogue, and that was to get away from a zero-sum, win-lose dynamic between the two countries and see if we couldn’t find genuine common ground on which to do some good things. And in that sense, I think both of us made real accomplishments.
Shekhar Gupta: Well, that’s the point. Because, apart from the engagement on the nuclear issue, the fact is that Jaswant Singh brought in a completely new paradigm in the Indian worldview, which was not pro-West but which was Westernised in a way. And you know where he was coming from. There were 40, 45 years of socialism and aggressive non-alignment. So I think while he may have accomplished a bit more on the nuclear issue, the US and the West also gained a lot more because India changed its worldview entirely.
Strobe Talbott: Well, let me make one other point. I’ve conceded a considerable amount here, namely that my good friend and counterpart Jaswant Singh accomplished on behalf of his government more in the non-proliferation area than we on the American side wanted to accomplish. But the last chapter of the book is called “Unfinished Business”. This story is not over yet. There is still a big question out there: What will India do with regard to, in some sense, institutionalising its moratorium on the testing of nuclear weapons? What will it do in order to achieve a treaty that cuts off the production of fissile material? What will it do to constrain, and thus stabilise, the competition with its neighbours over ballistic missiles and nuclear weapons? And the fact that we did not achieve as much as we wanted during the Clinton administration doesn’t mean that that issue is off the table. I think your government is going to have to come back to that. And it’s a political issue now.
Shekhar Gupta: Now, if this change had not come about, you know, the nuclear issue being one part of it, this change in the way India looks at the US and the West, and the way Jaswant Singh and you together shifted this paradigm in Indian foreign policy, do you think India would have had the same relationship with the US post-9/11? Or would India have related to the US the same way after 9/11?
Strobe Talbott: I’d like to make two points. I’d like to think that the United States under President Bush was better able to engage with India, including after 9/11, than it would have had it not been for the dialogue conducted in the Clinton administration. But there’s another point, too. The Bush administration was able to engage quite effectively with Pakistan and with President Musharraf after 9/11.
That was possible, I think, in large measure because the United States under President Clinton remained engaged with Musharraf even after the military coup, even after Kargil, even after all the difficulties both between the US and Pakistan and between Pakistan and India. And we were under a lot of pressure, and certainly a lot of advice from our Indian friends, going back to Kargil and the coup in 1999, to basically wash our hands of Pakistan. I think it’s a good thing we did not do that. I think it’s a good thing that President Clinton made a brief visit to Pakistan after his long visit to India.
Shekhar Gupta: But is that where he wagged his finger?
Strobe Talbott: Well, yeah, he went there largely to wag his finger, although he’s not a finger-wagger. He talked. He gave a tough-love message, is the way I would put it.
Shekhar Gupta: Well, from Clinton wagging his finger at Musharraf to his becoming now the stalwart ally, he’s come a long way, Musharraf. How do you look at Musharraf? One of your old colleagues has described him to me twice in three years as a work in progress.
Strobe Talbott: Well, let’s hope it’s progress in the right direction, and let’s hope that the work continues. I had a chance to see President Musharraf, and be part of a group that met with him in Davos, Switzerland, just a little over a week ago.
Shekhar Gupta: Yes, we were all there.
Strobe Talbott: I am pleasantly surprised that President Musharraf, given his history as the architect of Kargil, as an unreconstructed revisionist on the subject of Kashmir, has been willing to get it right on the third try. That is, Pakistan and India had an opportunity for a breakthrough over Lahore. Pakistan basically ruined it. Agra was a disaster. Now there’s a third chance, and it seems to have some real promise. But I must tell you, Shekhar, I think I’m probably not the only one who feels that this whole situation is fragile. And it’s fragile in part because so much depends on President Musharraf himself. He’s already been the intended victim of several assassination attempts. And so the question arises: Is the peace process only one bullet away?
Shekhar Gupta: And that’s my last question. The peace process is only one bullet away, may or may not be. At the same time, is Al-Qaeda only one successful assassination attempt away from getting the bomb? All the revelations that have now come out, Abdul Qadeer Khan…
Strobe Talbott: I understand what you’re saying. There is obviously a nexus or a connection between the Pakistani nuclear weapons capability and the danger of the bomb getting into other non-state hands. As a matter of fact, there’s a danger of it getting into other state hands. And the name AQ Khan, which I’ve been hearing here in India as long as I’ve been coming here, has only recently made its way into the newspapers in the United States. So there seems to be a welcome but very belated effort on the part of some Pakistani authorities to get hold of a very dangerous situation. The question is, is it too late or not?
Shekhar Gupta: That’s why the question is: Is the Bush administration making a mistake by leaving it all to a man instead of institutions or the system? It’s a mistake. We always accuse you of America, right?
Strobe Talbott: I know it sounds like exactly the same criticism against the Bush administration that was made against our administration for continuing to deal first with the Nawaz Sharif government and then with the Musharraf regime. I do not think it’s a mistake. Whenever I hear a criticism of the kind you just suggested, I always want to ask the person who makes the criticism: What exactly is the alternative? What are you suggesting we should be doing instead? Very often, when it was the Clinton administration receiving this criticism, either about Nawaz Sharif or about Musharraf, the Indian answer was either a non-answer or the answer was, “Have nothing to do with them. Dismiss them as a failed state, treat them as the rogue nation they are, and deal only with us.”
And we always refused to do that. And the Bush administration refuses to do that, and I think both the Bush administration and the Clinton administration have been right. Just as engaging India is important, and that’s the title of my book, we have to do whatever we can to remain engaged with Pakistan. Otherwise, Pakistan will become a self-fulfilling prophecy of a very negative sort.
Shekhar Gupta: And a nuisance state.
Strobe Talbott: Yes, and we’ve already seen quite a bit of nuisance from that area. But what we have to do is work with those forces that want to make it…
Shekhar Gupta: All I can say in this equation, there will always be more questions than answers, and it’ll only make life much more fun for people like you and me. In fact, more like you, who’ve seen the picture from both sides. So I wish you all the very best.
Strobe Talbott: Thank you very much, Shekhar.
Shekhar Gupta: Your book tells us more about what happened in those mysterious years than we’ve known all this while.
Strobe Talbott: I think it will.

title: Ex CJI Gavai flags SC Collegium’s ‘questionable’ functioning to President—‘SCs, STs, minorities left out’
description: A single community making up under 5% of the population in India secured over 40% of Supreme Court judgeships, Justice Gavai has said in letter to President Murmu.
author: Ruchi Bhattar
content:
New Delhi: Former Chief Justice of India (CJI) B.R. Gavai has written to President Droupadi Murmu over what he calls a “worrying trend” in judicial elevations and transfers that compromises diversity, inclusion and merit in India’s higher judiciary.
Sending the unprecedented and pointed communication to Rashtrapati Bhawan as a “concerned citizen”, Justice Gavai—who previously led the judicial appointment body—declared that the functioning of the Supreme Court Collegium is “now questionable”. In a three-page letter dated 27 November 2026, with copies marked to Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Law Minister Arjun Ram Meghwal, the former CJI stated he writes not in anger, but out of a sense of responsibility regarding recent developments that disregard equitable representation.
The second Dalit and first Buddhist CJI, Justice Gavai served from 14 May 2025 to 23 November 2025, a tenure of over six months.
A single community making up under 5 per cent of the population in India secured over 40 per cent of Supreme Court judgeships, Justice Gavai said in the letter, without specifying any one community. The former CJI believes that candidates from one particular section of society are being favoured to the detriment of marginalised groups, including Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, Other Backward Classes, minorities, and women, as well as other forward sections.
During his own tenure heading the collegium, Justice Gavai has noted how he strictly adhered to diversity and inclusion, striving to strike a balance among all sections of society. Circumstances now point to recommendations made with a primary focus on “appeasing and rewarding a single community”, he said.
Citing parliamentary records from March 2025, he noted that out of 715 High Court judges appointed since 2018, only 22 belonged to Scheduled Castes, 16 to Scheduled Tribes, 89 to Other Backward Classes, and 37 to minorities. Further, between January 2021 and January 2026, forward communities accounted for nearly 80 per cent of appointments, whereas OBCs—comprising almost half the population—received under 14 per cent.
Highlighting arbitrary high court transfers, Justice Gavai revealed that hard-working judges have faced punitive transfers to smaller courts, while others were rewarded with prominent postings based on community ties rather than merit. Referencing Professor George Gadbois’s landmark study which showed that one community held over a third of all Supreme Court judgeships between 1950 and 1989, he warned that unexamined ideas of who “looks like” a Supreme Court judge continue to persist.
Request for presidential intervention
Turning to constitutional provisions, Justice Gavai pointed out that Article 124(2) explicitly vests the appointment of Supreme Court judges in the President of India. He stressed that while judicial interpretations over recent decades have made collegium recommendations decisive, this “has not made the collegium unaccountable, nor it has relieved your high office of the President of the Republic of India of its duty to preserve protect and defend the Constitution”.
In his direct plea to Rashtrapati Bhawan, the former CJI clearly specified what action he expects from the President. Justice Gavai wrote: “I earnestly request you to acknowledge the issue at hand and intervene in the matter as you may deem appropriate to ensure all are reminded of constitutional duty of equal representation in one of the most significant pillar of Indian democracy.”
Reaffirming that the executive and legislature are equal stakeholders in judicial appointments, he urged immediate intervention to uphold equal representation across constitutional courts.
(Edited by Nardeep Singh Dahiya)
