title: A 'Fair Delimitation' Is Joined at The Hip to the Credibility of the Election Commission - The Wire
description: Regional parties, if planning to switch their stance, would do well to think of the changed mood of the nation after widespread protests have brought youth anger against the Modi dispensation and erosion of democracy to the fore.
author: M.K. Venu
content: Make no mistake, it will not only be the death of multi-party politics but the demise of democracy itself if some regional parties help in passing the delimitation bill during the specially convened four-day Parliament session starting November 30. Even if one rationally accepts that there is a need to expand the number of seats in the legislature to reflect the massive growth in population since the last census in 1971, there is no escaping the fact that this utterly malevolent exercise is being conducted against the backdrop of an Election Commission wilfully committing a massacre of the voters list in India. The nation is in ferment over millions of people facing disenfranchisement and the Supreme Court making the Election Commission roll back its illegalities on a daily basis. The Chief Election Commissioner has been virtually in hiding for months now. In the midst of all this, a delimitation Bill is being pushed in unseemly haste. Before some regional parties even think of considering support to or abstaining from the delimitation Bill voting, should they not address the bigger issue of Gyanesh Kumar’s removal and reconstitution of Election Commission which includes revamping the appointment process and rolling back the permanent immunity to the election commissioners? Sharad Pawar’s National Congress Party or DMK’s Stalin cannot afford to let the delimitation pass without addressing the real issue of the ongoing systematic destruction of the voters list which is clearly proving suicidal for India’s multiparty democracy. Pure common sense suggests that a complete reconstitution of the Election Commission and the overhaul of its appointment process must precede any delimitation exercise, if at all. One hopes the regional party leaders being wooed by Narendra Modi and Amit Shah understand the implications for Indian democracy and federalism if the Bill is pushed through without fully resolving the SIR scam. They would be walking into a trap laid by the Bharatiya Janata Party which has never tried to hide its intent of creating a one-party rule in the country. It began with the slogan of ‘Congress-mukt Bharat’ – Congress-free India – in 2014 and soon extended to ‘opposition-mukt Bharat’ after 2024 when PM Modi got a shock result in the Lok Sabha polls. It became a mission for the BJP to destroy regional parties after the Lok Sabha results. The massacre of the voters list in West Bengal is a prime example of this phenomenon. The regional parties like NCP and DMK must realise there will be no scope for electoral politics if the delimitation Bill is passed in the special session followed by the amoral appointment of Gyanesh Kumar as ex-officio member on the Delimitation Commission. Letting this happen will be the final nail in the coffin of India’s electoral democracy. One shudders to think of Gyanesh Kumar helping to redraw the constituency maps given the experience of Assam and Jammu and Kashmir where the experiment of gerrymandering was carried out. Still, one can be sure that all such acts of political chicanery would anger the awakened youth even more. Modi and Shah seem to think that their old playbook of brazenly manipulating their way to permanent power will work all the time. It has its own expiry date as the nationwide Gen-Z protest showed. The youth of the country are very angry over many issues. Rapid erosion of democracy is only one of them. Sheer hubris of authority and unbridled money power may give them confidence to pull off the delimitation bill. But how the nation, especially the youth, will react to this brazen act of bulldozing democracy with Gyanesh Kumar at the helm is something they will need to watch out for. The gulf between parliament and the people has been widening for some time now. People are losing faith in the capacity of institutions to address their grievances. Indeed our democracy is at a dangerous crossroads. Modi and Amit Shah could inadvertently become catalysts for a bigger mass movement than we have seen so far if a delimitation Bill is bulldozed through parliament. History shows such backlash always comes after hubris peaks to newer levels.

title: Sold, Booked, and Advertised: How Forest Hill Resort Kept Selling Through a 20-Year Legal Battle Until the ED Knocked - The Wire
description: The case against the resort had sat chargesheeted but unresolved for 18 years. Until it got the attention of the ED last week.
author: Arvind Chhabra
content: Chandigarh: When Enforcement Directorate (ED) teams raided the premises of Forest Hill Resort in Karoran on the outskirts of Chandigarh on November 20, they walked into an estate that for two decades has operated less like disputed forest land and more like a small private kingdom. The searches follow a July Special PMLA Court order in Mohali that permitted the ED to access records from an 18-year-old Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) chargesheet against Col. B.S. Sandhu (retd.), the WWICS founder, and others. Drive ten minutes out of Chandigarh, past its premier health institute Post Graduate Institute of Medical Education & Research (PGIMER), and the Shivalik foothills open up into a self-contained luxury enclave. A wrought-iron gate manned by uniformed security guards. A small gatehouse with a red-tiled tower. Beyond it, a 12-hole championship golf course, “soon to be 18,” they declare with pride, laid out against a wall of sal and khair trees, with sand traps cut into fairways that roll down toward a lake. Two helipads sit at the edge of the property, described in the resort’s own marketing deck as “a premise to the inception of helipads,” a first for the region’s private developments. A clubhouse restaurant called The Green Emerald serves what the brochure describes as “curated dining experiences.” There is a spa, a gym, tennis and squash courts, a golf academy with a pro shop, banquet lawns for weddings (with staff pointing to expansion underway which will make it an “envious place for the rivals”), and a conference hall for corporate offsites. On the lake, staff offer canoeing, kayaking, boating, and zorbing. On land, there is an adventure zone with a zip line, archery, ATVs, dirt bikes, segways, camel and horse riding through a partnership called “The Ranch,” and, this being the Shivaliks, wildlife safaris and stargazing. A tie-up with a luxury camping operator has already put two “jungle-colonial” cottages on the property, with teak wardrobes and hot showers, and more planned. A “Health & Wellness Retreat” sited by the lake lists ten specialised clinics on its signage, everything from a Pain Clinic and a Women’s Health Clinic to a Geriatric Clinic and an Infertility Clinic. There is talk of an “upcoming five-star luxury resort hotel,” a gated senior-living wing with its own hospital, and even a nursery. And this is not a passive asset sitting quietly through its legal troubles. Forest Hill Resort actively hosts events, and its own promotional material says so proudly: Punjabi music star AP Dhillon has performed here; so has a lineup for something called “Viber 8,” billed as “a thrilling musical festival”; an “Aiwaska Techno” music night; and even a car-launch event, complete with a vehicle parked mid-fairway in the promotional photos. Illustration via canva“FHR Members enjoy priority access to these events and promotions,” the deck notes, because behind all of this sits a membership model: buy a plot, a villa, or a “farm,” and you get a free lifetime membership to the Forest Hill Golf & Country Club, ordinarily priced at Rs 5 lakh. The same club, the same golf course, and the same brand are used to pitch an entire constellation of adjoining farm projects in the same contested belt, waving an international architectural masterplan as their credibility marker. A full-page advertisement in the local edition of a prominent national newspaper, carried on July 19, 2026, three days before the high court’s freeze order, captures the sales pitch in one line: “Come for the ESCAPE. Stay for the EXPERIENCE.” The resort brands itself, on the cover slide of its own investor presentation, as “an approved Eco-tourism Project (Approved under Govt of India policy for Eco-tourism),” a claim that, on the ground, still needs to be checked against any actual Union government approval. None of this, the golf, the weddings, the concerts, the wellness clinics, or the advertising, is happening in a legal vacuum. It is happening in the middle of one of Punjab’s longest-running land disputes. Twenty years, one unfinished demarcationThe dispute over Karoran’s forest status is old enough that reporters who covered its opening chapter as young journalists are now covering its latest one as veterans. It began in 2004, when the Punjab and Haryana high court took suo motu notice of construction at Forest Hill Golf & Country Club after a newspaper report, and ordered the club demolished, its power and liquor licence cut, and a CBI investigation opened, one arm to examine alleged official corruption in how the land was cleared, the other to map the full extent of landholding by Col. B.S. Sandhu (retd.), the WWICS founder, and his family and companies. The CBI’s Anti-Corruption Bureau in Chandigarh registered that case in 2006, invoking Sections 3A, 8, 12 and 13 of the Prevention of Corruption Act along with Section 120-B of the IPC for criminal conspiracy. It filed its chargesheet in 2008. That chargesheet has been sitting in the Special CBI Court for 18 years. In 2014, the Supreme Court weighed in. And this is the part the resort’s sales staff like to cite. The apex court set aside the high court’s blanket finding that all of Karoran was forest land, ruling that demarcation had to be done plot by plot, based on what the land records showed in 1980. What gets left out of the sales pitch is the second half of that judgment: the Supreme Court explicitly declined to touch the CBI’s investigation, which is precisely why that case has continued grinding forward, chargesheet and all, in the years since. A decade on, the demarcation the Supreme Court ordered still hasn’t been completed. It is the Punjab government’s own admitted position, restated in the July 2026 high court order, where the Additional Advocate General could not point the court to a single affidavit showing the exercise had been done. The high court noted, “The State of Punjab has, till date, not filed any affidavit reporting compliance with the directions issued by the Supreme Court in B.S. Sandhu. One affidavit of the Forest Department officials has been filed, but that would not serve the purpose, once the specific direction issued by the Supreme Court is to the State of Punjab, to carry out the necessary demarcation of forest land…” “Learned Additional Advocate General, Punjab, states that certain affidavits have been filed by the Chief Secretary, Government of Punjab, but our attention has not been invited to any affidavit which refers to the actual demarcation of ‘forest land’ in the area. Mere filing of affidavits without actually undertaking the requisite exercise for demarcation of ‘forest land’ would neither have the approval of this court, nor can it have any sanctity in the eyes of law.” The ED moves inIn July 2026, the case took on a new dimension. On the very day the high court issued its freeze order, a Special Judge (PMLA) in Mohali allowed the Enforcement Directorate to obtain the CBI’s original 2006 FIR, its 2008 chargesheet, and all supplementary chargesheets and relied-upon documents from the twenty-year-old probe. The case opened a money-laundering track on top of the corruption case, the ED’s argument being that the underlying CBI offences are themselves “scheduled offences” under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, which is what gives the agency jurisdiction to act at all. The move was not uncontested. Defence counsel for a co-accused named Rajiv Bajaj opposed the ED’s application, arguing the agency had not disclosed the registration details of its Enforcement Case Information Report (ECIR), effectively the ED’s own internal case file, nor demonstrated that the judicial records it wanted were actually indispensable to its investigation. The court was unmoved and allowed the ED’s request regardless. What this meant practically: a case that had sat, chargesheeted but unresolved, in a Special CBI Court for 18 years suddenly had a second agency, with a different and arguably sharper set of powers, asset attachment among them, actively working the same underlying facts. With ED teams raiding the resort premises last week, that money-laundering probe has moved directly onto the property. Project is “very much on”Two days after the July 2026 freeze order, after the high court had named Karoran specifically, and after the ED had opened its fresh probe, this correspondent called Forest Hill Resort’s sales office, posing as a prospective buyer. General Manager (Real Estate) Vikram Sharma told this correspondent the project was “very much on.” This correspondent visited in person and was walked through the golf course, the clubhouse, the lake, and the helipads, and offered plots in adjoining Tandi village at Rs 20,000 a square yard, and a separate acre at Rs 7 crore, with staff assuring him “all permissions are in” and “no legal hassles.” Asked about the high court order, Sharma said there was nothing to worry about legally. “See, the demarcation in Karoran and Nada was already complete,” he said, adding that the company would shortly move court to have both villages excluded from the freeze. (And it did.) Asked whether the Punjab government was doing the registry of land, Vikram Sharma was unfazed. Admitting that the land registry might have paused then, he added that it would resume within seven to ten days once “we get the high court’s clarification.” That claim ran directly counter to the high court’s order naming those exact two villages as undemarcated. Interestingly, in writing they try to be safer. Sales decks for adjoining farm plots pitched under the same club-membership model carry a printed disclaimer stating that land proposals in Nada and Karoran are “subject to the outcome of orders of the competent court.” Not far from Karoran, in Siswan village, the state’s own paperwork shows how enforcement actually plays out in this belt when the government does move: a status report shows small unauthorised structures, a furniture market, a fuel station, a juice shop, demolished within weeks of a court order, while larger farmhouse-scale violations are still working through “representations” and hearings months later. That is the pattern this story sits inside: courts that keep ruling, agencies that keep investigating, and a resort that keeps selling, hosting concerts, and running ads, seemingly confident that none of it will catch up in time to matter.Arvind Chhabra is a journalist.

title: We Women are Free: Why the Fight for Safe Streets Demands an End to Victim Blaming - The Wire
description: Locking women up in the name of 'protection' shields male predators and shifts the blame to women.
author: Ragini Nayak
content: “Unite to End Violence Against Women and Girls: Ensure Justice, Protect Survivors, End Impunity” is the theme of the United Nations’ ‘16 Days of Activism’ campaign, beginning on November 25, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women. Yet, decades of international declarations and campaigns later, a fundamental question remains: Why are women across the world made to bear both the guilt and the blame for sexual advances and offences committed against them?Ending impunity will remain a distant dream if the safety and security of women can be ensured only by locking them up. Across the world, and particularly in India, institutions too often respond to violence not by holding perpetrators accountable and making public spaces safer, but by restricting women’s freedom in the name of protection. The recent protests at Delhi University offer a telling illustration of this larger contradiction.The skies reverberated with cries of anger when, drenched in rain, holding placards and chanting slogans, hundreds of female and queer students marched on the historic pathways of Delhi University’s North Campus, under the banner of “Hum Auratein Azaad Hain (We, the Women, are Free)”.They were reacting to the horrific gang rape of a 17-year-old girl at South Delhi’s Aastha Kunj Park, but their collective fury targeted something much deeper: instead of acknowledging women’s right to public spaces, the institutional practice of imposing curfews and restrictions on women under the guise of “protection”.In Seeing Like a Feminist, Nivedita Menon argued that the language of “protection” can become a means of regulating women’s behaviour rather than transforming the structures that make public spaces unsafe. The absurdity of the Lady Sriram College administration’s defensive stance – instantly shifting classes online and policing women’s mobility – is a case in point for this deep-seated structural hypocrisy.Also read: Saakhi | The Rape in Astha Kunj and India’s Culture of Sexual ViolenceThis impulse to hold women responsible for the consequences of male behaviour is neither new nor incidental; it is rooted in a centuries-old patriarchal imagination that has consistently portrayed women as the source of male transgression. The most brutal tragedy for womankind remains that they are not just doomed with the burden of ‘the Fall’ but also with the blame of making men ‘fallen’.Woman was made the historical scapegoat for the ‘original sin’, and for centuries has been indoctrinated with the patriarchal thought that she has no choice but to bear the brunt of man’s ‘wanted’ or ‘unwanted’ desires and to believe that he is probably just ‘made this way’.‘He’ will whistle, wink, grope, assault, harass, rape – and ‘she’ will be the one told to stay indoors to prevent his transgression. This structural scapegoating mirrors the core thesis of Simone de Beauvoir’s The Second Sex, where she argued, “Thus woman is related to nature as she is to man; she is the prey of both; she is the temptation of both.”This age-old construction of woman as the source of male temptation continues to shape contemporary responses to sexual violence, where the responsibility for men’s conduct is routinely shifted onto women. It is significant that the Leader of Opposition, Rahul Gandhi, explicitly called out this victim-shaming/victim-blaming by proclaiming, “A system that blames the victim and shields the criminal. It is time to smash it!The solution is not to lock women inside. It is to make our streets safe, to confront the mindset of men who mistreat women, and to punish those who attack them.”It is high time that the easiest escape route for sexual aggressors should be closed. The idea that women are the driving cause behind men’s outrageous acts must be dismantled. And its logical progression – the argument that women are too provocatively dressed for men to control their sexual urges – must be struck at the root.Almost every woman who steps out of her house, walks through the streets or commutes on public transport is painfully aware of the reality of sexual molestation and the fact that perverse advances target almost any and every female form, irrespective of how that form is clad. Even today, there is no societal consensus on the fact that women have as much right to their bodies – and to how they choose to carry them – as men do, without being subjected to unsolicited invasion.I remember that in 2010, after completing the Delhi Half Marathon, actor Gul Panag complained that she was groped repeatedly by men in the crowd during the run. Sixteen years later, a woman journalist complained that an ACP groped and pushed her while she was covering a protest at Jantar Mantar.Also read: Raat Hamari Hai! When More Than 150 Women Came Together to Reclaim Public Spaces at NightYears apart, completely different women and circumstances, yet the same violation of women’s bodily autonomy in public space. And when a woman dares to confront it, the assault rarely ends with the invasion of her body. Instead, it is followed by the far more insidious violence of character assassination: What was she wearing? Why was she there? Why did she not resist?The gaze is conveniently shifted from the conduct of the perpetrator to turning the victim into the accused.In primary school, I was taught that “character is what you do when no one is watching”. However, as I grew up, I realised that my side of humanity’s character is judged entirely by “what we wear when everyone is watching”. Generally, the ‘character’ of a person is defined as the aggregate of features and traits that form their individual nature. Over the years, however, this definition has been usurped by our male counterparts.While a man’s character is built on qualities like honesty, competence, integrity, courage and intelligence, a woman’s character is rigidly defined only by her sexuality and her outward appearance –which is taken as a direct indicator of her sexual behaviour. This makes patriarchal compartmentalisation exceptionally easy. Women belong strictly to two extremes: they are either promiscuous ‘sluts’ or chaste ‘goddesses’.The task before feminist movements is not to persuade women to choose the other side of the binary – to replace the ‘Madonna’ with the ‘Whore’– but to dismantle the binary itself. Women need not reclaim one of the two. ‘Reclaiming’ these terms is not the answer; challenging their biased construct is.Women must subvert the identities that patriarchy has constructed for them; they must subvert the very terms on which the choice is imposed. The woman who is sexual and the woman who is chaste, the woman who covers herself and the woman who flaunts her body, the woman who desires and the woman who refuses – all remain equally entitled to dignity, safety and autonomy. Perhaps the real transgression for women, then, is to refuse to choose!Dr Ragini Nayak is a national spokesperson of the Congress party and former president of DUSU.

title: Delimitation or Seat-Chori? Real Story isn't States, it's the Maps
description: Delimitation Bill 2026: How redrawing Lok Sabha seats could benefit the BJP, what Assam and J&K reveal, and why the Delimitation Commission's composition matters. It raises questions about gerrymandering, population criteria and electoral boundaries.
author: Aditya Menon
content:
(Exposing the manipulation of India's electoral institutions is a key focus area in The Quint's reportage. Become a member and support our work.)
Many people are missing the point on the Delimitation Bill that the Modi government is set to re-introduce in a Special Session of Parliament on 30 November. The focus has disproportionately been on the share of each state, which is the main concern for parties like the DMK.
The real issue that will impact political equations is the redrawing of the electoral boundaries by the Delimitation Commission.
There are three reasons for this.
- The manner in which it was carried out in two states where delimitation of seats has already taken place: Assam and Jammu and Kashmir. In both states, boundaries were redrawn in a way that helps the BJP. In short, gerrymandering.
- The selective use of population as a criteria.
- The composition of the commission.
Delimitation in Assam and J&K
The basic principle of democracy is 'one person, one vote'. By extension, delimitation means that every seat has approximately the same number of voters.
If equitable division was the principle, each Lok Sabha seat in Assam should have 17.5 lakh voters. But in the Muslim-majority Dhubri seat, around 10 lakh extra voters were added. This means that the value of a vote in Dhubri is lesser than in other seats in Assam.
The extra 10 lakh voters added to Dhubri previously belonged to the Barpeta seat. The strategy was to move the Muslim-majority areas of Barpeta into Dhubri, making Barpeta a Hindu-majority seat overnight.
When the results came in, it was no surprise that the NDA won the seat for the first time in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections.
Selective Use of Population Criteria
Different standards were used in Assam and Jammu & Kashmir to change the boundaries of seats. In Jammu & Kashmir, the criteria of population was used to reduce the proportion of seats for the Muslim-majority Kashmir region and increase the proportion for the Hindu-majority Jammu region.
For example, the Anantnag Lok Sabha seat was reduced in population, and Muslim-majority areas in Jammu were added, even though the entire Pir Panjal mountain range lies between these two regions.
In Assam, the seats for Muslim-majority areas were reduced, despite a higher population, as we saw in the Dhubri example above.
The seats in Assam have been divided in a way that doesn't make geographic or demographic sense. Read this thread by information security and legal expert Srinivas Kodali to understand this.
The government seems to have divided seats in such a way that suits its own political calculations.
This can be understood through an important concept from US politics: gerrymandering.
What Is Gerrymandering?
Gerrymandering is the deliberate manipulation of electoral district boundaries to give one political party or group an unfair advantage, often resulting in strangely shaped districts. If one looks at the maps of seats in Assam, it is a classic case of gerrymandering.
There are two components to gerrymandering: packing and cracking.
Packing is the concentration of Opposition voters in a small number of seats. With this, the Opposition party wins these particular seats with large margins but loses everywhere else. Dhubri in Assam is a perfect example of packing.
Cracking: This strategy spreads Opposition voters across many seats. By doing this, the party in power keeps a majority in as many districts as possible. Barpeta Lok Sabha seat is an example of cracking.
Who Will be in the Delimitation Commission?
Under Clause 3(2) of the Delimitation Bill, 2026, introduced in the Lok Sabha on 16 April 2026, the proposed Delimitation Commission was to consist of three members, all appointed by the Central government:
- Chairperson: a sitting Supreme Court judge
- Ex-Officio Member: Chief Election Commissioner or an election commissioner nominated by the CEC
- State Election Commissioner (SEC) of the concerned state
The rules in the 2002 Delimitation Act were the same. But this is likely to become a cause of concern for the Opposition due to the allegations against current CEC Gyanesh Kumar.
Far from being removed, the Delimitation Bill will give Gyanesh Kumar far more powers than before. But it's not just about Kumar.
During the delimitation in Jammu and Kashmir, Opposition parties had accused the commission headed by Justice (Retd) Ranjana Desai of drawing boundaries in way that helps the BJP.
(A version of this story had been published in April 2026 when the goverment had last introduced the Delimitation Bill. This story is being updated and published afresh in light of new developments)

title: बाइक के हेलमेट से एयरबैग निकलने वाला वीडियो असली नहीं, AI है
description: AirBag Helmet Viral video: सोशल मीडिया पर एक वीडियो वायरल हो रहा है, जिसमें एक बाइकर किसी वजह से जमीन पर गिर जाता है  कुछ यूजर्स का दावा है कि यह चीन का एक नया आविष्कार है जहां ऐसे बाइक हेलमेट बनाए गए हैं जिनमें एयरबैग लगे होते हैं.
author: ऐश्वर्या वर्मा
content:
सोशल मीडिया पर एक वीडियो वायरल हो रहा है, जिसमें एक बाइकर किसी वजह से जमीन पर गिर जाता है और उसके गिरते ही चारों ओर एयरबैग खुलता हुआ दिखाई देता है. कुछ यूजर्स का दावा है कि यह चीन का एक नया आविष्कार है जहां ऐसे बाइक हेलमेट बनाए गए हैं जिनमें एयरबैग लगे होते हैं.
- आजतक, ABP न्यूज और Zee News सहित कई न्यूज वेबसाइट्स ने इसी जानकारी के साथ यह वीडियो शेयर किया है लेकिन इसके साथ ही इन्होने यह भी बताया है कि उन्होंने इस वीडियो की सत्यता की स्वतंत्र रूप से पुष्टि नहीं की है.
- हालांकि, वनइंडिया न्यूज और लोकमत टाइम्स ने इस वीडियो के साथ ऐसा कोई डिस्क्लेमर नहीं जोड़ा था.
लेकिन...?: यह वीडियो AI से बनाया गया है और इसमें इस तरह के किसी हेलमेट के असली दृश्य नहीं दिखाए गए हैं.
हमने सच का पता कैसे लगा ?: इस वीडियो को ध्यान से देखने पर हमें इसमें कुछ गड़बड़ी नजर आई; उदाहरण के लिए, इस वायरल क्लिप की शुरुआत में एक स्मार्टफोन की स्क्रीन पर यह वाहन दिखाई नहीं दे रहा था.
वीडियो में आगे चलकर, राइडर की जैकेट की बाईं बांह पर एक सफेद पट्टी दिखाई देती है, जो वीडियो के अंत तक आते-आते लाल पट्टी में बदल जाती है.
- इसके बाद हमने वीडियो के कुछ हिस्सों पर 'रिवर्स इमेज सर्च' ऑप्शन का इस्तेमाल किया, जिससे हमें पता चला कि यह 'जीरो ग्रेविटी गैंग' (Zero Gravity Gang) नाम के एक फेसबुक पेज से लिया गया है.
- इस पेज ने 2 अक्टूबर को यह वीडियो शेयर किया था, जो अब वायरल हो गया है. यह पेज अक्सर भविष्य की तकनीक (फ्यूचरिस्टिक टेक) से जुड़े ऐसे ही वीडियो पोस्ट करता रहता है.
यह पुष्टि करने के लिए कि क्या वीडियो AI से बनाया गया है या नहीं, हमने इसे AI से बने कॉन्टेंट की पहचान करने वाले टूल Hive Moderation पर चेक किया.
यहां इस वीडियो के AI से बने होने की संभावना 99.9 प्रतिशत पाई गई.
हमने इसे Buffalo University के Deepfake-o-Meter पर भी चेक किया. इनके दो अलग-अलग डिटेक्टरों ने इस वीडियो के AI से बने होने पर 100 प्रतिशत भरोसा जताया.
निष्कर्ष: AI से बना एक वीडियो शेयर किया जा रहा है, जिसमें दावा किया गया है कि यह एक ऐसे चीनी हेलमेट का असली वीडियो है जिसमें एयरबैग लगे हुए हैं.
(अगर आपके पास भी ऐसी कोई जानकारी आती है, जिसके सच होने पर आपको शक है, तो पड़ताल के लिए हमारे वॉट्सऐप नंबर 9540511818 या फिर आईडी webqoof@thequint.com पर भेजें. सच हम आपको बताएंगे. हमारी बाकी फैक्ट चेक स्टोरीज आप यहां पढ़ सकते हैं.)

title: Viral Video of Rajnath Singh Commenting on BJP’s ‘Rafale Scam’ Is a Deepfake
description: Fact-Check: A deepfake is going viral on social media, claiming to show Defence Minister Rajnath Singh stating that during Operation Sindoor, without Rafale jets, Pakistan would have shot down India's entire squadron.
author: Anika K
content:
A video is going viral on social media, claiming to show Defence Minister of India Rajnath Singh stating that during Operation Sindoor, without Rafale jets, Pakistan would have shot down India's entire squadron.
The claim: In the video, Singh can be heard saying, "Countless scams took place during Congress (Indian National Congress) rule. So what if the BJP (Bharatiya Janata Party) was accused of one Rafale scam?"
- He goes on to say, "If we hadn't had the Rafale during the Operation Sindoor war, and we were fighting relying on the Congress-era MiG-21 Bisons, Pakistan would probably have shot down our entire squadron."
How did we find out?: We ran a keyword search related to the viral video and couldn't find any reports on it.
- Next, we ran a reverse image search on the video and found a report by ANI with the same visuals.
- According to the report, the video shows Singh at Kalaburagi, Karnataka, calling out Congress leader Rahul Gandhi.
- He says that during both the 2007 and 2012 Gujarat Assembly elections, when PM Narendra Modi won in Gujarat, the Chief Election Commissioners were appointed by Congress.
- He goes on to say, "So is Rahul Gandhi questioning the impartiality of all former Election Commissioners?"
- There is no mention of Operation Sindoor or Rafale jets.
- The Hindu reported on Singh's public address at a rally in Kalaburagi, where he stated that the BJP will launch a nation-wide campaign, 'Save Democracy and Remove Anarchy'.
- According to the report, he accused the Congress of "attempting to destablise the Union Government and undermine democractic institutions in its pursuit of power".
- BJP released a press release which summarises everything that Singh discused during the ‘Loktantra Bachao, Arajakta Hatao’ Padyatra.
- There is no mention of Operation Sindoor or ‘Rafale Scam’.
Is it AI?: We ran the video through Hiya Deepfake Voice Detector, a tool that detects AI-generated audio, and it flagged the audio as AI.
- We also ran the video through DeepFake-O-Meter, and four of its detectors flagged it as AI.
Conclusion: The video is a deepfake and doesn't show real footage of Rajnath Singh commenting on BJP's ‘Rafale Scam’.
(Not convinced of a post or information you came across online and want it verified? Send us the details on WhatsApp at 9540511818 , or e-mail it to us at webqoof@thequint.com and we'll fact-check it for you. You can also read all our fact-checked stories here.)

title: Literature Festivals in India This Winter 2026–27: How To Choose the Right One for You
description: From Jaipur and Kerala to Wayanad and Bengaluru, explore India’s winter literature festivals in 2026–27, their dates, ticket prices and experiences.
author: Avantika Krishna
content:
If your idea of a good weekend involves listening to a favourite author, discovering new books or spending hours discussing stories, the next two months offer plenty to look forward to. India's winter literature festival season gets underway today, 27 November, with events opening in Dehradun and Lucknow.
Seven more festivals are scheduled across December and January, giving book lovers plenty of time to plan a trip. But how do you choose the one that suits you? In January 2025, Nisha Retnamma, an author living in the UAE, flew to Kozhikode for the Kerala Literature Festival because it let her "meet and listen to all your favourite authors from across the world". Keep her test in mind: whose voices do you most want to hear?
Which voices are you here for?
Start with language. If you want to hear writers in Hindi, Urdu and other Indian languages, head to Koshala from 27 to 30 November 2026, where live mushairas, kavi sammelans and translation studies fill the programme, and tickets start at Rs 100 on BookMyShow.
If you are curious about languages you rarely hear, wait for the Hyderabad Literary Festival, from 22 to 24 January 2027, at Sattva Knowledge City. Sessions on indigenous and endangered languages sit beside a poetry stream called Kaavya Dhaara, and entry is free. Jaipur also devotes a Bhasha Swarmala series to India's languages in its 20th edition.
Do you want a crowd, the sea or quiet?
Prefer a crowd? Join the Jaipur Literature Festival, from 14 to 18 January 2027, at Hotel Clarks Amer. Jaipur resident Rohit Mathur, who loves attending such events, says, "The global presence of Jaipur excites me", and the programme gives him plenty to chase, from debates with prize-winning authors to pop-up bookshops and evening concerts.
General registration starts at Rs 200, and students pay Rs 100 for all five days.
Want the sea? The Kerala Literature Festival, from 21 to 24 January on Kozhikode Beach, marks its tenth edition with Australia as its guest nation, and the waves soften the crowd. Author Martin Goodman, who attended in 2026, enjoyed being able to "breeze into conversation beneath a crescent moon", although two sessions he turned up for were cancelled. Keep a backup in mind.
English literature student Athira Gopinath says she would not miss it at any price. Delegate registration is free online.
Want quiet? Wayanad, from 20 to 23 December, is held in a gram panchayat rather than a city, with campfire readings and a heritage walk among its signature events. Novelist KR Meera, who has attended many festivals in big cities, predicted before its first edition that the "participation of the local people is going to be unique".
The biennial event drew over 110,000 visitors in 2024, and a one-day adult ticket costs Rs 50. The festival's own website lists 19 December as the start, so confirm before you book.
How do you like to listen?
The Bangalore Literature Festival's 15th edition, from 11 to 13 December at Freedom Park, a former colonial jail, is free with online registration. Bindu Manoj, who has attended since the festival began, felt after the 2017 edition that the early years were "the best with more literature", so read each programme before you commit.
Writers can use LitMart, where 10 shortlisted finalists pitch manuscripts to a jury, and Hyderabad runs a similar platform called Meet My Book.
Dehradun, from 27 to 29 November, suits readers who enjoy cinema alongside books, with filmmakers Imtiaz Ali and Vishal Bhardwaj on the programme and free online registration.
The Exide Kolkata Literary Meet, from 23 to 27 January at Alipore Museum, offers free entry on a first-come, first-served basis and a junior meet for young readers. The Mathrubhumi International Festival of Letters, from 28 to 31 January at Kanakakkunnu Palace in Thiruvananthapuram, closes the season under the theme 'Era of Riddles'.
Check the calendar, then choose
Dehradun and Koshala overlap, and Kerala, Hyderabad and Kolkata all share 23 and 24 January, so pick one for that weekend. Jaipur ends three days before Kerala begins, so a determined reader can attend both.
Dehradun, Bangalore, Hyderabad and Kolkata are free, while Jaipur and Wayanad charge for passes. Kolkata's dates come from a single listing, so check its website before you travel.
Now finish one sentence: "I want to hear..." If your answer is a favourite novelist, head for Jaipur or Kerala. If it is a poet in a language you cannot yet read, follow the mushairas to Lucknow. If it is a story told around a campfire, book Wayanad.
Then open that festival's website and confirm the dates. Which festival would you choose?

title: How Indian Villages and Fishing Communities Are Helping Protect Endangered Pangolins and Whale Sharks
description: From over 300 villages banning pangolin hunting to Gujarat’s fishers rescuing whale sharks, discover how Indian communities are protecting endangered wildlife.
author: Raajwrita Dutta
content:
On 24 November 2026, Ngoushutho Ngouri spotted an unusual animal crossing a road near a residential area in Meluri, Nagaland. It was a Chinese pangolin, a critically endangered mammal threatened by hunting and the illegal wildlife trade.
Ngouri alerted forest officials, who rushed to the spot, examined the animal and found it healthy and uninjured. The pangolin was safely released into a forest habitat away from human settlements.
Just weeks earlier, the local community had come together over a shared love for football and made a collective decision to protect this very animal.
Across Nagaland, Manipur and Gujarat, similar efforts are showing how everyday decisions by residents, village leaders, farmers and fishers can help protect some of the world's most threatened species.
A football tournament with a purpose
In October 2026, eight football clubs from neighbouring villages came together in Nagaland for a rather unusual sporting event: the Pangolin Cup.
Organised by the Wildlife Trust of India (WTI), in collaboration with the Meluri Range Sports Association and the Nagaland Forest Department, the six-day tournament attracted at least 10,000 participants and spectators.
Between the excitement of football matches, residents learnt about pangolins, why they are hunted for their meat and scales, and how these animals help maintain forest ecosystems by feeding on ants and termites.
What followed went well beyond the football field.
The Pochury Hoho, the apex leadership body of the Pochury Naga community, passed a resolution banning pangolin hunting across 30 villages. Anyone found hunting or trading the animal would face a fine of Rs 50,000.
Weeks later, Ngouri's decision to alert forest officials offered a tangible example of how such awareness could translate into action.
Over 300 villages unite to protect pangolins
Elsewhere in Nagaland, village councils are using traditional systems of governance to protect wildlife.
In February 2026, the United Sangtam Likhum Pumji, the apex body representing the Sangtam Naga community, banned pangolin hunting across 42 villages in Kiphire district.
Following months of discussions with conservationists, village councils took responsibility for enforcing the ban, with violations handled by customary courts.
As reported by Mongabay, such resolutions are helping communities use their customary laws to protect endangered wildlife.
Neighbouring Manipur has seen similar efforts.
In August 2024, the Tangkhul Naga Awunga Long, the apex body representing the Tangkhul Naga community, signed a resolution banning pangolin hunting and consumption across 230 villages.
In April 2025, when farmers discovered a Chinese pangolin in farmland near Tangkhul Khullen village, they informed community leader Kashung Tennyson. The animal was subsequently rescued and released into the wild.
Together, these three community resolutions cover more than 300 villages, bringing local residents and traditional institutions into the fight against wildlife trafficking.
Fishers who cut their nets to save whale sharks
Thousands of kilometres away, along Gujarat’s coast, another community is helping protect the world's largest fish.
Until the early 2000s, whale sharks were hunted along the Gujarat coast for their fins, liver oil, skin and meat.
In 2004, WTI launched a conservation initiative in partnership with the Gujarat Forest Department and Tata Chemicals, working with fishing communities to raise awareness about the endangered species.
Over the years, fishers began voluntarily releasing whale sharks that accidentally became entangled in their fishing nets. Some even cut their expensive nets to free the animals, with a compensation programme helping cover their financial losses.
According to WTI, Gujarat’s fishing communities have helped release 1,042 adult whale sharks and 22 young ones.
In November 2026, these communities received national recognition from the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change for their contribution to whale shark conservation.
The initiative has also expanded to Kerala, Lakshadweep and Goa, where fishers are being trained to recognise and safely release whale sharks.
For a resident walking along a village road, a farmer working in his field or a fisher heading out to sea, an unexpected encounter with an endangered animal can become an opportunity to save its life.
By bringing conservation into their sports, traditions, livelihoods and everyday decisions, these communities are showing how ordinary citizens can play a meaningful role in protecting India's wildlife.

title: Delimitation Bill: DMK Sets Terms for Tamil Nadu Support
description: The DMK may support the Delimitation Bill if Tamil Nadu’s 7.18% seat share is protected. The debate tests federal balance and political trust.
author: R.K. Radhakrishnan
content:
The Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) is waiting to examine the Delimitation Bill, and senior leaders told Frontline that if the demands put forth by the party were met, it was open to supporting the Bill. Given the fact that the government has called for a special session on November 30, it appears that the demands of the DMK have been accommodated.
“Our most important demand is that if the number of parliamentary constituencies is increased, Tamil Nadu’s existing 7.18 per cent share of seats should not go down,” DMK president and former Chief Minister M.K. Stalin, told Frontline in an informal conversation on November 26. “We have already articulated our demands when we had organised the meeting to oppose delimitation in its current form,” he added.
The Delimitation Bill, 2026 (Bill No. 109 of 2026) was introduced in the Lok Sabha on April 16, 2026. It provided for the constitution of a Delimitation Commission to readjust and reallocate seats in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies. The Bill stipulated that the exercise would be based on the latest published Census figures available when the Commission was constituted. A related proposal, contained in the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026, sought to raise the maximum strength of the Lok Sabha from 550 to 850 (815 for States and 35 for Union Territories). However, the Constitution Amendment Bill failed to secure the two-thirds majority required in the Lok Sabha. Consequently, the Delimitation Bill became infructuous and was not proceeded with.
Earlier delimitation exercises were undertaken in 1952, 1962, 1972, and 2002. The 2002 Delimitation Commission completed its work in 2008. The freeze on the allocation of seats among States, originally introduced through the 42nd Constitutional Amendment in 1976, was extended by the 84th Amendment in 2001 until the first Census after 2026.
Stalin and other leaders burnt a copy of the Bill on April 16, just ahead of its introduction in the Lok Sabha. He was clad in black, and hoisted a black flag, and declared that the DMK would agitate and win against the draconian Bill. That session of the Lok Sabha was not prorogued as the BJP kept looking for MPs to shore up its numbers. The DMK’s reported change in stance seems to indicate that the BJP has managed to muster the numbers.
The DMK’s other demands include fair delimitation that is subject to scrutiny, no detrimental clauses related to the exercise, a redrawing process based on consultations, and a 25-year freeze on any further tinkering with constituencies.
One DMK leader said that it was wiser to negotiate a way forward than to blindly oppose the Bill. “The BJP will simply sit tight and allow the Bill to lapse. If the Bill is not passed, and the Presidential assent obtained and gazetted ahead of December 31 [2026], the delimitation provisions will anyway kick in. In that case, the delimitation will be carried out as per population for the existing constituencies,” said former MP and senior DMK leader, T.K.S. Elangovan. “Tamil Nadu will lose seats in this scenario, as happened in an earlier occasion. We demand fair limitation,” he added. There are 543 seats in the Lok Sabha now, and the Constitutional limit is 550 seats.
While the BJP is desperate for the DMK’s support in the Lok Sabha, given its 22 MPs in the Lower House, whose votes would be critical to the passage of the Bill, the DMK would find it difficult to explain any decision to support the proposal to the people of Tamil Nadu, having questioned the BJP’s motives ahead of the 2026 Tamil Nadu Assembly election.
At a meeting in Chennai in 2025, the DMK had brought together national leaders to demand fair delimitation. The party also passed a resolution in the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly for fair delimitation. DMK’s demands were again conveyed to the BJP when it reached out to it about a month ago. Apart from insisting that the State’s share of seats should not fall below its current 7.18 per cent, the DMK demanded that the “existing proportion of parliamentary representation among States, as determined on the basis of the 1971 Census and frozen, must remain unchanged for another 25 years”.
The DMK said that these were two critical demands and it was the same as it had made in 2025. “We remain firm on both these positions today and will continue to do so. There is no change in this position, and there is no question of compromise,” Stalin said.
Referring to the speculation in a section of the media that the DMK had succumbed to pressure from BJP, the DMK reacted through a social media post: “...the grumbling of backstabbers will not shake our position in any way. The shameless, ungrateful lot who abandon their principles for positions of power must understand this.”
One leader, who did not want to be quoted, said that this was aimed at the Congress for the manner in which it had tried to paint the DMK as a party that did not honour its word.

title: Vande Mataram: Kashmir Mufti Declares Standing Un-Islamic
description: Kashmir's grand mufti bars Muslims from standing for Vande Mataram, as clerics oppose coercion at public events and question the politicisation of religious institutions.
author: Gowhar Geelani
content:
Jammu and Kashmir’s grand mufti, Nasir-ul-Islam, on Thursday, November 26, issued an edict (fatwa) against standing up during the rendition of “Vande Mataram”, declaring the participation of Muslims in the song impermissible under Islamic law, or the Shariat.
The grand mufti said it was not about showing disrespect towards any song, but that Islamic law clearly defines certain red lines for the followers of the Islamic faith. “To recite‘Vande Mataram’ or to stand up for the song is completely un-Islamic,” the Srinagar-based Mufti Nasir-ul-Islam told Frontline. A faithful Muslim, he said, could not read it either out of volition or under duress. Those who participated “wittingly or unwittingly” in functions where it was played could not escape responsibility by arguing that they had no choice.
Nasir-ul-Islam said that Islam attaches the greatest importance to one’s parents after the Creator. Still, if they demand anything against the Shariat, one may “unfurl the banner of revolt”. “Well, the Creator [Khaliq] is more important than creation [Makhlooq],” he said. Muslims, he added, worship only Allah, seek help from Him alone, and are not allowed to worship anyone else. “It is a matter of our faith and belief and there cannot be any compromise on this; this is our red line,” Nasir-ul-Islam said.
A rendition of “Vande Mataram”at the Jammu and Kashmir Waqf Day function in the summer capital, Srinagar, on Monday, November 23, drew objections from religious groups. On Wednesday, a group of Muslim scholars apologised and offered “prayers of repentance” (tauba) for standing while the song was played.
The Jammu and Kashmir Waqf Board, headed by the BJP’s local leader Darakhshan Andrabi, organised the inaugural Waqf Day function at Srinagar’s Sher-e-Kashmir University of Agricultural Sciences and Technology. All six stanzas of the song were played.
Union Minister for Minority Affairs and Parliamentary Affairs Kiren Rijiju attended the function. Others present included Muslim scholars from different schools of Islamic jurisprudence, the National Conference leader and parliamentarian Mian Altaf Larvi, and the Jammu and Kashmir Peoples Conference leader Imran Reza Ansari, a Shia politician from north Kashmir.
Videos showing some Muslim scholars from Kashmir and Jammu standing up for the song drew criticism on social media. The Srinagar-based Muttahida Majlis-e-Ulama (MMU), a grouping of Islamic organisations and Muslim institutions, issued a statement saying it had taken “strong exception to the playing of ‘Vande Mataram’ at the first-ever Waqf Day ceremony organised by the BJP leader Darakhshan Andrabi”. “The concept of Tawheed [oneness of the Almighty] is non-negotiable in Islam,” the MMU said. The religion, it added, strictly prohibits associating any partner with Allah or attributing divinity to any individual, object, land, or creation.
The MMU said that the All India Muslim Personal Law Board had in the past clarified the Islamic position on “Vande Mataram” and opposed its mandatory rendition. Kashmir’s chief cleric, Mirwaiz Umar Farooq, formerly chairman of the moderate faction of the All Parties Hurriyat Conference, heads the MMU. “It is unacceptable for us, as Muslims, to worship anyone except Allah,” he told Frontline. It was “equally regrettable”, he said, that a Jammu and Kashmir Waqf Board function had been politicised by playing the song when there was no legal obligation to do so.
The MMU also said it would seek legal opinion and submit a formal representation to the authorities against what it called the forced imposition of the song at government functions, educational institutions, and other public events.
On Friday, November 27, Mirwaiz Umar Farooq told Frontline that the authorities had placed him under house arrest to prevent him from addressing the Friday congregation at Srinagar’s historic Jamia Masjid. “The authorities regularly prevent me from discharging my religious obligations and duties by placing me under house arrest,” he said. Their sole aim, he alleged, was to deny him an opportunity to speak on social, environmental, religious, and political issues.
Mirwaiz Umar alleged that Kashmir’s well-respected Islamic scholar and patron of the MMU, Maulana Rahmatullah Qasmi, has been summoned to the police station after his statement on the latest controversy. Maulana Qasmi Sahib, the Mirwaiz alleged, was “reprimanded”. “Can we no longer raise our voice to safeguard our religious beliefs and sentiments?” Mirwaiz Umar questioned.
The Sunni Muslim scholar from south Kashmir, Maulana Abdul Rashid Dawoodi, who has faced criticism for attending the function, challenged Muslim clerics to issue an unambiguous fatwa on standing during the rendition of “Vande Mataram”. Explaining his participation, Dawoodi told reporters that he had neither read the words of the song nor accepted its contents, and had stood only because of protocol. “God is my witness; I did not read any words of the song by heart,” he said. Dawoodi added that he received no money and spent his own to attend Waqf Board events. “I am being singled out; my person is being targeted.”
Dawoodi has praised Andrabi and her leadership on several occasions, saying that the income of the Jammu and Kashmir Waqf Board and the functioning of the organisation have improved since she took over as its chairperson. He urged Islamic scholars to settle whether standing for“Vande Mataram” amounts to polytheism. “If any Islamic organisation of repute declares that standing for ‘Vande Mataram’ is akin to polytheism and is un-Islamic, let it issue a formal edict [fatwa],” he said.
Nasir-ul-Islam and Maulana Rahmatullah Mir Qasmi, head of the Darul Uloom Raheemiyyah seminary in Bandipora, also released a video statement congratulating the scholars who had apologised and offered “repentance prayers”. Rahmatullah named Maulana Farooq, the imam of Rajouri; his close aide Maulana Basharat from Poonch; the imam of the Railway Station Mosque in Jammu; Maulana Ilyas of Manjakot; and Pir Syed Aijaz and Maulana Zakir, imams of the mosque in Jammu’s Bathindi area. The scholars, he said, had realised their mistake, offered prayers of repentance, and read the Kalima [the Islamic declaration of faith] again. They had declared that they unwittingly erred by standing for the song. “We are all humans, and humans make mistakes,” Rahmatullah said.
Legal backing
In Jammu, imams belonging to different schools of Islamic jurisprudence addressed the media and apologised for standing during the rendition. They also said they had read the Kalima again and offered tauba. Rahmatullah said he was concerned that Muslim children, students, and employees from Jammu and Kashmir were being coerced into going against the tenets of Islam by being made to stand up for “Vande Mataram”. The scholars at the Srinagar function, he said, “should have summoned the courage” to say they would not compromise on their faith. They should have refused to attend an event that, he alleged, was used as a political platform. He also said that a Supreme Court ruling barred anyone from being forced to recite the song.
In Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986), the court protected schoolchildren who stood respectfully but declined, on grounds of conscience, to sing the national anthem. On March 25 this year, it refused to entertain a challenge to a Union Home Ministry circular on “Vande Mataram”, observing that the protocol was advisory.
On September 22, a bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant said orally that it expected the 1986 principle to govern the 2026 amendment penalising intentional disruption of the song’s singing. Conscientious objectors, including those with religious objections, should not face penal consequences, it indicated.
Challenges to the ministry’s January 28 and July 9 orders prescribing the six-stanza version are pending before the court. Rahmatullah said he had earlier told Andrabi not to misuse her authority as chairperson of the Waqf Board and to avoid coercing people in such a manner. “The issue of faith and belief in Islam is very sensitive,” he said. For Muslims, he added, employment, status, money, dignity, family, and other things had no value when it came to their basic faith. “Darakhshan Andrabi Sahiba is like our sister, but unfortunately, she is operating in this manner,” he said.
In a video statement, the grand mufti reiterated that prostration (sajdah) was an act of worship reserved exclusively for the Creator. “It is forbidden for Muslims to worship idols, statues, objects or land,” he said.
Gowhar Geelani is a senior journalist and author of Kashmir: Rage and Reason.

title: India’s Labour Codes: A Year Later, Questions Remain
description: India’s four labour codes continue to face scrutiny a year after implementation, with questions over workers’ rights, job security, wages, and social security.
author: TEAM  FRONTLINE
content:
On November 21, 2025, the Union government brought into force four new labour codes, consolidating 29 existing central labour laws into a single framework. The move, presented as a major overhaul of India’s labour regulation, has profound implications for wages, job security, social security, and the relationship between employers and workers. The codes have faced sustained opposition from trade unions, which argue that several provisions weaken collective bargaining, make retrenchment easier, and dilute existing labour protections. The government, meanwhile, has defended the reforms as a means of simplifying regulation, extending social security, and creating a more flexible labour market.
A year later, the debate is still on. The rollout of rules across States has been uneven, while questions over the actual reach of social security and the consequences for workers remain central to the discussion. Frontline brings together a selection of its reporting and analysis to trace the history of these reforms, examine their implications across different sections of the workforce and place the current debate in the context of India’s longer retreat from established labour protections.

title: India Emerges Biggest Gainer As Zara, H&M Shift $254 Million In Orders From Bangladesh
description: Global fashion retailers such as Zara and H&M moved close to 10 per cent of their monthly orders, worth about $254 million, out of Bangladesh betw
author: Arun Dhital
content:
News Brief
Arun Dhital
Nov 27, 2026 | Updated 06:17 PM GMT+5:30
Save & read from anywhere!
Bookmark stories for easy access on any device or the Swarajya app.
Global fashion retailers such as Zara and H&M moved close to 10 per cent of their monthly orders, worth about $254 million, out of Bangladesh between 1 and 18 November, with India taking the bulk, three factory owners told Reuters. Labour unrest and rising costs drove the shift.
The owners, who sought anonymity, said Marks & Spencer and Celio also moved business. Inditex, Zara's parent, declined to comment, while the others did not respond.
The Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) puts protest-related production losses above $400 million in a sector generating over 80 per cent of export earnings. Vietnam, Cambodia and Indonesia are also drawing buyers.
On Wednesday, Bangladesh approved a 36 per cent minimum wage hike for garment workers, far short of demands to more than double pay, sparking fresh clashes with police. Labour Ministry secretary Abdur Rahman Tarafder called it "satisfactory".
BGMEA director M. Mohiuddin Chowdhury said, "The wage increase has added to costs at a time when buyers are demanding lower prices and competition from rival sourcing countries is intensifying."
"Price becomes secondary when brands are under pressure to meet strict delivery deadlines," he said, noting rival hubs deliver within 60 to 90 days, against about 120 in Bangladesh.
"Since November 1, most of my buyers have stopped placing orders because of the unrest," said Khan Monirul Alam, managing director of Alps Apparels Group. "They are telling us our orders have been shifted, postponed or cancelled and that they have already found alternative solutions."
Energy shortages worsened by the Middle East crisis and tensions over Sheikh Hasina's possible return from India have added to worries.
"The challenge is restoring buyers' confidence before temporary shifts become long-term sourcing decisions," Chowdhury warned. "Brands have options. They will not wait for us if instability persists."

title: RVNL Achieves 6.59-Km Tunnel Breakthrough In Rudraprayag On Rishikesh-Karnaprayag Rail Line
description: Rail Vikas Nigam Limited (RVNL), a PSU under the Ministry of Railways, on Friday (27 November) completed the breakthrough of the nearly 6.59-km Tunnel
author: Arun Dhital
content:
News Brief
Arun Dhital
Nov 27, 2026 | Updated 06:07 PM GMT+5:30
Save & read from anywhere!
Bookmark stories for easy access on any device or the Swarajya app.
Rail Vikas Nigam Limited (RVNL), a PSU under the Ministry of Railways, on Friday (27 November) completed the breakthrough of the nearly 6.59-km Tunnel-14 on the Rishikesh-Karnaprayag rail project in Uttarakhand's Rudraprayag district.
Excavation was carried out under tough geological conditions, including loose soil beneath populated areas, unstable slopes and the need for controlled blasting to limit risks to nearby settlements.
RVNL said a key challenge was digging a 110-metre section of the triple-track tunnel through loose soil at Portal-1 (T14P1), where the overburden was just 20 to 30 metres.
Because this stretch lies below inhabited areas, engineers used specialised methods such as pre-excavation and multi-drifting.
At Portal-2 (T14P2), the team encountered slope instability and ground settlement in the Marora area. Engineers stabilised the slope using micropiles driven 30 to 35 metres deep, rock bolts measuring 15 to 20 metres and consolidation grouting.
"Specialized ventilation systems were deployed for fresh air supply and temperature regulation throughout the 4.7 km Portal-1 drive," the railway PSU said.
The 125-km line is being built at a cost of Rs 37,119 crore. RVNL Chairman and Managing Director Saleem Ahmad recently said the project has reached 79 per cent overall progress, with about 97 per cent of tunnel excavation done, and is targeted for completion by December 2029.
Sanctioned in the Union Budget 2010-11, the line runs through Dehradun, Tehri Garhwal, Pauri Garhwal, Rudraprayag and Chamoli districts, linking religious towns like Devprayag and Karnaprayag with Rishikesh and the national capital.
Most of the project is tunnels, with 16 main tunnels spanning 104 km and 12 escape tunnels of around 98 km.
Once operational, the rail link is expected to enhance connectivity across the Himalayan region, make Char Dham shrines more accessible, bolster border links, support tourism and local economies and substantially reduce travel time.

title: Centre Rules Out New Expressways Plan In Tamil Nadu, Backs Widening Of Road Instead: Report
description: The Centre is unlikely to approve any new expressway in Tamil Nadu soon and will upgrade existing highways to ease congestion. It has also declined to
author: Arun Dhital
content:
News Brief
Arun Dhital
Nov 27, 2026 | Updated 04:49 PM GMT+5:30
Save & read from anywhere!
Bookmark stories for easy access on any device or the Swarajya app.
The Centre is unlikely to approve any new expressway in Tamil Nadu soon and will upgrade existing highways to ease congestion. It has also declined to support the state's planned industrial corridors linking Chennai, Coimbatore and Thoothukudi, The New Indian Express reported.
This was conveyed when State Highways Minister Aadhav Arjuna met Union Road Transport and Highways Minister Nitin Gadkari in New Delhi on 17 November.
The Singaperumal Koil (CPRR)-Madurai greenfield expressway, for which the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) is preparing a detailed project report, may also be deferred.
The Centre is expected to clear eight lanes for GST Road's Chengalpattu-Madurai stretch and six lanes beyond up to Kanniyakumari. The state had sought eight or 10 lanes along all 740 km.
“They categorically ruled out taking up any new expressway projects in TN, either fully or partially,” a senior official said. The Tamil Nadu State Highways Authority will build the industrial corridors and has invited tenders for their DPRs.
NHAI officials linked the Centre's stand to heavy bank borrowings, delays in projects such as the Chennai-Bengaluru Expressway and Vikravandi-Thanjavur four-laning, and difficulty in sourcing earth.
The state's first greenfield highway, the Rs 10,000-crore, 277-km Chennai-Salem expressway proposed in 2018, was dropped after protests over land and the environment.
Gadkari asked NHAI to work with the state on easing congestion at five key entry and exit points around Chennai, with elevated corridors proposed on four routes.
The Chennai-Bengaluru Expressway is ready in Karnataka and nearly done in Andhra Pradesh, but 18.5 km of its 106-km Tamil Nadu stretch is incomplete.
NHAI, which has spent over Rs 16,000 crore on the project, is awarding a tender for 15 km of the Arakkonam-Kancheepuram section, a roughly 18-month job.
An official said soil availability has improved slightly under the new government.

title: ‘I’m not so brave’: Azam Khan on prison, Yogi, Owaisi and Muslim politics in UP
description: Atul Chaurasia spoke to the embattled Samajwadi Party leader, out on bail after more than five years in prison, on Muslim politics, his rivals, and a career that has stayed at the centre of Uttar Pradesh’s political landscape.
author: NL Team
content:
Atul Chaurasia spoke to the embattled Samajwadi Party leader, out on bail after more than five years in prison, on Muslim politics, his rivals, and a career that has stayed at the centre of Uttar Pradesh’s political landscape.
Understanding the politics of senior Samajwadi Party (SP) leader Azam Khan is no simple task. To his supporters, he is an outspoken leader who has fought many battles; to his critics, he is a polarising, communal figure. Outside his home in Rampur, a large crowd of supporters, party workers, and political figures had gathered, many of them having travelled from districts across western Uttar Pradesh to meet him.
Out on bail after more than five years in prison, the embattled politician discussed Muslim politics and representation, his political adversaries, leaders such as Asaduddin Owaisi, Chandrashekhar Azad, Rahul Gandhi, Akhilesh Yadav, and Yogi Adityanath, and his concerns about the future of his Mohammad Ali Jauhar University in Rampur.
During this conversation, Azam Khan answered several significant questions, while also candidly admitting to some of his own political missteps. Acknowledging his fear of those in power, he remarked, “I am not so brave that I wouldn’t be afraid of such powerful people.”

title: आज़म खान इंटरव्यू: मुस्लिम लीडरशिप की होड़ और जेल से पैदा हुई जिद
description: In an exclusive NL interview, Azam Khan discusses UP Assembly elections, Muslim politics, the Samajwadi Party, Congress alliance and the future of opposition politics.
author: अतुल चौरसिया
content:
आज़म खान से यह बातचीत उस शख्स को समझने की कोशिश है जिसकी राजनीति, बयान और उनके साथ बीते पांच साल में हुआ बर्ताव, सब कुछ उत्तर प्रदेश की सियासत के केंद्र में रहा.
समाजवादी पार्टी के वरिष्ठ नेता आज़म खान की राजनीति को समझना आसान नहीं है. उनके समर्थकों के लिए वह एक बेबाक और संघर्षशील नेता हैं, तो आलोचकों के लिए उनकी छवि ध्रुवीकरण करने वाले सांप्रदायिक नेता की है. पांच साल से ज्यादा जेल में बिताने के बाद बाहर आए आज़म खान से हमारी मुलाकात इन्हीं गुत्थियों को समझने का जरिया बनी.
रामपुर में उनके घर के बाहर समर्थकों, पार्टी कार्यकर्ताओं और नेताओं का हुजूम था. पश्चिमी उत्तर प्रदेश के अलग-अलग जिलों से लोग उनसे मिलने पहुंच रहे थे. मीडिया इंटरव्यू का सिलसिला देर रात तक चला. हमारी बारी आई तो कमर में तेज दर्द के चलते आज़म खान ने हाथ जोड़ लिए. इंटरव्यू अगले दिन सुबह 11 बजे के लिए टालना पड़ा. अगले दिन भी वही भीड़, वही इंतजार. जब बातचीत शुरू होने वाली थी, तभी बिजली चली गई. करीब 15 मिनट तक बिजली लौटने का इंतजार करते हुए हमने इधर-उधर की बातें की. इंटरव्यू के दौरान भी बिजली आती-जाती रही.
लेकिन इन तमाम अड़चनों के बीच हुई इस बातचीत में आज़म खान ने कई अहम सवालों के जवाब दिए. सत्ता में बैठे लोगों से अपने डर को स्वीकार करते हुए उन्होंने कहा, “इतने बहादुर नहीं हैं कि इतने ताकतवर लोगों से डरें नहीं.” उनकी राजनीतिक गलतियों का सवाल आया तो उन्होंने माना, “बिल्कुल हुई हैं, बिल्कुल हुई हैं.”
बातचीत में मुस्लिम राजनीति और उसके प्रतिनिधित्व से लेकर ओवैसी, चंद्रशेखर, राहुल गांधी, अखिलेश यादव और योगी आदित्यनाथ तक का जिक्र आया. उन्होंने अपने राजनीतिक विरोधियों पर भी बात की, रामपुर की यूनिवर्सिटी और उससे जुड़े भविष्य की चिंता जाहिर की. आज़म खान के जवाबों से आप सहमत हों या असहमत, लेकिन उन्हें सुनना और उनसे सवाल करना जरूरी है.

title: 1 lakh workers plan to protest in Delhi. What are their demands, and will they be allowed to march?
description: CITU’s three-day mobilisation seeks a minimum wage, pensions, permanent jobs, women workers’ rights and the repeal of the four labour codes.
author: Tapasya
content:
CITU’s three-day mobilisation seeks a minimum wage, pensions, permanent jobs, women workers’ rights and the repeal of the four labour codes.
The Centre of Indian Trade Unions (CITU), a CPI(M)-aligned workers’ organisation, has called for a march from Ramlila Maidan to Parliament from December 1 to 3. They are demanding a minimum wage of Rs 42,000 a month, universal pension of Rs 21,000, repeal of the four labour codes, and restoration of the erstwhile rural employment scheme, MGNREGA.
The CITU leadership has dubbed it a “historically unprecedented gathering”, estimating that over one lakh workers across India will descend on Delhi. CITU national president Sudip Datta told Newslaundry that more than 55,000 train tickets had already been booked by workers joining the march, and that over 50,000 women workers including ASHAs, anganwadi and mid-day meal workers are expected to lead the march.
Datta said that they have sought permission from the Delhi Police to assemble at Ramlila and then march to Parliament, but the police have not granted it yet. “The police have promised permission for using Ramlila grounds and we will begin putting up tents and setting up toilets at the venue,” he said.
A ‘reception committee’ for organising the march was set up in early October headed by economist Prabhat Patnaik with CITU General Secretary and former MP Elamaram Kareem as its convener. To raise funds and make arrangements to accommodate people, CITU said it has raised money from its more than 7 million members, and also through crowdfunding.
On consultation with the government, the Indian Labour Conference, the labour ministry’s main tripartite forum, has not met since 2015. The conference brought together the government, employers and workers to discuss production and workers’ welfare. CITU says other statutory tripartite bodies still exist, but have been captured by entities close to the government and large corporations.
Newslaundry spoke with CITU leaders and read a booklet it has published for the march to understand what the workers are marching for and how they arrived at these demands.
Raising the minimum wage to Rs 42,000
One of the major demands of CITU is to increase the minimum wage to Rs 42,000 a month for all workers. This includes a minimum income of Rs 42,000 for self-employed workers who earn by directly providing goods or services without drawing a regular salary or wages from a fixed employer.
India’s National Floor Level Minimum Wages, set by the Centre in 2019 as the lower limit for state governments to decide the minimum wage, stands at Rs 178 per day, or Rs 4,628 a month for 26 days of work.
The amount is “grossly inadequate even for a subhuman existence,” CITU says in a booklet it has published for the march.
The demand is based on the Aykroyd formula and the norms adopted by the 15th Indian Labour Conference in 1957. These calculate a minimum wage by treating a worker’s family as three “consumption units”: one for the worker, 0.8 for the spouse and 0.6 for each of two children. The norms fix 2,700 calories a day per unit and 66 metres of cloth a year, along with housing, fuel and miscellaneous needs. In its 1992 Reptakos Brett judgment, the Supreme Court added a 25 percent allowance for children’s education, medical care and contingencies such as old age or marriage.
CITU says its team used this formula and current prices of essentials to arrive at the Rs 42,000 demand. The Rs 21,000 pension demand follows the same logic, said R Karumalaiyan, a CITU national secretary. “It is a general norm that pension is 50 percent of the last basic pay. Using the same method, we have demanded a Rs 21,000 old-age pension.”
“Workers' rights can only be ensured if you have a proper political-economic framework. The policy-framework to incentivise the rich and hope that the benefits will trickle down to the working class has failed,” Datta told Newslaundry.
Taxing the ultra-rich
On November 19, addressing the annual meeting of the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce & Industry (FICCI), Prime Minister Modi acknowledged that income tax benefits, reduction of corporate tax from 30 to 22 percent and GST reforms for ‘ease of doing business’ had not translated to more employment or wage increases.
CITU stressed that the government has constantly worked for corporate interests at the expense of workers and citizens.
On November 24, economist Jayati Ghosh spoke at CITU’s press conference at the Press Club of India in New Delhi in support of the march. She called the current situation an “inequality emergency”, saying that wages for most workers in India have fallen behind rising prices of basic necessities like food.
“When it comes to inequality, we are back to the colonial times,” she said, citing research by the World Inequality Lab at the Paris School of Economics.
Under CITU’s proposal, the state would cover the difference for workers earning less than Rs 42,000 a month. Put simply, a worker in a sector such as agriculture, transport, trade or construction who earns Rs 10,000 a month would receive the remaining Rs 32,000 from the public exchequer. CITU says this would be funded by taxing the ultra-rich, and has proposed a 10 percent wealth tax and a 33 percent inheritance tax on the richest 1 percent of the country's population.
“We have calculated the gap between Rs 42,000 and the average real wages of 14 crore workers across four sectors: agriculture, transport, trade and construction. A tax on the super-rich will be enough to subsidise the gap. It will increase workers’ purchasing power, which will come back to the government as taxes on goods and services that they consume,” Datta explained.
Repealing the labour codes, restoring MGNREGA
In 2025, 29 central labour laws were replaced by four labour codes, namely the Code on Wages, the Industrial Relations Code, the Code on Social Security, and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code.
Various trade unions, including the RSS-affiliated Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh, have criticised the codes for diluting labour rights and the workers’ right to unionise.
CITU has criticised the Code on Wages for neither clearly defining the minimum wage nor setting out how it is to be calculated. Instead, the Code puts the onus on the states, giving only broad directions on what should be included in the calculation. The union’s objection to the Industrial Relations Code is that it extends the mandatory strike notice, earlier required only in public utilities, to all industrial establishments. Its objection to the Code on Social Security is that it offers no concrete framework for unorganised-sector workers.
The labour organisation has also demanded the restoration of the rural job guarantee scheme, MGNREGA, which was replaced last year by the VB-G RAM G Act. The new law raises the guaranteed minimum workdays from 100 to 125, but it shifts the scheme from a demand-driven to a supply-driven model. Work will now depend on the panchayat’s pre-approved work plans.
According to observers, the new law places a greater fiscal burden on the states. Under MGNREGA, the Centre bore the full wage cost and 75 percent of the material cost. The VB-G RAM G Act instead splits costs between the Centre and the states in a 60:40 ratio, except in the Northeastern states, where the split remains 90:10. This will hurt poorer states such as Bihar and Jharkhand.
Recognising women workers
Anganwadi workers, mid-day meal workers and ASHA workers, who are overwhelmingly women, are not recognised as workers but are designated as “volunteers” or “honorary workers”, even though they form the backbone of India’s frontline public health and nutrition services. They receive a “base honorarium” of as low as Rs 2,500 a month, with top-ups that vary by state.
CITU is demanding that these workers be regularised as employees, with higher wages and coverage under the Employees’ Provident Fund and other benefits.
AR Sindhu, national secretary of CITU, also cited the government’s own figures that 75 percent women who have passed Class 12 do not have paid work. She stressed that the new labour codes allow women to work night shifts with their consent but “there is no precondition for their safety”.
According to a 2023 State Bank of India report, unpaid work by women contributed Rs 22.7 lakh crore or 7.5 percent of India’s Gross Domestic Product.
Sindhu told the press that women from all sectors, from anganwadi, mid-day meal and ASHA workers to IT workers and gig workers, will be joining the march on December 1.
Filling vacancies, improving workplace safety
The CITU leadership has raised the issue of 8.23 lakh vacant jobs across central government departments, and increased contractual work that denies benefits like gratuity, provident fund and medical insurance.
It is demanding permanent jobs and better safety measures to protect workers from workplace accidents. Between 2018-22, 3,176 workers were fatally injured in India’s factories, according to the labour ministry.
The organisation also condemned the Jan Vishwas Act, 2023, which has decriminalised offences by employers that were previously punishable with imprisonment. Now they attract only monetary penalties.
“Decriminalising the employer who kills through negligence while criminalising the worker who strikes for safety are not two separate policy choices – it is one coherent design, built to shift risk downward and shield capital from consequences,” CITU’s march-booklet says.
In addition, the organisation has also demanded that the Election Commission’s Special Intensive Revision (SIR), which has excluded millions of voters from the electoral roll, be scrapped. The disenfranchisement not only takes away the right to vote but also “disentitles many working people from social welfare benefits” as voter cards become mandatory for workers’ registration in social security schemes, the march-booklet says.
