title: Former CJI Gavai writes to President Murmu, alleges community bias in judicial appointments
description: Gavai Asserts That The Primacy Of Collegium Recommendations Does Not Make The Collegium Unaccountable Or Absolve The President Of Her Constitutional Duties
author: PTI, Our Web Desk
content:
Voicing strong dissent and disappointment over recent appointments and transfers in the higher judiciary, former Chief Justice of India BR Gavai on Friday urged President Droupadi Murmu to intervene to deal with low OBC, SC, ST and minority representation in the high courts and the Supreme Court.
Justice Gavai, the first Buddhist and the second Dalit after K G Balakrishnan to head the Indian judiciary, who has been strongly defending the collegium system of judges appointing judges, expressed serious concern over what he termed a growing trend of caste-based preferences, lack of inclusivity and disregard for merit in appointments and transfers in the higher judiciary.
Justice Gavai was succeeded by present CJI Surya Kant after his retirement on November 23, 2025.
"When I was a part of the collegium and was Chief Justice of India, I always followed the principles of diversity and inclusion. Adequate representation was ensured to different sections of the society including those belonging to the forward section of the society and also to the marginalized section of the society including scheduled castes, tribes, other backward classes, minorities and women…," he said.
Without naming his successor, the former CJI said, "However, in the recent past disturbing events have unfolded, showing complete disregard to principles of merit and inclusivity."
"I am constrained to voice my dissent and disappointment as evidently appointments and transfers are being done in complete disregard to ethos of diversity, inclusion and merits taking into consideration other irrelevant factors," he said.
Justice Gavai, in a three-page letter to the President, who hails from a Scheduled Tribe, alleged that candidates from "one particular section of the society" are being favoured.
"Candidates belonging to one particular section of the society are being favoured for recommendation/elevation to the exclusion of everyone else including marginalized communities including scheduled castes, tribes, other backward classes, minorities, women and even persons from forward sections of the society who are not from a particular community," he said without naming that section.
After the retirement of Justice Gavai, seven new judges – Sheel Nagu, Shree Chandrashekhar, Sanjeev Sachdeva, Arun Palli, V Mohana, Sunita Agarwal, D K Upadhyay and Apresh Kumar Singh – have been appointed as SC judges by the collegium headed by present CJI Surya Kant.
Justice Gavai urged the President to "acknowledge the issue at hand and intervene in the matter" to ensure that all are reminded of the constitutional duty of equal representation in the higher judiciary.
The former CJI referred to the data of the government and said that out of 715 high court judges appointed since 2018, only 22 belonged to Scheduled Castes (SCs), 16 to Scheduled Tribes (STs), 89 to Other Backward Classes (OBCs) and 37 to minorities.
Roughly three of every four judges of constitutional courts came from the general category, the former CJI said in his letter.
"For appointments between January 2021 and January 2026, the reported share of the forward communities is close to 80 per cent," he said, adding that the OBCs, perhaps 40 to 50 per cent of the total population, have received under 14 per cent share in higher judiciary.
Caste is not recorded for Supreme Court appointments, he said and termed "silence" itself as part of the problem.
"A community that is under 5 per cent of the country's population has had over 40 per cent representation in the Supreme Court which has risen manifold in the recent past. While I admit that this is not something new and that is precisely why it is increasingly becoming unforgivable," he said.
In the letter, whose copies have also been sent to Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Law Minister Arjun Ram Meghwal, the ex-CJI said that he was writing as "a concerned citizen" who had been both a member and the head of the collegium "whose working is now questionable".
He said recent events have created "compelling circumstances" supporting a perception that recommendations are increasingly made to appease and reward a single community.
He cited political scientist George Gadbois's study of the apex court's first four decades, which found one community, then about one-nineteenth of the population, held over a third of judgeships between 1950 and 1989.
The study referred to disproportionate representation given to the Brahmin community.
"Seventy-five years into the Republic, the profile of the Court has barely moved. Each of us bears some share of that failure, and I say so plainly. It is because I know how such patterns persist, through familiarity, through networks, and through unexamined ideas of who 'looks like' a Supreme Court judge, that I can no longer stay silent," he said.
He also questioned High Court transfers and Chief Justice appointments, without naming anyone.
"Even in the case of the recent recommendation of transfer from one high court to another high court there is a perception that merit has been ignored and other similar factors have weighed in," he said.
"A chief justice, who was transferred from one HC to another smaller HC and thereafter from that HC to one of the smallest High Court, has now been rewarded, for being from a particular community, by transfer to a prominent High Court," he claimed.
Justice Gavai said as a result, a meritorious and hard-working chief justice of a High Court has been transferred to a smaller High Court to make way for him.
"It is not only demoralizing for such a meritorious chief justice but also has a chilling effect on all hard-working judges including persons belonging to marginalized sections of the society," he said.
He said the executive is an "equal stakeholder" in appointments and transfers.
He added that Parliament and the executive have often asked the collegium to include names from marginalised sections.
In March 2026, Justice Gavai called the collegium system the most workable model at present, while criticising executive delays in clearing recommendations and saying the executive must comply once the collegium reiterates a name.
In practice, the President acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers in such matters.

title: Analysis finds glaring errors in Uttar Pradesh, Karnataka final voter rolls after SIR
description: Mess After Clean-up; Aman Bhargava’s Report Says SIR Process Does Not Appear To Treat Voters Evenly And What Happens To You Varies With Where You Live, And Possibly With Which BLO You Get, Which Electoral Officer You Get And How Your Data Was Entered
author: Arnab Chatterjee
content:
An independent researcher has flagged a series of errors in the electoral rolls of Karnataka and Uttar Pradesh post the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process that is meant to clean up the voter lists.
In the final roll of Uttar Pradesh, as many as 23,261 people were found to be on the voter roll more than once in their own booth, 1,752 cases were found of the same voter ID on the roll in two constituencies, 1,828 houses were found with at least 100 voters from at least 50 families, according to the analysis report by Aman Bhargava from Diagram Chasing.
While the SIR revision struck off 58,850 cards as repeats, the Election Commission added at least 18,519 new duplicates, the report said.
It also flagged 12.7lakh voters with no real house number and identified 101 pairs of voters who are each other's father.
Seven new voters in Powayan were given voter ID numbers that belonged to someone else, the report said, citing official Election Commission data.
According to the EC data, more than 2.04 crore voters have been removed from Uttar Pradesh's electoral rolls after the SIR. For every 573 people struck off the draft roll, only one came back, the report said.
“Much of the debate has been about whether the SIR affected people by religion. Religion is not recorded in the rolls, so my analysis cannot determine whether it has been a factor. What the rolls do record is the age and gender of voters, and there the pattern is clear; compared to young men, young women were left off far more frequently. In Uttar Pradesh, women under 35 were left off the draft roll at twice the rate of men, mostly marked as 'shifted'", Bhargava told The Telegraph Online.
He was referring to UP chief minister Yogi Adityanath’s earlier claim that 1.27 crore Hindu voters were missing from Assembly lists compared to panchayat rolls.
According to Bhargava’s report, women aged 25 to 29 were removed at 2.3 times the rate of men across all of UP's 403 constituencies.
Official removal reasons show that under-35 women were three times more likely than men to be marked as “shifted.” The other categories (absent, dead, and duplicate) are much more alike between men and women.
However, more men than women were added during claims and objections, widening the under-35 gender gap, the report found, after comparing the number of voters removed before the January 2026 draft roll (ASDDR) with additions on the April 2026 final roll, by age group and gender.
More women than men were struck off before the draft, it said, while 5.9 lakh more men than women aged 18 to 24 were added to the final roll.
Bhargava also pointed out that the SIR impacted registered transgender voters at a far higher rate than men and women. A total 38 per cent of registered transgender voters were removed, against 23 per cent of men and women.
“In 316 of the 386 constituencies with transgender voters on the 2024 roll, their removal rate was higher”, he said.
Bhargava also clarified that although voter deletion does not directly indicate a vote swing, but in 307 of 378 constituencies the margin of deleted or removed voters was more than the 2022 victory margin.
The report also flagged other inconsistencies in the final electoral rolls, including invalid house numbers and names. It identified 10.8 lakh instances of such errors, of which 7.2 lakh involved names entered in place of house numbers.
The analysis also found 2.1 lakh cases in which a relative's name was printed twice, 1.4 lakh instances of voters' names appearing twice, and 5,056 cases in which a title was printed instead of a relative's name.
Karnataka SIR
“The Election Commission says Karnataka's final voter roll leaves out no eligible citizen and includes no ineligible person. The rolls say otherwise,” the report said.
It contradicted the EC’s “no ineligible person is included” tagline by citing several lapses: 8,992 people on the roll more than once in their own booth, 461 cases of the same voter ID on the roll in two constituencies, 381 house numbers with more than 100 voters, 20.7 lakh voters with no real house numbers, 296 cases where two voters are each other’s fathers.
As for the EC’s “no eligible citizen is left out” tagline, the report found that 3,115 voters were told they are not on the 2002 roll even though they are. It also found that 332 voters were marked dead and then added back to the final roll, and 234 cases where new voters held a removed voter's ID.
“Voter IDs are supposed to be unique, but my analysis found repeatedly that voter IDs are being reused,” Bhargava said.
For example, in the Shorapur constituency, a certain Gousiya Begam appeared five times in the final electoral roll with identical details, including father's name, house number, age and gender, but different voter ID numbers.
Two other 18-year-old voters, Abdul Rahiman and Shankarnag, were each listed twice on the same page. The report found that this was not an isolated case. While 762 duplicate entries were deleted during the revision, another 8,268 were added.
At least 8,992 voters now appear more than once within their respective polling booths, with identical personal details across entries. Together, these voters account for 18,271 voter ID cards bearing different identification numbers.
The report also flagged around 10,000 entries in which something other than a voter's name appeared in the name field.
“The SIR process does not appear to treat voters evenly and what happens to you varies with where you live, and possibly with which BLO you get, which electoral officer you get and how your data was entered,” it said.
The analysis involved digitising Election Commission electoral rolls using optical character recognition (OCR) and matching records through voters' Electoral Photo Identity Card (EPIC) numbers.
For Karnataka, it used five datasets: the 2002 roll, January 2025 pre-revision roll, 2026 draft and final rolls, and the ASDDO list.
For Uttar Pradesh, the datasets included the 2024 General Election roll, January 2026 ASDDR lists, the January 6 draft roll, the April 10 final roll and the 2027 draft roll.

For Karnataka, it used five datasets: the 2002 roll, January 2025 pre-revision roll, 2026 draft and final rolls, and the ASDDO list. For Uttar Pradesh, the datasets included the 2024 General Election roll, January 2026 ASDDR lists, the January 6 draft roll, the April 10 final roll and the 2027 draft roll.
The digitisation and analysis involved Diagram Chasing, Mathakaavalu, Edellu Karnataka and s1d Labs led by Sarthak Sidhant.

title: ‘Continuous state of contestation’: CDS flags changing nature of warfare, stresses military readiness
description: Citing Operation Sindoor, Gen Raja Subramani Said Its Second Phase Demonstrated India's Ability To Integrate Military Capabilities Across Domains And Maintain Escalation Dominance
author: PTI
content:
Chief of Defence Staff Gen N S Raja Subramani on Friday said India was facing a changing security environment in which the line separating war from peace was becoming increasingly indistinct, with countries locked in what he described as a "continuous state of contestation".
Speaking on the future of warfare and India's readiness for multi-domain operations, he warned that adversaries were also targeting the country's thinking and perceptions through "cognitive warfare".
The CDS stressed the need to strengthen military capabilities across all domains and said efforts were under way to modernise the armed forces' electronic warfare architecture.
Citing Operation Sindoor, he described its second phase as an example of effective joint and integrated multi-domain operations. He said India had retained control over the escalation matrix and achieved escalation dominance, adding that the operation had delivered a "decisive victory" for the country.
Former CDS, Gen Anil Chauhan (retd), who was the Chief of Defence Staff during Operation Sindoor last year, moderated the session hosted by think-tank Vivekananda International Foundation in Delhi.
Gen Raja Subramani, in his address, underlined the evolving nature of technology and the warfare, however, cautioning that technology superiority is "only transitory" and this will need constant improvement to stay prepared for future wars.
He emphasised that a whole-of-nation approach is needed to fight and sustain a prolonged war.
The general officer said multiple-domain operations is not about combining all the capabilities, rather it implies integrating different capabilities to "pose multiple dilemma to an adversary".
The CDS shared that the military is working with the three services to "modernise our electronic warfare architecture".
The general officer, elaborating on multi-domain operations, said integration of military-space architecture and the ability to communicate effectively are key to carrying out such operations.
Also, cyber defence is an integral component of multi-domain operations, he added.
The CDS further said an integrated command and control system is a prerequisite for conducting multi-domain operations.
On military preparedness, at a time when multiple conflicts are underway, Gen Raja Subramani said, "We need not look at a prescribed template. We need to have our own template."

title: William and Kate on Earthshot Prize green carpet in Mumbai
description: The pair arrived at the ceremony where five £1m prizes were awarded to projects aimed at solving climate challenges.
content:
William and Kate on Earthshot Prize green carpet in Mumbai
Prince William was joined by Catherine at this year's Earthshot Prize ceremony in Mumbai, which rewards people who create solutions to the world's climate challenges.
The pair walked the event's green carpet wearing outfits from Indian designers - William wore a bespoke Bandhgala, a classic Indian formal jacket, and Catherine was dressed in an Anarkali dress by Mahima Mahajan.
Founded by Prince William, Earthshot awarded five £1m prizes to projects including an effort to bring more electric rickshaws to India, and to ban "forever chemicals" in France.
Bhutan won the Protect and Restore Nature prize for its environmental policies that help to safeguard water supplies for nearly a fifth of the world's population.
William and Catherine's visit to India is the first time the couple have been on an official overseas trip together in four years, following Catherine's cancer treatment.

title: Prince and Princess of Wales play street cricket in Mumbai
description: William and Catherine met locals on their visit to India, ahead of a meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi later in the week.
content:
Prince and Princess of Wales play street cricket in Mumbai
The Prince and Princess of Wales played a game of street cricket in a business district in Mumbai, as they began a three-day official visit to India.
They were joined by cricketing superstar Sachin Tendulkar, to the delight of local children who only found out who their VIP guests were at the last minute.
It marks the first time in four years that the royal couple has been on an official overseas trip together - following Catherine's treatment for cancer.
The pair will attend a number of engagements over the coming days, including events for the Earthshot Prize which was founded by Prince William.
They are also set to meet Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi later in the week.

title: Delimitation Bill: Modi govt just a whisker away from 2/3 majority in Lok Sabha, 3 parties hold key
description: An analysis by ThePrint shows just an abstention by one opposition MP & non-availability of two jailed members will push Bill through, provided three fence sitters support govt.
author: Ananya Chaba
content:
New Delhi: The Narendra Modi government seems to be a whisker away from the two-third majority in Parliament required to pass the Constitution Amendment Bill that proposes to provide a proportionate increase of 50 percent in Lok Sabha seats across all states and links the delimitation exercise to women’s reservation.
The Bill also proposes to freeze each state’s share of parliamentary representation till 2051. Cleared by the Union Cabinet Friday, the Bill will be introduced Monday in the Lok Sabha, when the House meets for a special session.
According an analysis by ThePrint, just an abstention by one opposition MP and non-availability of two jailed members, Amritpal Singh and Abdul Rashid Sheikh, will push the Bill through, provided the three fence sitters—Nationalist Congress Party’s Sharad Pawar faction, Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) and the Yuvajana Sramika Rythu Congress Par (YSRCP)—come around to support the Bill.
The amended Bill as cleared by the Union Cabinet seems to address the conditions put forward by the three parties. Together, these regional parties have a combined strength of 34 MPs.
In the DMK’s case, it is about maintaining the proportion of seats which the Bill addresses while the other two parties are also softening their stand. On Friday, DMK president M.K.Stalin reiterated two demands: that Tamil Nadu’s existing 7.18 percent share of the Lok Sabha seats be protected in the event of an expansion of the House, and that the existing proportions of parliamentary representation among states remain frozen for another 25 years.
Nationalist Congress Party (Sharadchandra Pawar) has formally extended support to the Delimitation Bill, its spokesperson Jitendra Awhad announced.
Meanwhile, the opposition INDIA bloc allies are meeting Saturday to take a stand on the revised Constitutional Amendment Bill involving delimitation. The special sitting of the Parliament will start Monday, with the Lok Sabha sitting Monday and Tuesday and the Rajya Sabha on Wednesday and Thursday.
Also Read: Women’s reservation is the pretext, delimitation is the plan
How numbers currently stack up in Lok Sabha
In April, the government fell 54 votes short of securing the requisite majority in the Lok Sabha for the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, which sought to enable delimitation based on the 2011 Union Census.
Seven months on, as it prepares to make a second attempt at pushing through the legislation, shifts in political alignments have altered the parliamentary arithmetic.
In June, 20 of the 28 Lok Sabha MPs of the All India Trinamool Congress broke away from the Mamata Banerjee-led party and announced their merger with the Nationalist Citizens Party of India (NCPI).
The rebellion dealt a blow to the INDIA bloc, leaving Mamata’s faction with just eight MPs. Though the breakaway group is not formally part of the ruling National Democratic Alliance (NDA), it is aligned with the BJP.
The INDIA bloc also lost the support of the DMK and its 22 Lok Sabha MPs in the aftermath of the Tamil Nadu elections that took place in April.
On the other hand, the NDA has made gains. The merger of six MPs from the Uddhav Thackeray-led Shiv Sena with the Eknath Shinde faction has taken its strength in the Lok Sabha to 13.
The ruling alliance gained another MP earlier this week when the Shiromani Akali Dal returned to its fold, six years after walking out of the NDA over the now-scraped farm laws.
The current strength of the Lok Sabha stands at 540, with three seats lying vacant. Of these, 300 MPs, or nearly 56 percent, belong to the NDA, while 180 are from the INDIA bloc. Of the remaining 60 MPs, seven are Independents while others belong to parties and factions outside the two alliances.
While the political churn may have helped the government, the NDA still remains short of the two-thirds mark in a fully voting Lok Sabha. The focus shifts to parties outside the ruling alliance and the stand they take on the proposed legislation.
Where NDA can find numbers
Unlike an ordinary Bill, a Constitution Amendment Bill requires a special majority to get through Parliament. With the current strength of the Lok Sabha at 540, the number the government needs to muster is 360 at present.
The Sharad Pawar-led NCP faction, which remains part of the INDIA bloc, has eight MPs in the Lok Sabha. The Jagan Mohan Reddy-led YSRCP, which has 4 MPs and backed the Constitution Amendment Bill in April, appears inclined to do so again, but with a condition. Party sources told news agency ANI that its support would be contingent on the legislation safeguarding regional representation.
ThePrint mapped eight possible combinations of support from the three parties, taking as its starting point a tally of 324 votes in favour of the proposed amendment.
This baseline assumes support from all NDA MPs, barring the Speaker, the 20 Trinamool rebels, the United People’s Party Liberal (UPPL), the All India Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen (AIMIM), the Bharat Adivasi Party (BAP), the Zoram People’s Movement (ZPM), and Independent MP Umeshbhai Babubhai Patel.
The DMK, with its 22 MPs, can make the biggest difference to the government’s tally. Its support alone would take the number of votes in favour of the amendment to 346. If the NCP (SP) comes on board as well, the tally rises to 354.
Even if all three parties were to throw their weight behind the legislation, however, the government would have 358 votes—two short of the requisite majority in a fully voting Lok Sabha.
However, the two-thirds mark is not set in stone. Since the threshold is determined by the number of MPs present and voting, every absence or abstention on the non-supporting side brings down the number of affirmative votes the government needs.
Should the two above-mentioned jailed MPs be absent, the two-thirds mark will come down to 358—precisely the number the government can muster with the backing of all three regional parties.
Additionally, the government can get the Bill through the Lok Sabha even without the YSRCP’s four votes. With the DMK and the NCP (SP) on board, the absence or abstention of eight non-supporting MPs will be enough for its tally of 354 to meet the requisite majority.
The renewed delimitation push, then, can hinge as much on the votes it secures as on those that are not cast.
(Edited by Tony Rai)

title: ‘Must be dealt with iron hand’: SC’s blistering criticism of Vijay govt & temple board in Deepam row
description: Top court suspends Board of Trustees of the temple & appoints two former judges to run the shrine. Bench rejects collector’s interim status report, calls it 'crocodile tears'.
author: Bhadra Sinha
content:
New Delhi: Observing the Board of Trustees of Arulmigu Subramaniaswamy Temple were in flagrant violation of its 20 November order to light the lamp on Karthik Purnima, the Supreme Court Friday suspended its functioning and appointed two former judges to run the Hindu shrine.
S. Vaidyanathan, former chief justice of Meghalaya High Court, and V. Parthiban, a former judge of Madras High Court, would immediately take charge of the temple’s administration as its receivers.
Prima facie satisfied that a case of contempt was made out against the Madurai collector, the deputy commissioner of Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department, who serves as the executive officer of the temple, the Board and other authorities, the court said the chain of events that unfolded in the case would indicate that the “executive authorities seemed to have acted at the dictates of their political bosses.”
The events, a bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and J.M.Pancholi said, has to be unearthed to not only save the court’s dignity, but also to maintain purity in the administration of justice.
It issued contempt notices to each one of them, in addition to the members of the Board.
The Tamil Nadu chief secretary was directed to place details, including the emails, telephone calls, messages, if any made, forwarded, exchanged between the officials with the all detailed records regarding the matter. The state’s top civil servant has to appear in person on the next hearing on 15 December.
Also Read: Deepathoon Deepam row: Temple board cites traditional rules, shrine officials dispute their role
‘Last resort’
Fully satisfied that the Board failed to administer the temple, the bench said appointment of receivers was a measure of “last resort, intended to safeguard the institution and ensure that its administration respects its traditions, rituals and sanctity”.
The bench was particularly critical of the Board’s resolution, which, it said, reflected its “categorical” stand not to implement the court’s orders. The resolution, while denying permission to the authorities to light the lamp at the hill top, noted that the top court should be apprised about the customary and agami practices of the temple, which did not require the lighting of the lamp at the hill top, but the mandapam (pillared hall or pavilion).
“This is serious infraction on their part, which is also aided by other officials,” the court said, adding the resolution on its face firstly disclose wilful and flagrant disobedience of its interim order. Secondly, it shows a deliberate attempt to undermine the court’s authority and brazen disregard of the undertaking given to the high court.
In the interim order, the SC had directed the Tamil Nadu government to allow lighting of the Deepam at Deepathoon on 24 November. This was a one-time measure until it disposed of the government’s appeal against a Madras High Court order directing the state to facilitate the lighting of the lamp at the Deepathoon pillar and not the mandapam, which was the customary practice till then.
But, in a status report filed 25 November, the collector tendered an apology for not complying with the court order and blamed the Board for the disobedience, saying its resolution denied permission to the administration to light the flame.
This was followed by a contempt petition and an additional application, demanding action as well as implementation of the 20 November order. It was argued that the authorities not just defied the SC order but also breached its undertaking before the HC the next day to comply with the top court’s directive.
The SC’s Friday order was on these applications. It pulled up the police and directed the commandant, Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF), Chennai, to forthwith take over the security of the temple and the entire hill and ensure devotees carry out the rituals peacefully.
The court directed the DGP, the IGP, the Madurai commissioner and the government to ensure smooth transition of handing over security arrangements. The CRPF was directed to maintain peace even at the local dargah and ensure devotees are able to perform their respective rituals without any obstruction.
Dargah & the lamp
With regard to Muslim devotees wanting to offer prayers at the dargah, also present at the top of the hill, the bench directed that the lamp would be lit by the devotees or the temple administration and be at a place that is at least 50 meters away from the dargah from all sides.
For this, it said, the CRPF can take necessary steps as permissible to protect the dargah. Those visiting the dargah should be in no way hindered, stopped, or prevented from offering their prayers there.
The bench found “some force” in the submission and contention of the applicants that even though the auspicious occasion to light the lamp at Deepathoon pillar was over, it should nevertheless be lit during the Tamil month of Kardigai.
“Having regard to the significance of the festival and of the day on which the Deepam was originally directed to be lit, we direct the receivers to ensure lighting of Kardigai Deepam at Deepathoon tomorrow, i.e., 28 November, at such time as it may be fixed in consultation with the sthanikars using the flame lit at Uchai Pillaiyar Mandapam on 24 November, provided that the said flame is still burning or by making alternative arrangements,” it ordered.
As per the order, the receivers shall administer the temple in keeping with its traditions and rituals, preserve its sanctity and comply with the applicable law, rules and regulations. They have the liberty to approach the court for clarification or further directions, if need be. The government shall extend all logistic support to the court receivers, the bench ordered.
Considering the authorities neither implemented the order nor attempted to purge the contempt, the top court vacated its order that stopped the operation of the HC judgement and directed the receivers to permit every devotee to light the lamp on the Tirupakundram, keeping in mind the security aspects.
Also Read: A temple, a dargah and a disputed pillar: The legal battle over Thiruparankundram Deepam
‘Conscience shaken’
The Board’s resolution, the top court said, shook its “conscience.” It observed the court “in fact had heard both the sides at length on temple traditions before passing its interim order”.
Thus the statement carried unwarranted insinuation that the court had failed to uphold the traditions canvassed before this court, the bench said, adding that the Board never appeared before it to contest the matter by impugning its 20 November interim order.
The Board’s statement compounds the “affront” to the authority of this court, which speaks with the authority of the Constitution, the bench said. Hence, its orders command obedience and the authorities are warranted to act in aid of the court.
“But when an executive authority that presumes to decide whether an order of this court deserves to be obeyed, arrogates to itself a power the Constitution has never conferred upon it, it amounts to willful defiance and is a flagrant breach of constitutional duty,” the bench observed.
“It obstructs the administration of justice and strikes at the very root of the rule of law.”
The affront, it said, is all the graver when it comes from the authorities whom the Constitution commands to act in the aid of this court. “The willful non-compliance of the order of the court, especially by the executive authorities cannot go unnoticed and it has to be dealt with iron hands.”
The failure to light the lamp, viewed in conjunction with the adoption of a resolution contrary to the express direction of the court and the invocation of the temple tradition to justify the force for its time, discloses a willful and flagrant disobedience of the order, the court remarked.
On the collector’s interim status report, the court said though it tendered a formal apology, the officer attempted to shift the blame for non-compliance entirely on the temple administration.
“We are surprised that the collector, who is the district magistrate, can take such a stand. His powers are wide enough. His hands are quite long which can be used for implementation of orders of this court,” it said.
The preliminary report was not satisfactory, it said, because it did not reflect what actually transpired on that day.
Noting that the report was nothing but “crocodile tears,” the bench said it reminded of the quote, ‘you play dead and I act or pretend to cry’.
“We are prima facie satisfied that the order of this court dated 20 November has been willfully disobeyed despite the undertaken given before the High Court that the order would be complied in letter and spirit,” the bench said, issuing the contempt notices to the chief secretary, the DGP, the secretary to the state government, the collector, the Board trustees among others.
The top court said these notices should be served personally within three days and a personal affidavit should be filed confirming the service of notice. The SC registry shall forward copies of the order to the chief secretary to apprise the “utter and apparent disregard” of constitutional duty by the officers concerned, it added.
“This court has, however, intervened where the authorities interested with the administration of public institutions have failed to discharge their duties,” the bench said.
(Edited by Tony Rai)

title: After VanDyke chargesheet, NIA opens fresh UAPA probe into ‘anti-India’ elements in Myanmar
description: The latest FIR was filed on orders from the MHA, which on 7 September cited “credible information” about certain proscribed organisations.
author: Mayank Kumar
content:
New Delhi: The National Investigation Agency (NIA) has registered a fresh case under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967 (UAPA) to probe ethnic armed organisations and other “anti-India elements” operating from Myanmar for committing terrorist activities in Manipur. According to the latest FIR, these organisations were supplying arms, ammunition and explosives to the proscribed and insurgent organisations in India.
This FIR was filed two days after not invoking similar provisions of the anti-terror law in the chargesheet against seven foreign nationals, including a US national, Matthew Aaron VanDyke, in a similar case of training the ethnic armed groups in Myanmar, which were allegedly supporting certain proscribed Indian insurgent groups, in the previous case.
The agency arrested them on similar grounds for imparting training to Ethnic Armed Groups (EAGs), who were also allegedly known to be supporting some proscribed Indian Insurgent Groups by way of supplying weapons and other terrorist hardware and training theт thus affecting national security and interest of India.
The fresh FIR was filed on 10 September—two days after the chargesheet against the US national VanDyke and six Ukrainian nationals (Hurba Petro, Slyviak Taras, Ivan Sukmanovskyi, Stefankiv Marian, Honcharuk Maksim, and Kaminskyi Viktor) on the grounds of illegally crossing over to Myanmar and returning to India through an illegal route.
While seeking their remand in March this year, the agency told the court that the accused persons made “important disclosures” related to the “conspiracy,” including them being in “direct touch” with terrorists “carrying AK-47 rifles.”
However, the fresh FIR did not clarify whether it was registered based on disclosures allegedly made by the foreign nationals arrested in March this year.
Security agencies in the past have flagged the movement of cadres of the Indian Insurgent Groups (IIGs) to Myanmar for training in sophisticated weapons and return to Manipur, where ethnic clashes have continued intermittently since May 2023.
The latest FIR was filed on orders from the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), which on 7 September cited “credible information” about certain proscribed organisations— People’s Liberation Army (PLA), People’s Revolutionary Party of Kangleipak (PREPAK), and People’s Revolutionary Party of Kangleipak-Progressive (PREPAK-Pro)- operating from Myanmar to commit terrorist activities in the state of Manipur. The MHA ordered the agency to register a case and conduct a thorough probe to uncover the larger conspiracy.
The NIA FIR read, “….And whereas, these organisations based in Myanmar are supplying and causing to supply arms, ammunition and explosives to the proscribed organisations and insurgent organisations in India, and have also been raising, providing and transmitting funds through illegal and clandestine channels, knowing and intending that such arms, ammunition, explosives and funds are being used for the commission of terrorist acts within the territory of India.”
Additionally, the MHA had also cited the continuous conspiracy by these outfits to commit terrorist acts, including targeted killings of innocent civilians and attacks upon security forces, with the deliberate aim of inflaming enmity and hatred between different ethnic and community groups in the region, provoking violence and displacement, and striking terror among the people.
Based on the MHA’s inputs, the NIA had registered a case against unknown suspects under section 25 of the Arms Act, 1959; sections 5 & 6 of the Explosive Substances Act, 1908; and sections 17, 18, 38, 39, and 40 of the UA(P)A, 1967.
The NIA FIR further read, “And whereas, the Central Government is of the opinion that a scheduled offence under the National Investigation Agency Act, 2008 has been committed and the case is related to providing material and financial support to proscribed organisations and insurgent organisations in India by certain ethnic armed organisations and other anti-India elements based in Myanmar and having regard to the gravity of the offence, its grave ramifications, and the need to unearth the larger conspiracy, the matter requires thorough investigation by the National Investigation Agency in accordance with the provisions of the National Investigation Agency Act, 2008….”
The development came after the NIA filed a chargesheet against the foreign nationals without invoking provisions of the UAPA, citing the absence of “conclusive evidence” to establish that their activities were against India’s national interest.
Notably, the agency has a jurisdiction to probe cases outside India only if the alleged offences either affect India’s national interest or interests of Indian nationals.
Instead, they were charged under the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025. The Foreigners Regional Registration Officer (FRRO) subsequently paved the way for their discharge from the case and return home. While VanDyke returned to India in October this year to attend court proceedings, the six Ukrainians had moved exemption pleas, which the court allowed.
Explaining the agency’s rationale for not invoking UAPA provisions so far, the NIA Director General Rakesh Aggarwal earlier this month said the specific segment of the probe concerning the identification of the IIGs was still underway, and a chargesheet will be filed if the investigation establishes such facts.
Aggarwal said last week after the conclusion of the anti-terror conference in New Delhi, “They came to India on a valid visa, but they had crossed over to Myanmar illegally, where they had trained certain insurgents, some of whom are suspected to be IIGs (Indian insurgent groups). So far in the investigation, it has been proven that they came on valid visas to India and crossed over to Myanmar through an illegal route and again entered India through an illegal route when they were arrested.”
He further said that this part of the investigation had been completed and the facts established, with a chargesheet filed. He said, “The second part of the investigation is being carried out to ascertain exactly who the IIGs trained. Unless we establish the identities of those trained by them, it will not be possible to charge them under the UAPA.”
A lot of data is being analysed to establish the identity of the IIGs who were beneficiaries of their training, the NIA chief had said, adding that if the offence is established, the NIA can charge-sheet them.
(Edited by Anupama Yadav)

title: Wire Impact | ECI Tells West Bengal to Settle the Cases of Voters Left ‘Under Adjudication’ - The Wire
description: The Wire had reported, on November 13, that the commission’s own figures for these voters did not match the rolls.
author: Aparna Bhattacharya
content: Kolkata: The Election Commission of India (ECI) has told West Bengal’s Chief Electoral Officer (CEO) how to deal with voters still marked “under adjudication”, more than seven months after the state’s electoral roll was frozen for the Assembly election.In a letter dated November 27, 2026, “Clarification on Electors under Adjudication in West Bengal”, the commission’s Secretary, Pawan Diwan, wrote that cases in which judicial officers had passed orders but had not e-signed them “may be treated as decided” and referred to electoral registration officers (EROs). The EROs are then to update the roll “as per decision written by the Judicial Officers”.Cases that judicial officers have yet to decide “may be referred to the concerned EROs, being the statutory authorities, for taking appropriate decisions”.The letter comes two weeks after The Wire reported, on November 13, that the commission’s own figures for these voters did not match the rolls. The CEO’s office had told the Calcutta high court that 815 cases across the state had not been decided by judges, while 5,004 had been decided but not signed.The rolls of just 11 of Murshidabad’s 22 constituencies, examined by The Wire, recorded 29,347 voters still under adjudication. They included Md Selim Reza, a government schoolteacher who had served as a Booth Level Officer (BLO) during the revision, and whose own name had been left undecided since February.The commission’s letter responds to three letters from the CEO’s office, dated October 17, October 28 and November 4, seeking clarification.What the clarification saysThe letter sets out what should happen to four groups of voters.Those under adjudication whose cases were decided but not signed are to be treated as decided. The EROs are to update the roll according to what the judicial officer wrote. Those whose cases were never decided will go to the EROs for a decision.Voters deleted by judicial officers who have not appealed need no action, the letter says, since they have been excluded by a judicial officer’s order. Voters whose appeals have been decided by a tribunal, and who have been excluded, are to have the tribunal’s decision implemented.For voters deleted by judicial officers whose appeals are still pending before the tribunals, the letter asks that the Supreme Court’s directions of November 23 on prioritising appeals be followed. It adds that if such voters submit Form 6, the application to be added to the roll, “EROs should not process it till decision has arrived in such cases from Appellate Tribunal”.What it meansFor voters with orders already written, the letter ends a wait that began when the roll was frozen on 6 April. Judges’ decisions that were never signed, among them, by the commission’s own report at the freeze, 44,027 voters found eligible, can now be entered on the roll.The letter dated November 27, 2026, from the ECI to the West Bengal CEO, which sets out what should happen to four groups of voters whose cases were left ‘under adjudication’.For those whose cases were never heard, it hands the decision back to the electoral registration officer. In February, when the Supreme Court sent pending cases to judicial officers, lakhs of voters whose cases EROs had already decided were moved to the judges as well, as The Wire has reported. Now, the cases the judges never reached are being sent back to the EROs.The letter sets no deadline for EROs to decide the cases sent back to them, and does not say how many voters remain under adjudication. It does not explain why the CEO’s figure of 815 undecided cases is a fraction of the number recorded on the rolls.For voters whose appeals are still pending, the letter closes one door. They cannot apply afresh through Form 6 while their appeals remain undecided. More than 21 lakh appeals for inclusion are pending before the tribunals. On 27 November, petitioners told the Supreme Court that voters whose appeals remain pending when municipal elections are held should be allowed to vote.Tribunal judges’ pay raisedIn a separate notification issued the same day, the commission raised the honorarium paid to the former high court judges who sit on the SIR’s appellate tribunals in West Bengal. Former high court judges will now be paid Rs 2.5 lakh a month, and former chief justices of high courts Rs 2.6 lakh, with effect from November 20.Under the commission’s notification of April, 7 they had been paid Rs 1.5 lakh and Rs 1.6 lakh respectively for a base period of two weeks, and Rs 25,000 for every week after that. The revision followed a recommendation from the Calcutta high court’s internal committee on the SIR, conveyed to the Chief Election Commissioner by the high court’s Registrar General on 20 November.The ECI has also raised the honorarium paid to the former high court judges who sit on the SIR’s appellate tribunals in West Bengal.The commission asked the CEO to have the notification published in the state Gazette the same day, and to release the honorarium immediately. In August, the high court’s Registrar General had written to the commission that a meeting of the tribunal judges had found a “severe lack of ministerial and secretarial support” in hearing and disposing of appeals.For our full coverage on the SIR and the issues it has brought to citizens, click here.

title: Revised Delimitation Bill Puts Spotlight on Shifting Alliances and Cracks in Opposition Unity - The Wire
description: A copy of the Bill has not yet been made available to MPs, questions remain over whether the opposition INDIA bloc will be able to repeat its feat in April with the NCP(SP) skipping the INDIA bloc’s Saturday meeting and speculation over how DMK will vote.
author: Sravasti Dasgupta
content: New Delhi: The Union government’s move to bring an amended delimitation Bill has put the spotlight on shifting alliances and raised questions about whether the opposition INDIA bloc will be able to repeat its feat in April, when it unitedly defeated the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill brought by the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)-led National Democratic Alliance (NDA) in the Lok Sabha.In April, the constitutional amendment had received 298 votes in favour and 230 against, with the government falling short by 54 votes to get it passed. But since then, the BJP has gained in numbers through defections in the Trinamool Congress (TMC), Shiv Sena (Uddhav Balasaheb Thackeray) and Aam Aadmi Party (AAP). Crucial to the opposition INDIA bloc’s numbers is the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK), which exited the alliance following the Congress ending its alliance with the party after the Tamil Nadu Assembly elections. While the Congress has said that it is reaching out to all opposition parties, including the DMK, within the INDIA flock too, speculation has also grown over whether Nationalist Congress Party (Sharadchandra Pawar) (NCP (SP)) will vote in support of the BJP, with the party’s working president and MP Supriya Sule only saying that the party’s stand will become clear once the bill is seen. Former Tamil Nadu chief minister M.K. Stalin in a statement said on Friday that keeping with the resolution passed by the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly and the resolutions adopted at the Joint Action Committee meeting for fair constituency delimitation, the DMK remains firm on its two positions.This includes that if the number of parliamentary constituencies is increased, under no circumstances should Tamil Nadu’s share fall below its current 7.18% and the existing proportion of parliamentary representation among States, as determined on the basis of the 1971 Census and frozen earlier, must remain unchanged for another 25 years.“The DMK remains firm on both these positions today and will continue to do so. There is no change in this position, and there is no question of compromise,” he said.The NCP (SP) on the other hand has maintained ambiguity over whether it will support the BJP, with MP Supriya Sule saying that the legislation will have to be seen first, while MLA Jitendra Ahwad after meeting party supremo Sharad Pawar saying that the party supports delimitation as it has to conducted. “The discussion wasn’t about our party’s official stance. The general point being made was that the delimitation process is a constitutional requirement… A decision has been made to support the delimitation process, and we will indeed support it. We will support the delimitation,” said Ahwad to reporters on Friday evening.On the other hand, Sule said that she is not “aware” of the agenda.“I am not aware of the details. The session has been announced, but I do not have the agenda. Our party is a very disciplined party, and the whip is issued by our senior leader Amol Kolhe when the dates are announced. I have not seen the bill yet, so how can I state the party’s position on it? I do not know anything about this matter,” she said.Earlier this week, Sule had fuelled speculation of supporting the BJP after she said that the party would support the bill “if it is in country’s interest.”While INDIA bloc leaders are set to meet on Saturday, Sule has said she will remain in Mumbai over the weekend, with Pawar still in the hospital.Meanwhile the Congress on Friday too held a meeting of its leaders in New Delhi, while another meeting of the INDIA bloc will be held on Saturday.Following the meeting Congress MP Gaurav Gogoi said that communications have been sent to other members of the INDIA bloc.“This will be a joint meeting with other political parties. As per the information available with me, the government is attempting to bring back the Delimitation Bill. Congress’ demand has been clear right from the beginning; we have said that the current strength in Lok Sabha should be upheld,” he said. “Second, 33% women’s reservation should be done on the current strength. Third, the proportion of the strength of various states in Lok Sabha should be upheld for the coming 25 years. This is our clear demand. But on the pretext of women’s reservation, PM Modi and HM Amit Shah want to do delimitation.”Earlier on Friday, Congress general secretary K.C. Venugopal had said that the party is reaching out to all opposition parties including the DMK.“We are approaching everybody because I think the DMK has always stood by the Constitution of India. I think whoever loves the Constitution of India cannot support this kind of divisive agenda. So, we will approach all other opposition parties, as we did earlier,” he said.Even within the Congress, there have been murmurs of MPs not voting unitedly with MP from UP’s Sitapur Rakesh Rathore saying that he has felt ignored by the party.Ahead of the elections in Uttar Pradesh, Samajwadi Party (SP) chief Akhilesh Yadav on the other hand has sought to make his party’s stand clear on Friday by saying that delimitation will be the BJP’s “biggest mistake.”Following the defections in the TMC, with 20 MPs moving to join the Nationalist Citizens Party of India (NCPI), the faction has the largest strength in the Lok Sabha after the BJP, Congress, SP and DMK. While the rebels are likely to support the BJP, the Mamata faction has questioned how they can vote with their disqualification petitions still pending with Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla.“Will these traitors now be allowed to vote on the Delimitation Bill in the Lok Sabha? Are their votes legal? How can they vote when they should have been disqualified by now?” said TMC MP Sagarika Ghose. With copies of the proposed delimitation bill not available to MPs until late on Friday evening, the Congress has questioned the Modi government’s moves, accusing the BJP of “plotting to fraudulently manufacture a two-thirds majority in the Lok Sabha.”“It is extraordinary and totally unacceptable that the Lok Sabha is scheduled to debate the Constitution Amendment Bill and other Bills on Monday, November 30th and till 1800 hrs on Friday, November 27, the Bills have NOT been shared with the MPs. Games continue to be played by the PM-HM jodi,” said Congress MP Jairam Ramesh.Earlier on Friday, Ramesh called the delimitation bill and the bid to manufacture majority in parliament, “an attack on the Constitution of India.” “It must and will be opposed with full force,” he said.

title: West Bengal Final Electoral Rolls to be Published on February 8, EC Approves Polling Station Changes - The Wire
description: The integrated draft electoral rolls will be published on December 15, 2026, claims and objections can be filed by voters from December 15, 2026 to January 14, 2027. These are to be disposed of by February 1, 2027.
author: The Wire Staff
content: New Delhi: The Election Commission of India (ECI) has revised the schedule for the Special Summary Revision (SSR) of electoral rolls in West Bengal on Friday (November 27) and approved a proposal to rationalise and shift polling stations in the state. The revision uses January 1, 2027 as the qualifying date, which means anyone who turns 18 on or before that date can be enrolled as a voter. The final rolls will be published in the state on February 8, 2027.In a letter to the West Bengal chief electoral officer, dated November 27, the EC said it had accepted the proposal sent by the state’s election office on November 18. Under the revised schedule, the rationalisation and rearrangement of polling stations is to be completed by December 3, 2026.The integrated draft electoral rolls will be published on December 15, 2026, claims and objections can be filed by voters from December 15, 2026 to January 14, 2027. These are to be disposed of by February 1, 2027, and the final rolls will be published on February 8, 2027.Also read: Bengal Police Are Demanding Documents From Voters Awaiting SIR Tribunal Orders. The CEO Office Doesn’t Know WhyThe commission has directed that the modified schedule should be given wide publicity through all available media and political parties should be informed in writing.In a separate letter issued today, the commission said it had approved the proposal on rationalisation and shifting of polling stations contained in three letters from the state’s home (elections) department, dated November 13, 14 and 20. The letter does not list the stations affected or the new locations.“In this context, all the political parties shall be informed and wide publicity shall be done in the concerned polling areas to create awareness among voters about the new locations of the polling stations. All concerned officials may also be informed accordingly for necessary action,” the EC said.For our full coverage on the SIR and the issues it has brought to citizens, click here.

title: Char Dham Helicopter Accidents Expose Safety Failures
description: Uttarakhand's booming religious tourism industry faces scrutiny after fatal helicopter crashes expose gaps in aviation safety, regulation and infrastructure.
author: Vedaant Lakhera
content:
On October 30, a helicopter carrying pilgrims from Badrinath, one of the four Char Dham shrines in Uttarakhand, crashed near Joshimath in Chamoli district. All six people aboard died: the pilot, Himanshu Sabharwal of Delhi, and five men from Bengaluru, identified as Prathapa Bachihalliy, V.B. Shankar Gowda, Sudhir K., S.S. Nataraja, and Arun Salunke. The Trans Bharat Aviation aircraft left Badrinath at about 1:14 pm for Dehradun, and the Uttarakhand Civil Aviation Development Authority (UCADA) lost track of it on its monitoring system as it crossed the Joshimath valley, the authority’s chief executive, Prateek Jain, told the Press Trust of India. UCADA grounded Trans Bharat’s entire fleet, and the Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) is investigating.
Earlier that day, the India Meteorological Department had issued an orange alert for Chamoli, warning of thunderstorms, lightning, hail and gusty winds of 40–50 kmph. Officials have not linked the weather to the crash or established its cause. Why did the helicopter take off?
Helicopter flights to Kedarnath began around 2003, and the Char Dham circuit by air took shape around 2010–11. The market has since grown into a network of private operators selling pilgrimage packages to all the shrines, and UCADA manages it. Since the BJP won the mandate in 2017, the State has promoted religious tourism as its main economic driver, and Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami has said his government wants to make Uttarakhand the “spiritual capital of the world”.
According to the Uttarakhand Tourism Department, Jageshwar Dham received 1,74,119 pilgrims in the first half of 2026, about two and a half times the 67,875 in the same period of 2025. Purnagiri Dham recorded 20,91,788 pilgrims by June, up from 14,35,290 a year earlier, though neither shrine is on the Char Dham route.
However, experts argue that the state has focused very little on developing adequate infrastructure to accommodate the scale of tourism it is promoting.
Minister of State for Civil Aviation Murlidhar Mohol told the Rajya Sabha on July 21, 2025, that the Char Dham Yatra had seen six helicopter accidents in five years: one each in 2022, 2023, and 2024, and four in 2025 until June. Two of the 2025 crashes were fatal. Six people died at Gangnani in Uttarkashi on May 8 and seven near Gaurikund on June 15, bringing the year’s toll to 13. On March 23, 2026, the Ministry of Civil Aviation told the Rajya Sabha that India’s helicopter accident rate in 2025 was 0.53 per 10,000 flying hours, the highest in five years.
A parliamentary standing committee on transport, tourism and culture, chaired by Rajya Sabha member Sanjay Kumar Jha of the Janata Dal (United), said in an August 2025 report that state agencies manage high-risk helicopter operations with limited central oversight. It urged a uniform national framework, terrain-specific training for mountain pilots and a helicopter oversight cell at the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA), the regulator of civil aviation and air safety. After the October 30 crash, the committee scheduled a meeting with officials of the Ministry of Civil Aviation and the DGCA on November 13 to deliberate on why accidents on the Char Dham route have not stopped.
Authorities say they have acted since 2025. UCADA cut helicopter services on the 2026 Yatra by up to 30 per cent, ETV Bharat reported, and the Ministry of Civil Aviation said the first phase of operations, which ended on June 26, carried more than 78,000 pilgrims without an incident.
Uttarakhand has over 100 helipads. However, only two of them have air traffic control (ATC) units–one at Sahastradhara in Dehradun and a temporary one at Sitapur, near Sirsi, under the supervision of Airports Authority of India officials. In high-altitude regions–like the Char Dham route–ATC support becomes critically important, where choppers are flying through narrow river gorges surrounded by steep mountain walls, and without ATC regulating aircraft spacing, two helicopters flying in opposite directions in poor visibility have almost no room to swerve and find themselves in fatal situations. The Ministry of Civil Aviation said in June that land has been identified for permanent ATC facilities at Badrinath and Kedarnath, with interim arrangements in place until they are built.
What the report found
A report by Martin Consulting LLC, exclusively accessed by Frontline, says most risks in Indian helicopter operations stem from inadequate operational-support infrastructure and operators’ pursuit of profit. The firm’s CEO, Mark D. Martin, an aviation safety expert with more than 35 years of experience, also spoke to Frontline for this article. The report says private operators at Katra, the base town for Vaishno Devi pilgrims in Jammu and Kashmir, are not permitted to run their own fuel trucks and depend on a “barrel” fuel farm, which it identifies as a source of heightened risk. It also describes the Katra helipad’s geographical location as a potential flight-safety hazard. The report calls the regulatory framework “inconducive” and names currency fluctuations, interest rates and fuel costs as the main sources of financial pressure on operators, saying lease terms will have an “aggressive effect” on the profit-and-loss statement.
The report analysed 15 incidents and accidents from 2019 to 2024, eight of them in Uttarakhand and five at the Kedarnath helipad. The operators in the State include Kestrel Aviation, Himalayan Heli, Aryan Aviation, Trans Bharat, Heritage Aviation, and Global Vectra, all licensed by the DGCA as Non-Scheduled Operators.
The report found that incidents attributed to maintenance deficiencies, crew actions or controlled flight into terrain, in which a serviceable aircraft is flown into the ground or an obstacle, were mostly linked to operators with a documented history of safety lapses and regulatory violations. It named Heritage, Kestrel, Aryan and UTair as operators “constantly under the DGCA surveillance scanner”.
All three Kestrel Aviation incidents the report lists involve the AW119 helicopter, including the April 2023 tail-rotor fatality at Kedarnath, in which an individual walked into the rotating tail rotor. The report calls the series “alarming”. Heritage Aviation had three incidents, among them the August 2019 crash at Moldi, on a flood-relief flight, that killed three people. UTair Aviation is on the DGCA’s surveillance list, and Global Vectra is separately on a safety watch list of the Oil and Natural Gas Corporation.
The report says investigators’ findings of the 2019 crash in Moldi reflect the same concerns as the other incidents: no risk assessment, the pilot’s failure to reconsider takeoff, a helipad that lacked prescribed requirements, “complacency” and no clear division of responsibilities. The same operators recur across categories of incidents while remaining under close DGCA scrutiny, and the report reads this pattern as a systemic problem of compliance culture.
The report rates the surveillance system at Sahastradhara helipad as “red” because it lacks radar and ADS-B coverage, which would enable communication between aircraft and the ground station. As a result, all air traffic must coordinate with Jolly Grant Airport in Dehradun. Hangar facilities are also rated “red”, as the State government is the only operator with a hangar at the helipad; no private non-scheduled operator has one. The absence of Doppler radar, which helps forecast weather conditions and wind speeds, is another concern, given that most crashes are attributed to unexpected weather changes. Access to weather data is also limited: UCADA provides only “basic” information, leaving pilots to make decisions with inadequate meteorological inputs.
According to the report, operators operating out of Dehradun’s Sahastradhara conduct informal safety assessments of their own. They maintain a WhatsApp group through which weather updates concerning arrivals and departures are circulated, while real-time data from the Kedarnath weather station are also relayed to the group. Additionally, the operators coordinate access to a shared CCTV surveillance network monitoring entry and exit points. “Even a wild guess would not say CCTV cameras are being used to monitor weather conditions,” Martin told Frontline.
The AAIB also found that UCADA had no formal procedure for sharing weather information and asked the DGCA to direct it to create one.
Martin said the wrong types and models of helicopters are being deployed for terrain that, he said, reaches about 4,600 to 5,200 metres (15,000 to 17,000 feet) and is “extremely inhospitable and demanding, with deep ravines, gorges, and other formidable geographical features”. He named adverse weather as the principal contributing factor in accidents there. He called the upkeep of the helicopters “the worst ever” and said Kestrel Aviation has the worst safety record among the operators. The DGCA suspended Kestrel in June 2025 after one of its helicopters made an emergency landing on a highway. Martin proposed that the State form its own team of safety inspectors. “There is an urgent need for the state to constitute its own dedicated team of safety inspectors, who would conduct rigorous on-site inspections… ensuring compliance with an iron fist,” he said.
Wing Commander Vineet Sharma, an experienced helicopter pilot, told Frontline that the helicopters private operators use are ill-suited to the terrain and weather. “Most of these helicopters are single-engine helicopters, with no radar system and no autopilot,” he said. The Federation of Indian Pilots made the same points in a letter to the Prime Minister seeking a national helicopter safety review, adding that the helicopters fly with a single pilot and only by visual flight rules. Sharma said two pilots are advisable on such routes, “But there are allegations that these operators fly single-pilot to sell one more seat and make more money”. A second pilot, he said, can offer input and help with decisions in bad weather.
When weather closes in after a departure from Kedarnath or Badrinath, Sharma said, the safest course is to turn back and land at the helipad, but operators pressure pilots to continue. “We have lost many lives and many pilots because of this,” he said. Martin spoke of the passengers’ stake: “These are pilgrims whose dream is to go and pay their respects at these shrines. The least we can do is be honest with them and provide a safe way for them to travel.”
The two-pilot order
The DGCA and UCADA met on October 31, and charter helicopters on Char Dham routes from Dehradun must now carry a co-pilot, Jain told the Press Trust of India. On November 1, the DGCA directed UCADA to ensure that pilots obtain separate clearance for every flight leg, replacing approval for a whole itinerary. However, this has faced considerable resistance as operators wrote collectively to the DGCA calling the two-pilot requirement commercially unviable. “This year, the Yatra was already nearing its conclusion, so the directive by the DGCA had little effect. However, when the Yatra resumes next year, the regulator will insist on two-pilot operations. Operators will have to restructure their salary arrangements to accommodate the additional costs. If they refuse to comply, the Yatra may not happen. This way, the operators are trying to strong-arm the DGCA by threatening to disrupt the continuation of the pilgrimage,” Sharma observed.
Officials have not publicly linked the weather to the October 30 crash, and the accounts published so far do not say who cleared the Trans Bharat flight to leave Badrinath under an orange alert or what weather information the pilot had.
Frontline has sent queries and reached out to the DGCA, UCADA, and the Uttarakhand Tourism Department and will update this article when they respond.
