title: Edward Anderson on the Global Networks of Hindu Nationalism
description: The historian discusses how Hindutva networks operate across India and the diaspora, shaping politics, caste, identity, and minority rights.
author: Abhish  K. Bose
content:
In August, Mohan Bhagwat, chief of the RSS, addressed a packed Madison Square Garden, 12 years after Narendra Modi filled the same arena. Weeks later, Bellingcat, a Netherlands-based investigative journalism group, reported that $117.8 million had moved through two US charities linked to the Hindu nationalist movement between 2020 and 2024. In California, a bill to outlaw caste discrimination remains stalled three years after it was vetoed.
The three episodes, within months of each other, have put the financial and political machinery of diaspora Hindutva back in the spotlight. Historian Edward Anderson has spent the past decade studying that machinery—the temples, charities, campus groups and messaging networks that connect Hindu nationalism in India to its following abroad. In 2024, he published Hindu Nationalism in the Indian Diaspora: Transnational Politics and British Multiculturalism (Penguin/Hurst/Oxford University Press), drawing on years of fieldwork among Hindu organisations in Britain and beyond. His research covers Indian politics and contemporary history, diasporas and migration, transnational networks, and multiculturalism.
In this interview, Anderson argues that diaspora Hindutva is neither a pure export from India nor something that grew up entirely on its own abroad. Money still flows mainly from the diaspora to India, largely through charities. Messaging, organisation, and anxieties move in both directions. He discusses the networks that built this politics, the caste tensions now surfacing within it, and how living as a minority abroad reshapes a majoritarian politics back home.
Excerpts:
Diaspora Hindutva was built between the 1960s and the 1990s on temples, the Hindu Swayamsevak Sangh (HSS), the Hindu Swayamsevak Sangh (HSS), and hundi collections and gala dinners. Is the money still flowing from the diaspora to India, or has that reversed? And what are the channels now?
It’s an important question, but I would slightly reframe it. Shakhas, the VHP, HSS, and charitable activities were all part of the story, but my book is as much about people, networks and ideas as money. And it starts earlier: the first overseas shakha was founded in Nairobi, Kenya, in 1947, two decades before the Sangh took root in Britain. It’s also worth stressing at the outset that Hindutva is a political ideology, distinct from Hinduism, and the organisations we’re discussing don’t speak for many Hindus abroad—a large proportion of whom are indifferent to, or actively opposed to, Hindu nationalism.
On money, the evidence still points overwhelmingly one way: from the diaspora to India, mostly through registered charities. My research hasn’t really focused on financial flows, but Bellingcat reported in October that two US charities it links to the Hindu nationalist movement received $117.8 million between 2020 and 2024, much of it granted abroad, chiefly to projects in India. Beyond charities, a great deal moves through family remittances, which are almost invisible to researchers. US PACs are a different matter: foreign nationals can’t legally contribute to American elections, so that is Indian American money in US politics rather than money from India.
What has shifted is the direction of organisation and narrative. Since 2014, the Indian state and the BJP have become far more active patrons of the diaspora, through stadium spectacles and the Overseas Friends of the BJP. The RSS has followed: in August the leader (Sarsanghchalak) of the Sangh, Mohan Bhagwat, addressed a packed Madison Square Garden, twelve years after Modi did. Although it’s worth noting that the first RSS Sarsanghchalak to travel overseas was back in the mid-1990s, and many Sangh leaders do travel quite widely. Also, much of what diasporic Hindus consume online now flows outwards from India, and this can be quite influential; the BBC found that more than half of 2,00,000 tweets about the 2022 Leicester unrest originated there. In short, money still largely flows home, but messaging goes in both directions—often from India to the diaspora.
Sewa International and the HSS are registered charities in the US and UK, though their political link to the Sangh is open knowledge in India. How does money move under the labels of “culture” and “disaster relief”?
In most cases, the mechanism is quite straightforward and largely legal. Organisations register as charities in Britain or the US with educational, religious or relief objectives. They then raise money, some of which is used to make grants to “partner” organisations in India that run schools, hostels, clinics, cultural activities, and so on.
The important thing to understand is that, for the Sangh, sewa (service) has never been separate from its wider project. This has always been a key aspect of how the Hindu nationalist movement seeks to influence and ultimately transform society. And it is one of the main ways in which the movement has grown, particularly where the Indian state has been weak or absent. For instance, schools in remote parts of India can also transmit a particular vision of Hindu identity, and journalists’ investigations have documented anti-minority content in some of these projects. So money doesn’t need to be “diverted” into politics to be politically consequential—it helps to build the infrastructure and consciousness through which the movement grows. Charity law asks whether money was spent on charitable purposes; it doesn’t necessarily ask what kind of society those purposes are building.
A clear example from the UK is the fundraising that followed the Gujarat earthquake in 2001. Sewa International UK, at that time described as a “service project” of the HSS, raised several million pounds that year. Exposés, such as a 2002 Channel 4 investigation and a 2004 report by the campaign group AWAAZ, argued that many donors didn’t realise their money was going to the HSS, or that funds went to Sangh affiliates rather than to purely non-partisan relief work. The Charity Commission did open an inquiry, but its report was, many felt, rather cursory and equivocal—not helped by the fact that its investigators were refused visas to visit India. Similar allegations were made in the US about the India Development and Relief Fund.
But it’s difficult to give a comprehensive answer: the line between humanitarian and ideological work is blurred—often deliberately so—and the paper trail is very hard to follow.
Is anyone in America or Britain actually watching these charities, or do free speech and charity laws make them untouchable?
People are certainly watching, but mostly not those with the power to act. Much of the most rigorous scrutiny now comes from journalists, researchers, and activists rather than from regulators. In Britain, the Charity Commission has investigated a couple of charities, but nothing really came of it. What has changed recently is the political temperature. The US Commission on International Religious Freedom has called for sanctions on the RSS, and when Mohan Bhagwat visited New York in August, around ninety American politicians pledged not to accept RSS-linked donations. There are Indian and Indian origin activists in many countries around the world, representing a wide range of identities and political perspectives, who are vocal in their repudiation of communalism and ethnic nationalism. And this reflects a rich and long tradition of progressive politics of Indians overseas
Who calls the shots—Delhi or the diaspora? Is the diaspora an autonomous lobbying force, or a disciplined extension of Delhi’s foreign policy?
I think the honest answer is: neither, exactly. One of the central arguments of my book is that diasporic Hindutva is neither simply an export from India nor something that has grown up entirely organically abroad. Influence runs in several directions, and it varies a great deal from one organisation to another.
The Overseas Friends of the BJP is, by definition, the wing of a political party. In the US, it is registered as a foreign agent of the BJP, and during the 2019 general election in Britain, it said it would campaign against Labour in 48 marginal constituencies. The HSS overseas branches are connected to India through the RSS’s global division, the Vishwa Vibhag (based in New Delhi), and through visiting pracharaks and training camps. They often emphasise their autonomy, and they are also strikingly “vernacularised”—a shakha in New Jersey or Leicester feels quite different from one in Nagpur.
There are also a range of new groups that have emerged in recent years which I have used the term “neo-Hindutva” to understand: these may have close and direct links to the Sangh, or they may have connections which are much more convoluted or nebulous, but still they promote Hindutva politics in different ways. They are often shaped by domestic politics (i.e. that of the UK, US, etc.), and for pragmatic and other reasons tend to obfuscate their connections to Indian networks and ideologies.
It is also worth asking: which Delhi? The government and the RSS are obviously not the same thing. As Christophe Jaffrelot observed in an interview I published with him a few years ago, Modi and Amit Shah have concentrated power in ways that have at times sidelined the RSS. Tensions between the VHP and BJP have also surfaced at various points in time.
The past couple of years have also shown the limits of any “disciplined extension”. Many Hindu nationalist activists in America backed Trump, but his second term has brought tariffs on India, restrictions on skilled-worker visas and a good deal of openly anti-Indian rhetoric on the MAGA right. Delhi’s interests, the diaspora’s interests, and the ideological affinities of diasporic Hindutva haven’t always pulled in the same direction.
The first generation built temples; the second built campus groups. Are you seeing a shift from inherited identity —“I am Hindu because my parents are”—to ideological identity—“I am Hindu because of Hindutva”?
I think there’s a bit of both, and it’s not necessarily a linear path. Yes, some second- and third-generation Hindus may be finding their identity in ways which go beyond the culture they inherit from their parents. Clearly, online spaces facilitate this kind of enculturation in ways which previously didn’t exist. But at the same time, groups like the HSS and VHP overseas often deliberately cater to parents’ desire for their children to be exposed to Indian heritage, values, and a sense of belonging. The ideological component may be secondary or even not very well understood. And ideological identity can cut both ways: a younger generation of diasporic Hindus has also articulated a Hindu identity explicitly against Hindutva; Hindus for Human Rights is one such example.
You have tracked this politics moving from VHS tapes to WhatsApp to Reels. Does living as a minority in Leicester or New Jersey, while watching a majoritarian-strong state back home, make the diaspora more anxious than Hindus inside India?
I think there’s something in this. In India, the idea that Hindus are under siege has no demographic basis—it rests on a politics of fear and what has been called “saffron demography” (which has clear parallels with the white nationalist “Great Replacement Theory” in the West). In Britain, by contrast, Hindus genuinely are a minority, and not only in relation to the white majority; there are considerably more Muslims than Hindus in the UK. So narratives of a community under threat land differently. And they also resonate with wider narratives of Islamophobia, which have also been particularly powerful in the twenty-first century “War on Terror” context. They can speak to real experiences of racism and marginalisation, and to a sense of being outnumbered by another minority—while people can, at the same time, take pride in an assertive, Hindu-majority state back home. Those two feelings, of vicarious strength and local vulnerability, may seem contradictory, but they can reinforce one another.
The shift in media is enormously important here. When Hindutva circulated through pamphlets, magazines, and VHS cassettes, organisations had a good deal of control over what was produced and shared. WhatsApp and short-form video have largely dissolved that control, and a lot of the content now originates in India. Christophe Jaffrelot once made the point that segregation makes demonisation easier, because people have no first-hand knowledge of the “Other”. Algorithmic feeds can have a similar effect.
I would add two caveats, though. First, the anxiety isn’t simply manufactured; in the US, there has been a real and worrying rise in anti-Indian hostility during Trump’s second term. Second, the flow runs both ways. Romila Thapar has suggested that the “mentality of the ghetto” among India’s Hindu majority is itself partly shaped by the experience of Hindu minorities abroad. The diaspora may export its anxieties as much as it imports them.
Groups like the Hindu American Foundation (HAF), VHP-America, and Overseas Friends of BJP (OFBJP) now lobby Congress and Parliament in the language of religious freedom and pluralism. Has that succeeded in making Hindu nationalism mainstream in western politics? What actually counters it?
The organisations you mention are very different from one another, and some reject the Hindu nationalist label outright, so I’d rather talk about a broader pattern than pin it on particular groups. This is something I’ve tried to capture with the term “neo-Hindutva” that I mentioned earlier: a range of groups, often specifically diasporic (i.e. without direct counterparts in India), with positions closely aligned with Hindu nationalism, but expressed in the language of minority rights, multiculturalism, and civil liberties. That makes them legible, and often sympathetic, to politicians who would be unlikely to ever knowingly endorse a majoritarian movement.
Measuring success and impact is always difficult, but clearly some of these organisations have managed to present themselves as the voice of Hindus (even Indians) abroad. The language of “Hinduphobia” has moved from the margins into mainstream political spaces. Some politicians, from different parties, are openly sympathetic to the BJP and have hosted various Hindutva figures in Parliament (not without great controversy). And campaigns to block legislation on caste discrimination have had success, at least for now, both in California, where the bill was vetoed in 2023, and in Britain, where the government shelved plans to legislate in 2018.
But I’d be careful about saying that Hindu nationalism itself has become mainstream. What has been mainstreamed is a set of claims made in the name of “the Hindu community” by organisations whose ideological commitments many politicians don’t really understand. The strategy depends, to some extent, on that ideology staying in the background—which is why scrutiny and visibility matter.
And a lot of people have countered this—there is a long and rich tradition of progressive and radical politics in the Indian diaspora. For instance, we can see considerable efforts from Dalit and Ambedkarite organisers, who have done more than anything else to put caste on the legal agenda in the West. Progressive Hindu voices matter too, because they make it much harder to present criticism of Hindutva as an attack on Hindus (although of course this rhetoric is deployed). You also have many other identities and groups within the Indian diaspora presenting a version of their community which is counterposed to Hindutva: people from the left, feminists, secularists, and people from India’s many religious minority communities.
Your work shows these institutions have historically been upper-caste-led. With Equality Labs, the Cisco case and Dalit-Bahujan organising abroad, is “Hindu unity” fracturing? Is caste in the US workplace the new legal-political frontier?
Caste exposes a contradiction at the heart of Hindutva. As a majoritarian project, it needs a single, unified Hindu community, and the Sangh's historic answer to caste has essentially been to ask people to set it aside—to think of themselves as Hindus first. But, as various scholars have argued, that denial of caste conflict is manageable only up to a point, and the upper caste roots of the Hindu nationalist movement are hard to deny. Caste manifests differently in the diaspora. Some have suggested that certain elements are diluted and the salience of hierarchy and caste practices can be reduced. But that is certainly not always the case. Migration, and especially skilled migration to the US, has produced a diaspora that is disproportionately upper-caste, and its institutions have generally reflected that. Dalit and Bahujan organising challenges the idea that caste was left behind in India, and lived experience shows that caste also migrates: into offices, marriages and temples. So yes, I think it's fair to say that the workplace has become an important frontier. The response from much of the Hindu nationalist ecosystem has followed a fairly consistent pattern: minimising the extent of caste discrimination in the diaspora, presenting caste legislation as something that singles out and stigmatises Hindus (or can even be framed, in decolonial terms, as a divisive and orientalist imposition). You ask whether “Hindu unity” is fracturing? I think many would say that the idea of a monolithic “Hindu community” was always more an aspiration than a reality, and caste is where that becomes particularly hard to ignore.
Does BJP support among Indians in North America stem from a belief that an “assertive India” raises their own status there? If so, how do they reconcile championing majoritarianism at home while benefiting from pluralism and minority protections abroad?
Let me answer this from the British side, since that’s where most of my research has been focused—though much of what I’ll say applies across the Atlantic too. Status could definitely be part of it, and in Britain it has a particular postcolonial edge. For generations of migrants to the old imperial metropole, there was an association with being from a former colony and part of what people used to call the “Third World”. India is now a place British politicians court, given its economic and geostrategic significance. And British Indian voters are also important in UK elections. This is part of the context behind David Cameron introducing Modi to 60,000 people at Wembley in 2015. The same has been seen on the other side of the pond: the “Howdy Modi” rally in Texas in 2019, at which Trump and the Indian Prime Minister were hand-in-hand.
It’s certainly plausible that BJP support among Indians overseas is partly about an assertive and ostensibly patriotic form of politics resonating with people who may feel a degree of dislocation. That said, we should be careful about scale. Surveys suggest that support for Modi is lower and more divided in Britain than in the US—it also might be waning somewhat, and in any case support for Modi isn’t the same thing as commitment to Hindutva.
Your second question captures one of the paradoxes that first drew me to this subject: why would people support a majoritarian ideology in India while negotiating recognition as a minority in Britain? It is often dismissed as hypocrisy, but I think it is more interesting than that. Many simply don’t accept that India’s minorities are oppressed, because Hindutva casts Hindus as the historic victims. There is also a tendency to distinguish between “good” minorities and others. From the Rushdie Affair onwards, and especially after 9/11 and 7/7, some British Hindus rejected the catch-all “Asian” label and distanced themselves from British Muslims, presenting Hindus as a model minority. And rights language tends to be used selectively—invoked against “Hinduphobia”, resisted when it comes to adding caste to equality law.
What is striking in Britain at the moment is that, for some, the tension is resolved differently—by embracing a more restrictive nationalism here too. Recent polling suggests that support for Reform UK among British Indians has risen sharply since the 2024 election, albeit from a low base, and some Reform supporters draw explicit parallels between Farage and Modi.
Abhish K. Bose, a journalist based in Kerala, with 18 years of experience, previously worked as a staffer at The Times of India and The Deccan Chronicle-Asian Age.

title: Brights’ Society: Building a Community of Rationalists
description: At Pune’s Science for All meeting, rationalists challenged religious dogma, misinformation and shrinking support for science, calling for a stronger public scientific temper.
author: Mallika Ravikumar
content:
Kumar Nage was 10 when he lost his parents. Born in 1978 into a traditional Maharashtrian household, he found himself in an orphanage in Karambavane in Ratnagiri district, with a head full of questions.
“If there is a compassionate God out there, why has he left me in this condition?” he asked. “Why are my relatives, even the religious ones, not helping me?” The quest for answers led Nage to books, from works by the Marathi thinker Narhar Kurundkar to articles by the rationalist Narendra Dabholkar, founder of the anti-superstition organisation Maharashtra Andhashraddha Nirmoolan Samiti. “It changed my outlook completely,” says Nage.
Decades later, the ground gave way yet again when Dabholkar, his guide and mentor, was shot dead on a Pune street on the morning of August 20, 2013.
“It shattered me,” Nage recalls. “I became suicidal. Dabholkar had spent his whole life driving positive change. Why would anyone kill such a man? I could not understand it. I still cannot.”
Nage found a release for his grief in collective work. Today he is at the head of Brights’ Society, a platform active since 2014 that brings together atheists, agnostics, sceptics, and freethinkers so that rationalist thought can flourish. Its supporters range from the writer Javed Akhtar to former Maharashtra Chief Minister Prithviraj Chavan, both of whom were in Pune this November.
On November 21 and 22, Brights’ Society held its annual meeting at the Inter-University Centre for Astronomy and Astrophysics (IUCAA), on the campus of Savitribai Phule Pune University. Titled “Science for All” and co-organised with VicharVedh, this was the Society’s biggest edition yet, with a record number of registrations and participants from across the world.
The thread running through the two-day seminar was that the scientific method is a way of living as much as a laboratory protocol, one that involves following evidence, questioning authority, and refusing to accept an idea just because it is old, fashionable, or comfortable. Its other premise was that the wonder of science ought to belong to everyone and not to a privileged few.
Rationalism is no Western import into India, where more than two millennia ago the Charvaka, or Lokayata, school rejected the afterlife, the authority of the Vedas, and priestly rituals. Yet the conference came at a time when the scientific temper appears to be under attack in India and across the world. Misinformation, conspiracy theories, miracle cures, invented history, and fake babas abound, while champions of an unscientific outlook, including vaccine sceptics and climate deniers, have travelled from the fringe into the mainstream and found eager audiences.
Two days of questions
Akhtar opened the first day with a thought for reflection. “We routinely confuse the terms religious and communal,” he said, explaining that those bent on mischief exploit the confusion. The foremost communal leaders, in his view, were not religious people, and he cited Mohammad Ali Jinnah and V.D. Savarkar. “They made use of religion to get power.”
Religion itself, Akhtar suggested, grew out of the worship of what people feared or did not understand, such as earthquakes, floods, and diseases. “As science answered those questions, god disappeared from those domains.”
Those who persecuted Galileo, said Akhtar, did not know better, but people today do. If science has helped send rockets to precise locations on the moon, he asked, how can anyone continue to think like Galileo’s persecutors? The problem, he argued, begins early. “Telling a child about religion is like breaking their knees in childhood. Then, when they grow up, they are expected to run a race. How is it possible?”
If the scientific temper means questioning everything, it must also include questioning reason itself, and the veteran journalist Kumar Ketkar offered that counterweight. Drawing on the Nobel Prize-winning physicist Robert B. Laughlin’s book The Crime of Reason, Ketkar spoke of the outer limits of reason and of “mindless science”: the quest to live forever, artificial intelligence, and other technologies with the power to destroy the world.
Chavan turned the discussion to funds, recalling that when he was Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Science and Technology, India spent about 1 per cent of its GDP on science and technology, and he had wanted to raise this to 2 per cent. “I couldn’t do it, because there were other priorities,” he said.
The latest government figures, tabled in Parliament in July, put India’s research and development spending at 0.84 per cent of GDP in 2023-24. The corresponding shares were about 3.4 per cent in the US and 2.7 per cent in China in 2024, and 6.3 per cent in Israel in 2023.
Spending on science, Chavan argued, will rise only if civil society puts pressure on its elected representatives. “Only an increase in priority and government expenditure on science education will eventually translate into a society with a scientific temper.”
Chavan then presented the Jayant Narlikar Award to the scientist, poet, and science communicator Gauhar Raza, whose acceptance speech referred to the “bombardment of religious messages” a child receives daily from birth. “The only daily contact a child has with science is a 45-minute period at school,” said Raza, before highlighting the anti-science atmosphere prevailing in the country.
Scholars also spoke on access to knowledge and its democratisation, why the scientific temper matters, whether knowledge has a language, the problem of misinformation, and the materialist and rationalist traditions of India and the West.
Popular culture had its voices too, among them the actor Suvrat Joshi, who hosts the Marathi science podcast Soppa Karun Sangto (Let me put it simply) and spoke about using social media to make science fun and engaging for ordinary people. “The West can say art for art’s sake because they have progressed. We have a lot of problems here, so art has to be for a higher sake, for a better world,” said Joshi. “And I decided to use my storytelling for promoting rationality and science.”
The Society paid tribute to the astrophysicist Jayant Narlikar, IUCAA’s founding director, and his successor, the physicist Naresh Dadhich, both champions of the scientific temper who died in 2025. Narlikar’s daughter Leelavati recalled how her father, an ardent science communicator who loved talking to children about the marvels of the universe, made great efforts to reply to every postcard that brought him a question about science. Dadhich’s wife, Sadhana Dadhich, spoke about how her husband often argued passionately to persuade others to adopt a rational and scientific outlook on life.
On the second day, the veteran journalist Suresh Dwadashiwar received the Charvaka Award and used the occasion to rescue the term from caricature. Charvaka, he said, is not a vyakti (person) but a vichar (idea), and those who adopt that philosophy keep alive an ancient legacy of India. The popular couplet Yavat jivet sukham jivet / rinam kritva ghritam pibet (live happily as long as you live; borrow if you must, but drink ghee) has long been used to paint the Charvakas as crude hedonists. Dwadashiwar argued that it is, in fact, a Vedantin verse put into their mouths to ridicule them.
Comedy had its place as well, with stand-up sets on both days by two artists. Masoom Rajwani performed an act titled Stand Up for Science, while Varun Grover delivered the valedictory address. Both used satire to take apart unreason, defend the scientific temper, and comment on the times.
The first morning opened with Amrish Mishra’s rendition of the ghazal “Main na Hindu na Musalman” (I am neither Hindu nor Muslim), and the evening belonged to the sky, with astronomers leading a stargazing session on the IUCAA campus.
Among the many quotable lines heard over the two days, a few by the poet Uday Prakash, which Grover recited at the end of his set, went to the heart of the meeting. Their point is that the dead neither think nor speak, and that people who give up thinking and speaking, die too.
For many in the audience, though, the real gift was the chance to find one another and to bond with fellow rationalists who had dared to question the tenets they were raised with and decided to leave religion behind.
“There are many rational people,” says Nage. “The challenge is bringing them together.” Asked why freethinkers need to organise at all, he says reason has its own battles to fight, against laws on hurting religious sentiments and hostility from conservative groups. “That is why we must come together.”
For Brights’ Society, which seeks dialogue between atheists and the rest of society, the Pune meeting was a step towards that goal. More information about the group is available here.
Take assistance to overcome suicidal thoughts. Private and government helplines are available in every city.
Mallika Ravikumar is a former practicing lawyer and is now a writer published by Penguin, Hachette, and Speaking Tiger, among others, and writes on Indian history, nature, and culture.

title: Bangladesh Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmed claims India did not help Bengalis but weakened Pakistan in 1971: How Islamists are gaslighting its population to rewrite Bangladesh’s history
description: Since Sheikh Hasina’s ouster, Islamists of various hues are crawling out of the woodwork and veering Bangladesh towards Islamism. Bangladesh Speaker Uddin Ahmed is a prime example of this trend. | OpIndia News
author: Jinit Jain
content:
Bangladesh is facing one of the most difficult periods of its 55-year history. Months into pervasive anti-Hindu violence, Bangladesh has taken another hard turn to Islamism as its political representatives are now going all out in their efforts to appease Pakistan. On Wednesday, Bangladesh Parliament Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmed whitewashed the Pakistani massacre of Bangladeshis during the Liberation War of 1971, then proceeded to accuse India of not helping Bengalis but merely weakening Pakistan.
Ahmed, who is currently on an official visit to Pakistan, made the remarks while speaking to reporters at the Parliament House in Islamabad, where he recalled the events surrounding the war and the fall of Dhaka.
“India did not help the Bengalis but weakened Pakistan,” Ahmed said, attempting to recast India’s role in the liberation of Bangladesh as an act motivated chiefly by hostility towards Pakistan rather than the plight of millions of Bengalis who were being subjected to brutal military repression.
It is an atrocious statement to make, particularly coming from someone occupying the highest legislative position in Bangladesh. Ahmed is not an ordinary politician making an opportunistic remark to score points with a foreign audience. He is the Speaker of the Parliament of a country whose very existence is the result of the brutal repression unleashed by Pakistan against its Bengali population and the subsequent liberation war.
And yet, here he is, sitting in Islamabad, attempting to peddle a narrative that conveniently whitewashes the crimes committed by the Pakistani military and reduces India’s intervention in 1971 to a geopolitical manoeuvre aimed at weakening its western neighbour.
Ahmed’s remarks are not merely an insult to India. They are an insult to the millions of Bengalis who suffered under the Pakistani military, to the families of those who were murdered, to women who were subjected to horrific sexual violence, and to those who sacrificed their lives to ensure that Bangladesh could emerge as an independent nation.
The fact that Bangladesh’s Parliament Speaker is now attempting to whitewash those atrocities while standing on Pakistani soil tells us a great deal about how Bangladesh has gone to the dogs following the ouster of Sheikh Hasina.
A Bangladesh Parliament Speaker who appears more interested in pleasing Islamabad than remembering his own country’s history
Hafiz Uddin Ahmed’s comments did not emerge out of the blue. His entire visit to Pakistan appears to have been an exercise in signalling the warmth of the emerging relationship between Dhaka and Islamabad, particularly after the ouster of Sheikh Hasina and the Islamist takeover of Bangladesh in 2024.
Ahmed is on an official visit to Pakistan from November 23 to 29 at the invitation of Pakistan’s National Assembly Speaker Sardar Ayaz Sadiq. It is the first official visit to Pakistan by a sitting Speaker of Bangladesh’s Parliament. During the visit, Ahmed has met Pakistani President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, while expressing confidence that bilateral relations between the two countries would strengthen.
It is ironic that someone who is at the highest legislative position in Bangladesh is openly wooing the leaders of a country that sought to subjugate his nation not so long ago.
It would be one thing if Bangladesh and Pakistan were simply seeking to improve diplomatic relations. Countries routinely engage with former adversaries, and diplomatic engagement does not necessarily mean forgetting the past.
But Ahmed has gone much further. Instead of acknowledging the historical reality of Pakistan’s brutal military crackdown against the Bengali population in 1971, he has chosen to question India’s role in the liberation struggle and repeat a narrative that Pakistan has long attempted to propagate.
Ahmed claimed that Bengalis were demanding democracy in 1971 but were denied their rights. Yet, while speaking about the events of that period, he conveniently omitted the most important part of the story: it was West Pakistan and the Punjabi Muslim leadership that denied the rights of people of East Pakistan.
The 1970 general elections had produced a decisive victory for Sheikh Mujibur Rahman’s Awami League, which secured a majority in Pakistan’s National Assembly. The party had won an overwhelming mandate in East Pakistan and, by virtue of its electoral victory, was entitled to form the government.
But Pakistan’s political and military establishment refused to allow the transfer of power. Instead, the crisis was met with repression, military action and violence. The Pakistani Army launched Operation Searchlight in March 1971, unleashing a brutal campaign against Bengalis.
Ahmed’s selective recollection of history is therefore particularly revealing. He remembers the demand for democracy. He remembers the political crisis. He remembers the role India played. But the Pakistani Army’s atrocities appear to have conveniently disappeared from his account.
That is not historical analysis. That is historical whitewashing.
The Pakistani Army did not merely suppress a political movement: it unleashed a campaign of terror
The Pakistani Army’s atrocities in East Pakistan were not some incidental collateral consequence of a military operation. Violence against civilians became an instrument of the Pakistani state’s attempt to crush Bengali aspirations for independence.
The military targeted students, intellectuals, political activists, civilians and members of the Hindu minority. Universities and residential neighbourhoods became sites of violence. People were killed, homes were destroyed, and communities were terrorised. Mass graves and killing sites subsequently became grim reminders of what had happened.
The Jathibhanga massacre is one such example of the brutality inflicted upon Bengalis, particularly Hindus, during the Liberation War.
On April 23, 1971, thousands of Hindu civilians from villages in the Thakurgaon region were attempting to flee towards India to escape the violence. They gathered at Jathibhanga, hoping to cross the border and seek refuge. Instead, Pakistani military personnel and local collaborators reportedly surrounded them and carried out a massacre.
The victims were predominantly Hindu men from the Rajbanshi and Bengali communities. Reports and local accounts describe thousands being killed during the massacre, with bodies subsequently buried or disposed of near the river.
The tragedy left behind hundreds of widows and families whose lives were permanently destroyed. The massacre remains one of the most horrific episodes of violence recorded in the Thakurgaon region during the Bangladesh Liberation War.
A memorial was subsequently established at the site. Commemorative events have been held over the years, with survivors and families of victims demanding justice and remembrance.
These are the people Ahmed has effectively insulted through his attempt to rewrite the history of 1971.
When he claims India did not help Bengalis but merely weakened Pakistan, he is not making a harmless diplomatic observation. He is attempting to erase the context in which India intervened. He is ignoring the violence that forced millions to flee East Pakistan and seek refuge in India. He is ignoring the atrocities that made the liberation struggle inevitable. And he is ignoring the sacrifices made by Bengalis who fought for an independent Bangladesh.
India did not manufacture Bangladesh’s liberation struggle
The Pakistani establishment has always had a convenient explanation for the loss of East Pakistan: India supposedly engineered the separation, weakened Pakistan and exploited its internal crisis.
This narrative allows Pakistan to avoid confronting the uncomfortable reality that its own political and military leadership destroyed the possibility of a united Pakistan by refusing to respect the democratic mandate of East Pakistan and subsequently unleashing violence against its population.
In fact, India maintained a remarkable restraint throughout the turbulent period when Pakistan was unleashing horror upon its Bengali-speaking population in the hopes of quelling a rebellion. It was only after Pakistan launched preemptive air strikes on Indian air bases that Indira Gandhi, India’s then Prime Minister, declared a war on Pakistan.
India, meanwhile, was faced with an enormous refugee crisis as millions of people fled East Pakistan and crossed into Indian territory. The humanitarian and economic consequences were immense.
To reduce India’s role to an attempt to “weaken Pakistan” is therefore an exercise in dishonesty. It is an attempt to strip the 1971 war of its historical and humanitarian context and portray India’s intervention as an act of aggression against Pakistan rather than a response to the crisis created by Pakistan itself.
Ahmed may be attempting to curry favour with his hosts in Islamabad, but his remarks cannot erase the history of 1971.
Islamists who hid behind Bangladeshi nationalism are now showing their true colours
It has been Bangladesh’s misfortune that Islamists who hibernated after the 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War have started showing their true colours after the ouster of Sheikh Hasina, which has catapulted them and their political allies to positions of influence and power in the country.
For years, political actors who had sympathies for Pakistan, or whose ideological positions were deeply hostile to the secular and nationalist foundations of Bangladesh’s liberation, had to operate within a political environment shaped by the memory of 1971.
They could not openly glorify Pakistan without facing the historical baggage associated with the country. They could not casually whitewash the Pakistani Army’s atrocities without confronting the fact that Bangladesh’s independence was achieved after a bloody liberation war against Pakistan.
But the political upheaval following Sheikh Hasina’s ouster has altered the landscape.
Now, those who once had to cloak themselves in the language of Bangladeshi nationalism appear increasingly comfortable expressing positions that align with Pakistan’s interests. The attempt to portray India as the real villain of 1971, while downplaying Pakistan’s atrocities, is one such manifestation.
Being in power has seemingly emboldened them to believe that they can rewrite history.
And this is precisely the kind of historical revisionism that Pakistan has perfected over decades.
Pakistan has always attempted to rewrite the history of its wars with India
Pakistan has repeatedly demonstrated that when facts do not support its narrative, it attempts to manufacture a different version of reality.
The country has lost multiple wars and military confrontations with India. Yet its political and military establishment has consistently attempted to portray those defeats as victories, or at the very least, as episodes in which Pakistan emerged triumphant against overwhelming odds.
The Pakistani public is often fed narratives that bear little resemblance to the actual events on the battlefield. Military defeats are presented as strategic successes. Losses are minimised. Indian victories are denied or disputed. And whenever uncomfortable facts emerge, the Pakistani establishment attempts to bury them under propaganda. The same was witnessed after the Kargil war in 1999.
The same pattern was visible during Operation Sindoor in May 2025.
Following India’s strikes against terror camps and PAF bases in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied territories, the Pakistani establishment and its media machinery attempted to construct a narrative around so-called Indian aircraft losses. The claims were repeatedly amplified even as India provided its own account of the operation and released material documenting strikes against terror camps and military infrastructure.
The Pakistani narrative was built around mythical claims of Indian losses, with the country attempting to present itself as having inflicted a decisive defeat on India. The reality, however, was far more uncomfortable for Islamabad.
Pakistan was forced to seek de-escalation. The Pakistani Director General of Military Operations contacted his Indian counterpart, and the two sides agreed to halt military action. The Pakistani DGMO is reported to have told his Indian counterpart that they have had enough of BrahMos hitting targets in Pakistan, and now the tensions could cool down.
And Hafiz Uddin Ahmed appears to be attempting the same thing when he claims India did not help Bengalis but merely weakened Pakistan.
Ahmed’s remarks about Kashmir reveal where his sympathies lie
Ahmed’s comments during his Pakistan visit have not been limited to 1971. He has also echoed Pakistan’s long-standing position on Kashmir, saying that the dispute should be resolved in accordance with United Nations resolutions.
He has also accused Sheikh Hasina of seeking refuge in a country he described as hostile to Muslims, referring to India, and claimed that she would be sent to prison if she returned to Bangladesh. Ahmed further suggested that Bangladesh could approach the International Court of Justice if India refused to extradite Hasina, although he did not explain the legal basis for such a move.
The Speaker has also described the Awami League as a “terrorist party” and praised the February 2026 elections in Bangladesh as free and fair.
Taken together, these statements paint a picture of a political leader who appears increasingly comfortable adopting positions that align with Islamabad’s interests.
His remarks about Kashmir, his criticism of India, his attempt to portray India’s role in 1971 as an effort to weaken Pakistan, and his praise for the growing relationship between Dhaka and Islamabad are not isolated statements. They form a broader political narrative.
A Bangladesh that once emerged from Pakistan after a bloody liberation war is now witnessing its Speaker travel to Islamabad and question the role of the very country that helped its people escape Pakistani military repression.
The irony of Bangladesh’s Speaker praising Pakistan while rewriting 1971
Ahmed also claimed that nearly the entire stadium in Dhaka supported Pakistan during the football final of the 2026 SAFF Championship, in which India defeated Pakistan 2–1.
He claimed that 99.9 per cent of the spectators were supporting Pakistan and that the Pakistani team had won the hearts of the people despite losing the match.
The claim was intended to demonstrate the growing warmth between Bangladesh and Pakistan. In fact, it underlines the desperation in Dhaka to woo Pakistan while simultaneously downplaying the atrocities committed by the Pakistani Army against the people of Bangladesh.
In essence, what Bangladesh is trying is to erase its history, wipe out the very cause of its existence.
Bangladesh can engage with Pakistan without pretending that the Pakistani Army did not commit atrocities in 1971. Bangladesh can pursue diplomatic relations with Islamabad without portraying India’s intervention as an act of hostility towards Bengalis. Bangladesh can even seek a pragmatic relationship with Pakistan without erasing the sacrifices made by its own people during the Liberation War.
Ahmed’s remarks, however, appear to cross that line.
Pakistan’s propaganda is now finding an audience in Bangladesh
For decades, Pakistan has attempted to deny, minimise or distort the events of 1971. It has never adequately confronted the crimes committed by its military in East Pakistan. It has never shown the kind of remorse that would be expected from a country whose armed forces inflicted such horrific suffering upon an entire population.
Instead, Pakistan has repeatedly attempted to blame India for the disintegration of the country.
Now, Bangladesh’s own Parliament Speaker appears to be lending credibility to that narrative.
The question is will Bangladeshi population allow their leadership to carry on with such brazen historical distortion or will they attempt to bring them to reckoning?
Because if Bangladesh’s Speaker can stand in Islamabad and claim that India did not help Bengalis but merely weakened Pakistan, then the problem is no longer just Pakistani propaganda. It is the complicity of the Bangladeshi masses who expect Ahmed to work in the interests of the country.
The question Bangladesh’s youth must now ask themselves is this: Did they rise against Sheikh Hasina only to replace her government with one that is now busy whitewashing the Pakistani Army’s atrocities against their ancestors and rewriting the history of the Liberation War?

title: Supreme Court Hands Thiruparankundram Hill Security To CRPF, Orders Karthigai Deepam At Deepathoon On 28 November
description: The Supreme Court on Friday (27 November) handed security of the Thiruparankundram temple and hill in Madurai to the Central Reserve Police Force (CRP
author: Arun Dhital
content:
News Brief
Arun Dhital
Nov 27, 2026 | Updated 04:23 PM GMT+5:30
Save & read from anywhere!
Bookmark stories for easy access on any device or the Swarajya app.
The Supreme Court on Friday (27 November) handed security of the Thiruparankundram temple and hill in Madurai to the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF), after the state police failed to enforce its order on lighting the Karthigai Deepam at the Deepathoon pillar.
The CRPF will ensure the temple and dargah run peacefully and devotees can perform rituals.
The court ordered the temple receivers to light the Deepam at the pillar on Saturday (28 November), after consulting the priests. It also lifted the stay on the Madras High Court order, allowing devotees to light lamps there.
Pulling up the state government, the bench termed non-compliance with its 20 November order "flagrant" and prima facie "contempt of court" and "wilful disobedience". Its orders bind the state and its officials and are not open to negotiation, the court said.
"Time has come to deal with such situations with an iron hand, else it will lead to constitutional chaos," it added.
It suspended the temple's Board of Trustees and appointed two former High Court judges as administrators. "Trustees have categorically taken a stand that they would not implement the orders of this court," the bench said, flagging "administrative chaos" in Tamil Nadu, or at least Madurai.
The court found a prima facie case against the Madurai District Collector, the trustees and the HR&CE Department chairman. Allegations that officials acted at the behest of political leaders would be examined, it said.
The Chief Secretary must file an affidavit on officials' messages, emails and phone calls, and appear in person at the next hearing.
"Any attempt to pollute the stream of justice by any person, howsoever high he may be, would not be tolerated," the bench warned.
On 24 November, a police-escorted team had lit the lamp only at the customary mandapam near the Uchipillaiyar temple.

title: Karnataka Approves Rs 2,321-Crore Plan To White-Top 88 Bengaluru Roads, Tenders In Three Months
description: The Karnataka government has approved a Rs 2,321-crore project to white-top 88 roads spread across Bengaluru's five city corporations, with tenders li
author: Arun Dhital
content:
News Brief
Arun Dhital
Nov 27, 2026 | Updated 03:59 PM GMT+5:30
Save & read from anywhere!
Bookmark stories for easy access on any device or the Swarajya app.
The Karnataka government has approved a Rs 2,321-crore project to white-top 88 roads spread across Bengaluru's five city corporations, with tenders likely to be floated within three months.
Bengaluru Smart Infrastructure (B-SMILE) will execute the project at an average cost of Rs 17.7 crore per kilometre.
The detailed project reports for the roads will follow the TenderSURE model of urban design, with continuous footpaths, pedestrian crossings, upgraded junctions and landscaping.
Several Central Business District stretches figure on the list. Cubbon Road will be white-topped along its full length, from Minsk Square to the Dickenson Road junction, while Langford Road, Victoria Road and Old Airport Road have also been included.
The 10-km Bannerghatta Road high-density corridor will be handled as a separate package and split between the Central and South corporations.
Of the total outlay, Rs 1,848 crore is set aside for civil works and Rs 220 crore for water supply and sewerage works by the Bangalore Water Supply and Sewerage Board (BWSSB).
Another Rs 49 crore will go towards shifting Bescom and KPTCL utilities, and Rs 204 crore covers contingencies, price escalation, consultancy and other charges.
The BWSSB had first sought Rs 890 crore for its works along these roads. The figure was brought down to Rs 317 crore after discussions, and the project now provides Rs 220 crore.
The allocation aims to ensure the roads are not dug up again once white-topping is done.

title: India-EU Free Trade Pact Set For 16 December Signing During PM Modi's Brussels Visit, Expected To Enter Into Force By March-April 2027
description: Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal confirmed today (27 November) that the India-European Union free trade agreement is expected to be signed
author: Swarajya Staff
content:
Economy
Swarajya Staff
Nov 27, 2026 | Updated 03:54 PM GMT+5:30
Save & read from anywhere!
Bookmark stories for easy access on any device or the Swarajya app.
Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal confirmed today (27 November) that the India-European Union free trade agreement is expected to be signed later this year and could come into effect by March or April 2027.
The EU Ambassador to India Jean-Eric Paquet also revealed today that the landmark pact will be formally signed on 16 December during Prime Minister Narendra Modi's visit to Brussels.
The agreement, described as the "mother of all deals", concluded negotiations on 27 January this year after nearly two decades of talks.
India and the EU together represent approximately 25 per cent of global GDP and one-third of international trade worth around $11 trillion.
The European Commission submitted proposals to the Council of the EU in September seeking authorisation to sign and formally conclude the agreement.
Once signed, the deal will undergo scrutiny and approval by the European Parliament before entering into force.
Ambassador Paquet noted that the agreement is projected to enter into force in the first half of 2027, cutting tariffs to zero on 99 per cent of Indian trade volume entering Europe.
The pact will create a market of approximately 2 billion people across the world's fourth-largest economy and the second-largest economic bloc.
FICCI President Anant Goenka last week urged Indian businesses to prepare for the trade pact, noting that legal vetting is currently underway.
The EU was India's third-largest goods trading partner in 2025, with bilateral goods trade worth 118 billion euros.
Products accounting for 90.7 per cent of Indian exports by value would become duty-free when the agreement takes effect, with immediate tariff cuts covering sectors such as textiles, leather and footwear.

title: TV Newsance 357 | Grand theft journalism, PM’s Gen Z hunt, and baba-giri
description: Your bi-weekly dose of everything that passes for news on Indian television.
author: NL Team
content:
Your bi-weekly dose of everything that passes for news on Indian television.
This week, Abhinandan Sekhri fills in for Manisha Pande, who is on a much-deserved break.
The biggest breaking news on Indian TV wasn’t menghai, pollution or berozgari – it was GTA 6. Shiv Aroor turned the NDTV newsroom into a gaming lounge decked up with a PlayStation, Sudhir Chaudhary gave Decode a GTA makeover, and Aishwarya Kapoor and Anjana Om Kashyap had only one thing on their minds: GTA 6.
For the uninitiated, GTA 6 is a lawless universe where you do whatever you can get away with. Sound familiar? In the game, you run cars over people; in real life, bulldozers run over homes. In the game, you rob banks; in real life… Well, Sudhir has plenty to say about that too.
Meanwhile, NDTV’s owner Gautam Adani seems to play by his own rulebook as well – check out The Indian Express report on how a Rs 227 crore wildlife conservation penalty magically shrank to Rs 2.27 crore.
Not to be left behind, PM Modi compared his tenure to GTA 6. Ramayan also released this month, Modi Ji, yet you picked the video game. Cue the flood of netas posting about it in a desperate bid to woo Gen Z.
After all that virtual chaos, you need some spiritual peace, right? Who better to deliver it than our babas?
Dhirendra Shastri, also known as Baba Bageshwar, made remarks comparing two major Hindu deities that would easily land you in jail if you happened to be Muslim, a real journalist or both. Topping it all off, Baba Ramdev, who claims to have found cures for cancer, AIDS and COVID, called someone else a pakhandi.
Watch the full episode and let us know your thoughts in the comment section below.

title: असम सरकार ने सचिवालय के कर्मचारियों पर लागू किया ड्रेस कोड, टीशर्ट और चप्पल पर पहनने लगी रोक
description: सरकार के मुताबिक, सभी को सलाह दी गई है कि वे आधिकारिक कार्यों और कार्यक्रमों के दौरान ऐसा पहनावा अपनाएं जो शालीनता, मर्यादा, पेशेवर व्यवहार और गंभीरता को दर्शाता हो।
author: Jyoti Gupta
content:
असम सरकार ने शुक्रवार को राज्य सचिवालय ‘जनता भवन’ में कार्यरत सभी अधिकारियों और कर्मचारियों के लिए पहनावा संबंधी दिशा-निर्देश जारी किया, जिसके तहत कार्यालय समय और आधिकारिक कार्यक्रमों के दौरान जींस, टी-शर्ट, आदि पहनने पर रोक लगा दी गई। सामान्य प्रशासन (सचिवालय स्थापना) विभाग की ओर से जारी इस परामर्श में कहा गया कि यह देखने में आया है कि कई सरकारी अधिकारी आधिकारिक कार्यों के दौरान ऐसे कपड़े पहनते हैं, जिन्हें देखने में शालीन नहीं माना जाता और इससे सरकारी कर्मचारियों की सार्वजनिक छवि प्रभावित होती है और सरकार को भी असहज स्थिति का सामना करना पड़ता है।
आदेश के मुताबिक, सचिवालय परिसर में कार्यरत कर्मचारियों के बीच गरिमा, अनुशासन और मर्यादा का उच्च स्तर बनाए रखने के उद्देश्य से पहनावा संबंधी दिशा-निर्देश जारी किए गए हैं। आदेश में स्पष्ट किया गया कि नए ड्रेस कोड के निर्देश तत्काल प्रभाव से लागू होंगे। सरकार ने कहा कि ये दिशा-निर्देश ‘जनता भवन’ में कार्यरत सभी संवर्गों के अधिकारियों और कर्मचारियों पर समान रूप से लागू होंगे।
अयाह शाह विधानसभा में BJP लगाएगी जीत की हैट्रिक या SP का खुलेगा खाता? जानें क्या है जातीय समीकरण
सचिवालय के कर्मचारी क्या पहन सकेंगे?
सरकार के मुताबिक, सभी को सलाह दी गई है कि वे आधिकारिक कार्यों और कार्यक्रमों के दौरान ऐसा पहनावा अपनाएं जो शालीनता, मर्यादा, पेशेवर व्यवहार और गंभीरता को दर्शाता हो। पुरुष अधिकारियों और कर्मचारियों के लिए केवल औपचारिक कपड़े पहनने की अनुमति होगी जिनमें पैंट-शर्ट के अलावा कुर्ता, धोती-पायजामा और अन्य शालीन पारंपरिक भारतीय परिधान शामिल हैं।
टी-शर्ट और जींस जैसे अनौपचारिक कपड़े पहनने पर रोक लगाई गई है। सामान्य प्रशासन विभाग के उप सचिव मानस ज्योति बरुआ के हस्ताक्षर से जारी परामर्श में महिला अधिकारियों और कर्मचारियों के लिए शालीन सलवार-सूट, साड़ी और मेखला-चादर पहनने का निर्देश दिया गया है। महिलाओं के लिए भी टी-शर्ट, जींस जैसे अनौपचारिक परिधानों पर प्रतिबंध लगाया गया है।

दिल्ली के जामा मस्जिद पुलिस स्टेशन में एक 30 साल के व्यक्ति ने थाने के अंदर पुलिसवालों पर चाकू से हमला कर दिया। इस हमले में सब इंस्पेक्टर समेत 9 पुलिसवाले घायल हो गए। आरोपी अपनी पॉकेट में चाकू लेकर थाने के अंदर पहुंचा और पुलिसकर्मियों पर हमला कर दिया। और अधिक पढ़ने के लिए यहां क्लिक करें…

title: कांग्रेस को झटका! परिसीमन विधेयक का समर्थन करेगी शरद पवार की पार्टी
description: Delimitation Bill: न्यूज एजेंसी एएनआई ने सूत्रों के हवाले से जानकारी दी है कि परिसीमन विधायक शुक्रवार को संसद सचिवालय के पोर्टल पर अपलोड किया जाएगा।
author: जनसत्ता न्यूज डेस्क
content:
शरद पवार की पार्टी एनसीपी (एसएसीपी) संसद में परिसीमन विधेयक का समर्थन करेगी। एनसीपी (एसएसीपी) के नेता जितेंद्र आव्हाड ने मीडिया को यह जानकारी दी।
उन्होंने शुक्रवार शाम मुंबई में मीडिया से बात करते हुए कहा कि परिसीमन संवैधानिक होता है। यह आज नहीं तो कल करना ही है। उन्होंने कहा कि यह पूरी तरह स्पष्ट है कि परिसीमन विधेयक का समर्थन किया जाएगा।
कांग्रेस बोली- परिसीमन के जरिए संविधान बदलने की कोशिश
कांग्रेस ने शुक्रवार को आरोप लगाया कि पिछले लोकसभा चुनाव में ‘400 पार’ नारे के साथ विफल रहने के बाद मोदी अब परिसीमन के जरिये संविधान बदलने की कोशिश में जुटी है, लेकिन वह अन्य विपक्षी दलों के साथ मिलकर इसके खिलाफ लड़ाई लड़ेगी।
कांग्रेस संसदीय दल की प्रमुख सोनिया गांधी के आवास पर हुई पार्टी की संसदीय रणनीतिक समूह की बैठक में अगले सप्ताह प्रस्तावित संसद की बैठक तथा परिसीमन से संबंधित संविधान संशोधन विधेयक को लेकर पार्टी की रणनीति पर चर्चा की गई।
इस बैठक के बाद लोकसभा में कांग्रेस के उप नेता गौरव गोगोई ने मीडिया से बातचीत से कहा कि सरकार का लक्ष्य परिसीमन के माध्यम से लोकसभा की सीटों की संख्या बढ़ाकर वह काम करने का है, जिसे वह पिछले लोकसभा चुनाव में 400 पार के नारे के बावजूद नहीं कर पाई थी। उन्होंने आरोप लगाया कि पीएम मोदी और गृह मंत्री अमित शाह महिला आरक्षण की आड़ में परिसीमन आयोग के गठन और परिसीमन की प्रक्रिया को आगे बढ़ाना चाहते हैं।
गौरव गोगोई ने कहा कि कांग्रेस की मांग स्पष्ट है कि लोकसभा की मौजूदा सीटों की संख्या और हर राज्य की लोकसभा सीटों की सीटों की संख्या को भी बरकरार रखा जाए तथा इसमें 25 साल तक कोई बदलाव नहीं होने चाहिए। उनके मुताबिक, कांग्रेस की मांग यह भी है कि 543 सीटों में ही महिलाओं को 33 प्रतिशत आरक्षण दिया जाए।
उन्होंने आरोप लगाया, ”सरकार पहले मतदाता सूची के विशेष गहन पुनरीक्षण (एसआईआर) और मतदाता सूची में कथित हेरफेर के जरिये यह तय करने की कोशिश कर रही है कि कौन मतदान कर सकता है और कौन नहीं। अब परिसीमन के जरिये यह तय करने की कोशिश की जा रही है कि कौन कहां मतदान कर सकेगा।”
यह भी पढ़ें: परिसीमन पर एमके स्टालिन की दो टूक- कोई समझौता नहीं, ‘पीठ में छुरा घोंपने वालों’ पर भी साधा निशाना

title: ‘पुरानी गलतियां न दोहराएं…’, चंद्रबाबू नायूड ने परिसीमन बिल और महिला आरक्षण पर विपक्षी नेताओं से की अपील
description: सीएम नायडू ने कहा कि उनका मानना ​​है कि प्रधानमंत्री ने जो किया है, वह एक असाधारण कदम है। अब सभी को एक आम सहमति पर आना होगा। यह देश के लिए एक ऐतिहासिक अवसर है। अगर देश जीतना चाहता है, तो सभी को महिलाओं का सम्मान करना होगा।
author: जनसत्ता न्यूज डेस्क
content:
आंध्र प्रदेश के मुख्यमंत्री एन. चंद्रबाबू नायडू और केंद्रीय मंत्री एच.डी. कुमारस्वामी ने परिसीमन बिल और महिला आरक्षण को लेकर साझा प्रेस कॉन्फ्रेंस की। उन्होंने विपक्ष के नेताओं से अपील की कि वे अपना रुख इस पर साफ करें।
उन्होंने आगे कहा, मैं सभी से अपील करता हूँ कि पुरानी गलतियों को न दोहराएं। महिला आरक्षण कोई नई बात नहीं है; यह लंबे समय से लंबित मुद्दा है।
यह सबका साथ, सबका विकास है- चंद्रबाबू नायडू
मुख्यमंत्री चंद्रबाबू नायडू ने कहा कि आज मैं प्रधानमंत्री की ओर से शुरू की गई एक ऐतिहासिक पहल का समर्थन करने के लिए आया हूँ। यह ‘सबका साथ, सबका विकास’ है। मैं उन्हें बधाई देना चाहता हूँ। महिलाओं के आरक्षण का मुद्दा तीन दशकों से लंबित था। मैं इसका प्रत्यक्ष गवाह हूँ। अब यह साकार हो रहा है, जिससे देश में एक उम्मीद जगी है।
राज्यों के हित में है बिल- नायडू
चंद्रबाबू नायडू ने कहा, “अब 50 प्रतिशत आरक्षण की बात हो रही है यानी हम सीटों की संख्या बढ़ाने जा रहे हैं, सीटों में 50 फीसदी की बढ़ोतरी होगी। कल तक हम सभी डरे हुए थे। अगर आप दक्षिण भारत के संदर्भ में 1971, 2011 या 2026 की जनगणना को देखें, तो यहाँ एक बड़ी समस्या खड़ी हो सकती है। ऐसा इसलिए है क्योंकि हमने शुरुआत में ही परिवार नियोजन (family planning) की पहल कर ली थी। अब हमारा (आंध्र प्रदेश) प्रजनन दर (fertility rate) 1.6% है, जबकि रिप्लेसमेंट स्तर 2.1% होना चाहिए। पूरा दक्षिण भारत इसी समस्या का सामना कर रहा है। इसलिए, मैंने जनसंख्या प्रबंधन का आह्वान किया है जिसमें बड़े परिवारों को प्रोत्साहन देना और अधिक बच्चे पैदा करने को बढ़ावा देना शामिल है। केंद्र सरकार ने हर राज्य के लिए सीटों में 50% की बढ़ोतरी करने की पहल की है। इससे हम सभी को बहुत राहत मिलेगी।”
मुख्यमंत्री ने परिसीमन बिल पर तर्क देते हुए कहा, “मैं कुछ तर्कों का बहुत स्पष्ट रूप से जवाब देना चाहता हूँ। आज की स्थिति में, आंध्र प्रदेश के पास 25 सीटें हैं। भविष्य में, 50 फीसदी की बढ़ोतरी के साथ, ये बढ़कर 38 हो सकती हैं- जो कुल का 4.6% होगा, यानी अनुपात वही रहेगा। तमिलनाडु के पास आज 39 सीटें हैं, जो बढ़कर 59 हो सकती हैं – यानी 7.18%, अनुपात वही रहेगा। कर्नाटक के पास आज 28 सीटें हैं; ये बढ़कर 42 हो सकती हैं – यानी 5.16%। तेलंगाना के पास 17 सीटें हैं, जो भविष्य में 26 हो सकती हैं – यानी 3.13%। केरल के पास 20 सीटें हैं, जो बढ़कर 30 हो सकती हैं – यानी 3.68%। सभी दक्षिणी राज्यों को मिलाकर अभी 129 सीटें हैं। परिसीमन और बढ़ोतरी के बाद, ये 195 हो जाएंगी। 23.76% का यही अनुपात बना रहेगा। ऐसा होने वाला है… मैं सभी विपक्षी दलों से एक सीधा सवाल पूछना चाहता हूँ। आगे का रास्ता क्या है? इस देश में, हमने आम सहमति के जरिए कई सार्वजनिक नीतियां लागू की हैं।”
विपक्षी दलों से पूछा क्या है समाधान?
चंद्रबाबू नायडू ने कहा, “मैं सभी विपक्षी दलों से पूछता हूँ – इसका समाधान क्या है? कांग्रेस पार्टी – राहुल गांधी कल तक केरल का प्रतिनिधित्व कर रहे थे, वे वहां से सांसद थे। अब प्रियंका केरल का प्रतिनिधित्व कर रही हैं। इसके अलावा, वे तीनों राज्यों में सत्ता में हैं। तमिलनाडु में वे सरकार को समर्थन दे रहे हैं। अगर नवीनतम जनगणना के आधार पर परिसीमन होता है, तो दक्षिण भारत को बहुत बड़ा नुकसान उठाना पड़ेगा; उनकी आवाज ही दब जाएगी, जिससे काफी नाराजगी पैदा होगी। इन सब चीजों के लिए सबसे अच्छा रास्ता क्या है? सीटों में 50% की बढ़ोतरी और महिलाओं के लिए 33% आरक्षण। यह सभी के लिए फायदे की स्थिति है। इससे हर कोई संतुष्ट होगा। हमारा मानना है कि प्रधानमंत्री ने जो किया है, वह एक असाधारण कदम है। अब सभी को एक आम सहमति पर आना होगा। यह देश के लिए एक ऐतिहासिक अवसर है। अगर देश जीतना चाहता है, तो हमें अपनी महिलाओं का सम्मान करना होगा।”
अपना रुख स्पष्ट करें- CM नायडू
नायडू ने आगे कहा, “मैं सभी राजनीतिक दलों से अपील करता हूँ कि वे अपना रुख स्पष्ट करें। हर राजनीतिक दल को साफ तौर पर और बिना किसी दुविधा के अपना पक्ष रखना चाहिए। पिछली बार हमने देखा था कि कुछ राजनीतिक दलों ने कार्यवाही में बाधा डाली, संसद में हंगामा किया और अंततः किसी तरह इन विधेयकों को रोक दिया… महिलाओं की भी अपनी आकांक्षाएं हैं। वे राष्ट्र निर्माण में भागीदार बनना चाहती हैं। मैं सभी से आग्रह करता हूँ कि पुरानी गलतियों को न दोहराएं… महिला आरक्षण कोई नई बात नहीं है; यह लंबे समय से लंबित मुद्दा है। महिलाएं इसकी हकदार हैं। अब समय आ गया है कि सभी लोग महिलाओं का समर्थन करें और उनके साथ खड़े हों।”
‘गलत पक्ष में न रहें’
मुख्यमंत्री ने विपक्षी नेताओं से अपील करते हुए कहा, “सबसे एक बेहद सिंपल अनुरोध है- इतिहास के गलत पक्ष में न रहें। हम इतिहास रचने जा रहे हैं। ऐसा होकर रहेगा। इस ऐतिहासिक क्षण में, सभी राजनीतिक दलों और सभी नेताओं को सही पक्ष में होना चाहिए। इससे भारत को एक शानदार लाभ मिलेगा। मैं असल में इसकी सराहना करता हूँ क्योंकि मैं पिछले तीन दशकों से इसका इंतजार कर रहा हूँ। अब महिलाओं के लिए आरक्षण की हमारी आकांक्षा या लक्ष्य हकीकत बनने जा रहा है।”
यह भी पढ़ें: कांग्रेस को झटका! परिसीमन विधेयक का समर्थन करेगी शरद पवार की पार्टी
शरद पवार की पार्टी एनसीपी (एसएसीपी) संसद में परिसीमन विधेयक का समर्थन करेगी। एनसीपी (एसएसीपी) के नेता जितेंद्र आव्हाड ने मीडिया को यह जानकारी दी। पूरी खबर पढ़ने के लिए यहां क्लिक करें

title: Two Men Arrested In Pune Gang-Rape Case
description: Pune police have arrested Ganesh Shankar Pathak and Shrenik Pramod Chavan for allegedly gang-raping a 27-year-old woman at a lodge in Kondhwa. The incident, which occurred on November 22, involved the woman's partner, Chavan. Authorities are also investigating if the victim was drugged. The accused are currently in police custody.
author: Text Feed
content:
Pune police have arrested two men, including the victim's partner, in connection with the alleged gang-rape of a 27-year-old woman at a Kondhwa lodge, prompting an investigation into potential drugging.
Key Points
- Two men, Ganesh Shankar Pathak and Shrenik Pramod Chavan, were arrested in Pune for allegedly gang-raping a 27-year-old woman.
- The alleged incident took place on November 22 at a lodge in Kondhwa, with the accused reportedly warning the victim against disclosing it.
- Police are investigating whether the woman was given any drugs or intoxicating substances during the alleged assault.
- The accused have been remanded in police custody till November 30 under sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS).
Two men have been arrested for allegedly gang-raping a 27-year-old woman at a lodge in Kondhwa area of the city, police said on Friday. Ganesh Shankar Pathak (28) and Shrenik Pramod Chavan (36), both residents of Parvati area, were arrested by Yerawada police. The woman and both accused were friends, and she was in a relationship with Chavan, police said.
Investigation Underway In Kondhwa Incident
According to senior police inspector Umesh Geete, the woman and Chavan had recently had a dispute over some issue.
The accused allegedly took the woman to a lodge in Kondhwa on November 22. The duo allegedly gang-raped her and warned her against disclosing the incident to anyone, inspector Geete told PTI.
The duo were arrested under sections 70(1) (gangrape) and 123 (causing hurt by means of poison, etc, with intent to commit an offence) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS). A court remanded them in police custody till November 30.
Police are also investigating whether the woman was given any drugs or intoxicating substances, inspector Geete said.

title: Friend Arrested For Ludhiana Trader's Ice Pick Murder
description: A Ludhiana-based garment trader, Pankaj Arora, was allegedly murdered by his friend, Mickey Ahuja, and two accomplices. The victim was kidnapped on November 25, killed with an ice pick, robbed of gold ornaments, and his body was dumped in a Bathinda canal. The accused have been arrested.
author: Text Feed
content:
A Ludhiana garment trader was allegedly murdered by his friend with an ice pick over a financial dispute, leading to the arrest of the accused and two associates.
Key Points
- Ludhiana garment trader Pankaj Arora was allegedly murdered with an ice pick by his friend Mickey Ahuja and two associates.
- The victim was reportedly kidnapped on November 25 from Ludhiana and taken to Bathinda, where the killing occurred.
- After the murder, the accused allegedly looted Arora's gold ornaments, including a chain, five rings, and a bracelet weighing around 150 gm.
- The body was subsequently dumped in a canal at Rampura Phul in Bathinda district.
- Mickey Ahuja, a hosiery owner, and his two associates have been arrested in connection with the crime.
A man allegedly killed a Ludhiana-based garment trader with an ice pick and threw his body into a pond in Bathinda district, police said on Friday.
Details Of The Alleged Crime
After the killing, the accused allegedly looted the victim's gold ornaments  a chain, five rings and a bracelet weighing around 150 gm  before dumping the body in a canal at Rampura Phul in Bathinda.
Mickey Ahuja, a hosiery owner, allegedly kidnapped his friend Pankaj Arora (45), a garment trader in Ludhiana, before killing him with an ice pick and dumping the body in the pond, police said.
The accused, along with his aides, first called the trader out on November 25 on the pretext of settling some financial dispute. He was then taken away forcibly from Ludhiana to Bathinda and attacked with an ice pick, DCP (City) Alam Vijay Singh said.
Mickey and two of his associates have been arrested, the DCP said.

title: Why Uttarakhand HC Quashed Rape Conviction In Champawat Case
description: The Uttarakhand High Court overturned the conviction of a man accused of raping a mentally-challenged woman in Champawat, citing the prosecution's failure to establish charges and serious procedural flaws by the trial court, including unreliable witness identification and improper video evidence handling.
author: Text Feed
content:
The Uttarakhand High Court has overturned a man's conviction in a 2021 alleged rape case of a mentally-challenged woman, highlighting critical procedural lapses and insufficient evidence by the trial court.
Key Points
- The Uttarakhand High Court set aside a man's conviction in a 2021 alleged rape case of a mentally-challenged woman in Champawat.
- The High Court questioned the trial court's procedure and evidence appreciation, noting the prosecution failed to establish charges.
- Key issues included unreliable witness identification, lack of FSL/medical links, and the sessions judge improperly viewing video evidence privately.
- The original conviction by the Champawat Sessions Court on February 4, 2025, had sentenced the man to 20 years rigorous imprisonment.
- The High Court ruled that the trial court's procedure was contrary to the principles of natural justice and established law.
The Uttarakhand High Court has set aside the conviction of a man in a 2021 case involving the alleged rape of a mentally-challenged woman in Champawat district, saying the prosecution failed to establish the charges against him.
Trial Court's Procedural Lapses Questioned
On February 4, 2025, the Champawat Sessions Court had convicted the man under Section 376(2)(l) of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and sentenced him to 20 years of rigorous imprisonment, along with a fine of Rs 1 lakh.
Setting aside the conviction and sentence, a bench of justices Ravindra Maithani and Siddharth Sah raised serious questions over the procedure adopted by the trial court and its appreciation of evidence.
The case dates back to August 2021, when a video purportedly showing the man engaging in a sexual act with the woman with mental illness under a tin shed at the Tanakpur Roadways bus station went viral on social media.
Following directions from the Sub-Divisional Magistrate of Purnagiri (Tanakpur), an FIR was registered at Tanakpur police station on August 26, 2021, and the man was subsequently arrested.
During the investigation, the woman's statement could not be recorded owing to her mental condition. However, relying on witness testimonies and the video, the sessions court convicted and sentenced the man.
Evidence Scrutiny And Unreliable Identification
Hearing the appeal, the high court found that the prosecution had failed to establish the charges against the man.
The bench observed that neither the forensic science laboratory (FSL) report nor the medical report linked the man to the alleged offence.
It also found the identification of the accused by witnesses directly before the court, nearly a year later, unreliable, particularly since the face of the person in the video was not clearly visible and no test identification parade had been conducted during the investigation.
The high court further took exception to the sessions judge viewing the video privately in chambers instead of playing it in open court, independently identifying the accused and relying on such identification as a basis for conviction.
The bench held that the procedure was contrary to the principles of natural justice and established law.

title: Bhiwandi Shawarma Food Poisoning Cases Rise To 130; FDA Suspends 3 Hotels, Civic Body Launches Bulldozer Drive
description: Bhiwandi's shawarma-related food poisoning cases have risen to 130, with 107 patients still hospitalised. The FDA suspended three hotels over hygiene violations, while municipal authorities launched a bulldozer drive against unauthorised food stalls. The outbreak, the second major incident this year, has raised concerns over food safety monitoring across Bhiwandi.
author: Danish Azmi
content:
Bhiwandi: The number of people affected by food poisoning after consuming chicken shawarma at a food outlet in Bhiwandi has risen to 130, prompting the administration to intensify its crackdown on food establishments across the city. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has suspended three hotels for unhygienic conditions and violations of food safety norms, while the Bhiwandi-Nizampur City Municipal Corporation (BNCMC) has launched a bulldozer drive against illegal food stalls and roadside vendors.
The anti-encroachment drive began late on Friday evening and was underway at the time of filing this report.
107 Patients Remain Hospitalised
The affected people had consumed chicken shawarma at AK Shawarma, located near Vanjarpatti Naka. The victims include 64 men, 39 women and 27 children. While 23 patients have been discharged after treatment, 107 remain admitted to various hospitals. Two women and two children have been shifted to Thane for advanced medical care. Hospital authorities said the condition of all patients was stable.
Three Hotels Suspended After FDA Inspections
Following the food poisoning outbreak, the Thane FDA has intensified inspections of hotels and food establishments across Bhiwandi. During the inspections, three hotels — Rizwan Hotel in Bhusar Mohalla, Hotel Moonlight in Shantinagar and Anand Hotel on Kalyan Road — were suspended for unhygienic conditions and non-compliance with prescribed norms.
FDA Assistant Commissioner Santosh Sirosia said several shortcomings, particularly related to cleanliness and hygiene, were found at the establishments. Notices were issued to the respective hotel operators before suspension orders were initiated.
FDA teams are currently inspecting food establishments in different parts of the city. Sirosia said action would continue against operators found violating food safety standards. Hotels and food stalls across Bhiwandi are now under the department's scanner.
Bulldozer Drive Against Illegal Roadside Stalls
Meanwhile, the BNCMC's anti-encroachment department launched a crackdown on unauthorised food stalls and roadside handcarts under the leadership of Ward Committee 1 Officer Sameer Jawre.
The drive covered the stretch from Khandupada to Vanjarpatti Naka and Naddi Naka on Friday evening. Bulldozers were deployed to remove illegal stalls, handcarts and other encroachments obstructing roads and public spaces. The operation continued late into the night.
Officials said that following instructions from the municipal commissioner, action against unauthorised stalls was being carried out across all five ward committees.
Also Watch:
Second Outbreak Raises Food Safety Concerns
In June this year, 107 people had suffered food poisoning after consuming food from a shawarma outlet in Khandupada. The latest outbreak, affecting another 130 people, has once again raised serious questions about food safety monitoring and the effectiveness of routine inspections in the city.
The recurrence of such incidents has exposed gaps in the enforcement of food safety regulations. The administration now faces the challenge of ensuring regular inspections and strict compliance by food businesses, rather than limiting enforcement to demolition and inspection drives after major outbreaks.
